en: [I bow] to the Supreme Lord, who sits upon the peak of Kailāsa, who is the destroyer of Time and Kāmadeva, who is gracious, and who is the cause of bliss for the world. Āk_1.1.1.
Having prostrated with supreme devotion, Bhairavī offered this hymn of praise:
"O God of gods, Great God, destroyer of the poverty of rebirth! (Āk 1.1.2)
Be gracious, O embodiment of compassion; be pleased, O Supreme Lord!
[Reveal] the secrets of the divine scriptures, such as the Kula, Kaula, and others. (Āk 1.1.3)
O embodiment of auspiciousness, through your grace I know [this];
O Lord of All, I desire to hear your divine elixir. (Āk 1.1.4)
It destroys old age, birth, and disease, and bestows supernatural powers such as the ability to travel through the air;
it pacifies poverty and suffering, and grants boons such as the state of Brahmanhood. (Āk 1.1.5)
Īśvara said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, benefactress of all the worlds!
All that arises from the Sūta, who is dear as his own life to the Pure Self. (Āk 1.1.6)

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, for the sake of benefiting the entire world, [I shall describe] the most secret of secrets, the beneficial origin and characteristics of the Lord of Mercury (Rasendra). Āk 1.1.7.
I shall explain all of that; listen now, O Bhairavī.
(The Origin of Mercury) By the lords of the gods, by divine sages, and by Gandharvas, Uragas, and Kinnaras... [Āk 1.1.8]
You were entreated by those desiring the birth of a prince for the destruction of the demon Tāraka and for the protection of the worlds. (Āk 1.1.9)
Then, O beloved, as we sported for a very long time in a cave of the Himalaya mountain with the desire for a son, our time passed away. (Āk 1.1.10)
Sent by the gods to cause him to abandon his passion that agitates the three worlds, Agni approached through the window, having assumed the form of a dove. (Āk 1.11)
O Goddess, seeing that, out of shame I abandoned the sexual union;
our blazing radiance was cast into the mouth of the Fire-god. (Āk 1.1.12)
Scorched by that [fire], Agni immersed it in the Gaṅgā;
and because of that, the Gaṅgā too became heated and cast it out again. (Āk 1.1.13)
Having reached the outside, that [essence] became twofold: one for the birth of Skanda, and the other arose as pure mercury, which carries one across the ocean of calamities. (Āk 1.14)
Situated within five wells each a hundred yojanas deep, his impurities became minerals, jewels, and divine objects. (Āk 1.15)
Through the specific qualities of various particular fields, this mercury (rasendra)—which destroys birth and poverty—has attained distinct names, colors, and other attributes. (Āk 1.16)
At the time of dissolution, those five wells indeed became known as the "Mukhas";
along with their respective colors, they were cast down by Nivṛtti in the millions. (Āk 1.1.17)
O Goddess of the gods, there are five colors associated with all living beings:
in the east is white mercury, which removes diseases through its various colors. (Āk 1.1.18)
O beloved, the mercury located in the south is flickering, blue in color, free from defects, extremely dry, and exceedingly volatile. (Āk 1.1.19)
From him were born the lords of serpents, free from the defects of old age and rebirth;
in the western direction, however, was the one named Sūta, yellow in color and very harsh. Āk 1.1.20.

O Goddess, though it may be possessed of all defects, it becomes pure through the eighteen rites; it bestows all accomplishments and grants the attainment of the body, metals, and so forth. (Āk 1.1.21)
In the northern direction there is the red [substance], free from all defects;
by means of that very elixir (*rasāyana*), the gods have become exempt from birth, old age, and death. (Āk 1.1.22)
In the middle, however, the mixed [taste] is to be known, endowed with all the qualities of the [other] tastes;
on the outside, the taste has the luster of the moon and sun, and is endowed with defects. (Āk 1.23)
And that mercury, purified by eighteen refinements, becomes the bestower of accomplishment; for mercury is indeed the Great Lord (Maheśvara) in the very form of the immortals. Āk 1.1.24.
And those two, though exceedingly difficult to obtain, fulfilled [his desires] even slightly;
for even the bestower of success in all other undertakings [is attained] through ritual actions. (Āk 1.1.25)
He who knows the descent of the *rasa*, which is utterly pure through eighteen [factors] and swiftly bestows accomplishment, is the most excellent of righteous beings. (Āk 1.1.26)
One shall obtain longevity, happiness, continuity, wealth, and health;
through the synonyms and etymologies of *rasa*, one crosses beyond the ocean of birth, disease, old age, death, and poverty. (Āk 1.1.27)
Because it grants the further shore (*pāra*) by that very means, it is celebrated as *pārada*;
and because it acts upon mercury, secondary minerals, metals, and so forth, it is called *rasendraka*. (Āk 1.28)
Because he is the essence extracted from every limb, he is called Sūta;
since he produces all spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), he is therefore remembered as Sūta. (Ākāśabhairava Tantra 1.29)
Since it is the essence of my body, it is therefore proclaimed as "Rasa";
it is praised for the destruction of old age, death, poverty, and disease. (Āk 1.1.30)
Therefore, O fair-faced one, he is called *rasa* because of his nature as a *dhātu*; since he is the essence (*rasa*) of all *dhātus*, he is thus declared to be *rasa*. (Āk 1.1.31)

Mercury (pārada), the lord of juices (rasendra), is a benefactor due to its similarity [to the body]; it bestows all accomplishments, removes diseases, and is the primary agent in the work of alchemy (rasakarma). (ĀK 1.1.32)

O Dear One, mercury (sūta) is the king of essences (rasendra) in the operations of the elements and in the accomplishment of alchemy, because it is capable of all actions and because it is everything. Āk 1.1.33.
O Goddess, this is declared to be the Miśraka [type], which bestows all accomplishments;
[it contains] the impurities residing in the mercury, [and yields] the stainless Amoghasiddhi mercury that grants all accomplishments. (Āk 1.1.34)
O beloved, having beheld me, all the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, entreated me with various hymns of praise. (Āk 1.1.35)
"O Śaṅkara, by the mere sight of the king of elixirs (rasendra), humans, birds, beasts, and others attain various kinds of supernatural powers (siddhi); therefore, please prevent this. (Āk 1.1.36)
Therefore, he was joined with the three types of coverings (kañcuka) and defects (doṣa); from that time forward, however, he has been free from both the defects and the coverings. (Āk 1.1.37)
Purified by the eighteen refinements, mercury becomes the bestower of success. (The states of mercury: fuming, crackling, and the frog-leap; Āk 1.38.
Trembling and non-trembling—these are the five states of rasa. (The movements of rasa:
There are five movements of rasa; in water, there is a movement like that of water. (Āk 1.1.39)

O Goddess, when it is smoke, its movement is like that of smoke; when it is a layer [of ash], its movement is like that of a swan; when it is dross, its movement resembles that of dross; and the fifth is a movement like that of a living being. (Āk 1.1.40)
Four destinies are visible; the fifth destiny is invisible.
O Dear One, the four destinies are to be obstructed by means of mechanical devices, medicinal herbs, and so forth. (Āk 1.41)
The fifth destiny is to be obstructed by means of meditation, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth.
(Natural defects:
Likewise, [the elements] are the earthly, the watery, the fiery, and the airy. (ĀK 1.1.42)
The celestial [wind] is called Gajacarma, Puṇḍarīka, and Visarpakṛt;
the yellow [wind] is called Raktacarma, Nāraṅga, and Raktabinduka. (Āk 1.43)
The unbearable fire and the frog are known as the innate impurities (*naisargika-mala*).
(The adventitious defects *aupadhika-doṣa* are:
Kālikā, Malinī, Kapotī, and Raktakañcukā. (Āk 1.44)
Salomī, Girijā, and Piṅgalī—these seven are known as the adventitious sheaths (kañcukas) proclaimed in relation to mercury (pārada), O beloved. (Āk 1.1.45)
(Defects arising from processing): Poison, lead, and tin—these three are known as the defects arising from processing.
(The nature of the defects).
The [planet] Bhauma causes leprosy, and the [planet] Āpya increases the aggravation of the humors (doṣas).
That which belongs to Agni causes a burning sensation; that belonging to Vāyu produces piercing pain;
the defect arising from the ether (nābhasa) causes deafness; and that which consists of elephant-hide or elephant-skin [causes] numbness. (Āk 1.1.47)
Puṇḍarīka causes herpes; Visarpa causes erysipelas; Hāridra is said to cause leucoderma; and Raktacarma causes redness of the skin and eyes. (Āk 1.1.48)
The orange, the udumbara fruit, kuṣṭha, the red-seeded plant, and the lentil cause smallpox;
asahyāgni causes delusion, and the frog causes skin-nails. (Āk 1.49)
O Goddess, impurity causes fainting; it is likewise known as arising from the humors (*doṣa*).
*Kālikā* is black in color, and *Malinī* is the seizure of impurity. (Āk 1.1.50)
The female pigeon (kapotī), svarasāda, visphoṭa, raktakañcukā, salomī, and girijā cause vomiting; the latter also induces numbness. (Āk 1.1.51)
Piṅgalī destroys the eyes; the defects are said to arise from the bark.
Viṣa bestows death, Nāga [bestows] stupor, and Vaṅga [is used] for the worship of the gods. (Āk 1.1.52)
Diseases arising from incompatible combinations produce a foul odor;
[this refers to] the movement of the *rasa* to another location.
A woman who has bathed after her first menses, being beautiful and endowed with auspicious marks... [Āk 1.1.53]
Wearing pure garments, anointed with garlands and perfumes, and beautifully adorned,
she was mounted upon a noble horse, yet entirely devoid of sexual passion.
Having first worshipped Gaṇanātha, Bhairava, and the Guru,
and having meditated upon Rasendrabhairava— the mercury situated within the well, O Beloved— Āk_1,1.55.
One should look [at her] quickly and then depart, never looking back again;
this is the maiden who accomplishes the horse-mantra within the distance of a yojana. (Āk 1.1.56)
At that moment, desiring to seize it, the prince leaps up from the middle of the well and runs after it. (Āk 1.1.57)
Having traveled for as many as a yojana, he would again enter a well in an instant; and he was stationed in each of those pits that had been dug all around. (Āk 1.58)
Having become pure, the master of mercury should take that lord of mercury, which has fallen from the mouth of fire due to its weight into the place called Darada. (Āk 1.1.59)
In that region, that charioteer, an expert in alchemy and skilled in the Tantras, having placed [the substance] in an earthen vessel called a *pātana*-yantra, returned. (Āk 1.1.60)
O Goddess, mercury is taken up; it is said to be free from defects, even so by the perfected ones and the Vidyādharas here and there at all times. (Āk 1.1.61)
O Goddess, the lord of mercury (pāradendra), which bestows success, exists as something deposited. (Āk 1.1.62)
Āk, 1, 2: Śrī Bhairavī said: [I bow to] the giver of the instruction on mercury (rasa), his disciple, and the woman Kākinī.
I ask about the worship with nectar; explain it to me exactly as it is. Āk 1.2.1.
Śrī Bhairava:
(The characteristics of the instruction on mercury) Listen, O Bhairavī; I shall tell you all of that which is unprecedented.
The teacher should be possessed of knowledge, skillful, virtuous, endowed with good qualities, and pure.
He was a knower of Dharma, true to his word, and proficient in the science of alchemy;
he understood the reality of the Vedas and Vedānta, was stainless, and was devoted to Śiva. Āk 1.2.3.
Always devoted to the Goddess, ever-peaceful, skilled in the pavilion of aesthetic flavor (rasa), accomplished in mantra, a great hero, and intent upon the sacrifice to the deity. (Āk 1.2.4)

One who knows the procedure for the initiation of mercury (rasadīkṣā) [should know] mantras, medicinal herbs, great elixirs (mahārasa), the enumeration of passions (rāga), the ritual of seed-syllables (bījakalpa), the union of couples (dvandvamelāpana), and the fluxing agent (biḍa). Āk 1.2.5.
Dyeing, clarification, oiling, and the leaf-processes of transmutation;
the enhancement of color, softening, and the digestion of both the "child" and the "old" [metals]. (Āk 1.2.6)
He who knows both Khecarī and Bhūcarī shall be a guru.
(The characteristics of a disciple:
He is devoted to the guru, of virtuous conduct, and free from greed and deceit. Āk 1.2.7.
Free from desire and free from egoism, truthful in speech and established in his restraints, devoid of laziness, knowing his own duty, devoted to the six duties, and wise. (Āk 1.2.8)
Free from hypocrisy, violence, and the like, initiated into the practices of Śiva, he is an exceedingly accomplished practitioner, tranquil, and devoted to the performance of mantras. (Āk 1.2.9)
That disciple who is self-controlled, capable, and free from envy should be recognized as such.
(The characteristics of the Kākinī:
She has curly, glossy hair and eyes as long as lotus petals. Āk 1.2.10.
Her nose and hair were long and prominent; she was adorned with lips as beautiful as coral;
her teeth were like pomegranate seeds; her neck was like a conch shell, and her breasts were high. (Āk 1.2.11)
She was graced by the noose-like embrace of her arms, soft as a garland of *śirīṣa* flowers; her chest was broad, her navel deep, and her slender limbs were tremulous. (Āk 1.2.12)
With a flat belly, adorned with the line of hair and three folds, possessed of broad hips and plantain-like thighs, my beloved is most fortunate. (Āk 1.2.13)
Her shanks are like the trunk of a plantain tree, her lotus-feet are pale-red, endowed with bright and stainless nails, and she possesses the auspicious gait of a royal swan. Āk 1.2.14.
It is made beautiful by the sweet warbling of the black cuckoo, the Indian cuckoo, and other birds;
it is adorned with the temples of the God of Love, resembling the foliage of the *pippala* tree. (Āk 1.2.15)
A young woman, dark-complexioned, affectionate, beautiful, and endowed with auspicious marks, who is skilled in the arts of kissing, touching, embracing, and sexual union. (Āk 1.2.16)
She who is in her menses during the dark fortnight is known as a *kākinī*;
she may be accepted whether she is born of her own [appropriate] caste or even of another caste. (Āk 1.2.17)

In the work with mercury, in initiation, in ritual application, and in alchemy (*rasāyana*), [the attainment of] the state of a *kākīnī* [is required]; in the absence of a *kākīnī*, there may be another young woman of beautiful form. (Āk 1.2.18)
If that woman gives one niṣka of sulphur combined with cow’s ghee every morning for twenty-one days, she shall become like a kākīnī. (Āk 1.2.19)
He was righteous, fearful of sin, powerful, and possessed of the highest wisdom;
he was most excellent in justice, impartial toward all, and proficient in the science of flavors. (Āk 1.2.20)
The king and his minister were both experts in all the scriptures;
they were preeminent in devotion to all forms of dharma and promoters of the path of justice. (Āk 1.2.21)
(The Construction of the Alchemical Laboratory) O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall describe the alchemical laboratory (*rasaśālā*) for the Lord of Mercury (*rasendra*);
it should be established in a region that is free from disease and devoid of disturbances. (Āk 1.2.22)
In a land blessed by faithful beings, abounding in wealth and grain, characterized by excellent governance, full of prosperity, free from calamity, and beyond reproach.
In that city, rich with all social classes and filled with great devotees of Maheśvara,
there too was the victorious site, pure and well-protected.
In a place free from the crowding of snakes, beasts, birds, and the like, on level ground adorned with walls, moats, and bolts; Āk 1.2.25.
It was filled with oranges, pomegranates, and large citrons;
with palmyra palms, hintāla trees, vakuḷa flowers, coconut trees, and sour *pāṭala* fruits. Āk 1.2.26.
Adorned with *aśoka*, *jambu*, *panasa*, *sāla*, and *puṃnāga* trees, and with *kapittha*, *pūga*, *sarala*, *devadāru*, and *subilvaka* trees; Āk 1.2.27.
It was adorned with *dhātrī*, *nyagrodha*, *varaṇa*, *madhūka*, and *āmra* trees, and filled with *ketakī*, *mallikā*, *jātī*, *yūthikā*, and *mālatī* flowers. Āk_1.2.28.
With the *māgadhī*, *kunda*, *kurava*, and *tilaka* flowers; with the *śatapatraka*; and with the *kumuda*, *utpala*, *kalhāra*, *puṇḍarīka*, *ambuja*, and *utpala* lotuses. (Āk 1.2.29)
It was surrounded on all sides by lakes of cool water, adorned with swans, cranes, kāraṇḍava ducks, and ruddy geese. (Āk 1.2.30)
In a most beautiful and wonderful garden, adorned with lovely blossoms swaying in the cool breeze, one should construct a refectory. (Āk 1.2.31)
O Goddess of the gods, it is beautiful with sixteen pillars, square, well-proportioned, pleasing to the mind, and adorned with intoxicated elephants. (Āk 1.2.32)
It was provided with windows, secured with doors and bolts, adorned with banners on its walls, and radiant with all necessary furnishings. (Āk 1.2.33)
The guardians of the quarters were painted upon it, Vināyaka was duly worshipped there, Umā and Maheśa were installed, and it was protected by door-keepers. (Āk 1.2.34)

One should construct a medicinal kitchen, resounding with divine musical instruments such as kettledrums, trumpets, and bells, and endowed with the auspicious characteristics of a building site. Āk 1.2.35.
In the hall, an altar should be constructed—extremely firm, resembling a mirror, inlaid with bricks, beautiful, provided with stairs, and possessing the proper characteristics. (Āk 1.2.36)

Smeared with the dung of a tawny cow and surrounded by golden jars, one should prepare a noble throne for the Lord of Mercury upon the altar. (The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of the Lord of Mercury) Āk_1,2.37.
One should properly draw a two-cubit diagram on an auspicious seat using vermilion:
a six-pointed star within a lotus of eight petals, and outside of that, another eight-petaled lotus. (Āk 1.2.38)
One should place a lotus that is square and adorned with four gates within the yantra, and install a rasa-liṅga there, worshipping it with flowers and other offerings. (Āk 1.2.39)
(Rasa-sandhyā) Now I shall explain the twilight rite (sandhyā) which bestows the fruits of alchemical work.
Having bathed, being pure and anointed with unguents, one should enter the laboratory of mercury. (Āk 1.2.40)
Wearing white garlands and garments, with self-restrained mind and conquered senses, controlled in speech, devoted to the guru, truthful, and firm in his vows. (Āk 1.2.41)

Having sat down upon a soft, variegated woolen blanket, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with water that is endowed with the power of speech, illusion, and prosperity, and whose essence consists of the Self, knowledge, and Śiva. (Āk 1.2.42)
Saying "I purify the reality," one should drink [the water] three times according to the rule;
O Dear One, one should meditate upon the Varada-gāyatrī and recite it three times. (Āk 1.2.43)
O Bhairavī, hear the Rasabhairava-gāyatrī according to its true essence:
*Aiṃ raseśvarāya vidmahe rasāṅkuśāya dhīmahi tannaḥ sūtaḥ pracodayāt*.
Resembling ten million suns and like ten billion moons.
The radiant deity has five faces, three eyes, and the moon as his crest;
he possesses eighteen arms, is peaceful, and is devoted to the fivefold cosmic functions. (Āk 1.2.45)
Raseśvara wears white garlands and garments, has a serpent as his sacred thread, resembles crystal, and is mounted upon a corpse. Āk 1.2.46.

And [he saw] Nīlakaṇṭha, the omniscient one, adorned with all ornaments, the bestower of boons, the science of alchemy (rasaśāstra), mercury (pārada), the serpent, and the nectar of immortality (sudhā). Āk 1.2.47.
O Īśvarī, [he holds] a conch, medicinal herbs, a bow, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and an arrow; a hand-drum, a sword, a mace, and fire. Āk_1.2.48.
Holding health, a divine garland, and fearlessness in his eighteen hands, he bears Rasāṅkuśī upon his own lap and has the bull as his vehicle. (Āk 1.2.49)

Having meditated upon Śiva, who is beautiful with his mass of matted hair, whose face bears a gentle smile, and who is the Bhairava of aesthetic flavor (rasa), one should [meditate] on Rasāṅkuśī in his lap. Āk 1.2.50.
She holds a goad and a rosary in her two right hands, and she bears a noose and the gesture of fearlessness in her two left hands. (Āk 1.2.51)

The goddess has four arms, is red in color, possesses three eyes, and has the moon as her crest-jewel; she wears red garments, has a neck like a conch shell, and is composed of compassion. (Āk 1.2.52)
One should meditate upon the auspicious Goddess Rasāṅkuśī, radiant with jewel ornaments, graced by a gentle smile, and facing the Lord. Āk 1.2.53.
Then, having taken the ashes, the wise one should hold them with his left hand;
he should not let them fall down, but rather take cow dung into a vessel.
Having dried it, O Dear One, one should burn it in the sacrificial pit and maintain [the fire] in sequence;
then the re-extraction should be performed with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta. (Āk 1.2.55)
Having consecrated it again with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, one should perform inspection, sprinkling, striking, and likewise sprinkling. Āk 1.2.56.

One should deposit [the mantras] in their respective locations—on the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the two feet—in sequence, using the five mantras beginning with Īśāna. (Āk 1.2.57)
The Great Lord Rasācārya should smear all his limbs with ashes using those five substances and perform the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the rules. (Āk 1.2.58)
O Pārvatī, having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should sprinkle consecrated water held in the left hand upon the head while reciting the root mantra. (Āk 1.2.59)
Having sipped water again that has been consecrated with the root mantra, one should then drink it three times from the right hand as an act of ritual purification (ācamana). Āk 1.2.60.

O Pārvatī, having offered the *arghya* with the root mantra and having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*) three times, the noble-minded practitioner should then mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times. (Āk 1.2.61)
And one should offer this *rasa-sandhyā* to the *sūta*, O Goddess;
thus one should perform the *sandhyā* that destroys all sins at the three times of day. (Āk 1.2.62)
(The extraction of the root mantra of Rasāṅkuśī and Rasāṅkuśī):
O Dear One, I shall describe the sequence for extracting the root mantra; listen.
[It consists of] Vāk, Māyā, and Kamalā, followed by Rasānām Īśvaraḥ ending in the dative case. (Āk 1.2.63)
Then the station of Mahākāla, then the station of Mahābala;
then the station of Aghorabhairava, and then the station of Vajravīra. (Āk 1.2.64)
This entire sequence of syllables beginning with *krodha* and ending with *kāla* is conjoined with the Perfectly Awakened One (*sambuddhi*).
It is joined with the final letter of the *ka-ṣa-ṣa-ta-varga* groups, followed by the sound *da*, and provided with a bindu. (Āk 1.2.65)
This is the five-syllable peak (kūṭa); then, joined with the act of attracting (karṣaṇa) and also accompanied by the visarga, this peak consists of four syllables, O Dear One. (Āk 1.2.66)
This mantra of Rasendrabhairava consists of thirty-two syllables;
it is concealed in all tantras, a secret that is extremely difficult to obtain. (Āk 1.2.67)
O Bhairavī, listen; I shall declare the mantra of Rasāṅkuśā:
Vāṅ, Māyā, Bhuvaneśī, Ramā, and Makaraketana. (Āk 1.2.68)
The mantra of the goddess Rasāṅkuśā, ending with "namaḥ" and consisting of twelve syllables, is proclaimed for you as follows: [Oṃ] Rasāṅkuśāyai namaḥ. (Āk 1.2.69)
The meter of Rasabhairava is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh;
Nandikeśa is declared the seer (ṛṣi), and the deity is the venerable Rasabhairava. (Āk 1.2.70)
The seed-syllable *raṃ* is the *kīla*, while the final letter is said to be the *śakti*.
For Rasāṅkuśā and Skanda, the seed-syllable is *ardraṃ* and the *kīlaka* is *rasaḥ*. (Āk 1.2.71)
Salutation to that which is known as Śakti, the secret and supreme mantra.
(The Worship of the Rasa-liṅga) O Bhairavī, listen to the worship of the Rasa-liṅga according to its true nature. Āk 1.2.72.
Placing the left foot forward, one should enter the sacrificial hall;
seated upon a soft seat, pure and with a restrained mind. (Āk 1.2.73)
Having restrained the vital breaths and formed the formal resolve, one should contemplate the venerable Guru situated upon the head—
resembling pure crystal, profoundly tranquil, and bestowing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should first remember their names and obtain their permission;
[then one should address] those beings who dwell in heaven and those on earth who create obstacles.
"May those great elements that exist in the netherworld perish by the command of Śiva.
With this very mantra, one should scatter unbroken grains (*akṣata*) in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (Āk 1.2.76)
Reciting "puṣpamastrāya phaṭ," he should cast [the flower] into the intermediate space;
and reciting "sarvaśatrupramathanī," he should place it on his right heel. (Āk 1.2.77)
One should strike it on the ground three times; then there shall be breath control (prāṇāyāma).
To the south of the auspicious seat of Rasendra, there is a square [mandala]. (Āk 1.2.78)
One should fashion a very beautiful mandala measuring one cubit and a half;
it should consist of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and a square in successive order. (Āk 1.2.79)

One should worship Indra and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas), preceded by their respective names and ending with "namas," using flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava). (Āk 1.2.80)
O Śivā, one should worship the heart and the other limbs with the seed-syllables of speech (vāṅ), illusion (māyā), and Lakṣmī (kamalā) in the east, south, west, and north respectively. Āk 1.2.81.
One should worship the two eyes in the corners of Īśāna, Agni, Asura, and Marut;
and the weapon-mantra, ending in *phaṭ* and in the dative case, in all directions. (Āk 1.2.82)
One should display the eight finger-snaps and then bring forth the support;
right there, one should invoke the fire-mandala, which has the seed-syllable as its root. (Āk 1.2.83)
There, one should worship the ten digits of Agni in sequence with perfumes and unbroken rice grains;
then, taking up the vessel, one should contemplate it as the solar orb. (Āk 1.2.84)
There, the twelve digits of the Sun (Mārtaṇḍa) should be worshipped with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice;
one should fill the arghya vessel with water mixed with the finest fragrances. (Āk 1.2.85)
One should contemplate the lunar orb and worship them there;
having drawn a triangle in the center, one should inscribe the seed-syllable of Śakti. (Āk 1.2.86)
There, one should scatter fragrant flowers and recite the root mantra three times;
one should hold four vessels in the four directions, beginning with the east. (Āk 1.2.87)
One should fill those [vessels] as before and worship them with perfumes, flowers, and consecrated rice;
one should then sprinkle them with water from the central vessel while reciting the root mantra. (Āk 1.2.88)
One should offer one's own limbs as vessels and all things as materials for worship;
one should then prepare a square mandala with a welcoming entrance. (Āk 1.2.89)
As before, one should fill five vessels with pure water;
one should place mercury in the central one and cast gems into the southern one. (Āk 1.2.90)
One should place gold in that left vessel and set kuśa grass near it;
in the vessel situated near the jewel-vessel, there should be the eight fragrant substances (aṣṭagandha). Āk_1.2.91.
For each vessel, one should draw a triangle endowed with Māyā;
one should place scented paste, unbroken rice, and flowers, and consecrate them three times with the root mantra. (Āk 1.2.92)
One should consecrate the vessel of nectar seven times with the root mantra, and likewise consecrate the articles of worship and oneself with the water from that very vessel of nectar. (Āk 1.2.93)
One should sprinkle the body, the head, the pedestal, and the lamp;
Meru is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) of the seat, and Sutala its metre (chandas). Āk 1.2.94.
The Blessed One is proclaimed as the deity in the form of a tortoise.
O Goddess Earth, the worlds are supported by you; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, support me, O Goddess, and make this seat pure.
With this very mantra, one should scatter a flower upon the seat. (Āk 1.2.95)
(The Purification of the Elements):

I shall now explain the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). The earth element is yellow, accompanied by the vajra; it is solid, joined with the seed-syllable *laṃ*, and extends from the base of the big toe to the knees. (Āk 1.2.96)
One should meditate upon her, from the knees up to the hips, as being white and in the form of a liquid, accompanied by the seed-syllable *vaṃ* and topped with a half-moon. Āk 1.2.97.
From the hips up to the heart, one should meditate externally upon the syllable *raṃ*, red in color and adorned with a svastika, situated within a triangle. (Āk 1.2.98)
O Goddess, the wind should be meditated upon from the heart up to the throat, having the luster of collyrium, accompanied by the seed-syllable *yaṃ* and adorned with six dots (*ṣaḍbindu*). Āk 1.2.99.

O Goddess, one should meditate upon the sky as a six-cornered [triangle] extending from the region of the ears to the aperture of Brahmā, circular, joined with the seed-syllable *haṃ*, and intensely black. (Āk 1.2.100)

O Supreme Goddess, having merged the earth into water, that [water] into fire, that [fire] into air, and that [air] into space, one should establish [the consciousness] at the end of the twelve [fingers]. (Āk 1.2.101)
O Dear One, one should dry up one's own body from the *mūlādhāra* by means of the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, piercing through the six *ādhāras* as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*). (Āk 1.2.102)
One should burn the entire body with the seed-syllable *raṃ*, and then flood it;
[the body] becomes liquefied by the seed-syllable *vaṃ* from the lunar orb at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). (Āk 1.2.103)
O Śivā, one should bathe the body with the flowing nectar;
from the ether one should take the wind, and from that, one should draw forth the fire. (Āk 1.2.104)
Water should be drawn from fire; from those [waters], one should take earth.
In this way, one should employ the five elements in their respective places. (Āk 1.2.105)

O Goddess, one should meditate on the personification of evil (pāpapuruṣa), black in form, situated in the left side of the belly; one should visualize him as having emerged, bearing a sword and a shield. Āk 1.2.106.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the *rasāṅkuśa* mantra upon the fingers, the heart, and so forth:

*Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kṣmauṃ kṣmaṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ phaṭ raseśvarāya mahākālabhairavāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ / raudrarūpāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalalocanāya avatara 2 avatāraya 2 jalpa 2 jalpaya 2 śubhāśubhaṃ kathaya 2 kathāpaya 2 mama mahārakṣāṃ kuru kuru kāraya /* [Perform the placement with the *rasāṅkuśa* mantra upon the fingers, the heart, and other parts: *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kṣmauṃ kṣmaṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ phaṭ*. To the Lord of Taste (*raseśvara*), to Mahākālabhairava, for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*! O you of fierce form, with dark and tawny eyes, descend, descend! Cause to descend, cause to descend! Speak, speak! Cause to speak, cause to speak! Tell me of the auspicious and the inauspicious! Cause to tell, cause to tell! Perform great protection for me, perform it, cause it to be performed!]
2. Grant me, grant me the perfection of alchemy (rasasiddhi)! 1888.
Homage to the Heart of Mahākālabhairava!
As before, svāhā to the Head of Mahābalabhairava!
As before: *vaṣaṭ* to Aghorabhairava for the crest-lock (*śikhā*);
as before: *hūṃ* to Vajravīrabhairava for the armor (*kavaca*);
as before: *vauṣaṭ* to Krodhabhairava for the three eyes (*netratraya*).
As before, [the mantra] for Kālabhairava is *astrāya phaṭ*.
Thus is the finger-assignment (*aṅgulinyāsa*). Having pronounced each seed-syllable, the fourth is the "Taste-hook" (*rasāṅkuśa*). (Āk 1.2.107)

One should place the five seed-syllables in the five locations beginning with the heart; then, with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should display the crest-gesture (coṭikā) in the cardinal directions. (Āk 1.2.108)

O Goddess, one should then perform the deposition of the *mātṛkā*, the deposition of the *kalās*, the deposition of the *pāñjya*, and the *kolaka*; thereafter, one should carry out the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*). (Āk 1.2.109)
Indeed, by means of retention (kumbhaka), one causes the heart-lotus to fully blossom;
and within the pericarp of that heart-lotus, one should contemplate the embodiment of aesthetic flavor (rasa). (Āk 1.2.110)
One should worship with mental offerings such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should adorn one's own body with perfumes, flowers, and the like, according to one's pleasure. (Āk 1.2.111)

Thus should the internal sacrifice be performed; one should then carry out the external sacrifice. Having sprinkled the *liṅga* with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and having effected the purification of the *liṅga*, [one should proceed]. (Āk 1.2.112)
O beloved, having placed the *vardhanī*—filled with water and clothed in a garment—on the right side, one should worship it according to the prescribed rite. (Āk 1.2.113)
On the pedestal, one should fashion a square with vermilion powder;
within that, one should draw a hexagon with a straight golden rod. (Āk 1.2.114)
O Dear One, one should worship the eight-petaled lotus, which has four doors and a square ground-floor chamber on its exterior, and the guardians of the directions (dikpālas). Āk 1.2.115.
And Nandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Riṭi, and the mighty Mahābala;
Kumbhakarṇa, Sugrīva, Bhṛṅgaka, and Dṛḍhāyudha. (Āk 1.2.116)
Having placed two each at the four gates, beginning with the east and worshipped them,
[one should place] gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, kāntaloha, śaṭha, and iron.

O Maheśvarī, having worshipped two [deities] each in the directions starting from the east in sequence, one should worship Śukra in the eastern part and Graha in the southeast within the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha). Āk 1.2.118.
One should worship Rudra in the south, Samīraṇa in the southwest, Śiva in the west, Vahni in the northwest, and Umā in the north. (Āk 1.2.119)
One should worship Pāvaka in the northeast; then, at the tips of the eight petals starting from the east, [one should place] sulphur, orpiment, green vitriol, and realgar. (Āk 1.2.120)
Kaṅkuṣṭha, mākṣika, nṛpāvarta, and gairika;
likewise, the lepikā, the kṣepikā, the krāmikā, and the rañjikā. (Āk 1.2.121)
Lohaṭī, Bandhakārī, Bhūcarī, Mṛtyunāśinī, Vibhūti, and Khecarī—these are the ten dūtīs in their proper sequence. (Āk 1.2.122)
They are to be worshipped on an eight-petaled lotus, in the petals above, below, and [the others], as ruby, pearl, lapis lazuli, sapphire, emerald, and coral. (Āk 1.2.123)
Gomedaka and puṣparāga gems, which grant all accomplishments, one should worship at the tips of the petals of the second eight-petaled lotus. (Āk 1.2.124)
The Rudras have eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes;
their crowns are adorned with the crescent moon, they have blue throats, and the bull is their emblem. (Āk 1.2.125)
O Maheśānī, all those eight Vidyeśvaras, each bearing their respective colors, are to be worshipped in the second eight-petaled lotus. (Āk 1.2.126)
Rasaka, vimala, tāpya, capala, tuttha, and añjana—these six, O friends, placed upon the tips of the petals of the hexagon, bestow all accomplishments. (Āk 1.2.127)
One should worship these six—diamond, vaikrānta, diamond-ore, magnetite, borax, and bhūnāga—as well as the *śaktis*, within the hexagons. (Āk 1.2.128)
Cinnabar, realgar, bitumen, and orpiment—these four supreme powers (parā-śakti) are located in the pericarp, starting from the east. (Āk 1.2.129)
Cinnabar is Mālinī-śakti; Sasyaka is Parā-śakti;
Śilājatu is Aparā-śakti; and Agnijāra is Parāparā. (Āk 1.2.130)
One should worship these [deities] situated in the enclosure of Rasa with their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in *namaḥ*, using the dative case. (Āk 1.2.131)
In the center, however, one should worship Rasabhairava amidst the divine powers (divyaśaktis), once twenty-seven niṣkas of pure gold have been melted. (Āk 1.2.132)
With a one-pointed mind, one should place nine niṣkas of mercury into a well-characterized linga-shaped mold made of beeswax. (Āk 1.2.133)
O Śivā, when the molten gold has been heated, one should cast the mercury into it;
after a moment, once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, that mercury-liṅga should be placed within milk. (Āk 1.2.134)
Having set it aside and taken it up again, one should remove the impurity on the upper part;
then, having rubbed and smoothed it, one should sprinkle the *liṅga*. (Āk 1.2.135)

In this manner, one may fashion a liṅga according to one's capacity, using silver or other metals—either individually or combined—or using the essences (sattva) of mica and similar substances. (Āk 1.2.136)
The Rasaliṅga is said to be of two kinds, O beloved: with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
The liṅga with parts is that which was described previously; the partless one is the mercury alone. (Āk 1.2.137)
For those desiring worldly enjoyment, as well as for those seeking liberation in its entirety or in part, the Rasaliṅga bound with gold is [worshipped by] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Vahni. Āk 1.2.138.
They worshipped Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and Nandin with lingas fashioned from silver; you have worshipped a mercury-linga bound with the essence of mica. (Āk 1.2.139)
The goddesses Ramā and Vāṇī, along with Kubera, Indra, and Varuṇa, worshipped the one bound in *tāmra*;
while Yama, Vāyu, and Nairṛta worshipped the one bound in *kānta*. (Āk 1.2.140)
The Siddhas, Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, and great ṛṣis are bound by the Vaṅga; the Nāgas, Vasus, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Kinnaras are bound by the Nāga. (Āk 1.2.141)
The Bhadrakālīs, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas are bound by the *tīkṣṇa* [knot];
and Durgāmbā, the Apsarases, Guhyakas, and Asuras are bound by the *muṇḍa* [knot]. (Āk 1.2.142)
Yogins such as Bhṛṅgin and others worship the partless *rasaliṅga*;
those humans who desire fruits have been told of these various *rasaliṅgas*. (Āk 1.2.143)
They should worship these with diligence at all times for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
Now hear about the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃsthāpana*) for the aforementioned *rasaliṅgas*. (Āk 1.2.144)

Having restrained the vital breaths according to the rule, O Śivā, one should meditate upon the supreme Power of Breath (Prāṇaśakti), who is seated upon a red lotus situated in the midst of an ocean of blood. (Āk 1.2.145)
She wears red garments and is red in hue, adorned with a crown of various jewels;
her hair-knot is like a digit of the stainless moon, and she has eyes like the sun, fire, and the moon. Āk 1.2.146.
Her cheeks were reddened by the rays of her ear-ornaments,
and she was graced by a bridge of the nose shaped like a *śrīparṇī* flower.
She is resplendent with lower lips like coral and rubies,
and adorned with smooth teeth shaped like kuruvinda seeds.
Her neck, as beautiful as a conch shell, was adorned with a pearl necklace,
and she was decorated with finger-rings, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
She holds a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and flower-arrows, and bestows fearlessness;
her lotus-like hands are beautified by a vessel filled with blood. Āk 1.2.150.
Adorned with a necklace and saffron paste shining upon the slopes of her full breasts,
she was further embellished by a girdle, anklets, bracelets, and ornaments for her toes.
With a one-pointed mind, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) for the *liṅga*.
O Dear One, [the mantra is]: "The goad, the bed, and the noose; *haṃsaḥ so’ham* (I am He).
May the life-breath of such-and-such a *liṅga* be here as its life-breath."
The life-force (*jīva*) of that *liṅga* resides here.
May all the sense-faculties of that *liṅga*—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, and smell—having come here, remain happily for a long time. I am that *Haṃsa*, *svāhā*. *Ya-ra-la-va-śa-ṣa-sa-ha-oṃ*.
O Dear One, having uttered this mantra— *kroṃ hrīṃ āṃ*— one should invoke the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
Of this *Śrī-prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra*, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (*ṛṣis*).
The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are the meters;
the goddess Śrī Parāśakti is the deity;
Āṃ is the seed-syllable.
Hrīṃ is the Śakti; Kroṃ is the Kīlaka. This is the application (viniyoga) for the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) of this Liṅga.
One should first worship the seat with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth. (Ākāśabhairava Tantra 1.2.152)
Hāṃ, salutation to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti).
Hrīṃ, salutation to the Tortoise (Kūrma).
Hrūṃ, salutation to Ananta.
Hraiṃ, salutation to Earth;
Hrauṃ, salutation to the bulbous root;
[salutation] to the sprout, the stalk, the pericarp, the petals, the filaments, and the pericarp; in its center, [salutation] to Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, Aiśvarya, Adharma, Ajñāna, and Avairāgya.
Salutation to Anaiśvarya.
O Maheśvarī, one should invoke the Lord seated upon the heart-lotus together with the Goddess, along with his retinue and endowed with the powers of his own limbs. (Āk 1.2.153)

One should establish the liṅga upon the pedestal with the root mantra; one should offer arghya with water from kuśa grass, pādya with scented water, and the ācamana should be performed with gold. (Āk 1.2.154)
O Pārvatī, the Śāmbhavī bath should be performed with water containing jewels, using the entire root mantra, the eleventh Rudra, and the Pavamāna hymn. (Āk 1.2.155)
With camaka hymns, the Puruṣasūkta, fruits, and even the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with coconut water, sugarcane juice, and fragrant scented water. Āk 1.2.156.
Having bathed the liṅga, O Śivā, one should then establish it upon the pedestal.

Around the liṅga, in the eight directions, [one should worship] with "Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; to Jyeṣṭha; to Rudra; to Kāla; to Kalavikaraṇa; to Bala; to Balavikaraṇa; to Balapramathana; to Sarvabhūtadamana," and [in the center] with "to Manonmana."
Having worshipped with flowers in the presence of Śiva:
*oṃ hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* / *oṃ hrīṃ śirase svāhā* /
Oṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock; oṃ hraiṃ, huṃ to the armor; oṃ hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.
Oṃ hraḥ astrāya phaṭ / Hrāṃ to Īśāna, obeisance! Hrīṃ to Tatpuruṣa, obeisance!
Hrūṃ, homage to Aghora.
Hraiṃ, homage to Vāmadeva.
Hrauṃ, homage to Sadyojāta.
O Dear One, one should offer a handful of flowers to the deity with the root mantra. (Āk 1.2.157)

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Śiva using the six-limbed application of the root mantra; furthermore, one should place the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, on the right side of the liṅga. Āk 1.2.158.
Brahmā, the earth, water, Viṣṇu, Rudra, fire, Īśvara, wind, as well as ether and Sadāśiva. (Āk 1.2.159)
The wise one should worship, in due order, Śrīkaṇṭha, Amṛtāṃśu, Bhairava, and likewise Bhāskara, as well as Paraśiva and Parātmā. (Āk 1.2.160)
On the left side of the *liṅga*, however, are the seven Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, as well as Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, Durgā, Skanda, and Vināyaka. (Āk 1.2.161)
The Yoginīs, the Kṣetrapālas, and the Śaktis of the primordial seats—Oḍyāṇa-Śakti, Jālandharī, Pūrṇā, and Giri, O Dear One. (Āk 1.2.162)
O you who are worshipped by the gods, one should worship Rudra-śakti as Kāmeśvarī, as well as Lopāmudrā, Kubjikā, and likewise Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī. (Āk 1.2.163)
O Pārvatī, the sweet and other tastes, fragrances, all grains, divine herbs, nectar, wine, poison, and the minerals such as leather; Āk 1.2.164.

The senses, the mind, the intellect, the ego, and consciousness, as well as the objects of perception such as sound and the rest, and the limbs of the body—these are to be worshipped, O Śāmbhavī. (Āk 1.2.165)
On the western side of the Liṅga are the oceans, rivers, and streams;
the mountains, headed by Meru; and the nine planets, beginning with the Sun. (Āk 1.2.166)
The circle of luminaries, the Pole Star, the Śiśumāra, and Prajāpati;
the Kalās, Kāṣṭhās, Ghaṭikās, Muhūrtas, Prahars, and the Day. (Āk 1.2.167)
Night, the fortnight, the month, the seasons, the times, and the years; the ages, the kalpas, the directions, the stars, and the lunar day, O Śivā. (Āk 1.2.168)
And the netherworlds, the lords of the nāgas, as well as the Rudras of the fire of time, yakṣas, piśācas, bhūtas, rākṣasas, and likewise the sons of Danu. Āk 1.2.169.
O Dear One, having worshipped in due order the Guhyakas, the wicked Vetālas, diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā), as well as mantras, weapons, and missiles; Āk 1.2.170.
On the front part of the *liṅga*, however, the lineages of gurus are to be worshipped:
the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the sages, the yogins, and the exponents of Brahman. (Āk 1.2.171)
The Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and likewise the two Aśvins;
the Vasus, the foremost of the Apsarases, and the nine rasas beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra). Āk 1.2.172.
Song, dances, their various divisions, as well as the ten beginning with Kāśyapa; the Rudras together with the Manus are to be worshipped, as are the Bhāskaras and the three Vahnis. (Āk 1.2.173)
The Viśvedevas, the ancestors, the mothers, the ancestral deities, the family preceptors, the masters of the Rasas, the ancient teachers, and those who worship Śiva. (Āk 1.2.174)
The ten births beginning with the fish, the Jina, the Lokāyatika, all the worlds beginning with hell, the Garuḍas, and the eggs of the Garuḍas. Āk 1.2.175.

All the Brahmāṇḍas, those moving in the sky, those moving on the earth, and those moving in the water—all these deities should be worshipped with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. (Āk 1.2.176)

O Dear One, with flowers, perfumes, and unbroken grains (akṣata) accompanied by the respective names in the dative case, one should offer a pair of garments and likewise two sacred threads (upavīta) to the deity. (Āk 1.2.177)
He offered the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), divine fragrances, unbroken grains, and flowers— always excluding those of the *kaitaka* jasmine— as well as divine split bamboo mats.
And its flowers are the kahlāra, kamala, utpala, and kairava;
as well as the jātī, campaka, punnāga, pūga, and nāraṅga.
One should offer māgadhī, mādhavī, mallī, yūthikā, and so forth, as well as damanī and maruva, to the Lord of Mercury (Rasendra). Āk 1.2.180.
One should offer incense of ten ingredients, lamps, cakes, food, ghee, milk-rice, vegetables possessing the six flavors, and accompanied by pure, excellent perfumes. (Āk 1.2.181)
One should present the food offering (*naivedya*) consisting of things to be licked, sucked, and so forth, to the Lord of Mercury (*pāradendra*);
and, O Goddess, one should give water for washing the hands with scented water. (Āk 1.2.182)
Well-scented betel nuts mixed with camphor, and bright white betel leaves complete with their stalks. (Āk 1.2.183)
One should offer powdered pearls, betel, a mirror, a pair of fly-whisks, an umbrella, dance, and song. (Āk 1.2.184)
O Dear One, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) during all the ritual services;
O Śivā, one should offer all the services with the root mantra and recite the hymn of praise. Āk 1.2.185.
Having meditated upon the god Rasendrabhairava and the goddess Rasāṅkuśā, one should worship Māheśvara, Vinatā, and the others with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (Āk 1.2.186)

With the thumb and the ring finger, one should offer [the oblation] accompanied by the finest fragrance; with the root-mantra, one should offer it to the God, to the Goddess, and to the lineage of gurus. (Āk 1.2.187)
One should also offer libations in sequence to the goddesses residing in the enclosures:
"Hrīṃ! I worship the form of Ānanda-Śiva. Hrīṃ! I worship the form of Parānanda-Śiva."
Hrīṃ, I worship the form of Śiva, the bliss of the supreme and the non-supreme.
Hrīṃ, I worship the form of the Siddha of bliss. Hrīṃ, I worship the form of the Siddha of supreme bliss.
Hrīṃ, I worship the perfected form of Parāparānanda. Klīṃ, I worship the form of Ānandaguru.
Klīṃ, I worship the form of Parānandaguru.
"Klīṃ, I worship the form of the Guru, the bliss of the supreme and the non-supreme;
having offered them the prasāda and being personally authorized by them... (Āk 1.2.188).
One should know that the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self) and the *vidyātattva* (the principle of knowledge) are located at the navel;
the *śivatattva* (the principle of Śiva) is in the heart, and indeed the *sarvatattva* (the principle of all) resides in the palate. (Āk 1.2.189)
Having thus meditated upon the three principles (tritattva) along with the grace accompanied by mantras,
one should then, O Dear One, remember the blazing light situated within [the self].
And one should accept the favor as desired in this world frequented by the gods;
through the *mūrchā* [offering], the ancestors are gratified and all the deities rejoice. (Āk 1.2.191)
"Out of ignorance [... he is indeed I, there is no doubt.
(The Sequence of the Offering of the Lord of Mercury) "Excellent fragrant rice, pure blood, ghee, and honey. (Āk 1.2.192)
Having joined them together and divided them into five sections, one should offer them in sequence:
in the south, north, east, west, and the center. (Āk 1.2.193)
Then, having recited those various mantras, the person should offer the bali;
[beginning with] the Praṇava, Māyā, Kamalā, and the Goddess who grants sons. (Āk 1.2.194)
Then [to him] named Vaṭukanātha, tawny, resplendent with a mass of matted hair: "O Piṅgala, O three-eyed one, accept, accept this offering and worship, svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to all the Siddha-yoginīs and to all the Mothers!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to all the spirits and to all the lords of spirits!"
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Sthānakṣetrapāla, accept, accept this offering and worship, svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Rasendra Kṣetrapāla, Lord of the Kings of Kings, accept, accept this offering and worship, svāhā!
One should present the offering, O Śivā, for the pacification of all obstacles.
Then, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times in front of the mercury.
Then, O Goddess, one should recite a hymn for the gratification of Rasabhairava;
when Rasabhairava is pleased, all the gods will be satisfied. (Āk 1.2.196)
This rite of daily worship has been proclaimed; it is difficult to find everywhere.
Know me, O Goddess, to be mercury (*pārada*); he who remembers me, O Beloved, is equal to me. (The fruit of the worship of mercury). *Āk* 1.2.197.
Mercury (pārada), however, is superior to me both because it belongs to me and because of its essential nature;
the recollection, sight, and likewise the touch of mercury is meritorious. Āk 1.2.198.
Worship, consumption, and giving—this sixfold merit has been proclaimed; it possesses a threefold nature: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasa. (Āk 1.2.199)
It is sattvic, bestowing liberation, pure, youthful, and adorned with two arms;
it holds a full vessel and a subtle staff, has two eyes, and wears a garland of small bells. (Āk 1.2.200)
The *rājasa* [form] bestows enjoyment; it is red in color, adorned with a crown and a moon-crest, four-armed, youthful, blue-throated, and three-eyed. (Āk 1.2.201)
One should meditate upon him who bestows all sovereignty, holding a trident, a vessel, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
he is of the nature of *tamas*, black in color, and has blazing hair rising upward. (Āk 1.2.202)
O Goddess, one should meditate upon the previously described Rasa, who has eighteen arms and three eyes;
he bestows all accomplishments and grants the fruit of all desires. (Āk 1.2.203)
The remembrance of the King of Essences destroys all calamities;
O Bhairavī, by meditating on Him seated within the lotus of the heart, sins are destroyed. (Āk 1.2.204)
Beholding the Lord of Pāra, one destroys the sins accumulated across the three periods of time;
likewise, by beholding the multitude of divine liṅgas extending from Setu to Kedāra. (Āk 1.2.205)
Whatever merit a mortal obtains from visiting all the sacred fords on earth as far as the ocean's edge, that shall become ten millionfold [by this means]. (Āk 1.2.206)
Through bathing, drinking, and other such acts, that merit becomes multiplied ten millionfold;
O Goddess, even a million killings of cows and hundreds of abortions [are thus purified]. (Āk 1.2.207)
Thousands of killings of Brahmins are destroyed by the sight of the mercury, as is [the merit of] the gift of ten million cows and a hundred crores of gold. (Āk 1.2.208)
O beloved, the merit that comes from a thousand horse-sacrifices is attained by the sight of this nectar; furthermore, touching it destroys the sin of approaching those who should not be approached.

The sin of seizing the property of others and the evil acquired through the slaughter of living beings—whether on the earth consisting of seven continents, in the netherworld, in the sky, or in heaven—[is all destroyed]. Āk 1.2.210.

Whatever merit one gains by worshipping those lingas through the worship of rasa (mercury), that same merit is obtained by performing worship at the divine, self-manifested (svāyaṃbhuvā) lingas. (Āk 1.2.211)
Whatever merit is gained from the worship of the Rasaliṅga, that shall be its fruit;
it is the state attained by yogins devoted to the eight limbs and by those who discourse on Brahman.
One attains that state through the worship of the *rasaliṅga*, wherein the mercury is contained within saffron, agallochum, musk, and camphor. (Āk 1.2.213)
One should offer the solidified mercury to the Liṅga for the sake of accomplishing one's desired aims;
by consuming the king of mercury, all sin is destroyed. (Āk 1.2.214)
One should dry up the self, which has been defiled by the impurity of beginningless illusion; one shall swiftly remove the disease of existence and destroy the threefold torment. (Āk 1.2.215)

Whatever fruit may arise from giving gold equal in size to Mount Mahāmeru, that same fruit is obtained by the gift of the king of elixirs (rasarāja) over the earth bounded by the four oceans. (Āk 1.2.216)
In the form of Brahmā he is the pure essence; in the form of Viṣṇu he is that which has become solidified;
in the form of Rudra he is reduced to ashes; and as Sadāśiva, he is the bound mercury (sūta). Āk 1.2.217.
O Maheśvarī, the lord of mercury (pāradendra) can assume any form at will like a leech, take the form of Time (kāla), and possess defects; it may be fainted, reduced to ashes, or bound. Āk 1.2.218.
This compassionate Lord of Mercury (Rasendra) removes disease, death, and poverty;
O Lord of Mercury, you swiftly grant [these] through sound, touch, smoke, and ash. (Rasendrastotra 1.2.219)
O bestower of the siddhi of moving through the sky, protect me from the end of ten billion gold pieces;
salutations to you, the death of Death; salutations to the self of all virtues. (Āk 1.2.220)
Salutations to the destroyer of wrinkles and grey hair, the bestower of great vitality, the slayer of weapons and missiles, and the one who has crossed the ocean of illusion. (Āk 1.2.221)
O Lord of Mercury, salutations to you, the god of love in the dalliance of beautiful women;
O embodiment of nectar, destroyer of the three humors, salutations to you whose essence consists of the six tastes. (Āk 1.2.222)
To you who are the form of earth due to density, the form of water due to fluidity, radiant due to the predominance of fire, and the form of air due to mobility. Āk 1.2.223.
Salutations to you, whose form is the subtle essence; salutations to you who possess the nature of the elements.
Salutations to you who are fit for yoga; be gracious, O one worshipped by the immortals. Āk 1.2.224.
O Purifier, you remove diseases such as consumption and leprosy that arise from the slaughter of cows, Vedic scholars, brahmins, kings, lords, teachers, heroes, and others. Āk 1.2.225.
O mercury, you are the savior of those whose senses and objects have perished and who lack knowledge;
for even by the application of a mere atom, you are superior to all medicinal herbs. (Āk 1.2.226)
O Destroyer of all defects and Dispeller of aversion, salutations to You!
By You were created the gods, beginning with Mahendra, as well as Brahmā and the others, who are Your portions (kalās). Āk 1.2.227.
The moon, sun, planets, and stars; Śiva, Bhairava, and the Śaktis; the worlds with their qualities of knowledge and ignorance; and the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas. (Āk 1.2.228)
O glorious Lord of Mercury (Sūtendra), all divine medicinal herbs, even those that grant every supernatural power, are not worth a sixteenth part of you. (Āk 1.2.229)

O Lord of Sūtas, while Śambhu himself is present before one's eyes—endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and bestowing various supernatural powers—what need is there for anything else? (Āk 1.2.230)
O Kojañjala, by practicing [the yoga] therein, yogins always attain the state of immortality and the inexhaustibility of metals such as gold. (Āk 1.2.231)
O Lord of Sūtas, how can that man who does not know you—the supreme one whose nature is both visible and invisible, and who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation—know me? (Āk 1.2.232)
You alone are the teacher, mother, father, brother, wealth, knowledge, refuge, and friend of all beings; who else besides you is a benefactor? (Āk 1.2.233)

O Lord of Mercury (Rasendra), in your yoga, in your scripture, in your hymn, and in your alchemy (rasāyana), whoever in this world is endowed with devotion is none other than I; of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.2.234)
O Mercury, even one who is proficient in the knowledge of Brahman, if he reviles you, must be shunned by all people; I am not at all able to protect him. (Āk 1.2.235)
For one who says of you, "You do not exist," there is no accomplishment anywhere;
but for one who says of you, "You exist," there shall always be accomplishment. (Āk 1.2.236)
O Sūta, whoever in this world—whether of noble birth or of low lineage—refines you, the king of mercury, by means of the eighteen processes; Āk 1.2.237.
He is meritorious, he is observant of vows, he is blessed, he is praiseworthy, and he is wise; he is a true man, he is omniscient, he is perfected, and he is a deity. (Āk 1.2.238)
That family is purified, the land is meritorious, and the king is endowed with victory; that city is always festive, and his mother has achieved her purpose. (Āk 1.2.239)
Beholding him, touching him, and likewise speaking with him is meritorious;
by means of direct perception and other valid cognitions, O Mercury, you are Sadāśiva.
O Lord of Alchemy, by your grace, metals such as iron attain the state of diamond and the nature of gold; likewise, O proud one, doe-eyed women [attain beauty]. (Āk 1.2.241)
Resplendent with breasts as high, full, and rounded as ruddy geese,
they were fickle and attached to the god of love, graced by lips like coral.
With curved and sharp nail-sprouts resembling the beaks of parrots, their arms were as beautiful as garlands of *śirīṣa* flowers, and their radiance was equal to wreaths of *campaka*. (Āk 1.2.243)
Adorned with a line of body hair arising from their deep navels, they possess grace in every limb; they become lovely, affectionate, and submissive. (Āk 1.2.244)
Just as fire would burn a heap of dry wood, O Lord of Mercury, so too [does it consume] birth, poverty, death, suffering, and great diseases. (Āk 1.2.245)
If one should hold you within the fire for the purpose of digestion (jāraṇa) for a certain number of days, one shall dwell happily in the world of Śiva for as many thousands of kalpas. (Āk 1.2.246)
O Lord of Sūtas, whatever wealth a person may expend on your behalf, you shall grant them that riches increased many millions of times over. (Āk 1.2.247)
This supreme, transcendent knowledge is difficult to find in all the worlds;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is meritorious, and increases one's sons and health. (Āk 1.2.248)
O Lord of Sūtas, those who revile you—cats, donkeys, crows, jackals, bulls, dogs, eunuchs, the blind, the deaf, and the dull-witted—[are like these]. (Āk 1.2.249)
Mutes, hunchbacks, the lame, those with missing limbs, the barren, and the diseased, as well as fishermen and evildoers, are born in many successive lives. (Āk 1.2.250)
Whoever should engage in mixing their goods or cooked food with those who revile you, or share a seat, a bed, a meal, or conversation with them; Āk_1.2.251.
"He shall become most wicked and must be abandoned, excluded from all religious duties.
Thus, O Bhairavī, has this hymn to Pāradendra been proclaimed by me. (Āk 1.2.252)
Whoever should recite or listen with devotion at the three junctions of the day for the sake of attaining mastery over the tastes (rasasiddhi),
[shall be freed] from the sins of killing a Brahmin and other major and minor transgressions.
O Goddess, by the three ritual acts, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt—whether in a terrible battle, a great forest, being lost in the directions, or in the perils of enemies. (Āk 1.2.254)
O Goddess, when crossing a river, or in danger from thieves, tigers, and the like, one should recite this hymn while meditating upon the illustrious Rasabhairava. (Āk 1.2.255)
Having thus praised the King of Alchemists (Sūtarāja), one should offer all ritual action [to him]:
"The mercury is the giver, the mercury is the enjoyer, the mercury is the agent, and the cause. (Āk 1.2.256)
The taste is both the priest and the oblation; the taste is eternally all-pervading.
With this very mantra, one should offer it to Rasendra. (Āk 1.2.257)
Then, having meditated as before, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the root mantra;
then, having formed the withdrawal mudrā (*saṃhāramudrā*), one should cause the Lord of Mercury (*raseśvara*) to flow into the river. (Āk 1.2.258)
The teacher of aesthetic relish (rasadeśika) should place the deity, together with his limbs, retinues, and powers, within the heart-lotus;
he should contemplate the true state [of identity], thinking, "I am Śiva. (Āk 1.2.259)
Having swept the place of worship and sprinkled it with water, the preceptor should then go to the sacrificial hall and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). (Āk 1.2.260)
In the hall, in the southeast quarter, there is a *yonikuṇḍa* with three girdles, strewn according to rule with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the east and the north. (Āk 1.2.261)

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the root mantra and having practiced breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should have the five elements consecrated by one's own wife or by a twice-born man. (Āk 1.2.262)
Having brought the fire and placed it in the sacrificial pit, one should then kindle it—[visualizing] the Fire with tawny matted locks, three eyes, and white garments. (Āk 1.2.263)
The god is seated upon a red lotus, adorned with garlands and ornaments;
he has seven hands, four horns, two heads, and three feet. (Āk 1.2.264)

Having meditated upon the bull, bound in three places and bearing weapons such as the spear and others, one should perform all the ritual services for him, beginning with the offering of water for honor (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya). Āk 1.2.265.
One should worship Jātavedas with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and excellent flowers; therein, having meditated upon him, one should invoke the deity Rasabhairava. (Āk 1.2.266)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the deity and offer oblations with the root mantra;
O Dear One, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over sesame seeds, clarified butter, and rice.
One should perform twenty-eight [recitations] or offer the first oblation from the root-mantra;
then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should maintain concentration in the heart.
Thus has the procedure for daily worship been declared to you, O Goddess worshipped by the gods. (Āk 1.2.268)
Āk, 1, 3 (The Sequence of the Initiation of Taste):
Now I shall proclaim the initiation that bestows all accomplishments.
And that [wisdom] is said to be fivefold, according to the distinctions of the pledges (samaya) and so forth. Āk 1.3.1.
The first initiation is called Samaya; the second is known as Sādhaka;
the third is termed Nirvāṇa; and the fourth is designated as Ācārya. (Āk 1.3.2)
The fifth, known as "the perfected" (siddha), is generally difficult for men to find.
A disciple endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, devoted, humble, and pure—Āk 1.3.3.
Having prostrated before the Guru with the eight limbs and praised him in many ways, he should then request the Guru, saying: "Please favor me with initiation. (Āk 1.3.4)
Having received initiation according to the prescribed rules, the disciple becomes a perceiver of all truths.
(Regarding the auspicious lunar days and other factors suitable for initiation: Aśvinī, Mūla, Revatī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, and Punarvasu; Āk 1.3.5.
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Anurādhā (Maitra), Hasta, the three Uttarās, Maghā, and Aśvinī are the most excellent lunar mansions for the rite of initiation (dīkṣā). (Āk 1.3.6)
The third, the fifth, the seventh, the fourteenth, the eighth, the full moon day, the tenth, and the thirteenth. (Āk 1.3.7)
These lunar days are the primary ones; among the weekdays, Monday, Thursday, Friday, or Sunday is most auspicious for the initiation into the *rasa* [alchemical] practice. (Āk 1.3.8)
(The Sequence of Initiation into the Samaya):
During the bright fortnight, under an auspicious conjunction, avoiding the *karaviṣṭi* yoga, and at the equinoxes or solstices when endowed with the strength of the moon and stars. (Āk 1.3.9)
On the day of an eclipse, on Śivarātri, on one's own birth-star, during an auspicious moment, under a benefic planet, and in a Siddhi-yoga, the supreme guru should bestow initiation. (Āk 1.3.10)
Then, having entered the Rasa-shala, which was radiant with all its equipment, strewn with flower garlands, and adorned with lofty arches and banners; (Ak 1.3.11)
Having performed the daily worship and the fire-ritual, one should follow the sequence of initiation;
on the right side of the deity, one should spread out a layer of rice grains. (Āk 1.3.12)
In the center of that, one should place a prastha of fine rice;
above that, one should set down a water-pot wrapped with a white thread. (Āk 1.3.13)
Wrapped in two garments, provided with the five jewels of a charioteer, purified by the five types of earth, sprouts, and bark, and filled with water. (Āk 1.3.14)

One should contemplate this jar, known as Śiva and possessing the form of Śiva, as being endowed with *dūrvā* grass, the finest fragrant sesame, gold, *darbha* grass, and unbroken rice grains. (Āk 1.3.15)
Having placed on its left side the jar known as the *vardhanī*, which is the form of Śakti and endowed with all the aforementioned substances. (Āk 1.3.16)
One should draw the Sarvatobhadra, the Śrīgaurītilaka, the Nandyāvarta, and the Svastika all around, adorned with five colors. (Āk 1.3.17)

Having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the supreme teacher, having taken his own seat, likewise performs three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma). (Āk 1.3.18)

For the sake of increasing this disciple’s lifespan, health, prosperity, and progeny, and for the sake of liberation and the eight supernatural powers, one should worship Śiva after forming the formal resolve (saṃkalpa). (Āk 1.3.19)
One should worship the Śiva-kumbha and the Vardhanī with perfumes, flowers, unhusked grains, incense, lamps, food offerings, and visual offerings, along with the various ritual services. Āk 1.3.20.
One should recite the root mantra of Rasāṅkuśī one thousand times, and offer oblations into a triangular sacrificial pit endowed with the proper characteristics ten times that amount. (Āk 1.3.21)
Then, one should offer fruit combined with the three sweets (trimadhu) and endowed with the finest perfumes;
and on the fourth day, one should worship the deities of the enclosures (āvṛti-devas) in sequence, using their respective names in the dative case.
Having uttered [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā, one should offer the oblation.
O Goddess, having first worshipped the triad of Śivas, one should then worship the triad of Siddhas. (Āk 1.3.23)
Then, O Goddess, the supreme guru, having worshipped the three gurus, the elders of the lineage, and the yoginī, and having received their permission, [proceeds]. (Āk 1.3.24)
I worship him who possesses power, the form of Śiva as Bliss (Ānanda-Śiva-mūrti), and likewise I worship the form of Śiva as Supreme Bliss (Parānanda-Śiva-mūrti). Āk 1.3.25.
In this way, one should worship the form of the three Siddhas together with the seed-syllable Śrī;
likewise, one should worship the form of the three Gurus joined with the Māra seed-syllable. (Āk 1.3.26)
Having grasped the three principles (tattvas), one should again perform the ritual placement (nyāsa);
having become the very body of Śiva oneself, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva. (Āk 1.3.27)
The seer of Śiva should look upon the disciple, who is joyful and empowered, and having stationed him at his own left side, he should place [the vessel] upon his head. (Āk 1.3.28)
Having consecrated the ashes with the root mantra and covered his eyes with a cloth, he should sprinkle water from the Śivavardhanī vessel upon his head. Āk 1.3.29.
One should worship Śiva along with his retinue three times in one’s own right hand;
this is to be known as the Śiva-hand, which severs the bonds of worldly existence. (Āk 1.3.30)
One should recite the root mantra of Aṅkuśī three times and impart the instruction of the mantra into the right ear of the disciple. (Āk 1.3.31)
First the mantra of Gaṇapati, and then the mantra of Kṣetrapāla;
the seer is Gaṇaka, and the meter is remembered as Nyṛc-gāyatrī. (Āk 1.3.32)

The deity is to be known as Gaṇapati, and the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed with the seed-syllable; the third letter of the first group of consonants, joined with the half-moon, is that which is called Gaṇa. (Āk 1.3.33)
One should utter the mantra ending in "namaḥ," joined with the name of the Lord in the dative case;
[the deity] bearing a noose, a goad, a sweetmeat, and his own tusk. (Āk 1.3.34)

Having meditated upon Gaṇanātha, who has the face of an elephant, the luster of coral, who wears the crescent moon as a crown, and who is pot-bellied, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. (Āk 1.3.35)
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the fire-oblation (homa) ten times [the number of recitations], offering oblations of molasses and sesame seeds;
one should also worship Kṣetrapāla, accompanied by Kaṣabindu and Caturthikā. (Āk 1.3.36)

Having recited the mantra ending with "namas," one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) using the seed-syllable; the meter is known as Paṅkti, and the sage is Bhṛgu, while the deity is Bhairava. (Āk 1.3.37)

Four-armed, adorned with a trident, a vessel, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; resembling a dark cloud, decorated with serpent ornaments and a garland of tinkling bells. (Āk 1.3.38)
Having meditated upon the three-eyed one with curved fangs, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
then perform libations and fire-offerings ten parts of that amount, using milk-rice soaked in the three sweets. (Āk 1.3.39)
Having instructed him thus, "Go forth," he should observe the conventional rules of conduct;
perform service to the deity and attend upon the guru. (Āk 1.3.40)
One should perform the recitation without weariness and listen to the scriptures with reverence;
remain constantly devoted to the path of conduct previously described. (Āk 1.3.41)
Bowing down with palms joined in reverence, O Lord, I shall do exactly as you have commanded. By your grace, O Śrīnātha, I am blessed and my purpose is fulfilled. (Āk 1.3.42)
Thus the disciple, strengthened by the conduct of the observances (samaya), should make this request;
having risen very early in the morning, he should also remember his gurus upon his head. (Āk 1.3.43)
Having performed the necessary duties and bathed, he should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at the bank of a river, a lake, a pond, or in pure water. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.3.44)
Having sipped water and performed the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the daily libation (*nityatarpaṇa*);
first [offering to] the triad of Śivas, Vighnanātha, Kṣetrādhipa, and Hari. (Āk 1.3.45)
One should [worship] Brahmā, the Sun and other planets, Durgā, the Mothers, and the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga; thereafter, one should recite the three Siddhas. (Āk 1.3.46)
Ādinātha, Mīnanātha, Gorakṣa, Koṅkaṇeśvara, Jālandhreśa, Kandhanīśa, Oḍḍīśa, and Ciñciṇīśvara. (Āk 1.3.47)
Then one should satisfy these nine known as the Nāthas, beginning with Cauraṅgin:
Cauraṅgin, Carpaṭin, Ghoḍācūlin, and then the two Rāmas. (Āk 1.3.48)
Bholagovinda-siddha, Vyāḍi, and likewise Nāgārjuna; Koraṇḍa, Śūrpakarṇa, Muktāyī, and likewise Revaṇa. (Āk 1.3.49)
One should satisfy the sixteen Siddhas: Siddha Kukkurapāda, Śūrpapāda, Kaṇerika, and the one named Kiṅkiṇika. Āk 1.3.50.
Then, having satiated the three elders—the mother, the father, and the guru—and having satiated the preceptor, the brother, the friend, and others born of one's lineage; Āk_1.3.51.
Having sipped water according to the prescribed rule, he should then perform the worship of the deities on the bank of a river, by a pond, in a cow-pen, or likewise in a temple. (Āk 1.3.52)
Having spread out sand in a clean place in a circular shape, one should invoke the Lord of Day, who is pale-red and possesses the form of Śiva. (Āk 1.3.53)
The supreme [deity] has two arms and possesses a pair of lotus-eyes;
he is radiant, adorned with red garlands, garments, and unguents, and seated upon a lotus throne. Āk 1.3.54.
Having meditated, one should worship Vighneśa and Bhairava with red flowers;
having meditated upon those two as previously described, one should worship them both with red flowers. (Āk 1.3.55)
One should perform prostrations with the eight limbs twelve times;
then, establishing [the deity] within one's own heart, one should go to one's own guru for the sake of service. (Āk 1.3.56)
Thus has been described the initiation of the *samaya*; now the initiation of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is being told.
[The initiation of the practitioner] concerns a true disciple who is devoted to the conduct of the *samaya* and whose mind is matured. (Sādhakadīkṣā) Āk 1.3.57.
On an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, he should initiate [the disciple] by means of the initiation known as that of the practitioner (sādhaka).
The Guru should perform the occasional worship and cause the disciple to be invoked. (Āk 1.3.58)
One should oneself, being of the nature of Śiva, visualize the disciple as being within the womb of Gaurī;
having spread sacred ash upon the ground, one should draw three corners there. (Āk 1.3.59)
Having seated the disciple there and bound his eyes, [the teacher performs] the *garbhādhāna*, the *puṃsavana*, and then the *sīmantonnayana*. (Āk 1.3.60)
One should perform the birth-rite (jātakarma) as part of the initiation (dīkṣā), and assign a name;
during the rite of the vow (vrata), one should sprinkle [the child] with ashes while reciting the root mantra. Āk 1.3.61.
Having meditated upon the son of Gaurī, one should perform his initiation;
having beheld him with the vision of Śiva, one should place the ashes of Śiva upon his head. (Āk 1.3.62)
Having placed the root mantra [there], one should worship it ten times;
and into his right ear, one should impart the ten-syllable mantra. (Āk 1.3.63)
(The Rasagāyatrī:

[One should recite] the mantra of Rasendrabhairava, the Gāyatrī known as "Rasa," followed by the seed-syllable of the fire-god with the nasal drop (bindu), and then the word for "Rasendra. (Āk 1.3.64)

One should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) using the word "Bhairava" in the dative case, followed by the weapon-mantra (astramantra) in ten parts, and the fire-seed syllable (vahnibīja) joined with the long vowels. Āk 1.3.65.
The seer is named Aghora, the meter is Virāṭ, and the deity is Maheśvara;
one should perform a preliminary service consisting of a hundred thousand recitations, with the fire-oblation and libation being one-tenth of that amount. (Āk 1.3.66)
With a steady mind, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) using sesame seeds, clarified butter, and rice;
one should recite the previously mentioned *rasagāyatrī* one hundred thousand times and perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (Āk 1.3.67)
O Dear One, having offered one-tenth of the oblations with clarified butter, sesame seeds, and rice, he should give the rosary, the mercury-linga, and the Rasāgama to the disciple. (Āk 1.3.68)
Having become possessed of the conduct previously described, one should worship the mercury-liṅga;
one should achieve mastery over the meaning of one's own scriptures and perform the purification of the lord of mercury (sūtendra). Āk 1.3.69.
"One should command the disciple who is constantly devoted to service of the guru.
[The disciple replies: "With palms joined in reverence and bowed down, I shall carry out your command. (Āk 1.3.70)
Thus has been described the initiation for practitioners known as Nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, which is highly praised.
Having first performed the daily rites (*nityakriyā*) and the occasional worship (*naimittikārcana*), [the teacher proceeds]. (Nirvāṇa-dīkṣā) Āk 1.3.71.

As before, one should place the *śivakumbha* and other vessels, and the *vardhanī*, in their proper order; having spread ashes to one's left, one should draw a hexagon within an earthly enclosure (*bhūgṛha*). (Āk 1.3.72)
Having settled the disciple [in his seat], the Guru should sprinkle him with the water contained in the pitcher;
he should then cast upon his head ashes consecrated with the root mantra. (Āk 1.3.73)
One should offer fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, and tie a bracelet on the right hand, measuring from the big toe of the foot up to the *brahmarandhra*. (ĀK 1.3.74)
The best of gurus, having consecrated the thread with its root mantra and rendered it fragrant, places that "Hand of Śiva" upon the disciple's head. (Āk 1.3.75)
Having instructed the supreme twelve-syllable mantra Rasāṅkuśā, the preceptor should bestow upon the disciple that which has Rasabhairava as its presiding deity. (Āk 1.3.76)
O Dear One, one should perform the assignment (nyāsa) of the seers, meters, and deities as previously stated;
then one should likewise perform the libation (tarpaṇa), the fire-oblation (homa), and the meditation (dhyāna) as before. (Āk 1.3.77)
Having risen and bowed many times to the Guru, one should recite hymns of praise;
the Guru, for his part, should indeed give the disciple a tiger-skin seat upon which [he may sit]. (Āk 1.3.78)
One should give a bellows filled with cloth—a bellows for medicinal herbs—after having taught the science of mercury; "O disciple, become a physician! (Āk 1.3.79).
