"You have become Rudra in form; be for the welfare of all beings.
Thus the Guru should instruct the disciple, and then the disciple, with a joyful mind, [should respond]. (Āk 1.3.80)
"I have accomplished my task, I am purified, and I have crossed the ocean of saṃsāra"—thus the disciple should inform the guru after praising him in many ways. (Āk 1.3.81)
This has been declared as the initiation of nirvāṇa; now follows the consecration of the teacher (*ācāryābhiṣecana*).
[This is] the initiation of the teacher for this high-souled disciple who has been initiated into nirvāṇa. (Ācāryadīkṣā) Āk 1.3.82.
The most excellent of gurus should perform the initiation of the teacher (ācāryadīkṣā) according to the rule;
he should arrange everything just as in the case of the initiation for liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā). Āk 1.3.83.
In particular, one should place a water-pot before Śiva and Vardhanī, provided with silver, perfumes, metals, gems, and collections of divine medicinal herbs. (Āk 1.3.84)
Furthermore, one should place everything else into this [vessel] like the auspicious jar (śivakumbha).
Having touched the Guru-jar, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times. (Āk 1.3.85)
Know this large jar to be the Guru; one should worship it with the Guru-mantra and with the sixteen services, beginning with invocation, the seat, and the water-offering (arghya). (Āk 1.3.86)
There, one should worship the lineage beginning with Śiva together with the Guru, as before, while the disciple is seated with a one-pointed mind. (Āk 1.3.87)
As before, one should sprinkle water upon the Śiva-vardhanī;
and as before, [one should perform the rite] with the Śiva-hasta, which conveys the instruction of the root mantra. (Āk 1.3.88)
Having placed the lineage of gurus as well as the Guru upon his head,
he should worship them with perfumes, garlands, and lamps, beginning with the ritual of invocation.
One should worship in due order with food offerings endowed with the finest fragrances;
the Guru should perform the sprinkling with water from the jar using the five types of sprouts. (Āk 1.3.90)
One should [worship] one hundred times with the root mantra, twenty-one times with the lineage of Śiva, and likewise with the lineage of the Siddhas and the lineage of the Gurus. (Āk 1.3.91)
To a disciple who is devoted to the guru, endowed with power, and wise,
[one should give] necklaces, armlets, bracelets, rings, and crowns.
Vehicles, seats, umbrellas, chowries, and fans; a pair of jeweled earrings; and an inexhaustible vessel filled with abundant prosperity. Āk 1.3.93.
A helmet with a turban, an excellent silk tunic, a meditation belt, a yoga staff, and likewise the uḍyāṇabandha; Āk 1.3.94.
"You should likewise grant him that command: 'Now you are the preceptor;
today you are the master; you are blessed; become the guide for all. (Āk 1.3.95)
"Be an expounder of the divine Rasāgamas, a knower of their true principles"—thus should the Guru instruct the disciple who is prostrate and devoted to the Guru. (Āk 1.3.96)

Thus, this initiation by the Teacher is now described as the Siddha-initiation (*siddhadīkṣā*). [The Siddha-initiation lasts] for nine nights, or seven nights, or five nights, or three nights. (Siddha-initiation) Āk 1.3.97.
The twenty-one heroes (vīra) endowed with power (śakti) should be worshipped daily; likewise, an equal number of yogins, youths, maidens, and women should be worshipped. Āk 1.3.98.

Having gratified [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, blossoms, and the offering of excellent fruits and scents, one should also present garments, ornaments, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). Āk 1.3.99.
Then, having touched with both hands the head of the disciple—who is seated on his seat, endowed with devotion, and pure—at his right ear, [the teacher] [imparts] the mantra. (Āk 1.3.100)
One should initiate the fire together with its seed-syllable and the moon together with the visarga;
[one should contemplate] the letter *ra*, resembling a flame of fire, arisen from the *mūlādhāra*. (Āk 1.3.101)

Having crossed the lotus of the six supports, one should contemplate the letter *sa*, which has become liquefied at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and takes the form of the moon. (Āk 1.3.102)
The perfected one should contemplate the mantra as flooding all his limbs—the cause of dissolution and maintenance arising from inhalation and exhalation. (Āk 1.3.103)
Having thus constantly understood with the mind that [the mantra] is always the essence of all mantras, consists of all deities, is meritorious, and bestows all accomplishments. (Āk 1.3.104)

Know this mantra of the essence (rasa-mantra) to be the giver of liberation while living, pure, supreme, consisting of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, and composed of fire and moon; worship it. Āk 1.3.105.
It consists of twenty-one thousand six hundred [verses] and has been set in motion day and night; fix your mind upon it. (Āk 1.3.106)
The seer of this mantra is Jīva, and its metre is said to be proclaimed as Ityuktā;
Raṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), while Saṃ is proclaimed as the power (śakti). Āk 1.3.107.

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs joined with the long letter *ra* (repha), and then, O Goddess, one should meditate [on the deity] in the lotus of the heart, resembling ten million suns and moons. (Āk 1.3.108)
Having meditated upon that essence which resembles pure crystal, which is the further shore of saṃsāra, and which is thus of an undivided form, one should attain identity with it. (Āk 1.3.109)
(The Hymn to the Partless Essence) You are the essence, you are Śiva, you indeed are Śakti, and you are Bhairaveśvara;
you are Brahmā, you are Rudra, you are the Sun, and you are the Moon of cool rays. Āk 1.3.110.
You are the earth, you are the water, and you are the fire; you are the wind, you are the ether, and you are the supreme space. You are the individual soul (jīva), and you are the ultimate goal.
You are the perfected one, you are the awakened one, you are the fragrant one, and you are the god of love;
you are the guardian of the world, you are Tārā, you are Mātṛkā, and you are Gajānana.
You are Skanda, you are the Guru, and you are the pure progenitor of all beings;
you are the sacrificer, you are Hari, you are the three sacred fires, and you are the officiating priests.
By worshipping you, all the deities are worshipped;
when you are satisfied, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are fully satisfied. (Āk 1.3.114)
By drinking the water from your feet, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords;
Śiva beholds with favor him who gazes upon you with true devotion. (Āk 1.3.115)
Whoever should recite your name, for that person there shall be the fruit of all mantras;
wherever you are present even for a single moment, that place is called a field of merit. (Āk 1.3.116)
O Lord of Siddhas, whoever you behold is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Īśvara;
for wherever you eat a morsel of food, there indeed lies the three worlds.
O Protector, that by which you are sustained and by whom this world is preserved for even a moment—He alone must certainly be the Supreme Self, eternally conscious and blissful. (Āk 1.3.118)
Thus, for you, the perfected yogi whose mind is resolved,
the traditional duties of caste and stage of life arise from the discernment between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Sin and merit, pleasure and pain, cold and heat, the pleasant and the unpleasant, bathing and not bathing, loss and gain, purity and impurity, fear and fearlessness. (Āk 1.3.120)
There is nothing here to be grasped or not grasped, nor hunger or thirst;
one may eat and move about according to one's own desire, happy and with a joyful mind. (Āk 1.3.121)
Free from the sense of "mine" regarding all undertakings, his wife, and his kinsmen, he becomes initiated after thus accepting the teacher's instruction. (Āk 1.3.122)
From this day forward, you are to be revered; do not offer salutations to anyone.
You are my equal, you are a perfected one, and you are now liberated while living.
Having spoken thus, the most excellent of teachers embraced Siddha for a moment and said: "This is declared to be the initiation of Siddha, which bestows union with Śiva. (Āk 1.3.124)
"Difficult to find in all tantras, it has been revealed out of affection for you;
O Goddess, it should be understood as such—difficult to find even within the [esoteric] observances. (Āk 1.3.125)
Āk, 1, 4 (The Refinements of Taste): Śrī Bhairavī.
"O Lord, please explain to me correctly the processing of mercury.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"O Supreme Goddess, there are eighteen processes for mercury. (Āk 1.4.1)
Having worshipped those perfected ones (siddhas) and practitioners (sādhakas) according to the rule, I shall explain them to you;
first is the rite of sweating (svedana), and second, O Dear One, is the rite of rubbing (mardana). Āk 1.4.2.
O Śivā, fainting is the third stage, falling is the fourth;
the fifth is known as obstruction, the sixth as restraint, and the seventh as regulation. Āk 1.4.3.
The eighth, O Goddess, is illumination (dīpana); the ninth is after-treatment with oil enema (anuvāsana);
the tenth is movement (cāraṇa), O Goddess; and digestion (jāraṇa) is the eleventh (the number of Rudras). Āk 1.4.4.
The twelfth is *garbhadruti*, the thirteenth is *bāhyadruti*;
the fourteenth is called *rāga*, and the fifteenth is *sāraṇā*. (Āk 1.4.5)
The sixteenth is known as *anusāraṇā*, and the seventeenth as *pratisāraṇā*;
the eighteenth is *vedhana*, [applied] to the body and to metals. (Āk 1.4.6)
(The Method of Refining the Mercury):
Now, O Pārvatī, I shall describe the refinements of the king of mercury.
One should draw a hexagonal mandala on the southern side of the linga. (Āk 1.4.7)
Outside of that, one should place an eight-petaled lotus and a square, adorned with doors in the cardinal directions; O Śivā, one should install [the deity] within its pericarp.
A mortar made either of copper or of magnetite, marked with a line of gold;
within it, one should place exactly one hundred palas of the king of essences (mercury). Āk 1.4.9.
Having cast in half of that, or half of that again, the practitioner of mercury should worship with devotion; thereafter, he should perform the purification (*saṃskāra*). (Āk 1.4.10)
(Sudation;
the method of fermenting grain-vinegar):
[It is prepared] with barley, wheat, rice, black gram, green gram, chickpeas, and so forth.
And with various kinds of grain, such as *śyāmāka* and *kodrava*, which have been dehusked.
O beloved, one should place grain in a clay jar with four times as much water;
one should protect it with effort until it reaches the state of acidity. (Āk 1.4.12)
In the midst of that, [one should place] *haṃsapādī*, *mīnākṣī*, two kinds of *punarnavā*, *citraka*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, and *śatāvarī*. (Āk 1.4.13)
Having cut sarpākṣī, girikarṇī, muṇḍī, sahadevikā, and triphalā into pieces, one should throw all of these [into the vessel]. (Āk 1.4.14)
And from one-fourth part of grain, this excellent grain-acid (dhānyāmla) is produced; it is especially recommended for tasks such as the sweating (svedana) of mercury. Āk 1.4.15.
One should place the king of fluids (rasarāja), along with the powder of soot, *citraka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and jaggery, into a heated mortar made of *kānta* iron. (Āk 1.4.16)
Burnt horn, brick, maiden, salt, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *māgadhī*, mustard seed, as well as *vandhyā* and *karkoṭakī*. (Āk 1.4.17)
Having added these fractional parts of the *sūta* (mercury) to that [mixture], one should rub it;
then, having repeatedly added *dhānyāmla* (sour gruel), one should proceed in this manner for three days. (Āk 1.4.18)
O beloved, one should thoroughly wash the juice with warm *aragvadha* (soṣṇāranāla);
[then add] salt, *rāji*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), radish, and excellent *citraka*. (Āk 1.4.19)
Punarnavā, meṣaśṛṅgī, meghanāda, durālabhā, fresh ginger, haridrā, nāgabalā, and navasāra; (Āk 1.4.20).
Having ground [the ingredients] finely with sour grain-liquor (dhānyāmlaka) in equal proportions, one should apply it to a cloth;
once it has reached the thickness of a finger's breadth, one should pour the previously mentioned liquid into it. (Āk 1.4.21)

Having bound that [substance] and placed it in a copper vessel, one should then put it into a jar filled with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and subject it to heating day and night using the apparatus known as the *dolāyantra*. Āk 1.4.22.
Having extracted it, one should wash the king of elixirs again with warm *āranāla* in a shallow bowl; in this manner, one should perform this twenty-one times. (Āk 1.4.23)
O Dear One, one should then grind the perspired king of elixirs.
(Grinding) Now, therefore, I shall describe the rite of grinding; listen, O Bhairavī! Āk 1.4.24.
The substances such as the powder and so forth are as before; take *viśālā*, *rājavṛkṣaka*, *aṅkola*, black *dhuttūra*, and the three pungents (*trikaṭu*) in equal parts. (Āk 1.4.25)

One should add mercury, equal in weight to one-sixteenth part of the entire [total], into a heated mortar and grind it with the previously mentioned grain-ferment (dhānyāmla) for another day and night. Āk 1.4.26.
Then, one should wash it in an earthen vessel with warm *āranālaka*;
in this manner, the rubbing and washing should continue for twenty-one days. (Āk 1.4.27)
Having thus ground the mercury, one should then cause it to coagulate;
or else, the mercury that has been processed with mica or processed with the seed-mantra is likewise ground. (Āk 1.4.28)
The stainless [soul] takes up colors through substances such as powders and the like;
[this is] *mūrchā*.
Now I shall explain *mūrchā*; listen with attentiveness. (Āk 1.4.29)
Black mustard, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *citraka*, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), *kṣīrakanda*, *sūraṇa*, *sarpākṣī*, and *kākamācikā*. (Āk 1.4.30)
Blue vacā, balā, kanyā, kṛṣṇonmatta, as well as akulī, white aparājitā, aṅkola, gojihvā, and likewise garuḍī. (Āk 1.4.31)
Mercury should be rubbed with the juices of these [plants], either individually or all together, along with the milk of *Ravikṣīrī* for a period of days. (Āk 1.4.32)
One should grind it in a heated mortar and place that mercury in a crucible; having sealed it, O beloved, one should cook it again in the *bhūdhara* apparatus. (Āk 1.4.33)

One should perform grinding with juices derived from medicinal herbs such as *rājikā* for twenty-one days and then carry out heating in an earthen crucible; thus the mercury becomes fully activated. (Āk 1.4.34)
O Goddess, one should perform the rite for its arousal;
[this is] the rite of arousing.
Thus, one should wash the swooned mercury with sour gruel. (Āk 1.4.35)
O beloved, one may also raise the mercury with warm water;
or, through the application of a *pātanāyantra* (sublimation apparatus), the raising of the mercury occurs. (Āk 1.4.36)
(Regarding *pātana*):
O Pārvatī, the precipitation (*pātana*) of the king of mercury is said to be threefold;
it is called upward precipitation (*ūrdhvapāta*), downward precipitation (*adhaḥpāta*), and lateral precipitation (*tiryakpātana*). (Āk 1.4.37)
(The Procedure for Upward Sublimation) I shall describe the sublimation of mercury: *pāṭhā*, *brāhmī*, *citraka*, *śāṅgerī*, *kākamācī*, *maṇḍūkī*, and *girikarṇikā*. (Āk 1.4.38)
Kumārī, jayā, bhṛṅgī, gojihvā, śaṅkhapuṣpikā, bhūpāṭalī, nirguṇḍī, kākajaṅghā, and śatāvarī. (Āk 1.4.39)
Ginger, *devadālī*, *tilaparṇī*, *nīlikā*, *āragvadha*, milky tuber, *aṅkola*, and *devadāru*. (Āk 1.4.40)

One should grind these juices, either all together or individually, for one day in a heated mortar (taptakhalva); that copper, with mercury as the fourth part [of the total], [is thus processed]. (ĀK 1.4.41)
Having ground that [mercury], one should cause it to fall into an upward-dropping apparatus for a day;
then, taking that pure mercury which has adhered to the upper part, one should grind it again. (ĀK 1.4.42)
Combined with copper as before, one should cause it to fall [into the crucible] by means of the juices of the previously mentioned herbs;
in this manner, one should rub it repeatedly seven times. (Āk 1.4.43)
One should cause the mercury, purified by upward sublimation, to fall downward.
(The procedure for downward sublimation:
Now I shall describe downward sublimation; [one should take] the three pungents, salt, and varā. (Āk 1.4.44)
One should add *citraka*, black mustard, and drumstick—all equal in quantity to mercury—and grind them with fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmlaka*) in a heated mortar. (Āk 1.4.45)
One should smear the upper vessel with that paste and seal it properly;
then, one should apply a light *puṭa* (firing) to the back of the upper vessel. (Āk 1.4.46)

Thus one should perform downward precipitation (*adhahpātana*) seven times again and again; once the substance has been purified by downward precipitation, one should practice transverse precipitation (*tiryakpātana*). (ĀK 1.4.47)

(The Procedure for Horizontal Distillation) I shall describe horizontal distillation: take equal parts of mercury and paddy-rice mica (*dhānyābhraka*), grind them with fermented rice water (*dhānyāmla*) for one *yāma*, and place them in a horizontal distillation apparatus (*tiryakpātanayantra*). (ĀK 1.4.48)
One should cook it thus with fierce fire seven times again and again; when it has been processed in this way three times, one should then arrest the mercury. (Āk 1.4.49)
Or mica, or sulphur, or honey-gold, or even vimalā;
or gold, or silver, or kānta iron, or indeed tīkṣṇa iron. Āk_1,4.50.
Each [substance] should be purified and given in a quantity equal to one-quarter part of the copper;
one should then perform mardana and pātana in succession using the juices of pāṭhā and other herbs. Āk 1.4.51.
Whatever substance the mercury (sūta) is endowed with, it bestows the qualities of that very substance.
During the process of precipitation (pātana), mercury abandons lead and tin through the addition of copper.

Alternatively, mercury becomes purified when precipitated in the *dīpikā* apparatus; (this is *nirodhana*) the mercury becomes thoroughly processed by the five operations beginning with *sveda*. (ĀK 1.4.53)
For the purpose of nourishing the *sūta*, one should perform the rite of "obstruction" (*nirodhana*).
Now, regarding the rite called obstruction, one should grind salt with water. (Āk 1.4.54)
Having poured the liquid into the middle of the vessel, one should place salt on top of it; then, having added a little water, one should seal it with a shallow bowl. (Āk 1.4.55)
One should properly apply a plaster to the joints and thereafter roast it gently;
in this manner, O dear one, one should perform the rite of confinement seven times. (Āk 1.4.56)
By this, the mercury (sūta) becomes nourished and freed from its state of impotence;
perfected through the practice of restraint, it becomes potent and well-controlled. (ĀK 1.4.57)
(Niyāmana) Furthermore, O fair-faced one, I shall describe the rite of *niyāmana*:
barley, *ciñcā*, milk-lily (*kṣīrakanda*), *sarpākṣī*, salt, and *bhṛṅgarāja*. (Āk 1.4.58)

Having ground karkoṭakī, nimba, and vanyā together with all [the other ingredients] in fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), and having stirred it with sour gruel (āranāla), one should foment it with those liquids for a day. (Āk 1.4.59)
One should cause that [substance] to burn in the restraining machine for seven days.
(Dīpana) Now, therefore, O Pārvatī, I shall describe to you the ritual of dīpana. Āk 1.4.60.
Svarṇapuṣpī, marīca, the three alkalis (trikṣāra), pañcapuṣpikā, bhūkhaga, the five salts (pañcalavaṇa), rājikā, and the roots of śigru and mūlaka. (Āk 1.4.61)
Kāsīsa, vijayā, kanyā, pātālagaruḍī, kaṇā, kṣīrakanda, karkoṭī, girikarṇī, jayā, and honey. (Āk 1.4.62)
One should make a paste of *citraka*, *kākajaṅghā*, and all the sour substances; with that one should rub the mercury, and also grind it with those juices. (Āk 1.4.63)

One should cook it in a swinging vessel (ḍolāyantra) for one day, and likewise seven times; thus one should perform the grinding and the heating, for the mercury, when ignited, seeks to consume its food. (Āk 1.4.64)
In this manner, one should fumigate that purified, ignited mercury.
(Anuvasana):
Now follows the procedure for the anuvasana treatment; the mercury, having been ignited in an earthen vessel—Āk 1.4.65.
Having cast it [into the vessel], one should subject it to a strong heat with the juice of ripe *jambīra* fruits;
one should do this for seven days, and thereafter one should perform the process of sublimation (*cāraṇa*). (Āk 1.4.66)
O Dear One, mercury, when purified by the nine procedures beginning with sweating, becomes the destroyer of all diseases and is freed from the seven impurities (*kañcuka*). Āk 1.4.67.
Śrī Bhairavī said:
"O Śaṅkara, you have taught the practices beginning with *svedana* (perspiration);
speak [further], for by your grace I shall listen without doubt to the practices beginning with *cāraṇa*. (Āk 1.4.68)
Śrī Bhairava said:
Well asked, O illustrious lady! Listen now to that [teaching] concerning the movement [of the breath] and so forth.
(The Procedure for Movement)
Now, O Supreme Goddess, I shall describe the practice of moving through the clouds. Āk_1,4.69.

Whether facing forward or turned away, whether in the rasa or at the opening of the latent impression (vāsanā), one should gradually cause the sky to move through the sequence of swallowing the embryo and the flour-paste. Āk 1.4.70.
(The Practice with the Face-to-Face) Here, O Goddess, the practice with the face-to-face (*samukha-cāraṇa*) is first clearly explained:
"With the face-to-face, one swallows the morsel; without the face-to-face, one is incapable of swallowing. (Āk 1.4.71)
Therefore, one should perform the "opening of the mouth" (*mukhīkaraṇa*) of the lord of mercury (*rasendra*).
(The first method of opening the mouth:
In the middle portion of a brick, [one should make] a deep, circular, and level [depression]. (Āk 1.4.72)
Having made a pit, one should place the perfumed mercury therein;
one should then confine it with a clean cloth using a tenth part of the liquid. (Āk 1.4.73)
Having placed the fragrance above that, one should seal it with a shallow bowl;
on top of that, one should apply a small lid, repeating this process again and again until the fragrance has been fully absorbed. (Āk 1.4.74)
Having repeatedly cast it [into the crucible], one should cause it to circulate a hundredfold and then let it fall;
one should filter that Lord of Essences through a thick cloth four times its size. (Āk 1.4.75)
Having placed it in a bamboo tube and closed its opening, one should cook it in a vessel filled with cow urine for twenty-one days;
then, one should place it again in a heated mortar.

It should be ground for three days with *jambīra*, *mātuluṅga*, and *amlavetasa* along with *bhūkhaga*, and for another three days with *bhūnāga*; thereafter, it should be placed inside the belly of a brick.
One should take one niṣka each of powdered paddy-rice, mica, and sulfur;
each being ten niṣkas, they should be ground with jambīra juice for one watch (yāma). Āk 1.4.78.
With this, one should smear two pits between the bricks;
having then cast twenty niṣkas into each pit, [one should place them] above that. (Āk 1.4.79)
One should apply another brick, firmly plastering the joint with saline clay, and then bake it in the flame of a lamp for a period of seven days. (Āk 1.4.80)
Having removed that brick while it is still cool to the touch, one should extract the juice; having rendered it free of dross once more, one should repeat this process three times. (ĀK 1.4.81)

When this is done, the mercury (rasendra) attains the state known as "divine" (sukha). (This is the second method of making [the mercury] "mouthed. Furthermore, I shall describe another supreme method of making it mouthed. (Āk 1.4.82)
One should grind the best mercury (rasendra) for three days with an equal amount of jīva, bhū, and nāga;
then, one should place it inside a crucible smeared with bhūlatā. (Āk 1.4.83)
Above that, one should apply a paste of *bhūlatā*, seal it, and dry it;
then, having smeared it with fresh cow dung, one should place it so that it is submerged up to the foot. (Āk 1.4.84)
And in that pit, a sealed crucible (puṭa) should be placed over a fire of husks and dried cow-dung;
at the end of the day, having extracted it, one should grind and cook it as before. (Āk 1.4.85)
One should perform this again thirty times; thus the mercury, with its mouth as fire, becomes a secret elixir that swallows [all impurities] and bestows all accomplishments. (Āk 1.4.86)

(The third method of making [the mercury] face-upward: Furthermore, I shall describe another supreme method of making it face-upward: one should cook the mercury in a vessel filled with cow’s urine using a *ḍolāyantra* (swinging apparatus). (Āk 1.4.87)
O fair-faced one, when the mouth of the crucible has been properly heated twenty-one times within a bamboo tube, it becomes fit for the transmutation of mercury. (Ākāśabhairava-tantra 1.4.88)
(The fourth method of making manifest:
Between two bricks, there should be a pit four finger-breadths deep; ten *niṣkas* of pure fragrance and ten *niṣkas* of *dhānyābhra* [should be placed therein]. (Āk 1.4.89)
Having ground it for one *yāma* with *jambīra* juice, one should smear two pits with that paste in equal portions and then cast [the substance] into the pits. (Āk 1.4.90)
That perfumed mercury, weighing twenty niṣkas or more, should be placed upon another brick, made firm with smooth clay and salt. (Āk 1.4.91)
Then, O Dear One, one should smear it and ignite a lamp-fire beneath;
after it has been sewn together for seven nights, one should extract it once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body. (Āk 1.4.92)
Having discarded that dross, one should treat the mercury as before for three times;
by doing so, the mouth of the mercury indeed becomes beautiful. (ĀK 1.4.93)
(The method of mouth-free circulation): By the power of divine herbs, the mercury circulates without a mouth;
or else, through contact with *vajra* and *vaikrānta*, it causes the mica and other minerals to circulate. (Āk 1.4.94)
Sixty-four *niṣkas* of mercury, four *niṣkas* of *vaikrānta* ash, and one *niṣka* of *vajra* ash [should be processed] with the juices of divine herbs. (Āk 1.4.95)
Having rubbed everything for seven days, that mercury should process [substances] such as mica; [this is] the "processing by means of the mouth of the vessel" (*vāsanāmukhacāraṇa*).
One should digest sulfur in mercury using the "swing" (*dolā*) method previously described. (Āk 1.4.96)
In the yantra, the mercury becomes sixteenfold through the process of perfuming (*vāsanā*). (This is the consecration of mica, the purification of mica fit for ingestion.
I shall now describe to you the consecration of the mica that is ready for ingestion. (Āk 1.4.97)
(First Method) One should grind dead mercury with blood, alkalis, water drops, the three types of *tumburu*, and the group of acidic substances (*amlavargaka*). (Āk 1.4.98)
The alchemist should practice that for seven days, either facing the subject or with his face turned away.
(This is the second method.
Dead mica, plantain, radish, and śatāvarī—Āk 1.4.99.
O Dear One, one should grind punarnavā, meghanāda, yavaciñcā, śigruka, and sūraṇa with their own juices and then saturate [the powder] with them. Āk 1.4.100.
The alchemist should practice that for seven days, either facing [the fire] or with his face turned away.
(Third Method) Into a copper vessel, he should place salt, Sarjika, Ṭaṅkaṇa, Bhūkhaga, and... Āk_1,4.101.
Having cast it into the stalk of Arana for three days so that it becomes fermented, one should drive away the serpent within it and crush it into a hundred pieces, O Dear One. (Āk 1.4.102)

In the process of silver-making, one should saturate tin with its own juices for seven days; then mercury, whether "facing" (samukha) or "faceless" (nirmukha), should be processed with it. Ākāśa 1.4.103.

(Fourth method: One should grind [the substance] with *dhānyābhra* and cow’s milk for one day; then, having sealed it in a crucible (*saṃpuṭa*), one should cook it again in a *kapotapuṭa*. (Āk 1.4.104)
One should thus roast it four times and likewise grind it again;
it should be ground three times with the juice of plantain and three times with the juice of radish. (Āk 1.4.105)
Kākamācī, meghanāda, matsyākṣī, punarnavā, apāmārga, citraka, vidārī, bhṛṅgarāja, and muni. (Āk 1.4.106)
One should cook it thus four times and likewise grind it again;
having ground it with each of these individually, one should perform the *puṭapāka* (herb-pottery baking) separately for each.
One should then process that mica with *musalī*, *yavaciñcikā*, *taṇḍulī*, *kadalī*, *śigru*, *varī*, *arka*, and *punarnavā*. (Āk 1.4.108)
Each of those fluids should be processed separately for one day each;
then that abhraka, O worshiper of the gods, truly moves within the lord mercury. Āk 1.4.109.
(Fifth method: One should grind *dhānyābhra* with the milk of a goat for the duration of one *yāma*.
Having sealed that *abhra* in a crucible, one should roast it in a fire-pit known as the *kapota*-puṭa. (Āk 1.4.110)
In this manner, there should be fourteen days; thereafter come the rambhā, arka, pīluka, nāgavallī, musalī, kuberākṣī, and śigruka. (Āk 1.4.111)
O beloved, having taken the single juice of these—tumbī, tumburu, aṅkola, balā, and apāmārga—along with vyōṣa and kāñjika; Āk 1.4.112.
Having placed it inside a vessel, one should cook it for three days in a *ḍolāyantra* (swing-furnace);
then, having extracted the previously mentioned *abhra* from that, one should further process it. (Āk 1.4.113)
Equal parts of ṭaṅkaṇa, tuvarī, and sindhukāsīsa, along with a tenth part of abhraka—all of this should be thoroughly ground together. (Āk 1.4.114)
The mercury may process that mica either with its face turned toward it (*samukha*) or away from it (*nirmukha*).
(Sixth method:
One should repeatedly heat lead that has been melted a hundred times in the juice of *muṇḍī*. (Āk 1.4.115)
One should grind paddy-iron (dhānyābhra) with that liquid, place it in a crucible, seal it, and cook it in a crucible known as the "pigeon" (kapota); this process should be repeated seven times.
In this manner, [one should] grind it seven times with the juices of ginger and seven times with the juices of *citraka*;
having added an equal amount of sulfur, one should rub and then saturate it in sequence. (Āk 1.4.117)
It should be processed for one day with the juices of muṇḍī as previously mentioned, with the juice of bījapūra, and with breast milk; then that mercury shall act upon the mica.
In this way, all seeds, the essence (sattva) of mica, all metals such as gold, and various other essences [are to be understood]. (Āk 1.4.119)

Whatever pairs of substances, all kinds of gems, or anything else worthy of being processed may exist, each of those should be ground like clouds; the mercury then courses through them all. (ĀK 1.4.120)

(Seventh method: Having ground *dhānyābhraka* with the juices of *tilaparṇī*, one should roast it three times; then, by means of rubbing, one should saturate the mercury with it seven times. (ĀK 1.4.121)
It suddenly attains the state of flour and in an instant moves through the sky. (The eighth method:
The three alkalis, the five salts, potassium carbonate, green vitriol, and borax. Āk_1,4.122.
Earth-born mercury, gold, vitriol, saurāṣṭrī, vatsanābha, tuvarī, and vetasāmla—all these taken in equal parts. (Āk 1.4.123)
One should grind *dhānyābhra* in equal parts with fermented rice water (*dhānyāmla*) for one day, along with the milky sap of *arka*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *meghanāda*, and *punarnavā*. (Āk 1.4.124)
Radish, *citraka*, plantain, *kākamācī*, *śatāvarī*, *apāmārga*, *tālamūlī*, *vidārī*, *taṇḍulī*, and *muni*. (Āk 1.4.125)
Mīnākṣī, śigru, bṛhatī, kumārī, yavaciñcikā, balā, tumbī, kuberākṣī, vyoṣa, tumburu, and pīlunī. (Āk 1.4.126)
Aṅkola and phaṇivallī—O Goddess, having ground all these in equal parts, one should form a paste with four times as much fermented rice-water (dhānyāmla). Āk_1,4.127.
One should repeatedly cast the liquid into that [vessel] a hundred times;
then, one should thoroughly grind the previously mentioned abhra with the liquid paste for one watch (yāma). Āk 1.4.128.
One should cook it in a crucible called *kapota* in this manner twenty times, adding an equal amount of sulfur along with the juices of the aforementioned medicinal herbs. (Āk 1.4.129)
It should be impregnated for three days with juices derived from *bījapūra* fruits mixed with *sastanya* [milk products];
this mineral (abhraka) is supremely beneficial for the digestion of mercury (*sūta*). (Āk 1.4.130)
Coupled substances, celestial essences, various seeds, all metals such as gold, and diverse kinds of jewels. (Āk 1.4.131)
The union and the vajra-seed are prescribed for the movement;
one should perform all of this in the manner previously described. (Āk 1.4.132)
Then the lord of mercury moves through all of that, being fit for such movement.
(The ninth method:
Into the vessel, however, [one should place] ferrous sulfate, borax, honey, and sulfur. ĀK 1.4.133.
One should throw the three alkalis, the five salts, and sour substances into [the mercury] for a moment;
then, as prescribed in the *Divyābhiṣeka-yoga*, one should dissolve the snake-mercury a hundred times.
One should imagine that lead and other substances worthy of being moved are [transformed] by this [mantra]:
varī, punarnavā, raṃbhā, gavākṣī, and yavaciñcikā. (Āk 1.4.135)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should process vajra and abhraka with the juices of śigru and meghanāda for seven days in due order. Āk_1,4.136.
That mica [should be processed] with *nāgavallī*, *koberī*, or *śigruka*;
or with *bāṇa*, *aṅkola*, *balā*, *ārambhā*, *sphotā*, or *pīluka*. (Āk 1.4.137)
Or else, O beloved, [the juice] of the *ālambuṣā*, *ahimaruci*, *musalī*, or *tumburu*, or even of *kharamañjarī* or bitter vegetables.
One should steam this for three days with one of these juices combined with *vyoṣa* and mustard; then, one should add *ṭaṅkaṇa* and rock salt (*saindhava*) to it. (Āk 1.4.139)
Having added green vitriol and alum according to the method of the first pressing, this mercury shall move through the mica, whether facing it directly or not. (Āk 1.4.140)
By the power of that mica, the pill (*golaka*) shall become a bestower of success.
(The tenth method: One should steam the mica for a day with fermented grain liquids (*dhānyāmla*) and sour substances (*amlavarga*). (Āk 1.4.141)

Then, having ground together the three sages (the three myrobalans), meghanāda, the bulb of rambhā, and radish in snuhī milk, one should burn them in a crucible known as the "pigeon" (kapotaka). Āk 1.4.142.
Matsyākṣī, ginger, kākamācī, punarnavā, apāmārga, and arūpūga—with the juice of these [one should perform the rite]. Āk 1.4.143.
Furthermore, one should add each [substance] one by one, beginning with abhraka;
it should be cooked for one day in a *ḍolāyantra* together with the milk of *snuhī*. (ĀK 1.4.144)
Then, when this thick [substance] has dried in the shade, one should take avasāraka, nimba, vacā, kāsīsa, and sour chickpea water separately. (Āk 1.4.145)
One should place a sixteenth part of mica into a copper vessel and rub it; by means of this application in an iron vessel, the mercury becomes mobile. (Āk 1.4.146)

(Eleventh type: One should grind grain-mercury (*dhānyābhra*) firmly for one day with the juice of the *somavallī* plant; thereafter, one should subject it to three *puṭa* treatments with the juice of the *somavallī*. (Āk 1.4.147)
O Goddess, one should meditate sevenfold; then the mercury flows into that thick mass. (The twelfth method: Having sprinkled it a hundred times with *sāranāla* and with this [substance], Āk_1,4.148.
One should wash the cloud-like substance a hundred times along with the copper vessel; one should process that mercury in a mortar—of this there is no need for deliberation. (Āk 1.4.149)
(Gandhakabhāvanā) Listen, O Pārvatī, to the cultivation of the fragrance for the purpose of application: saurāṣṭra, ajamoda, sarjī, and tin. Āk_1,4.150.
One should grind sulfur with the juice of *śigru* and saturate it with that;
after the sulfur has been ground for seven days, one should administer it to the mercury. (Āk 1.4.151)

It maintains the passion (rāga) of the lord of mercury (rasendra) during the ripening and digestion of the seeds; it is the best for all operations in the clipping of the wings of the lord of mercury. (Āk 1.4.152)
One should perfume the fragrance by means of the juices of *palāśa* flowers, the liquids from the leaves of the *śāka* tree, and the juices of *viṣṇukrāntā*, for seven days. (Āk 1.4.153)

One should cause that fragrance to permeate the mercury by means of the brick-oven apparatus (*iṣṭakāyantra*). [Regarding] the best divine roots for the permeation of mica (*abhra*), I shall now tell you those supreme divine roots for the permeation of mica. (Āk 1.4.154)
Vajrī, Rambhā, Haṃsapadī, Ciñcikā, Vyāghrapādikā, Maṇḍūkī, Bṛhatī, Puṅkhā, Kumārī, and likewise Lāṅgalī. (Āk 1.4.155)
Sarpākṣī, agnidhamanī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, indravāruṇī, ṣaṇḍajārī, and karkoṭī are renowned as divine roots (divyamūlikā). (Āk 1.4.156)
(The Roaming of Sulfur and Abhraka):
Now, therefore, I shall briefly explain the process of roaming (*cāraṇa*).
Having cast an equal amount of *dhānyābhraka* into molten sulfur, one should apply it. (Āk 1.4.157)
This renowned formulation of Gandhābhra is excellent for the practice of flight;
it consists of ten niṣkas of mercury, whether with or without a face. (Āk 1.4.158)
One should grind two niṣkas of the Gandhābhra compound in whatever manner is appropriate;
then, one should enclose that powder with a layer of Nāgapiṣṭī according to the ritual rule. (Āk 1.4.159)

O Supreme Goddess, for the work of gold one should wrap it with the paste of tin; for the work of silver, with the paste of copper; and for the perfection of the body, [one should wrap it] with the paste of mercury. Āk 1.4.160.
When the odor has vanished, one should cook that paste for three days;
one should cook that paste in a *dīpikāyantra* and cause it to fall downward. (Āk 1.4.161)
One should grind that liquid as before into a paste, excluding the wrapping;
when the mercury has flowed for three days, one should cook it in the presence of sulfur and cause it to fall downward. (Āk 1.4.162)
One should add that mercury sixty-four times its weight into a heated mortar;
then, having ground it for one day with divine herbs, one part of consecrated mica (abhraka) should be added. Āk 1.4.163.
One should place that in a *cāraṇā* apparatus combined with the juice of *jambīra* fruit;
having left it in intense sunlight for a day, the mercury (*sūta*) flows through that thick substance. (Āk 1.4.164)
Thus, the process of moving the leaf-like and cloud-like [substances] is said to consist of repeatedly swallowing the mass of the embryo; likewise is the movement of the sattva-cloud. Āk 1.4.165.
O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the processing (*cāraṇa*) as far as possible;
first, one should process mercury with mica in the proportion of one sixty-fourth part. (Āk 1.4.166)
This [measurement] shall be one-thirty-second part, then a sixteenth part, an eighth part, a fourth part, and a second part, respectively and equally. (Āk 1.4.167)
It becomes twofold, fourfold, eightfold, sixteenfold, thirty-twofold, and sixty-fourfold in succession. (Āk 1.4.168)
The cutting off of wings, faultlessness, lightness, suitability for being swallowed, openness, resistance to fire, pervasiveness, and lack of motion. (Āk 1.4.169)
The instability of the lord of mercury arises from the ingestion of mica;
however, I am pleased with him who performs the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of the lord of mercury. (Jāraṇā, Āk 1.4.170)
Let there be no doubt in your mind: *jāraṇā* bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess, *jāraṇā* is difficult to obtain; it is not attained without good fortune. (Āk 1.4.171)
Digestion (*jāraṇā*) is of two kinds: the digestion of the "child" (*bālajāraṇā*) and the digestion of the "adult" (*vṛddhajāraṇā*). (The sequence for digestion:
One should first digest the sky (*gagana*), and thereafter all other substances. (Āk 1.4.172)
O Bhairavī, one should digest all the alloys, the seeds that have been cooked,
and the gems such as rubies and others, in their proper sequence.
(The method for producing the essence of mica for the purpose of digestion;
the first method:
The essence of the sky (mica), fit for digestion by the king of mercury, shall now be described.
And one should duly process grain-cloud mica (dhānyābhraka), which is designated as "vajra."

The consecration (abhiṣeka) should be as before; in that [consecration], the substance to be heated (tāpya) should be one-tenth [of the quantity]. One should grind the five products of the buffalo and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) until they reach the consistency of a karṣa. (Āk 1.4.175)

One should form pills and cause the essence (satva) to fall out using a crucible-furnace (koṣṭhīyantra); then, one should blow [the mixture] containing a fourth part of the essence placed in a crucible with lead (tāpya). Āk 1.4.176.
Having performed this four times, that essence is the best for the digestion of mercury, for alchemy, for medicinal purposes, and for all ritual actions. (Āk 1.4.177)
(Second method:

One should take dead mica, one-fourth part of that [mercury], lead equal to one-quarter of that, and honey equal to one-quarter of that; by means of five [doses] of buffalo and cow [milk], one should precipitate the brilliant essence. (Āk 1.4.178)

That sattva and one-fourth part of that [sattva] of honey-ore (mākṣika), along with an equal amount of realgar (śilā), should be blown in a smeared crucible; the resulting *sattva* will be like gold. (Āk 1.4.179)
One should perform this four times; then the mercury swallows that sattva.
(The third method:
Take sixteen parts of dead mica and one-fourth part of tin. (Āk 1.4.180)

Having added an equal amount of orpiment (*tālaka*) to the five products of the buffalo (*pañcamāhiṣagavya*), one should cause the being to fall; that is the fourth [type of] orpiment (*haritālaka*). (Āk 1.4.181)
Having cast it in four successive times, the mercury devours that sattva of abhraka; (this is the fourth method: the softening of the sattva of abhraka).
Having placed it within a diamond crucible, one should likewise [place] solid mercury of equal measure.
Having added glass and borax and sealed [the crucible], one should blow it with a fierce fire;
then one should throw that [mixture] into the group of acidic substances, along with the seed of the *ciñcā* tree and the leaf of the *snuhī*. (Āk 1.4.183)
Having ground it again in that same manner with the addition of glass (kāca) and borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), one should heat it thus seven times, with repeated sprinkling each time. (Āk 1.4.184)
That essence of mica becomes bright and soft when subjected to cāraṇa;
this is the fifth method.
One part each of mercury, ṭaṅkaṇa, and tāpya [should be taken] separately. (Āk 1.4.185)
One-third part of purified lead, ten parts of mercury, mica, alkali of barley, burnt hair, alkali of *sarja* resin, and *guggulu*. (Āk 1.4.186)
Combined with the five parts of a goat and joined with sour substances and urine, one should grind it as before; thus the essence is precipitated, soft and stainless. (Āk 1.4.187)
(The crucible coating for the union of couples:
the first method) O Pārvatī, I shall describe the crucible coating for the union of couples. Āk_1,4.188.
Having ground together equal parts of ram's horn, hoof, guñjā, ṭaṅkaṇa, and poison with the fat of a large frog, one should smear the crucible. (Āk 1.4.189)
All sentient beings meet together and are ground in a crucible:
equal parts of guggulu, dhātakī flowers, jaggery, and the three alkalis. (Āk 1.4.190)
Then, having ground these with breast milk, one applies them as a coating inside a crucible; this is the "union of pairs" (the second method).
Aśmabhedin, lāṅgalī, bhūlatā, and marīcaka— (Āk 1.4.191)
One should grind the fruit of cotton and *śakragopa* insects together with breast milk; with that very mixture, one should coat the interior of the crucible. (Āk 1.4.192)
In that [crucible], all living beings and all great essences, as well as metals primarily consisting of gold, meet together through the blowing of a fierce fire. (Āk 1.4.193)
(Third method: Having ground together the flesh of a *cucundarī* (musk rat), *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and poison in equal parts, one should smear it inside a crucible and place [the mercury] therein. (Āk 1.4.194)
Whatever may be suitable for a dual application, all of that should be gathered through suction.
(The fourth method: Apāmārga reduced to ashes and rubbed with Kaṅguṇī oil. (Āk 1.4.195)

One should smear the crucible with that [substance] and place the double-substance (dvandvadravya) inside; it will merge through intense heating by blowing and by the addition of the respective "killer" (māraka) powder. (Āk 1.4.196)
(The Union of Pairs) For this very reason, I shall explain the union of pairs; listen!
[Take] *varṣābhū*, plantain root, *kākamācī*, and *punarnavā*. (Āk 1.4.197)
Gold, human skull, guñjā, ṭaṅkaṇa, and mica—when their essence is placed in a crucible and heated, the gold and mica merge in an instant. (Āk 1.4.198)
Having powdered mica and saturated it with the juice of *kākamācī*, one should combine it with the juice of *kapittha* and with mercury (*sūta*) and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*). (Āk 1.4.199)
Tin and mica, placed inside a tin leaf and heated, will merge;
having melted them with mustard oil, one should add the ash of Apāmārga. (Āk 1.4.200)
Gold-colored mica [is obtained] from nāgatāpya; star-like mica from haritāla;
copper-colored mica from sulphur; and sharp mica from sindhu and hiṅgula. Āk 1.4.201.
Vanga-mercury combined with yellow orpiment, lead-mercury with realgar, Langali, yak-tail hair, cotton seeds, and horse-gram; Āk 1.4.202.

The creeper of the earth (*bhūlatā*), the stone-subduer (*aśmadamanī*), woman’s milk, and the earthworm (*suragopaka*)—these, when combined in pairs and smeared inside a crucible, are well-melted with a fierce fire. (Āk 1.4.203)
All those who are as pure as lovely clouds or mountains meet together in an instant. Then, the flesh of a muskrat combined with poison and borax [is used]. (Āk 1.4.204)
From the application of a coating to the crucible, it effects the fusion of all dual substances:
borax, beeswax, rhinoceros horn, frog fat, and meat. (Āk 1.4.205)
By applying a paste of *guñjā* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, one merges with all living beings;
[likewise] by means of *ṭaṅkaṇa*, wool, mica, lac, earwax, collyrium, and *karkaṭa*. (Āk 1.4.206)
All substances are combined with the milk of a woman, along with *dhātakī*, *guggulu*, molasses, *sarja* resin, barley-gruel, and borax. (Āk 1.4.207)
Pounded with breast milk, this pair is recommended for rejuvenation (rasāyana);
whatever fine powder there may be should be combined with the previous paste. (Āk 1.4.208)
When placed in a blind crucible and blown with a blowpipe, the mixture instantly melts when sown with *tāpya*, *rasaka*, *sasyaka*, and *darada*. (Āk 1.4.209)
That substance would become dense and firm when blown [with fire], and then it would coalesce;
one should then combine all the mercury, secondary minerals, and metals together in one place. (Āk 1.4.210)
(First Type) They enter into mutual union and flow together like water;
this applies to whatever powder of vajra, clouds, or sattva, as well as any powder of metal. (Āk 1.4.211)
One should cast the two [substances] together in equal measure into the crucible of the union of pairs; through heating, their fusion occurs. (Āk 1.4.212)
(Second method:
One should grind ṭaṅkaṇa with the juice of the plantain root and smear it [inside] the crucible;
O Dear One, by blowing [the fire], white mica and tin will unite. Āk 1.4.213.
(The third method:
Having ground together *vanaśigru*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *guñjā*, and a human skull, one should smear a crucible with that [mixture] using the water of a woman’s breast milk. (Āk 1.4.214)
Having powdered the essence of tin and white mica, one should cast it [into the crucible] and blow upon it;
they will undoubtedly unite, which is excellent for the work of silver. (Āk 1.4.215)

(Fourth Method) Having powdered white mica (*śvetābhra*) and mercury (*pārada*) in a ratio of one part mercury to one-fourth part of the mica, one should grind them together with an equal amount of borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) using *kākamācī* juice. (Āk 1.4.216)
Having made a ball from those fluids, one should wrap it with a sheet of tin; having coated it with an amount equal to white mica-essence, one should heat it inside a sealed crucible. ĀK 1.4.217.
The union should be perfect, and it should be primary in the work of silver; (this is the first method for the smearing of the crucible in the alchemical union of vajra and gold).
Now, therefore, follows the application of the ointment of the dual fusion of diamond and gold. Āk 1.4.218.
Having ground *guñjā* seeds, which resemble a lovely face, together with the double amount of *bali* and the breast-milk of women, one should likewise place it inside a crucible.
This Vajramelāpa has been described by me.
(The second method: Silādhātu, Kāntamukha, Śaśadanta, and Gandhaka. (Āk 1.4.220)
Having ground equal parts of *amlavetasa* and plastered it onto the crucible, gold and diamond will indeed unite within that crucible; of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.4.221)
(The third method:
One should grind together crab bone, mineral ore, buffalo horn-dust, eye-secretion, borax, and wool, all in equal parts, with the breast milk of a beautiful woman. (Āk 1.4.222)
With this ointment, one should coat the crucible; gold and diamond will then fully unite.
(The fourth method: Borax, the mouth of *kāntaloha*, the excrement of a young calf, and the bone of a bee. (Āk 1.4.223)
One should rub human hair and bones with breast milk;
gold and diamond will certainly merge when smeared with this inside a crucible. (Āk 1.4.224)
(Fifth type:
Equal parts of iron filings, borax, realgar, magnetite, glass, honey, crab shells, the milky sap of *snuhī*, and the milky sap of *arka* [should be combined]. (Āk 1.4.225)
One should rub everything with breast milk and apply it as a coating for the crucible; this is the crucible-coating known as the "union of diamond and gold. (Āk 1.4.226)
One should smear the interior of the crucible with those substances by which even a vajra would be reduced to ashes;
one should blow it with a fierce fire, and there will be the fusion of gold and vajra. (Āk 1.4.227)
(The Alchemy of Vajra and Gold;
the first method) Now, therefore, O Mistress of the Gods, I shall explain the alchemical union of vajra and gold.
Gold should be twelve parts, and pure mercury half of that. (Āk 1.4.228)
Half a part of the best mercury (rasendra), half a part of lead ash (nāgabhasma), and half a part of killed diamond (mṛtavajraka)—
these four should be ground with acidic liquids in a heated mortar.
Having extracted [the substance] during the union of the two [substances], one should seal it in a crucible and heat it;
by force, that will then merge—of this there is no need for deliberation. (Āk 1.4.230)
(Second method:
One should then soak the killed *vajra* in the milk of a female *śārivā* for one day;
having formed it into a ball (*golaka*), one should grind it and leave behind one part. (Āk 1.4.231)
One should take three parts of the king of fluids (mercury) and four parts of gold; having ground them into a paste with acid, one should form it into a ball. Āk 1.4.232.
Having ground that, one should wrap it and enclose it with a birch leaf;
one should place it upon a heap of grain for a fortnight, and then remove it again and again. (Āk 1.4.233)
If one blows [upon it] with force, it certainly melts; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
(The third method: One should wrap a vajra with a gold leaf consisting of sixteen parts. (Āk 1.4.234)
One should quickly cast that into a smeared crucible; having made it into powder, one should either cast in a portion of gold, white glass, or human skull. (Āk 1.4.235)
Having stopped it, one should blow forcefully; in this manner, one should do so again and again, repeatedly casting white glass or even a human skull [into the fire]. (Āk 1.4.236)
In this manner it melts exactly seven times, and then it is processed once more; one should add sixteen parts of powdered diamond to this gold. (Āk 1.4.237)
Having repeatedly cast either glass or a human skull into a crucible smeared as before, one should blow strongly seven times; thus it will surely fuse. (Āk 1.4.238)
In this manner one should perform it for the third time, and likewise for the fourth.
(The Consecration of Pairs) Now, therefore, I shall explain the consecration of those in pairs. Āk 1.4.239.
One should grind together equal parts of green vitriol, the five salts, copper pyrite, sulfur, potassium carbonate, and the three alkalis with fermented rice gruel. (Āk 1.4.240)
One should place that paste in a copper vessel in the sun for three days; into that, one should quickly cast lead a hundred times, melting it again and again. (Āk 1.4.241)
One should saturate it a hundred times with *sauvīra* (antimony) kept in a copper vessel;
that mercury, thus prepared as a pair, may digest whatever substance is suitable for digestion. (Āk 1.4.242)
Tin is used for silver work, and lead is used for gold work.
Now, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, I shall fully explain the method for preparing matured seed-mercury. (Āk 1.4.243)
(The first method:
O beloved, when gold has been liquefied, an equal amount of lead and mica should be combined with it;
one should blow the mixture until twelve times the weight of lead has been processed, until only the gold remains. Āk 1.4.244.
This is known as the "ripened seed"; one should digest it in mercury gradually.
(The second method: One should smelt together equal parts of yellow mica-essence and gold. Āk 1.4.245.
One should smelt it until twelve times the weight of gold remains as residue; then, one should again slowly smelt yellow mica-satva ten times its weight. (Āk 1.4.246)

This shall be the third procedure: when the seed has been cooked until only gold remains, one should take mercury from lead, copper, and the sky [space] in proportions of four, three, two, and one parts respectively. (Āk 1.4.247)
One should grind it in a coated crucible, seal it, and heat it strongly;
then, having ground that residue with honey and acidic liquids, one should cook it in a *puṭa*. (Āk 1.4.248)
Again, having ground that [mercury] with an equal amount of *ākṣīka* salt and acidic substances, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
Having applied five such *puṭas* in this manner, one should process it into molten gold. (ĀK 1.4.249)
One should heat it ten times until the seed becomes fully ripened.
(The sequence of the four seeds:
Now, O fair-faced one, I shall explain the four seeds. Āk_1,4.250.
These are, in truth, the seeds of the crooked blood-red serpent;
the seed of gold and the seed of the Naga are recommended for the work of gold-making. (Āk 1.4.251)
The seed-syllable *tāra* and the seed-syllable *vaṅga* are taught for the rite of silver; the seed-syllables *hema* and *tāra* are used for alchemy (*rasāyana*). Āk 1.4.252.
The seed of the *nāga* plant and the seed of the *vaṅga* plant are not for the purpose of alchemy;
these four seeds serve to pacify disease. (Āk 1.4.253)
Otherwise, O Śāmbhavī, these seeds must not be applied at all. (The Procedure for the Golden Seed;
the First Golden Seed)
Either sulphur, or pyrite, or iron pyrites, or talc. Āk 1.4.254.
Having powdered either pure stone, or vaikrānta, or añjana, or kharpara, or kāntamukha, in equal parts; Āk_1,4.255.
One should repeatedly cast [the mercury] into molten gold a hundred times. (This is the second seed-gold, perfected by the ash of a nāga.
Mercury, cinnabar, kuṣṭha, iron, parpaṭika, and mica—Āk_1,4.256.
O Dear One, take equal parts of mercury, copper, realgar, and antimony, and add one-sixteenth part of each of these; then [process them] with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*. (Āk 1.4.257)
One should crush those leaves and smear them upon pure lead;
after roasting it in thirty-two *puṭas*, the lead will be reduced to ash, which one should then carry. (Āk 1.4.258)
When the previously poured liquid has flowed out equally in a hundredfold stream, one should likewise strongly melt the remaining gold until it is pure gold. (Āk 1.4.259)
(The third [method]: the seed of gold perfected by the ash of tin.

Alternatively, one should reduce tin to ash with calamine, conch-shell, mica, and mercury, along with the alkali of *ciñcā* fruit, equal in measure to tin, and rubbed with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*. (Āk 1.4.260)
One should seal it with sixteen layers and process it a hundred times in gold;
thus is the fourth [method], the successful copper-ash which serves as the seed for gold.
Alternatively, one should kill the equal amount of sulphur above and below the copper. (Āk 1.4.261)
Having cast [the powder] into it, one should seal it and roast it eight times; then that copper should be processed with gold.
(The fifth seed of gold is thus perfected by means of sharp-iron ash.
Alternatively, one should kill the sharp-iron and apply cinnabar equal in weight to the sharp-iron. (Āk 1.4.262)
Having rubbed it with breast milk, one should then perform a *puṭapāka* with a one-sixteenth part of *tīkṣṇa* (iron sulfide);
having added cinnabar (*hiṅgula*), one should rub and then perform *puṭapāka* in succession. (Āk 1.4.263)
In this manner, one should process that sharp [substance] sixteen times in gold;
when the gold has been liquefied a hundredfold, one should process it in that same direction within the liquefied gold. (Āk 1.4.264)

(The sixth: the golden seed) Having heated that gold twice as much and purified it, one should smelt it firmly; having powdered it with two or three *puṭas*, it becomes killed with five [applications]. (Āk 1.4.265)
One should smelt that repeatedly until it is melted ten times over;
thus it becomes divine, bestowing all spiritual accomplishments.
This is known as the "gold-seed" (*hemabīja*); it is beneficial for the digestion of mercury.
(The seventh gold-seed:
The essence of *sasyaka*, *abhra*, and *vaikrānta*, along with gold, *mahiṣī*, and *ravi*. (Āk 1.4.267)
One should grind it finely, seal it in a closed crucible (*liptamūṣā*), and blow it with a bellows; once it has melted, one should blow it again in an open crucible (*prakaṭamūṣā*). Āk 1.4.268.
One should add a small amount of honey, adding it again and again until only gold remains; then, one should pour that [mixture] into it. (Āk 1.4.269)
One should blow upon gold, lead, copper, and iron in succession as before;
likewise, one should process the pyrite and blow upon it until only gold remains. (Āk 1.4.270)
This is known as the "gold seed" (*hemabīja*); it is beneficial for the digestion of mercury.
(The eighth gold seed:
One should grind together equal parts of mica (*abhra*), its essence (*satva*), and auspicious copper. Āk 1.4.271.

Having heated all the washed tāpya twice the amount of the abhraka, one should forcefully blow it in a crucible smeared with the *dvandva* mixture; thereafter, one should powder that residue (*khoṭa*). (Āk 1.4.272)
It should be rubbed with the juices of divine medicinal herbs and firmly sealed within a crucible;
likewise, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, then powder it, rub it again, and seal it once more. (Āk 1.4.273)
Thus, having been cooked in five layers, one should carry it into molten gold;
as long as it has not increased tenfold, one should blow it openly in a crucible.
Then, having repeatedly cast pure copper into that [crucible], one should blow upon it and heat it until only gold remains; O Dear One, this is the seed of gold.
(Ninth: the golden seed) Take equal parts of the ashes of *tīkṣṇa*, *arka*, and *nāga*, along with an equal amount of the powder of *tāpya*.
One should cause this to flow into molten gold until it becomes ten times [the original weight]. (Āk 1.4.276)
O beloved, this is the seed of gold (*svarṇabīja*); it remains as pure gold until the end.
(This is the tenth seed of gold.
One should strongly melt together equal parts of dead silver, copper, iron, and steel. (Āk 1.4.277)
Then, one should grind that residue in a crucible smeared with a pair [of substances];
that powder should then be slowly introduced into molten gold. (Āk 1.4.278)
O Dear One, blowing [the crucible] while repeatedly adding pyrite powder ten times [the weight of the gold], until only the gold remains—this is the seed of gold. Āk 1.4.279.

(Eleventh: The Golden Seed) One part of lead and four parts of copper, along with a sattva derived from *rasaka*, should all be blown [into a flame] and ground into powder within a crucible smeared with a double-layered coating. (Āk 1.4.280)
One should slowly process that powder into six times its weight of molten gold;
as long as it takes for the gold to remain as the residue, so long shall it be the "gold-seed" (*svarṇabījaka*). (Āk 1.4.281)
(Twelfth: The Gold Seed) One should kill copper with *tāpya* (calamine); one should then slowly cause it to be carried into lead (*nāga*).
Blowing repeatedly while adding the powder of *tāpya* until it is a hundredfold [the original amount], [the process is complete]. (Āk 1.4.282)
One should smelt that [ore] in gold, increasing the heat thirty-two times in succession; as long as there remains only gold, so long shall it be the seed of gold. (Āk 1.4.283)
(The thirteenth: the golden seed.
One part of the essence of *kharparī*, two parts of the essence of mica (*abhra*), and three parts of copper powder—having placed these in a coated crucible, one should blow upon them. (Āk 1.4.284)

One should grind that residue and mercury-cinnabar (tāpya) in equal parts, rub them with acidic liquids, place the mixture in a sealed crucible (saṃpuṭa), close it, and roast it again in a mild fire. (Āk 1.4.285)
Thus cooked in five layers, one should cause that powder to flow into molten gold, multiplied a thousandfold, until only the gold remains. (Āk 1.4.286)
By heating these two together according to the proper method, this becomes the seed of gold.
(The fourteenth seed of gold:
Take one part of iron-ore essence and two parts of pure copper. Āk 1.4.287.
One should powder it after having placed it in a sealed crucible (liptamūṣā) and heated it strongly while closed;
then, one should powder that [resulting] tāpya and grind it with an equal amount of acid. Āk 1.4.288.
Having sealed that in a *saṃpuṭa* vessel, one should cook it in a *puṭa*; then one should grind it again.
Having thrown it into honey as before, O beloved, one should rub it and cause it to fall [into the crucible]. (Āk 1.4.289)
O beloved, one should process that powder through five layers of filtration;
as long as it is processed a hundred times in gold, so long will it become the seed of gold.
(Fifteenth: The Golden Seed) Honey, sulphur, yellow orpiment, realgar, vaikrāntaka, kāntamukha, sasyaka, vimalā, and collyrium. Āk_1.4.291.
One should also process mercury, powdered a hundredfold, with gold, along with iron-parpaṭī, tāpya, kaṅkuṣṭha, vimalā, and abhraka. (Āk 1.4.292)
Through repeated applications of the combination of dead copper, stone, mercury, snuhi-milk, arka-milk, and cinnabar, the naga attains a state devoid of life. Āk 1.4.293.
With mercury, realgar, purified tamarind alkali, as well as lead, killed tin, killed lead, or killed copper or killed iron; ĀK 1.4.294.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should cause each [atom] to be carried into the finest gold;
when the serpent [of impurity] is obstructed within the gold, it is transmuted through hundreds of multiples.
(Through the digestion of lead and other metals in gold, there occurs a change of color:

Lead that has been digested [in gold] has the luster of *rocanā* (yellow pigment); tin that has been digested is greenish-yellow (*hārīta*) and bears a coppery hue; iron that has been digested is equal to the sun; and tin (*vaṅga*) that has been digested resembles the *japā* flower. (Āk 1.4.296)
(First, the seed-syllable *tāra*):
White mica, iron pyrites, copper sulfate, and realgar, as well as *kharpara*, all in equal parts, and *kuṭila* four times that amount. Āk 1.4.297.

One should pound everything together, grind it into powder, and reduce it to ash using five *puṭas*; then, once the silver (*tāra*) has been melted, one should slowly and gradually blow [the fire] until it is increased a hundredfold. Āk 1.4.298.
This is known as the seed-syllable *tāra*, which is supremely beneficial for the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
(The second *tāra*-seed-syllable: Just as crookedness [in gold] is removed by means of *tāpya* [calamine], so too should [the mercury] be killed by means of *tāpya*. (Āk 1.4.299)
That portion is equal to the *tāla*, and that same amount is [added] to molten silver;
it should be increased gradually until it becomes thirtyfold. (Āk 1.4.300)
This is known as the *tāra-bīja* (silver-seed); one should cause that to digest mercury.
(The third *tāra-bīja*:
O Dear One, one should grind together equal parts of *tīkṣṇa*, tin (*vaṅga*), and *vimalā* into a powder. (Āk 1.4.301)
One should blow upon that *khoṭaka* when it has been smeared with the *dvandvamela*; that *khoṭa* should then be powdered with acids, rubbed, and subjected to *puṭa* firing. (Āk 1.4.302)
O Dear One, one should perform this five times; then that ash is produced.
When the star has moved away, one should carry that ash along evenly and steadily. (Āk 1.4.303)
O Bhairavī, by blowing upon it ten times, this excellent seed-syllable *tāra* becomes [powerful] for the digestion of the king of mercury. (Āk 1.4.304)
(The fourth is the seed-syllable *tāra*):

One should grind together in equal proportions white mica (*śvetābhra-sattva*), mercury (*kuṭila-tāra*), and copper pyrite (*ākṣīka-sattva*); having placed this mixture in a coated crucible, one should heat it. (Āk 1.4.305)
One should process that powder with silver and add an amount equal to the silver; one should continue adding silver until it has become tenfold through the addition of *ākṣīka*. (ĀK 1.4.306)
This seed-syllable *tāra* is proclaimed to be supremely beneficial for the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
O Goddess of Gods, [one should take] three, two, and one part respectively of *tīkṣṇa*, *tāla*, and *amalā*. (The fifth is the *tāra* seed-syllable. Āk 1.4.307.

Having placed the powdered [substance] in a smeared crucible, one should blow it with a fierce fire; that resulting residue (khoṭa) should be ground into powder, digested with acids, and subjected to puṭapāka. (Āk 1.4.308)
When that silver has been liquefied seven times, one should then add ten parts of copper;
having repeatedly added palm-wood powder, one should blow the furnace until only silver remains. (Āk 1.4.309)
This seed-syllable of silver (tāra-bīja) is excellent; it is supremely beneficial for the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
(The sixth silver seed-syllable: Kharparī, Tāla, white *abhrasattva*, silver, and *mākṣika*. (Āk 1.4.310)
One should blow [the fire] until all the tin is equalized and entirely placed within the crucible;
one should then powder it, rub it with acidic liquids, and thus roast it seven times. (Āk 1.4.311)
One should blow that powder into molten silver ten times while smelting it;
as long as silver remains, so long shall it be the seed of silver. (Āk 1.4.312)
(The seventh is the seed-syllable *tāra*.
One should form a binary compound of white-cloud-like *satva* and tin (*vaṅga*) as before;
having added *tālaka* to that powder in a one-quarter proportion, one should rub it with acidic liquids. (Āk 1.4.313)
One should seal it in that [crucible], throw in the *tāla*, and perform the grinding and sealing as before;
thus one should perform five sealings, and then one should cause that powder to flow into the molten metal. (Āk 1.4.314)
In silver, that seed of *tāra* becomes twelvefold;
(the eighth is the seed of *tāra*) white cloud-essence (*śvetābhrasatva*), tin (*vaṅga*), and half as much fine powder of iron (*tīkṣṇacūrṇaka*).
One should blow [the crucible] containing everything inside it using sharp, clear, and stainless [iron];
then, having ground that with acidic liquids and crushed it, one should seal it and cook it in a *puṭa* (burial) fire. (Āk 1.4.316)
One should then melt that [silver] five times in molten silver, blowing the furnace while adding cinnabar (tālaka) until it has increased a hundredfold. (Āk 1.4.317)
As long as there remains a residue of *tāra* (silver), so long shall it be the seed of *tāra*.
I shall now explain the seed of *tāmra* (copper) for the purpose of digesting (*jāraṇa*) mercury. (This is the seed of copper. Āk 1.4.318.
O Goddess, one should place equal parts of gold and copper, along with an amount of mākṣika equal to those two, inside a sealed crucible; then one should heat it thoroughly. (Āk 1.4.319)
One should thus blow [the crucible] ten times, repeatedly adding honey;
this is known as the copper seed (tāmrabīja), which resembles the rays of the sun. (Āk 1.4.320)
(First, the seed of the Naga):
Take equal parts of mica and *rasaka*, and four times as much *nāgabhasma* (mercury oxide); one should smelt them, grind them into powder, and then fix it with *mākṣika*. Āk 1.4.321.
Having combined this with an equal amount of powdered stone, one should then sow it; O Dear One, one should blow it into molten gold that has been liquefied a hundred times. Āk 1.4.322.
This is declared to be the first *nāgabīja* (lead seed); it produces and digests [mercury].
(The second *nāgabīja*)—I shall now describe the excellent *nāgabīja*, which is supreme for the digestion of mercury. (Āk 1.4.323)
Then, O Dear One, one should blow [the crucible] with mercury, mica, copper, and iron in increasing proportions;
and that seed, killed by mākṣika, should be cast out. (Āk 1.4.324)
Tin, struck by *tāpya*, should be carried thirty-two times in gold;
lead, having obtained *śilājatu*, is declared to be thirty times [the amount] in the seed of mercury (*nāgabīja*). (Āk 1.4.325)
(The sequence for the seed of tin:
I shall explain the seed: tin, antimony, and pyrite.
One should blow [the mixture] while equal parts, and then grind that same amount of pyrite and antimony together. (Āk 1.4.326)
One should rub and roast it with acidic substances; after sixteen such roastings, it becomes ash.
When mercury is melted, one should cause the ash of tin to be absorbed into it a hundredfold. (Āk 1.4.327)
O Goddess, one should take thirty-two times as much cinnabar (tālaka) as that mercury;
this is to be known as the seed of tin (vaṅgabīja), and it should digest the mercury within the ore. (Āk 1.4.328)
(On the Application of Viḍa in Digestion) O Goddess worshipped by the gods, I shall now declare the applications of *viḍa* suitable for the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*).
(1. Vaḍavānalaviḍa)
Sauvīra, gandhaka, kāṅkṣī, kāsīsa, vyoṣa, and saindhava.
One should saturate all of this— sauvarcala salt, sarjikā, and that which grows on the banks of the Mālatī— with the juices from the roots of the śigru plant for seven days.
This *viḍa* is excellent for the process of *jāraṇā*, and it is known by the name Vaḍabānala (the Mare’s Fire).
(2. Vaiśvānara-viḍa) O Dear One, one should soak conch shell burnt with the milks of the *arka* plant and then roast it in a *puṭa*. Āk 1.4.331.
This great substance known as Vaiśvānara-biḍa is said to be capable of splitting [mercury] a hundredfold;
it consists of equal parts of sulphur, conch-shell powder, rock salt, and poison. (3. Jvālāmukha-biḍa) Āk 1.4.332.
This *viḍa* salt, having been processed one hundred times with cow urine as well as with the juice of *śigru* roots, is declared by the name Jvālāmukha. (Āk 1.4.333)

(4. Agnijihvakabiḍa) O beloved, borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) should be processed a hundred times with the juices of *palāśa*; this *biḍa* salt, known by the name Agnijihvaka, is the best for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of metals. Āk 1,4.334.
(5. Vaḍabābila):
One part each of kāntāsyam, sulphur, and cūlī are the "iron-impregnator" (*lohajāra*).
[One should take] cūlī, sulphur, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *tāla*, realgar (*bhūkhaga*), and *ṭaṅkaṇa*. (Āk 1.4.335)
One should cook this [preparation] with alkaline urine; it is known by the name Vaḍabāmukha (6. Mahāvaiśvānara Viḍa).
[It contains] devadālī, mokṣaka, nicula, and punarnavā. (Āk 1.4.336)
One should not excessively dry out the leaves of the palāśa, kāñcana, vāsā, eraṇḍa, vāstuka, sesame, or even the entire plantain tree when they have been cut. (Āk 1.4.337)
Thereafter, one should add eight times the quantity of urine;
having burnt a radish with its roots and an equal amount of sesame stalks, [these should be added]. (Āk 1.4.338)

Having thrown the two alkalis into the previous liquid and kept it in the sun for three days over a strong fire, one should filter it through cloth and cook that liquid in an iron vessel. (Āk 1.4.339)
Whenever many bubbles and vapors arise, [one should apply] the three alkalis, the three pungents, sulphur, ferrous sulfate, and the five salts. (Āk 1.4.340)
One should add powdered *saurāṣṭrī*, asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*), and *cūlī* in equal parts;
one should stir it with an iron ladle until it reaches the consistency of molasses. (Āk 1.4.341)
Having extracted it, one should place it in an iron casket for seven days;
then, one should keep it again for seven days within a heap of grain buried underground. (Āk 1.4.342)
One should maintain the *biḍa* salt in the heat for seven days; this is the great *vaiśvānara-biḍa*.
It should be processed a hundred times with the sour juice of *jambīra* and the juice of wild *śigru*. (7. Vahni-biḍa) Āk 1.4.343.
One should process sulfur; this is the *viḍa* known as "fire.
Likewise, *navasāra* (saltpeter) combined with fragrance also becomes that *viḍa*. (Āk 1.4.344)

(8. Citrabhānubiḍa) One should take sulfur, the alkali of *nicula*, *guñjā* seeds, borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), and the root-seed of *devadālī* in equal parts, and then saturate [the mixture] with all of these. Āk 1.4.345.

This *biḍa* salt, processed seven times with the juices of bitter *kośātakī* and likewise with the acidic group of substances, becomes "Citrabhānu"; it is the foremost for the digestion of gold. (Āk 1.4.346)
(9. Mahābiḍa) Having burnt equal parts of the three—radish, ginger, and fire—one should place them in cow urine and cause it to be strained through a cloth. (Āk 1.4.347)
By this, the great *mahābiḍa* fragrance is perfected a hundredfold.
(10. Another *mahābiḍa*:
) *Tāla*, *śilā*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, conch shell, salt, and oyster shell. (Āk 1.4.348)
One should cook it slowly over a fire with urine and sour liquids; this is the great *viḍa* salt, known as *vajrānalaviḍa*.
Then, having burnt a conch shell with the milks of the sun-plant (*arka*), one should saturate it a hundred times. (Āk 1.4.349)
Having ground it with the group of sour substances and sealed it, one should cook it with five *puṭas*;
then, having added an equal amount of *ṭaṅkaṇa* alkali that has been saturated with the group of sour substances, [one should proceed]. (Āk 1.4.350)
O beloved, having taken realgar, fragrance, cinnabar, coral, and then *nṛpāvarta*, one should take equal parts of these five along with conch powder. Āk_1,4.351.

One should macerate it with the group of sour substances for three days; it becomes a great *viḍa* salt known by the name Vajrānala, which is prescribed as a *khoṭa* for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury. (Āk 1.4.352)
One should always employ mercury in the process of *sāraṇā* within the crucible of the union of pairs (*dvandvamelāpa*);
indeed, in an instant, it dissolves even diamonds and other such substances. (Āk 1.4.353)
(12. Another *viḍa*):

O Goddess, powdered conch shell that has been burnt and drenched a hundred times with the milk of *ravikṣīrā*, when subjected to many *puṭa* cycles, is praised as a *viḍa* for the process of *jāraṇā*. (Āk 1.4.354)

(13. Baḍabāmukho viḍaḥ) Either a hundred times one should boil the powder of sulphur with cow's urine, or the powder of burnt conch-shell steeped in water from the roots of the *śigru* tree. (Āk 1.4.355)
One hundred times, the submarine fire (*vaḍavāmukha*)—
the universal alchemical flux (*sarvajārakabiḍa*)—
should saturate sulfur combined with poison and rock salt using the juices of *kanyā*, *dhuttūraka*, and *karavīra*. (Āk 1.4.356)
When processed a hundred times with liquid substances in a *gharma* vessel, this *viḍa* salt becomes a universal activator (*sarvajāraka*).
(15. Another *viḍa*:
one should soak *gandhasaindhava* with the juice of the leaves of *tāmravallī*. Āk 1.4.357).
Within seven days this [substance] becomes perfected; one should employ it for the digestion of gold.
(16. Siddhabīḍa) Take one *pala* each of rock salt (*saindhava*), realgar (*kunaṭī*), and sulfur (*gandha*). Āk 1.4.358.
One should grind three palas of each of these, including the creeper-like hair (bhūlatā), dry them, and cook them;
one should perform this process eight times. This is known as *siddhabiḍa*. (Āk 1.4.359)
(The Digestion of Abhraka):
Now, O Pārvatī, I shall describe the process of digesting mica; listen.
Sixty-four niṣkas of mercury, well-conducted, [should be placed] in a heated mortar. ĀK 1.4.360.
One should pour a single purified piece of gold into that [liquid], along with the three alkalis, the five salts, earth, *khaga*, sour substances, and *javetasa*. (Āk 1.4.361)
One should add sixteen parts of mercury along with the juice of jambīra fruit and grind it for exactly one prahara in a *kūrmayantra* provided with medicinal fluxes (*viḍa*). (Āk 1.4.362)
Having cast it into [the crucible] and processed it for a day, the mercury becomes digested;
this mercury, having been placed in a heated mortar (taptakhalva), along with *rājī*, jaggery, and wool-fiber (*ūrṇaka*). (Āk 1.4.363)
Brick, house-soot, rock salt, and mercury—each of these taken in a sixteenth part [of the total] should be ground with the group of acidic substances for one day. (Āk 1.4.364)

Having formed a mass in the intense heat and bound it in a *poṭala* (pouch) within that liquid, one should cook it for a day in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) filled with the group of acidic substances. Āk 1.4.365.
At each mouthful, however, one should perform this [meditation] while awaiting the next morsel;
if a morsel has not been digested, it should be processed in the "tortoise-machine" (*kacchapayantra*). (Āk 1.4.366)
In this manner, by means of the sequence of morsels alone, one should digest the [elements] beginning with space (ākāśa),
starting from the sixty-fourth part and continuing up to the limit of sixty-fourfold multiplication.
In the best of mercury (*rasendra*), one should cause the *grāsa* to be digested by giving it again and again.
(The characteristic of the digested mica-mercury:
When the mercury has been digested with a sixty-fourth part of the essence of the sky (*vyomasatva*), [the process is complete]. (Āk 1.4.368)
This wielder of the staff, resembling a leech, is indeed [the portion] in the thirty-second part;
in the sixteenth part he is equal to a crow, and in the eighth part he is equal to excrement. (Āk 1.4.369)

O Goddess, when processed in a fourth part [of the liquid], it becomes like the cream of curd; when processed in two parts, it becomes like fresh butter and takes on the luster of a cow's udder. (Āk 1.4.370)
When the mercury has fully digested the mica, it becomes a hundredfold penetrator;
