when it has digested double that amount of the solid [mica], it should penetrate by a thousandth part. (Āk 1.4.371)
O beloved, when four times the amount of abhraka has been digested [in the body], one attains a lifespan of ten thousand years;
when eight times the amount of gagana has been digested, one attains the lifespan of Brahmā and possesses the power of piercing a target at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas].
When sixteen times Viṣṇu’s lifespan has been digested, the mercury is a "piercer of ten million" (koṭivedhaka);
when thirty-two times [Viṣṇu’s] lifespan has been digested, it is a "piercer of ten billion" (daśakoṭi) with the lifespan of Rudra. (Āk 1.4.373)
When sixty-four times the amount has been digested, one attains eternal life for ten billion years;
when the mica has been fully digested, the mercury abandons all defects.
It abandons all internal [impurities] and consumes all metals; (the cutting of the wings) it does not fall down from the machine, nor does it fly upward. Āk 1.4.375.
Not belching, tawny in color, it remains motionless within the fire;
O Goddess, it emits droplets, and the mercury becomes like one whose wings have been clipped. (Āk 1.4.376)
When it is properly digested, the mercury becomes a child; when digested fourfold, it becomes a youth;
and when digested sixfold like the sky (ākāśa), the mercury is designated as an old man. (Āk 1.4.377)
The "child" pierces with *kalka*; the "youth," by means of leaf-unguents;
but this "matured" mercury, when "aged," pierces the metals. (Āk 1.4.378)
A childly physician cures disease but is not capable of alchemy (rasāyana);
a youth is skilled in alchemy; an elder may be [skilled] in both the body and metals. (Āk 1.4.379)
(The method for digesting other substances:
In the absence of *ghanasattva*, *kāntasattva* is given;
in its absence, *tīkṣṇa* should be used. In this manner, one should cause the pairs [of metals] to be digested. (Āk 1.4.380)
Then, one should cause the mercury that has been thoroughly digested to digest the binary compounds;
once freed from the binary compounds, the king of mercury does not act upon the mica-leaf.
Therefore, O worshiper of the gods, one should certainly process mercury with mica combined with metals such as gold, or with lead-mica, tin-mica, or copper-mica. (Āk 1.4.382)
One should digest either blue mica, golden mica, or mica from *tāpya*;
just as the essence of mica is digested, so too should one digest the binary compounds (*dvandva*). (Āk 1.4.383)
Then one should digest the ripened seeds of the juice of the seed of the couple (*dvandvabīja*).
(The fruit of digestion: O Goddess, the mortar is called the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*), and the mercury-king (*rasendra*) is called the linga. (Āk 1.4.384)
Rubbing sandalwood is prescribed as its "morsel" (grāsa) for worship;
when the mass of sins is being exhausted, the digestion of mercury (rasajāraṇā) becomes easy. (Āk 1.4.385)
And when *jāraṇā* has been attained, knowledge that bestows liberation arises; O beloved, how can there be liberation as long as one does not know *jāraṇā*? (Āk 1.4.386)
O Dear One, for the lord of practitioners, *jāraṇā* is that which makes liberation manifest;
for the sake of *jāraṇā*, the mercury is held in the fire for as many days as required. (Āk 1.4.387)
He who holds mercury in fire for even one day, or half of that, enjoys happiness in the world of Śiva for as long as a thousand kalpas. (Āk 1.4.388)
His sins, accumulated over many births, are destroyed;
he becomes a friend of Suvarṇaretas, and likewise attains the mercury of a golden body. (Āk 1.4.389)
It does not burn in the fire of the smelter, it is friendly toward water, and it is pure when squeezed through cloth four times its size; such is gold. (Āk 1.4.390)
When the process of straining has occurred and the morsel has emerged entirely without residue, that becomes the sustainer of the staff; then the essence is the digested morsel. (Āk 1.4.391)
Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ phaṭ! O Lord of Taste, for the offering of all sentient beings, seize, seize the morsel! Hrīṃ svāhā! (The melting of the embryo;
the accomplishment of the seed-syllable fit for the melting of the embryo.)
First Category:
I shall now explain the internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) of the processed mercury.
Listen, O Bhairavī, to the seed-substances (*bīja*) suitable for causing internal liquefaction. (Āk 1.4.392)
Equal parts of nāgabhasma, mākṣika, and gandhaka should be powdered and processed by blowing into molten gold that is three times the weight [of the mixture]. (Āk 1.4.393)
This putrid seed melts instantly within the womb of mercury. (The second method: Having repeatedly processed lead with gold while repeatedly adding powdered mica, [the seed is produced]. Āk_1,4.394.
In the Nāgakṣaya hell, one must repeatedly offer a nāga three times over until only gold remains; it must be offered again and again. (Āk 1.4.395)

This seed indeed melts through rubbing within a liquid containing mercury (the third method). One should blow upon equal parts of gold and the essence of *tāpya* placed inside a crucible. (Āk 1.4.396)
While that is melting, one should repeatedly add equal amounts of copper powder;
likewise, three times the amount of the essence of honey (mākṣika-sattva) should be added again and again.
This seed of the lord of mercury dissolves within the womb through rubbing. (The fourth method: Then, one should repeatedly melt an amount of purified iron equal to the gold. Āk 1.4.398.
One should make the leaves prickly with thorns and smear them with salt ground with sour substances and an equal amount of fragrance, O Pārvatī. (Āk 1.4.399)
One should cook those leaves in a crucible until only gold remains;
this is the seed of the lord of mercury (rasendra), which dissolves through rubbing within its womb. Āk 1.4.400.
(Fifth Method) One should grind rock salt (*sindhūttha*) equal in weight to the [mercury] with sour gruel (*amlaka*).
One should cook it in a closed crucible (*saṃpuṭa*), then grind it again and cook it once more. (Āk 1.4.401)
Again and again, twelve times, one should rub this equal amount of ash derived from a snake with acidic liquids upon a gold leaf using this [formula]. (Āk 1.4.402)
Having smeared it repeatedly, one should blow upon it seven times; thereafter, one should cause that [substance] to flow.
First, one should cause it to be infused seven times with the ingredients ground into a paste. (Āk 1.4.403)
This seed of the lord of mercury dissolves within [the crucible] through grinding.
(The sixth method: Ferrous sulfate, borax, sulfur, pyrite, black salt, and realgar; Āk 1.4.404.
One should grind all these together with sour chickpeas for the duration of a day;
by this grinding, the seed of mercury dissolves within its womb. (ĀK 1.4.405)
(The success of the crucible apparatus in causing the melting of the embryo:
Suvarcala, kāsīsa, yavakṣāra, ṭaṅkaṇa, mākṣika, saindhava, cullī, sāmudra, and likewise rājikā. (Āk 1.4.406)
Equal parts of *kāṃkṣī* and camphor, rubbed with the milky sap of *arka* and *snuk*, should be used as a coating for the crucible;
one should apply this along with *viḍa* salt to a thickness of one finger-breadth. (Āk 1.4.407)
This crucible apparatus is excellent for the process of melting the core (garbhadruti); (Methods of Core Melting;
First Method).
Gold, copper, dead iron, and sharpened steel are colored by the ripened seed. (Āk 1.4.408)

One should firmly cause all the seeds that cause the melting of the embryo to circulate; once it has melted, repeatedly blowing while adding the powder of *tāpya* (calamine) again and again. (Āk 1.4.409)
O Goddess of the Gods, as long as the copper and the sharp [impurities] have not been exhausted, this seed of the lord of mercury remains within the womb; through rubbing, it dissolves. (Āk 1.4.410)
(Second Method) Gold that has been struck with gandhaka and the processing of ripened seed— one should smear both of these in a crucible, seal it, and heat it strongly. Āk 1.4.411.
That powder, when sprinkled, melts thoroughly within the liquid *rasagarbha*.
(The third method: When gold has been liquefied, dead copper and sharp iron [are added] very gradually. (Āk 1.4.412)
One should cause it to circulate sixfold until that mercury dissolves, O Beloved;
[this is] the fourth method.
It renders great essences and flavorless substances, as well as depleted metals, inexhaustible. (Āk 1.4.413)
By adding equal parts of copper and sulfur,
one should cause this to be processed hundreds of times until only an inexhaustible residue remains.
An equal portion of the king of essences certainly dissolves within the womb [of the crucible].
(The fifth method:
One-sixty-fourth part of the processed lord of essences. Āk_1,4.415.
One should place the seed for causing the embryo to flow into a heated mortar along with realgar, red orpiment, vitriol, sulphur, blue vitriol, and borax. (Āk 1.4.416)
One should grind all of this with sour chickpea water for the duration of this day;
having added a sixteenth part of this to the mercury, one should cause the seed (bīja) to be given as well. (Āk 1.4.417)
Wherever [the object] is, it dissolves at that very moment.
(The sixth method: One should collect the alkaline ash produced from Apāmārga and Palāśa. (Āk 1.4.418)
Ṭaṅkaṇa, barley-alkali, kāsīsa, suvarcala, sea salt, rock salt, rājī, honey, and navasāra. (Āk 1.4.419)
Equal parts of camphor and honey, rubbed with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, should be used to coat the crucible; one should then proceed with *viḍa* salt as well. (Āk 1.4.420)

One should apply a plaster of one finger's breadth and place the previously prepared [substance] therein; having sealed it, it should be steamed for one day over a fire of dried cow-dung, whereupon it will melt completely. (Āk 1.4.421)

Thus, the substance to be melted is to be processed until the seed is sixfold. (13. External liquefaction) O Śivā, I shall explain to you the ritual of external liquefaction in its proper sequence. Āk_1,4.422.
Listen to the method by which the liquefaction of mica and other minerals occurs.
(The Liquefaction of Mica) Now I shall describe the liquefaction of mica, as well as the bulb of the *kañcukī* plant. (Āk 1,4.423)
One should cast *kapitindu* and hair-oil (*keśataila*) three times each into a crucible; having melted that iron-slag (*abhra-sattva*), it becomes a liquid metal (*druti*). (Āk 1.4.424)

(Regarding the liquefaction of gold: O Dear One, one should repeatedly saturate the fruit-powder of *devadālī*, *śakagopa*, and *aśvalālaka*, along with *ṭaṅkaṇa*, using the juice of *jālinī*. (Āk 1.4.425)

One should melt gold and pour into it a flux equal in weight to the mercury; [this is] the flux of all gems. One should take the three alkalis, sour chickpeas, asafoetida, and amlavetasa. (Āk 1.4.426)
Likewise, having ground *jvālāmukhī* salt with the juice of *sthalakumbhī*, and with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, one should gently [place] the diamond within that globule. (Āk 1.4.427)
One should place that [substance] inside a jambīra fruit and cook it for three days in a dolāyantra; when this is done, the melting of the diamond occurs just like that of mercury. (Āk 1.4.428)
For gems such as rubies and others, there is indeed liquefaction (*druti*).
(Regarding *drutimelāpana*:
O Bhairavī, listen to the true nature of the fusion (*melana*) of these liquefied substances as I describe it. Āk 1.4.429.
Black aloe-wood, musk, *brahmabīja*, honey, woman’s menses, poison, asafoetida, garlic, borax, and turmeric. (Āk 1.4.430)
One should triturate these together with mercury (sūta) that has been liquefied in a heated mortar (taptakhalva).
[The herbs are: pāṭhā, vandhyā, tālamūlī, nīlī, and the three types of citraka. (Āk 1.4.431)
Lotus rhizome, milk-rhizome, *balā*, *guñjā*, fresh ginger, horse saliva, neem leaves, and breast milk—each taken in equal measure. (Āk 1.4.432)
One should cause the clear juice of these, filtered through a cloth, to be taken; having repeatedly added this to mercury combined with fluxes, one should thoroughly rub it. (Āk 1.4.433)
All the fluxes merge into mercury; of this there is no doubt.
By means of that very [mercury] into which the fluxes have merged, one obtains the kacchapa machine. Āk 1.4.434.

One should mix [the substance] with *limpecca* by means of the *biḍa* process and digest it gradually; in this manner, one should cause the mercury-king to digest the flux six times over. (Āk 1.4.435)
(14. Rañjana) Listen, O Pārvatī, to the process of coloring mercury that has been liquefied and matured; therefore, I shall also describe to you the coloring of the coloring-seeds. Āk 1.4.436.
(The Method for Dyeing Oil):
*Palāśa* flower, *mañjiṣṭhā*, red *karavīra* flower, *khadira* flower, red sandalwood, and likewise *kukkuṭī*. (Āk 1.4.437)
For two nights, one should grind together sarala, devadāru, japā flowers, and other red flowers with lac-dye water. (Āk 1.4.438)
This oil, four times the quantity of blood-born red flowers, should be combined with four times the liquid so that oil remains as the final residue. (Āk 1.4.439)
One should sprinkle the seed upon it twenty-one times;
O worshiper of the gods, one should likewise dye all the ripened seeds in this manner. (Āk 1.4.440)
(The coloring of lead seed):
Having taken lead in an iron pan, one should kindle a fierce fire beneath it;
one should cast the seeds of the *palāśa* leaf into it and stir them about. (Āk 1.4.441)
Having rubbed it with a *palāśa* staff for four *yāmas*, it turns to ash.
One should grind that ash together with an equal amount of sulfur in an acidic liquid for one *yāma*. (Āk 1.4.442)

Having sealed it, one should roast it in a *gajapuṭa* fire; when it has cooled by itself, one should remove it, add mercury equal to one-fourth its weight, grind it together, and cook it again in a *puṭa*. (Āk 1.4.443)
In this manner, after seven such cycles, the nāga will become red in color;
one should then take the powder of the five parts of the vāśā plant and the powder of the kakubha tree. Āk 1.4.444.
One should grind together the flowers of the *śigru*, *kiṃśuka*, *koraṇḍa*, and *śāka* plants, along with *nāginī*, *ahimāra*, *kumārī*, and *nāgakanyā*. (Āk 1.4.445)
Having placed all of this—one part of each—and two parts of realgar (manaḥśilā) into a vessel, together with four times as much cow’s urine; (Āk 1.4.446).
One should cook it until only one-quarter remains, repeatedly adding [the ingredients] during the first watch of the night;
one should cook it on the hearth, stirring with Brahma-sticks for seven days. (Āk 1.4.447)
When this mercury (nāga) has been melted in the ripened seed, one should cause it to flow out three times;
thus the seed becomes colored, and it shall be the primary [reagent] for the coloring of mercury. (Āk 1.4.448)
(The method for coloring the seed: One should blow [the fire] upon equal parts of calamine essence and powdered black mica-essence.
When that has melted, one should gradually add calamine powder and dead copper. (Āk 1.4.449)
O Supreme Goddess, that seed becomes threefold and is coloring. (Another method:
One should grind together equal parts of iron sulfate, honey, sulfur, and vermilion. Āk 1.4.450.

O beloved, having ground the group of red substances in cow’s urine, one should grind them in their juice and dry them seven times; then one should powder that and cast it [into the preparation]. (Āk 1.4.451)

Having added equal parts of tin and copper that have been alloyed together, one should melt them strongly; then one should quench them in a mixture of jyotiṣmatī oil and the group of red minerals (raktavarga). Āk 1.4.452.
Furthermore, O beloved, having added an equal amount of the previous powder, one should heat it;
one should sprinkle it in this manner seven times, whereby the seed becomes a colorant for mercury. Āk 1.4.453.
(Another method:

Then, one should liquefy bright and pure sattva with equal proportions [of mercury]. Cinnabar (darada), processed three times in cow’s urine together with the group of red minerals (raktavarga), [is then added]. (Āk 1.4.454)
One should throw an amount equal to that into it and heat it in this manner seven times;
by repeatedly throwing in cinnabar (darada), there shall be the seed that colors mercury. Āk 1.4.455.
(Another method:
One should smelt together equal parts of thick mercury, a snake, and gold;
and in an iron pan, one should also smelt the red group of minerals, along with honey-ore (*mākṣika*), red ochre (*gairika*), and realgar (*śilā*). Āk 1.4.456.

One should grind it finely and sow [the seed] into that [substance] equally and repeatedly; this shall become the seed, which effects the coloring of mercury (*sūtendra*), after ten such cycles. (Āk 1.4.457)
(Another method:
Red-colored realgar should be processed with the juices of *yavaciñcā* twenty times with care; one should then apply it as a paste with that [mixture]. (Āk 1.4.458)
One should cook nāgapatra in a leaf-cup until it reaches the state of powder;
then take three parts of mercury (rasaka) and one part of cinnabar (darada).
Take one part each of realgar, sulphur, and rhinoceros horn;
one should sprinkle them with the sour juice of *mātuluṅga* and apply a paste made from them as an ointment. (Āk 1.4.460)
One should cast that respective previous nāga into the interior of the crucible and then blow it;
once it has melted, one should lift it out, smear the crucible [with the residue], and blow it again. (Āk 1.4.461)
In this manner, the naga [metal] should be smelted seven times until it becomes like gold.
(Another method:
The essence of yellow abhraka and the aforementioned naga [metal], taken in equal parts—Āk 1.4.462.
One should cause the consecrated [substance] to be joined in pairs according to the previous yoga; by means of this dual yoga, the casting of the molten metal should be performed. (Āk 1.4.463)
The seed of the ripened [plant], having been dyed three times, becomes auspicious. (This is the dyeing of the silver-seed.
Now then, O Pārvatī, hear the procedure for the dyeing of silver seeds. Āk_1,4.464.

Piercing) One should grind an equal portion of yellow orpiment with the processed mercury, using the oils of *dhūrta* and the juices of divine herbs for one day. (Āk 1.4.490)

Āk, 1, 5 (The Sequence of Specific Digestion):
Śrī Bhairavī said:
"O Sadāśiva, you have previously described the general process of digestion (*jāraṇā*);
now tell me, O Lord, about the specific digestion, so that I may understand it. (Āk 1.5.1)
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the process of digestion known as *bhūcara* (the earth-walker).
(This is the *bhūcarī* digestion.)
One should mix black, yellow, and red [pigments] with copper and iron. (Āk 1.5.2)
When pure *śulba* (copper) has been digested twenty-two times, one should then gradually mix with it half as much *gandhanāga* (antimony). ĀK 1.5.3.
It should be given together with gold, sixteen parts for each part of mercury;
when the fragrant naga (gandhanāga) is digested, then the mercury becomes bound. (Āk 1.5.4)
When the gold has been digested, one should then dye it with half as much dead metal (mṛtaloha), using copper killed by sulphur, along with pyrite, cinnabar, and iron. (Āk 1.5.5)
One should kill pure gold by means of a *puṭa* [firing]; one should add six times the amount [of the reagent].
When the seed of gold has been digested in the *sūtaka* [mercury], it becomes fourfold. (Āk 1.5.6)
One should recognize it as having bound passion; the mercury becomes gold-colored.
Situated within the *sāraṇā* apparatus, one should cause it to flow together with that very [substance]. (Āk 1.5.7)
Having processed it with one-third [of the additive], one should again cause it to be digested in that very same [substance];
thus it is digested, processed, and then again digested and processed. (Āk 1.5.8)
Through the application of the sevenfold chain, the mercury becomes a "piercer of the peak" (koṭivedhī).
The process of digestion (jāraṇā) pertaining to the earth-dweller (bhūcarī) has been declared; now hear the process of digestion pertaining to the sky-dweller (khecarī). Āk 1.5.9.
One should cause inferior gems to be rendered as the residue of mercury (*rasocchiṣṭa*) through the *khecarī-jāraṇā*;
one should then add seeds of bitter gourd (*kaṭutuṃba*) equal to half of that amount. (Āk 1.5.10)
The wise one should prepare a paste combined with *mahājāra* and place the mercury in the middle of that, inside the mouth of a *vajramūṣā* crucible. (Āk 1.5.11)
Having thus combined *kataka* and gold, one should grind them together; then, one should apply a paste of rubies and cause a "swallow" (*grāsa*) to be given to the mercury. (Āk 1.5.12)
Having bowed to the guru and the deities, and having paid homage to all the Siddhas and especially to the goddesses, one should consume [the substance] with great effort. (Āk 1.5.13)
Then fainting and burning of the limbs arise; of this there is no doubt.

Accompanied by the sounds of conchs and trumpets, together with Siddhas and Vidyādharas,

Then, having been well-polished, cast down, and freed from all defects,

One should digest sharp sulfur and mercury using the tortoise apparatus (*kūrmayantra*);

Having added mica, magnetite, and likewise conch-shell navel, together with the primary and secondary minerals and accompanied by a great fluxing agent (mahājāra). Āk 1.5.34.

in the fourth, it is shaped like a ball; and in the fifth, it has the brilliance of fire. (Āk 1.5.80)

O Goddess of gods, the characteristics of mercury (rasarāja) that has been processed sequentially are as follows: in the sixth stage it is Sūryaprabha, and in the seventh it is Tejaḥpuñja. (Āk 1.5.81)

One should cause [the mercury] to swallow an equal portion, then a double portion, then a fourfold portion, and likewise an eightfold portion, O Goddess; one should thus digest it according to the qualities of the digits (kalās). Āk 1.5.82.
O Goddess, multiplied by thirty-two and then by sixty-four in succession,
the qualities arising from the purificatory rites produce intensity through sweating and purity through rubbing. (Āk 1.5.83)
From *mūrchana* comes freedom from defects; from *utthāna*, the destruction of putrefaction;
from *pātana*, it becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*); and from *rodha*, there is nourishment. (Āk 1.5.84)
Through restraint comes steadiness; through illumination, the fire blazes face-to-face;
through perfuming, there is union with yoga; and through movement, there is the practice of power. (Āk 1.5.85)
From *jāraṇā* comes binding (*bandhana*) properly; from the two types of *drāvaṇa*, oneness (*ekatva*);
from *rañjana*, its redness (*raktatva*); and from the three types of *sāraṇā*, its pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*). (Āk 1.5.86)
You are "Krāmin" because of your power of transference and because of your penetration even into bodies and metals. Āk 1.5.87.
Having bowed her head to Śambhu, the daughter of the Mountain-king questioned him regarding the sequence of piercing the body (dehavedhakrama).
Śrī Bhairavī said: "O Lord, the piercing of the body has previously been described by you in brief. (Āk 1.6.1)
"Explain that piercing of the body so that I may understand it correctly. Śrī Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (Āk 1.6.2)

O Goddess of the Gods, for yogis who are engaged in worldly enjoyments, one should perform the piercing of the body by means of the fivefold medical procedures (pañcakarma), beginning with ripening (pācana). Āk 1.6.3.
(Regarding the five actions; 1. ripening: One should gradually purify the humors aggravated by salt and other [factors].
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, one should consume food with digested essence in that very same sequence. (Āk 1.6.4)
Having become one who eats light food during the day, one should stir these three—small grains, *adhākī*, and ginger—measuring one *pala* each, into water. (Āk 1.6.5)
Having boiled down the remaining eight [ingredients], one should drink it every night for three days;
immediately thereafter, one should drink the decoction of *varā* for three days as before. (Āk 1.6.6)
Thus one should extend the digestive process; then one should perform oleation.
(2. Oleation:
During the day, one should eat rice with ghee and goat's meat in the proper measure. Āk 1.6.7.
During the day, the wise man should eat light food consisting of clarified butter, rice, or mung bean soup;
at night, he should drink cow's ghee mixed with rock salt. (Āk 1.6.8)
One *niṣka* of Saindhava salt and four *niṣkas* of ghee, along with oil of *bhṛṅga* and *āmalaka*, one should sprinkle over the entire body. (Āk 1.6.9)
In this manner, one should perform oleation for seven days; it is supremely beneficial. (3.
Fomentation) Fish, meat, black gram, sesame, barley, and *jāmalaka* flour—Āk 1.6.10.
All this would constitute one *prastha* [measure] of *ekāṣṭhīlā*, *aguru*, *balā*, *rāsnā*, *vyāghrī*, *ghanāpatra*, *kauśikā*, *ativiṣā*, and *niśā*. (Āk 1.6.11)
The wise person should place all of this—two pala each of curd, milk, water, and sour gruel—into a clay vessel containing two āḍhaka of [the base substance] and boil it together. Āk 1.6.12.
One should cause his body to be steamed by its heat for the duration of two ghaṭikās;
one should perform this sudation for seven days, as it is supremely beneficial. (Āk 1.6.13)

(4. Emesis) One fruit of *madana* and sixteen parts of water should be boiled down until one-fourth remains; once that water has been strained through a cloth, [the following should be added]. (Āk 1.6.14)
One should add one *karṣa* each of long pepper (*pippalī*), *indrayava*, liquorice (*yaṣṭī*), and salt;
drinking this in the morning will cause vomiting that destroys all diseases. (Āk 1.6.15)

(5. Purgation) One should finely grind together mercury, borax, sulphur, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) in equal parts, along with an amount of *jepāla* equal to all of these. Āk 1.6.16.
One should consume a dose of exactly two *guñjā* seeds together with jaggery;
this is declared to be a purgative that destroys all diseases. (Āk 1.6.17)
This is declared as the "fivefold action" (*pañcakarma*); one should perform it in sequence for the purpose of purgation.
(Regarding the formulations for cleansing the *doṣas*:
one should drink one *kuḍuba* daily of *ketakī*, breast-milk, and *jambīra*. Āk_1,6.18.
For seven days, in the morning, one should remove the defect of saltiness by adding one pala of triphalā into sixteen palas of water. (Āk 1.6.19)

One should boil that [mixture] until one-fourth remains; when it has cooled, one should drink one *pala* of honey from it for three days in the morning. This is the supreme remedy for removing the defects caused by alkaline substances. (Āk 1.6.20)
One should drink *viḍaṅga* together with *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and the fruit of *ketakī*, boiled for three days; when drunk, it removes the disorder of acidity (*amladoṣa*). (Āk 1.6.21)
Alternatively, one should drink for three days a mixture of one *pala* of the juice of *tintriṇī* and alkaline water, combined with one *karṣa* each of *yavakṣāra* and sugar. (Āk 1.6.22)
This destruction of the defects of acidity has been described in the context of *rasāyana*.
[One should take] one *karṣa* each of *vacā*, *biḍālapādī*, *pālāśa* seeds, and *jantughna*. (Āk 1.6.23)
One should consume one karṣa of jaggery and all of that [powder] together, and drink warm water;
if this is done for three days in the morning, it will result in the expulsion of worms. (Āk 1.6.24)
Śyāmā, agni, viḍaṅga, vāśā, trikaṭu, the three fruits (phalatraya), rock salt (saindhava), devadāru, and mustā—each of these should be taken in equal parts. (Āk 1.6.25)
One should lick one karṣa of these with ghee every morning; within seven days, it conquers all diseases. Having thus purified the body, one should eat śāli rice with milk. (Āk 1.6.26)

Having attained perfect strength, one should then employ the elixir (*rasāyana*): [the fruit] produced from the celestial tree, combined with milk, clarified butter, *āmalaka* juice, and honey. (The Application of the Elixir) Āk 1.6.27.
Having extracted oil from all of that, one should drink two palas of it every day;
within a month, beauty and intelligence will surely arise—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.6.28)
In the second month, one should drink that which was previously mentioned, four *palas* of it;
by this, the humors and the disorders arising in the eyes are pacified. (Āk 1.6.29)
Furthermore, in the third month, one should consume a dose of six *palas*; by that, one will surely attain a divine body and become possessed of great splendor. (Āk 1.6.30)
(The Procedure for Consuming Āroṭa Mercury):
Now, O Supreme Goddess, the āroṭa mercury should be consumed gradually;
it has been precipitated and killed in sequence from iron, copper, mica, and silver. (Āk 1.6.31)

This mercury, the essence of the Arōṭaka, is the supreme means for achieving the perfection of the body; it is mercury that has been refined by the seven purificatory processes, beginning with sweating. (Āk 1.6.32)
O Goddess, the *sūta* known as *tvāroṭaka* is exhilarating and intoxicating;
it is excellent for alchemy (*rasāyana*) and the pacification of diseases, bestowing all virtuous qualities. (Āk 1.6.33)
One should consume equal parts of kānta-loha, abhra-sattva, and āroṭa, along with two guñjās each, together with honey, ghee, and triphalā, for one month. (Āk 1.6.34)
In this manner, it should be consumed gradually according to the sequence of two, three, four, five, and six [guñjās] per day;
thus, by the end of sixteen months, the dose reaches sixteen guñjās. (Āk 1.6.35)
And if one should prepare it thus with the juice of *āroṭaka* for my beloved, dear as life, he shall be freed from wrinkles and graying hair and live for a hundred autumns. (Āk 1.6.36)
(Āroṭarasa):
Having equalized iron essence, mica essence, and mercury digested with gold, one should likewise add the *āroṭaka* [catalyst] to all of this. (Āk 1.6.37)
For this is the preparation of the field that brings about a lifespan of a thousand years;
a seed sown in unsuitable ground does not sprout anywhere. (Āk 1.6.38)
Therefore, he who applies the impurity (sūtaka) without first preparing the field will not find his merit to sprout, just as a seed does not grow in saline soil. Āk 1.6.39.
(The Procedure for the Use of Mercury Bound in a Casing):

I shall now describe in due order the supreme method for the mercury bound in a casing as previously mentioned, as well as the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), along with its prescriptions and prohibitions. (Āk 1.6.40)
Listen attentively, O Pārvatī; out of affection for you, I shall tell you of the supreme transmuting agent (*krāmaṇa*) for mercury: lovely women, clouds, gold, and diamonds. (Āk 1.6.41)
Without transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), the mercury will not succeed in [the transformation of] the body or metals.
A dose the size of a *guñjā* seed, bound into a pill (*khoṭabaddha*) and combined with honey for transmutation, [should be used]. (Āk 1.6.42)
One should practice in this manner for one month, and then again according to the prescribed sequence up to sixteen months, just as in the case of the essence of the roasted grain.
He attains a lifespan of a hundred years, freed from all diseases; by using even a single *pala* [of this medicine], he is not overcome by illnesses. (Āk 1.6.44)
In the second [month] there shall be an increase of semen; in the third he becomes strong;
in the fourth he destroys gray hair; in the fifth he conquers wrinkles. (Āk 1.6.45)
In the sixth [repetition], one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing and an eloquent speaker; in the seventh, the eye diseases are removed;
in the eighth, one attains the vision of Tārkṣya, the lifespan of Brahmā, and the prowess of Brahmā. (Āk 1.6.46)
If one employs nine palas, there will be the attainment of success (*siddhi*) and the gathering of powers;
if one employs ten palas, one becomes a second Śaṅkara. (Āk 1.6.47)
O beloved, a person should consume mercury the size of a *māṣa* bean to attain a lifespan of a thousand years;
one should consume mercury the size of a barley grain to attain a lifespan of ten thousand years. (Ākāśabhairava Tantra 1.6.48)

A wise person should consume mercury the size of a grain of rice to attain a lifespan of one hundred thousand years; when consuming it for ten million years, he should eat it the size of a mung bean. (Āk 1.6.49)
All this transmutation of the essences (rasas) should be performed as previously described;
that mercury (sūta), bestowing a lifespan of a thousand years, brings about the state of Brahman. (Āk 1.6.50)
The elixir that bestows a lifespan of ten thousand years grants the state of Viṣṇu, and the elixir that bestows a lifespan of a hundred thousand years brings about the state of Rudra. (Āk 1.6.51)

The processed mercury (*sūta*) bestows a lifespan of ten million years and also grants the state of Śiva; moreover, mercury matured in honey (*mākṣīka*) truly bestows the status of the Giver of Wealth (*Dhanada*). (Āk 1.6.52)

When digested by pure silver, it bestows the state of Indra; when digested by mica, it grants the nature of the Sun; when digested by copper, it confers the status of Brahmā; and when processed with silver, it yields the state of Viṣṇu. (Āk 1.6.53)
When processed with gold, mercury bestows the state of Rudra; when processed with diamond, it bestows the state of Īśa;
and when processed by means of liquefaction, it bestows the state of Sadāśiva. (Āk 1.6.54)
The state of being of the nature of Truth-Consciousness-Bliss is attained through the *sūtaka* [elixir] processed with the seed;
however, by means of the common *tīkṣṇa* [elixer], a man attains the state of Rudra. (Āk 1.6.55)
In this way, whoever should consume the digested iron—that is, the mercury reduced to ash—will become water-like by means of water and attain the state of dry land by means of dry land. (Āk 1.6.56)

O Goddess, by your splendor you are the essence of fire, and by the wind you assume the form of air; you are yourself the manifest agent and destroyer, the one who bestows both curses and grace. (Āk 1.6.57)
Wherever the practitioner discards urine or feces, even a stone or a piece of clay touched there becomes gold. (Āk 1.6.58)
From the perspiration of that body, one should pierce eight metals;
all of that becomes divine gold when twelve *pala*s have been consumed. (Āk 1.6.59)
Alternatively, one should consume the burnt mercury (bhasmasūtaka) along with silver, copper, tin, and bell-metal; through its sweating, they attain the state of silver. Āk 1.6.60.
Alternatively, one should consume sharp, well-digested mercury-ash;
when tin is touched by its urine, it attains the state of silver. (Āk 1.6.61)
O Goddess, by each single application, the immobilization of lead and mercury occurs; one should consume a dose of mercury the size of a *guñjā* seed that has been processed with gold. (Āk 1.6.62)
Two *guñjās* of [mercury] processed with silver (*tāra*) and three [guñjās] of [mercury] processed with copper (*ravija*);
one *māṣa* of sharp iron (*tīkṣṇa*), mica (*abhraka*), and magnetite (*kānta*), or it may be one or two *guñjās*. (Āk 1.6.63)
One should consume digested vajra and vaikrānta, measured at the size of a mustard seed, combined with lead, tin, fat, insects, poison, and artificial poisons. (Āk 1.6.64)

One should forcibly expel the bound medicinal paste mixed with urine during the process of *rasāyana*, once it has gradually become fire-resistant through the absorption of gold and silver. (Āk 1.6.65)
And this king of essences, when bound, becomes the bestower of the perfection of the body;
[it consists of] vajra, magnetite, mākṣika, vaikrānta, abhraka, and gold. (Āk 1.6.66)
Aged by these [substances], mercury is recommended for *rasāyana* according to what is available;
likewise, exactly six secondary minerals (*uparasa*) are intended for consumption in *rasāyana*. (ĀK 1.6.67)
One should consume one pala of well-burnt, aged ashes; for ten thousand years, he lives with a body as firm as a diamond. (Āk 1.6.68)
And thus one should consume twelve palas of the digested *tīkṣṇa* [mercury];
living in this manner for a great kalpa, one shall go to Śiva at the end of the dissolution. (Āk 1.6.69)
By one pala of the ash that has digested iron wire, one attains the lifespan of Brahmā;
by two palas, the lifespan of Viṣṇu; and by three palas, the lifespan of Rudra. (Āk 1.6.70)
But in the fourth case, O Goddess, a man shall attain the state of Śiva once three *pala* of the golden-aging ash-elixir have been consumed in succession. (Āk 1.6.71)
Eighty-eight thousand yoginīs, arrogant with pride, remain as his servants; such a man may become one who can assume any form at will. (Āk 1.6.72)
Whatever form one meditates upon, one shall assume that very form;
wherever [the meditations] dissolve, there alone does the accomplishment dissolve. Āk 1.6.73.
O Goddess of Gods, when twelve *māṣa* of gold ash have been consumed, one should take a dose of the size of a single *guñjā*, having ascertained one's own digestive strength (*agnibala*). (Āk 1.6.74)
One should eat betel-leaf with ghee and honey and enjoy a beloved woman;
for when the *bhasmasūtaka* has been consumed, even a subtle fault becomes one indeed.
O fair-limbed one, after three weeks, a man becomes blinded by passion;
within a single day, he may agitate a thousand women. (Āk 1.6.76)
O lady of excellent hips, through union with a woman, impurity (sūtaka) spreads throughout the body;
O Goddess, without union with a woman, even his indigestion is digested. Āk 1.6.77.
If the semen is discharged through sexual intercourse, a danger to life arises within three weeks; therefore, one should abstain from sexual intercourse for that duration. (Āk 1.6.78)
Conversation with a young woman should be carried out, as should the massaging of her limbs;
for by the mere touch of her, the *rasa* permeates the body. (Āk 1.6.79)
Just as the sight of a beautiful woman brings delight, so does that *sūtaka* (the impurity of birth) instantly take hold, O Goddess of Gods. (Āk 1.6.80)
O Goddess, the support of that [vagina] which is like a holy fig tree (aśvattha), being even and auspicious—such indeed is the vulva (bhaga) in the vessel of alchemy (rasāyana). Āk 1.6.81.
One whose vulva is fleshless, elongated, and likewise withered and veiny—one who causes suffering and poverty—should be avoided in the practice of *rasāyana*. (Āk 1.6.82)

On a bright fortnight, on an auspicious day endowed with the strength of the moon and stars, at a favorable moment, the twice-born man, having meditated upon Śiva, the sacrificial fire, the Brahmins, and his guru, [should proceed]. (Āk 1.6.83)

Being contented and of a cheerful mind, one should consume the mercury that bestows success. An excellent application for inducing its movement (*krāmaṇa*) is a nasal drop (*nasya*) consisting of milk, gold, and ginger. (Āk 1.6.84)
Collyrium made from the six metals, beginning with gold, is the supreme *krāmaṇa* (transmuting agent).
Hereafter, I shall explain what is beneficial and what is harmful regarding the consumption of mercury (*rasasevā*). (On the wholesome and unwholesome in the service of mercury) Āk 1.6.85.
Red rice, wheat, cow's milk, ghee, curd, meat from wild animals, mung beans, sugar, honey, and rock salt. (Āk 1.6.86)
Haṃsodaka, vāstuka, meghanāda, punarnavā, paṭola, alābu, kadalī, dhānyaka, ikṣu, and pomegranate. (Āk 1.6.87)
One should always consume coconut water and betel-leaf;
and one should anoint oneself with sandalwood, saffron, and musk. (Āk 1.6.88)
Fragrant flowers, soft beds, beloved women, discourse on the knowledge of the auspicious Self, gentle speech, and a state of ease. (Āk 1.6.89)
Divine and pure garments, a shadow that moves only slightly, the recitation of the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, joy, gentle laughter, and purity. (Āk 1.6.90)
Beholding dance, listening to song, worshipping Śiva, saluting the gods, the fire, the guru, and the brahmins, and the preservation of the sacred revelation. (Āk 1.6.91)
Concentration, compassion for living beings, truthful speech, and that which is beneficial and pleasant—such activity of speech, body, and mind leads to the cessation of suffering. (Āk 1.6.92)
All this, O beloved, regarding the transmutation (*krāmaṇa*) of the lord of mercury (*rasendra*), has been told;
now listen, O beloved, as I describe what is harmful for the consumption of mercury. (Āk 1.6.93)
Excessive eating, excessive drinking, excessive sleep, and excessive wakefulness; eating at improper times, excessive attachment to women, and even total lack of attachment. (Āk 1.6.94)
Inappropriate laughter and derision, joy, anger, excessive longing, much talk, playing in water, suffering, and excessive brooding; (Āk 1.6.95)
Kaliṅga, kāravella, kūṣmāṇḍa, and likewise karkaṭī; kākamācī, kulattha, kārkoṭī, and kusumbhikā. (Āk 1.6.96)
Sesame, linseed oil, black gram, pigeon pea, and lentils; buttermilk with rice, fermented grain-water, and that which is bitter, pungent, sour, or salty. (Āk 1.6.97)
Alkali, honey, slimy substances, and pitta-inducing parūṣaka; preparations of buffalo milk, vidara, and mango. (Āk 1.6.98)
Eating offerings consisting of oranges, bilva fruits, lakuca fruits, and śigru;
touching fire; and striking cows or brahmins with one's feet. (Āk 1.6.99)
Beating maidens, young horses, cattle, and the like; the killing of living beings; and even the cutting down of trees—these constitute a grave sin (pātaka). Āk 1.6.100.

The seven vices beginning with dice, the shadow of an *aśvattha* tree and a *kapittha* tree, as well as a phallic emblem, a woman, a hellish being, a bed, a leopard, and a *vibhītaka* tree. (Āk 1.6.101)
One should discharge feces and urine in a place away from crossroads, and [avoid] Śiva, the twice-born, gurus, women, heroes, and those of self-restraint. (Āk 1.6.102)

For those who have heard the *samaya*, for rivers, sacred bathing places, waters, and men, [there is no fault] regarding onion, asafoetida, garlic, black mustard, and the two types of *bṛhatī*. (Āk 1.6.103)
Nishpāva beans, leaping, applying ointments, the night, ornaments, and being delighted;
sleep, wine, spirits, cocks, and the flesh of aquatic creatures. (Āk 1.6.104)
Sharp, hot, heavy, constipating, dry, and parched meat; honey;
eating from plantain leaves or bronze vessels; and exposure to the heat. (Āk 1.6.105)
These groups of substances are prohibited in the practice of *rasāyana*.
If one should consume them through negligence, diseases born of unwholesome habits arise, and transformation [or decay] occurs instantaneously. (Āk 1.6.106)
When mercury is undigested, there may occur emaciation, fainting, vertigo, fever, exhaustion, trembling, obstruction of feces and urine, colic, and shivering. (Āk 1.6.107)
Insomnia, lethargy, hiccups, coughing, labored breathing, yawning, loss of appetite, diarrhea, and stiffness of the limbs, eyes, and belly. (Āk 1.6.108)
In the chest, ears, belly, feet, penis, head, and joints, there indeed arise burning sensations, a breaking pain in the limbs, and all other diseases. (Āk 1.6.109)
This formulation is now described by me for the purpose of pacifying indigestion caused by [excessive] rasa:
*rājakośātakī*, *puṅkhā*, *garuḍī*, and *kāravallikā*. (Āk 1.6.110)
Kārkoṭī, kākamācī, devadālī, and parājitā—each of these one pala, in four palas of cow urine. (Āk 1.6.111)
One should boil [the ingredients] until one-fourth remains, then add one karṣa of clear rock salt;
one should drink that decoction, which is beneficial for indigestion caused by meat. (Āk 1.6.112)
One shall become happy after three days; the transference of the mercury occurs.
The mercury causes pain in that particular limb; one should thoroughly massage it. (Āk 1.6.113)
Or, O slender-limbed one, the Rasa flows unhindered through the breast; (this is the piercing of the seven constituents).
First, O Goddess, is the piercing of the skin; second is the piercing of the blood. (Āk 1.6.114)
The third would be the piercing of the flesh, the fourth the piercing of the fat; the fifth would be the piercing of the bone, and the sixth consists of the marrow. (Āk 1.6.115)
The seventh is the piercing of the white [element]; likewise, the eighth is the piercing of the channels (nāḍī).
The ninth is the piercing of the eyes, and the tenth is the all-pervading piercing.

Through the transmutation by mercury (rasavedha), lead becomes gold; through the transmutation by copper (raktavedha), tin becomes gold; and through the transmutation by meat (māṃsavedha), steel becomes gold. (Āk 1.6.117)

Through the piercing of the marrow (medas), the thread becomes gold; through the piercing of the bone, silver; through the piercing of the marrow (majjan), it becomes gold; and through the piercing of the metals, they become gold. (Āk 1.6.118)
O Dear One, by piercing with white [mercury], an earthen vessel becomes gold;
when the semen has been digested by the diamond [vajra] and the marrow has been processed with mica, it pierces [the metal]. (Āk 1.6.119)
Gold-digested mercury, O beloved, pierces the bone; silver-digested mercury pierces the marrow;
lead-digested mercury pierces the fat; and mercury [digested with] iron pierces the flesh. (Ākāśabhairava Tantra 1.6.120)
When digested by *śulba*, it is a "piercer of red"; when digested by *kānta*, it consists of mercury;
when bound by *tīkṣṇa*, it has a blue luster; and with copper, it possesses a reddish radiance. (Āk 1.6.121)

Resembling the moon when made of silver, and possessing the brilliance of gold when made of gold, the smoke-observing [practice], when placed in the mouth, leads to the state of moving through the sky after one month. (Āk 1.6.122)
But when held in the mouth, it pierces by touch and bestows perfection after two months;
with three months it pierces a hundred crores, and with four months it pierces ten crores. (Āk 1.6.123)
With five [months] one becomes a piercer of ten million; with eight, furthermore, ten thousand;
with nine months, a thousand; and with ten months, a hundred. (Āk 1.6.124)
Through contact with his urine, feces, phlegm, and bodily impurities, whatever metals exist upon the earth attain the state of gold. (Āk 1.6.125)
By piercing with sixty-four parts during the eleventh month, and by piercing with thirty-two parts after a year, one should pierce the body. (Āk 1.6.126)
Completely freed from all diseases and devoid of wrinkles and grey hair, he cannot be cut by weapons nor burned by fire. (Āk 1.6.127)
Possessing the speed of the wind and great splendor, like a second god of love, he becomes visible by his own will and likewise becomes invisible. (Āk 1.6.128)
By the mere touch of which all metals turn to gold—
even when that world has perished in a single, terrible ocean, and both the stationary and moving beings have vanished.
Where the gods dissolve, there the perfected one (siddha) likewise dissolves.
Āk, 1, 7 (The Origin of Rubies and Other Jewels):
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, in a cave, were the Daughter of the Mountain and the Lord.
Let them remain for a long time playing together, each desiring to conquer the other. (Āk 1.7.1)
Then a great flow of semen in the form of mercury occurred between the two;
by the power of that flow, the stones became pierced. (Āk 1.7.2)
Rubies and other precious gems, metals such as gold and the like, minerals beginning with sulfur, divine stones, medicinal herbs, and creepers. (Āk 1.7.3)
Of all those previously mentioned, which are of various colors, many kinds, and bestowers of various siddhis, the great vajra is the most excellent. Āk 1.7.4.
O Goddess, I shall describe to you in due order its birth, characteristics, ritual refinement, worship, and fruit; listen attentively, O beloved. (Āk 1.7.5)
(The characteristics of the vajra and the divisions of the vajra:
The twice-born, the kṣatriyas, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras follow in order;
they are white, red, yellowish, and black, as well as various other kinds. (Āk 1.7.6)
O beloved, they should be known in sequence as female, male, and neuter;
they are white, filled with fruit, luminous, and most excellent. (Āk 1.7.7)
But those [lines] devoid of seed-syllables (bīja) should be known as male;
they are rich in strength, endowed with sattva, and serve as the cause for the progression of the metals. (Āk 1.7.8)
They quickly bind the mercury and bestow success upon all;
they produce elixirs, nourish the body, and indeed grant the eight supernatural powers. (Āk 1.7.9)
Those women are remembered as radiant with the seed-syllables of the six corners;
they bestow physical luster, procreation, enjoyment, splendor, and happiness. (Āk 1.7.10)
O Leader of the Gods, one should know that those who are long, triangular, and slender are neuter; they have diminished vitality, little vigor, and are prone to wandering. (Āk 1.7.11)
The eunuchs [are for] those who are neuter; women [are for] women; men are beneficial to all.
They possess qualities corresponding to their birth, such that their energy, their nature, and their virtues are alike. (Āk 1.7.12)
Just as they possess beauty, so too do the twice-born practice moral conduct;
thus they destroy wrinkles, gray hair, and disease, while the kṣatriyas remove death itself.
The Vaiśyas provide stability to the body; the [Rājanya] ones effect the transmutation of metals;
the Śūdras arrest the aging process and destroy various diseases. (Āk 1.7.14)
(Vajra-consecration:
Now I shall speak of the vajra-consecration; listen, O beloved!
[The plants] Śyāmā, Śamī, Meghanādā, Varṣābhū, Dhūrtaka, and Kodrava. (Āk 1.7.15)
Meṣaśṛṅgī, ākhukarṇī, kuluttha, amlavetasa, madana, agasti, and nirguṇḍī—[the preparation] is joined with the fresh juices of these. (Āk 1.7.16)

One should cook it for a day in a dolāyantra (swinging vessel) placed inside the bulb of a vyāghrī plant; then, having extracted it, one should coat it with buffalo dung and heat it over a fire of dried cow-dung. (Āk 1.7.17)

One should burn it for four watches of the night, and at the end of the night, one should sprinkle [the site] with horse urine, the milk of the *snuhī* plant, and the juice of *kulattha* beans. (Āk 1.7.18)
One should cook, burn, and likewise sprinkle [the seeds] seven times; thus, those born of the twice-born classes become purified and grant success. (Āk 1.7.19)
(Vajrarasāyana) O Goddess of the Suras, I shall describe the vajra-ash, which is fit for an elixir: vaikrānta, tāpya, gandhāśman, śilā, mākṣika, and tālaka. (Āk 1.7.20)
One should grind together antimony, ṭaṅkaṇa salt, and the bones of a crab; having placed this mixture into a ball with breast milk, one should then put it into a crucible. (Āk 1.7.21)
One should first heat it very intensely and afterwards cook it in a "gaja-puṭa" (elephant-seal) furnace;
taking that very same *vajra*, within that [furnace] measuring sixteen *mātrās*.
One part of mercury, processed with the ripened seed [of the plant], should be rubbed with breast milk; these two should then be cooked again in a *gajapuṭa* fire. (Āk 1.7.23)
Thus, from that sixteen-fold [process], one should make that vajra firm, endowed with the essence of digested seeds; it shall become an elixir (rasāyana) of ashes. Āk 1.7.24.
Listen, O Rudrāṇī, I shall describe the divine vajra-rasāyana;
one should perform the ritual for the purification of the body and so forth as previously stated. (Āk 1.7.25)
On an auspicious lunar mansion and at a favorable moment, endowed with the strength of the moon and stars,
one should first worship Śiva, Agni, the Guru, the cow, the Brahmin, and the physician.
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, one should consume that ash in the measure of a barley grain, along with one *guñjā* measure of the essence of mica and gold ash. (Āk 1.7.27)

Having purified his body, he should lick [the powder] with honey and ghee in the morning, consisting of one, two, three, or four parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā), for a period of sixteen months. (Āk 1.7.28)
Having increased [the dose] every month up to sixteen barley-grains,
one should likewise follow the sequence of increasing by a *guñjā* for the triad of ashes beginning with *kānta*.
O beloved of mine, one should take two niṣkas of powdered triphalā along with ghee and honey as desired; the previously mentioned ritual restrictions should be abandoned. Āk 1.7.30.
If one consumes even a single *pala* of vajra-ash daily in due course, it destroys wrinkles, gray hair, and disease, and bestows a lifespan of a hundred years. (Āk 1.7.31)
With two palas one lives for a thousand years; likewise, with three palas for ten thousand;
with four palas the lifespan is a hundred thousand; and with five palas, it is a million. (Āk 1.7.32)
A lifespan of ten million years and six palas; the lifespan of the Lord of the Gods (Indra) as the seventh;
the lifespan of Brahmā as eight palas; and the state of Viṣṇu as nine palas. (Āk 1.7.33)
O Goddess, the state of Rudra is the tenth; beyond that is the state of Īśvara;
and in the twelfth [state], he fully bestows the state of Sadāśiva and adamantine ashes. (Āk 1.7.34)
Omniscience, omnipresence, and likewise wandering at will—
this I shall proclaim as the Vajra-food, the supreme elixir for well-being. (Vajraudana) Āk 1.7.35.
Once the vajra has been purified as before, one should begin the soft ritual:
it should be placed within a mother-vāhaka bird and wrapped in the flesh of a partridge. (Āk 1.7.36)

One should then wrap that again with the juices of *tīkṣṇaka*, *antānana*, and *rasa*, separately in each of the following: horse gram (*kulattha*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), rice-water (*nīra*), and *kodrava* grain. (Āk 1.7.37)
One should cook it thus for three days and then wrap that vajra with the leaves of betel that has been growing for three years, or else with those of cotton. (Āk 1.7.38)

The movement [of the semen] situated between the knees, which becomes soft after two watches (yāma), is called "Vajra-food" (vajraudana); now "Vajra-fluidity" (vajradruti) is being described. (Āk 1.7.39)
(Vajradruti):
The three alkalis, chickpea sour, asafoetida, and *amlavetasa*; *jvālāmukhī* and *ikṣuraka*, together with the juice of *sthalakumbhī*. (Āk 1.7.40)
Having ground together the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, one should place the diamond gently into that mass;
then, having placed it in a *jambīra* fruit, one should cook it for three days in a *dolāyantra*. (Āk 1.7.41)
When this is done, the diamond undergoes liquefaction like [other] metals.
(The extension of the process for liquefying other substances:
When this is done, the liquefaction of gems such as rubies and others likewise occurs. Āk 1.7.42.
Just as ores such as mica and other minerals certainly melt when this is done, so too do mercury, gems, and pearls, along with *amlavetasa*, melt. (Āk 1.7.43)
One should cultivate it for seven days in the heat and then place it in a citron;
after three weeks in a heap of grain, it becomes thoroughly liquefied through the process of *puṭapāka*. (Āk 1.7.44)
(The Qualities of Vajra Ash:
O lady of excellent limbs, just as it is with the vajra, so too with its liquefaction and softness; the ash becomes a conqueror of old age, poverty, and death. Āk 1.7.45.
In the case of *rasāyana*, there is happiness arising from the softness of the ash and the liquefaction;
however, in *rasāyana* the [result] is male and female, whereas in *krāmaṇa* it is neuter. (Āk 1.7.46)
Possessing the six tastes and cooling potency, it destroys all diseases, pacifies all humors, and is a source of all happiness—an elixir of life. (Āk 1.7.47)

It bestows the brilliance of lightning, firmness of body, clarity, and smoothness; it is emollient, promotes beauty, strength, and longevity, and destroys the misfortune brought by the planets. (Āk 1.7.48)
The purification of vaikrānta is like that of diamond, using clay, cow-urine, and ash;
its varieties include gold. Now I shall describe the most excellent elixir of mercury (*hemarasāyana*); listen! (Āk 1.7.49)

The origin of gold was explained previously; nevertheless, it may be of three kinds: one arises from the transmutation by mercury (*rasavedha*), while the other originates from a [natural] field (*kṣetra*). Āk 1.7.50.
And another [type] arises from an alloy of metals; these are respectively superior, middling, and inferior, and they are yellow, red, and yellow-red in color.
Saffron, white, and red [are used] during the processes of rubbing, cutting, and heating;
such is the divine gold for the purification of gold, made into a plate and reduced to small fragments. (Āk 1.7.52)
Halinī, kañcukī, kanda, snuhī, arka, agnikarañjaka, dhūrta, guñjā, iṅgudī, cīra, mūla, tāla, and aśvagandhikā; Āk 1.7.53.
Having ground this indravāruṇī and its roots with buttermilk, one should smear gold plates with it and heat them in the fire. (Āk 1.7.54)

One should immerse it seven times each in urine, stirred oil, water with *kulattha* beans, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and in the midst of *jambīra* juice and the milk of the sun-plant (*arka*). (Āk 1.7.55)
One should smear, heat, and sprinkle [the substance] repeatedly, even up to seven times; [using] ant-hill earth, the essence of soot, brick, and strong red ochre. (Āk 1.7.56)
Having ground together four-colored *abhraka*, *tāpya*, *darada*, *tālaka*, and *śilā* with the juice of *jambīra* and having smeared it onto a leaf, one should seal it in a *puṭa*. (Āk 1.7.57)
O Goddess of the Gods, having ground together kānta, kaṅkuṣṭha, mercury, vimalā, sūta, and bhūlatā with sour gruel, one should prepare pills weighing one niṣka each. (Āk 1.7.58)
One should not make it less than four *palas*, nor more than four *palas*.
The gold and copper, having been rolled together, should be melted until they are made uniform. (Āk 1.7.59)

Into that [mixture], once it has become liquid, one should drop each pill individually; ten times the amount of gold should be applied externally, and the pills should be dried in due order. (Āk 1.7.60)
One should blow upon it slowly in this manner until only the gold remains;
that becomes pure, divine, and the remover of old age, death, and disease. (Āk 1.7.61)
Gold resembling the leaf of the *ciñcā* tree, a purified gold leaf, and mercury—
one should grind these together in a secluded place with acidic liquids and then apply that paste. (Āk 1.7.62)
One should heat a paste made from equal parts of sulphur and mercury inside a crucible;
then, one should add a sixteenth part of the mercury ash to the gold powder. (Āk 1.7.63)
One should grind it thoroughly with sour juice and cook it in a *bhūdhara* crucible;
in this manner, one should add the mercury at each firing until sixteen cycles are completed. (Āk 1.7.64)
This mercury-ash, when processed (*niruttha*), becomes the bestower of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). [This is] the gold elixir (*hemarasāyana*).
Having purified the body through purgatives, emetics, and so forth, on an auspicious day— (Āk 1.7.65)
One should worship the Lord, the Brahmins, the sacred fire, the guru, and the physician as one's foremost;
with a pure heart, one should partake of the divine elixir of gold. (Āk 1.7.66)
One should lick the mercury-ash and the iron-ash, each measuring one *guñjā*, along with the gold-ash measuring one *māṣa*, mixed with the best honey and clarified butter. (Āk 1.7.67)
As previously stated, up to the sixteenth month of the vajra stage, the practitioner of *rasāyana* should perform the procedure while abandoning the previously mentioned rules. (Āk 1.7.68)
Listen, O Daughter of the Mountain, to the wonderful method of service regarding the golden elixir (*hemarasāyana*): by consuming a single *pala*, one becomes free from all diseases. (Āk 1.7.69)
Then, O Dear One, by the application of two *pala*s, one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair; and with three *pala*s, there shall be perfection of speech and divine vision. (Āk 1.7.70)
By the use of four *pala*s, one is indeed not afraid of poison, tigers, or snakes;
likewise, by five *pala*s alone, one attains divine self-knowledge. (Āk 1.7.71)

O Goddess, by means of the six-pala formulation, the state of Siddha and Sādhya shall be attained; likewise, by means of the seven-pala formulation, the state of a Vidyādhara shall be attained. Āk 1.7.72.
Likewise, through the union of eight *palas*, one becomes adept in moving about at will;
and even with a ninth *pala*, one is endowed with the qualities of the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*).
Likewise, O Goddess, by ten palas one may attain the status of Mahendra;
with eleven palas, one attains the state of Brahmā—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.7.74)
O beloved, with twelve *palas* one attains the state of Viṣṇu, and with thirteen *palas* one may reach the station of Rudra. (Āk 1.7.75)
Likewise, with fourteen *pala*s one attains the state of Īśvara;
with fifteen *pala*s one reaches the supreme state of Sadāśiva. (Āk 1.7.76)
Likewise, with sixteen *palas*, there may be the embodiment of Being-Consciousness-Bliss;
he is the omniscient one, the creator of all, the destroyer, the protector, and the omnipresent one. (Āk 1.7.77)
(The Alchemy of Gold) I shall now proclaim the alchemy of gold; listen, O Pārvatī, at this moment!
The fruit-dust of *devadālī*, *śakragopa*, and *aśvalālikā*— Āk 1.7.78.
O Dear One, one should saturate borax many times with the juice of *jālinī*;
there, one should melt gold and cast [the powder] equal in weight to mercury (*sūta*) into it. (Āk 1.7.79)
One should prepare this elixir like gold, using ash as the service;
it is sweet, bitter, and astringent, cold and hot, a rejuvenative tonic. (Āk 1.7.80)
It is pleasing to the heart, bestows luster, is pure, beneficial for the eyes, heavy, and scraping;
it grants fortitude, memory, longevity, health, policy, and success in speech. (Āk 1.7.81)
It destroys diseases such as consumption and insanity, pacifies the humors (doṣas), is unctuous, appetizing, promotes digestive fire, increases virility, and enhances strength. (Āk 1.7.82)
(The beloved, its varieties, and its definition):
Now I shall proclaim the beloved, the elixir of love;
may the divine medicinal herbs be the bestowers of all accomplishments. (Āk 1.7.83)
From them, Śambhu himself, accompanied by Śarvāṇī, [obtained] that which is beloved, most excellent, and a remover of wrinkles and grey hair—the Tāṇḍava dance at the end of the aeon. (Āk 1.7.84)
There he discharged it with great violence, and drops of sweat were produced;
wherever they fell, they indeed acquired the nature of magnets. (Āk 1.7.85)
Many [types of land] arise in arid regions, and some in ordinary lands; they may exist or not exist in water-abundant areas. By nature, they are remembered as being of five kinds. (Āk 1.7.86)

O Goddess, there are the *bhrāmaka*, *cumbaka*, *karṣaka*, and *drāvaka* types, as well as *romaka*; these are respectively single-faced, two-faced, three-faced, four-faced, and all-facing. (Āk 1.7.87)
Among those five types, yellow, black, and blood-red—whether mixed or separate—the presiding deities for each of them appear in sequence. (Āk 1.7.88)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Bhūta, and Mātṛkā are proclaimed [as the presiding deities].
Yellow in color, it penetrates through touch; black is the best for alchemy (rasāyana). (Āk 1.7.89)
Rakta salt causes the binding of mercury; Miśra removes all diseases;
Romaka destroys fear of evil planets; and Drāvaka is the most excellent of all. (Ākāśa 1.7.90)

I shall describe the characteristics of the superior, middling, and inferior types of lodestone—namely the *karṣaka*, *cumbaka*, and *bhrāmaka*—in their respective order; thereafter, one should cause the iron to revolve. Āk 1.7.91.

Therefore, it is called "the attractor" (bhrāmaka), "the magnetizer" (cumbaka) because it magnetizes iron, "the drawer" (karṣaka) because it draws iron toward itself, and "the liquefier" (drāvaka) because it causes [metal] to melt. (Āk 1.7.92)
That which causes the hair to bristle and the pores to open is called *romaka*; it is declared to be the most excellent.
That with many openings is superior, while that with four or five faces is the highest grade.
The medium [type] should have two or three faces, while the inferior should have one face;
it is beneficial for destroying all diseases when used as a *bhrāmaka* or *cumbaka*. (Āk 1.7.94)

O beloved, this lovely iron (kānta) is of five kinds: the attractor (karṣaka), the liquefier (drāvaka), the excellent one for use in alchemical elixirs (rasayoga) and rejuvenation (rasāyana), and the goad for the elephant of mercury (rasadvipāṅkuśa). Āk 1.7.95.
That which is touched by wind or sunlight should never be taken;
O fair-faced one, having lifted it with both hands, the beloved should be grasped. (Āk 1.7.96)

(The subduing of a lover’s essence): O Dear One, having first worshipped Durgā, Gaṇeśa, and Bhairava, one should burn the lover with a fierce fire and sprinkle him with water infused with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (Āk 1.7.97)
One should grind that desired substance finely with glass, sea salt, and borax, along with lac, guggulu, guñjā, wool, clarified butter, honey, and beeswax. (Āk 1.7.98)
With rabbit bones, small fish, and the pastes of *bhallātaka* and sesame; likewise with the ashes of *sarja*, the ashes of barley, *rāla*, and *cirabilva*. (Āk 1.7.99)
With equal parts of the horns of a young elephant, a female buffalo, and a female deer, one should grind these in equal proportions with goat's milk until they become smooth. (Āk 1.7.100)
O Goddess of the Suras, having finely ground together the five products of the cow—beginning with curd and ending with cow dung—one should prepare pills weighing one *karṣa* each. Āk 1.7.101.
In a crucible or a blowpipe, using firm khadira wood coals, one should gradually place five pills at a time therein. (Āk 1.7.102)
By churning for three nights with that beloved as the churning rod, pure mercury will fall out;
having reduced all of that to fine particles, one should combine it with equal parts of medicinal substances such as glass (kāca) and others. Āk 1.7.103.
One should blow it intensely once it has entered the crucible; thus, O Dear One, it should be smelted three times.
When done in this way, that lovely essence becomes the most excellent essence. (Āk 1.7.104)
(The nature of the beloved [substance]):
When drops of oil placed in water within a vessel made of *kāntaloha* do not spread, these black specks are indeed *caṇas*; of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.7.105)

There would be no scent of crushed asafoetida; a wave of milk would take the shape of a mountain peak; a jackal would never fall to the ground, nor would it ever abandon its bitter nature. (Āk 1.7.106)
Hot water thrown into that iron becomes cool in an instant. (This is the purification of iron.
It should weigh no less than five palas and no more than fifteen palas. Āk 1.7.107.
One should boil sixteen palas of triphalā with four times that amount of water until it is reduced to one-fourth; then, one should immerse the leaves in that decoction. (Āk 1.7.108)
One should dry those smeared with rabbit blood again in the sun;
likewise, one should heat curd, oil, Sauvīra, and clarified butter again.
O Dear One, an ointment made from honey, arka-milk, jambīra, and the juice of kulattha causes drying, burning, and sprinkling respectively. Āk 1.7.110.
One should divide each [element] sevenfold and thus abandon the defects of the mountain (iron ore).
(The mantras for the purification of metal:
First the mantra, then the ritual action; the mantra to be employed is now declared. (Āk 1.7.111)
The word *udbhavodbhava* should follow [the name], ending in the dative case and placed after *amṛta*;
it ends with *svāhā*, and the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) comes at the beginning—this is the mantra established for the act of crushing. (Āk 1.7.112)
Oṃ amṛtodbhavodbhavāya svāhā.
This mantra, "rakṣāyai lohanarayor ayam ekodbhavaḥ," is for protection.
He who should recite it in its place ending with "phaṭ" instead of the word "svāhā"—Āk 1.7.113.
Oṃ amṛtodbhavāya phaṭ praṇavordhvaṃ namaścaṇḍavajrapāṇaye, and thereafter: mahāyakṣasenādhipataye namaḥ. (Āk 1.7.114)
The word *su* is repeated twice for the sake of the power of the Great Vidyā; then follows *svāhā*. This mantra is proclaimed for the rite of offering (*balikarman*). (Āk 1.7.115)
Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍavajrapāṇi, the great lord of the yakṣa army; homage! Suru suru, to the one possessing the power of great vidyā, svāhā!
(Regarding iron ash:
Then, these iron leaves should be finely pulverized.
Having placed the powder of magnetite into an iron vessel, [one should treat it] with the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
One should sprinkle it with water using a ladle while stirring it, and cook it until it has formed into a mass;
then, taking that [mass], one should place it upon a pure layer of clay.

One should properly place it within a hollow pit sixteen finger-breadths deep; having laid down dried cow-dung from the forest, one should burn the cow-dung situated in the middle of that. Āk 1.7.118.
One should keep it for a day and night, avoiding wind and sunlight;
then, taking it up again in the morning, one should rub it with a decoction of *varā*. (Āk 1.7.119)
In this manner, one should perform [the process] with the vessel and the crucible through successive cycles of heating and sealing;
thus one should proceed for seven days, and indeed, vermilion (hiṅgula) should be added therein. (Āk 1.7.120)
One should grind the sixteenth part of iron with breast milk, then perform cooking in a vessel and apply sixteen *puṭas* (roastings) in a sealed crucible (*saṃpuṭa*). (Āk 1.7.121)

O Goddess, that ash should be rendered "niruttha" (purified) and employed in alchemy (*rasāyana*). [Regarding the immortalization of iron ash: There should be as much *triphalā* as there is [iron ash], and water four times that amount. (Āk 1.7.122)

One should boil [the ingredients] until eight parts remain; then, O beloved, one should cook ghee equal in measure to that decoction and an amount of *kāntaloha* ash equal to the ghee in a copper vessel.
Stirring with an iron ladle while that juice is drying, one should cook it over a mild fire until [the consistency] is equal to iron, then add sugar. (Āk 1.7.124)
This is called *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the process of immortalization), the supreme [method] that carries all yogas. (The varieties of metal-purification:
O Dear One, I shall now explain the purification of metals; it is of three kinds. Āk 1.7.125.
They are described as soft, medium, and hard: that which resembles a citron is soft; that which resembles a ball of dough is medium; and that which resembles sand is hard. Āk 1.7.126.
(The Procedure for the Practice of the Elixir of Magnetic Iron) Now I shall explain the practice of the ash of magnetic iron (*kāntaloha*):
on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, after having worshipped the Lord and other deities. (Āk 1.7.127)
O beloved, having first purified the body through purgatives and other means, one should consume the divine, perfected elixir of beautiful ash—the ash of mica (abhrabhasma). Āk 1.7.128.
One should consume it for one month; thereby the body becomes purified.
One *māṣa* of *kānta*-iron ash and one *guñjā* of mica ash [should be taken]. (Āk 1.7.129)
Having purified oneself through acts such as bathing and giving gifts, one should lick two niṣkas of powdered triphalā mixed with honey and clarified butter every morning. (Āk 1.7.130)
From that iron [vessel], cow's milk is sixty times more effective;
it should be warm as it flows from the udder, but in its absence, one should take milk mixed with an equal amount of water.
O beloved, one should boil the milk until the water is evaporated and then drink it;
however, if that is unsuitable, one should drink a decoction of *varā* or a medicinal extract (*kaṣāya*) of *guḍūcī*. (Āk 1.7.132)
One should consume this for one month, then gradually for two, three, and four months;
every month, there is an increase of one *māṣa* and one *guñjā* of the ashes of *kāntaloha* and mica. (Āk 1.7.133)
Thus, until the end of sixteen months, there is an increase of sixteen measures;
one should perform the ritual while abandoning the previously mentioned [restrictions], and shall attain accomplishment. (Āk 1.7.134)
By the practice of this for one year, there is the destruction of minor ailments;
by the practice of this for two years, there is the eradication of major diseases. (Āk 1.7.135)
After three years it destroys gray hair; after four years it removes wrinkles;
after five years it wards off untimely death; and in the sixth year, one shall attain a lifespan of a hundred years. (Āk 1.7.136)
In the seventh year, O beloved, one attains a radiance like that of the sun; in the tenth year, there is a union with spiritual perfection (siddhi);
and in the eleventh year, one attains the state of a Vidyādhara.
In the thirteenth year he attains divinity, and in the fourteenth, the status of Indra;
likewise, in the fifteenth year, he shall become beloved by all the world.

In the sixteenth year, the eight Siddhis shall be attained; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī. (The process of liquefying Kāntaloha: Just as gold is liquefied, O Dear One, the liquefaction of Kāntaloha occurs as previously described. Āk 1.7.139.
The liquefaction of *kānta* iron becomes ash, like the ash of ordinary iron.
(Regarding the varieties of iron and their qualities:
*Kiṭṭa*, *muṇḍa*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *kānta* follow one after another in ascending order of quality. Āk 1.7.140.
They become rich in qualities by ten, a hundred, a thousand, and then a hundred thousand respectively;
moreover, when increased by a hundred, it becomes a beloved elixir (*rasāyana*) of medicinal herbs. (Āk 1.7.141)
It pacifies the three humors, is divine, removes all diseases, bestows luster, is pleasing to the taste, beneficial for the eyes, heart-pleasing, life-prolonging, and pure. (Āk 1.7.142)
It provides stability and firmness to the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) and is a powerful elixir (*rasāyana*).
Now, I shall explain *abhra* (mica) in due order, beginning with its origin, its varieties, and its characteristics. (The Origin of *Abhraka*, its Varieties, and its Characteristics) ĀK 1.7.143.
In the delightful Śvetadvīpa, you exist as the primordial power Purādiśakti, together with Indrāṇī, Kamalā, Vāṇī, Gāyatrī, and others. (Āk 1.7.144)
Accompanied by the divine wives of the sages, headed by Arundhatī, Mahāmāyā—whose nature is consciousness, existence, and bliss—sportively played. (Āk 1.7.145)
Then many drops of tears of joy fell from his eyes onto his silken garment; thereupon, the river of the Lord of Rivers became sweet with the flow of that emotion.
Having cast that garment on the shore and bathed, he went to Kailāsa;
meanwhile, by the force of a whirlwind, that garment fell into the Ocean of Milk. (Āk 1.7.147)
Then, from that ocean of milk being churned by the gods and asuras, there arose that cloth of dust known as the fourfold *abhraka*. (Āk 1.7.148)
The black cloud-like [complexion] became like collyrium from the application of the Goddess's body;
her red hue took the form of dust, and her linen garment became white. (Āk 1.7.149)
Having observed that fourfold cause for the binding of mercury—which is an elixir that removes disease and bestows all perfections—[one should proceed]. (Āk 1.7.150)
Thus all the gods spoke, [offering] that which was equivalent to nectar itself:
"The white [stone] for silver works; the other three are for gold. (Āk 1.7.151)
All [mercury]—whether red, yellow, white, or black—is suitable for application in alchemy (*rasāyana*).
Red mercury is a hundred times more potent than white, and yellow mercury is a thousand times more potent than red. (Āk 1.7.152)
It should be known that black iron is a hundred thousand times more effective than yellow iron for alchemy (*rasāyana*);
each of these arises in four varieties according to their respective origins. (Āk 1.7.153)
The pināka, the dardura, the nāga, and the vajra—these are the four kinds [of thunderbolts].
One should employ the vajra as the primary one and avoid the other three. (Āk 1.7.154)
The Pināka, cast into the fire, releases a mass of petals;
having bound the impurity consumed by it, it kills the cause of disease. (Āk 1.7.155)
Dardura, when cast into fire, produces the croaking sound of a frog;
it generates the incurable disease known as *aśmarī* (urinary calculi). (Āk 1.7.156)
When mercury is cast into fire, it emits a hissing sound;
by the service of that [mercury], the great leprosy known as *maṇḍala* will certainly arise. (Āk 1.7.157)
(Regarding the characteristic of the graspable:
Through the service of these three, a collection of diseases arises;
however, vajrābhra situated in fire shall never undergo any transformation. (Āk 1.7.158)
Therefore, vajrābhraka should be consumed, for it conquers wrinkles, grey hair, and death;
it should be taken from a mine deeper than a king’s cubit using a pickaxe. (Āk 1.7.159)
(Vajrābhra: Examination:
Of Inferior Quality)
A gem that is heavy, broad-leaved, glossy, with petals that can be detached easily, and which resembles glass, moonstone, or dross—such a one should never be used. (Āk 1.7.160)

One should strongly heat *vajrābhra* (diamond-ore) possessing the previously mentioned characteristics in the milky sap of *arka*, in fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), in cow’s urine, and in the decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (This is *dhānyābhraka*. ĀK 1.7.161.
And here, having properly released the petals from those [medicines], one should cast that [powder] three times into the juices of meghanāda and āmla. (Āk 1.7.162)
Having ground it finely in a cloth, one should let it dry in the intense heat of the sun;
then, having placed it together with grains and bound it up, one should immerse it again in *kāñjika*. (Āk 1.7.163)
One should rub it firmly with both hands until a fine powder flows out into sour gruel (kāñjika); that should be dried in the sun—this is known as *dhānyābhraka*. (Āk 1.7.164)
(The extraction of the essence of mica:
O Dear One, the extraction of the essence of mica occurs in the same manner as that of magnetite (*kāntaloha*).
[The substances used are: gold, silver, *mākṣika*, *vaikrānta*, honey, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*. (Āk 1.7.165)
One *niṣka* each of *guñjā*, jaggery, ghee, and *bhallātaka* should be ground with the juice of *arka* and made into pills weighing one *karṣa* each. (Āk 1.7.166)
When this mercury, possessing the nature of a cloud, has been driven forth by means of a hundred *niṣkas*, one should cast in the pills;
the pills should be cast very slowly, at intervals of exactly one *ghaṭikā* each. (Āk 1.7.167)
As long as that sattva remains, it should be processed by those who are untiring;
this *abhraka*-sattva is indeed a Rasāyana fit for the gods. (Āk 1.7.168)
Having powdered the essence of mica (*abhrakasatva*), there are *meghanāda*, *punarnavā*, *sūraṇa*, the leaf of *arka*, *mustā*, *jambīra*, and *tālamūlikā*. (Āk 1.7.169)
Triphalā, vajravallī, śāṅgerī, and likewise marica; the group of sour substances (amlavarga), the root of the banyan tree, kārpāsa, muni, and śigru. Āk 1.7.170.
Ekavīrā, kokilākṣī, sarpākṣī, tulasī, vacā, peṭārī, vākucī, and kanyā—[one should apply these] separately with the juices of each one. Āk 1.7.171.
One should perform mardana, gharmapāka, sthālīpāka, and puṭa, each for one day in succession; thereafter, [the process is performed] with darada and honey.
One should add a sixteenth part of the mercury and grind it with the juices of the best [herbs];
one should thus perform this for up to sixteen puṭas, O Bhairavī. (Āk 1.7.173)
