he is the creator, the destroyer, the protector, and the sovereign Lord who bestows grace upon all. (Āk 1.11.28)
Possessing divine vision and a vajra-body, he is Bhairava himself in person;
[his chariot] is adorned with golden bells spread over half a yojana. Āk 1.11.29.
Resplendent with the beauty of moving bees, adorned with various rubies, embraced by golden garlands, and enchanting with the sound of bells. (Āk 1.11.30)
It was filled with divine, blazing, and great-sounding conchs and trumpets, along with lutes, flutes, mṛdaṅga drums, murajas, and other musical instruments played in unison. Āk 1.11.31.
It was filled with various kinds of cymbals and other divine sounds, and was accompanied by Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and Kimpuruṣas singing. (Āk 1.11.32)
Adorned with sparkling rubies, armlets, necklaces, bracelets, and rings, and equipped with golden anklets, they were decorated with divine ornaments. Āk_1,11.33 //
Adorned with divine garlands and ornaments, anointed with divine perfumes, clad in celestial raiment, and possessing beautiful forms, they were overwhelmed by the intoxication of love.
Then celestial women, having approached him, said:
"O Siddha, you who have shaken off all weariness, what task shall we perform? O Lord, let a command be given. (Āk 1.11.35)
More than a hundred thousand daughters of the Siddhas wait upon him;
wherever he goes, there we shall follow him, gathered around him. (Āk 1.11.36)
He repeatedly took possession of various celestial dwellings adorned with gold and rubies, as well as divine waters for bathing and drinking. (Āk 1.11.37)
He dwells at will in all the worlds, such as Vajrī and others;
he is worshipped by the hosts of gods and siddhas, just as this Bhairava is.
Enjoying all pleasures and free from hunger and thirst, he shall enjoy the company of hundreds of thousands of yoginīs while contemplating bliss. (Āk 1.11.39)
O fair-faced one, even at the time of the end of a great aeon, when this world has been utterly destroyed,
it dissolves into the supreme ether, wherein the deities also dissolve.
O beloved, by the power of this elixir, one becomes known as the "Destroyer of Death," indestructible, unbreakable, and incapable of being consumed by fire.
O Maheśvarī, this king of mantras, which bestows the perfection of all elixirs (rasāyana) and grants the accomplishment of alchemy (rasasiddhi), shall now be declared. (Āk 1.11.42)
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, O Śrī Bhairava! Āk 1,11.43.
Āk, 1, 12 (Attainment of Siddhi at Śrīśaila):
Śrī Bhairavī.
"O Lord, it is heard that on Śrīśaila various accomplishments (siddhis) are easily attained, producing immediate conviction; O Master, tell me of those various [accomplishments]. (Āk 1.12.1)
Śrī Bhairava said: Listen, O beloved, I shall tell you all that which brings about immediate success:
[the mantras] from Kailāsa, Mandara, Meru, the Vindhya mountain, and the Himālaya. (Āk 1.12.2)
The divine Śrīparvata is superior to Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, and even Ṛśya-giri; it is frequented by the lords of yogis who have attained perfection.
Therein, O beloved, are all the sacred fords, lakes, and rivers;
there are lingas that bestow perfection, as well as creepers, stones, and trees. (Āk 1.12.4)
Clay, tubers, water, leaves, flowers, fruits, and such like things exist which bring about all accomplishments. Āk 1.12.5.
"O Īśānī, I am Śrīparvata; I am that mountain manifest before you. Know that mountain to be my immobile form, served by the gods. (Āk 1.12.6)
That which exists here and nowhere else, and that which is situated elsewhere—this is the divine Linga to be touched, the stainless Jyotirlinga. (Āk 1.12.7)
O Supreme Goddess, the one renowned as Śrī Mallikārjuna is situated on the left side of this Liṅga, while Ghaṇṭāsiddheśvara stands [on the right]. Āk 1.12.8.
A bell hangs at the gate and a sacred bathing pool is present;
it must be attended by those who have fasted for three days, remaining vigilant and unwearied. (Āk 1,12.9)
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should bathe Śiva continuously;
O Dear One, one person should bring water while another brings it from the reservoir.
O beloved, another should ring the bell until the end of the fourth watch;
when the Lord of Bell-Siddhis is pleased, he shall grant even them the power of movement through the sky. (Āk 1.12.11)
O Dear One, to the south of this Ghaṇṭāsiddheśvara, one should dig down knee-deep; there, a luster like that of yellow pigment (rocanā) is seen. Āk 1.12.12.
O beloved, having gathered that clay, one should drink a karṣa measure of it mixed with milk for seven days; he shall become truly immortal. (Āk 1.12.13)
In front of Śrī Girīśa, a great stone in the shape of an elephant constantly exudes divine-smelling *suguggulu* resin by day and by night. (Āk 1.12.14)
One should take that [substance] with a ladle made of *palāśa* wood into a vessel of *alābu*;
having mixed it with sulfur, one should consume a quantity of one *karṣa*. (Āk 1.12.15)
By practicing daily for the duration of a month, one shall thereafter attain perfection; ever-joyful, youthful, and steadfast, he shall live as long as the moon and stars endure. (Āk 1.12.16)
When the face of the Mleccha has fled, one should cast that guggulu [incense] into it;
then, ten million parts of copper will become divine gold. (Āk 1.12.17)
(The Moon-Water at Mallikārjuna:
To the west of the god Mallikārjuna is the Moon-Pond;
on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, the supreme practitioner should perform the rite there. (Āk 1,12.18)
Fearless and free from conceptual construction, staying near water and devoid of clothing, one should recite the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra at night. (Āk 1.12.19)
At midnight, when the water is touched by the moon, one should then pour one's own añjali of water into the opening of that sacred bathing place. Āk 1.12.20.
When the moon passes over after touching it, then one should take that water; the wise man who drinks it immediately shall live as long as the moon and stars endure. Āk 1.12.21.
That man shall possess a vajra-body, a gentle form, and a peaceful nature;
at the eastern gate of Śrīgiri, there exists Tripurāntaka. (Tripurāntaka 1.12.22)
In a region to the north of the god, a tamarind tree is seen;
at its root resides the Lord Śrī Bhairava himself. (Āk 1.12.23)
One should dig the earth to the depth of a man's measure; then, right before it, there will be seen a heated pit with blue water that bestows divine accomplishments. (Āk 1.12.24)
Having tied leaves of the *tattinṛṇīka* plant in a cloth, one should cast them into that sacrificial pit; then they become large fish. (Āk 1.12.25)
Having taken them, the wise man should cook them with wood from the *tintriṇī* tree in this manner, gradually;
he should avoid their heads, thorns, and cavities. (Āk 1.12.26)
The practitioner, desiring success, should consume the entire remainder;
by that, a fainting spell shall occur for a mere moment, after which he awakens. (Āk 1.12.27)
One who sees a hole in the earth shall live for ten thousand divine years.
(Maṇipalli) is located two *gavyūtis* to the west of Tripurāntaka. (Āk 1.12.28)
There is a village called Maṇipalli; to its western side there is a certain mountain, and behind that is Ekavāṭaka. (Āk 1.12.29)
One should see [the entrance] and enter there facing east; then one should proceed facing south for a distance of about ten bow-lengths. (Āk 1.12.30)
There, having taken stones shaped like mango fruits and possessing a fiery luster, one should tie them in a cloth; that cloth will turn red. (Āk 1.12.31)
One should place that cloth, together with a stone, into the midst of milk;
then the milk will become red in color, and the supreme practitioner should drink it. (Āk 1.12.32)
Within seven days, accomplishment arises; one becomes a vajra-body of great strength.
One shall live as long as the moon and stars, for an entire eon, free from conceptualization. (Āk 1.12.33)
To the north of Tripurāntaka is the excellent Kokilābila;
there dwells Jagatprakāśa, having performed the purification of the body. (Āk 1.12.34)
The wise practitioner, having induced vomiting and so forth, should enter that cave;
there, within a distance of ten *cāpa*s, are stones resembling cuckoos.
Taking some seeds, they placed sesame seeds upon them; seeing that they burst open as a result of this, they rubbed them against one another. (Āk 1,12.36)
One should throw those [substances] into milk; that milk will turn black.
By drinking that milk for just one month, one will attain a divine body. (Āk 1.12.37)
He shall live for three days of Brahmā, free from wrinkles and grey hair;
with speed like the wind, he perceives the openings upon the surface of the earth.
To the east of Tripurantaka, at a distance of just one yojana, there is a deity who is the lord of the city of heaven; one should dig in front of him. (Āk 1.12.39)
And there, O fair-faced one, stones resembling the hoods of serpents, which have the quality of touch, emerge from the earth to a depth of one knee. (Āk 1.12.40)
To the west of the god Tripurāntaka, at half of half a yojana, there is a divine entrance to a subterranean cavern, located within a distance of three bow-lengths.
One might go to where there is a date tree, black in color and laden with fruit;
having drunk the juice of those fruits, one would experience a momentary fainting spell. (Āk 1.12.42)
He becomes awakened and perfected, and shall live as long as the moon and sun endure.
At the southern gate of Śrīgiri are Vajreśvara and Sureśvara.
O Goddess of the Gods, while standing, one should dig into the earth; there, stones resembling *śrīphala* fruits that differ in their tactile qualities are to be collected. (Āk 1.12.44)
In that place there is one called Rāmeśvara; in its vicinity, one should dig up stones shaped like rudrākṣas, which possess various distinctions of touch. (Āk 1.12.45)
At the site of Jyotisiddhavaṭa, there stands a single tree named Āvartaka to the south; it is situated near that, toward the west. (Āvartaka) Āk 1.12.46.
There exists a mountain there; one should dig it up [to find] stones resembling palm fruits. One should heat them thoroughly, and all that shall become gold. (Āk 1.12.47)
At its very southern gate is Kuṇḍaleśvara;
one should dig the earth near it to the depth of a knee and extract [the image]. (Āk 1.12.48)
There are stones with a reddish luster, shaped like *śrīphala* fruits, which possess the power of transmutation through touch;
for indeed, there is a sacrificial pit near the deity Puruṣeśvara. (Āk 1.12.49)
There exist two trees called Guñjāriḍḍha; one should eat their leaves.
Within seven days, one becomes perfected (siddha), freed from old age and death. (Āk 1.12.50)
(Hastiśilā):
There, one should dig at the Hastiśilā stone to the right to the depth of a hand's measure;
therein, those stones shaped like jambu fruits, known as "touch-stones," are to be taken. Āk 1.12.51.
It is renowned by the name Hastiśiras and is known as Hastiśilā;
it is one yojana in extent on its southern side. (Chāyāchattra) Āk_1,12.52.
The form of Śiva, proclaimed by Śiva, exists as a parasol of shadow;
it is circular, measuring one hundred cubits, and one should go beneath its opening. (Āk 1.12.53)
He too is not seen by anyone, yet he becomes a perfected one (siddha) at that very moment;
by his own will, equal to Rudra, he indeed sports throughout the three worlds.
Or he may accomplish the eight siddhis, for he is the bestower of all attainments;
mercury, mica, sattva, gold, and mercury [themselves] increase in quality progressively.
One should rub it thoroughly with sour gruel, form it into a ball, and wrap it;
having tied that ball to the tip of a long bamboo pole, [one should recite] the mantra of Śrī Kālikā. (Āk 1.12.56)
One should recite [the mantra] and place it there with that umbrella of shade; thus, within a sphere bound to the tip of a bamboo pole, an auspicious pill (ghuṭikā) is produced. (Āk 1.12.57)
One should hold that [substance] within the mouth, and at that very moment one becomes a sky-walker (khecara).
Having bound the stone and the palm-leaf with cloth and wrapped them around the tip of a bamboo pole... (Āk 1.12.58)
Having sat under a parasol made of shadows, one should anoint those two eyes;
one will see a treasure situated in the earth—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.12.59)
One should place a sword bound to the tip of a bamboo pole within the shadow of the parasol;
having empowered that sword with the Kālikā mantra, one should hold it in the hand. (Āk 1.12.60)
The steadfast one becomes a hero who conquers the three worlds within the triple universe;
having bound gorocanā to the tip of a bamboo pole, he should place it under a parasol of shadow. (Āk 1.12.61)
Having applied a tilaka on the forehead with that, one may bring the world under one's control;
likewise, one should apply it to collyrium made from *srotoñjana* or place it upon a parasol. (Āk 1.12.62)
Anointed with that collyrium, he cannot be seen even by the gods;
having fastened the sandals as before, one should cause the parasol of his shadow to be placed [over him]. (Āk 1.12.63)
Having placed the sandals upon his feet, those two sandals would carry him wherever he desired to go. Āk 1.12.64.
As before, one should place a red cloth over the shadow-canopy;
by wrapping that cloth around the painting, one becomes invisible in an instant. (Āk 1,12.65)
Once the cloth has been thoroughly cleansed, that [image] will subsequently appear; of this there is no doubt.
Having combined the lovely sky and gold with mercury, one should rub them together. (Āk 1,12.66)
The wise one should tie it, rolled into a ball, with a cloth to the tip of a bamboo pole;
he should place it under a parasol in the shade and consecrate it with the Kālī mantra. (Āk 1,12.67)
This shall be a piercing by touch; this is the truth, the truth, O fair-faced one.
At the western gate of Śrīśaila, the deity Brahmeśvara resides. (Āk 1.12.68)
And Goddess Durgā is situated there at the ninth step,
and then [the sites] on the Tuṅgabhadrā River and those of Brahmeśvara.
At the gateway, these four touch-stones (sparśaka) are the color of mung beans;
and the grove of tamarind trees stands in the southwest of Brahmeśvara.
And there is a sacrificial pit there, beneath a tamarind tree where Caṇḍikā resides; she constantly stands on one foot, gathering those tamarind fruits. (Āk 1.12.71)
Having cast them into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should bind them with a cloth and perform the ritual bath;
at the conclusion of the bath, one should take them up, for they indeed become fish. Āk 1.12.72.
One should cook those [grains] with fuel-wood, discarding the bones, tail, and heads;
one should give one portion to the deity and a second to guests. (Āk 1.12.73)
One should consume a third part oneself; one becomes unconscious in an instant.
This perfected one becomes divine and beholds a subterranean cavern upon the earth. (Āk 1.12.74)
For he is liberated from old age and death, and cannot be slain even by those free from decay;
there exists a village called Bhīmapāduka to the north of Alampura. (Āk 1.12.75)
One should dig the earth for a distance of one cubit at the side of that village;
for there will be stones shaped like hoods, which possess the quality of touch. (Āk 1.12.76)
There is a goddess named Yogīśvarī, the deity of that city of Alaṃpura;
in front of her is a beautiful cave, and in the middle of it, one should dig into the earth. (Āk 1.12.77)
Stones resembling mica should be taken with the urine of a cat;
having mixed them together, one should cast them into molten tin, and it will attain the state of silver. (Āk 1.12.78)
The best of practitioners should drink those stones with honey and clarified butter;
having become perfected, he becomes divine, conquering wrinkles, graying hair, and death. (Āk 1.12.79)
At the northern gate of Śrīparvata, there dwells a deity named Maheśvara; there is also a Bhramarāmrava tree, from which one should fetch its fruit. (Āk 1.12.80)
And one should burst it open; then bees emerge from within, still alive. One should avoid all those bees. (Āk 1,12.81)
One should cook its fruits in an alkaline solution until they are soft; one may drink milk as much as possible.
A momentary fainting spell may occur because of that, and at the end of the fainting spell, one should drink milk again. (Āk 1.12.82)
One should perform this with diligence for twenty-one days;
by that means, one will possess a vajra-body, free from wrinkles and grey hair. (Āk 1.12.83)
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas shall live as long as the sun and stars;
O beloved, by that very moment he becomes equal to the wind in speed. (Āk 1.12.84)
Then, by means of the fruit of the mango tree itself from which the bees have been removed, one thousand palas of tin, when melted, will become silver. (Āk 1.12.85)
One should create a cavity in a mango fruit and exclude the bee;
into its center, one should place one *karṣa* of mercury and the essence of black mica. (Āk 1.12.86)
Having closed the mouth and smeared it with cow dung, one should dry it in the shade and cook it for one *prahara* over wood of that same [tree]. (Āk 1.12.87)
Having made it naturally cool, the wise one should place it in his mouth; he attains the state of a sky-walker (khecarī), free from wrinkles and grey hair. (Āk 1.12.88)
One shall live as long as the moon and sun, possessing eloquence equal to that of Brahmā;
one should cast the essence of black clouds (sūta) into a mango fruit as previously described. (Āk 1.12.89)
Having coated it with cow dung and clay, one should bake it with forest stones;
once cooled, the mercury should be extracted and licked together with honey and clarified butter. (Āk 1.12.90)
By taking a dose the size of a *guñjā* berry at the end of a month, a human becomes a child;
equal to nine elephants in strength, he lives for one day of Brahmā. (Āk 1.12.91)
To the north of Śrīgirīśa, on the Śuklaparvata mountain, he who is renowned throughout the three worlds is to be worshipped with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra). Āk 1.12.92.
With the mantra "Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ," the practitioner, free from conceptual construction, should behold a celestial palace in the sky in the western direction. (Āk 1.12.93)
For it is divine, manifoldly beautiful, and produces immediate conviction;
thereafter, having crossed the great river, one should proceed toward the western quarter. (Āk 1.12.94)
And a cave is seen there; one should enter it facing westward.
Fearless, alone, and free from conceptual construction, one should travel three yojanas therein. (Āk 1.12.95)
There, a grove of plantain trees extending five yojanas is seen;
in its midst is a lake filled with clear water and a noble throne.
One should behold that great, divine seat as resembling crystal;
one should utter this mantra and perform prostration like a staff. (Āk 1.12.97)
Oṃ hrīṃ, to the Lord of the Sovereigns of Speech and Knowledge, hrīṃ oṃ svāhā.
Having bathed there, O fair-faced one, the practitioner should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times, subsisting on bulbs and roots or as he pleases, O beloved. (Āk 1.12.98)
Within the lion throne, one should behold the Lord, resembling crystal, four-armed, three-eyed, and bearing the crescent of the pure moon. (Āk 1.12.99)
To him who has a blue neck, who is adorned with serpents, whose weapons are the battle-axe and the deer,
who grants boons and fearlessness, who is most excellent, and who is worshipped by the preeminent gods.
And one should perform prostrations with the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) repeatedly with mantras and hymns;
then, being pleased, that Śiva grants the desired boon. (Āk 1.12.101)
There is a hundredfold abode, where there is a well as if it were nine hundred;
there are likewise that many groves and Nandana-like forests.
There are nine hundred ponds and an equal number of openings;
there are as many wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), and all of these bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
There dwells a yakṣiṇī renowned by the name Mohalī, who grants desired boons;
she says: "Give me enjoyment, if you desire success. (Āk 1.12.104)
"O Goddess, I shall grant her enjoyment; this must be said here by him:
'One should offer her bulbs, roots, fruit, or milk-rice. (Āk 1.12.105)
That yakṣiṇī spoke again: "As long as I hold my son upon my breast while he eats, I shall grant you a great boon."
"If you release it then, I shall kill you mercilessly.
Thus, Cīra, being free from fear, acted; had he done so, he would have attained success. (Āk 1.12.107)
O Maheśvarī, one should go to that lake in the northern direction at a distance of half a *yojana*; there, O Goddess, stands divine sandalwood filled with flowers.
Merely by smelling those flowers, hunger and thirst do not afflict one;
or else, one may eat a single fruit of it as is appropriate. Āk 1.12.109.
By merely consuming it, that person shall possess a vajra-body;
he shall go a quarter-yojana toward the southeastern direction. (Āk 1.12.110)
There, the Nandana grove is seen, thick with pomegranate trees;
whoever eats its fruit shall live for a thousand yugas. (Āk 1.12.111)
Proceeding for a distance of half a *krośa* from the eastern side of that very lake, one will find the Nandana grove, filled with *dhātrī* fruits. (Āk 1.12.112)
The wise man who eats its fruit shall live for three *saṃvartaka* kalpas; he should then proceed for one *yojana* to the western part of that lake. (Āk 1.12.113)
Therein lies the Nandana grove, filled with *śrīphala* fruits; whoever eats that fruit lives as long as the moon and stars endure. (Āk 1.12.114)
In that very Nandana grove, there shall be a blue-colored *liṅga*;
through its northern gateway, the immensely powerful Nāga shall enter.
There, a great and formidable serpent possessing seven hoods appeared, making a terrifying sound;
such was this great naga, repeatedly uttering the sound "huṃ huṃ."
"The practitioner, desiring success, should pay homage with great effort. Thus spoke the Great Naga: "I grant you invisibility. (Āk 1.12.117)
The practitioner should go to that very place where there is a divine maiden at his own western gate, while reciting the great mantra. (Āk 1.12.118)
That maiden gives a necklace and does not grant entrance;
one should wear that necklace around the neck, and by that means, one becomes Sarasvatī. (Āk 1,12.119)
Therefore, one should go toward the southern gate, which causes extreme fear;
there one will see a person with disheveled hair, squinting eyes, and naked.
Having seen the illustrious Kṣetrapāla, who is blue in color and holds a mace in his hand, one should pay homage by reciting the mantra and offering hymns that ward off obstacles. (Āk 1.12.121)
"Hā hā he he huṃ huṃ phaṭ huṃ svāhā"—by this very mantra, even the Kṣetrapāla quickly becomes propitiated. (Āk 1.12.122)
He bestows welcome but does not grant entry;
then one should proceed to the eastern gate, where the Lord of the Gaṇas resides.
The most excellent practitioner should worship what is situated there and enter;
a divine liṅga is seen there, and a beautiful bow is also present. (Āk 1.12.124)
One should worship that Lord with the mantra *oṃ huṃ*;
there, the wise person should fast and recite [the mantra] day and night. (Āk 1.12.125)
"The Lord becomes manifest and indeed grants the supreme boon"—such are the Siddhis that exist in the Kadalī forest. (Āk 1.12.126)
Right there, at a distance of only one *yojana* from the eastern side of the lake, the entrance to Padmāvatī’s subterranean chamber is marked by letters inscribed at its door. (Āk 1.12.127)
The practitioner, having purified himself through emetics and other such means, should enter there;
and having gone a hundred *apāntaras* within that place, he will find a drum (*mṛdaṅgaka*).
Upon seeing it, one should play it; then, from hearing its sound, Padmāvatī herself comes and bestows the nectar of immortality. (Āk 1.12.129)
By drinking it, he will become perfected and attain immortality; then, having approached him, you should entreat him to come into my presence. Āk 1.12.130.
"O Lord, having come together in my divine abode, which is filled with five hundred maidens, may you remain as my husband until the end of Brahma's lifespan. (Āk 1.12.131)
At its conclusion, you will go to the eternal abode; of this there is no doubt.
It is located to the southeast of that former pond. (Āk 1.12.132)
The deity Kadambeśvara is also present as a Kadamba tree in front;
having taken leaves from there, one should smear them with pungent oil. (Āk 1,12.133)
The wise man should either smear [the fish] with oils produced from the seeds of that [tree], or cook them with its wood;
those fish should then be placed in a copper vessel. (Āk 1.12.134)
One should avoid the bones, the head, and the tail, but one should consume [the rest] combined with honey and clarified butter.
By using that, one becomes accomplished, equal to Rudra, and possessed of great strength. (Āk 1.12.135)
And that tree is located on the riverbank in the vicinity of Kuṇḍaleśa; accomplishment occurs through the method as before, and not otherwise. (Āk 1.12.136)
To the north there is Puṣpagiri and Kapoteśa is also found;
one should perform three circumambulations and proceed toward its summit. (Āk 1.12.137)
For that practitioner, there will be the state of moving through the sky; of this there is no doubt.
To the northeast of that [place], the Chedikī gateway is situated. (Āk 1,12.138)
There, facing north, one should enter with care at a distance of three bows;
having ground a stone shaped like a mouse in buttermilk, a person should drink it. (Āk 1.12.139)
He will quickly fall into a swoon and live for three days of Brahmā;
he will pierce all metals by mere touch, without a doubt. (Āk 1.12.140)
Having fasted by day and night, one shall attain success before the deity;
there exists a pair of deities to the south of Kapoteśvara.
One should bury [the image] up to the navel between the two deities;
there are stones there resembling yellow orpiment, which one should remove. (Āk 1,12.142)
Having ground [the powder] with honey and ghee, whoever drinks it shall become immortal.
One should bury [the image] one cubit deep to the northwest of Kapoteśa. (Āk 1.12.143)
In that place, there are stones shaped like pigeons known as "touch-stones.
Having performed worship to the deity, one should collect one of them. (Āk 1.12.144)
In the northeast of Śrī Girīśa, there is indeed the Bhṛgupātana; near that is a divine pool, from which one should take the clay. Āk 1.12.145.
One should blow upon that [substance] mixed with the five products of the cow using a fire of *khadira* wood;
from it, a blue metal will fall when heated with honey and clarified butter.
One should sprinkle that with sevenfold-washed [liquor] and place that pill in the mouth;
the perfected one becomes equal to Viṣṇu, omniscient, omnipresent, and happy. (Āk 1.12.147)
One *krośa* from the mountain peak where Bhṛgu leapt down is Dadhikavāṭaka;
at its summit, there is always a mountain known by the name Acchataila. (Āk 1.12.148)
To the west of that is a bilva tree; in the midst of it, after traveling five bow-lengths, one should see a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) there, containing a liquid like lac. Āk 1.12.149.
One should take [the mercury] in a gourd vessel; that elixir is a "piercer of ten million" (koṭivedhaka).
It was the rampart of Candragupta to the west of Śrīgirīśa. (Āk 1.12.150)
In the midst of that is a dwelling, and a shrine (caitya) is situated to its east;
to the east of the shrine is a divine stone, resembling a mung bean in appearance, known as "Touch. (Āk 1.12.151)
There dwells the elephant Mohana; having mounted him with a concentrated mind, one should pluck a blade of grass from his back, and all of it shall become gold. (Āk 1.12.152)
To the north of that elephant, one should dig the earth to the depth of a knee;
there will be stones resembling the color of jambu fruits, which are characterized by their tactile sensation. (Āk 1.12.153)
One should dig the earth beneath an elephant to the depth of a knee;
from that, one obtains a supreme pill (*ghuṭikā*) in the form of a triangle, perfected for the purpose of piercing a target at a distance of one hundred thousand [bow-lengths]. (Āk 1.12.154)
To the northwest of Mallinātha, having bowed, there is the supreme Devahrada;
there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) there where stones have the appearance of mung beans and are known for their healing touch.

O Dear One, the auspicious *liṅga* there, which resembles a tortoise and is characterized by touch, should be gathered after worshipping it on the full moon day under the asterism Kṛttikā. (Āk 1.12.156)
Beyond that distance of two gavyūtis is remembered the Nīlavanī;
its linga and its water are praised as being blue in color. (Āk 1.12.157)
Stones resembling horses, mangoes, or crows are "touch-penetrating" (sparśavedhaka);
one should bury them inside a temple at a depth of one cubit in the ground. (Āk 1.12.158)
Those stones shaped like mice are known as *sparśasaṃjñā*; they are found to the southwest of the illustrious Lord of the Mountain and are renowned by the name Guṇḍīprabhā. (Āk 1.12.159)
One should burn yellowish clay from its foremost pit in a crucible;
from it there emerges gold, pure and fit for the gods, most excellent. (Āk 1.12.160)
There also dwells Bhṛṅgacūta, which, as before, bestows spiritual accomplishments;
likewise, there is the auspicious Tambīpura and the vast, holy site (tīrtha). Āk 1.12.161.
The wise one [should know] that Sadāphala is renowned to its northeast;
and to the southwest of Śrīgiri, there is the place known as Mahānanda.
The wise one should proceed by the Ghaṇṭāpatha toward its northeast; there resides Kālakaṇṭheśa, and in front of him is a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Āk 1.12.163.
In that case, there exists the accomplishment (siddhi) of the elixir (sūta) which resembles the indragopa insect;
by sprinkling [it], the seven metals become gold when heated. (Āk 1.12.164)
In the northeast of Śrī Girīśa is the glorious Mālinīśvara;
to the north of that is the famous mountain known as Tūma. (Āk 1,12.165)
In front of that, there are auspicious darbha grasses with the appearance of tridents;
one should bury them up to the navel and remove the blue earth from beneath them. (Āk 1.12.166)
One should cook it with wooden sticks of *akṣa* wood for the gods, guests, and the fire in that order;
one should assign one portion each to them and take the fourth part for oneself. (Āk 1.12.167)
Having attained perfection, he shall live for ten thousand kalpas with great strength and prowess;
there, near the Lord of Ilā, stands Koṭīśvara.
The flower and leaf at its tip possess the power to effect penetration by touch;
there resides the Lord Acaleśvara, the supreme agent of penetration by touch. (Āk 1.12.169)
One yojana to its south is Cāmareśvara;
beyond that is Svarṇaśilā, and above that is Naramāṃsaka.
Or the wise one should throw cow-flesh [into the fire] and kindle it with bādhara wood;
then, at dawn, that stone appears resembling gold. (Āk 1.12.171)
One should stir the garment of a woman who has recently menstruated with her menstrual flow upon a stone, and then cast it into a small vessel of water. (Āk 1,12.172)
By the mere touch of that, even the earth and stones situated on the ground where the venerable Guru resides would become the finest gold upon licking them. (Āk 1.12.173)

One should consume one *karṣa* of that powder together with an equal amount of *triphalā*; by doing so, one conquers wrinkles and graying hair within a month and may live as long as the moon and stars endure. (Āk 1.12.174)
To the southwest of Śrīgirīndra is the Lord Paṭāhakarṇa;
twenty-five dhanus to the northeast of that [is his location]. (Āk 1.12.175)
One should dig there a pit two cubits deep and two cubits wide; one should collect those stones that are shaped like the hollow of a joined earthen bowl. (Āk 1.12.176)
One should make them red-hot like fire and sprinkle them with juices produced from *kūṣmāṇḍa* plants;
from the midst of that, one should offer a portion of fresh butter (*navanīta*) to the deity. (Āk 1.12.177)
One should give one part to a guest and lick one part oneself;
by day and by night there may be fainting, yet one becomes naturally free from sleep. (Āk 1.12.178)
Free from wrinkles and gray hair, a man shall live for ten thousand years;
O beloved, this is the second stairway to the touchable and lovely state. (Āk 1.12.179)
All the stones on both sides of that deity are white and yellow; all these are smooth to the touch, and one should collect a single one from among them. (Āk 1.12.180)
For to the east of that deity there is a well, and there are stones resembling frogs known as Sparśa. (Āk 1.12.181)
To the north of that Lord stands the great Liṅgādri mountain;
to its northern direction lies a river flowing toward the east. Āk 1.12.182.
Indeed, on the western side of the river there is a tawny-colored *liṅga*;
there is also a pool there called Pūrṇaśailodaka, which grants instantaneous piercing [of the spiritual centers]. (Āk 1.12.183)
Two yojanas to the south of Maheśa stands Caṇḍikā, renowned by the name Piṇḍikā; [she is located] from her northwestern corner. (Āk 1.12.184)
For within that [ocean] there is a blind well, and therein are stones the color of mung beans;
some resemble myrobalan fruits, and they are all designated as "tangible objects. (Āk 1,12.185)
And the procedure for all the substances mentioned here is now stated:
if one should grind something coarse, one must indeed make it fine within a crucible. (Āk 1.12.186)
O Dear One, one should cause all metals to revolve within it;
all that becomes gold, and one may thus produce it as desired. (Āk 1.12.187)
If one places a subtle [substance] among all molten metals, then by its mere touch, all those metals indeed attain the state of gold. (Āk 1.12.188)
In the northwestern direction, during the era of Mallinātha, there is the shrine named Sarveśvara;
it is located two yojanas from that place on the royal highway toward the southern quarter.
Upon arriving there, a ḍoṅgalikā plant is seen at its summit;
it bears black dhātrī fruits, and one should eat them. (Āk 1.12.190)
For seven days, until satisfied, one who possesses a vajra-body, liberated from old age and death, shall live for three hundred kalpas. Āk 1.12.191.
And to the south of that, in the great forest of Kākalārī, there stands a plantain tree (stambakadalī); the practitioner should enter there. (Āk 1.12.192)
One should go for the distance of half a *krośa*, and a pool of mercury will be seen;
having placed it in a gourd vessel, he shall become one who possesses the power of ten million-fold penetration (*koṭivedhin*).
There is seen a stone image of Śikhaṇḍin, blue in color;
at the tip of its face is a pool, a span in size and intensely dark blue. (Āk 1.12.194)
If a dry bamboo stalk is placed within it for a moment, it becomes fresh;
leaves and flowers likewise become so in a single day—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.12.195)
Having added one *prastha* of mercury to that, one should add an equal amount of water;
one should drink that along with honey, and fainting occurs at that very moment. (Āk 1.12.196)
In an instant he shall attain wisdom and live for a thousand yugas;
on the southeast side of Śrīgiri is Ghaṭikāsiddha, the sky-walker.
In front of that, on the ground, the wise man should dig five cubits deep;
there will be stones shaped like jujube fruits which grant the power of flight. (Āk 1.12.198)
One [seal] should always be worn on the mouth by those perfected ones (*siddha*) who desire the power of moving through the sky.
(The Sequence of Accomplishment) The procedure for all the aforementioned accomplishments at Śrīśaila is now declared. Āk_1,12.199 //
Having first performed the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa), one should subsequently recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
indeed, by means of the Aghora-mantra at the end, one will swiftly attain each respective siddhi. (Āk 1.12.200)
(Now the ritual placement: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the heart of the one who dwells on the great mountain;
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head of Jyeṣṭhā.
Oṃ hrīṃ, vaṣaṭ to Raudrī, the crest-lock. Oṃ hrīṃ, huṃ to Kanakakuṇḍalinī, the armor.
Oṃ hrīṃ, vauṣaṭ to Saṃjīvinī, the eyes.
Oṃ hrīṃ mālinyai astrāya phaṭ.
Oṃ huṃ śivāya namaḥ; one should place [this] on the two feet. Oṃ vaṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ; [one should place this] on the two shanks.
Oṃ paṃ, homage to Padminī at the secret place; oṃ kāṃ, homage to Kanyākumārī at the navel;
oṃ glauṃ, homage at the belly.
Oṃ drāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Durgā; on the chest. Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Vindhyavāsinī; at the base of the throat. Oṃ laṃ, obeisance; on the neck.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Aṣṭabhujā; [place this] on the two arms.
Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Sarvatomukhinī; [place this] on the mouth. Oṃ, obeisance to Prakāśikā; [place this] on the two eyes.
Oṃ, salutation to Mahiṣamardinī; [one should place this] on the two ears.
Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to Sarvāṅgasundarī; one should place this on the head. Having thus performed the protection of the limbs, one should worship the field (kṣetra).

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Sovereign Goddess; obeisance to the Dweller in the Mandala! Krāṃ krīṃ krūṃ! Strike, strike! Cook, cook! Churn, churn! Cause [her] to descend quickly! Cause [her] to descend quickly! Come, come, O you who are adored by the worlds! Svāhā! With this mantra, one should invoke the deity.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Tribhuvaneśvarī; grant your presence, grant it, svāhā!
With this mantra, one should worship the deity of that field.
Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇavarṇinī Aparāmukhī in the east.
Oṃ, salutation to Sudhāvarṣiṇī in the southeast;
Oṃ, salutation to Parvatākṛṣṇavarṇinīraudramukhī in the south;
Oṃ, salutation to Bālārkavarṇinīmahālakṣmī in the southwest.
Oṃ Khaṃ! Homage to the one with the color of a red mountain, the crusher of the great Mahiṣāsura, in the west.
Oṃ Māṃ! Homage to the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevī) who possesses all colors and the syllable Hūṃ, in the northwest.
Oṃ, salutation to Siṃhavāhinī in the north;
Oṃ, salutation to Śivāśivāśivā, who holds a trident in her hand, in the northeast;
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Manonmanī in the sky.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mahāmohinī in the netherworld (pātāla).

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hroṃ hrauṃ hraṃ, O Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), paralyze, paralyze! Delude, delude! Reveal, reveal! Render unconscious, render unconscious! Klīṃ, churn, churn! Attract, attract! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
And one should worship in the center.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), protection, and worship, one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times for that rite.
Thereupon, one attains success (*siddhi*).
The mantra is as follows:
*oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hraṃ aghoratara prasphura prasphura prakaṭa prakaṭa kaha kaha śama śama jāta jāta daha daha pātaya pātaya oṃ hraiṃ hrāṃ hraṃ aghorāstrāya phaṭ*.
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times.
Then, appearing in a dream, the deity grants a boon. (Āk 1.12.201)
Āk, 1, 13 (Gandhaka):
Śrī Bhairavī.
Having bowed her head to Śambhu, the Supreme Goddess praised him:
"By your grace, I have heard the divine elixir of all things. (Āk 1.13.1)
O Maheśvara, tell me in due order about the origin of Gandhaka, its varieties, its purification, its medicinal application, and the fruit of its elixir. Āk 1,13.2.
Śrī Bhairava said: O Goddess, listen; I shall proclaim the elixir of sulfur (gandhaka-rasāyana).
Long ago, O Goddess, in Śvetadvīpa, which was radiant with creepers and wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma), [this was revealed].
It was strewn with various clusters of jewels and filled with diverse flowers and fruits,
frequented by groups of *siddhas*, *vidyādharas*, and women, as well as by throngs of *kiṃnarīs* and *apsarases*.
Sporting with many beautiful women, you are radiant with intoxication, delighting in the music of flutes and lutes and the enchanting sounds of various instruments. (Āk 1,13.5)
O Goddess of the gods, O you who are worshipped by the deities, you dance with great joy to the sounds of cymbals, small drums, and kettledrums, and to the clapping of hands. (Āk 1.13.6)
Then she became subject to her season and a great flow of menses issued forth;
by that fragrant menses, your garment was turned red. (Āk 1.13.7)
Having discarded that red garment and bathed in the great ocean of milk,
you returned to Kailāsa surrounded by many celestial nymphs.
O Goddess of the Gods, that cloth of dust was cast by the wind into the great ocean of milk; there that cloth remained submerged for a long time. (Āk 1.13.9)
Born together with the nectar from the great ocean being churned,
he delighted both the asuras and the suras with his praiseworthy fragrance.
By that very name, Śakra and the other preeminent gods said:
"O beloved of my heart, let this perfume be known by his name, for it has arisen from him. (Āk 1,13.11)
This fourfold blood of yours is divine and supremely strength-bestowing;
this sulphur is capable of binding mercury and of digesting it. (Āk 1,13.12)
"Whatever qualities exist in the lord of mercury (rasendra), those same qualities exist in sulfur (gandhaka)," so said Indra and the other gods, delighted by the fragrance of the sulfur. (Āk 1.13.13)
From that time forth, O beloved, this sulphur has been renowned in this world as "the Kṣatriya," resembling the Japā flower; it is the most excellent, O beloved. (Āk 1.13.14)
The yellow one is indeed a Vaiśya and is middling; the white one is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa and is the lowest;
the black-colored one becomes a Śūdra, O Dear One, and is the lowest of the low. (Āk 1.13.15)

Red in color, it pierces iron; yellow in color, it is an elixir; white in color, it is for medicinal purposes; and black, it is for application as an ointment against skin diseases such as leprosy. Āk 1,13.16.
(The Purification of Sulphur):
Now I shall describe the purification of sulphur, which bestows success:
sesame leaves, *ajamodā*, *brāhmī*, *bhṛṅgī*, and *dhuttura*. (Āk 1.13.17)
The powdered sulphur should be processed with the juices of these [plants] for one day;
having placed it in a vessel of magnetite (kāntapātra), one should cook it with an equal amount of clarified butter. (Āk 1.13.18)
Having cooked that with a mild fire, one should indeed pour it into goat's milk;
having added a little cow's milk and ghee, one should seal the mouth of the vessel. (Āk 1.13.19)
One should sprinkle powder over that which is bound with a clean cloth;
having then enclosed the earthenware vessel (śrāvaka) above it, one should place it within a pit. (Āk 1,13.20)
Having placed a soft pouch made of forest-lotuses over it, sulphur melts;
then one should repeatedly saturate and dry it three times with *tilaparṇī* and other herbs. (Āk 1.13.21)
Having taken that [substance], one should liquefy it by soaking it seven times with fish gall;
then one should grind it together with the powder of *jālinī* seeds. (Āk 1.13.22)
Then it should be processed seven times with the juice of *bhṛṅga* in the intense heat of the sun;
having thoroughly washed it with water, one should dry it and then cook it again. (Āk 1.13.23)
Then, having placed that purified sulphur for a moment in the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* within a beautiful vessel smeared with ghee over a mild fire, it becomes pure. (Āk 1.13.24)
In the practice of alchemy (*rasāyana*), it should be employed so as to bring about happiness.
(The Alchemy of Sulfur): One should perform purification of the body through emetics and purgatives, as previously described. (Āk 1,13.25)

At an auspicious hour and under a favorable constellation, having worshipped the Supreme Śiva, Gaṇādhipa, Kṣetrapāla, the venerable Guru, and the physician in due order, [one should proceed]. (Āk 1.13.26)
One niṣka of powdered triphalā, one niṣka of guggulu, and pure sulphur weighing one guñjā—one should lick these together with castor oil. (Āk 1.13.27)
It should be consumed every day according to the sequence of increasing by one *guñjā*, until on the sixteenth day it reaches the measure of sixteen *guñjās*. (Āk 1.13.28)
Then, at the end of sixteen days, that [medicine] should be consumed every day;
it should be measured as sixteen *guñjā*s, being an unprecedented and supreme *triphalā* preparation.
One who desires success should not increase the dose beyond this;
by employing it for one month in this manner, one shall eliminate the eighteen types of leprosy. (Āk 1.13.30)
Likewise, it [cures] urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, cough, dyspnea, consumption, fever, ulcers, fistula-in-ano, and other diseases arising from the eighty types of wind disorders. (Āk 1.13.31)
By practicing for two months, it bestows great luster;
O Dear One, by three months, there shall be the pacification of all diseases. (Āk 1.13.32)
Then, through practice for six months, even an old man shall attain youth; likewise, O Śāmbhavī, by practicing for a year, one becomes perfected.
Through the application of its urine and dregs, copper attains the state of gold;
the wise one should perform both the prescribed rites and prohibitions as previously described. (Āk 1.13.34)
He who partakes of the pure and meritorious elixir (rasāyana) consisting of the [six] tastes and so forth, he alone shall have accomplished his purpose and is honored even by the gods. (Āk 1.13.35)
Having bathed in all sacred fords and being endowed with the fruits of all vows, one shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices, beginning with the horse sacrifice. (Āk 1.13.36)
Blessed, most meritorious, supreme, and praiseworthy by the wise, he is the knower of yoga, the omniscient one, the benefactor of all, and the Lord. (Āk 1.13.37)
Pure, omnipresent, tranquil, heroic, and radiant with the quality of sattva—for him there is no dissolution into the body; indeed, being invisible, he attains the state of Śiva. (Āk 1.13.38)
Āk, 1, 14 (Poison; The Origin of Poison).
Śrī Bhairavī said:
"O Lord, I have heard all about the divine elixir (*rasāyana*) that contains every essence;
now tell me of the origin of poison, its nature, its application, and its fruit. (Āk 1.14.1)
Śrī Bhairava said:

When the Ocean of Milk was being churned by the Siddhas, Kinnaras, lords of the Guhyakas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, who had made Mount Mandara their churning-stick, [the following occurred]. Āk 1.14.2.
On one side were all the gods, beginning with Brahmā;
on the other, the lords of the Danujas, along with vast numbers of Daityas of great strength and prowess.
From him were born the jewels, such as the Kaustubha; the wish-fulfilling cow;
the Kalpa tree; Mahālakṣmī; and the great elephant Airāvata.
Likewise, Uccaiḥśravas, the moon, Dhanvantari the best of physicians, the nectar of immortality, and the divine creeper that bestows celestial perfections. (Āk 1.14.5)
Then, from the mouth of the Naga king, exhausted by his circling of Mount Mandara, a fierce flame of poison arose, terrifying to the world. (Āk 1.14.6)
Today, from the further churning of the ocean of milk,
the great poison Kālakūṭa has emerged, resembling the God of Death at the end of an aeon.
Then, beholding that [fire] resembling the fire of universal destruction, the gods became terrified;
with dejected minds, they approached me while offering hymns of praise. (Āk 1.14.8)
"O Lord, supreme among all, protect us! O guardian of those who have come for refuge!"—thus did those gods and asuras offer praise in many such ways. (Āk 1.14.9)
Then, with a smiling face, I drank that Kālakūṭa poison;
whatever remained there and there fell upon the earth in many places. Āk 1,14.10.
In some places, O beloved, it exists in the form of its root; in others, in the form of bark;
in some places, in the form of leaves; and in some places, in the form of water.
In this way, many kinds of poison have arisen and spread here and there;
among them, O beloved, the best is the bulbous-root poison, the eighteenfold poison.
I shall now describe in order the ten types of poison: Kālakūṭa, Dardura, Hālāhala, Meṣaśṛṅga, Mohada, Granthi, and Karkaṭa. Āk 1.14.13.
Raktaśṛṅgī, haridrā, and keśara are recorded as the tenth;
these ten types of kṣveḍa are not to be employed in alchemy (rasāyana). Āk 1.14.14.
(Regarding the eight kinds of poison: O Goddess, *śvetaśṛṅgī*, *vatsanābha*, *sarṣapa*, *śṛṅgī*, *vālukam*, *mustaka*, *saktuka*, and the eighth is *kardama*. Āk_1,14.15.
Eight varieties to be employed in alchemy (rasāyana) have been proclaimed:
Kālakūṭa, which has the luster of a crow’s beak and resembles a frog. Āk 1.14.16.
Dardura is blue in color and equal to hālāhala poison;
meṣaśṛṅgī, however, resembles the horn of a ram and causes delusion. (Āk 1.14.17)

O Goddess, the *raktanīlaprabha* is marked by knots; the *granthika* is likewise joined with knots; the *karkaṭa* has a tawny appearance; and the *raktaśṛṅgin* is a highly poisonous [gem]. (Āk 1.14.18)
Blackish-brown, reddish, yellowish, greenish, and like the filament of a lotus—thus it is of ten kinds. (Āk 1.14.19)
That which resembles a white-horned cow or a white-toothed elephant, and is pale like vatsanābha, and is marked with spots shaped like mustard seeds, is *sarṣapa* [poison]. (Āk 1.14.20)
Śṛṅgī should be known as having the form of a horn; vāluka has the form of sand; mustaka has the form of musta grass; and saktuka is white in color. (Āk 1.14.21)
O Goddess, the form of beeswax is the supreme poison, *kardama*;
when it is broken into pieces of poison, drops are seen within them. (Āk 1.14.22)
The [mercury] of the Brahmins and other castes is, respectively, white, red, yellow, and black;
it is white for alchemy (*rasāyana*), red for subjugation (*vaśya*), and [black] for the work with mercury (*pāradakarma*). (Āk 1.14.23)

In minor rites they should be yellow; for killing, however, they are black in color. O Goddess, poison becomes nectar through proper application, but through improper application it becomes poison. (Āk 1.14.24)
Therefore, poison should be consumed with reason, never without reason; for poison is equal in its potency to mercury, mica, gold, and magnetite. Āk 1.14.25.
(Visa-śuddhiḥ) One should bind [the poison] onto a cloth smeared with oil of red mustard seeds; after three days have passed, one should extract the poison together with borax. Āk 1,14.26.
One should grind it into a fine powder and cause it to be prepared; thus it becomes purified.
O fair-faced one, when employed for medicinal cures or as an elixir (*rasāyana*), it shall grant success. (Āk 1.14.27)
(An Elixir of Poison):
Having purified the body through emetics and other means, and eating wholesome food, one may consume poison.
It should be taken gradually, starting with a mustard seed and then a black mustard seed. (Āk 1.14.28)
Mudga beans, rice, barley, and masha beans—these should be consumed with sugar; when combined with poison (kṣvela), it becomes nectar (amṛta). (Āk 1.14.29)
Bitter, sour, and salty [tastes] should be abandoned; physical exercise, heat, sunlight, and the like should be avoided;
and oils, mustard seeds, and solid foods should be eschewed during the practice of the elixir of immortality (*viṣarasāyana*). (Āk 1.14.30)
Cow’s milk, ghee, buttermilk, unctuous curd, and sugar—these substances of sweet taste should be consumed; otherwise, they become causes of morbidity. (Āyurvedadīpikā 1.14.31)
(Viṣopadravās taccikitsā ca) O Dear One, when consumed in the proper measure, poison becomes nectar;
if it exceeds the proper measure, even nectar turns into poison. (Āk 1.14.32)
If [the enema] is administered excessively due to negligence, then distressing urges arise;
there may be difficulty during the first urge, and trembling during the second. (Āyurveda-kalpa 1.14.33)
In the third [stage], there is burning with thirst; in the fourth, the breaking of movement;
in the fifth, the mouth becomes frothy; and in the sixth, the breaking of the neck. (Āk 1.14.34)
In the seventh [period] there is no rising from bed, and in the eighth there would be death;
therefore, O fair-faced one, a remedy must be applied quickly. (Āk 1.14.35)
If that mercury (kṣvela) is even slightly excessive, it causes various diseases, as well as delusion, forgetfulness, and pain, and furthermore leads to vomiting and diarrhea. (Āk 1.14.36)
Hoarseness of voice, stammering, burning sensation, as well as vertigo, earache, dyspnea, cough, and other diseases arising from Vāta. (Āk 1.14.37)
When excessive signs are seen upon the body of the beloved, then one *niṣka* of *ṭaṅkaṇa* and four times as much clarified butter [should be used]. (Āk 1.14.38)
To avoid that, one should drink either *taṇḍulīyaka* with water, or the marrow of *putrajīva*, or a *niṣka* of its fruit mixed with water. (Āk 1.14.39)
Or one should take *haridraka* weighing two *paṇas*, or *vacā*, or *devadālī*, or *sarpākṣī*, or *sārbuṇī*, measured with human urine. (Āk 1.14.40)
One should take paṭolī and giriparṇī separately with human urine as an antidote for poison; this is the Gāruḍa mantra, enclosed by the four syllables *lāṃ*, *yāṃ*, *vāṃ*, and *hāṃ*. (Āk 1.14.41)
Likewise, [there are] the rites of paralyzing (*stambhana*), stunning (*stobhana*), driving away (*nirvāha*), and neutralizing poison (*nirviṣīkaraṇa*).
By means of this mantra—*lāṃ proṃ lāṃ*—one performs the rite of paralyzing.
Having consecrated a jar of cold water with this mantra, one should pour the water over the head of the person afflicted by poison.
Poison does not take hold.
With this *stobhana* mantra—*yāṃ proṃ yāṃ*—one should blind the peacock of the one afflicted by poison.

With this *nirvāha* mantra—*vāṃ proṃ vāṃ*—having consecrated either a staff of *arka* wood or a staff of *dhuttūraka* wood, and having touched all the limbs of the one afflicted by poison, one should cause the poison to be expelled.
"Hāṃ proṃ hāṃ! By means of this mantra for neutralizing poison, one should wipe all the limbs of the person afflicted by poison with a staff for the purpose of detoxification; he becomes healthy.
O Dear One, if the digested poison remains in the body, there should be emesis until the bile [is expelled]. (Āk 1.14.42)
One who eats the root of *taṇḍulīyaka* should perform purgation until the end of the undigested matter (*āmānta*).
He should consume meat with ghee; this will remove the toxic effects of poison. (Āk 1.14.43)

O Goddess, he who consumes the aforementioned measure is liberated from great disease; through practice for six months, there is the destruction of old age, graying hair, and fragmentation [of the body]. (Āk 1.14.44)
By employing it for a year, one may live as long as the moon, sun, and stars;
this elixir of poison (viṣa-rasāyana) should be administered during the cold, winter, and spring seasons. (Āk 1.14.45)

This [practice] should never be employed during the summer, the rainy season, or autumn; nor for those suffering from wind-disorders, the elderly, pregnant women, or those afflicted by hunger, thirst, heat, or travel. (Āk 1.14.46)
Eunuchs, those with indigestion, those with an excess of bile and anger, and those afflicted by consumption are never fit for the elixir of mercury. (Āk 1.14.47)
Āk, 1, 15 (Divine Medicinal Plants and Elixirs):
Śrī Bhairavī.
O Lord, free from impurity and māyā, who removes the afflictions of old age and birth!
By Your grace, the elixir of mercury and other substances has been understood. (Āk 1.15.1)
"O Lord, from this point forward I wish to serve you in some way, O Master—whether by means of a comfortable method or by employing divine medicines and elixirs. (Āk 1,15.2)
"Tell me that divine [mantra] of such a kind which bestows all accomplishments.
Śrī Bhairava:
(1. Brahmakalpa)
The Ritual for Brahmavṛkṣa Oil: I shall now describe the divine medicinal elixir (*rasāyana*) beginning with the *brahmavṛkṣa* and other such substances. (Āk 1.15.3)
In that regard, first listen, O Goddess, to the elixir of the Brahma-tree:
one should take the seeds of the Brahma-tree, having removed their husks. (Āk 1.15.4)
Having dried it in the intense heat of the sun, one should reduce it to a fine powder;
then one should saturate it for seven days with either the juice of *dhātrī* fruit or with milk. (Āk 1.15.5)
One should cast them into a wheel-pressing machine and then extract that oil; oil produced in this manner destroys the humors (doṣas) and is a rejuvenative elixir (rasāyana). Āk 1.15.6.
One *prastha* of oil produced from the seed of *brahma* and an equal amount of clarified butter (*ājya*) should be placed in a smooth vessel and then set within a heap of grain. (Āk 1.15.7)
Therefore, O Goddess of the gods, one should collect the oil every half-month;
having purified the body through purgatives and other means, and having worshipped the fire, the guru, and the twice-born. (Āk 1.15.8)
Having mixed two palas of cow's milk with one niṣka of that oil, one should drink it in the morning; thereafter, one should eat wholesome food and remain self-controlled. (Āk 1.15.9)
In this manner, on the second day as well, with an interval of one day between each, there shall be an increase of one niṣka in succession until it reaches sixteen niṣkas. (Āk 1.15.10)
This is indeed declared to be the supreme dose for this oil.
Upon drinking it, a momentary fainting occurs; one should then sprinkle water on the face. Āk 1.15.11.
When he has awakened, one should give him milk-rice mixed with ghee and sugar;
by the use of oil in this manner for a month, a man becomes a possessor of knowledge. (Āk 1.15.12)
In the first [period], he grasps [knowledge] at once, is very handsome, and remains as if sixteen years of age;
in the second, he possesses the strength of a nāga and is free from all diseases.
In the fourth month, the steadfast one will gradually attain strength equal to Indra;
in the fifth month, he will possess a vajra-body, divine vision, and become a sky-walker. Āk 1.15.14.

Endowed with the qualities of *aṇimā* and the rest, omnipresent and existing at all times, in the sixth month he himself becomes the creator, the enjoyer, and the destroyer, like the Trinity. (Āk 1.15.15)
O Goddess, by practicing this for one year, one becomes Sadāśiva in person.
As long as one subsists on oil, one should eat rice with milk. (Āk 1.15.16)

Having purified his body through emetics and other means, and having performed worship of the physician and the twice-born, he should in the morning take one *kuḍuba* of cow’s milk and oil produced from the seeds of the *kiṃśuka* tree. (Āk 1.15.17)
Having combined two *kuḍuba* measures as previously described, one should drink them together.
By the mere act of drinking that, a fainting fit shall occur, and it will cause him to lie down in ashes. (Āk 1.15.18)
Upon awakening after seven nights, while remaining as if bound upon his bed, he should not move his limbs; thus he becomes one with unblinking eyes. (Āk 1.15.19)
O Bhairavī, when the oil has been digested and the process is complete, consciousness returns;
one should then give him cow’s milk every day for ten days. (Āk 1.15.20)
He shall cast off the skin from his body like a snake sheds its slough, and he shall subsist constantly on milk for twenty-one days. (Āk 1.15.21)
The wise one becomes a master of speech, retaining what he has heard in an instant;
hearing from afar and possessing divine vision, that sagacious person shall live for a day of Brahmā. (Āk 1.15.22)
(The Ritual for the Sprouts of the Brahma-Tree):
On an auspicious lunar mansion, one should collect the sprouts of the Brahma-tree—those that are free from worms and insects, tender, and beautiful. Āk 1.15.23.
One should dry it in the intense heat of the sun, having ground it and filtered it through cloth; then one should carefully place it in a new vessel. (Āk 1.15.24)
With his body purified by emetics and other therapies, observing celibacy, having conquered his senses, avoiding foods that are alkaline or sour, and subsisting on milk and śāli rice; (Āk 1.15.25)
One should always drink lukewarm water and resort to a bed in a windless place;
for one month, one should consume a quantity of one karṣa combined with cow's buttermilk. (Āk 1.15.26)
In the second and third [months], there is an increase by one *karṣa* respectively;
in this manner, until the end of the sixteenth month, one should drink a *kuḍuba* of *satakra*. (Āk 1.15.27)
Thus, the man who constantly practices this, whose hair is curled and glossy,
and who possesses the strength of an elephant in rut, shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
(The Ritual for the Flowers of the Brahmavṛkṣa):
The wise person should dry the flowers of the Brahmavṛkṣa in the shade;
he should grind them into powder, strain them through a cloth, and place them in a new vessel. Āk 1.15.29.
Twenty palas of flower powder and twenty-four palas of cow’s ghee, mixed together in one portion, should be placed within a heap of grain. (Āk 1.15.30)
At the end of the month, one should extract it after dividing it into fourteen parts;
each part should be consumed individually in this manner for three months. (Āk 1.15.31)
He should eat from a vessel of metal, avoiding salt, sour substances, and the like;
subsisting on milk-rice, if afflicted by thirst, he should drink a decoction of *khadira* wood. (Āk 1.15.32)
Within three months, his body becomes like a vajra; of this there is no doubt.
Firm and possessing the strength of ten thousand nāgas, he moves with the speed of the wind. (Āk 1.15.33)
By using its ash, even excrement and urine can pierce all metals and turn them into gold. (Ākāśagarbha 1.15.34)
He shall live for a day of Brahmā and rejoice visibly with the deities. (This is like the seed of the Brahma-tree:
One should grind the seeds of the Brahma-tree and place them in a jar. (Āk 1.15.35)
One should place honey, clarified butter, and sugar together upon a heap of grain; after a month has passed, one should collect it and take a quantity of exactly one *karṣa* every day. (Āk 1.15.36)
The pure-souled one should consume it and afterwards drink cow’s milk;
the increase should continue only until it reaches one *pala*, for it should not exceed that. (Āk 1.15.37)
In this way, within a year, perfection arises that is free from death;
pure and possessing strength like an elephant, he shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā. Āk 1.15.38.
One should prepare a fine powder from the bark of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree; one should saturate a *pala* of it with cow’s milk and drink it every day. (Āk 1.15.39)
The wise man, having conquered his senses and eating wholesome food for one year, shall certainly live for ten thousand years and become a perfected being (siddha). (Āk 1.15.40)
(The Ritual for the Exudation of the Brahmavṛkṣa):

One should consume equal parts of *brāhmī*, *madhuka*, clarified butter, and the exudation produced from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree; one should take one *pala* of this mixture and drink milk afterwards. (Āk 1.15.41)
Thus, by the practice of Ekābdayoga, the pure knower, possessing an auspicious appearance and free from wrinkles and grey hair, shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
(The Ritual for the Five Limbs of the Brahmavṛkṣa):
One should duly collect the five limbs of the Brahmavṛkṣa tree; having dried them in the shade, one should grind them into powder and purify them with a cloth. (Āk 1.15.43)
A pure person should lick a measure of one karṣa with honey and clarified butter at the break of dawn;
within a year, that man becomes free from wrinkles and graying hair. (Āk 1.15.44)
(The Ritual Manual for the Secret *Dhātrī* at the Root of the Brahma-Tree):
One should split an exceedingly thick and long Brahma-tree, leaving three cubits remaining at the root, and then construct a pit at its tip. (Āk 1.15.45)
O beloved, one should fill that [hole] with ripe *dhātrī* fruits;
then, one should block that pit with the remaining pieces of the wood from which they were cut. (Āk 1.15.46)
The wise man should wrap it properly with *kuśa* grass from root to tip and smear it with clay and cow dung; thereafter, he should wrap it with a cloth. (Āk 1.15.47)
Furthermore, the wise one should smear [the vessel] with clay and cow dung and let it dry;
once it is thoroughly dry, he should fill it completely around the edges with dried cow-dung cakes.
Once it has been burnt and has become cool, one should take that thick fruit-juice and place it in a vessel filled with honey and clarified butter, along with those *dhātrī* fruits. (Āk 1,15.49)
Dwelling happily either in an underground cell or in a windless place, he should always eat as he pleases, subsisting on milk, with his senses subdued. (Āk 1.15.50)
Within six months, he perceives flaws and hidden treasures upon the earth;
like a snake shedding its skin, the man shall live for a Brahma-yuga.
(2. The Ritual of the White Brahmavṛkṣa;
The Ritual of the Five Limbs of the White Brahmavṛkṣa) O Dear One, one should grind the five limbs of the white *pālāśa* tree and dry them.
O beloved, one should lick that which has fallen from the garment in the shade, mixed with honey.
By taking a quantity of one karṣa for three months, a person shall conquer old age and death;
after a year, having attained the lifespan of Brahmā, he becomes perfected and omnipresent. (Āk 1.15.53)
(The Ritual for the White Brahma-seed):
One should collect the seeds of the white *pālāśa* tree one by one; by consuming them daily with goat’s ghee for a month, one shall conquer death and old age. (Āk 1.15.54)

Preceded by the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), he shall live for a *brahmayuga*—a thousand years—having mastered those [substances] previously mentioned among the red *pālāśa*, oil, bark, leaves, and so forth. (Āk 1.15.55)

Those qualities exist in the white *pālāśa* tree, bestowing success upon the practitioner. (The ritual procedure for the *brahmavṛkṣa*) I shall now describe the ritual procedure for the *brahmavṛkṣa* and its mantra. (Āk 1.15.56)
Oṃ hrīṃ, make [everything] nectar, make [everything] nectar; obeisance to Amṛtamālinī.

One should first perform twenty thousand recitations as the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). She holds in her lotus-like hands a jar of nectar, a rosary, a garland, and the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*). (Āk 1.15.57)
One should meditate upon Amṛtamālinī, who bears a noose of pearls;
during an eclipse, one should consume [the substance] seven times for one hundred and eight repetitions. (Āk 1.15.58)
During times such as lunar or solar eclipses, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times; without this, there will be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (Āk 1.15.59)
Success shall be swift through the mantra; one should practice preceded by the mantra.
(3. The Ritual of Muṇḍī) Now I shall proclaim Muṇḍī, who bestows the desired objects upon practitioners. Āk_1,15.60
And it may be of four kinds: red, yellow, white, or black;
[it should be prepared] under the asterism Puṣya, on a Sunday, on the full moon day, or under the asterisms Revatī or Śravaṇa. (Āk 1.15.61)
Or one may take her during an eclipse or at times of auspicious conjunctions (*siddhayoga*);
she is the maiden from the fields (*kaidārī*) who has shorn her hair (*muṇḍinī*), preceded by offerings and worship. (Āk 1.15.62)

Having performed his bath and observing silence, he should collect [the water] while reciting the mantra: "Oṃ, to the one born from nectar, make it nectar, make it nectar, svāhā! Hrīṃ Saḥ! He should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) by reciting this mantra twelve thousand times. (Āk 1.15.63)
The root, the stalk, the fruit, the flower, and the leaf are declared to be the five parts;
one should properly take that five-part muṇḍī with cold water. (Āk 1.15.64)
Having washed it, one should dry it in the shade and then powder it; having strained it through a cloth, one should place it in a new jar in due order. (Āk 1.15.65)
A person with a purified body should drink one *karṣa* of that powder with cow’s milk; once the medicine has been digested, the person should first drink clarified butter (*ghṛta*). (Āk 1.15.66)

Then one should eat food that is free from salt, oil, sour substances, and the like; it should consist primarily of sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika*) cooked in ghee, sweetened with honey, and accompanied by an abundance of milk. (Āk 1.15.67)
Within six months, perfection is attained; one casts off the skin like a serpent, becoming free from gray hair and the like, possessing divine vision and a firm body. (Āk 1.15.68)

A man who possesses the strength of a rutting elephant, is steadfast, youthful, and has a body full of vigor, shall achieve all perfections within a year and attain the lifespan of Brahmā. (Āk 1.15.69)
When consumed with ghee, that *muṇḍī* shall yield its former fruits.
(4. The Ritual Manual of *Devadālī*) Now, O Goddess, I shall describe the elixir (*rasāyana*) of *devadālī*. (Āk 1,15.70)
Devadālī is considered to be of three types: white, black, and yellow;
the white variety alleviates diseases, while the black and yellow varieties are especially effective. (Āk 1.15.71)
O Pārvatī, honored by the gods, it yields fruit in the practice of alchemy (*rasāyana*) and in the working of metals during lunar and solar eclipses and on the full moon day. (Āk 1.15.72)

On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, or on the fifth, according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the rite preceded by mantras on an auspicious day and under an auspicious lunar mansion. (Āk 1.15.73)
Oṃ amṛtagaṇarudragaṇāntāya svāhā. Having recited this one hundred and eight times, one should perform the offering preceded by the bali. Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya phaṭ svāhā.
This is the mantra for binding the crest-lock of the practitioner.
Furthermore, the wise one should dry the five limbs of the *devadālī* plant in the shade. (Āk 1.15.74)
One should thoroughly cleanse it with cloth and consume it with cow's milk;
then the wise one should cook it in an iron vessel over a gentle fire. (Āk 1.15.75)
One who has purified their self should lick one karṣa of this with honey and clarified butter for seven days;
their wisdom shall become divine, and by using it for a month, diseases will be removed. (Āk 1.15.76)
By consuming these for two months, one certainly beholds hidden treasures and the like.
[One should take] the juice of *dhātrī* fruit, honey, the juice of *devadālī*, and ghee. (Āk 1.15.77)
One should take one *karṣa* of each [ingredient] daily in a light dose;
after twenty-one days, one becomes wise and a retainer of what has been heard. (Āk 1.15.78)
One should grind the five ingredients and purify them with a cloth;
one should always drink [the powder] with the water of Śiva, or with milk, or with cow urine. (Āk 1.15.79)
As before, she bestows success and removes all forms of skin disease;
