*oṃ glauṃ sauṃ hrīṃ khecarabhūcaradivyayogini imāṃ rakṣa rakṣa sarvaśatrupramathini svāhā*.
This is the mantra for binding with threads.
One thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra, the leader of mantras, should be performed every day.

In this manner, the practice should be performed for seven days; on the fifth day, one should meditate upon Amṛteśvarī, who resembles jasmine, the moon, and camphor, and is clad in white garments. (Āk 1.15.358)
Moistened with white garlands and unguents, adorned with ornaments of pearls, she holds a rosary in her right hand and a jar filled with nectar in her left. Āk 1.15.359.

Below that, on the right and left, one should visualize her standing there holding a book of consciousness (*saṃvit*); then, one should perform the ritual cutting (*lavana*) accompanied by mantras. (Āk 1.15.360)
One should collect [the fruits] that are glossy, possess seeds, and have leaves.
Oṃ klīṃ vaṃ saṃ krauṃ! O you who arise from the nectar of Śiva’s bliss, grant victory in the conquest of the three worlds, svāhā!
This is the mantra for preservation.
One should dry it for seven days in a clean place with mild sunlight. (Āk 1.15.361)
One should place those leaves in a new vessel and grind them into a fine powder;
having heated two pots, one should first roast [the powder] in one of them. (Āk 1.15.362)
Then one should seal it in another [vessel] in this manner, repeating the process again and again;
the expert should continue cooking it until it reaches the state of perfect maturity. (Āk 1.15.363)
O Goddess, O beloved, the Guñjā, the Unmattā, and the Vallī—using the sap of their leaves repeatedly, one should prepare seven distinct pots for each of them separately. Āk 1.15.364.
Muṇḍī, brāhmī, kumārī, varī, dhātrī, the two types of kaṭu, and sugandhikā are to be known in sequence, each measuring one pala. (Āk 1.15.365)

The *jayā* fruits, ground into powder, should be added in an amount equal to all those [other ingredients]; white sugar should be added in an amount equal to everything, and one should pour in cow's milk in an amount equal to that. (Āk 1.15.366)
Having cast sugar into the midst of milk, the physician should bring it to the consistency of a thin thread;
then he should add the powder of the plants beginning with *muṇḍā* and ending with *vijayā* into it. (Āk 1.15.367)
Having thus stirred it and brought it down to coolness, one should add honey and half as much sugar, then pour in an equal amount of cow's ghee, and mix them thoroughly together. (Āk 1.15.368)
Having placed two handfuls [of grain] upon the heap of grain, one should recite the mantra of Mahāvaṭuka every day a thousand times, or as many times as one is able. (Āk 1.15.369)
Hrīṃ śrīṃ! To Mahākālāgnibhairava, whose body is embraced by the Mothers of all Siddhis and by Brahmā, the dryer of all calamities, huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṃ!
This is the mantra for cooking with fire.
Having extracted [the substance] after a month, one should consume it according to the rite, [in a dose] the size of an āmalaka fruit.
Dwelling in a windless chamber, subsisting on milk-rice, he has his senses fully subdued.
One should meditate upon the deity as instructed by the guru, or upon the supreme reality,
twice or thrice a day, according to the strength of one's service in due order.
Thus, after three years, freed from old age and wrinkles, he attains the siddhi of moving upon the earth and shall live for three hundred years. (Āk 1.15.372)
Vārāhī, triphalā, citra, and aśvagandhā should be combined in sequence;
thus, one should add two, three, or four parts of aśvagandhā and the others respectively. Āk_1,15.373.
One should easily stir this equal amount with *vijayā* and honey; it should be kept in the sun for a fortnight and repeatedly heated. (Āk 1,15.374)
One should consume [it] like an āmalaka fruit; after eight months, one becomes radiant as the sun, and after a year, the practitioner becomes free from old age and death. (Āk 1.15.375)
O Goddess of the Gods, recite this mantra with devotion for the perfection of the body:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ mahāvyomabhāskarāya dīpimātṛkāliṅgitavigrahāya tejasāṃ nidhiṃ kuru kuru ṭhaṃ*. This is the Sūryapāka mantra.
Three palas of jayā and two palas of yaṣṭī powder.
One *pala* each of *elā*, *bhadrā*, and powdered *citrāmūla*, half a *pala* of powdered *śrīkhaṇḍa*, and sugar equal in weight to all these combined. Āk 1.15.377.

The wise man should mix half a *niṣka* of gold powder with one *niṣka* of Himalayan sandalwood (*himavālukā*), thoroughly knead it all with clarified butter, and place it under the moonlight. (Āk 1.15.378)
O Dear One, beginning from the fifth day of the bright fortnight until the end of the lunar half-month, one should practice the meditation on the moon;
having worshipped according to the rite, one whose inner chamber is purified should lick [the elixir]. Āk 1.15.379.
I shall state again its mantra, which bestows all accomplishments:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ mahāśaśāṅkakiraṇavisphārabhairavāya amṛteśvarīmātṛkāliṅgitavigrahāya visphuraṇaṃ kuru kuru huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṃ*.
This is the mantra for the ripening of the moon (*candrapāka*).
For such a ritual procedure, three kinds of mantra have been proclaimed.
One should perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite for each individual mantra ten thousand times;
the fire-sacrifice (*vahnipāka*) is to be carried out during the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha. (Āk 1.15.381)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the ripening of the Sun starting from the month of Phālguna;
the ripening of the Moon starting from Kārttika shall be a bestower of success. (Āk 1.15.382)
Muṇḍī combined with citraka and nirguṇḍī destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha);
if brāhmī is joined with kumārī, it destroys epilepsy (apasmāra). (Āk 1.15.383)
Jayā combined with varā and vyōṣa causes the destruction of wasting diseases; and jayā combined with the leaves of kārpāsa and matsyākṣī removes pitta. Āk 1,15.384.
Combined with the alkali of *snuhī* and *arka* leaves, it removes abdominal tumors and colic;
combined with the powder of *vacā* and *dūrvā*, it bestows the increase of wisdom. (Āk 1.15.385)
Combined with yaṣṭīgandhaka, it removes skin diseases and bestows nourishment;
combined with the mucilage of śālmalī and sugar, it increases virility. Āk 1.15.386.
Combined with pāṭhā, tiktā, and the three pungents (trikaṭuka), it removes diseases caused by phlegm;
when joined with white guñjā, it destroys great poisons for men. (Āk 1,15.387)
Combined with *vyāghāta* powder, it destroys leprosy;
combined with wild pepper and castor, it destroys wind disorders. (Āk 1.15.388)
These twelve yogas correspond to the twelve months; the practitioner should recite the three mantras in each respective month. (Āk 1.15.389)
By this yoga, the practitioner becomes truly free from old age and death;
there is no doubt about this, O fair-faced one—this is the truth, the absolute truth. (Āk 1,15.390)
Mercury, sulfur, the three aromatics, black mica, rudrākṣa, and gold ash should be ground together with the juice of jayā and processed by maceration for one fortnight. Āk 1.15.391.
One should roast it in a *bhūdhara* crucible or a *saṃpuṭa* apparatus, and then grind it into powder;
this [powder] should be combined with four times its weight of jaggery, sugar, and ghee. (Āk 1.15.392)
She should be served with a measure of one niṣka, either in the morning or in the evening;
and one should recite the Mahāvaṭuka mantra up to one hundred thousand times, O beloved. (Āk 1.15.393)
In the sixth month, there will be accomplishment; one becomes free from old age and death, possesses the speed of thought, and gains the strength of ten thousand elephants. (Āk 1.15.394)
And having attained the vajra-body, he shall live as long as the moon and stars;
[this is achieved] with the powder of a banyan sprout combined with sugar, honey, and clarified butter. Āk_1,15.395.
If one practices *jayā* for three fortnights, it brings all the world under one's control;
when combined with the powder of *apāmārga* and mixed with ghee, *jayā* [achieves this]. (Āk 1.15.396)
One should constantly recite the mantra; after six months, one becomes immortal.
The excellent white *jayā*, *citraka*, *trivṛtā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and *vṛṣā* [are the ingredients]. (Āk 1.15.397)
Dūrvā grass, bhṛṅga, marīca, madhuka, ajājī, saindhava salt, karpūra, and kacora—each of these in equal parts—with the powder of jayā added in equal measure to all. Āk 1.15.398.
One should stir it with the three honeys and place it in a smooth vessel; by consuming one karṣa at dawn, one shall become a possessor of siddhi within a month. Āk_1,15.399 //
One might become like a god for a year and live for three divine days by taking equal parts of powdered aśvagandhā, vacā, vyoṣa, and jayā. (Āk 1.15.400)
One should lick [the mixture] combined with the three sweets; after three years, one becomes equal to a deity.
Eight parts of hemp powder and four parts of *muṇḍikā* [are required]. (Āk 1.15.401)
Two parts of *brāhmī* powder, one part of *vājigandhā*, two parts of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and likewise two parts of *varā*. (Āk 1.15.402)
One part of stone, one part of sulfur, one part of the king of mercury (rasarāja), and half of that amount of gold ash. Āk 1.15.403.
One should add pearls equal in measure to that, and coral equal to the pearls;
having mixed them with honey and clarified butter, one should place them in a smooth vessel. (Āk 1.15.404)

Having prepared a decoction of grain for seven nights and performed three hundred thousand recitations, one should consume a pill weighing one *niṣka*, subsisting on a diet of milk while keeping the senses subdued. (Āk 1.15.405)
From the mandala, one becomes a destroyer of all diseases; after a year, one possesses flowers like fire;
after half a year, one becomes Bhairava; such a person shall live as long as the moon and stars endure. (Āk 1.15.406)

Śivamūlikā, taken in equal parts with the three aromatics (trisaugandhika), the best of the three aromatics (varā), and the three acrids (vyoṣa), and licked with honey and ghee, cures cough and increases the digestive fire. (Āk 1.15.407)
If consumed primarily with sweet substances, it conquers diseases such as cough and dyspnea;
combined with turmeric, it destroys all types of urinary disorders (meha). (Āk 1.15.408)
Maṇḍūkaparṇī together with vacā bestows speech and intelligence;
so too do drākṣā, sitā, vallakī, kharjūrī, and dugdhapiṇḍikā. (Āk 1.15.409)
Mixed with the juices of *kandalī* plants, it is known as "all-tasting" (*sarvasvādu*).
When combined with coconut water and rendered fragrant with camphor, [it is called *sarvasvādu*]. (Āk 1.15.410)
Endowed with all sweetness, it is perfected as a subduer of bile and an increaser of virility;
its milk possesses four times the quality of sweetness, becoming like honey in its ripening. (Āk 1.15.411)
Having filtered that through a cloth, one should add camphor to it;
then, one should drink it along with cardamom, all the sweet substances, and *jayā*. (Āk 1.15.412)
The seed of *jayā*, cast together with cloth into water mixed with milk, bestows the power to approach a hundred women and increases bile, the heart, and nourishment. (Āk 1.15.413)
O Dear One, one should cook the remaining fourth portion over a gentle fire;
having turned it into curd according to the rule, one should then churn it and extract [the butter]. Āk 1.15.414.
One should add fresh butter there, along with camphor, cardamom, sugar, and honey;
this brings about nourishment, longevity, and luster, while increasing strength and health. (Āk 1,15.415)
That which has been washed a hundred times with breast milk is called "hundred-washed" (śatadhauta).
Likewise, [one may use] nāgakeśara, kacchūra, lavaṅga, elā, and agaru. Āk 1.15.416.
Camphor, sandalwood, musk, *takkola*, and saffron—these, along with an equal amount of *jayā* seeds, should be ground together with cow’s milk. (Āk 1.15.417)
The wise one should fashion pills according to the measure of a niṣka or half a niṣka;
having scented them with fine flowers, he should place them along with betel leaf in his mouth. (Āk 1.15.418)
It purifies the mouth, removes foul odors, and is pure;
it bestows fragrance and clarity, and grants joy to the mind. (Āk 1,15.419)
One should throw dhātakī flowers, nutmeg, ginger, and jayā in quantities equal to all of those together into cow’s milk mixed with half as much water. Āk 1.15.420.
One should strain the remaining milk through a cloth and saturate it with the three sweets;
known as Siddhayoga, it bestows virility, longevity, and strength. (Āk 1.15.421)
Alternatively, a powder composed of *ajamodā* mixed with *niśā* (turmeric) dust, when used alone, destroys ringworm and skin eruptions. (Āk 1.15.422)
When combined with *tālī*, *jayā* destroys hemorrhoids as well as swelling;
when combined with *śilā*, it should be known that *vijayā* is a pacifier of itching.
The wise one should prepare *jayā* in a pot with oil, and afterwards in molasses, until it reaches a thick consistency; he should always consume it together with ghee. (Āk 1.15.424)
Manifestly, it is a synonym for Cupid, bestowing pleasure upon many women.
Pathyā, bhallātaka, jaggery, and sesame seeds—these, taken in equal parts, [constitute the remedy]. (Āk 1.15.425)
Vijayā, taken in equal parts with those [other ingredients], destroys the six types of hemorrhoids;
likewise, yavānī, the two types of jīraka, and ajamodā, each in equal proportions. (Āk 1.15.426)
The wise should consume Vijayā, which is equal in potency to this [Harītakī], along with clarified butter; it cures sandhivāta, vertigo, vomiting, insanity, and headache. (Āk 1.15.427)

Having made a pill from sugar, honey, and all types of *māgadhī* (long pepper) in equal parts with *jayā*, and having caused it to drip in clarified butter, they know this as the "five-fold antidote" (*pañcāgada*). (Āk 1.15.428)

It destroys heart disease, splenic disorders, abdominal ailments, and fistula-in-ano; it contains *citraka*, stimulates the digestive fire, possesses excellent qualities, and breaks the force of colic pain. (Āk 1.15.429)
Combined with trikaṭu, it destroys wind; combined with sugar, it subdues pitta.
The seeds of śvetādrikarṇikā and vijayā, taken with donkey urine—Āk 1,15.430.
When used as a nasal medication (*nasya*), it removes epilepsy and destroys malevolent spirits, ghosts, and the like.
One should consume the powder of *jayā* with honey and clarified butter until it resembles the size of an *āmalaka* fruit. (Āk 1.15.431)
Vijayā is supreme for producing eloquence of speech and an increase in vigor;
it may be taken with honey and ghee, or with dhātrī, musta, or their own expressed juices. (Āk 1,15.432)
When used at night, *jayā* bestows clarity of vision upon men; it extends youth and stability, and shall become a supreme promoter of longevity. (Āk 1.15.433)
Jaggery, abhayā, and vijayā break up chronic skin diseases; cleaning the teeth with a jaya twig makes the teeth firm. (Āk 1.15.434)

If the purification of the sense of taste is performed using *vijayā* wood smeared with oil, it will destroy the impurities and foul odors on the tongue; thus, one's capacity for perceiving tastes will become authentic. (Āk 1.15.435)
One should cook *jayā* in coconut milk over a gentle fire; having smeared it with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one should drink it at night and thereby enjoy a hundred women. (Āk 1.15.436)
Equal parts of ginger and *harītakī*, along with an equal amount of *jayā*, and sugar equal to the sum of all these should be combined; this formulation is "Enchanting the Three Worlds. (Āk 1.15.437)
One should prepare equal parts of trikaṭu, madhuka, cavya, the four aromatics (cāturjāta), fruit (musta), varā (chebulic myrobalan), gostanī (long pepper), and pippalīmūla. Āk_1,15.438.
The marrow of *priyāla* is equal to those [other ingredients], and *jayā* is equal to all of them combined;
when these have been cooked with three times as much jaggery, one should add their powder, O Auspicious One. (Āk 1.15.439)
Having stirred [the ingredients], one who desires [success] should make *kandarpa-modakas*, which pacify all diseases, destroy the three *doṣas*, and bestow strength. (Āk 1.15.440)

The wise man, having purified his digestive tract, should consume these aphrodisiacs and nourishing substances three times a day at the three junctions of the day; after three years, such success as this is attained. Āk 1.15.441.
One who always employs this [remedy] becomes free from old age and death. [The ingredients are:
long pepper, long pepper root, ginger, cinnamon, cardamom, and cinnamon leaves, taken in equal parts. (Āk 1.15.442)
With these, one should prepare *modakas* equal to *vijayā*, using wheat flour and twice as much jaggery. (Āk 1,15.443)
One who restrains the senses and eats a *karṣa* measure every day will, within a year, be endowed with strength and nourishment, and be free from wrinkles and grey hair. (Āk 1.15.444)
With chickpeas, mung beans, green gram, or pigeon peas, likewise with sesame seeds, or with dehusked flat beans fried in ghee and mixed with jaggery. (Āk 1.15.445)
Having combined *vijayā* with equal parts of *satrijāta*, *savyoṣa*, and *jīra*, one should prepare pills (*modaka*) weighing one *karṣa* each. (Āk 1.15.446)
One of purified intellect should eat each one daily, both morning and evening;
they remove all diseases, increase virility, and bestow strength upon the intellect and the senses. (Āk 1.15.447)
Takola, sandalwood, camphor, and nāgakesara; cardamom, cloves, madhuka, long pepper, and likewise black pepper—these should be used. (Āk 1.15.448)
Vijayā and white sugar in equal parts with all [the other ingredients] is auspicious and balanced;
this powder named Pañcabāṇa removes all diseases. (Āk 1,15.449)
By using it for twelve years, one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair.
The excellent *trijātaka*, a piece of the moon, and the three pungents are the seed-mantra. (Āk 1,15.450)
Equal parts of these, along with sugar of identical quality, stirred with honey and licked, is an appetite-stimulant that bestows perfection upon the body. (Āk 1.15.451)

Śatāvarī combined with an equal amount of uttamā, vyōṣa, and twice as much musalī, along with an equal amount of jayā and an equal amount of sugar, bestows virility, longevity, and strength. (Āk 1.15.452)
Ginger combined with sugar taken in the morning promotes longevity;
jayā prepared with milk, when consumed at night, is aphrodisiac and strengthening. Āk 1,15.453.
When consumed with honey before a meal along with *vājigandhā*, it brings about strength and nourishment; this proven preparation is a supreme elixir (*rasāyana*). (Āk 1.15.454)
Having cooked the seeds of *markaṭikā* (without their skins), equal parts of *māṣa* flour, and *jayā* in buffalo milk, it should be consumed at night; it produces extreme virility. (Āk 1.15.455)
One should [process it] seven times each in the sun with the juices of śālmalī, picchavarī, bhṛṅga, and amṛtā, using the reflected rays [of the sun] in a vessel of iron.
One should subsequently perform the visualization and grind that [substance] together with an equal amount of *jayā*;
one should lick a *karṣa* of it with honey, which destroys old age and death. (Āk 1.15.457)

One should take the five parts of the *śālmali* tree together with an equal amount of powdered *vijayā*; one should lick a *karṣa* of this mixture with honey and clarified butter, which destroys wrinkles and graying hair. (Āk 1.15.458)
Then, on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, one should take *hastikanda* together with its roots;
having dried it in the shade, one should powder it and mix it with an equal amount of *jayā*. (Āk 1,15.459)
One should then stir it with honey and place it in a greased vessel;
after keeping it for twenty-one days in a heap of grain, one should then remove it. (Āk 1.15.460)
One should consume one pala daily in two meals;
meanwhile, one should avoid pungent and sour foods, eating instead soft soups and grains. (Āk 1.15.461)
The meat of wild animals is sweet, light, pacifies pitta, and is beneficial.
One who has the luster of the rising sun, is intelligent, possesses a melodious voice like the cuckoo, and is endowed with strength—Āk_1,15.462.
One travels a distance of one hundred yojanas in a single day by taking equal parts of powdered *muṇḍī* and powdered *jayā*, combined with honey and clarified butter. (Āk 1.15.463)
One should lick one *karṣa* every morning daily; this promotes longevity and nourishment.
One should practice this for twelve years, consuming it in combination with clarified butter. (Āk 1.15.464)

By consuming cow’s milk and *ṣaṣṭika* rice, free from salt, sourness, and alkaline substances, one becomes free from wrinkles and old age; one appears youthful and possesses a light body. (Āk 1,15.465)
One should collect the leaves, flowers, and fruit of the white Brahmavṛkṣa tree;
one should dry them in the shade and reduce them to powder, mixing that with an equal amount of Vijayā pollen. (Āk 1.15.466)
One should lick one karṣa of this with honey and ghee for a year, and one will attain youth;
O Dear One, one should also fry jayā seeds and sesame seeds with jaggery.
Having prepared sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) soaked in cow’s ghee, one should eat them in the morning;
they enchant the mind and accomplish union with a beloved woman. (Āk 1.15.468)
One should cook the *jayā* leaves together with seasonings suitable for cooking;
one should then fry them in cow’s ghee along with jaggery, *elā*, pungent spices, and cumin. (Āk 1.15.469)
This prepared dish, named Vyañjanayogarāja, is pleasant to consume;
it consists of rice, vijayā seeds, and peeled mung beans. (Āk 1.15.470)
One should place [the substance] inside a coconut with a large cavity and seal the opening;
having smeared the exterior with cow-dung and clay, one should dry it over a gentle fire. (Āk 1.15.471)
One should cook it inside a coconut and collect that liquor;
one should consume it along with the three sweets according to one's strength. (Āk 1,15.472)
This yoga brings about great virility and bestows manhood even upon eunuchs.
One should place the seeds of *vijayā* tied in a cloth into cow’s milk. (Āk 1,15.473)
When that milk is reduced by half and cooled by the breeze of a fan, [one should add] the seeds of vārāhī and markaṭī, camphor, cardamom, and cloves. (Āk 1.15.474)
One should add the three sweets and the three aromatics in equal proportions;
having mixed them together, one should drink it at night, for it is a supreme aphrodisiac. (Āk 1.15.475)
This is the Vārāhī-yoga, which cuts away impotence and other such defects;
one should grind that seed, boiled in milk, into a fine paste with a stone. (Āk 1.15.476)
One should smear the juice of the uttamakanyā plant onto a bronze vessel and keep it in intense sunlight; from that, one should extract the oily essence.
One should perform the administration of nasal therapy (nasyakarma) with that [oil] combined with other unctuous substances;
it removes diseases located above the clavicle, as well as cough, dyspnea, and so forth. (Āk 1.15.478)
Whatever medicine is prescribed for whichever specific disease, when combined with that [mantra], it becomes perfected and will remove that very disease. (Āk 1.15.479)
And I shall describe its qualities; listen to them, O Maheśvarī:
moisture of the tongue, happiness of mind, contentment, and the fulfillment of one's intentions. (Āk 1.15.480)
One will possess eloquence of speech, a radiant countenance, and a fondness for physical exercise;
one will be devoted to bathing, meditation, and worship, and will be eager for sweet tastes. (Āk 1.15.481)
Eating choice foods, drinking cool water, intent on conversation, devoted to looking about as he pleases, and eager for the company of women. (Āk 1,15.482)

Pervaded by compassion for all beings, his intellect dissolved in the knowledge of reality, he was solely devoted to the composition, narration, understanding, and exposition [of the Dharma]. (Āk 1.15.483)
One shall achieve victory in debates, in battle, and in the wrestling ring;
moreover, there are many other qualities that are difficult to find elsewhere. (Āk 1,15.484)
(Regarding victory, non-harm, and accomplishment:
O Supreme Goddess, listen to those transformations that indeed arise when the price for this accomplishment is exceeded by consumption. Āk 1,15.485.
With reddened eyes, and with the surface of his tongue, lips, and palate dried up;
first, the tip of the nose dries, followed by difficulty breathing and heat in the sides of the body. (Āk 1.15.486)
In the second [stage], there is the closing of the eyes and the body becomes covered with scales;
in the third, there is a burning sensation in the feet, hands, and eyes, along with a faltering voice.
In the fourth [stage], one is afflicted by hunger and thirst, with eyes rolling from sleep;
in the fifth, speech becomes faltering, and one forgets what was said moments ago. (Āk 1.15.488)

When the sixth transformation has arisen, it causes the loss of mindfulness of the mind; in the seventh, there is a loss of strength in the hands and a lack of appetite for food in the body. (Āk 1.15.489)
Great waves of exhilaration arise again and again;
in the eighth [dhyāna], there is confusion of the directions, tranquility, knitting of the eyebrows, and excessive weeping. (Āk 1.15.490)
In the ninth [stage], there is the sound "huṃ" from the ears, fainting, loss of memory, and timidity;
belching, moaning, rolling on the ground, and wretched speech. (Āk 1.15.491)
Speaking otherwise than the truth is a secret; he does not know happiness, and even suffering becomes mild for him, O beloved, as his limbs become perspiring. (Āk 1.15.492)
There are many other disorders; their treatment consists of purgation, sour tastes, and subsequently bathing the head with cold water. (Āk 1.15.493)
His body was adorned with garlands and anointed with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, and cool water, becoming fragrant and refreshing. Āk_1,15.494.
She possessed beds of jasmine, Arabian jasmine, *cāmpeya*, lotus, and water-lily, as well as couches shining with coils of lotus stalks and leaves of the plantain tree.
One should chew camphor, cardamom, cloves, *takola*, and *kaṭukī* fruit together with betel leaf, while fanning oneself with a palm-leaf fan. (Āk 1.15.496)
He should wear fine, fragrant saffron-colored garments;
and for two muhūrtas during the moonlight, he should gaze at the moon reflected in his bracelet. (Āk 1,15.497)
Intent on a firm embrace of her pair of full and elevated breasts, he should lie down;

Administering nasal drops through both nostrils destroys old age and death;
such a person shall live for three hundred years, free from all diseases. (Āk 1.16.11)
For men whose life-force has departed due to disease, water-snare [drowning], delusion, or poison, one should administer nasal drops mixed with white *puṃs* [semen]. (Āk 1,16.12)
O sinless one, they will undoubtedly revive with oil mixed with the ashes of the dead; thus has the previously mentioned "science of reviving the dead" been described. (Āk 1.16.13)
(Other formulations for elixirs: Cardamom, chebulic myrobalan, sweet flag, the fruit of *kākatuṇḍī*, *maruṣkara*, *sahadevī*, neem leaves, and the tuber of *lāṅgalī*. Āk 1.16.14.
One should dry equal parts [of the ingredients] in the apparatus and extract the oil from the *pātāla* [vessel].
O beloved, one should take that oil as a nasal drop (*nasya*) at intervals of seven days. (Āk 1.16.15)
When the nasal medication has been administered in this manner for a year, a man shall live for a thousand years;
he should also drink half a pala of oil combined with the root of *nīlikā*. (Āk 1.16.16)
Within a year, one becomes perfected, free from wrinkles and grey hair;
after three years, one lives for a day of Brahmā, possessing the speed of the wind and great strength.
One should prepare one *prastha* each of *bhṛṅgarasa* and black cumin; blue lotus and licorice (*madhuka*) shall each be half a *prastha*. (Āk 1.16.18)
One should cook five palas of sesame oil with all these ingredients together;
when only the oil remains, that oil destroys both old age and death. (Āk 1.16.19)
Half a niṣka, one niṣka, and one and a half niṣkas respectively—this is said to be the measure of oil; [using it], one shall live for three hundred years. (Āk 1.16.20)
Having cast one *pala* of *iṣṭikā* into water, one should drink one *karṣa* of it;
after a year, it destroys graying hair, and the man shall live for a thousand years. (Āk 1.16.21)
Sarpākṣī, kākamācī, sahadevī, bhṛṅgarāja, the fruit of kākatuṇḍī, nimba leaves, and the seeds of vākucī. Āk 1.16.22.
The root of *devadālī* with its taproot, the root of *brāhmī*, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), the root of *vājigandhā*, and the leaf of blue *koraṇḍa*. (Āk 1.16.23)
One should thoroughly soak equal parts of the powder and the juices for seven days, then dry the resulting powder in the shade, saturated with the three sweets (trimadhu). Āk 1.16.24.
One should consume two karṣas daily; by doing so for a year, one conquers old age.
Endowed with great strength, one may live happily as long as the moon and stars endure. (Āk 1.16.25)
(The Ritual Manual of Mahākāmeśvara):

Four types of *jātaka* wood, *coraca*, sandalwood, water, grapes, *tugā*, *reṇuka*, musk, *tagara*, moon [white sandalwood], saffron, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *kuṣṭha*, *aśvagandhā*, *abdaka*, *kaṅkola*, *amaradāru*, *citraka*, poison, two types of cumin, rock salt, *bhārṅgī*, *gokṣura*, *devapuṣpa*, *musālī*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *balā*, and *phenaka*. (Āk 1.16.26)

Rambhā-kanda, the three fruits (triphala), the three pungents (trikaṭuka), nutmeg (jātīphala), vāśaka, tālīśa, kaṭukī-phala, gaja-kaṇā, māṣa, amṛtā, sugar (śarkarā), picchā, bhṛṅga, vidārī, madanaka, the seed produced from kacchū, śālmalī, aṅghri, punarnavā, agaru, śatāvarī, and likewise dīpyaka. Āk 1.16.27.

One part of mercury, one part of mica, and an equal amount of *vijayā* (conch-shell), with all these ingredients combined in equal proportions, mixed with sugar, honey, and clarified butter, and scented overnight with flowers such as *jātī*, *campaka*, and *ketaka*—one should consume half a *karṣa* of this at night; it is the Great Lord of Desire (*Mahākāmeśvara*), which grants the perfection of the body and fulfills all desires. (Āk 1,16.28)

For men, drinking milk as an after-drink is beneficial for increasing and strengthening the semen; likewise is drinking water infused with the roots of the *śālmali* tree, or whatever else is semen-prolific (*śukrala*).

It is a great liquefier that grants supreme bliss through pleasure to mature and beautiful women; it is submissive, possesses the essence of the fleeting passion of love during union, and bestows the delight of the arts of play. (Āk 1,16.29)
In sexual union with an elderly woman, it destroys the pride of young men; it is the source of eternal bliss, its taste having been relished even by the primordial beings.
It brings about the perfection of speech and the composition of excellent poetry; it bestows happiness, health, exceptional youth, and the totality of the arts. (Āk 1,16.30)

It removes old age and bestows strength; it casts away death and dispels the multitude of diseases. It produces luster and leads to uprightness. For one devoted to the practice of yoga, success becomes easily attainable; it most certainly ordains the destruction of the succession of sins and grants offspring to women. (Āk 1,16.31)
It quickly destroys the accumulation and the wasting of diseases; it strikes down the great host of *rudra*-fevers, brings the breath (*śvasana*) to dissolution, and cuts off the onset of coughing.

It splits asunder the six types of hemorrhoids (*durnāman*), removes all violent pains from disease, lops away the flood of urinary disorders (*meha*), and, through its application, utterly destroys blood-bile dysentery (*śoṇitadara*). (Āk 1.16.32)

When [the digestive fire] is diminished, it bestows abundant nourishment; when full, it restores the excessively worn-out and blazing fire; and for those with weak digestion, it thoroughly cuts away the *grahaṇī* disorder as well as all remaining humors (*doṣas*).

It is the most excellent among all rejuvenators (*rasāyana*s); through its daily consumption, it perfectly brings about the perfection of the body for the wise, for those seeking enjoyment, and for yogins. (Āk 1.16.33)
(Extension of the combination of mercury, mica, and so forth to the *mūlikā* rituals:
"In these rituals concerning the *mahāvṛkṣa* and others that have been taught, this common application must be performed by practitioners who desire success. (Āk 1.16.34)
A man should employ and consume either one *guñjā* of pure mercury or two *paṇas* of *vābhraka*, and likewise *kāntaloha*. (Āk 1.16.35)
Through the application of mercury, mica, and iron, one attains immediate perfection;
for like a body devoid of life or a flower lacking fragrance, [the body is useless otherwise]. (Āk 1.16.36)
In the same way, the medicinal preparations (mūlikākalpa) devoid of mercury do not bestow success;
therefore, when accompanied by mercury, they grant immediate accomplishment. Āk 1,16.37.
(Anointing elixir; Mahānīlī oil:
O beloved, one *prastha* of the juice of *mahānīlī* and one *prastha* of the juice of *bhṛṅga*.
One *prastha* of the juice of *dhātrī* fruits and [one *prastha*] originating from *kākatuṇḍī* fruits.
One should combine one *prastha* of decoction made from sesame, one *prastha* of oil, and one *āḍhaka* of cow’s milk; then add one *pala* of *kākatuṇḍī* fruit. (Āk 1.16.39)
O Dear One, having ground three palas of *āmalaka* and one pala of the powder of *bhṛṅga* and *nīlī* leaves, one should add all of that to it and cook it over a gentle fire. Āk 1.16.40.
Then, having boiled the remaining oil, one should strain it through a cloth;
having anointed the head with this oil, one should perform a head massage. (Āk 1.16.41)
One should perform this elixir daily as an ear-ornament; thus the hair becomes like bees [in color] and the hearing acquires the clarity that reaches to the ends of the quarters. (Āk 1.16.42)
Diseases above the collarbone are destroyed, and likewise, it becomes beneficial for the feet.
(Candanādya-taila): Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron; likewise—Āk_1,16.43.
The two types of uśīra, kaṅkola, nutmeg, cloves, nalikā, nalada, spṛkkā, turuṣka, sthāṇu, and locana. Āk 1.16.44.
Hareṇu, tagara, lac, nakha, sthauṇeyaka, murā, nalada, āmalaka, kuṣṭha, coraka, and the fruit of kaṭukī. Āk 1.16.45.
Prapauṇḍarīka, kharjūra, padmaka, jātipattrikā, śaileya, dhātakī flowers, sarala, and elavāluka. (Āk 1.16.46)
O beloved, one *karṣa* each of *pūgīphala*, *saptaparṇa*, and *tāmalaka*, along with one *prastha* of oil and cow’s milk. (Āk 1.16.47)
One should cook all that until it is reduced to one āḍhaka, and then carefully collect the remaining oil;
into that, one should add musk, musk-deer musk, camphor, and saffron. (Āk 1.16.48)
The wise person should separately extract [the oil] and perfume it with flowers such as *jāti*;
with that, one should perform anointing on the lower body to destroy foul odors. (Āk 1.16.49)
Though he may be about eighty years of age, he shall appear as if sixteen; handsome and increasing in whiteness, he will be the pride and delight of the world of women. (Āk 1.16.50)
He who enjoys the company of a hundred women shall live for a hundred autumns.
(The Elixir of Rubbing) Now I shall describe the rubbing [massage] which destroys wrinkles and graying hair. Āk 1.16.51.
One should grind equal parts of mercury and fragrance with breast milk from a woman, along with muṇḍikā, meghanāda, viṣṇukrāntā, and likewise munī. (Āk 1.16.52)
One should macerate *sarpākṣī* with their juices for one day;
this [mixture] should be ten times the amount of sesame and barley alkali. (Āk 1.16.53)

All this—along with honey and clarified butter—is used for anointing the body; by this, wrinkles and graying hair are destroyed, and one shall live for three hundred years after a year [of practice]. (Āk 1.16.54)
Having become one with a divine body, the practitioner shall live; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should grind a lotus flower together with its stalk and mercury for seven days. (Āk 1.16.55)
Then, one should rub the body with the auspicious water belonging to oneself;
after a year, success arises as before, [resulting in] a divine form. (Āk 1.16.56)
O Goddess, one should grind the lord of elixirs (sūtendra) with the ash of Śiva and the root of Brahmadaṇḍī for seven days; one should thoroughly rub it together. Āk 1,16.57.
Success arises after a year, and one’s form becomes divine as before;
one should saturate a *surabhi* flower with pungent oil for seven days. (Āk 1.16.58)
If one eats half a leaf daily, after a year one will have a body like a diamond;
possessing a lifespan of three hundred years and a golden complexion, one will be free from wrinkles and gray hair. (Āk 1.16.59)
A person should lick one karṣa of powdered kuṣṭha mixed with honey and ghee every morning;
having a body as fragrant as the śatapuṣpa flower, he shall live free from wrinkles. (Āk 1.16.60)

(Recipes for dyeing the eyebrows: Having stirred together the fruit of *kākatuṇḍī*, *kāntacūrṇa*, and oil from the seeds of mango, one should place it in a vessel and bury it for a month in a heap of grain. (Āk 1.16.61)
Having extracted [the juice], one should smear it on the head; by means of this, a nasal treatment (*nasyakarma*) is performed.
Within three days the hair will become beautifully blue-black, and within six months there will be a complete dyeing of the hair. (Āk 1.16.62)
One karṣa of harītakī, two palas of iron powder (kāntacūrṇa), and one pala of lead powder (nāgacūrṇa) should be ground together with sour curd. Āk 1.16.63.
Having anointed [the head], one should apply it to the crown of the head and massage it for half a nāḍikā;
then, having wrapped it with castor leaves, one should bind it again with a cloth. (Āk 1.16.64)

One should bathe again for three days as before, and [perform] the coloring of the hair with *nīlikā* and *bhṛṅga* together with their roots, along with iron powder equal in measure to *varā*. (Āk 1.16.65)
One should soak the powder in goat’s urine for one day;
having performed the bathing and other rites as before, the coloring of the hair is done as previously described. (Āk 1.16.66)

O beloved, one should take the seeds of *guñjā* (without their husks), *cailā*, *devadāru*, and *kuṣṭha* in equal parts; this powder should be saturated with the juice of *bhṛṅga* for one day. Āk 1.16.67.
The wise man should cook any other powder with oil over a gentle fire;
by anointing with this oil and ghee, one's hair becomes like a black bee. (Āk 1.16.68)
Equal parts of burnt elephant tusk and *rasāñjana*, ground together with goat’s milk and applied as an ointment, results in the darkening of the hair. (Āk 1.16.69)
Equal parts of black earth, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the juice of *bhṛṅga*, and iron powder should be mixed together and confined in a vessel for one month. (Āk 1.16.70)
By applying that ointment for five months, the hair shall become black;
having ground the fruit of the *dhātrī*, the *japā* flower, and iron dross, one should apply it to the head. (Āk 1.16.71)
One should apply that [mixture] for three days; by this, the hair will become like a black bee.
The powder is like vermilion (sindūra), and the *sāṃbraṇī* is equal in measure to those two. Āk 1.16.72.
Having ground together gorocanā, black sesame seeds, and śatapuṣpā with the water of the Śiva-mantra, an application as a paste immediately dyes the hair. (Āk 1.16.73)
One should grind all this kākamācī in an iron vessel;
by means of that very [mixture], after a day has passed, it is the supreme dye for the hair. (Āk 1.16.74)
A paste made from white mustard, *sarja* resin, and barley-alkali, ground with sour gruel and the juice of *nāgapuṣpa*, should be used as an ointment for dyeing the hair. (Āk 1.16.75)
One should grind the powder of plantain root, as well as vermilion and charcoal, with the juices of citron in an iron vessel using an iron pestle. (Āk 1.16.76)
By applying it for a single day, the hair becomes dyed;
[the ingredients are] green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), blue lotus leaves, curd, and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*. (Āk 1.16.77)
Iron powder in equal proportions, when applied as a paste, dyes the hair;
one should also rub the leaves of the *koraṇṭa* with *nāgadaṇḍa*. (Āk 1.16.78)
And by applying that for three days, the hair becomes like a black bee;
[the ingredients are] excellent *bhṛṅgī*, mango seed, lotus stalk, and *priyaṅgu*. (Āk 1.16.79)
Indigo, turmeric, iron, and lead, powdered together with neem oil, should be stirred in a vessel made of magnetite (kāntaloha) and left to infuse for one month. Āk 1.16.80.
With that, the black hair is smeared and dyed, becoming like bees;
likewise, black sesame seeds and *kākamācī* seeds in equal proportions [are used]. (Āk 1.16.81)
That [substance] should be extracted from an oil-press; by means of it, the coloring of the hair is achieved.
One *karṣa* of *japā* juice mixed with honey should be administered as nasal drops (*nasya*) for seven days. (Āk 1.16.82)
After that, one should dye the hair; for this is the best of all nasal preparations.
Having ground triphalā and iron powder with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, [one should apply it]. (Āk 1.16.83)
This oil should be mixed with an equal amount of *bhṛṅga* juice;
then one should cook the whole mixture over a gentle fire until only the oil remains. (Āk 1.16.84)
One should place that oil in a smooth vessel on the ground for a month;
previously, one should have smeared the head with oil and [covered it] with leaves of the *kāravallī* plant. (Āk 1.16.85)
One should wrap it with a cloth and keep it in a windless place while consuming a milk diet;
one should wash it with decoctions of triphalā for seven days, O beloved. (Āk 1.16.86)
One should perform the coloring of the skull for as long as one lives, without a doubt;
[using] the seeds of *śrīālīkākatuṇḍī* with the juices of *nirguṇḍikā*. (Āk 1.16.87)
It should be infused separately with the juices of hibiscus flowers for four days;
that oil should be distilled using the *pātālayantra*, and an ointment should be made from it. (Āk 1.16.88)
One should place it upon the head and wrap it with *gandharva* leaves;
then, the wise one, dwelling in a place devoid of wind, should cover it with a cloth. (Āk 1.16.89)
One who subsists on milk should perform a bath in *kāñjika* for seven days;
thus, one's hair will become like a black bee for as long as one lives—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.16.90)
Having ground together equal parts of *jalamaṇḍanikā*, *kākamācī*, and *bhṛṅga*, one should cook oil; then, one should prepare a soup and subsequently smear it with that oil. (Āk 1.16.91)
One should smear the head with that for seven days to dye the hair;
one should arrange the bathing, eating, and sleeping as before. (Āk 1.16.92)
Having ground it with the juice of the best *bhṛṅgarāja*, one should smear it onto a vessel of *kāntaloha*;
having placed it face-down, one should [rinse] it in the morning with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*. (Āk 1.16.93)
Having ground it again, one should lick the head [of the preparation] and wash it with water decocted from the three myrobalans (*triphalā*);
one should perform this for twenty-one days as before and obtain the same result. (Āk 1.16.94)
Having ground *garala* and black cumin and sealed their opening, the wise man should dig a hole in the muddy courtyard of the house and place them there. (Āk 1,16.95)

After six months, one should properly extract that which has become liquefied and black; one should place a *karṣa* of it in the middle of the head, and perform the wrapping and so forth as before. (Āk 1.16.96)
One should dye the hair from birth; that is the dyeing for the *kāpālika*.
*Bhṛṅgī*, indigo, *varā*, black iron, and the seed of *madana* [are used for this]. (Āk 1.16.97)
Koraṇṭaka flower, powder derived from the bark of the arjuna tree, and the root of the lotus and the jambu tree—all these taken in equal parts. (Āk 1.16.98)
One should place it in an iron vessel and bury it in the ground for a fortnight;
one should then remove the paste from the vessel, and take four times as much oil as there is of that paste. Āk 1.16.99.
Four times the amount of oil should be juice of *bhṛṅga*, and four times that should be a decoction of *varā*; one should cook all of this over a gentle fire. (Āk 1.16.100)
One should cook the residue of the oil, having ground it in an iron vessel; then, for the sake of testing it, one should apply a drop of it to a crow's wing feather. (Āk 1.16.101)
If the medicine is blackened by oil, it will be a bestower of success;
the practitioner should have it boiled in that vessel for one month. (Āk 1.16.102)

By repeatedly smearing his hair with the juices of the tamarind (*ciñcā*), the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*), and the *palāśa*, as well as with the resin of the *vāsā* plant, his hair becomes like a black bee after six months.
One should quickly stir the mercury contained in the vessel until it turns to ash;
one should then cook that mercury-ash along with one *pala* of iron powder. (Āk 1,16.104)
Two palas of the best powder, three palas of pomegranate rind, and one pala of this [other ingredient], all equal in measure, [should be mixed] with sour gruel in an iron vessel. (Āk 1,16.105)
One should stir and cook it slightly for a moment in that iron vessel, then keep it in the sun after it has been saturated with the juices of *bhṛṅga* and *koraṇṭa*. (Āk 1.16.106)
It should be processed for twenty-one days, repeatedly made into a liquid; hair smeared with that very substance becomes like the color of a peacock's tail feathers. Āk 1.16.107.
In the applications of collyrium and lac, whether prescribed or otherwise mentioned, one should apply an ointment at night and likewise wrap [the eye] with castor leaves. Āk 1,16.108.
This rite of morning ablution is remembered as common to all.
(Instruction on the locations suitable for gathering divine herbs:
In a cremation ground, in water, on a path, in a house, or likewise in a temple. Āk 1,16.109.
In a place filled with excrement and urine, in a village, in a cow-pen, beneath a tree, in the shade, in a place abounding in poison, in a cold spot, or in any other afflicted location; Āk 1,16.110.
In such places as these, a proven root-herb should not be taken; rather, it should be sought in a forest, on a mountain, at the bank of a river, or in a pure grove of ascetics. Āk 1.16.111.
In a pure field attached to stone, in a field of accomplishment, on the shore of the ocean, on Śrīparvata, on the Snowy Mountain, at a lake, in a secluded pool— Āk 1.16.112.
One should take the roots that have grown, which bestow the perfection of the body;
[this is] the procedure for taking divine medicinal herbs during the rite of binding protective cords for all perfected roots. (Āk 1,16.113)
In the [cycles of] destructions, upheavals, and dissolutions, the divine Manus are indeed described in succession; they are remembered as being common to all.
On the very day before, having bathed well, having cleansed his teeth,
having anointed himself, wearing clean garments, joyful, and with a restrained mind— Āk 1.16.115.

Remaining silent and provided with perfumes and unbroken rice grains, he should go to the previously sought root that grants one's desired aims, which has been encircled by a protective thread. Āk 1.16.116.
Having cleared away the grass all around and dug [the ground], one should sprinkle it with water;
having performed worship with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, one should bind it with a thread. (Āk 1.16.117)
Accompanied by the mantra, the supreme practitioner, having fasted and subdued his senses, should say:
"Stay right here, O auspicious one; become the accomplisher of my task. (Āk 1,16.118)
My task has been accomplished; therefore, you shall go to heaven.
Oṃ hrīṃ! Salutations to you, O you who are born of nectar, who increases strength and virility! Grant me strength and long life; destroy my sin far away! Hrīṃ phaṭ!
With this very mantra, it should be wrapped three times with thread.
Having touched it, one should bind the protection and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Then, having risen at dawn and performed the daily rites, being pure— Āk 1.16.120.

Having approached that root and having worshipped it with all the ritual services such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should offer an oblation (bali) together with its causal formula. Āk 1.16.121.
The wise one should dig while reciting the mantra; this mantra is also declared: "With that by which Brahmā digs you, with that by which Bhṛgu digs you... (Āk 1.16.122).
"By that same path through which Indra, Varuṇa, and Viṣṇu have passed, I shall approach you;
I shall dig you up with my own hand, purified by mantras. (Āk 1.16.123)
Having thus made the supplication at the outset, one should subsequently recite the mantra:
*oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ taṃ amṛteśvari ehi ehi mama sakalasiddhiṃ kuru huṃ phaṭ*.
With this very mantra, one should bury the root of accomplishment. (Āk 1,16.124)
Then, having uprooted it, one should pray with palms joined:
"May you not fly up, may you not fall down, and may you not become otherwise.
Oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍa huṃ phaṭ svāhā!"
O Supreme Goddess, one should uproot [the plant] with this very mantra;
having taken it while its roots are uncut, it should be wrapped in a pure cloth. (Āk 1.16.125)
Having placed it in a small cloth bundle within his own home in a clean spot, he should joyfully deposit it in his storehouse; thereafter, he may break his fast. (Āk 1.16.126)
Oṃ, homage to Bhairava, the bestower of great siddhis, the deliverer from calamity, hūṃ phaṭ!
By this very mantra, one should take [the child] and bring him home. (Āk 1.16.127)
Āk, 1, 17 (The Elixir of Life for the Morning Drink):
Then the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, with a joyful mind, asked:
Śrī Bhairavī said:
O Ādibhairava, Lord of Gods, cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction! (Āk 1.17.1)
O All-Knowing Śiva, Lord of the World, by your grace, O All-Pervading One, I have heard of various divine elixirs (rasāyana). Āk 1,17.2.
It is easy to accomplish, easily obtained, divine, and provides immediate proof;
it is especially suitable for children, women, eunuchs, the elderly, and those afflicted by disease. (Āk 1.17.3)
"O God, O treasure-house of compassion, tell [me] what is suitable for those worthy of elixirs. Then Bhairava, who terrifies worldly existence, with his lotus-face smiling, [spoke]. Āk 1,17.4.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is suitable for all, which brings happiness, which is purifying and easily attainable, and which destroys external and internal impurities. (Āk 1.17.5)
Because she protects all the worlds that have been born, as well as the life-breaths of all living beings—the entire universe consisting of all the gods—O Beloved. (Āk 1.17.6)
It pacifies the three humors, provides happiness, is wholesome, and excels all other tastes;
it possesses the six qualities beginning with life-sustenance, is endowed with intense potency, and bestows strength. (Āyurvedadīpikā 1.17.7)
Life and strength for living beings generally have their root in fire; water is the fuel for that fire. Therefore, a wise person should drink water. (Āk 1.17.8)
The three fires—the lightning fire, the submarine fire, and the digestive fire—are those that have water as their fuel;
for others, however, wood and the like are indeed their fuels. (Āk 1.17.9)
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall speak of the auspicious elixir of water; listen.
One should fill a new jar in the morning with purified waters. (Āk 1,17.10)
Whether with water from the Ganges, or from rivers, or from tanks, or from lakes, or even from wells, or with water from the hot season or the rainy season— whatever is available.
One should place that jar on a pedestal at night, when its defects have vanished and it is bathed by the divine rays of the sun and the nectar-beams of the moon. (Āk 1,17.12)
It was perfumed with aloeswood, eaglewood, camphor, and sandalwood,
and scented with *pāṭalī*, *ketakī*, jasmine, *mallikā*, and blue lotuses.
When fanned repeatedly and gently with a palm-leaf fan smeared with ushira-root paste and sprinkled with water, it is called *haṃsodaka*. (Āk 1.17.14)
Before the rising of the constellation Anurādhā, one should drink water that has not been touched by feces or urine;
thereafter, one should perform the evacuation of feces and urine. (Āk 1.17.15)
Performing the rites such as the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana) and other duties, he may eat according to his own desire;
however, like a child of one year, he should always drink water only a pala at a time. (Āk 1.17.16)
In this manner, the wise one should increase by one *pala* each year until the end of the sixteenth year, reaching a total of sixteen *palas*. (Āk 1.17.17)
After sixteen years, one should consume sixteen handfuls of water;
in this manner, one should constantly and respectfully practice this until the age of twenty. (Āk 1.17.18)
By this, all diseases are destroyed without a doubt;
one shall live for a hundred years, endowed with intelligence, strength, sensory faculties, and happiness. (Āk 1.17.19)

One should drink eight palas of this decoction, spread out [for digestion], for the sake of longevity; one should take water according to the strength of one's digestive fire, either every three days or every five days. (Āk 1.17.20)
After seven days, the wise man should likewise increase it by one handful (prasṛta) at a time; furthermore, he should gradually increase it until it reaches one kuḍava. Āk 1.17.21.
It should be consumed up to sixteen *prasṛtas*;
beyond that, as the water increases, so the disorder is pacified. (Āk 1.17.22)
One may drink water for six months, or a year, or until the end of one's life;
as there is increase, so there is decrease, down to the measure of a single mouthful. (Āk 1.17.23)
One should abandon the fast during the day or night if one eats unwholesome food;
however, if there is extreme physical exertion, one may take as much as a handful [of food]. (Āk 1.17.24)

One should drink it—whether one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters of a measure—like a service-offering with palms joined, combined with any one of honey, ghee, oil, milk, clarified butter, water, or other such substances. (Āk 1.17.25)
Or else, one should quickly destroy the disease of wind (vāta) by means of medicines located within it;
and having consumed the medicine that pacifies each respective disease, [the affliction is cured]. (Āk 1.17.26)
Then one may drink water after a muhūrta has passed, or when the [previously consumed] water has been digested, or at the end of a meal, or at night. (Ākāśagāminī 1,17.27)
If a fast is undertaken when a disease such as fever has arisen, one should drink half [the prescribed amount] of the previous [liquid], and thereafter eat light food as is comfortable. (Āk 1,17.28)
If the fast is for the purpose of a vow, then that milk or a *pala* [of food] may be taken at night;
O Goddess, by not eating during the night, the water in one's stomach dries up. (Āk 1,17.29)
One should always drink water with effort, either half-full or with palms joined;
a wise person should drink water so as to maintain equilibrium between the food, the vital essence, and the digestive fire in all circumstances. (Āk 1,17.30)
If the voiding of feces and urine occurs before the *brāhma-muhūrta*, then one should void the feces and urine only after drinking water. (Āk 1.17.31)

If one drinks even a small amount of purified water after voiding feces or urine, or if one drinks water at night when the proper time is unknown, one must drink water again in the morning. (Āk 1.17.32)
One should drink water either by the quarter-measure, the fourth part, or by the handful (añjali).
(Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome in the ritual of drinking water:
wheat, sixty-day rice, barley, and the meat of wild animals. Āk 1.17.33.
Clarified butter, curd, milk, whey, fresh butter derived from cow's products; honey, sugarcane juice, pomegranate, grapes, plantains, dates, and sugar. Āk 1.17.34.
Mango fruit, emblic myrobalan, fresh coconut water, and the leaves and fruits of the pumpkin, bottle gourd, and neem; Āk 1.17.35.
The leaves, flowers, and fruit of the *śigru*; the juices made from *mudga* soup;
as well as *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *goraṇṭī*, and the two types of *jīvantī*. (Āk 1.17.36)
Rājavṛkṣaka, śothaghnī, cillī, or laghucchadā; śatāvarī, taṇḍulī, matsyākṣī, and vidārikā. (Āk 1.17.37)
Upodakī, vārttākī, the fruits of kāravallī, small kośātakī, lakṣmī, paṭola, and tālamūlaka. (Āk 1.17.38)
The flower of the *mocā* plant, the fruits of the *daṇḍa*, the *kṣudradantikā*, the *sadāphala*, the *matsyāṇḍī*, ginger, and rock salt. (Āk 1.17.39)
Phalapūra, āmlaka, ripe dhātrī fruit, alarkaka, vāyasī, kuntalī, and likewise vasukanyālikā. (Āk 1.17.40)
Cumin, sarasī, śārṅgerī, cakramardaka, maṇḍūkaparṇī, the leaves of pālakyā, and likewise gāṅgeruka. (Āk 1.17.41)
Ākhukarṇī, the leaf of kāsamarda, and likewise gāṅgeruka; and for the purpose of seasoning, kaiḍarya, rock salt, uṣaṇa, and jāraka. (Āk 1.17.42)
All [these fruits] are generally sweet, delicious, cool, and provide comfort; however, the unripe fruit of the *kataka* and the *pathyā* (harītakī) should be smeared with salt. (Āk 1.17.43)

One should partake of the stalks, flowers, roots, and filaments of the blue lotus and the white water-lily, along with unctuous substances, while bathing, wearing white garments, and remaining pure. (Āk 1,17.44)
Anointment with musk, sandalwood, camphor, and snow;
a gentle breeze; garlands of flowers; moonlight; and jewel ornaments. (Āk 1.17.45)
One who consumes water should eat food that is wholesome, appetizing, watery in nature, predominantly sweet, and well-prepared, accompanied by ghee and milk. (Ātreya Saṃhitā 1.17.46)
One should chew betel leaf with camphor while seated comfortably;
in the evening one should drink coconut water, and at night milk with sugar.
A bed of *śālmalī* cotton and sleep at night according to one's pleasure; as well as foods that are deficient, excessive, constipating, obstructive, hot, or harsh. (Āk 1.17.48)

Food that is dry, unpalatable, unstable, heavy, or slimy; eating at improper times; and [the consumption of] fermented grain-porridge, *bṛhatī*, the two types of *coṣa*, *alābu*, and *nirūḍhaka*—[these are causes of disease]. (Āk 1,17.49)
Kulattha soup, kāliṅga, guñjā, vṛkṣaphala, as well as onion, garlic, all tubers, and likewise white mustard; Āk 1.17.50.
Meat from non-arid regions, fish, a meal consisting of some milk-rice, food with unmentioned vegetables, fruit, and meat accompanied by milk. Āk 1.17.51.
All milky juices, all sweet flavors, sesame oil, and its paste—the medicine is prepared by combining these. (Āk 1.17.52)
Excessive talkativeness, the heat of the sun and its shade, the distress of improper reflection, grief, the burden of vehicles, fear, as well as laziness and extreme passion; Āk 1.17.53.
Carrying a burden on the head, crossing water, fasting, physical exercise, envy, sleeping during the day, and likewise staying awake at night; Āk 1.17.54.
A headwind, frost, dusty ground, a room filled with smoke, a bed made of cotton—these are unfavorable. (Āk 1.17.55)
Fire, producing fatigue and perspiration, as well as wearing warm clothing, wearing silk garments, striking the thighs, and sitting on a hard seat; Āk 1.17.56.
The water of hot springs, alkaline wells, and saline pits is pungent and bitter;
asafoetida is sour, astringent, and bitter, and it is drying. (Āk 1.17.57)
Wine, fat, marrow, urine, and foul waters;
intoxication, cold, ill health, and food devoid of oil. (Āk 1.17.58)
Anointing with cold sour gruel is beneficial when there is no disease, as is a decoction; likewise, bathing the head even with warm water is drying and causes a burning sensation. (Āk 1.17.59)
One should avoid other censurable causes that provoke the *doṣas*. (The signs of having digested the water one has drunk:
Having drunk the water while healthy, sitting comfortably, restrained in speech, and pure—Āk 1,17.60.
One should discharge feces and urine, and avoid betel and similar substances;
however, if urine should still be discharged while one is drinking water, then [one must act accordingly]. (Āk 1,17.61)
One should know that the water has been digested when it passes out as urine without the use of medicine; then one is considered to be in a state of good health. (Āk 1.17.62)
When the yellow liquid has been completely discharged, hunger arises;
one should then perform an oil massage and follow the prescribed wholesome regimen. (Āk 1.17.63)
(The symptoms of indigestion from water and its avoidance:
Diseases arise without avoidance, not from lack of reflection:
fatigue, exhaustion, vomiting, aching in the head, and dizziness of the head. (Āk 1,17.64)

The stiffening and drying of fluids, as well as excessive secretions, the suppression of natural urges, abdominal tumors, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), loss of digestive fire, and the breaking pain in the limbs; Āk 1,17.65.
There is swelling throughout the entire body, in the groins, the chest, the heart, and the eyes;
there is cramping of the calves, labored breathing, aversion to food, and loss of appetite. (Āyurveda 1.17.66)

If urinary calculi, chronic rhinitis, cough, and difficult-to-cure diarrhea are dried up by water even once through practices such as dryness and physical exertion, [the patient will recover]. (Āk 1.17.67)
That is not to be known as a fault, provided that the stiffness of the fault does not occur repeatedly;
when the water has been drunk and [the system] becomes rigid, treatment is prescribed here. (Āk 1,17.68)
The wise person should cover the abdomen and the bladder with *kūṣmāṇḍa* leaves;
he should apply a plaster that facilitates the release of urine for the purpose of passing water. (Āk 1.17.69)
Alternatively, one should perform a bath with limbs smeared with clarified butter and *dhātrī* (myrobalan) as an elixir;
or one may drink milk with jaggery, or buttermilk mixed with sugar. (Āk 1.17.70)
Or else, having drunk coconut water mixed with sugar and gourd seeds, one whose water has been digested with difficulty should take clarified butter before eating. (Āk 1.17.71)
Alternatively, one should remain in water for a long time and bathe with *dhātrī* and other cooling substances;
or, if the water has become stagnant after being drunk, one should purify it with sweet and cold [remedies]. (Āk 1.17.72)
One should induce vomiting with a paste of *kṛṣṇā*, *madanaphala*, and *sindhūttha* mixed with honey;
or, having drunk powdered *pathyā* with coconut water, one should cause purgation. (Āk 1.17.73)

Alternatively, one may combine trijātaka, vyoṣa, krimighna, āmalaka, and abda, with trivṛt being equal in measure to all of these; indeed, sugar should be added in an amount equal to the total of all these ingredients. Āk 1.17.74.
Having made pills with honey, one should lick them for the removal of water-retention;
if consumed at night, they are excellent and destroy all morbid humors. (Āk 1,17.75)
One should place a wet cloth below the navel for a moment, or immerse oneself in cold water, or apply cool water to the head. (Āk 1.17.76)
Or he should plant it on a bed of moist sand, or he may sit in a fountain-house with seeds of *trapusa* and *urvāru*. (Āk 1.17.77)
Or one should drink saffron (*kāśmīraja*) with excellent grape juice;
or the seeds of *karkaṭī* should be drunk with grape juice. (Āk 1.17.78)
One should [use] the water used for rinsing rice, or madhuka, or sugar, along with grapes and jaggery, and dārvī, in combination with rice-water. (Āk 1.17.79)

Alternatively, one may take *goṣṭhanī* (milk) mixed with sugar and the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) fruits; or *varī* (śatāvarī) combined with sugar; or *drākṣā* (grapes) together with buttermilk. (Āk 1.17.80)
One should drink molasses with water or coconut water;
likewise, one may take a paste made from *tugākṣīrī* or the seeds of *karkāru*. (Āk 1.17.81)
Or one may take the root of *tāmalakī* for a kalpa, or the paste of *yaṣṭimadhu*, or the ripe fruit of *piśācakadalī*, combined with honey and sugar. (Āk 1.17.82)
Or with coconut water, or with buttermilk, or even with whey;
or with the juice of the root of the plantain tree, or with milks, or with the juices of *āmalakī*.
Or with the juices of amṛtā, or with the fresh juice of kūṣmāṇḍa, or with the juices of pomegranate, or likewise with the juices of abhīru. (Āk 1.17.84)
Or one may drink elā with sugar along with the juices of the alābu;
likewise, kadalī-kanda, yaṣṭyāhva, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and kaśerukā [may be used]. (Āk 1.17.85)
The five roots of *tṛṇa*, *śukrā*, and *śatāvarī*—a decoction made from these, beginning with the root of the plantain (*kadalī*), [is used]. Āk 1.17.86.
It should be drunk either with honey or with sugar for the purpose of releasing the body from water [urination].
(The virtues of drinking at dawn:
Water that is drunk thus during the Brāhma-muhūrta is a rejuvenative elixir. Āk 1,17.87.
It shall pacify all defects without exception and destroy even diseases;
it cures blood-wind disorders, wind disorders, heart disease, asthma, and cough. (Āk 1.17.88)

It cures hemorrhaging (raktapitta), various disorders of bile (pittas), malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), vomiting, anorexia, consumption (kṣaya), fainting, leprosy (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (meha), delusion, goiters, and tumors (arbuda). (Āk 1,17.89)
It cures abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, urinary stones, colic, flatulence, indigestion, cholera, worms, anemia, jaundice, chlorosis, and erysipelas. (Āyurvedadīpikā 1.17.90)
Wounds, swelling, leprosy, loss of digestive fire, the three types of poison, diseases of the regions above the clavicle, the private parts, epilepsy, and mental confusion. (Āk 1.17.91)
Free from fever, abdominal distension, stomach ailments, urinary obstruction, and hemorrhoids, and liberated from wrinkles and graying hair, one shall live for three hundred years. (Āk 1.17.92)
Steady-minded, strong, and wise, he becomes beloved and the very embodiment of desire for women.
(The Elixir of Nasal Inhalation: That man who drinks water through both nostrils in the morning, Āk 1,17.93.

One who eats wholesome food daily, taking only a śukti-measure [of the powder], and has conquered the senses, attains sharpness of the sense organs as well as the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair. (Āk 1,17.94)
One attains a lifespan of a hundred years through this elixir for the nostrils. (Āk 1.17.95)
Ātreya Saṃhitā, Chapter 1, Section 19: Seasonal Regimen (Ṛtucaryā) and the Division of Time (Kālavibhāga).
Śrī Bhairavī said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, the sequence of daily practice has been heard. O Lord, I desire to hear the occasional practice; please speak. (Āk 1.19.1)
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen to that, O Great Goddess; I shall describe the occasional rite.
For that [state] is dependent on time, yet it is eternal, imperishable, and immeasurable. (Āk 1.19.2)
Without beginning or end, subtle, gross, all-pervading, and eternal;
[he is] Brahmā and the others, the sun and the others, the great elements and the others, and that which is beyond them. (Āk 1.19.3)
All follow time; in their exertion they take the form of time.
Indeed, from time alone they are born, and into that same time they always dissolve. (Āk 1.19.4)
"That which is time is indeed myself, and you are the one who sets time in motion;
therefore, it is announced for the birth and death of those who bear life. (Āk 1.19.5)
For this time is indeed indivisible, yet it is nevertheless divided;
it is divided by the amount of time it takes for a sharp needle to pierce a petal of a lotus leaf. Āk 1.19.6.
That time is called a *lava*; thirty *lavas* constitute a *truṭi*. That which is this *truṭi* time, when doubled, becomes a *mātrā*. (Āk 1.19.7)
The closing of the eyelids and lashes is praised as a *mātrā*.
Eighteen *mātrās* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty *kāṣṭhās* make up a *kalā*. Āk 1.19.8.
Thirty *kalās* are said to be one *kṣaṇa*, and six *kṣaṇas* constitute a *nāḍikā*.
Two *nāḍīs* make a *muhūrta*, and four of those [muhūrtas] make a *yāma*. Āk 1.19.9.
O beloved, four *yāmas* constitute a day as well as a night;
such is the duration of day and night, though the forenoon consists of ten *nāḍikās*. (Āk 1.19.10)
At midday there are ten nāḍīs, and the same applies to the afternoon; likewise for the first watch of the night, the midnight watch, and the final watch of the night. Āk 1.19.11.
Fifteen days shall constitute the fortnight known as the bright (śukla);
the second shall be the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), and from two [such fortnights] a month is produced. (Āk 1.19.12)
Two months constitute what is known as a season (ṛtu); two seasons are designated as a period of time (kāla).
Three seasons form an ayana, and by two [ayanas] a year (saṃvatsara) is produced. Āk 1.19.13.
Time is divided into eighteen types; thus, the months beginning with Māgha occur in succession as the seasons of Śiśira and so forth. (Āk 1.19.14)
Winter, spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, and the cold season—these are the seasons; I shall describe their southern course, listen, O beloved. (Āk 1.19.15)
(The nature of the winter season:
Therein, the sun and the very quarters of the sky are obscured by masses of snow;
the wind, dull with smoke-colored dust, awakens the cold. (Āk 1.19.16)
Then the flowering *lavali* trees of Kubera caused the hair to stand on end;
bees were intoxicated by the fragrance of the blossoms of the *punnāga*, *lodhra*, and *phalinī*.
Elephants, horses, cows, buffaloes, crows, goats, and the like are full of pride; so too are birds and other creatures when covered by a mass of frost from the rivers. (Āk 1.19.18)
Behold these wells with their warm, steaming waters during the winter season;
for it is in this way that phlegm naturally accumulates during the cold season. (The nature of the winter season) Āk 1,19.19.
(The nature of the spring season:
In spring, the quarters of the sky are stainless, the sun possesses lovely rays, there is the movement of the Malaya breeze, and [the trees] are adorned with new sprouts. (Āk 1.19.20)
Everywhere the trees are in full bloom, rich with fresh bark and foliage, produced by mangoes, *aśoka*, *bakula*, *mādhavī* vines, and *campaka* flowers. (Āk 1.19.21)
The forest glade shines with flowers such as the *palāśa* and others, filled with the humming of wandering bees and the warbling of cuckoos. (Āk 1.19.22)
And there is an aggravation of phlegm; this time is indeed the very best.
(The nature of the summer season:
In summer, the sun is fierce and scorching, resembling the color of an *atasī* flower. Āk 1,19.23.
The earth and all directions were scorched; the essence of the entire world was dried up;
the quarters blazed intensely with forest fires, and the ground turned ashen gray.
The wind from the southwest blows most fiercely, and the gales become violent and unpleasant;
through heat, sweat, and the wind, living beings feel as if they were feverish. (Āk 1.19.25)
They are crowded with scorched wild boars, buffaloes, and elephants, and contain only small amounts of water that have become parched by the heat of the fierce sun's rays. (Āk 1.19.26)
The ponds and other bodies of water have become turbid, their aquatic creatures scorched by heat;
and the trees are covered with fallen leaves that are withered, dried up, and shattered. (Āk 1.19.27)
They were hot and devoid of shade, violently agitated by the wind; the leaves, creepers, and shrubs were withered, yet the *śirīṣa* trees were radiant with blossoms. (Āk 1.19.28)
From that, there is a daily depletion of phlegm and an accumulation of wind.
(The nature of the rainy season:
In the rainy season, the western wind blows and the earth is covered with new grass. Āk 1,19.29.
The entire earth, covered by clouds as dark as collyrium and scattered like *śakragopa* insects, is enchanting with all its crops. (Āk 1.19.30)
Covered by a mass of creeper-like eyebrows, moist with water and muddy, it was spread wide with tail feathers from the dancing play of flocks of intoxicated peacocks. (Āk 1.19.31)
The quarters of the sky were deafened by the terrifying croaking of frogs, while the air was thick with the fragrance of kadamba, plantain, jasmine, and kuṭaja flowers. Āk 1.19.32.
The long pond was completely filled with abundant water, its lotuses destroyed by the impact of torrents from rain-bearing clouds, yet its steps remained fully submerged in the flood.
The great rivers, possessing vast forms resembling confluences, with their waters turbid and both their banks filled to the brim; Āk 1.19.34.
The sky was illuminated by lightning flashing forth from thundering clouds,
made terrifying by the roar produced by the mutual collision of massed waters.
The forest was filled with joyful deer, buffalo, insects, and cātakas, while the orbs of the sun and moon were obscured by clouds shimmering with rainbows. (Āk 1.19.36)
At that time, phlegm is greatly diminished, wind is provoked, and bile is accumulated;
(this is the nature of the autumn season) in autumn, the rays of the sun are sharp and possess a shimmering luster. (Āk 1.19.37)
The paths were cleared by clouds that had released their waters and were now devoid of moisture;
all living beings rejoiced, drenched by the nectar-like essence of the moonlight. (Āk 1.19.38)
And the nights were enchanting, strewn with shimmering clusters of stars, beautiful with the clarity of the stainless sky, and providing the festival of amorous delights. (Āk 1.19.39)
The earth had its mud dried up and was filled with rice in ear;
the ponds were adorned with blossoming lotuses, water lilies, and blue lotuses. (Āk 1.19.40)

The lakes, filled with pure water, were crowded with flocks of delighted fish and swans and possessed waves as restless as playful women; they provided benefit through bathing and drinking. (Āk 1.19.41)
The quarters of the sky were adorned with the beautiful, blossoming camaras of the clear firmament, and were encircled by pure, fragrant cranes and jasmine flowers. Āk 1,19.42.

O Pārvatī, when the forest—filled with herds of elephants arrogant due to contact with the pollen of the seven-leaved tree—is consumed by fire, the wind becomes diminished and the bile is provoked. Āk 1.19.43.
(The nature of the times of inhalation and exhalation:
O Śivā, during the day and night, at the beginning, middle, and end, phlegm, bile, and wind become provoked; all the seasons proceed in their proper sequence. (Āk 1.19.44)
Day shall be of the nature of Agni, and night shall consist of Soma;
and then, O Goddess, there shall be two fortnights, namely the seasons of Hemanta and Śaiśira.
Those two seasons are the winter season; the hot [seasons] are spring and summer;
the seasons of the rainy period and autumn are to be known as the monsoon season. (Āk 1.19.46)
The northern course [of the sun] consists of those three seasons beginning with Śiśira;
it should be known as such, O Dear One, and that should be understood as the period of gathering (ādāna). (Āk 1.19.47)
By their very nature, the sun and the wind remove the earth's moisture and coolness;
however, it is by virtue of their path that they become so hot, harsh, and dry. (Āk 1.19.48)
The bitter, astringent, and pungent [tastes] take away the strength and vitality of living beings day by day; they become increasingly powerful in that successive order. (Āk 1.19.49)
The southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) consists of the three seasons beginning with the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*);
know this to be of the nature of Soma, traditionally known as "emission" (*visarga*). (Āk 1.19.50)
By their very nature, wind, the moon, and clouds are cool; moreover, they become exceedingly powerful through rain. Therefore, the sun becomes diminished in its brilliance. (Āk 1.19.51)
As this heat of the earth increases day by day for living beings, Time releases its power, so that they become increasingly more powerful. (Āk 1.19.52)
In this regard, the sour, salty, and sweet tastes are indeed unctuous; they are most abundant in late winter and early spring, and moderate in spring and autumn. (Āyurvedadīpikā 1.19.53)
In summer and the rainy season, the strength of all living beings becomes cold;
[this is the regimen for the winter season] because, at the onset of the cold, the strength of the bodily fluids is constricted by the chill. (Āyurveda 1.19.54)

Because the digestive fire of the stomach is concentrated within the abdomen rather than being dispersed, it is therefore more powerful; thus, if one eats only a small amount of food, that digestive fire remains potent. (Āk 1.19.55)
Fire is kindled by the wind and it digests the bodily constituents, such as the rasa and others;
therefore, when the cold season arrives, sweet, salty, and sour [tastes] should be consumed. (Āk 1.19.56)
Then, due to the length of the nights, hunger becomes even more intense at dawn; following the method for the daily routine, one should discharge excrement and urine. (Āk 1.19.57)
O Supreme Goddess, one should prepare everything, including the tooth-stick and so forth;
thereafter, one should perform an anointing of the head with oil that is suitable for it and relieves wind. (Āk 1.19.58)
Then, one should enjoy anointing the limbs and massage as much as possible and according to one's pleasure, as well as wrestling with skillful opponents as much as possible. (Āk 1.19.59)
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule with wheat, chickpeas,
and mung beans from which the oil has been removed, he should put on two light, warm, and very thick red silken garments.
Having put on two garments, one should apply anointment to the body with musk, saffron, and the resinous extract of black agallochum. Āk 1.19.61.
One should fumigate the body and the hair with the incense of black agallochum;
likewise, one should offer the flowers of campaka, bakula, śatapatra, and kaitaka.
Having smeared [the head] with saffron and other substances, one should wear it upon the head; likewise, molasses-liquor, the scum of wine, wine itself, and fatty meat. (Āk 1.19.63)

One should consume unctuous meat broth that is warm, preparations made from the flour of black gram and wheat, products derived from sugarcane and milk, and warm food produced from sesame. (Āk 1.19.64)
For bathing, pleasantly warm water; for a dwelling, a beautiful house; and for a bed, soft deerskins and woolen blankets, smooth and fine like cotton-wool. (Āk 1.19.65)
O Daughter of Śambhu, one should resort to that radiant place, strewn in succession with fine woolens and beautiful silks, where the rays of the sun do not reach from behind. Āk 1.19.66.
Those women with rounded, full, and elevated breasts constantly endure the heat of intense summer, sweat, and sandals, as well as dwelling within the inner chambers. Āk 1.19.67.
With beautiful hips rounded like the wheels of a chariot, adorned with thighs like plantain trunks,
they were intoxicated by the madness of drinking wine, and beautified by garments, garlands, and perfumes.
One should embrace beloved ones who are joyful; thus, no affliction born of the disorder of cold will arise.
[One should apply] musk, saffron, camphor, cloves, and nutmeg. (Āk 1.19.69)
There should be one *niṣka* each of the individual ingredients, with *sāra* derived from *khadira* wood;
one should add sixteen *niṣkas* total, and grind everything together with cold water.
One should prepare a pill in the form of black pepper that destroys foul odors;
this pill is proclaimed to be appetizing and a remover of wind and phlegm. (Āk 1.19.71)
