One should always consume betel leaf together with a pill as desired;
such is the conduct for the winter season, and one should practice it likewise during the cool season.

If phlegm (śleṣman) should become excessively accumulated, one should strictly observe the regimen prescribed for the winter season; for during this period, the cold becomes more intense and the wind arising from the withdrawal of energy (ādāna) becomes dry. (Āk 1.19.73)
(Vasantartucaryā) In the winter, however, the accumulated phlegm, melted by the rays of the sun in spring, destroys the digestive fire by its own watery nature. (Āk 1,19.74)
It produces every kind of disease; therefore, one should quickly conquer the *kapha*.
Now, O my beloved, I shall describe the conduct for the spring season. (Āk 1.19.75)
One should remove it by means of sharp collyrium, emetics, physical exercise, and rubbing with fragrant unguents; also by massaging with the feet and by bathing in warm water. (Āk 1.19.76)
Having put on garments dyed with astringent colors, safflower, or silk, one should fumigate one's limbs with camphor and agallochum. Āk 1.19.77.
One should anoint the body with musk, saffron, and the majesty of sandalwood pastes, as well as with mango, campaka, punnāga, betel nut, kesara, and pāṭala flowers. Āk 1.19.78.
Having smeared *mādhavī*, *ketakī*, *mallikā*, *aśoka*, and *navamālikā* with *javā* and other substances, one should carry *kalhāra* and *utpala*. (Āk 1.19.79)
Alcohol is said to be of five kinds, the supreme remover of all diseases;
these are declared to be *mādhavāriṣṭa*, *mārdvīka*, *āsava*, and *śīdhu*. (Āk 1.19.80)
That which is prepared from honey and intoxicating substances is known as *mādhava*; it is an intoxicant that has been buried in the earth for a long time. (Āk 1.19.81)

This [liquor] produced from *mārdvīka* grapes or from *gostanī* dates should be known as *ariṣṭa*; or it is called *āsava*, because it intoxicates or because it arises from the distillation (*savana*) of substances. (Āk 1.19.82)
Sugar is produced from sugarcane juice; these five are considered by me to be worthy of consumption—sweetened by the lotus-faces of beloved women and captivating to the heart. (Āk 1.19.83)
Fragranced with flowers and other scents, pleasing to the heart, and delighting the eyes of beloved ones; old [garments] are pungent, bitter, and astringent, and they remove phlegm. (Āk 1.19.84)
[One should offer] leaves, flowers, and fruits of the mātuluṅga, āmra, and jambū trees, along with friends, together with citron juice, fresh ginger, and garlic. (Āk 1.19.85)
Wild game meat, minced meat on a spit, and its broth prepared fresh; as well as aged honey, wheat, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, and śāli rice. (Āk 1.19.86)
One should consume vegetables, condiments, and drinks that alleviate phlegm;
however, one who does not drink liquor should instead take ginger-water, musta-water, or honey-water. (Āk 1.19.87)
Or one may drink water boiled with the heartwood of *khadira* and *asana*;
[one should dwell] in a garden with white palaces and the like, possessing the luster of radiant jewels.
In a beautiful pavilion adorned with mosaic floors, suited for amorous dalliance, delightful with the warbling of cuckoos, and radiant with fragrant flowers; (Āk 1.19.89)
The heat was warded off by the dense shade of many trees, and the sunlight was cooled on all sides by irrigation channels filled with water. (Āk 1.19.90)
Where the sweat of fatigue was stilled by the movement of the Malaya breeze, and which was gladdened by the stalks of trees made beautiful by various blossoms; (Āk 1.19.91)
It was sprinkled with the nectar from fragrant garlands hanging down, beautified by rows of *uśīra* and *pāṭalī* flowers, and spread over with lotus stalks. (Āk 1.19.92)
Seated upon a place strewn with flowers, radiant with the breeze from gently waving palm-leaf fans,
he was surrounded by women skilled in pleasant conversation and eager for sensual pleasure.
Delighting his beloved young women, who were the very essence of the pride of Kandarpa and wore fine, pure garments, he engaged in enchanting conversations with them. (Āk 1.19.94)
Accompanied by trusted friends, he should spend the midday happily; [he should avoid] things that are excessively cold, heavy, unctuous, sweet, sour, or salty. (Āk 1.19.95)

In the month of Madhu (Caitra), one should avoid sesame, sugarcane, milk products, sleeping during the day, excessively unctuous substances, fish, alkaline water, cakes, and anything that increases phlegm. Āk 1.19.96.
(Seasonal regimen for summer):

For in summer, the sun becomes exceedingly fierce; it dries up the fluids of the earth and destroys the unctuous qualities [of the body], whereby phlegm (kapha) undergoes depletion. (Āyurveda Sūtra 1.19.97)
By that means, the air should become purified with filled cool waters, fragrant with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron. Āk 1.19.98.
In water that was well-purified, scented with various blossoming flowers such as jasmine, and reaching up to the full breasts of amorous women; (Āk 1.19.99)
In a lake or a pond duly prepared according to the rules, [they were present] with their moon-like faces adorned by eyes reaching to their ears. Āk 1.19.100.
With arms as soft as śirīṣa flowers, radiant with ornaments of lotus stalks, and glowing with camphor, pearl garlands, flowers, and sandalwood paste; Āk 1.19.101.
With their waists and hips bound by garments of fine saffron-dyed silk,
they were made to resound with the cries of cranes attracted by the tinkling of their own anklets.
Accompanied by women skilled in water-sports, he should sport with them, his body and face sprinkled by the water released from their hands. Āk 1,19.103.
His body sprinkled by the water discharged from the mouths of the melting peaks,
he embraced them between his arms, repeatedly performing graceful movements.
Having emerged from the water and dried his body with garments, he should then comfortably brush out his hair and put on two clean, fine, and dyed robes. (Āk 1,19.105)
One should fumigate the body and hair with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor;
having smeared one's body with the paste of *śrīkhaṇḍa*, moon-fragrance, and musk.
Nepāla, mālatī, mallī, pāṭalī, and śatapatraka; saugandhika, maruvaka, and hrīvera, along with the products of deer and eggs. Āk 1.19.107.
One should wear flowers anointed with fragrant oils;
however, wine should not be drunk here, or else [only] by those accustomed to wine.
Only a very small amount of food should be drunk by him; if there is no satiety, then he may drink wine as he pleases, combined with much sweet water. (Āk 1,19.109)

If it were not so, O beloved, there would be a drying up of the bodily elements, accompanied by internal burning and delusion; one's limbs would become flaccid, and the strength of one's vital breath, intellect, and power would be exhausted.
One should resort to that which is sweet, cooling, unctuous, liquid, light, and wholesome;
one should immediately lick rice mixed with sugar, or the meat of wild animals. (Āyurveda 1.19.111)
One should drink unthickened meat broth, *rasālā*, or a refreshing beverage (*pānaka*); or else, one may consume the beneficial *pañcasāra*, *rāga*, or *ṣāḍava*. (Āk 1.19.112)
(Rasālā drink:
Curd mixed with sugar and black pepper and stirred by hand—this is known as rasālā; it may also be made from plantains, breadfruit, and mangoes. (Āk 1.19.113)
A beverage made from fruits with sugar-water placed in a new earthen vessel, known as "slightly sour," is beneficial. (Āk 1,19.114)
(Pañcasāra:
Grapes, dates, and madhūka flowers, as well as the ripe fruits of śrīparṇī, kṣudra-kharjūrī, and paripakva. Āk 1.19.115.
Having added water with sugar, one should grind it firmly with the hand; then, having placed it in a new earthen vessel, it should be strained through cloth on the following day. (Āk 1.19.116)
Known as *pañcasāra*, it is heart-pleasing and removes wind and phlegm; likewise, fruits combined with sweet substances such as sugar and honey [form] *rāga* and *ṣāḍava*. (Āk 1.19.117)
That which is transparent should be known as "attachment" (rāga), which destroys all torment;
if this very same [attachment] is thick, it is called "lickable" (lehya) or "six-flavored" (ṣāḍava). (Āk 1.19.118)
When that same [mixture] is purified with a cloth, it is called *peya-ṣāḍava*.
These five types of drinks are prepared with *pāṭalī*, *campaka*, and other [flowers]. (Āk 1.19.119)
Pure water scented with elā, placed in a new earthen vessel and cooled by a breeze from a fan made of uśīra grass and palm leaves. (Āk 1,19.120)
This is the general method of preparation, excluding the leaves of the *moca* and *coca* plants;
then, it is filled into a new vessel, sweet and pure. (Āk 1,19.121)
It was made fragrant with *pāṭalī*, *ketakī* flowers, and camphor; it was covered with thick cloth and rendered pleasantly cool by palm-leaf fans. Āk 1.19.122.
One may drink water [shaded] by *tāla*, *sāla*, *pūga*, and *kharjūra* trees, as well as by *nālikera*, *āmra*, *panasa*, *jambū*, *punnāga*, and *campaka* trees. (Āk 1.19.123)
[The trees were] adorned with clusters of fruits and flowers hanging down to the touch of hands,
and shone with their branches covered and interspersed by bunches of grapes.
The rays of the sun were warded off by various fragrant trees that delighted the bees perched upon clusters of *mādhavī* flowers with their songs. (Āk 1.19.125)
In the Mānasa lake, beautified by swans, cranes, and ducks, and cooled by the breezes from the ripples of streams flowing all around; (Āk 1.19.126)
In that place, which was beautified by the warbling of cuckoos amidst dancing peacocks and cranes, and where young women were bewildered by the chatter of mynas and parrots; Āk_1,19.127.
In a garden surrounded by young *kośīra* grass, sprinkled with water, and fashioned from the sprouts of lotus fibers, red lotuses, white lotuses, and blue lotuses; Āk_1,19.128.
It was hung with fragrant flower garlands, exceedingly cool, and provided with new canopies of shade fashioned from moist garments. (Āk 1.19.129)
In a beautiful Mādhavī bower, which removes all distress,
she was provided with plantain leaves, lotus stalks, flowers, and tender shoots.
A bed covered with beautiful and excellent cloths, sprinkled with cool water, exceedingly soft, and removing both fever and fatigue.
Sprinkled with fine droplets of water, cooled by frost and contained within leather garments, he was accompanied by his peers. Āk 1,19.132.
In this manner he should pass the midday, either in a fountain-house or while playing with the breasts,
hands, and faces of a beloved fashioned from ivory, from which [the liquid] flows.
To alleviate his fever, he rolled upon a cool, clear crystal slab smeared with camphor and sandalwood paste, which was cooled by the water of the *bālośīra* plant. (Āk 1.19.134)
Their limbs were cooled by a recent bath, adorned with ornaments of pearls, anointed with lotus-fiber paste and sandalwood, and encircled by bracelets of lotus stalks. Āk 1.19.135.
Delighting and amusing those women—who were dressed in pure white garments, exceedingly beautiful, and dispellers of heat—with kisses, embraces, and touches. Āk 1.19.136.
It was adorned with canopies fashioned from garlands of flowers,
and it shone like moonstones melting at the touch of the rays of the cool-rayed moon.
Seated upon the terrace of the palace, which was radiant with the beauty of moonlight and graced by gentle breezes, he [perceived] those called the rays of the moon.
Eat foods cooled by the rays of the moon and stars;
drink buffalo milk with sugar, which is strength-giving and beneficial. (Āk 1.19.139)
In the heat of summer, I am one whose body is adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste, whose limbs are draped in pure white garments, and who has completed his acts of pleasure. (Āk 1,19.140)
By means of the breeze from garments moistened with water, by the wind from palm-leaf fans, and by fanning with broad lotus petals raining down water; Āk 1.19.141.
And with peacock-feather fans, as well as yellow sandalwood, and with sweet garlands of camphor, jasmine, and pearls, O beloved. (Āk 1.19.142)
It resounded with the chirping of female and male śārika birds and parrots,
adorned with lotus stalks, and was graced by blossoming white, red, and blue lotuses.
And for him who is tormented by the heat of the summer season, that distress is removed by the application of camphor and sandalwood and by the company of lovely women. (Āk 1.19.144)
One should avoid flour-based foods, pungent, sour, salty, and dry substances, as well as physical exertion and exposure to the sun.
(The regimen for the rainy season) Now, therefore, O Bhairavī, listen; I shall describe the seasonal conduct pertaining to the rains. Āk_1,19.145.
In men whose bodily constituents have been depleted by excessive intake, the digestive fire, though diminished during the rainy season, quickly fails due to the humors. (Āk 1.19.146)
When the sun was hidden by masses of water-laden clouds in the sky, and there was a cool, chilling wind accompanied by a gale, [he entered the womb]. (Āk 1.19.147)

The wind may become excessively agitated due to the heat of the summer season, from the vapors rising from the earth moistened by clouds and the like, or from the very nature of the time. (Āk 1,19.148)
The bile becomes excessively aggravated by acidic foods, by impure waters such as those from spiders, and by foul weather; likewise, the digestive fire is provoked by such conditions.

By that very [excess], the fire (digestive heat) subsides, and the phlegm becomes aggravated and difficult to overcome; thus the humors become mutually corrupted, and from that arises the common state [of disease]. (Āk 1.19.150)
One should enjoy massage and the anointing of the head with Nārāyaṇa oils;
having bathed with plenty of warm water, one should cleanse the body. (Āk 1.19.151)
One should wear [a garment] that is red, white, or madder-colored;
O Śivā, one should fumigate the body with thick incense of agarwood. Āk 1.19.152.
One should worship with beautiful musk, saffron, the resin of black aloe-wood, *kuṭaja*, *ketakī*, jasmine, *maruva*, and *karavīra*. (Āk 1.19.153)
One should consume the meat of fatty or wild animals prepared with their juices, as well as well-prepared soups made from mung beans, āḍhaka beans, and kuluttha lentils. (Āk 1.19.154)
One should drink either the aged *maireya* wine known as *ariṣṭa*, or buttermilk mixed with *sauvarcala* salt and the powder of the five spices (*pañcakola*). (Āk 1.19.155)
A person whose digestive tract has been purified should consume all types of hot substances;
he should administer decoction enemas and partake of a diet consisting of aged grains. (Āk 1.19.156)
Whether celestial or from a well, boiled water is pleasant to drink;
on days of excessive wind and rain, it should generally be salty and sour. (Āk 1,19.157)
One should consume sweet, light, and honeyed side dishes that have been dried and polished, as well as oils, *vaṭaka* cakes, and *parpaṭa* pancakes. (Āk 1.19.158)
And let her wear betel-leaf as she pleases, combined with musk and nutmeg; let her have eyes like lotuses and wear garments perfumed with agallochum incense. Āk 1.19.159.
One should remain in a palace free from ground-moisture, delightful, devoid of the cold of frost, and perfumed with the incense of agaru, while staying amidst fragrant substances. Āk 1.19.160.
One should avoid sleeping during the day, river water, barley meal soaked in water and ghee, physical exercise, the rays of the sun, and excessive sexual union. (Āk 1.19.161)

(Seasonal regimen for autumn) Now, therefore, I shall describe the autumnal regimen; listen, O Vāṅmayī! In the rainy season, due to cold and rain, [the body is suddenly affected] by the rays of the sun. (Āk 1.19.162)
In autumnal rain, the bile of men whose bodies have been heated by the sun becomes especially aggravated; therefore, for the removal of that bile— // Āk_1,19.163 //
One should prepare a mild massage and rubbing with bile-subduing oil;
bathing with pleasantly warm water and wearing white or saffron-colored garments. (Āk 1.19.164)
Having held [the incense], one should smear the limbs with the smoke of agaru and karpūra;
likewise, the limbs should be smeared with bhadraśrī and hima, as well as with ketakī and bhallātaka.
One should consume *campaka* and lotus petals mixed with musk;
one should resort to purgation, venesection, and the tasting of bitter ghee. (Āk 1.19.166)
One should consume rice, wheat, mung beans, pointed gourd, honey, sugar, the meat of wild animals, and substances that are bitter, astringent, and sweet. (Āk 1.19.167)
But when hungry, one should eat light food, such as *dhātrī*, *śīthu*, ghee, milk, a beverage, barley-gruel, or fresh coconut water. (Āk 1.19.168)

One should drink "swan-water" (haṃsodaka)—which is purified by the rising of the star Agastya, free from poison, light, and cool, and rendered cold by being heated by the rays of the sun and moon. Āk 1,19.169.

At nightfall, having anointed himself with cool sandalwood paste, wearing fragrant garlands, dressed in freshly washed garments, and adorned with ornaments, he should enjoy a meal of mung bean soup while remaining at ease. (Āk 1.19.170)
Adorned with strings of pearls, anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste,
he dwelt in a palace surrounded by delightful gardens and made exceedingly beautiful by the moonlight.
Seated comfortably together with a young woman, he should enjoy the rays of the moon, tasting various kinds of sugarcane stalks and even wine that subdues bile. (Āk 1.19.172)
Drinking again and again, he remains in comfort, sporting with women;
he drinks alkaline substances such as nitre and salt, and cold drinks, eating until he is fully satiated. (Āk 1,19.173)
One should avoid sesame oil, the rays of the sun, daytime sleep, muscle fat, curd, pungent substances, intoxicants, the east wind, and anything that produces pitta. (Āk 1.19.174)

(The Practice Common to All Seasons) Now, O Śivā, the common practice shall be briefly described: one should generally consume sweet, sour, and salty [foods] at the onset of winter and the rainy season. (Āk 1.19.175)
In the spring, one should especially resort to bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes;
in the summer, one should resort primarily to sweet tastes; and again at the end of the rainy season. (Āyurveda-saṃhitā 1.19.176)
One should consume bitter, sweet, and astringent [foods] in succession during the rainy season;
in spring, one should eat dry and hot food, and in summer, unctuous and cold food. (Āk 1.19.177)
During the rainy season, the cool season, and winter, one should partake of food that is oily and very warm;
at the end of the rains, one should follow this same regimen with food that is dry and cold. (Āyurveda-saṃhitā 1.19.178)

One should daily consume the specific tastes prescribed for each respective season in abundance, as well as all other tastes in small quantities according to one's preference. (Āyurveda Sūtra 1.19.179)
The final week of one [period] and the seven days of the other—thus, fourteen days are known as the transitional period of the season (*ṛtusaṃdhi*). (Āk 1.19.180)
One should very gradually relinquish the conduct of the current season and, at the junction of the seasons, engage in the conduct of the coming season in due order. (Āk 1.19.181)

For diseases arise from the abandonment of wholesome substances and the consumption of unwholesome substances; therefore, one should gradually proceed toward the adoption of the former and the relinquishment of the latter. Āk 1.19.182.
By following the seasonal regimen (*ṛtucaryā*), one shall obtain long life and health.
(The sequence of the digestion of food and the sequence of the production of the bodily constituents and wastes.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, I shall explain the sequence of the digestion of food in brief. (Āyurveda-dīpikā 1.19.183)
And all the food that has been eaten is brought into the stomach by the vital air (prāṇavāyu); there, its mass is broken down by fluids and it becomes soft once again. 1,19.184.

The digestive fire (*koṣṭhāgni*), kindled by the *samāna* wind, digests that which has been brought to the stomach (*āmāśaya*) by the oily substance (*sneha*), just as the external fire does. (Āk 1.19.185)
The fire cooks the rice, the water, and the food contained within the vessel;
as soon as it is eaten, all of that becomes sweet, possessing the six flavors.
When being cooked by substances that generate *kapha*, such as those that are sweet and so forth, foam arises;
for foam is the essence of *kapha*, and it attains acidity through the process of burning (*vidāha*). (ĀK 1.19.187)
Having descended from the stomach, that bile becomes pure;
having reached the receptacle of digested food, it is further dried up by the fire. (Āk 1.19.188)
When condensed, it becomes fully matured; through great ripening, it becomes pungent.
It is of the earth, water, fire, and wind elements, but not of the ether element. (Āk 1.19.189)
The five heats digest the five foods, beginning with the earthy, as well as the five qualities of food once they have been digested, and likewise the qualities of the elements. Āk 1.19.190.
Each of these nourishes its own respective [beings] individually according to their pleasure;
likewise, the terrestrial [element] nourishes the terrestrial ones, and the others nourish those within the body in due order.
That digested food is of two kinds, distinguished as waste (kiṭṭa) and essence (sāra).
The waste is also twofold: the clear becomes urine, and the thick becomes feces. Āk 1.19.192.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the seven fires cook the essence according to their respective natures; once it has entered the constituent elements (*dhātu*), blood then arises from that rasa.
From flesh comes fat, from that bone is produced;
from bone comes marrow, and from that semen; from semen, O beloved, the embryo arises. (Āk 1.19.194)
I shall now describe how breast milk arises from the *rasa* (nutrient fluid) remaining after the formation of *prasāda*, and how blood arises from that;
likewise, the vessels (*sirā*) and tendons (*kaṇḍarā*) arise from the flesh, while the six layers of skin and the fat (*vasā*) come into being. Āk 1.19.195.
From fat, the sinews and joints [arise], and thereafter the remainder perishes;
the waste product of the nutrient fluid (rasa) is phlegm (śleṣman), and that of the blood is bile (pitta). Āk 1.19.196.

The waste product of flesh is the impurities of the body cavities; that of fat is the sweat; the hair of the body and the head arise from the bones; and from the marrow come the eyes, excrement, and skin. Āk 1.19.197.

Fat, semen, and ojas are known as the pure essences (śukla) of the tissues in their respective order; from the maturation of the tissues, waste products (kiṭṭa) arise as the impurities, while the refined essence (prasāda) becomes the next tissue. Āk 1.19.198.
Through mutual support, there is a succession of the moisture of the elements;
that essence which arises from food that has been properly digested is indeed the *rasa*. (Āk 1.19.199)
Therefore, rasa indeed increases the dhātus, such as blood and the rest.
Humans possess seven dhātus, just as women do. (Āk 1.19.200)
In men, semen resides in the head; in women, it resides in the delighted mind.
Yet, upon union with their husband, that semen flows into the abode of Smara (the temple of love).
And that [fluid], being clear and gentle like water, becomes for our embryo;
the food consumed day and night causes the increase of the semen. (Āk 1.19.202)
After seven days it becomes clear and white; after a month, indeed, it is capable of conceiving a fetus.
O Ambikā, in this very manner of sequential ripening, it becomes six months old.
By the power of aphrodisiac medicines, semen and other fluids are produced immediately;
there is always a transformation of the bodily constituents through movement and digestion. (Āk 1,19.204)
(The nature of the digestive fire:
The digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), the elemental fire (*bhautika*), and the fire of the bodily constituents (*dhātavīya*) are known as the fires.
Among these, the digestive fire is the most excellent, by which food is thoroughly digested. (Āk 1.19.205)
That alone is the root of all fires; when it perishes, they perish, and with its increase, they increase. That is the root of life and of strength. (Āk 1.19.206)
Therefore, O Goddess, one should protect that [body] with effort by means of wholesome and suitable food, drink, and medicinal herbs; for health is dependent upon them. (Āk 1.19.207)
That very fire is of four kinds: sharp, dull, balanced, and unbalanced.
When the *vāyu* is overwhelmed by *pitta*, the digestive fire (*pāvaka*) becomes sharp. (Āk 1.19.208)

Food that is eaten either improperly or in excess is quickly digested, yet it may produce diseases born of pitta; however, when the digestive fire is weak and the samāna wind is afflicted by kapha, [the food is not properly processed]. (Āyurveda 1.19.209)

Even food that is properly consumed, in measured quantity, and wholesome may take a long time to digest, causing dryness of the mouth, flatulence, heaviness, and rumbling in the intestines. (Āk 1,19.210)
One should repeatedly cause flatulence; this also cures diseases born of phlegm.
When the *samāna* wind is situated in its own place, the digestive fire is said to be balanced. (Āk 1.19.211)

Food properly consumed is digested at the right time and yields the fruit of health; however, when the *samāna* wind is displaced from its path, even excellent food will not be digested by an uneven fire. (Āyurveda-kalpa 1,19.212)

It may take a long time to digest poorly consumed food, or it may quickly produce diseases born of wind; therefore, O beloved, one should be vigilant and protect the equilibrium of the digestive fire. (Āyurveda 1.19.213)

A sharp fire cooks [the food] in two watches; a mild fire for six watches; one with moderate heat cooks the food with difficulty in four watches; and one with a pleasant fire cooks it comfortably in four watches. (Āk 1.19.214)
However, the fire situated at the navel of all living beings may sometimes be uneven, burning either quickly or very slowly. (Āk 1.19.215)
In elephants, camels, horses, and the like, the fire is the size of a thumb;
in domestic animals, humans, and wild beasts, the internal fire is the size of a barley grain. (Āk 1.19.216)
The digestive fire of vultures, owls, cranes, and the like is the size of a sesame seed;
the fire of creatures such as worms and insects is the size of a hair. (Āk 1.19.217)
The digestive fire, having been ignited, first digests food;
then, in the absence of food, it digests the humors (doṣas); and when the humors are exhausted, it digests itself. (Āk 1.19.218)
At the exhaustion of the elements, he should withdraw the vital breaths of living beings into the supreme element.
Āk, 1, 20 (Yogarasāyana):
Śrī Bhairavī said:
O God of gods, ocean of compassion, destroyer of Time and Kāma; O Eight-formed One, Great-formed One, devoted to the fivefold cosmic acts! Āk_1,20.1.
O Three-eyed One, O Destroyer of Tripura, you have manifested this entire world,
in which the moon is wearied by the hissing of the lord of serpents coiled in your matted locks.
O Lord with five faces smiling, whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire, whose cheeks are illuminated by the jewels on the hoods of the serpents serving as your earrings! Āk 1.20.3.
Adorned with lips as beautiful as young shoots with teeth like jasmine buds, you have a throat darkened by *hālāhala* poison and are decorated with the seven lords of serpents. Āk 1.20.4.
O you who shine with eighteen arms emerging from the great circle of serpents, endowed with all divine weapons, and clothed in the skin of a noble tiger! Āk 1.20.5.

O you whose pair of feet is illuminated by the rays from the blue lotuses on the crowns of the lords of gods and asuras, you who remove the birth, old age, and death of those established in yoga! Āk 1.20.6.
O manifestation of truth, consciousness, and bliss; O ocean of serene compassion;
O You who are accessible through the syllable *oṃ*; O stainless, inconceivable, unthinkable, and immeasurable One! Āk_1,20.7.
You are indeed the praiser, the object of praise, and the praise itself; you are the agent, the action, and the instrument of action.
For you alone are everything—be gracious, O Supreme Lord! (Āk 1.20.8)
By your māyā, the entire world is created, protected, and likewise destroyed;
you are earth, you are water, you are fire, you are wind, you are space, and you are the moon. (Āk 1.20.9)
You are the sun, you are the supreme self (paramātman), you are the qualities (guṇas), and likewise you are primordial nature (prakṛti);
you are the individual spirit (puruṣa), you are the mind (manas), and you are the intellect (buddhi), consciousness (citta), and the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti). Āk 1.20.10.
"And if it pleases your heart, O Lord, and is dear to you as life itself, command me to explain the entire science of alchemy (rasāyana) in full detail. (Āk 1.20.11)
O Lord, how is liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and what is the nature of yoga? O Lord of Gods, please grant us the easy means that removes worldly existence. (Āk 1.20.12)
Having heard the praise, Bhairava, with a smiling face and supreme joy, spoke to the auspicious Goddess, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains. (Āk 1.20.13)
Śrī Bhairava said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Illusion, Eternal One! You know everything;
nevertheless, O Sovereign Lady, you ask out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds."
I shall speak in brief; listen attentively, my dear.
Who else but you is dear to me for the discourse on the meaning of this secret? (Āk 1.20.15)

(The Characteristics of One Liberated while Living) Listen, O Goddess of Gods, I shall describe the characteristics of one liberated while living: desire, anger, fear, greed, pride, delusion, and envy. (Āk 1.20.16)
Pride, shame, lineage, moral conduct, contempt, hypocrisy, and deception;
ignorance, dullness, arrogance, cold, heat, and likewise the sun's glare. (Āk 1.20.17)
He who would renounce wind, pleasure and pain, evil and merit, the beneficial and the harmful, the threefold suffering, as well as son, friend, wife, and so forth— Āk 1.20.18.
Unattached to all sense objects and devoted to the contemplation of reality, one should be one whose heart is unstained, like a lotus leaf by water. (Āk 1.20.19)
One whose disposition is adorned with love, compassion, joy, and equanimity, and whose intellect is not averse to the task of attaining happiness in this world and the next; Āk 1.20.20.
For one who knows the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal possesses restraint of the internal organ;
being free from old age and death, he becomes one whose self is the essential flavor of Śiva. (Āk 1.20.21)

He should be known as one liberated while living, having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra; he is to be venerated by gods, daityas, and others, and he is the Guru, Śiva himself, who is to be served. (Āk 1.20.22)
O Maheśvarī, just as I am worthy of worship in all worlds, so too is he always fully honored by everyone in all worlds. (Āk 1.20.23)
But that liberation which occurs for living beings at the end of the body is purposeless;
for at the end of the body, all embodied beings attain liberation—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.20.24)
O Mother of Tripura, if liberation were attained simply by causing terror, then why were the donkeys, birds, bulls, and rams not liberated? (Āk 1.20.25)
O beloved, if liberation were to occur through the consumption of semen, feces, and urine, then how is it that monkeys, pigs, and the like have not attained liberation? (Āk 1.20.26)
It does not arise from immortality alone, nor from auspiciousness (*śivatva*) alone;
rather, it occurs through the union of these two, and this is known as *jīvanmukti*. (Āk 1.20.27)
At all times, liberation exists within the entire scripture as that which arises at the final moment;
yet it is not perceived, like a jewel held in the palm of one's hand—such is the state of Śambhu.
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall tell you that which is most secret, unspeakable, and difficult even for the gods to obtain: the eternal stability of the body. (Āk 1.20.29)
(The means for achieving stability of the body that accomplishes liberation while living; the perfection of yoga:
The auspicious state of Śiva-hood and the power of moving through space, which bestows all perfections.
Without the body nothing would exist; this body is the means for accomplishing everything.
Therefore, one should always protect the body with effort from all sides;
for upon the fall of the body there is the destruction of Dharma, and with the destruction of Dharma, there is the loss of ritual action. (Āk 1.20.31)
If action fails, how can there be yoga? If yoga is lost, consciousness would not exist.
If consciousness is absent, how can there be liberation? If liberation is lost, nothing remains. (Āk 1.20.32)
Even by means of hundreds of other methods, the body cannot be sustained forever;
however, mercury and breath-control (pavana) are the supreme bestowers of all perfections. 1.20.33.
Both wind and mercury, when coagulated, deadened, and bound, constantly remove diseases in due order, destroy death, and bestow the state of a sky-walker (khecarī). Āk 1.20.34.
The *rasa* was previously explained by me; now the *vāyu* is being praised.
From the restraint of the *vāyu*, knowledge arises; from knowledge, liberation is born. (Āk 1.20.35)
For all beings, the body is the root; the vital air (pavana) is the master of its stability.
From that supreme imperishable (akṣara), space (ākāśa) was produced. 1.20.36.
From that [space] comes wind, from that fire, from that water, and from that earth; the imperishable is the supreme cause of these five elements. (Āk 1.20.37)
Space consists of sound; wind consists of sound and touch;
fire consists of sound, touch, and form; and water is said to consist of these [and] taste. Āk 1.20.38.
Earth consists specifically of sound, form, touch, and taste;
O Dear One, it possesses the nature of sound, form, taste, touch, and smell. (Āk 1.20.39)
And the presiding deities of earth, wind, fire, air, and space are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva. (Āk 1.20.40)
The earth was submerged in lost waters and those [waters] were consumed by a great fire;
and that [fire], O Pārvatī, was extinguished by a fierce wind, and even that [wind] was likewise [extinguished].
Dissolved in the sky, they subsequently emerge from that space;
it stands both within and without, all-pervading, without support and without refuge. (Āk 1.20.42)
Meditating on space with the mind, one should sever the bond of existence;
[one should likewise master] the wind consisting of the life-force of the world, and the water that bestows consciousness and bliss. (Āk 1.20.43)
By means of yoga, he makes it motionless; like the wind, he becomes a traveler through the sky, burning the three worlds which are set ablaze by infinite suns and fires. (Āk 1.20.44)
Having meditated on fire within one's own heart, one is not afflicted by fire;
[one perceives] the surface of the earth being flooded by a multitude of waves of nectar.

One who meditates on the reality of the elements within their own mind is not troubled by water, even when the earth is submerged in a deluge of elements and overrun by beings that move through the sky. (Āk 1.20.46)
Constantly contemplating this in his heart, he has no fear of kings;
for whatever one contemplates in the mind, that very form one attains. (Āk 1.20.47)
Just as wood may attain the state of fire, or as an insect may attain the state of a bee, [so too does one attain perfection through] the limbs of yoga:
posture (*āsana*), regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*). (Āk 1.20.48)
Meditation is concentration; the limbs of yoga are sixfold in their sequence.
(1. The Rule for Posture) Indeed, there are eighty-four hundred thousand postures. Āk_1,20.49 //
Among those, two principal seats are known as Siddhapadmāsana.
Regarding Siddhāsana:
one should firmly join the perineum with the root of one foot. (Āk 1.20.50)
And one should place the other foot upon the root of the organ;
sitting with limbs steady and senses subdued, O Dear One. (Āk 1.20.51)
With the eyes motionless and the mind steady, looking at the space between the eyebrows—this is to be known as Siddhāsana, which bestows the path to liberation. Āk 1.20.52.
(The lotus posture:
Having placed the left foot upon the right thigh and the right foot upon the left thigh, with both hands positioned behind the back. (Āk 1.20.53)
And with the hands reversed, having firmly grasped the left big toe with the left hand and the right [big toe] with the right hand, [he should place them] upon his own chest. (Āk 1.20.54)
Placing the chin upon the chest, one with restrained senses should meditate on the tip of the nose;
this is known as the *padmāsana*, which destroys all diseases. (Āk 1.20.55)
(2. Prāṇāyāma;
Ajapāmudrā) At the location of the anus, however, is the foundation, a lotus with four petals.
It is endowed with the syllable *vādi-sānta* and possesses a radiance equal to the rising sun.
The Svādhiṣṭhāna is a six-petalled lotus endowed with the letters from *ba* to *la*;
it has the brilliance of lightning. Then, O Goddess, is the Maṇipūraka, which has the luster of a jewel. (Āk 1.20.57)
At the navel is the unstruck (*anāhata*) lotus, consisting of one hundred petals, joined with the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, golden-hued, and possessing twelve petals. (Āk 1.20.58)
In the heart, the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* are praised as the purification;
it is a great sixteen-petaled lotus adorned with the sixteen vowels. (Āk 1.20.59)
The wheel of command (ājñācakra) has two petals and is adorned with a lotus in hand;
O Goddess, the six wheels have thus been described in sequence as being white. Āk_1,20.60.
Below the navel and above the genitals is said to be the *kanda*, resembling the egg of a bird; therefrom the channels originate. (Āk 1.20.61)
There are twenty-two thousand [channels], among which ten are recorded as the principal ones;
the first channel is *iḍā*, and the second is *piṅgalā*.
Suṣumnā shall be the third, and Gāndhārī the fourth;
Hastijihvā shall be the fifth, and the swift Pūṣā the sixth. (Āk 1.20.63)
The seventh channel is known as Alambuṣā, and the eighth is remembered as Kuhū;
the ninth is indeed Śaṅkhinī, and the tenth follows in sequence. (Āk 1.20.64)
These channels are the carriers of the vital breaths (prāṇa), and they are known as the recitations (japa). They are prāṇa and apāna, as well as vyāna, udāna, and samāna. (Āk 1.20.65)
The ten winds—Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—reside within all the circles of the channels (nāḍī-cakras). (Āk 1.20.66)
Flickering through the left and right channels, both downward and upward, the individual soul (jīva) runs about under the sway of the prāṇa and apāna breaths and is not perceived. (Āk 1.20.67)
Just as a ball struck by two hands does not remain steady on the ground, so too the living being, enveloped by the inhaled and exhaled breaths, is not steady. (Āk 1.20.68)
In the drawing together of the prāṇa and apāna, one should likewise draw the prāṇa from the apāna;
it should go outward with the syllable *ha* and enter within with the syllable *sa*. (Āk 1.20.69)
"O Dear One, O Sovereign Lady, that *haṃsa*—which is 'I am He'—the living soul should constantly recite this mantra twenty-one thousand times and six hundred more. (Āk 1.20.70)
The number of repetitions of the Haṃsa-mantra is always completed within a single day and night;
this great mantra called Haṃsa is indeed proclaimed as the Ajapā. (Āk 1.20.71)
This Gāyatrī, known as Japā, bestows self-restraint and liberation;
there is no austerity, knowledge, or merit whatsoever equal to this recitation. (Āk 1.20.72)
For she is unutterable and devoid of phonemes, arising from Kuṇḍalinī;
indeed, this one who moves through the vital breath (prāṇa) should always be known by yogins. (Āk 1.20.73)
The Mother is the Kuṇḍalinī power, established above the kanda;
she is coiled eightfold, having the form of a sleeping serpent. (Āk 1.20.74)
Having closed that opening of the door of Brahmā with her own mouth, O Pārvatī, she should first awaken it by means of the application of fire. (Āk 1.20.75)
O Śivā, together with the mind and the vital breath, one should proceed through the central channel;
by forceful contraction, she shall open the gate of Brahman. (Āk 1.20.76)
Just as a needle leads to its thread, so does that [channel] lead to the aperture of Brahman (brahmabila).
Seated comfortably in the lotus posture, O beloved, with both hands turned upward— Āk 1.20.77.
Having placed the chin in the middle of the hollow of the arms, one should rest it upon the chest; firmly contracting the opening of the anus and the cavity of the lower wind (apāna). Āk 1.20.78.
O beloved, repeatedly and swiftly move the breath upward;
releasing the vital energy (prāṇa) through the power of Kuṇḍalinī, one enters the path to liberation. (Āk 1.20.79)
And he attains true awakening, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
then, he should wipe his limbs with the perspiration produced thereby. (Āk 1.20.80)
Subsisting on milk and eating measured food, he should renounce pungent, sour, and salty tastes;
with senses conquered, practicing celibacy, staying in a hut, and abandoning ritual action. (Āk 1.20.81)
Thus devoted to practice, he attains perfection within a year;
[namely,] Jālandhara, Mūlabandha, Oḍḍīyāṇa, and Khecarī—[the four] mudrās [of] prāṇāyāma. (Āk 1.20.82)
And whoever should perform the Mahāmudrā shall become a possessor of bodily accomplishment. O Śāmbhavī, I shall describe their characteristics, which are to be kept secret from you. (Āk 1.20.83)
(Jālandharabandha):
Jālandhara is the binding of the clusters of vessels in the throat;
having performed it and bent the neck downward, [the nectar] then flows from the crown of the head. (Āk 1.20.84)
Even if nectar were to flow from the sky and fall upon her breasts, it would not run away when her ears are pinched by the wind. (Āk 1.20.85)
It destroys the multitude of ear diseases; it becomes the supreme destroyer of death.
(The Root Lock) One should press the root lock, starting from the heel, against the region of the womb. Āk 1.20.86.
The yogi should contract the anus and draw the *apāna* upward;
when the *mūlabandha* is performed in this manner, the root of impurity is destroyed. (Āk 1.20.87)
When the prāṇa and apāna breaths are joined together, even an old man may attain youth;
by means of the mūlabandha, even death itself may be overcome by those who possess the sun-like vitality.
(The Oḍḍiyāṇa Bandha: Having firmly drawn up the wind from the opening of the navel upward into the abdomen, one should then bind the posterior stretch at Oḍḍiyāṇa. (Āk 1.20.89)
One should find rest in Mahāmāyā; this is proclaimed as the *udyāṇa* (the rising).
It is the blazing forest fire of death and the *vāḍava* submarine fire within the ocean of old age and disease. (Āk 1.20.90)
(Khecarīmudrā) One should insert the tongue into the cavity within the mouth and direct it toward the opening of the palate;
with a steady gaze, one should look at the space between the eyebrows while [the tongue] is inverted. Āk 1.20.91.
For this khecarī mudrā is to be kept secret and is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
because the tongue has gone to the sky (the palate), the mind consequently moves in the void (kha). (Āk 1.20.92)
This is renowned as Khecarī, which removes death, disease, and old age;
for one who is sealed by Khecarī, there is no sleep, hunger, or thirst. (Āk 1.20.93)
Fainting occurs, which is virtuous, and there is indeed no fear of the bondage of karma; even when united with a woman, the semen certainly does not fall. (Āk 1.20.94)
As long as the semen remains stable within the body, there is indeed no fear of death;
for one by whom the space-seal (nabhomudrā) is bound, the seed does not depart. (Āk 1.20.95)
If he should go [to another woman], his seed indeed enters the fire;
that seed, being itself obstructed by the power [of the other woman], ascends upward. (Āk 1.20.96)
As long as one is not bound by the *yonimudrā*, that mudrā is difficult to attain.
Seed is said to be of two kinds: semen and the great passion (*mahārāga*). (Āk 1.20.97)
The semen is located in the head, while the *rajas* is located in the womb;
the semen is white in color, whereas the *rajas* is said to have the luster of coral. (Āk 1.20.98)
The semen is eternally situated in the moon, and the menstrual blood is conjoined with the sun;
semen is Śiva and the blood is Śakti—their union is very difficult to attain. (Āk 1.20.99)
By the movement of the power (śakti) of the vital breath (marut), the subtle element (rajas) is led upward;
it then attains union with the bindu, and at that time, the divine body comes into being. (Āk 1.20.100)
In the mahāmudrā,
one should press the region of the womb with the base of the left foot,
and hold the extended right foot with both hands. (Āk 1.20.101)

Having placed the chin upon the chest, then having filled the abdomen with air by means of the wind, one should exhale, O Goddess, remaining in the bound posture (baddhāsana) and self-controlled (yamī). Āk 1.20.102.
This is proclaimed as the supreme Mahāmudrā, which purifies impurities;
it joins the sun and the moon, dries up the tongue [of craving], and destroys evil. (Āk 1.20.103)
Likewise, O beloved, one should press the region of the womb with the right foot, and having extended the left leg, one should hold it with both hands. Āk 1.20.104.

One should perform the remainder as previously described; thus, in both the right and left [movements], the practice should be simultaneous in its parts. One should avoid [any] unevenness in that. (Āk 1.20.105)
For him, whether wholesome or unwholesome, the six flavors—even when tasteless—as well as terrible poison, are digested like very pleasant nectar. (Āk 1.20.106)
Diseases such as abdominal tumors, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and skin diseases (kuṣṭha) undoubtedly perish;
this Mahāmudrā grants perfection, destroys [untimely] death, and overcomes the fear of old age. (Āk 1.20.107)
It should not be revealed, nor should it be given to just anyone, O dear one.
(3. Pratyāhāra) The yogin, seated in the *muktāsana* posture with his limbs, neck, and head held straight, [should practice]. Āk 1.20.108.
With eyes fixed on the tip of his nose, established in himself and staying in a small hut, he should mutter the *praṇava*;
[for him,] the three worlds, the three times, the three gods, and even the three lords [are conquered]. (Āk 1.20.109)
The three luminaries headed by the Moon, the three Vedas, the three fires, the triple power (śakti), the triple path, and the powers of Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu. (Āk 1.20.110)
That light in which the three phonemes shine is "Om.
He who [worships] that syllable Om with mind, speech, and action—Āk 1.20.111.
Whether walking, standing, reciting, waking, pure or even impure, he who meditates, chants, and practices becomes liberated from the bonds of existence. (Āk 1.20.112)
One would not be smeared by karma, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
when the wind moves, all the elements of the sense faculties move as well.
When the vital air (vāyu) is steady, everything beginning with the body becomes stable;
therefore, one should bind the breath, for when the breath is steady, the mind becomes steady. (Āk 1.20.114)
O Bhairavī, when the mind is steady, the individual soul also becomes steady; as long as the vital breath is restrained, so long is the consciousness perfectly stable.
As long as the seed remains within the space between the eyebrows, there is no fear of death;
the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be eternally thirty-six finger-breadths [in length]. (Āk 1.20.116)
Remaining in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), with the limbs straight and the mind steady, one should fill the vital air (prāṇa) through the left nostril alone. Āk 1.20.117.
One should retain [the breath] for sixteen measures, O Dear One, exhale for twelve measures, and perform the exhalation through the right nostril for ten measures. (Āk 1.20.118)
And again, O Dear One, one should fill [the breath] through the solar path as before;
having retained it, one should exhale through the left nostril. (Āk 1.20.119)
O Goddess worshipped by yogis, the method of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is said to be threefold: the inferior, the middling, and the superior, respectively. Āk 1.20.120.
This [first] prāṇāyāma is declared to be the lowest; therefore, the middling is recorded as being double that, and the highest is declared to be triple—such is this prāṇāyāma, O Īśvarī. (Āk 1.20.121)
But when one fills the left nostril with the lunar syllable, one should meditate upon [the syllable] resembling milk, situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar. (Āk 1.20.122)
But when one fills [the breath] through the right nostril with the solar syllable, one should always contemplate it as being located at the navel, resembling a blazing fire. (Āk 1.20.123)
Having thus meditated upon the two seed-syllables through both nostrils, the wise one who fills [the channels] will thereby achieve the purification of the *nāḍīs*. Āk 1.20.124.

Thus, through practice for three months, one gains the ability to retain the vital breath (vāyu) at will; the digestive fire (jāṭharo vahniḥ) becomes kindled, and the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda) arises. (Āk 1.20.125)
O Goddess, one shall attain health through the constant practice of yoga; however, in the first stage this is not yet the true Dharma, and in the second stage the body trembles. (Āk 1.20.126)
But when one rises during the third [watch], while remaining in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana),
the withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) occurs through the sixfold practice beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma), O Śivā.

Retention (dhāraṇā) is praised when performed according to the rule of twelve [moments]; meditation (dhyāna) arises from twelve moments of retention, and that [meditation] consists of twelve [moments]. Āk 1.20.128.

O Goddess, that is called *samādhi*, by which the visible world is perceived as beyond the beyond; in that state, which is both supreme and non-supreme, the accumulation of karma is exhausted. (Āk 1.20.129)
Birth and death do not occur, and old age and disease perish; through yoga practiced with correct method, one shall become long-lived and happy. Āk 1.20.130.
From practicing [yoga] improperly, there arise hiccup, diseases of the ear, headache, asthma, cough, and many other such disorders and defects. (Āk 1.20.131)
(Viparītakaraṇī Mudrā):
One woman comes from a gentle place and is enjoyed by two men;
thereafter, whoever that third person may be, he shall be freed from birth and old age. (Āk 1.20.132)
The sun, having the form of a blazing fire, is situated in the center of the navel;
the moon shines in the middle of the palate, raining down nectar with its face turned downward. Āk 1.20.133.
The sun, with its upward-turned face, swallows it by means of the brilliance of its rays;
that which acts in the opposite manner to this is the *viparītaka*. (Āk 1.20.134)
Having made the mouth like a crow's beak and drawing in the air with a whistling sound through the nostrils, one should then release that breath again. (Āk 1.20.135)
This yoga, known as "the cooling" (śītalīkaraṇa), removes fever and bile;
for one who drinks its nectar-like coolness, there is indeed no old age. (Āk 1.20.136)
O Dear One, for that yogi who drinks the vital breath with the tongue at the root of the palate, all diseases perish within six months. (Āk 1.20.137)
O beloved, for him who drinks the *soma* after turning the tongue upward, perfection (*siddhi*) arrives within half a month; indeed, no diseases afflict him. (Āk 1.20.138)
And by pressing the great cavity within the tongue with the tip of the tongue, and meditating upon Mother Ambā as a stream of nectar, one becomes a poet in half a year. (Āk 1.20.139)
For the yogi whose body has been drenched in nectar, after three years, the semen indeed moves upward; thus, the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest are perfected. (Āk 1.20.140)
The three kinds of poison shall not enter his body; likewise, there is neither old age nor death, nor fear of malevolent beings. (Āk 1.20.141)

(4. Dhāraṇā) Having ascended to the aforementioned posture, always devoted to breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and purified by withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), one should then practice concentration (*dhāraṇā*). (Āk 1.20.142)
O Śivā, that which is the immobility of the mind is known as *dhāraṇā*;
it is the individual fixing of the five elements, beginning with earth, within the heart. (Āk 1.20.143)
Square, golden, and marked with the letter *la*, the earth together with Brahmā should be meditated upon as situated in the heart for five *nāḍikās*. (Āk 1.20.144)
One should hold the vital breath (prāṇa) together with the mind right there, O Śāmbhavī;
this is the vidyā that causes paralysis, by which one attains mastery over the earth. (Āk 1.20.145)
Resembling a half-moon, as pure as camphor or snow, it is eternally situated in the region of the throat, joined with the letter *va* drenched in nectar. (Āk 1.20.146)
One should hold the water element conjoined with Viṣṇu there;
the vital breath, together with the mind, should be meditated upon for five nāḍikās. (Āk 1.20.147)
For this Vāruṇī lore, which removes poison, bile, and fever, was indeed devised by me alone for the swallowing of the Kālakūṭa. (Āk 1.20.148)

One should meditate upon the fire element (vahnitattva), which has the form of a triangle, shines like molten gold, is accompanied by the letter *ra*, has Rudra as its presiding deity, resides in the region of the palate, and possesses a blazing radiance. Āk 1.20.149.
In that very state, the yogi should hold the breath along with the mind for five *ghaṭikās*; this is indeed the supreme Vaiśvānarī [mudrā]. (Āk 1.20.150)
It destroys the fear of poison and fire, removes diseases such as wind and phlegm, is circular, has the luster of a blue cloud, and is established between the two eyebrows. (Āk 1.20.151)
The syllable *sa* is the air element (*vāyutattva*), which is eternal and has Īśvara as its deity;
therein reside five channels (*nāḍikā*) along with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*). (Āk 1.20.152)
One should retain this Vāyavīya vidyā, which bestows the power of moving through the air;
it resembles the water of a mirage and is conjoined with the letter *ha*. (Āk 1.20.153)
O Dear One, the deity beginning with Sadāśiva is always situated at the aperture of Brahmā; it is the element of space, formless, tranquil, and all-pervading. (Āk 1.20.154)
There, having restrained the breath together with the mind, one should hold it for as long as five *ghaṭikās*; this is the "Knowledge of the Sky," O Goddess. (Āk 1.20.155)
O Goddess, this knowledge has been declared as bestowing liberation and removing the suffering of yogins;
the earthly knowledge is considered paralyzing, while the watery is thought to cause flooding. Āk 1.20.156.
Then, the Vaiśvānara knowledge is proclaimed as the burner;
the Vāyava is said to be the agitator, and that which has the form of space is the pacifier. (Āk 1.20.157)
Gradually, the five vidyās should each be mastered individually; they bestow upon yogins fruits corresponding to their own names and functions. Āk 1.20.158.
This fivefold concentration, O Goddess, is difficult to attain on earth.
That unwavering reflection upon the principles (tattvas) is proclaimed as meditation (dhyāna). (5. Dhyāna) Āk_1,20.159 //
O beloved, meditation is renowned as being of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa).
That which is with attributes is accompanied by syllables; that which is without attributes is devoid of syllables. Āk 1.20.160.
A hundred thousand Vājapeya sacrifices and a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single moment of yogic meditation. (Āk 1.20.161)

With the mind turned inward and the gaze directed outward, sitting upright in the lotus posture—this is to be known as the yoga of meditation; it is auspicious and bestows immediate accomplishment. Āk 1.20.162.
O beloved, having meditated upon the Self in this first wheel at the *mūlādhāra*, which has the luster of gold, one should focus on the tip of the nose; thus one destroys all sin. (ĀK 1.20.163)
And at the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which has the luster of a jewel, one should contemplate oneself;
focused on the tip of the nose, that best of yogis is liberated from sufferings. (Āk 1.20.164)

Having visualized oneself within this maṇipūraka-cakra, which has the luster of the early morning sun, the self-controlled one, with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, can shake the three worlds. (Āk 1.20.165)

O Supreme Goddess, when the wheel at the heart-center, resembling a garland of lightning, has been thoroughly mastered through various forms of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) in the unstruck state (anāhata), [the yogi attains success]. Āk 1.20.166.
O Dear One, that yogi who meditates upon the self with eyes fixed on the tip of the nose becomes equal to Brahman, having brought the mind under control. Āk 1.20.167.
At the uvula, known as Viśuddhā, which resembles a golden campaka flower, one should meditate on oneself with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose and become filled with bliss. (Āk 1.20.168)
In the *lambikā*, filled with nectar and adorned by the lunar disc, one should meditate upon the Self with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose and become composed of bliss. (Āk 1.20.169)
O Goddess, one should meditate upon the Self in the form of collyrium between the eyebrows;
having conquered the vital breaths, the yogi becomes filled with the bliss of yoga. (Āk 1.20.170)

One whose eye is fixed between the eyebrows should meditate upon the Self, which is devoid of qualities, free from decay, auspicious, tranquil, higher than the highest, and consisting of the universal and the individual consciousness. Āk 1.20.171.
The yogi indeed becomes filled with the bliss of Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
This is known as the *ājñācakra*, located in the supreme, stainless void. (Āk 1.20.172)
Having contemplated the Self as auspicious, one becomes composed of knowledge and self-controlled;
it is stainless like the form of the sky and resembles the water of a mirage. Āk 1.20.173.
Having meditated upon the self as omnipresent, the self-controlled one attains liberation;
[the centers are] the anus, the genitals, the navel, the heart, and likewise the uvula. (Āk 1.20.174)
The uvula, the space between the eyebrows, the sky, and the aperture of Brahmā—these are known as your wheels, the places to be bestowed upon yogins. (Āk 1.20.175)

O Dear One, concentration (dhāraṇā) lasts for five ghaṭikās, meditation (dhyāna) is said to last for six nāḍīs, and absorption (samādhi) shall last for twelve days through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyamana). Āk 1.20.176.
(6. Samādhi) Just as the oneness of water and salt occurs through their union, that state of aesthetic equilibrium between the mind and the self is called samādhi. Āk 1,20.177.
When the mind dissolves at the end, upon the cessation of the vital breaths, then there arises a state of equanimity; that indeed is called samādhi. (Āk 1.20.178)
O Goddess, when the individual soul, with all its volitions completely dissolved, attains oneness with the Supreme Soul, that is called samādhi. (Āk 1.20.179)
When the mind functions toward the senses, having abandoned dependence on another, and the living soul has attained unity [with it], then there is neither sense-faculty nor mind. (Āk 1.20.180)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell;
the self, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor, the pleasant and the unpleasant. (Āk 1.20.181)
He who does not perceive cold or heat, nor wind or sun,
is not afflicted by the flood of his own karma, nor is he afflicted by anything at all.
He is not harmed by weapons, nor is he seized by mantras, yantras, or tantras;
he is neither afflicted by fire, nor by water, nor even by wind.
He is invulnerable to all embodied beings and worthy of honor even by the gods;
whether in eating, in recreation, in sleep, or in waking. (Āk 1.20.184)
O Yoginī, being engaged in all activities, one knows that reality which is without support, without form, without beginning or end, and without foundation. (Āk 1.20.185)
Without abode, free from conceptual proliferation, inactive, stainless, and great;
immovable, pure, eternal, devoid of qualities, the sky-like expanse consisting of consciousness. (Āk 1.20.186)
O Vindhyavāsinī, know this to be the reality of the state of Brahman: eternal bliss, infinite, all-pervading, omnipresent, and continuous. Āk 1.20.187.
One who is disciplined in yoga dissolves into the supreme reality, which is free from disease, without support, devoid of affliction, of great splendor, and without appearance. Āk 1.20.188.

Just as milk poured into milk, clarified butter into clarified butter, fire into fire, or water into water attains identity with that which it has been cast, so too does one merge into Brahman. (Āk 1.20.189)
(Regarding the fruit of yogic practice: All this divine elixir of vital air has been declared by me;
the meritorious soul who practices it has accomplished his purpose throughout the three worlds. (Āk 1.20.190)
Endowed with the fruit of all sacrifices, he has bathed in every sacred ford;
he is illustrious, he is the lord of yogins, and he alone is worshipped by the immortals.
O lady of beautiful countenance, that very one who is perfected and pure is equal to me;
my heart feels affection for him, and his mind is the dwelling place of mine.
His life is fruitful and both his lineages are purified; by the mere setting down of his foot, the earth is made holy. (Āk 1.20.193)
That earth where he has dwelt for even a moment is indeed a field of merit;
O beloved, blessed is his mother, and meritorious is his father.
By the sight of him, corpses such as those impaled on stakes would come back to life;
by his word alone, everyone—even the dead—attains both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
"By contact with its urine and impurities, even metals attain the state of gold;
how much more so, O Goddess, one whose prowess is equal to mine? (Āk 1.20.196)
Āk, 1, 21 (The Ritual for the Construction of the Hut for Attaining Yoga): Śrī Bhairavī said:
"A hut was mentioned by you previously; how is it to be constructed and of what nature?
O Śambhu, tell me, O Lord, for how long a time must one dwell there? (Āk 1.21.1)
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Tripurasundarī, listen well as I describe that hut;
having raised up the earth, O beloved, make it once again level.
One should gradually set up six pillars in each row, making them straight; then, having placed very firm wooden beams upon them, one should install the crossbeams above. (Āk 1.21.3)
After laying the bricks, one should thoroughly smear them with lime;
having constructed the parapet all around, one should fashion an auspicious wall with three enclosures.
One should construct a hut in the middle of that [space], and furthermore, one should dig a square pit measuring ten *prādeśas* deep, using the third enclosure as a guide. (Āk 1.21.5)
It was five *prādeśas* deep below and likewise above;
thus, with its ten spans (*vitastis*), it was inconceivable and enchanting.
The eastern gate is in the outer circle; O Śivā, the southern gate is in the second circle, while the western gate is prescribed for the third.
The measurement of the doors is said to be two spans; each door shall have a leaf, be free of gaps, and be provided with a bolt. Āk 1.21.8.
One should make the wall smeared with lime and the ground very smooth;
on the south and the north, there should be two inner altars within the enclosure.
It is three and a half spans wide and ten spans long;
its height is one span, and the middle part is three spans. Āk 1.21.10.
There, one should fill the walls of the hut with ash produced from cow dung and strained through a cloth, creating many extensive and variegated designs. (Āk 1.21.11)
Bhairava, resembling a dark rain-cloud, with blazing hair standing erect on his head, possessing an eye in his forehead and curved fangs, adorned with serpent-earrings. (Āk 1.21.12)
He has a snake as his sacred thread, wears a garland of small bells and skulls, is naked,
and has his feet and hair adorned by ten million crows.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, rings,
and other ornaments, he has ten arms, holding a *ḍamaru* drum, a goad, a sword, and a trident.
He grants boons with his right lotus-hands, while holding a serpent, a noose, a small bell, a honey-cup, and the dispeller of fear with his left arms. (Āk 1.21.15)
Richly adorned with black unguents and garlands, it destroys all diseases;
it is the slayer of ailments, spirits, serpents, and enemies, and the destroyer of fear from poison and the like. (Āk 1.21.16)
Then, O Dear One, one should draw the peaceful Mṛtyuñjaya Vaṭuka, white as mercury, the moon, or snow, appearing as a youth and adorned with two arms. (Āk 1.21.17)
Adorned with a girdle of small bells and beautiful earrings upon his ears, the child has three eyes and stands naked in form. (Āk 1.21.18)
Adorned with white garlands and unguents, and holding a full vessel to his left, he holds a staff in his right hand; he is the destroyer of death. (Āk 1.21.19)
One should first utter the seed-syllable of Māyā and this Vaṭuka;
for the sake of rescuing from calamity, one should write these two five-syllabled [mantras]. (Āk 1.21.20)
"Vaṭukāya" and "māyā" (hrīṃ) are known as the mantra of Vaṭuka;
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, this is declared to be the mantra for both forms. (Āk 1.21.21)
And if there is a yantra for this mantra, one should draw that yantra there,
[placing] Ramā, Bhuvaneśī, Kāma, and Cintāmaṇi in sequence.
First, one should write "Vaṭukāya" repeated [twice] in the pericarp;
then, one should write the remaining syllables, one on each petal, upon the eight petals. (Āk 1.21.23)
On the sixteen petals outside, one should write the sixteen vowels;
on the thirty-two petals, the thirty-two consonants from *ka* to *sa*. (Āk 1.21.24)
One should draw six *halas* on the petals and a *bhūpura* (fortified city) outside;
this is the *yantra* for deliverance from calamity and the warding off of untimely death. Āk 1.21.25.
It provides protection for all living beings afflicted by planetary influences; it brings women under control, as well as kings, men, and even animals. (Āk 1.21.26)
It constantly bestows various supernatural powers, removes all diseases and poisons, is radiant with necklaces and armlets, and deludes the entire universe with its splendor. (Āk 1.21.27)
One should meditate upon the Lord Mahāmṛtyuñjaya, and one shall become a conqueror of death. Thus [is formed] the third letter of the second group conjoined with the fifth. (Āk 1.21.28)
Then follows the word of the one to be protected (sādhya), joined with the vowel, the nasal drop (bindu), and the letter *sa*;
after that, the word "protect" (rakṣa) repeated twice; and again, the three seed-syllables as before. (Āk 1.21.29)

Having recited the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra in reverse order, one should mutter it; one should write the syllable *Bhaṃ* in the middle of the *Tāra*, with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) placed within it, upon the petals of the directions. (Āk 1.21.30)
One should write the final syllable sequentially upon the petals starting from the southeast;
having drawn a square enclosure (bhūpura) on the outside, one should draw it densely in all directions. Āk 1.21.31.
In the four corners is the syllable *ṭha*, a yantra consisting of Mṛtyuñjaya, which destroys untimely death, fever, disease, poison, and delusion. (Āk 1.21.32)
There, one should depict the god Cintāmaṇi, who grants whatever object is desired;
he is as beautiful as blue coral, three-eyed, and has a lovely countenance. (Āk 1.21.33)
One should meditate upon Ardhanārīśvara, who wears a crown of the moon, holding a noose and a red lotus in his left hands, and a trident and a skull-cup in his right hands. Āk 1.21.34.

Then, from the fire [letter] and the first of the groups [consonants], excluding the *ra* and *ma*, followed by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the end of the *sadya* [mantra], together with the sixth vowel and the nasal bindu. (Āk 1.21.35)
This is the auspicious mantra of the Cintāmaṇi, which bestows desired objects when contemplated;
it is encircled by the sixteen vowels and grants the wishes of the Cintāmaṇi. (Āk 1.21.36)
One should enclose it with the letter *ṭha*, which destroys fever, epilepsy, and death;
thereafter, one should draw the goddess Śāradā, the bestower of success. (Āk 1.21.37)

White as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon, she wears the crescent moon upon her crown; with her lotus-like hands, she holds a vessel of nectar, a rosary, and displays the *varada* and *abhaya* mudrās. Āk 1.21.38.
Wearing white garments and radiant with pearl ornaments, she bears the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśī), and the two words "vada vada. (Āk 1.21.39)
One should utter "Vāgvādinī" together with the name of the Buddha (Amitābha) and the wife of Agni (Svāhā).
This is declared to be the Śrīmātṛkā mantra, which bestows eloquence. (Āk 1.21.40)
Omitting the first two seed-syllables, one should recite the remainder as before;
this is the ten-syllable Śāradā mantra, which bestows the play of speech. (Āk 1.21.41)

One should first write the letter *vi* (the color of the sky), followed by the letter *su*, ending with *ya* and accompanied by the visarga, in the pericarp; one should also write the vowels upon the filaments. (Āk 1.21.42)
In the eight petals, the eight groups [of consonants] are proclaimed as follows: three beginning with *a-śa-hā*, and five letters beginning with *ka*. Āk 1.21.43.
One should draw the letters *ṭha* in the corners of the outer square and place them in the cardinal directions;
for this is the Mātṛkā-yantra, which removes poison, death, and disease. (Āk 1.21.44)
O Goddess, one should draw Aghora, who resembles a dark blue cloud, possessing cruel fangs and three eyes, and adorned by eight lords of serpents. (Āk 1.21.45)
With red unguents and garments, adorned with a red garland, [he holds] a battle-axe, a hand-drum, a sword, a shield, an arrow, and a bow. Āk 1.21.46.
Holding a trident and a vessel of abundance with his eight arms, he [beholds] Bhuvaneśī, the pair of whom is quivering; then, let the desired object flash forth. Āk 1.21.47.
Then there is a pair of forms that are terrible and even more terrible than the terrible, manifesting as a doubled pair with the sound "ka ha. (Āk 1.21.48)
O Goddess, there are two *vama* syllables, the word *bandha* repeated, two instances of *ghātaya*, and the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending with *phaṭ*. (Āk 1.21.49)
This mantra, consisting of fifty-one syllables and known as Aghora, is prescribed for the purpose of subjugation;
it possesses the appearance previously described and has the luster of molten gold. (Āk 1.21.50)

O Dear One, for the sake of liberation and for the purpose of conquering death, one should draw the white form previously described—the peaceful Aghorāstra weapon which bestows the accomplishment of all goals. (Āk 1.21.51)
The seed-syllable of Māyā, joined with the vowel and accompanied by the object of accomplishment (sādhya), should be placed in the center;
outside of that, one should likewise write the eight groups of consonants upon the filaments.
Then, one should write the letters of the mantra, numbering three (the qualities), upon the eight petals;
likewise, the remaining [letters] at the tips, and the armor (*kavaca*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras in its six corners. (Āk 1.21.53)
Outside of that, one should draw this Aghora yantra consisting of a city (bhūpura);
then, one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti in the center, surrounded by throbbing [rays]. (Āk 1.21.54)

Then, one should cause a pair [of syllables] to flash forth in the hexagon, and subsequently in the eight-petaled lotus, in sequence, with six, four, four, six, five, and four [syllables]. (Āk 1.21.55)
Then, one should draw [the diagram] with these remaining mantra-syllables according to the seasons;
within the hexagon, it is raised by means of the fire and weapon [mantras], its corners being devoid [of those syllables]. (Āk 1.21.56)

O Dear One, one should draw the Aghora Yantra surrounded by a Bhūpura (fortified city diagram), which removes serpents, enemies, thieves, minor ailments, epilepsy, spirits, and planetary influences. (Āk 1.21.57)
Furthermore, one should draw Mahāgaṇapati, resembling coral in color, with a crescent moon upon his crest, an elephant face, and three eyes. (Āk 1.21.58)
Pot-bellied, clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents,
possessing the beauty of ten mighty arms, and with a woman resting upon his left thigh.
Resplendent with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, signet rings, and earrings, he holds a fruit-filled vessel, a mace, a sugarcane bow, and a trident. (Āk 1.21.60)
With her ten hands, she holds a wheel, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, a cluster of rice stalks, and a jewel-filled vase with her teeth and mouth. (Āk 1.21.61)
He is embraced by Śrī, who rests upon his beautiful left thigh and holds a lotus in her hand;
he is a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for the desired objects of the world of devotees. Āk 1.21.62.
The Praṇava, Kamalā, Māyā, Kāmarāja, and Vasuṃdharā;
then, in sequence, the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati, and thereafter Mahāgaṇapati.
[The mantra consists of] the vocative case ending in the fourth case, followed by "vara" and likewise "varada";
then [the words] "sarvajanaṃ me ca vaśam ānaya. (Āk 1.21.64)
Having drawn the consort of Agni, one should write the twenty-eight-syllable mantra of Mahāgaṇapati, which destroys death and poverty. (Āk 1.21.65)

Having written the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa within a six-pointed star in a triangle, one should write the seed-syllables of Śrī, Śakti, Madana, and Bhū on the outside in the cardinal directions. (Āk 1.21.66)
In the hexagon, one should write the six seed-syllables, and in its junctions, the mantra for the limbs;
thereafter, one should write the mantras in groups within the centers of the eight petals. (Āk 1.21.67)

Then, one should write the Mātṛkā letters in direct order (anuloma) on the final syllable and the final petal, and in reverse order (pratiloma) upon the line; this [diagram] is then encircled by hooks and nooses. 1,21.68.
This auspicious and beautiful Yantra of Gaṇapati, ending with "gaja" and beginning with "śrī," is divine and increases longevity and health. (Āk 1.21.69)
One should draw these networks of yantras within the interior of the hut by the deity;
on the exterior surface of the hut walls, one should paint the color of Bhairava. (Āk 1.21.70)
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava, Kapālina, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhārabhairava, in sequence. (Āk 1.21.71)
On the inner wall of the second enclosure, one should draw eleven Rudras in sequence, each with three eyes, wearing matted hair crowned by the crescent moon. (Āk 1.21.72)
Outside of that, one should then draw the nine Nāthas, the nine Siddhas, and the sixteen [disciples] beginning with Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and Sananda.
Within the third enclosure, on the inner wall, the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī and the sixty-four Yoginīs should be drawn according to the prescribed rite. (Āk 1.21.74)
Outside that wall, in due order, are the guardians of the directions headed by Indra, the planets beginning with the Moon and the Sun, and the stars beginning with Aśvinī. (Āk 1.21.75)
The zodiac signs beginning with Aries should be drawn there, adorned with ornaments and holding weapons;
and on both sides of the door of the hut, one should depict Gaṇeśa and Bhairava. (Āk 1.21.76)
On the two sides of the door of the second enclosure are Śaṅkha and Padmaka;
and on those of the third enclosure are Garuḍa and Hanumān.
O Goddess, one should draw the two Bhayabhañjanas on both sides of the door in that place where a divine hut has been constructed by the best of yogins.
That land is most blessed, praiseworthy, a field of merit, and purifying;
and the people there are fortunate, possessing abundant wealth, and performers of meritorious deeds. (Āk 1.21.79)
The kingdom shall have abundant food, freedom from disease, and bring the happiness of health; it shall be free from calamities, blessed with timely rain, and filled with grain. (Āk 1.21.80)
It is free from the fear of thieves, disturbances, tigers, serpents, and the like;
and all sacred fords (tīrthas), such as the Gaṅgā and others, dwell there. (Āk 1.21.81)
Even the gods beginning with Indra, the planets beginning with the sun and the moon, the Yoginīs, the Bhairavas, the Siddhas, Gaṇeśa, Guha, and the Mothers; Āk 1.21.82.
For the monarch residing there, there shall be the attainment of victory and long life;
furthermore, there may arise the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin), resplendent with perpetual festivals.
Through the vision of the hut, barren women shall obtain the blessing of sons;
there is also the destruction of leprosy, epilepsy, possession by spirits, and other great diseases. (Āk 1.21.84)
Those who practice the elixir (rasāyana) should remain within a hut; they attain, with ease indeed, a perfection difficult even for the gods to obtain. (Āk 1.21.85)
(The *Amarīkalpa*):
O Goddess, I shall proclaim the wonderful, divine, most secret, and auspicious *Amarīkalpa*, which is faultless, easily obtained, and produced from one's own body. (Āk 1.21.86)
It bestows the eightfold sovereign powers beginning with *aṇiman*, as well as the accomplishment of bodily strength, alchemy, and so forth;
one whose body is purified by emetics and other means should avoid salt and sour flavors. (Āk 1.21.87)
But having entered the hut, O Goddess, the noble-minded one [prepared] the water of Śiva; with a vessel made of the wood of the large *kataka* tree, he [held] the drinking cup. (Āk 1.21.88)
And having ground triphalā, one should apply it within the interior of the cup;
[one should take] one karṣa with the water of Śiva at night, O beloved, while the vessel is turned face down. (Āk 1.21.89)
Having set it aside, one should discard the flow from the beginning and the end in the morning;
then, one should pour the middle streams into that vessel and subsequently add the three myrobalans (triphalā).
One should stir it with an immortal [elixir] and always drink it while facing east, after bowing to one’s chosen deity, the gurus, and the elders, and having worshipped Gaṇeśvara. (Āk 1.21.91)
One who is moderate in diet, restrained in conduct, and avoids wind and sun will become pure both internally and externally by means of a single enclosure alone. (Āk 1.21.92)
By the second maṇḍala, all forms of leprosy are destroyed;
by the third maṇḍala, the four kinds of poison are eliminated. (Āk 1.21.93)
By the fourth maṇḍala, it becomes like coconut water;
by the fifth, one's own water destroys impurities and foul odors. (Āk 1.21.94)
By means of the yoga of the sixth maṇḍala, the foul odor of the body is destroyed;
by means of the yoga of the seventh maṇḍala, there shall be sharpness of the sense faculties. (Āk 1.21.95)
Then, in the eighth mandala, one should consume a karṣa of powdered saffron along with the water of Śiva, continuing this until the fourteenth mandala.
