One shall be free from wrinkles and grey hair, and abandoned by the fear of great poisons;
in the fifteenth maṇḍala, one part each of *śṛṅga* and sulphur [is used]. (Āk 1.21.97)
One should drink twenty-one draughts mixed with the water of Śiva;
at the end of that, there shall be a mandala, and one becomes a partaker of the siddhis of the body and of metals.
O Goddess, one should likewise consume abhraka combined with varayā up to the twenty-second maṇḍala;
thus the self-controlled one should practice until the twenty-eighth maṇḍala. Āk_1,21.99.
Endowed with the strength of a rutting elephant, possessing the vision of a vulture, and free from disease,
he reached the twenty-ninth mandala, joined by an excellent woman.
O beloved, one should also drink the pure lizard mixed with the powder of its own entrails;
within thirty-five days, that man shall possess a vajra-body. (Āk 1.21.101)
Thirty-six mandalas and so forth, combined with the dust of the golden earth and accompanied by oneself and a cow, should be drunk until it has increased twofold. (Āk 1.21.102)
At the end of forty mandalas, the practitioner shall become a sky-goer (khaga) with his physical body;
however, when the forty-third mandala is reached, he becomes endowed with the nature of mercury (pārada).
One should drink ten thousand *varas* until reaching fifty mandalas;
endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, one becomes a sky-farer with a vajra-body. (Āk 1.21.104)
Endowed with the perfections (siddhis), free from fear, free from danger, and stainless,
he wanders at will through all the worlds for all time.
O Goddess, having first begun with the mandala, one should perform the rite daily;
one should stir it with water infused with *dhuttūra* juice. (Āk 1.21.106)
One should repeatedly rub all the limbs with that very ash,
especially with one's own urine when it is available at other times.
O Goddess, one should constantly practice [this] on the crown of the head, the nostrils, the ears, the eyes, and both hands and feet; thus a person shall become pure in body. (Āk 1.21.108)
O beloved, one who serves the immortal [goddess] should never cast his own excrement upon the ground; for such a man, it becomes the water of Śiva. (Āk 1.21.109)
One should drink every day all types of metal, divine gold that is difficult for humans to obtain, and a lizard accompanied by *vijayā*. (Āk 1,21.110)
Āk, 1, 22 (The Ritual of Vandāka):
Vandāka is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by the division of male and female.
A man whose leaf-like [body] is like the leaf of a date palm bestows all accomplishments. (Āk 1.22.1)
Strī-saṃjña is one who has little virtue but possesses the power of conduct;
Vandāka is one who grows from the foot; Śikharī is a tree-climber; and Tarurohiṇī is a creeper that climbs trees. Āk 1.22.2.
Vṛkṣādanī and Kāminī, as well as Vṛkṣarugbandha-bandhaka and Vandāka, are bitter and astringent; they remove phlegm, bile, and fatigue. (Āk 1.22.3)
It bestows the accomplishment of subjugation and other powers, is aphrodisiac, destroys poison, and is a rejuvenative elixir. (The procedure for extracting Vandākā:
Having observed a fast and bathed well, wearing red garlands and unguents, Āk_1,22.4.
Having loosened his hair and garments, with a restrained mind at night, he should circumambulate the tree, offering perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other such items. (Āk 1.22.5)
Having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly with the articles of worship, one should scatter an offering of curd and rice;
then, one should recite the Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha mantras one hundred and eight times. (Āk 1.22.6)
Having recited the mantra and cut it with a sword, one should collect the *vandāka* according to the prescribed rite; this procedure has been declared for all types of *vandāka*. (Āk 1.22.7)
On the day of Aśvinī, one who has observed the vow of purity should collect the shoots of the *aśvattha* tree according to the prescribed rite;
having ground them and stirred them into milk, he should drink it, and he will become as strong as a horse. (Āk 1.22.8)
Likewise, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, one should recite the Nṛsiṃha mantra while cutting down an Aśvattha branch with a sword and bring it back. (Āk 1.22.9)

Having rubbed [the herb] with water, smeared it upon one's forearm, and applied a tilaka-mark mixed with gorocana, one should look [at the person]; he will certainly become submissive to all. (Āk 1.22.10)
One should collect the vandāka from a banyan tree under the constellation Aśvinī according to the prescribed rite;
by binding it on the hand with a thread, a man becomes invisible. (Āk 1.22.11)
By grinding [the herbs] with milk, one will gain total control; by drinking it, one shall conquer diseases.
Under the asterism Aśvinī, one should collect the shoots of the Śirīṣa tree according to the prescribed rite.
One should bind it to the hand with a thread, and the paralysis of virility will certainly occur.
On the day of Aśvinī, the wise one should fetch a binding-cord made of *palāśa* wood. (Āk 1.22.13)
Whosoever ties it on the hand and touches [the woman], that woman shall come under his control;
by tying the *aṅkola* bond on the hand during the asterism of Aśvinī, one becomes beloved by the world.
Having taken Kuśa grass and Vandāka under the asterism Bharaṇī during an auspicious conjunction, one should bind it on the right hand; by that means, a person shall become invisible. Āk 1.22.15.

If one places a *phalguvṛndāka* plant under the constellation Bharaṇī within a heap of grain, there will indeed be an increase in that grain; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (Āk 1.22.16)
On the day of Bharaṇī, one should collect a bunch of jujube fruits according to the prescribed rite;
by tying it on the right hand, one shall obtain the desired fruit. (Āk 1.22.17)
Under the asterism Kṛttikā, one should collect *katakavandāka* according to the prescribed rite; one should place it in the middle of a wick and collect the soot from it. Āk 1.22.18.
By the mere application of collyrium to women, a husband will certainly become submissive.
Having purified oneself under the constellation Kṛttikā, one should fetch a *jambū* flower. (Āk 1.22.19)
Having drunk that paste ground with milk, one is liberated from diseases.
Under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should gather the Vandāka creeper of the Tinduka tree according to the prescribed rite.
Having tied it on one's hand, whatever person one touches shall become entirely submissive;
it is recommended for cataracts and similar ailments, as even an incurable condition is cured by the application of this ghee as an ointment. (Āk 1.22.21)
An eye-salve made from that same [substance] rubbed with honey is beneficial for the eyes.
Having obtained a ring made of *udumbara* wood under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should fashion it into a bracelet;
the sweetmeat placed in a vessel set upon that bracelet shall not diminish. (Āk 1.22.22)
One should collect the shoots of the Aśvattha tree under the Rohiṇī asterism according to the prescribed rite.
When the vandāka plant is kept in the house, constant prosperity arises.
One should collect the vandāka of the *kataka* tree according to the prescribed rite under the asterism Rohiṇī.
If one sees a treasure in the pair of eyes while applying collyrium, one should certainly bind that very object in the hand; then one will surely become a subduer of all. (Āk 1.22.25)
O beloved, one should collect the shoots of an Udumbara tree under the Rohiṇī asterism according to the prescribed rite;
by tying them on the hand, it quickly destroys quartan fever. Āk 1.22.26.
Under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should gather a binding-plant of citron;
by wearing it on the right ear, it is the supreme means for bringing the world under one's control. (Āk 1.22.27)
On the day of Rohiṇī, the Beloved of the World tied a sprig of Bilva to his hand;
on Mṛgaśīrṣa, he properly took a sprig of Śirīṣa. (Āk 1.22.28)
Having tied it in his hand, he should touch a woman or a man; he will certainly bring them under his control.
Under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa, one should take a *vandāka* plant produced from the *tintriṇī* tree. (Āk 1.22.29)
Having ground it with milk, one should drink it; the man becomes invisible.
He who drinks it with curd in the morning shall become a remover of all diseases. (Āk 1.22.30)
Having smeared all one's limbs with that [powder] ground with buffalo curd, one who enters the fire is not burned by the fire. (Āk 1.22.31)
In whose house the vandāka plant of the tintriṇī tree is established, for him there is no fear of thieves, and victory at dice shall be in his hand. (Āk 1.22.32)
One should collect the shoots of an Udumbara tree under the constellation Mṛgaśīrṣa;
having tied them in the hand, one should touch a woman, and that woman shall come under one's control. (Āk 1.22.33)
One should tie it in the hand of women or cast it into the midst of food; there will be an increase in food—of this there is no need for doubt. (Āk 1.22.34)
One should collect the tender shoots of the *nyagrodha* tree under the asterism of Mṛgaśīrṣa;
if one binds them on the right hand, one will certainly bring people under one's control. (Āk 1.22.35)
Taking the *vandāka* plant of *māṭarūṣa* as prescribed, and binding it on his hand, one playing with people at dice shall be invincible in gambling. (Āk 1.22.36)
Under the asterism Ārdrā, one should take the *taumbura* plant and collect the *vandāka* according to the prescribed rite;
he who drinks it with milk shall experience the dissolution of iron. (Āk 1.22.37)
On a Monday during the *ārdrā* asterism, or on a Sunday during the *puṣya* asterism, one should take a *vandāka* plant from a *tumburu* tree;
by binding it on the right hand, the immobilization of arrows (*bāṇastambha*) is produced. (Āk 1.22.38)
If a childless couple drinks bamboo shoots ground with milk under the asterism Punarvasu, they shall give birth to many sons.
Furthermore, during the asterism Punarvasu, one should fetch the Vandāka plant of the Naktamāla tree;
having ground it with milk, one should drink it, which destroys all diseases. (Āk 1.22.40)
By the mere measure of that powder, the seizing spirits and rākṣasas are destroyed.
Having gathered the bandhūka and vandāka plants under the Puṣya asterism, one should cause them to be deposited there. (Āk 1.22.41)
In that case, within the enemy's field, the destruction of the crops occurs;
if *karṇikāra* and *vandāka* are properly procured during the asterism of Āśleṣā, [the enemy's crops are destroyed]. (Āk 1.22.42)
Having tied it firmly to his hand, he brings [the person] under control by touching them with it; and one should collect the shoots of the *madhūka* tree under the asterism Āśleṣā. (Āk 1.22.43)

One should bind upon the right hand a *vandāka* plant from the *mucukunda* tree, which destroys the fear of tigers and other predators, having been gathered according to the prescribed rite under the asterism Maghā. (Āk 1.22.44)
If one causes it to be placed in the midst of grain, that grain shall become inexhaustible.
A sprout of the *vibhītaka* tree, taken during the two *phalgunī* constellations (the former ones), [should be used]. (Āk 1.22.45)
If one places it in the midst of grain, it shall become inexhaustible in an instant;
this same procedure is prescribed for the two Phalgunīs and also for Hasta. (Āk 1.22.46)
One should obtain a sprout of the Śāka tree according to the prescribed rite under the asterism Maghā;
this brings about an accumulation of grain at the door, and an increase in grain occurs.
On the day of Maghā when the sun is in that asterism, one should obtain a sprig of the mañjīvṛkṣa tree according to the prescribed rite;
by constantly wearing it upon the head, one’s prosperity shall come under control. Āk 1.22.48.
One should collect the sprouts of the *palāśa* tree according to the prescribed rite under the asterism Hasta;
by binding them on the hand or the head, one becomes a destroyer of seizing spirits such as tigers and the like. (Āk 1.22.49)
Likewise, having bound a sprout of the *tinduka* tree brought during the asterism of Citrā upon one's hand, one becomes victorious over all enemies. (Āk 1.22.50)
One should collect the *vandāka* creeper of the *kuṭaja* tree under the asterism Citrā according to the prescribed rite;
by binding it on the right hand, one shall obtain even that which is difficult to attain and desired. (Āk 1.22.51)
If one takes *likuca* and *vandāka* under the constellation Svāti and deposits them in whatever object, all that becomes inexhaustible; there is no doubt about this. (Āk 1.22.52)
One who ties a *babbūla* branch under the asterism Svātī, or a *badarī* branch under Anurādhā, and wears it on the hand—any woman touched by that [person] shall become submissive. (Āk 1.22.53)
Having brought a nurse’s gift according to the prescribed rite, he should cause it to be deposited in the house of a hostile shell-worker at Viśākhā. (Āk 1.22.54)
All intoxicants shall become undrinkable once that [impurity] has been extracted;
this occurs through the ritual performed under the constellation Anurādhā, using the *aindrī* plant and *vandāka* moss. (Āk 1.22.55)
If one places [the seed] among grain, it shall lead that grain to inexhaustibility.
Having taken a mango sprout under the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, one should bury it in the house of a courtesan. Āk 1.22.56.

She would truly become unfortunate; however, it is said that liberation is attained when the root is extracted according to the prescribed ritual, having first taken the vandāka plant from a khadira tree. Āk 1.22.57.
By tying it on his hand, a man who is unfortunate will quickly become fortunate;
that same substance, when ground with milk and drunk, destroys skin diseases and other ailments. (Āk 1.22.58)
On the day of the Sun (Sunday), one should collect *vandāka* from a cow-pen according to the prescribed rite;
if it is bound on the right hand, the subjugation of women becomes certain. (Āk 1,22.59)

That very [substance], having been prepared from *karavīra* flowers under the *pūrvāṣāḍhā* constellation, should be worn upon the head; then all accomplishments (*siddhi*) will certainly be attained. (Āk 1.22.60)
One who wears a *vandāka* [medicinal herb] produced from the *badarī* tree under the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā upon one's head in battle shall be invincible. (Āk 1.22.61)

A woman who is barren should drink [this] with milk; she shall obtain many sons. On a Sunday coinciding with the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā, one should take the Vandāka plant of the Kurava species. (Āk 1.22.62)
If one ties it on the right hand, that person indeed becomes invisible;
the *mandāra* binding should be taken under the constellation of Uttarāṣāḍhā. (Āk 1.22.63)
Alternatively, by binding a palāśa pledge in one's hand, one gains control; however, the vandāka plant produced from the *citraka* tree is not obtained even at the ear. (Āk 1.22.64)
One should smear a copper leaf with [the substance] rubbed with *kaṅkuṇī* oil;
by means of the *puṭapāka* method, it certainly becomes gold. (Āk 1.22.65)
One should collect the sprout of the castor plant (eraṇḍa) during the Śravaṇa-Arka [conjunction];
by binding it on the right hand, one will always be victorious at gambling. (Āk 1.22.66)

If one has duly gathered *badarī* and *vandāka* plants under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā and, having tied them in one's hand, touches whomever [with them], that person will certainly become a slave. (Āk 1.22.67)
Having ground *punnāga* and *vandāka* according to the prescribed method with milk, one who drinks it shall possess the strength of a great serpent (*mahānāga*). (Āk 1.22.68)
On a Sunday coinciding with the Maghā constellation, one should obtain a sprig of the *naktamāla* tree according to the prescribed rite;
by wearing it on the arm according to the rite, one will have no sight of *piśācas*. (Āk 1.22.69)
On a Punarvasu lunar mansion, one should collect the sprouts of the *tintriṇīka* plant according to the prescribed rite;
by binding them on the right hand, one will always be victorious at gambling. (Āk 1.22.70)
On a lunar mansion presided over by a beneficent star, one becomes invisible when holding a sprig of *vaṃśa* in the hand;
however, on the *uttarā* [nakṣatra], one should obtain a sprig of *śirīṣa* according to the prescribed rite.
One should bind it upon the head with the hand; it will become a remover of tigers and other seizing spirits (*graha*).
Under the asterism *Maghā*, one should place in the field a *vandāka* plant produced from honey. (Āk 1.22.72)
The binding of the beaks of birds and mice occurs [by this means].
One should collect the *vandāka* (flower-bud) of the *palāśa* tree under the asterism Hasta according to the prescribed rite. (Āk 1.22.73)
One should apply a medicinal paste to the penis; virility will certainly be stabilized.
Having ground the *vallīka* plant with honey, one should sprinkle it [on the organ] after mixing it with milk. (Āk 1.22.74)
O Goddess, that *vaṅga* [tin] becomes silver when processed seven times;
one should collect the tender shoots (*vandāka*) of the *palāśa* tree according to the prescribed rite under the constellation Hasta.
A man who drinks [the juice] with milk indeed becomes invisible;
likewise, one who takes the sprouts of the *tinduka* tree, gathered under the asterism of Citrā.
Having tied a cluster of *harītakī* fruits gathered under the constellation Pūrvabhādrapadā upon his hand, one becomes invulnerable to all enemies. (Āk 1.22.77)

Having drunk it ground into a paste with milk, one becomes equal to Vararuci; likewise, one who has gathered the *arkavandāka* plant under the *uttarā* asterisms and taken it under the *bhādrapadā* asterisms [attains the same]. (Āk 1.22.78)

One may utterly destroy poison, whether of stationary or mobile origin, by means of medicinal plasters and the like; having performed the protective rite with a branch of the Bodhi-vandāka tree under the constellation Revatī. (Āk 1.22.79)
Even a barren woman conceives by drinking that [medicine] with cow's milk;
likewise, one who has consumed a *vaṭa-vandāka* plant from a termite mound ground with honey during the asterism of Revatī. (Āk 1.22.80)
For eye ailments, it is most excellent; for disorders such as the obstruction of the eyes, one should take a *vaṭa-vandāka* plant under the asterism of Revatī and wear it on the arm. (Āk 1.22.81)
One endowed with the strength of a great elephant and born into a great assembly [is produced] from a Vandāka Rājavṛkṣaka tree uprooted under Viśākhā. (Āk 1.22.82)
The *vaṭavandāka* plant from a *rohiṇī* tree, when worn at the waist, wards off the fear of fire in the home for one staying at home and increases virility. (Āk 1.22.83)
A *vandāka* plant from an *aśvattha* tree, gathered under the asterism Revatī, is known to bestow pregnancy;
likewise, if a *vandāka* arising from a poisonous tree is gathered under Pūrvāṣāḍhā, it has the same effect.
Being smeared [with it], one utters the speech of spirits, piśācas, and the like;
one can cause food and a continuous stream of drinks to appear within a cooking pot. (Āk 1.22.85)
In gambling, one should employ the *jāmbavavandāka* which brings victory for Revatī;
one should employ the *kuravavandāka*, which stays in the hand and wards off arrows. (Āk 1.22.86)
The *vandāka* (mushroom) from a *madhūka* tree, when placed among grain, bestows an increase of grain;
the *vandāka* from a *palāśa* tree, when consumed with milk, bestows eloquence. (Āk 1.22.87)
If the *nimbavandāka* plant is placed inside the house of a prostitute, she will be brought under control in a wondrous manner from birth until the end of her life. (Āk 1.22.88)
Āk, 1, 23 (Distinguished Refinements of Taste):
Śrī Bhairavī.
"O God, O Śambhu, ocean of compassion, Lord of the gods, by your grace I have heard all about this divine elixir of all tastes. (Āk 1.23.1)
I shall announce another [teaching] that brings benefit to the entire world, for the elderly, women, children, eunuchs, and others who are afflicted by disease. (Āk 1.23.2)
"O Lord, for those who are incapable of alchemical elixirs (rasāyana), how can there be happiness?
O glorious Bhairava, you who favor all beings, please command us. (Āk 1.23.3)
Having heard the goddess’s hymn of praise, which bestows welfare upon all the world, and having heard her gentle smile, the Lord spoke these supreme words: Āk 1.23.4.
The Blessed Bhairava said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, since you are the mother of the worlds!
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall explain that benefit for the world which you have asked about."
I shall explain, in due order, the method for processing mercury and other substances which destroys all diseases; listen with careful attention. (Āk 1.23.6)
Rasendra, rasarāja, rasa, sūta, pārada, śivabīja, śiva, jaitra, rasaloha, and mahārasa; (these are the names of mercury). Āk 1,23.7.
Rasottama, Mahātejā, Sūtarāṭ, Capala, Amṛta, Dhuttūra, Lokanātha, Prabhu, Indra, and likewise Bhava. Āk 1.23.8.
He possesses the splendor of Rudra, he moves through the sky, he is the mercury-essence born of the inconceivable;
he is the immortal, the giver of bodies, Skanda, the Lord of Skanda, and the destroyer of death. Āk 1.23.9.
The divine elixir is considered the most excellent, bestowing fame and purifying; thus have been declared the thirty-three names of the divine essences. (Āk 1.23.10)
O fair-faced one, the king of elixirs (sūtarāja) when possessed of defects is like poison;
but the mercury free from defects is itself nectar—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.23.11)

Therefore, O Pārvatī, listen to the purification of mercury (pārada), which destroys defects; [it is taught by] the master of mercury, the best of physicians, who is self-controlled and knows the Aghora mantra. Āk_1,23.12.
(Refinements for the Purification of Mercury;
First Method) On an auspicious lunar mansion, under favorable ascendants, at a good moment, and on a propitious day.
As previously described, one should first perform the worship of the charioteer in a pure place. (Āk 1.23.13)
One hundred palas, or fifty, or twenty-five, or again ten, or five—O Goddess, it is not desired to be less than this. (Āk 1.23.14)
One should place mercury in a mortar made of iron or stone;
[then add] a sixteenth part (kalāṃśa) of the powder of brick and turmeric to the king of mercury.
O Dear One, having ground it for a day in a heated mortar with the sour juice of *jambīra* fruit, one should wash it with warm *sauvīra*; thus the defect of lead is destroyed. (Āk 1.23.16)
The defect caused by mercury is destroyed by *aṅkola* and *indravāruṇī*;
by *āragvadha*, the impurity; and by *citraka*, the defect caused by lead.

One should remove instability with *kṛṣṇadhūrta*, poison with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), mountain-born defects with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), and unbearable fire with *gokṣura*. (Āk 1.23.18)

For seven days, for the purpose of destroying the seven defects such as *vaṅga* and the rest, [the preparation should be made] with the respective powders in one-sixteenth part (*kalāṃśa*), combined with the juice of *kumārī*. (Āk 1.23.19)
After crushing it, one should subsequently wash it with warm *kāñjika*;
thus the mercury is freed from all impurities and its seven sheaths. (Āk 1.23.20)
If the mercury is to be employed in medical practice, it shall be a destroyer of all diseases.
(The second method: Devadāru, malayaja, jayā, and vāyasatuṇḍikā. Āk 1.23.21.
One should grind mercury for one day with the juice of *kumārī*, *musalī*, and *vandhyākarkoṭī*, and then place it again in a *pātanayantra*.
One should cause the pure mercury to fall [into the crucible] and join it for the physician’s work.
(The third method:
The burnt powder of stone and the juice of *niśākanyā* should be mixed with the liquid. (Āk 1.23.23)
One should rub it for one day and then cause it to fall [into the liquid] in the aforementioned apparatus; thus purified by this refinement, one should employ it in medical practice. (Āk 1.23.24)
(The fourth method: O beloved, having ground cinnabar for just one watch (three hours) with the juices of *pāribhadraka* or else with the juices of *jambīra*, one should cook it. (Āk 1.23.25)
O Goddess, in the *pātanaka* yantra, [the substance] is freed from its impure coating.
(The fifth method: One should grind *dhānyābhra* and mercury in equal parts with the juice of *punarnavā*. (Āk 1.23.26)
Having ground the mercury for a day in a heated mortar, one should cook it in a *vajramūṣā* crucible within a *bhūdharayantra*, and then grind it once again.
Having again performed the grinding and digestion with the previous liquids as before, one should place that [substance] ten times in the *pātana* (dropping) apparatus. Āk 1.23.28.
O Goddess, mercury becomes pure and is fit to be employed in alchemical elixirs and rejuvenation therapies. (The sixth method:
One should place sulfur, equal to one-tenth part of the mercury, into a heated mortar. (Āk 1.23.29)
One should grind it for one watch with the juices of *varā*, *jambīra*, *kanyā*, and *agni*;
one should cause it to fall in a *pātanāyantra* (sublimation apparatus), and thus perform this process seven times. (Āk 1.23.30)
O Dear One, there is grinding with fragrant substances and the process of precipitation;
O Goddess, mercury becomes pure and may then be employed in mercurial operations. (Āk 1.23.31)
(Seventh Method) One should cook vermilion with sesame oil, buffalo urine, liquor, sour gruel,
and beef in an iron vessel over a gradual fire. Āk 1.23.32.
One should stir that liquid repeatedly with an iron rod for seven days;
then, while it is still moist, one should saturate it with peacock bile in the sun for a day. (Āk 1.23.33)

One should cause mercury to fall in a *pātanāyantra* using a fierce fire; after four watches (*yāma*), it becomes pure mercury, capable of carrying the medicinal properties (*yogavāhaka*). (Āk 1.23.34)
(The *viḍa* salt fit for *jāraṇā* is like the submarine fire.
Listen, O Goddess, my dear; I shall explain the *viḍa* suitable for *jāraṇā*.
Having powdered burnt conch shell and impregnated it with the milk of the sun (*arka*) in the heat [of the sun], Āk_1,23.35.
Then, O Goddess, one should process it for one day and contemplate the essence of the smoke;
for one day, it should be placed in the intense heat of the sun with the juices of *jambīra* fruit.
O fair-faced one, one should boil the sixteen-part *suvarcala* with goat’s urine for four watches until it reaches a thick consistency. Āk 1.23.37.
In sixteen parts of human urine, one should carefully boil *kaṇṭakārī* together with its roots until it becomes thickened. Āk 1.23.38.
Tintriṇī-alkali, kāsīsa, sarja-alkali, and śilājatu—each of these should be processed separately with the juices of jambīra for four watches (yāmas). Āk 1.23.39.
Jepāla, realgar, salt-petre, rock-salt, guñjā, and borax should each be separately soaked with the juices of *śigru*. (Āk 1.23.40)
The thirteen substances beginning with conch-shell should be processed with the juices of *jambīra* fruits;
all of them, in equal parts, should be combined for one day and then filtered. (Āk 1.23.41)
He should always be known by the name Vaḍavānala;
likewise, he is used for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of gold and other base metals, as well as precious gems. (Āk 1.23.42)
And the secondary minerals, such as mica and others, should be applied with great care.
(The procedure for the ash of mercury; the first method.)
One should grind purified mercury and purified sulfur together with an equal amount of cow's ghee.
One should place the massified [substance] of a maiden within the interior of a petal,
wrap it thoroughly with thread, and then enclose it in a casket made of magnetite.
Having sealed it in a soft crucible, O Dear One, it should be heated three times; then, taking it out and placing it in a strong crucible, the wise one should close it and blow upon it. (Āk 1.23.45)
The king of elixirs (mercury) should be reduced to ashes when employed in alchemical transmutation (*rasāyana*). (Second method:
One should dry [the herbs] in the shade, as well as leafy vegetables and ripe fruits. Āk 1.23.46.
One should grind [the ingredients] with the milk of *arka* and smear the interior of the crucible (*mūṣā*) with it;
[then add] the residue of the placenta of a cow that has recently given birth. (Āk 1.23.47)
Afterwards, one should place mercury and the powder of sulphur into the middle of a crucible;
having cast them in and sealed it, one should heat it until the mercury is reduced to ashes. (Āk 1,23.48)
(The third type:
Vandhyā, Kārkoṭakī, Kākatuṇḍī, Kaṭutumbikā, Kañcukī, Nalikā, Kākamācī, and Kālamañjarī. (Āk 1.23.49)
Having ground all these kāka-jaṅghā plants, one should place them inside a crucible;
one should then macerate the mercury with the eight previously mentioned substances, beginning with vandhyā-mukhī. Āk 1.23.50.
Having placed that liquid into a smeared crucible and sealed it, one should cook it in the earth-oven;
thus, the smearing of the crucible should be performed eight times.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should repeatedly perform kneading and blowing;
the mercury (sūtendra) becomes "dead," fit for medical treatment and alchemy (rasāyana). Āk 1.23.52.
(Fourth Method) One should grind the solid mercury with the fourfold medicinal restrainers (*niyāmaka-auṣadha*) for four watches;
then, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire in twice the amount of sulphur oil. Āk 1.23.53.
One should cook the mercury in this manner until it attains the state of *khoṭa*;
then, having placed that *khoṭa* in an iron crucible (*saṃpuṭa*), the wise one should seal it firmly. (Āk 1.23.54)
Having ground iron slag with *pathyā* (yellow myrobalan) and water, one should draw a sealed vessel (*sampuṭa*).
Above that, having placed glass in the crucible (*śrāvaka*), one should cast in lead (*nāga*). (Āk 1.23.55)
O beloved, one should blow [on the bellows] only so long as that serpent-like [breath] flows;
the wise person should not blow at all until it reaches a state of rigidity. Āk 1.23.56.
When it has become hard again, one should blow upon it repeatedly as previously described; by blowing for three watches in this manner, the mercury is reduced to ashes. (Āk 1.23.57)

Mercury that has been reduced to ashes by means of roots but lacks the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*) should not be applied to the body or to metals; it is to be used only for medicinal purposes. (Āk 1.23.58)
(Fifth Method) One should grind pure mercury in double the amount of scented oil for one day; then, having ground it again, one should also treat it with *sarpākṣī* and *bhṛṅgarāja*. (Āk 1.23.59)
O Dear One, one should finely grind these with the juices of *viṣṇukrāntā* for three days, and then cook them in a *yantra* using the triple-union method (*trisaṃghaṭṭa*) eight times. Āk 1,23.60.
The lord of mercury, which destroys the multitude of diseases, should be turned into ash.
(The sixth method: The mercury should be rubbed for three days with the juices extracted from the roots of white *Aṅkola*. (Āk 1,23.61)
Having sealed it, one should place [the mercury] in a crucible and cook it in a *bhūdharayantra*;
the mercury attains the state of ash, becoming the supreme remover of all diseases. (Āk 1.23.62)
(Seventh method: One should grind *viṣṇukrāntā* and a sacrificial altar with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
The mercury should be rubbed with that paste seven times, having been revived after being swooned. (Āk 1.23.63)
Having placed that essence into a vessel for a disciple, one should repeatedly sprinkle it with those juices;
one should cook it for a day over a lamp-flame, until it becomes ash in the form of salt. (Āk 1.23.64)
(Eighth type:
The wise one should saturate *somarājī* and asafoetida with the milky sap of the *kākoduṃbarikā* tree; having done this seven times, he should repeatedly dry and grind it. (Āk 1.23.65)
One should throw the five parts (pañcāṅga) of *kākodumbara* into sixteen parts of water until one part remains; with that, one should grind the asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). (Āk 1.23.66)
Having placed that liquid into the crucible and sealed it within the retort,
one should then roast it in the earth-oven (bhūdhara) in this manner eight times, repeatedly.
And at each layer one should place that asafoetida; thus the mercury becomes dead.
(The ninth method: Likewise, the seeds of *urubūka* and those born from *apāmārga*. (Āk 1.23.68)
One should fill [the crucible] and, having placed that [substance] in the crucible, then throw the mercury (sūta) inside;
above that, one should place the previously mentioned powder and properly seal the crucible. (Āk 1.23.69)
In this manner, by four small, light packets, it shall be reduced to ashes. (The tenth method:
Within the bulb of the *kuḍuhuñcī* plant, soaked in the breast milk of a beautiful woman... (Āk 1.23.70).
Having cast in the liquid and sealed the mouth with a paste made from its marrow, the wise one should smear it with cow dung and heat it over a fire of cow dung. (Āk 1.23.71)

When this is done seven times, the mercury attains the state of ash. (The eleventh method: Equal parts of mercury and sulfur [should be processed] with the water from the roots of the *aṅkola* tree. Āk_1,23.72.
One should grind it for one day, seal it within the interior of a crucible, and roast it in a bhūdharayantra; at the end of the day, an ash is produced. (Āk 1.23.73)

(Twelfth Type) One should grind equal parts of processed paddy-cloud mica (*dhānyābhraka*) with the juices of the drugs used for killing [metals] for one day; then, using that paste, one should apply it as a coating to a cloth. (Āk 1,23.74)
Having made a wick from that cloth and holding it with a pincer, one should light it;
the liquid that falls into a bronze vessel will become black in color. (Āk 1.23.75)
Furthermore, that [substance] should be crushed by the Mārakas and cooked in a *pātanāyantra*;
it becomes "dead" in a single day, and its ash removes all diseases. (Āk 1.23.76)
(Thirteenth type:
Mercury should be rubbed with the oil of *kāladhuttūra*; then it should be ground for one day in a tortoise-shaped apparatus (*kūrmayantra*) by those skilled in the process. Āk 1.23.77.
It should be cooked until it turns to ash; it becomes white and destroys all diseases. (The fourteenth method:
One should grind pure mercury with half its quantity of pure sulfur. Āk 1.23.78.
One should heat mercury placed in a crucible for one day with the liquors derived from *māraka* herbs;
in a furnace known as the *bhūdhara*, it turns to ash in a single day.
(Fifteenth type:
O dear one, one should grind mercury with cloud-ash (*abhra*) and banyan-milk for three nights;
having placed it inside a crucible, one should cook it over a fire of dried cow-dung for one day. (Āk 1,23.80)
The lord of mercury, bright and the destroyer of all afflictions, becomes reduced to ashes; (this is the sixteenth method).
When the mercury has been opened and perfumed, [one adds] equal parts of gold. (Āk 1.23.81)
One should cause it to digest according to the previous method; then one should add an equal amount of sulfur.
Having placed the mercury in a crucible, it should be rubbed for one day with the juices of divine herbs. (Āk 1,23.82)
One should cook it day and night in a fire of dried cow-dung or in a fire of husks;
having extracted it, one should then subject it to sudation with substances derived from divine herbs. (Āk 1.23.83)
O Goddess of the Gods, having ground [the mercury] with equal parts of the seeds for four watches, it should be heated in a *vajramūṣā* crucible; the mercury will be reduced to ashes. (Āk 1.23.84)
One should always employ that divine ash for treating disease or as an elixir (*rasāyana*). (The seventeenth method:
When mercury has been properly digested, one should grind an equal amount of gold with acid. Āk 1.23.85.

Having washed that which has become a paste with sour gruel (kāñjika) and taken it again, one should add half a part of the pure powder, half of that amount of purified mercury (śuddhagandha), and half of that amount of borax (ṭaṅkaṇa). Āk 1.23.86.

One should grind that [substance] for an entire night with equal amounts of the liquid juices of women's menstrual flowers, and at the end of the day, one should then form it into a pill (*golaka*). (Āk 1.23.87)
The wise one should heat it in a *gaḍḍuka* apparatus over a mild fire for a day; then, having taken it out and pulverized it, he should add an equal amount of sulfur. (Āk 1.23.88)

It should be cooked for three days in a crucible (garbhayantra) over a mild fire of husks; O Goddess, the mercury will become ash, which, being "non-rearising" (niruttha), becomes an elixir (rasāyana). Āk 1,23.89.

(Eighteenth variety) Three karṣas of pure mercury and one karṣa of copper powder, O Dear One, should be ground thoroughly with acidic liquids for a day in a mortar; from that, [the compound] shall arise. (Āk 1.23.90)

One should wash that paste with water, and then, having taken all that pure metallic essence of honey (mākṣīkasattva), [one should process it] with the juices of the leaves of *cakramarda*. (Āk 1.23.91)
One should grind that paste thoroughly for three days in a crucible (*garbhayantra*),
O Goddess, and cook it for three days, day and night, over a fire of chaff.
In a fire of dried cow-dung, the resulting ash of mercury (sūtabhasma) removes disease and old age.
(The nineteenth method. Equal parts of mercury, gold, and the essence of *vyoma*, along with a *biḍa* salt equal to the gold—ĀK 1,23.93.
One should grind all that in a mortar for one day with the juices of plantain stalks;
then, for two days, with an equal amount of seeds produced from divine herbs. (Āk 1.23.94)
One should grind it together with the juice of plantains (*rambhā*) in a crucible (*garbhayantra*);
by cooking it according to the previous procedure, an auspicious mercury-ash (*rasabhasma*) will be produced. (Āk 1.23.95)

The lord of mercury (*rasendra*), which destroys old age, death, and disease, and bestows all accomplishments—[this] stainless essence (*vimalāsattva*) should be ground with an equal amount [of the other ingredients] for three days. (The twentieth method. Āk_1,23.96.
A paste should be made from the juice of *sinduvāra* leaves;
one should place that inside a glass flask (*kācakūpī*), and coat the flask with seven layers of clay and rags. (Āk 1.23.97)
One should dry it in a sand-oven (vālukāyantra) and cook it for a day over a mild fire;
thus the divine mercury ash (rasabhasma) is produced, which removes disease, old age, and death. (Āk 1,23.98)
(Twenty-first variety:
Two karṣas of mercury and half that amount of purified sulfur, along with an eighth part of the essence of honey and an eighth part of sulfur—one should grind all of this for one day. (Āk 1.23.99)
O Dear One, one should place that ball within the interior of a crucible using the essence of *nirguṇḍī* leaves;
then, having sealed the mouth of the crucible, one should insert it [into the furnace]. (Āk 1.23.100)
One should cook that crucible in a *gaḍḍukā* apparatus over a mild fire for one day;
the divine ash of the mercury will then be produced, resembling the reddish hue of vermilion. (Āk 1.23.101)
[This is] the auspicious [method], which destroys old age, death, and disease, and bestows all accomplishments;
(the twenty-second type:
mercury, interspersed with an equal amount of sulphur, [is placed] within the interior of a fired crucible. Āk 1.23.102.
Having added four times as much of the juice of *kākamācī* to those two, one should cover it, place it in a *gaḍḍukā* vessel, and cook it gradually. (Āk 1.23.103)
In the fire known as mild, medium, or fierce for four watches (yāmas), the auspicious ash of mercury (rasabhasma) is then produced, which destroys all diseases. (Āk 1.23.104)
(The twenty-third method:
One should grind mercury processed for a day with the milky sap of *snuhī*; in its absence, one should grind that mercury with the juices of *amlavallī* and an equal amount of sulphur. (Āk 1.23.105)
Having placed it in a crucible, the wise one should cook it as before;
this mercury, once dead, shall become a remover of all diseases. (Āk 1.23.106)
(The twenty-fourth method: One should grind *guñjā* fruit, equal in quantity to mercury, together with honey, borax, and lac, combined with the juice of *bhṛṅga* leaves, for one day. (Āk 1.23.107)
Covered in a crucible made of diamond, one should heat it with a gentle fire;
this mercury, which is an elixir and an aphrodisiac, becomes as white as the moon. (Āk 1.23.108)
(The twenty-fifth variety:
Equal amounts of pure *gandharasa* with the juices of *kīṭamāriṇikā*, or with those of *ajamārī* and *himārī*, or with the juice of white *aṅkola*. (Āk 1.23.109)
Then, having placed it in an earthen crucible, one should grind it for three days;
thereafter, [it should be heated] for one day in a fire of dried cow dung or for three days in a fire of chaff.
When cooked thereafter, the ash of the *sūta* (mercury) arises, which removes disease and old age.
(The twenty-sixth method) O Dear One, mercury purified through the process of causing the falling of copper and mica— Āk 1.23.111.
One should grind vajra-ash together with the juices of *haṃsapādī* and the seeds produced from divine herbs; then one should smear the interior of a vajra crucible with this. (Āk 1.23.112)
Having added the previous liquid to it and sealed it, one should then cook it for three days with a fire of chaff;
thereafter, having extracted it, one should add an equal amount of quicksilver.
Then, one should grind everything with the juices of *haṃsapādī* for three days; thereafter, one should cook it as before—this mercury will certainly turn into ash. (Āk 1.23.114)
The destroyer of old age, death, and disease, the bestower of all accomplishments, and auspicious—
(the twenty-seventh variety)—
one *karṣa* of perfumed mercury and eight *guñjā*s of gold. (Āk 1.23.115)
One should grind four *guñjā* of "dead-vajra" with the juices of *haṃsapadī* in a heated mortar; having placed it in a vajra-crucible, one should seal it. (Āk 1.23.116)
And having placed it in the earth-bearing machine (*bhūdharayantra*),
one should take that mercury again and grind it for three days in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*) with the juices of *haṃsapādī*.
One should cook it repeatedly in the *bhūdhara* furnace as before;
having thus performed a hundred *puṭas*, it will become a red-colored ash. (Āk 1.23.118)
It destroys old age, death, and poverty, and brings about the destruction of worldly existence.
(The twenty-eighth variety:
One part of pure mercury and one part of copper powder [should be combined]. (Āk 1.23.119)
One should grind that for a day with sour substances, wash it, and take the paste; then, equal parts of zinc ore and the paste [should be ground] with the juice of *cakramarda* leaves. (Āk 1.23.120)
One should grind everything for three days and place the entire mass in a crucible (golaka);
O Goddess of the Gods, it should then be cooked in a fire of husks for three days. Āk 1.23.121.
One should cook it day and night in a fire of dried cow-dung; the resulting ash becomes the *rasa*. (The twenty-ninth method:
Equal parts of mercury that has been made "mouthed" (*mukhīkṛta*), iron essence (*abhrasattva*), and gold—these three [are combined]. ĀK 1.23.122.
Having ground it with the juice of *raṃbhā* for one day until it becomes a paste as smooth as butter, one should then grind it with the seeds of divine herbs for three days. Āk 1.23.123.
One should cook it in a crucible and afterwards in a fire of dried cow dung; thus it becomes dead [mercury].
(The thirtieth method.
One part of well-digested mercury and an equal amount of vimalā should be [processed] with the juices of nirguṇḍī. Āk_1,23.124.
Having ground it for three days, one should place it inside a glass flask and cook it in a sand-bath apparatus; in four cycles, it will be reduced to ashes. (Āk 1.23.125)

(The thirty-first method: Equal parts of *tāpyasattva* (calamine essence) and sulphur, and mercury processed with the same amount [of these two], should be ground with *nirguṇḍikā* for one day; that ball (*golaka*) is then [further processed]. Āk 1.23.126.
Having made it enclosed within a diamond crucible (vajramūṣā), one should heat it in a *gaḍḍuyantra* furnace;
when cooked, it becomes red in color, and that mercury (*rasa*) destroys all diseases. (Āk 1.23.127)

(The characteristics of mercury ash: One should recognize from the mercury ash its indestructibility, its lack of residue, its stainlessness, its excellent state as ash, and its power to dissolve metals. (Āk 1.23.128)
(1. Gandhapiṣṭī;
first variety) Having powdered and purified the fragrance, [one should mix it] with the juice of the previously mentioned leaves.
One should likewise contemplate it sevenfold within the heat and with the menses of women.
Likewise, one should again rub the sulphur with human bile;
then, one *pala* of purified mercury should be placed in a shallow earthen dish and set in the sun.
Above that, having applied the stirred-up fragrance and rubbed it with the thumb, one should prepare the mercury;
it becomes a paste that bestows success in all rites. (Āk 1.23.131)
(The second method, *svarṇagandhapiṣṭī*): O Goddess, purified sulfur [is processed] with the juice of *tilaparṇī*.
One should grind it seven times, dry it, and then successively saturate it with the [decoction] while in the shade.
One should place one *pala* of purified mercury into the crucible;
then, one should place a gold *niṣka*-sized pellet into the crucible. (Āk 1.23.133)
There, O Śivā, one should place a small amount of menstrual blood, urine, and impurity into it, and then set that crucible in the middle of a sand-enclosed apparatus (*vālukāyantra*).
One should repeatedly add very small amounts of the previous fragrance until the scent of one karṣa has been digested by cooking over a mild fire. Āk_1,23.135.
Having removed it and allowed it to cool on one's own body, one should take out the golden sphere;
this divine gold-paste will grant all that is desired. (Āk 1.23.136)
(Third Method) One should saturate pure sulphur one hundred times with the juice of *markaṭī*;
then, having placed pure mercury in the shade, one should put it into a clay pot under the heat of the sun. Āk 1.23.137.
One should add a little bit of the previous fragrance and a little bit of *markaṭī* juice;
when the fragrance has been digested, liquid should be added—repeatedly adding fragrance and repeatedly adding liquid. (Āk 1.23.138)
When one-quarter of the portion has been digested and the fragrance becomes a paste, it becomes divine, fit for all rites, and difficult even for the gods to obtain. (Āk 1.23.139)
(Fourth Method) Having powdered pure fragrance, [one should treat it] three times with sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
three times with the acid of *jambīra* fruit, and three times with the juice of *haṃsapādī*. (Āk 1.23.140)
In this manner, one should wash the camphor seven times and then perfume it separately three times with the water of white *karṇikāra* flowers in the sun. (Āk 1.23.141)
One should smear two guñjas of camphor inside the yantra; there, one should throw in a niṣka and a half of powdered, perfumed [substance] that has been processed. Āk_1,23.142.
And above that, one should place a *pala* of mercury upon its back;
then an amount of camphor equal to the previous [mercury], and above that, one and a half *niṣkas*. (Āk 1.23.143)
Furthermore, having added sulphur and then cow’s urine, one should grind the root of the white mountain karṇikā with that paste. Āk_1,23.144.
Having covered it with that same earthen bowl, one should seal it and cook it gradually within a *jālikā* apparatus; thereafter, one should extract that divine [substance]. (Āk 1.23.145)
One should do this three times, and the fragrant paste will certainly be produced. (The fifth method:
One should place one *pala* of pure mercury into the middle of a mortar smeared with oil. (Āk 1,23.146)
One should take one *karṣa* of purified mercury and add the juice of *devadālī*;
by rubbing it with the fingers in the intense heat of the sun, it will become a paste. (Āk 1.23.147)
(Sixth Method) One should place one *pala* of mercury and half a *karṣa* of sulfur into a copper mortar; one should cook it over a mild fire for one *yāma*, stirring it with the thumb. (Āk 1.23.148)
Divine and auspicious, this fragrant powder accomplishes all rites.
(The Stilling of Powders) I shall now describe the stilling of powders derived from bitter *kośātakī*. (Āk 1.23.149)

Having ground the seed of the *caṇḍālinī* bulb together with an equal amount of milk produced from the breasts of a beloved woman, one should firmly apply that paste to a thickness of one finger-breadth.
Whether in the *vandhyā* tuber, or the *kṣīra* tuber, or in the *sūraṇa* tuber, or in the *vajra* tuber, or in the *kuḍuhuñja* tuber; Āk_1,23.151.
One should place that flour paste [into the vessel] and seal its opening with its own marrow;
having smeared that bulbous root (*kanda*) with clay, one should bake it in a *bhūdharayantra*. (Āk 1.23.152)
Day and night, one should turn [the vessel] up and down over a fire of dried cow-dung;
this is the prescribed method of cooking so that the bulbous root is not burnt. Āk 1.23.153.
Then, O Dear One, having brought together the paste (*piṣṭī*), it shall become solidified (*stambhitā*).
(The digestion of the paste [2])—O Śivā, the digestion of the solidified pastes will now be described. (Āk 1.23.154)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should place sulphur equal in weight to the powder [of mercury] inside a metal bellows;
and above it, O Mistress of the Gods, one should place the solidified sulphur-powder.
Above that, one should add powdered sulphur equal in weight to the flour;
having sealed it, one should cook and digest it gradually in a *bhūdhara* yantra.
Furthermore, O beloved, one should repeatedly apply the fragrance in this way for a hundredfold duration;
once the fragrance has been processed for a hundredfold time, one should extract the paste from the apparatus.

There shall be the digestion (*jāraṇa*) and coloring (*rañjana*) of all the medicinal pastes (*gandhapiṣṭī*). [This is] the killing (*māraṇa*) of the paste. I shall now explain the procedure for killing the digested pastes. (Āk 1.23.158)
Having cast the processed *gandhapiṣṭikā* into a heated mortar and ground it with the juices of divine herbs for a day, one should form it into a pill (*golaka*). (Āk 1.23.159)

Having ground the seeds of divine herbs with the fresh juices produced from those same divine herbs, one should coat the previously prepared ball inside a diamond crucible (*vajramūṣā*). (Āk 1.23.160)
Having cast [the substance] and sealed the mouth of the crucible, one should cook it in a *bhūdharayantra* for one day, O Dear One, while causing it to move up and down. (Āk 1.23.161)
Having gathered [the ingredients] as before, one should rub them with the previous waters;
O Goddess, one should enclose them in a *puṭa* as before, ten times in this sequence.

Without doubt, O Bhairavī, the powder of fragrant substances (gandhapiṣṭi) accomplishes all tasks; from the sequence of the preparation of this fragrant powder, the juices and ashes are produced. (Āk 1.23.163)
These are the foremost among all operations, especially in the operation of binding mercury (the first method).
(The Vaikrānta-bond:
O Bhairavī, listen now as I shall describe the methods for binding mercury. Āk_1,23.164.
One should place ten *niṣkas* of purified mercury into a mortar, and add one *niṣka* of pure sulfur, adding it very gradually. (Āk 1.23.165)
One should pound and rub it with a stone until it becomes a paste after the duration of a *yāma*;
[this should be done] either in *kṣīrakanda*, or in *vandhyākanda*, or in that which is born from *kuḍuhuñja*. (Āk 1.23.166)
When the bulb has been cooked and is auspicious, the wise man should place a paste of sulphur inside it; he should then place half a niṣka of vaikrānta ash at the top and bottom.
Having blocked the mouth with the marrow of that tuber and having smeared the exterior with a layer of clay one finger-breadth thick, he should then let it dry completely on all sides. Āk 1.23.168.
One should cook it eight times in a *bhūdhara* yantra using a *kaukkuṭa* puṭa over a fire of dried cow dung; furthermore, O Dear One, one should repeatedly turn [the vessel] upside down.
One should repeatedly turn it downwards and upwards;
having practiced this for one day, one should thereafter bake it with four measures of dried cow-dung.
Mercury becomes bound, resembling the seed of a ripe pomegranate; it is known as "bound by vaikrānta," and when powdered, it acts as a "yogavāhaka" (a carrier of medicinal properties). Āk 1.23.171.
(The second method:
the binding of fragrance.
Then, having bound that aforementioned fragrant paste in a cloth, place it within a sealed vessel.
Having placed a packet made of iron, with equal amounts of sulfur above and below, [one should proceed].
Having properly closed the crucible, one should cook it in the *bhūdhara* apparatus; and in this manner, one should do so repeatedly until the odor has completely vanished. (Āk 1.23.173)
O Maheśvarī, the mercury possessing these six qualities should thus be subjected to *jāraṇā*;
in this way, this mercury bound with sulfur removes all diseases. (Āk 1.23.174)
(The third type:
the *gandhakabandha*):
It is sixteen finger-breadths in length and as wide as a citron fruit.
A baked crucible, more firmly constructed, [is placed] in the middle of a sand-vessel (*vālukāyantra*).
One should make it submerged three-quarters of the way and situated with one-quarter of its height remaining outside;
into that, O Goddess of the Gods, one should cast one *pala* of mercury processed with fragrant substances.
Then, in the upper part of the crucible, one should place two palas of purified sulfur;
having properly sealed its mouth, one should heat it with a gentle fire. (Āk 1.23.177)

One should cook it until it is smokeless; once the smoke has ceased, it should be filled again with the juice of *kākamācī*. When that juice has been digested [absorbed], [the vessel should be removed]. (Āk 1.23.178)
O beloved, it should be filled again with the juice of *nāgavallī* (betel leaf), and then filled with the juices of *unmattaka*; one should cook it slowly over a mild fire. Āk 1.23.179.
Sulfur is digested by means of juices beginning with *kākamācī* and ending with *dhattūra*;
by cooking it in this manner, mercury becomes bound. Āk 1.23.180.
This is known by the name *Gandhakabaddha*; one should employ it in all yogic preparations.
(The fourth method: the binding of gold with sulphur.
First, the wise practitioner should prepare a paste of sulphur as previously described. Āk_1,23.181.
One and a half parts of pure gold should be combined with seven and a half parts of lead;
after being rubbed together with sour gruel for a watch (yāma), this is known as *hemapiṣṭikā*.
Having encased the fragrant powder with a coating of gold powder on the outside, it should be placed within an iron casket shaped like breasts and bound with cloth. (Āk 1.23.183)

Having prepared that paste and applied it, the wise one should place sulfur both above and below the paste; equal in amount to all [the other ingredients], he should then seal the joint with sour liquids and salts. (Āk 1.23.184)
When the mountain-press has been repeatedly exhausted again and again, one should add six times the amount of sulfur; thereafter, one should slowly remove the cloth. (Āk 1.23.185)
One should repeatedly digest an equal portion of sulfur very slowly;
however, one must not exhaust the sulfur entirely, for if it is so done, there will be a loss of the mercury.
When it has thus been processed a hundredfold, one should collect the fragrant paste; one should place the paste into a casket of gold of equal weight. Āk 1.23.187.
Having ground glass with the juices of *kanyā*, one should smear it on the outside to the depth of a finger;
then, having smeared it with borax, one should subsequently apply clay and salt in succession.
Each application of the coating should be made one finger-breadth in thickness; after each application has dried, it should be placed in a crucible-furnace and blown [with a bellows]. Āk 1.23.189.
By means of a sharp, curved tube and an intense fire, the strike occurs;
the pill (khoṭa) becomes like the rising sun, a divine elixir.

This is the "Gandhahāṭakabandha" (the fifth type, the sulphur-bond), which destroys old age, disease, and poverty; or else, having bound that sulphur-paste in a cloth, one [uses] the sulphur. (Āk 1.23.191)
Having applied an equal amount [of mercury] and then firmly sealed it within a crucible made of iron,
one should roast it in a *bhūdhara* furnace until the sulfur is fully digested.
In this manner, it should be given again and again until the mercury has absorbed six times its weight of sulfur;
thus bound with sulfur, the mercury becomes a conqueror of all diseases. (Āk 1.23.193)

(The sixth method: *mūlikābandha*) One should grind mercury for one day with the juices extracted from the roots of *kārkoṭī*. Then, one should place that ground mercury into a ball made from the roots of *markaṭī*. (Āk 1.23.194)
Having sealed that mass in a diamond crucible, one should cook it with a fierce fire;
this becomes a bound *khoṭa*, auspicious and effective for all purposes. (Āk 1.23.195)
(The seventh method: *mūlikābandha*) Having ground the root of the *arka* plant with the milky sap of the sun (*ravikṣīra*), one should smear it inside a crucible (*mūṣā*).
Having placed the colored mercury (*rañjitasūta*) within it, one should seal it and then close it up. (Āk 1.23.196)
One should confine it within a clay casket and then within an iron casket;
subsequently, one should cook it in a gajapuṭa fire, and the mercury will attain fixation (bandha).
(Eighth type: *mūlikābandha*) One should grind mercury with the juices of *jalakumbhī* for three days;
having fashioned a crucible from the leaves of *jalakumbhī*, one should place the juice therein. (Āk 1.23.198)
Having sealed it in a vajra-musha crucible and dried it in the shade, one should roast it gently with *chagaṇa* cakes, increasing the number by one each time, for thirty cycles. Āk 1.23.199.
Then it should be placed in a "gaja-puṭa" [furnace]; thus the mercury becomes properly bound.
(The ninth method: binding with roots.
Pure mercury should be rubbed for one day with the juices of Ekavīrā. Āk_1,23.200.
One should smear a vajra-mūṣā crucible with the paste of the root of *ekavīrā*;
having placed the aforementioned mercury (*rasa*) inside it, when it is heated, the mercury becomes bound. Āk 1,23.201.

(Tenth Type: Root-Binding) Mercury should be rubbed for three days with the juices extracted from reddish-white milk-tubers mixed with breast milk, and for another three days with the juices of *vajrakanda*. (Āk 1,23.202)
One should smear a vajra-mūṣā crucible with a paste of *kṣīrakanda*; having placed the previously prepared mercury therein, when it is heated, the mercury becomes bound. (Āk 1.23.203)
(Eleventh type: *Mūlikābandha*) Having ground the root and fruit of the *arka* plant, one should smear the crucible (*mūṣā*) with it;
into the middle of that, one should place a crucible fashioned from the root of the *puṅkhā* plant. (Āk 1.23.204)

Having placed the *sūtaka* (mercury) in the middle of that and having filled it with juices produced from the base of the arrow-shaft (*puṅkhā*), one should firmly seal the mouth of the crucible (*mūṣā*). Āk 1,23.205.
One should thus place the blindfolded crucible in the middle of a sealed pair (saṃpuṭa), and then carefully coat it with salt and likewise with clay. Āk 1.23.206.
Then, by means of the *puṭa* process, that mercury attains fixation (*bandha*) with just two grains of black mustard, along with the juice of *citraka* and rock salt. (Āk 1.23.207)

Pounded into a powder and consumed in the morning, it destroys all diseases. (The twelfth method: the binding of the root. One should grind mercury for one *yāma* with the water from the roots of the *kapittha* tree. (Āk 1,23.208)
One should seal the mercury-vessel within another blind vessel; then one should blow upon the vessel until it becomes like vermilion. Āk 1.23.209.
When this is done, this lord of mercury is bound; there is no doubt about this.
For this is proclaimed as the binding of the lord of mercury by means of a root-plant (*mūlikā*). Āk 1,23.210.
Thus these Sūtras have been killed, rendered unconscious, and brought under bondage;
each has been applied there through practices that carry the yoga. (Āk 1.23.211)
(The Method of Saturating the Mercury;
First Type) Now, the method for saturating pure mercury is described.
One should grind the mercury with meghanāda, vacā, hiṅgu, and garlic. Āk 1.23.212.
Having ground that ball for one day, one should wrap its exterior with asafoetida;
then, placed within a salt-vessel, one should cook it for one day over a fierce fire.
Having taken it up with the upper end, one should bind it firmly with a cloth;
having applied an equal amount of sulphur above and below, one should cook it over the fire of Soma.
When it has been digested, the fragrance should be added again, six times in equal amounts.
Once the sulphur has been digested sixfold, the medicine becomes a "mūrchita" compound that destroys diseases. (Āk 1.23.215)
(Second method:
One part each of purified sulphur, the essence of soot, and pure mercury should be ground together in a mortar for one *yāma* and placed in a glass vessel. Āk 1.23.216.
Having sealed it until the end of twelve yāmas, one should cook it in a sand-bath apparatus;
once it has cooled to its own temperature, one should break it open and discard the sulphur situated at the top. (Āk 1.23.217)
Having taken the mercury situated below, one should employ it in all formulations.
(The third method:
One should likewise mix purified mercury with an equal amount of sulfur and half as much rock salt. Āk 1.23.218.
One should grind it with the juices of white *jayantī* for three days;
having formed a ball and dried it thoroughly, one should seal it inside a crucible. (Āk 1.23.219)
Having dried it, one should blow upon it slightly and then cast it into very hot water;
having extracted the essence from that, it should be processed with the juice of the three tubers.

One should employ [this] in all diseases, or one should heat it in a *bhūdhara* [furnace] or cook it. (The fourth method: Half a part of mercury and one part of sulfur should be rubbed together with clarified butter to form a ball (*golaka*). (Āk 1,23.221)
Having prepared that, one should bind it in a cloth and cook it in a swinging-vessel apparatus (*ḍolāyantra*) for one watch (*yāma*) in cow urine, and for three days in human urine. (Āk 1.23.222)
One should dry it again by wrapping it in cloths and binding it firmly with clay;
once dried, having sealed it in a crucible, one should then cook it with a fire of chaff.
Having turned the upper part downward and the lower part upward, and so forth by means of such reversals, one should apply fomentation for three days. (Āk 1.23.224)
Afterward, having extracted that *sūta* which carries the yoga and removes disease, [one should take] the feces of a newborn infant and the seed of the *pālāśa* tree. (Āk 1.23.225)
One should grind together the blood of a Caṇḍālī woman, mercury, one-quarter part of mercury,
and ṭaṅkaṇa with the juices of jayantī for one day to form a pill (golaka).
Then, one should smear a copper casket with a paste of *sahadevī*;
having placed a ball (*golaka*) inside it, one should gently heat it for two watches (*yāma*). (Āk 1.23.227)
Then, having extracted it again from the middle of the sand-trap, one should smear the exterior with *citraka*, *sahadevī*, and sulfur. (Āk 1.23.228)

One should bind the [substance] in a crucible (sampuṭa) with cloth, coat it with clay, and let it dry; having sealed it in another crucible, one should bring forth the crucible once it has been heated. Āk 1,23.229.

The great mercury (*mahārasa*), acting as a vehicle (*yogavāha*), removes diseases when reduced to a fine powder; it should be prepared in a sealed crucible (*sampuṭa*) equal in weight to the mercury itself, according to the procedure seen in the scriptures. (Āk 1.23.230)
(Fifth Method) Mercury mixed with one part of fragrant substances should be rubbed for a day with the juices of *Dhattūra*.
It should then be placed in an *andhamūṣā* crucible and heated in a *bhūdharayantra* for a day until it becomes liquefied (*mūrchita*). Āk 1.23.231.
(Sixth Method) Having prepared a crucible six finger-breadths deep, well-fired, made of clay, and firm,
one should then smear the interior of the crucible with the roots of the *vartulapattra* plant. (Āk 1.23.232)
Having cast the *sūtaka* into the middle of that [mixture], one should fill the crucible with those liquids;
having sealed it, one should cook it in a *vālukāyantra* over a lamp-fire on the hearth. (Āk 1.23.233)
At the end of seven days, having extracted it, one should employ that [elixir] which removes old age. (The seventh method:
One should grind the juice thickly with *kuraṇḍaka* juices in the heat of the sun. (Āk 1.23.234)
One should rub [the substance] with the big toe using leaves from the *latākarañja* plant for one day; once it is thoroughly saturated, it may be employed in all medicinal formulations. (Āk 1.23.235)
(Eighth variety:

One should grind equal parts of ferrous sulfate (kāsīsa), rock salt (saindhava), and mercury (sūta). In the absence of ferrous sulfate, blue vitriol (phullatūrikā) should be used instead. (Āk 1.23.236)
One should add it little by little into the mortar; these three should be combined together so that each amounts to exactly one hundred *niṣkas*, neither less nor more at any time. Āk 1,23.237.
One should cook it for a day with a fierce fire using the *sthālīsampuṭa* apparatus;
then, having become bright and fixed at the top, one should extract the auspicious, sublimated substance. (Āk 1.23.238)
(Ninth Method) Now, another procedure for purified mercury that has been made to coagulate: dead gold equal in weight to the mercury, and sulphur equal to the weight of both. Āk 1.23.239.
It should be rubbed with the milky sap of the sun (ravikṣīra) for one day and then sealed in a *bhūdhara* crucible;
in a single day, the mercury becomes perfected as the *hairaṇyagarbhaka*.
Whether white, red, or black in color, that mercury which is heavy and returns to life after having been fainted is called *mūrchita*. (Āk 1.23.241)
(The Root-Bonds): Śrī Bhairavī said:
"O Lord, what kind of auspicious herb is it that causes the mercury to become solidified?"
By what means is ash produced, by what is the elixir (sūta), and by what is the binding of the pill (khoṭa)? Āk 1.23.242.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Bhairavī, to the secret of the binding of mercury according to its true nature;
it is not known even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods, O goddess worshipped by the celestials.
(The Ritual Manual for the Root of the Night-Walker):
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, there is a rākṣasa named Prayāga.
O lady of beautiful hips, by sitting upon his seat, a newborn child may be bound [to safety] in an instant. Āk 1.23.244.
The best of practitioners should take the leaves of the night-stalker;
then, O Goddess, they are pressed, and an excellent juice is produced. (Āk 1.23.245)
Having thoroughly rubbed the mercury with that [substance] for three days, the alchemist should quickly bind the *āroṭa* and digest the *gagana* (mica) therein. (Āk 1.23.246)
One should then process the sulphur with that very leaf-juice;
having been impregnated with it seven times, it is then combined together with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa).
O Goddess, when the mechanical device is possessed by the Vidyadhara, one should cause the sky to dissolve therein;
O Queen of the Gods, within a single month, it dissolves completely and perfectly. (Āk 1.23.248)
When the mercury has been properly digested in the sky, it becomes a "hundred-piercer" (*śatavedhī*).
Then, O Goddess, one should saturate sulfur with the juice of *niśācara* (night-walker). ĀK 1.23.249.
One should steep it seven times with the juice of the two-footed plant;
by applying a leaf-coating of *tāra* (silver), the best gold is obtained in half-and-half increments. Āk 1.23.250.
When this has been thoroughly digested in the sulphur, the mercury becomes a hundred-fold penetrator (śatavedhī).
The mineral calamine (tālaka) should then be processed seven times with the juices of night-roaming plants (niśācara). Āk 1.23.251.
By that very [process], one should kill vaṅga; one should extract nāga from tāra. One should digest that tāra with mercury (sūta); that mercury shall become bound (bandhita). (Āk 1.23.252)
One should cause the piercing with the wire to be performed at the sixty-fourth part;
that portion becomes excellent, bestowing virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation. (Āk 1.23.253)
One should have the flowers of the night-stalker (niśācara) ground into a fine powder; ten palas of this powder should then be saturated with the juices of the emblic myrobalan (dhātrī). Āk 1.23.254.
Having mixed it with ghee and honey, one should place it in a new vessel;
O Goddess of the Suras, it should be deposited in a heap of grain for three times seven days.
By merely consuming that, one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair;
one should then lick the fine powder of bark mixed with honey. (Āk 1.23.256)
O Dear One, by practicing this for half a month, there will be a reversal of the process;
through his urine and excrement, base metal becomes gold. (Āk 1.23.257)
By practicing for only one month, mercury becomes gold;
that fruit-oil should be extracted using the apparatus known as *pātāla*. (Mercury:: *paṭṭabandha*) Āk 1,23.258.
O Goddess of the gods, with that oil the wise one should cause the mercury to contract; at that very moment, O Goddess, the great essence becomes fixed in its seal (pāṭabandha). Āk 1,23.259.
O fair-faced one, a bracelet and a ring should be fashioned from mercury;
by means of that, the most wonderful "death through contraction" (saṃkocamaraṇa) should be performed.
(The Ritual Manual for the Woman-Lord) Furthermore, I shall explain another very rare method for the binding of mercury:
that medicinal herb which is the mother of the three worlds is the Woman-Lord (Aṅganāyikā). (Āk 1.23.261)
Mercury remains bound by mere contact with it;
the mercury [of the base metal] becomes [mercury] when this [base metal] has been rubbed for seven days with the juices of the great medicinal herbs.
O lady of excellent complexion, by means of a hundredth-part penetration (*vedha*) through churning that mercury for twenty-one days, one produces divine gold.
The mercury that pierces a target at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas] directly penetrates the eight metals;
O Goddess of the Gods, within twenty-one days it penetrates ten million. (Āk 1.23.264)
And in the fourth week, the mercury becomes "piercing through ten million" (koṭivedhī) by means of sweating,
heating, and rubbing, together with the juice of the great medicinal herb.
He whose range of movement is unimpeded bestows the *siddhi* of the *khecarī*;
he may enjoy a thousand women within the span of a single day. (Āk 1.23.266)
For he, with his shadow vanished and himself invisible, shall wander through the three worlds;
by the very juice of the great medicinal herb (mahauṣadhī), the restoration of the dead shall come to pass. Āk 1.23.267.
By this, O beloved, one should cause the vital essence (sūta) to be slain; reduce it to five states.
For the deceased [substance], one should administer snuff and massage the hands and feet. (Āk 1.23.268)
O fair-faced one, the life-force of even a dead man may enter it;
(this is the Narasāra-kalpa). Furthermore, I shall explain another method for the binding of mercury, which is very difficult to obtain. (Āk_1,23.269)
By the touch of human essence (*narasāra*), the mercury (*sūtaka*) is bound in an instant;
having added the juice of human essence to the mercury along with the dust of *dvipadī*, [the binding occurs]. (Āk 1.23.270)
At the end of the day, it undergoes binding and dyes all metals;
one should then saturate realgar with the essence of *narasāra*. (Āk 1.23.271)
If it grows without fragrance, it kills a serpent; however, when obstructed by the dust of a two-footed creature, the serpent shall be neutralized. (Āk 1.23.272)

O Goddess, when the mercury has been digested with the essence of Narasāra for six times the duration of the snake (six months), it becomes a "ten-million-penetration" (*koṭivedhī*) elixir, whether applied to silver or copper. Āk 1.23.273.
Having been processed seven times separately with the essence of human marrow and breast milk, one should administer a dose of that essence in the apparatus called Vidyādhara. (Āk 1.23.274)
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, the sky is digested in the mouthless one, O Mistress, by the essence of the best of men and by the essence of the female insect. Āk 1.23.275.
O Goddess, one may liquefy the sky, sharp iron, and serpents by means of the essence of human marrow, O Mistress, and by the essence of Hanumatī. (Āk 1.23.276)

O beloved, by means of the *niṣeka* [infusion] of the essence of human marrow (*narasāra*), along with *mañjiṣṭhā* and red sandalwood, divine gold is produced from the sun-like [substance]. (Āk 1.23.277)
O Goddess, one should sprinkle a serpent with the juices of the madayantī plant;
by being sprinkled seven times, it becomes divine gold at that very moment. (Āk 1.23.278)
Gold increased by one-eighth part is the medicinal substance for the work of gold;
vermillion should be infused seven times in the juice of *narasāra*. (Āk 1.23.279)
By that very [means], one should cause the fierce [substance] to be destroyed; it shall attain the state of being reduced to ashes.
That ash, when mixed with three times its quantity of powdered copper, will flow out by means of that. (Āk 1.23.280)
That silver, resembling gold when combined with one-eighth part of gold, or silver with an equal part of gold, becomes a two-colored alloy known as *patita*. (Āk 1.23.281)
The *rasaka* should be processed seven times with the juice of human marrow;
likewise, the lord of mercury (*rasendra*) should be processed seven times with that very same juice of human marrow.
One should grind that mercury and the mineral salt (rasaka), as well as sharp iron (tīkṣṇaloha) and lead (pannaga), together with the essence of human marrow (narasārarasa). Āk 1.23.283.
At that very moment, [the mercury] becomes bound by the *rasaka* and the *rasa*.
Likewise, one should color sharp lead and copper with the *rasaka*. (Āk 1.23.284)

By force, that gold is produced, possessing the luster of a pumpkin flower. (The *Kaṅkālakhecarīkalpa*) Furthermore, I shall explain another method for the binding of mercury, which is very difficult to obtain. (Āk 1,23.285)
O Supreme Goddess, there is a medicinal herb named Kaṅkālakhecarī; its oil should be collected together with the first Khecarī. Āk 1,23.286.
One should place it for one day in a vessel made of gold;
when the second day arrives, one should strike it with a diamond gem.
One should heat that [substance] in fire until it is well-heated and possesses a blazing luster.
(The Ritual of the Mantra-Lion-Throne) O Dear One, a certain medicinal herb belonging to the class of shrubs or creepers should be taken along with its seed-syllable. Āk 1.23.288.
The third goddess is named Mantrasiṃhāsanī Khecarī; one should collect that oil from the Pātālayantra into a copper vessel. Āk 1.23.289.
One should pour the essence of Khecarī into the midst of that oil, and place it within the Medinīyantra, O fair-faced one. (Āk 1.23.290)
O Goddess, having placed that [substance] along with the sky, earth, water, and mercury into the *pūrvauṣadhī* for one month, then, through churning, form a ball (*golaka*). (Āk 1.23.291)
Having tied it in a pouch, O Dear One, one should cause the mercury to digest the sky; when the sky has been fully digested, the bound mercury remains stable. (Āk 1.23.292)
Being blown upon with the blast of a bellows, it is not destroyed;
rather, the form of that which is fully digested becomes like crow-dung. (Āk 1.23.293)

When the sky has doubled and the [mercury] is digested, one should collect the eight metals. (The *Īrindirīkalpa*) Now I shall further proclaim another method for the binding of mercury, which is very difficult to obtain. (Āk 1,23.294)
The medicinal herb Irindirī, which has arisen from the body of Śiva, can digest sulphur; it can also digest orpiment. (Āk 1.23.295)
It indeed dissolves gold and it binds the lord of mercury;
it melts coral and likewise it dissolves the sky (mica).
She can cause even a vajra to be destroyed and she can destroy all sentient beings; she can dissolve all metals and she can also dissolve sentient beings. (Āk 1.23.297)
O fair-faced one, having placed it in cow-horn with *irindirīra* resin, it should be deposited in a heap of grain; thus the mercury remains in a solid state. (Āk 1.23.298)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, when the mercury has been digested in equal amounts of gold using the juice of a divine herb, it will transmute ten koṭis [of gold]. (Āk 1.23.299)
In the fifth [stage], one pierces through ten million times a hundred thousand; in the sixth, one pierces by touch;
in the seventh, one becomes a piercer by means of incense; and in the eighth, by mere looking. (Āk 1.23.300)
In the ninth [stage], one becomes a piercer of sound; beyond this, it does not exist.
Fools, deluded and devoid of the Kula-herbs, wander about like beasts. (Āk 1.23.301)
Furthermore, the accomplishment of ordinary grasses, herbs, and juices never arises;
therefore, with every effort, one must come to know the Kula-herb. (Āk 1.23.302)
The sixty-four divine medicinal herbs are established within the Kula;
yet the deluded do not know them, being infatuated by the delusion of Śiva. (Āk 1.23.303)
Non-divine grasses and herbs grow in mountain caves;
mercury is never bound by the essence of such grasses and herbs. (Āk 1.23.304)
One who is devoid of the family-herb (kulauṣadhi) would certainly not remain undecaying;
for those who are bereft of the family-herb cause even the sky to move. (Āk 1.23.305)
But that mercury, O lady of excellent hips, does not remain in the midst of fire;
it neither forms a solid mass (khoṭa), nor ash, nor indeed does it become a stable substance. Āk 1.23.306.
Certain substances undergo transformation and do not remain as they were;
gold does not remain the same when subjected to heating, or during the processes of filing, melting, rubbing, or cutting. (Āk 1.23.307)
O Dear One, that mercury does not undergo piercing (vedha) beyond a hundred [times] until it has been processed for one year; yet even tin, once so treated, becomes gold. Āk 1.23.308.
"Therefore, O Beloved, one should never give [it] for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa.
Śrī Bhairavī said:
"The mercury has become lifeless; how can it bestow life? (Āk 1.23.309)
"But how does Śaṅkara, who is himself lifeless, come to life by means of that which is lifeless?
Śrī Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, when the mercury (rasendra) has been rubbed with a divine herb... (Āk 1.23.310).
Then, O Pārvatī, the mercury becomes free from *kālikā*;
the mercury free from *kālikā* takes away the time of another. (Āk 1.23.311)
It pacifies the impurities of even the eight metals in an instant.
Who would describe as dead the mercury that has entered into a great swoon? Āk 1,23.312.
By the very essence of divine herbs, he whose consciousness was lost is restored;
