the mercury, composed of the five elements, remains as Sadāśiva himself. (Āk 1.23.313)
(The Kṣmāpālakalpa:
Furthermore, O Goddess, I shall explain another method for the binding of mercury;
with this [mercury], one may take away diamond and likewise gold by means of Kṣmāpāla. Āk_1,23.314.
One should bind together vajra-ash and gold-ash;
[this refers to] other *kulamūlika* rituals.
Having processed it in the juice of a night-stalker (*niśācara*), one should cause it to digest by means of human life-force. (Āk 1.23.315)
O auspicious lady, one should kill that *sūta* with the divine *jāgarī* herb;
he by whom that essence is consumed becomes Sadāśiva himself. (Āk 1.23.316)
By consuming a single *tolaka* of it, a person becomes capable of the "touch-transmutation" (*sparśavedhī*);
by the perspiration of his body, the eight metals are turned into gold.
That best of practitioners shall live for a hundred thousand years; moreover, from the sweat of his body, the king of essences (rasarāja) is bound [as a pill]. Āk_1,23.318.
O Goddess, the Lord of Creatures, possessing dark splendor, binds the *sūtaka* (impurity) in an instant;
yet, through the touch of the *jāgarī* [flower] and by means of the protector of the earth, it is bound [and removed]. Āk 1.23.319.
O beloved, when the *gagana* (mercury) is processed with the juice of *turuvallī* and then subjected to digestion in a *vālukāyantra*, it instantly becomes a solidified mass (*khoṭa*). Āk 1,23.320.
Having combined one *māṣa* of molten iron ball with one *māṣa* of gold ball,
one should grind them together with lime juice for three days.
One should smear one *karṣa* of *nāgapattras* with a paste of mercury;
then one should wrap them with *vṛścikālī* and subsequently smear that lump [with it]. (Āk 1.23.322)
O Goddess, one should kill the serpent; it becomes like a *śakragopa* insect.
One should smear one *karṣa* of silver leaves with the killed serpent. (Āk 1.23.323)
One should smear *vṛścikālī* and then smear its leaf;
that mercury (*tāra*), O Goddess, dies, becoming like the reddish glow of vermilion. (Āk 1.23.324)
By means of that very same thousandth part, one should cause the piercing with mercury (śulbavedha) to be performed;
divine gold is produced, fit for the ornaments of the gods.
O Pārvatī, that which is rich in milk, possesses many fruits, and has knotted joints—known by the name Vartulapatrā—is recommended for the binding of mercury. (Āk 1.23.326)

Once, having placed the mercury in a closed crucible (mūkamūṣā) within a paste of *kanda*, one should blow upon it with the breath from the mouth; thus bound, it is recommended for consumption. Āk 1.23.327.
The bulb of *raktakañcukī* ground with breast milk, when applied to a crucible according to the previous method, effects the binding of mercury. Āk 1,23.328.
One should blow upon the seed of *vṛścikāpattrikā* combined with women’s milk, just as before, so that the alchemist may consume the mercury for the sake of eating it. (Āk 1.23.329)
Taking vajrakanda, one should place the juice in the middle;
one should apply the puṭa called gajendra seven times and bring it to a state of binding.
The wise man should consume that essence; within six months he shall become immortal.
Taking the bulb of lāṅgalī and likewise the bulb of karkoṭī—Āk 1.23.331.
Having placed the mercury in the middle of that [substance], one should heat it and then grind it again;
it dies when blown with a fierce fire—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.23.332)
One should seal the mercury contained within a parrot’s beak and then heat it;
this will act as a penetrator by the hundredth part and bring about the perfection of the body. (Āk 1.23.333)
One should place the juice of *haṃsapādī* and mercury inside the hollow of a dried tuber;
by applying the "gajendra-puṭa" firing method, it dies—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.23.334)
And he becomes a piercer of a thousand [targets]; of this there is no doubt.
Having taken the foot of a swan and the beak of a parrot, one should grind them into a juice. (Āk 1.23.335)
Having placed [the substance] in the belly of a *krauñca* bird, one should then apply three *puṭas*;
there is no doubt that it dies, and the great mercury becomes capable of piercing a *lakṣa*.
(The Simile of the Firefly) Listen, my dear, to the description of the divine herb known as *tṛṇajyotis* (firefly-plant).
It burns constantly at night, O Pārvatī, but it does not burn during the day. (Āk 1.23.337)
If its root is placed in a small amount [of water], it will instantly turn into blood;
by means of the juice and scent of that root combined with mica (abhra) ground with the sour juice of *mātuluṅga*, [the same occurs]. (Āk 1.23.338)
A copper leaf, when smeared [with this], becomes gold after three smeltings (*puṭa*);
O Goddess of the Gods, the king of mercury, combined with the powder of its root, [achieves this]. (Āk 1.23.339)
Abhraka rubbed in the juice of *mātuluṅga* flows [as a liquid] in an instant.
(The Ritual of Uccāṭā) Now, O Dear One, I shall explain Uccāṭā, which effects the binding of mercury. Āk_1,23.340 //
A single stalk would not even suffice for the insertion of her hairs;
at its tip there would be a flower resembling the beak of a parrot. (Āk 1.23.341)
O Goddess of gods, its leaves resemble the plumage of a parrot;
its bulb is shaped like a tortoise, and its milky sap is like vermilion. (Āk 1.23.342)
O Pārvatī, when water flows from beeswax, one should take that [wax] and pierce all metals, and they become gold. Āk 1.23.343.
One should grind mercury, orpiment, and blue vitriol with the juices of uccaṭā;
heated in the sun, the mercury dies through the power of this divine herb. (Āk 1.23.344)
O fair-faced one, one should pierce all metals with a one-hundred-thousandth part [of the essence];
it should be repeatedly processed until it arises with a brilliance equal to the sun. (Āk 1.23.345)
(The Ritual of Red Snuhī):
One should pierce mercury, the latex of red snuhī, realgar, sulphur, mica, cinnabar, and the metals with a thousandth part [of the following]. Āk 1.23.346.
Having taken the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant, one should coat it with the powder of *niśā*;
having formed it into a pill, one pierces the elephant with that very substance at that very moment. (Āk 1.23.347)
(The Analogy of the Land-Lotus) Now, therefore, hear the procedure for the divine herb *sthalapadminī*.
It resembles a lotus in its leaves and is likewise similar in its flowers. (Āk 1.23.348)
If it breaks, milk will flow; it is blood-colored and very beautiful.
Having stepped upon it with the left foot, one should gaze at the circle of the sky. (Āk 1.23.349)
And one should see there the circle of planets and constellations joined with the stars;
O Goddess, at a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas, that should be known as the terrestrial lotus-pond. Āk 1,23.350.
Taking its five parts, combined with Haragaurī, joined with realgar and yellow orpiment, and mixed with honey; Āk_1,23.351.
One should grind it for seven nights and then use it to transmute copper;
O Goddess of the Gods, when pierced by even a thousandth part of it, it becomes gold. (Āk 1.23.352)

O Dear One, having taken its five limbs according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should cause the king of elixirs (sūtarāja) to circulate; then, having placed it in a silent crucible (mūkamūṣā), one should blow upon it.
It dies among the mice through contraction; of this there is no doubt.
With that very [substance], one should pierce all metals in a thousandth part. (Āk 1.23.354)
(The Ritual of Citraka): I shall now briefly explain the secret of Citraka.
Citraka is to be known as threefold: black, red, and *rasāyana*. (Āk 1.23.355)
White [mud] pacifies diseases; it is classified as superior, middling, or inferior.
A wise person should not extract black, red, or white [mud] during the winter season.
O Goddess, having uprooted black *citraka*, if it is not smelled by cows, one should throw it into milk;
the milk will turn black in an instant. (Āk 1.23.357)
One should grind mercury together with the powder of its five parts and blow it in a mūka-mūṣā crucible; it becomes a solid bolus (khoṭa) at that very moment. Āk 1,23.358.
Having put on red garments and being adorned with red garlands and unguents, one should [perform the rite] on the fifth day of the dark fortnight with red garlands and cooked rice. Āk 1.23.359.
O Great Goddess, having offered the oblation, one should extract red *citraka*;
with three doses of the powder of red *citraka*, one should drink [it] along with tin. (Āk 1.23.360)
Completely freed from all defects, it attains stability at that very moment;
its root is mercury, copper, and the sprinkling of *kuṅkuṇī* oil. (Āk 1.23.361)
By repeating this twenty-one times,
the copper will become pure when it has been smeared with the oil of red *citraka* and *bhallātaka*, and then subjected to the *puṭa* process.
O Goddess of gods, when combined with the leaf of *candrārka*,
the root-stalk (*kanda*) of *nāginī*, mercury (*sūtendra*), and red *citrasaṃyuta*, it becomes divine gold.
Through the application of leaf-paste and counter-infusions (*pratīvāpa*), even moonstone and sunstone become gold.
(The *Jyotiṣmatī* Oil Formula) Listen, O Pārvatī, as I shall describe the procedure for *jyotiṣmatī* oil. Āk 1,23.364.
There is a creeper named Jyotiṣmatī which resembles gold;
it is abundant with spreading vines, auspicious, and bears fruits of golden hue. (Āk 1.23.365)
In the first fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, having taken this supreme seed and having boiled it like sesame seeds, [one should apply it] either with the hands or with the feet.
Having taken its oil, one should place it in a copper jar;
one should then bury the jar in the ground and [heat it] gradually with a fire of husks from above. (Āk 1.23.367)
When six months have passed, that vessel shall become gold;
having made copper equal to gold, it should be mixed with oil and honey. (Āk 1.23.368)
By sprinkling it with this counter-application, that gold becomes equal to copper;
likewise, it may achieve a hundredfold penetration (*śatavedhī*). This is the unsurpassed jewel of knowledge. (Āk 1.23.369)
(The Chapter on Dagdharuhākalpa:
O beloved, I shall now describe the *dagdharuhā*, which binds mercury;
it should be known as the "touch-herb" (*sparśauṣadhī*), the accomplisher of all desires and aims. (Āk 1.23.370)
O Great Goddess, though that divine great herb is constantly severed and burnt by fire, it sprouts again in an instant once it has been consumed. Āk 1,23.371.
Her flower arises as red, yellow, white, or black; one should observe its well-formed leaves to be like those of the chickpea plant. Āk 1.23.372.
She is established on the bank of the Gomatī, at Gaṅgā, and on Mount Arbuda;
she is seen in the forest regions to the south of Ujjayinī.
The wise one, having combined its divine resin, which is marked with black streaks, with betel leaf, should have a pill prepared. (Āk 1.23.374)
Having pierced a thousand [times] all the molten metals within the midst of fire, it instantly transforms them into gold. (Āk 1.23.375)
In the same way, mercury dies when combined with *kānta* iron and gold.
(The Ritual of the Bitter Gourd) O Goddess, the bitter gourd (*kaṭutuṃbī*) is well-known; now hear of this divine herb. Āk 1,23.376.
Having collected its seeds, one should reduce them to a fine powder;
it should then be saturated twenty-one times with the juice of the *dhātrī* (myrobalan).
Having cast that very seed, combined with milk and *viśvabheṣaja*, into the apparatus, one should collect the oil and form it into a solid mass. (Āk 1.23.378)

One should cause the mercury to faint and then rub it with *cakramarda*; (this is the *lohadaṇḍakalpa*). It should be combined with cow-bile, peacock-bile, potassium carbonate (*kāṅkṣī*), and iron sulfate (*kāsīsa*). (Āk 1.23.379)
These [substances] are equal in weight to mercury, and their impurity (sūtaka) is the same for all;
they should be placed inside a ram's horn continuously for one month. (Āk 1.23.380)
One should pierce all metals with an iron rod;
likewise, sulphur should be processed twenty-one times with an iron rod.
It should be combined with iron ore itself and mixed with the juice of *jambīra*; together with its seed and mercury, it should be placed inside a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*). Āk 1.23.382.
One month spent underground indeed transforms silver into gold;
[using] one part of a leaf and five parts of silver. (Āk 1.23.383)
One should add one part of seed to five parts of thread;
these shall constitute twelve parts, all of which one should place upon the ground.
One should cause the infusion of this site to be performed with a fine staff;
at the end of twenty-five days, the finest gold is produced. (Āk 1.23.385)
(The Ritual of the Milk-Bulb) I shall now describe the procedure for the milk-bulb (*kṣīrakanda*), which likewise brings about all accomplishments.
Among its four colors, the red bulb is most highly recommended. (Āk 1.23.386)
This [vessel] is broken and would leak milk that is blood-colored yet beautiful, adorned by the thundering of clouds. (Āk 1.23.387)

The binding of the king of elixirs with smooth leaves resembling those of the *snuhī* plant, which are uniform and possess a fine golden luster, brings all sentient beings under control. (Āk 1.23.388)
Having collected its milk, the wise one should extract the silver;
by heating it with a fierce fire, beautiful gold is produced. (Āk 1.23.389)
The wise one should grind mercury with the resin of *tintriṇī* leaves mixed with a small amount of copper dust; thus, the binding of the mercury will occur. (Āk 1,23.390)
Having cast it into water, the pill becomes like a vajra.
(The Ritual of the Śāka Tree) O Goddess of Gods, having squeezed out the excellent juice of the Śāka tree, Āk_1,23.391.
Combined with red sandalwood, one should digest all metals;
all metals will merge and flow like water. (Āk 1.23.392)
Gandhaka, rasaka, tāpya, mercury, and red sandalwood, when combined with the juice of rudantī, cause silver to turn into gold. Āk_1,23.393.
One should carefully collect the resin of the Śāka tree and grind the powder of the root of the Śigru plant with that resin. (Āk 1.23.394)
Having coated copper leaves with [the medicine] and placed them in a crucible, one should heat them;
that molten gold will become divine and endowed with auspicious characteristics. (Āk 1.23.395)
One should gather the fully ripened fruits of the śākavṛkṣa tree; with their juice, the wise practitioner should perform a seven-night infusion. Āk 1.23.396.
One should smear silver leaves with that juice mixed with madder; when heated, they become gold. (Āk 1.23.397)
(The Ritual Manual of Devadālī): Hereafter, I shall describe the procedure for the great medicinal herb *devadālī*.
It is white for the alleviation of diseases, and black or yellow for the practice of *rasāyana*. (Āk 1.23.398)

On the full moon day, on the thirteenth day, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, or else on the fifth day of the dark fortnight, one should extract this [mantra] according to the prescribed rule. Āk 1.23.399.
O Goddess, the fruit of *devadālī*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, and *sūtaka* cause [the metal] to faint and quickly bind it; they turn copper into gold. (Āk 1.23.400)
Having ground the fruit of *devadālī*, its root, and the juice of *īśvarī* with water, one causes tin to solidify in an instant. (Āk 1.23.401)
(The Ritual Manual of White Guñjā): Now, therefore, O beloved, honored by the gods, I shall fully explain the procedure for white guñjā on the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Having placed earth in a skull, one should sprinkle it with water;
then, under the Puṣya conjunction, one should sow the seeds of white guñjā.
One should likewise perform the gathering [of the mantra] by means of the yoga that will be described:
*Oṃ namo bhagavati śvetavalli śvetaparvatavāsini*. (Āk 1.23.404)
"Perform, perform all tasks; homage, homage to the Unobstructed, svāhā!
Having taken pure copper and placed it inside a crucible... (Āk 1,23.405)
Silver weighing fifteen palas, together with half a karṣa of white guñjā seeds, becomes free from odor when [the latter] is placed within it. (Āk 1.23.406)
O Goddess, when the powder of *guñjā* seeds is combined with *brahmarīti* into a single mass, it becomes beautiful gold that serves as an ornament for the goddesses. Āk 1,23.407.
(The Binding of the Essence of the Scissors) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the binding of the essence of the scissors (*kartarīrasabandhana*),
when one’s mind is possessed by wrath during an encounter with the Asuras. (Āk 1.23.408)
The great Sudarśana discus was dispatched by the enemy of Mura;
thereupon, drops of sweat fell from his forehead. (Āk 1.23.409)
Having fallen upon the earth, those divine [weapons] became the essence of the *kartarī*;
and for the sake of protection, the *sudarśana* was stationed there by Viṣṇu.
Whirling like a wheel, it cuts down weapons;
it utters roars and thunderous sounds, and emits smoke and flames. (Āk 1.23.411)
By the mere sight of the Kartarī-dṛṣṭi, as well as the other, the Śabda-kartarī, which possesses a terrible power, is established for the sake of the welfare of the worlds. (Āk 1.23.412)
She, who is of the nature of the vital essence (*rasa*), is most terrible, yet she is the knower of the perfected ones (*siddhas*).
Whenever one should go to her field, one should then recite the *aghora* weapon-mantra. (Āk 1.23.413)
Then the wise one should again place the *ghora* [mantra] there, and subsequently place another;
having presided over the body by means of the direct and reverse orders, he should apply the *kartarī*.
One should seal that [mudrā] joined with the Aghora-weapon;
one should obstruct it with the Blazing [weapon], and paralyze it with the Illuminating [weapon]. (Āk 1.23.415)
One should join that [mudrā] with the *niṣṭhā* seal by means of the application of the *sthāna* [yoga].
(The water-bindings;
the moon-water-binding.)
Now, O Mistress, I shall explain the binding of mercury by means of lunar water.
Having seen the "moon-water" (candrodaka), especially on the full moon day,
the mantra-practitioner should diligently perform the ritual extraction there on that full moon day.
Having first performed the consecration of the field and worshipped the god Śaṅkara, [the water] emerges after piercing the earth and increases according to the waxing of the moon. Āk 1.23.418.
On the fourteenth day, the wise man, having worshipped that sacred field and having fasted for a day and night, should offer an oblation there. Āk 1.23.419.
Having gone near him on the night of the full moon, one who is well-versed in mantras should collect the "moon-water" while reciting the appropriate mantra. (Āk 1.23.420)
Having stirred it with honey and clarified butter, one should drink it with a concentrated mind;
by the mere act of drinking it, one becomes unconscious in an instant. (Āk 1.23.421)
Likewise, at the rising of the moon, one should arise; one should cause him to consume alkaline salt.
By practicing this for seven nights, he will become as stainless as the moon. (Āk 1.23.422)
By practicing for twenty-one nights, one lives for three days of Brahmā;
by practicing for one month, that person shall attain the lifespan of Brahmā.
One should grind mercury, gold, and the essence [of] the sky with "moon-water"; when blown [into a crucible] while situated within a crucible, it becomes a pill in that very instant. (Āk 1.23.424)
But this [elixir], by mere touch, shall transmute the eight metals; and that mercury, having been thoroughly fused with another mercury and with diamond (vajra), [achieves this]. 1,23.425.
One should pierce it with sixty-four parts; by doubling that, one obtains a thousand.
Then, the mercury, bound by ten *saṅkalikās*, is the size of a *guñjā* seed. (Āk 1.23.426)
By holding [this amulet] encased in three metals in the mouth, one shall become invisible.
*Oṃ namo rudrāya daṃṣṭrotkaṭāya vighnaṃ nāśaya nāśaya diśo rakṣa rakṣa rudro jñāpayati huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra for the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, who holds a trident in his hand; O you born of nectar, protect, protect! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
This is the mantra for the drink. (The binding of poisonous water.)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the binding of mercury with poison. Āk 1.23.427.
O Goddess, having gone there to that mountain region, one should recollect the thousand-fold Ghorā, which is rich with colors such as white and yellow and contains the supreme essence. (Āk 1.23.428)
In this [mirror], hair thrown upon it shatters; one's own reflection is not seen;
oil takes the form of a ball, whereas clarified butter spreads out. (Āk 1.23.429)
One should remove the scent from the fragrant substance; the paste acts as a salt.
Having understood this, one should place it in a bitter gourd using a leaf of the *palāśa* tree. (Āk 1.23.430)
Having ground together mercury, sulfur, and an equal amount of "Hara-seed" (cinnabar) with goat's milk, one should smear it upon a copper vessel. (Āk 1.23.431)
O Goddess, by means of that crucible, [the substance] becomes like the redness of vermilion;
O Goddess, with even a hundredth part of that, one may pierce all metals. (Āk 1.23.432)
By this method, O Goddess, the nāga attains the state of vermilion; by a thousandth part of that very substance, silver and gold are produced. (Āk 1.23.433)
Red, yellow, and likewise black [substances] perform successive effects;
[they may be placed] in a vessel made of the three myrobalans (triphalā), or in a vessel made of gourd (alābu). Āk 1.23.434.
Having taken it as before, one should wrap it on the outside with *pālāśa* leaves;
then one should place it in the midst of grain for twenty-one days. (Āk 1.23.435)
One should prepare a single drop in the midst of buffalo milk;
he who eats the milk-rice (pāyasa) combined with milk, honey, and clarified butter [attains success]. Āk 1.23.436.
O Goddess, for as many years as there are drops [of the mixture], one shall live with full strength;
[the ingredients are] lāṅgalī, house-soot, vermilion, and the two types of turmeric. (Āk 1.23.437)
One should grind together the horn of a ram, *śṛṅgī*, black *unmattā*, *aśvamāraka*, and mercury along with its seed, using poisonous water. (Āk 1.23.438)
A wise person should saturate it seven times with poisonous water;
or rather, one should saturate it until the powder is thoroughly rubbed, and then it shall become so. (Āk 1,23.439)
Having dissolved the naga with that [solution] by means of a sixteenth part, it becomes the void (kha).
One should then process what is contained in the crucible within a bamboo apparatus for three cycles. (Āk 1.23.440)
One should avoid its smoke, which greatly causes diseases of the limbs;
one should place that nāgasindūra in a vessel made of gourd.
One should transmute silver, copper, and other metals with a hundredth part of that powder;
having taken poison-water and refined tin, it becomes auspicious. (Āk 1.23.442)
Just as gold becomes bright when sprinkled with those waters,
one should take the "poison-water" and cast it into the supreme mercury.
One should grind together realgar, sulphur, poison, borax, and lāṅgalī in a mortar until it becomes a fine paste, and then smear this upon silver leaves. Āk 1.23.444.
When placed in an andhamūṣā crucible and heated, it becomes seedless gold.
*Oṃ hrīṃ nīlakaṇṭhāya ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. One should recite this ten thousand times (*ayuta*).
Thus ends the mantra for taking and drinking the water of immortality (*viṣodaka*).
Now, O Pārvatī, I shall describe the ritual procedure for the water of the *sañjīvanī* [life-restoring] plant. (The Ritual Manual of the Sañjīvanī Water) Āk 1.23.445.
O Goddess, worshipped by Śukra, O you who are praised by the gods, I was formerly propitiated by him for the sake of benefiting the Dānavas who had died in battle with the gods. (Āk 1.23.446)
I bestowed upon him the *saṃjīvanī* lore in the form of water;
by it, those Daityas who had died in the battle with the gods were restored to life. (Āk 1.23.447)
I shall relate to you correctly that which has been deposited in the world of mortals:
there is a most meritorious and pure mortal woman in the southern region.
On its southern bank, however, is the excellent city of Utpalī;
to the south of that is the mountain renowned throughout all the worlds.
It is seen as being named Kṛṣṇagiri, O Sarvamaṅgalā; there is a village very famous by the name Ambikā in its vicinity. Āk_1,23.450.
There too, having observed water in a vessel honored by the gods, one should take a dry bamboo cane and throw it into the middle of the water. (Āk 1.23.451)
Within a day and night, it certainly becomes green and glossy;
it sheds sprouts and leaves and appears exceedingly beautiful. (Āk 1.23.452)
Then, O Goddess, one should worship the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrādhipa), Gaṇeśa, Candra, and likewise the host of Yogins with offerings of oblations and flowers. Āk 1.23.453.
Oṃ, to Candra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the bearer of the trident! Oṃ, bind the directions, bind them! Bind the directions, bind them! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ!
Having consecrated sesame seeds and mustard seeds seven times with this mantra, the practitioner should scatter the mustard seeds in all directions. (Āk 1.23.454)
Having performed the protection ritual and being composed in mind, one should take water in a bitter gourd with great care and return to one's own place. (Āk 1.23.455)
Oṃ, homage! O Immortal One, you whose form is nectar, make [this] nectar, make it so! Thus Rudra commands, svāhā!
Having consecrated that water seven times with this mantra, along with one day’s worth of mercury and two māṣas of gold— Āk_1,23.456.
The wise man should rub [the body] with that water and drink it;
then, for twenty-one nights, he should diligently subsist on a diet of milk. (Āk 1.23.457)
He shall live for more than ten thousand kalpas, able to assume any form at will and possessed of great strength;
having traveled a hundred yojanas, he returns once again. (Āk 1.23.458)
Invulnerable to all beings, subsisting on food according to his own will, he becomes a sky-walker.
One should unite gold, mercury, and space together as one. (Āk 1.23.459)
One should grind it with that water and then subject it to heat for seven days;
that mercury will then pierce all metals by means of a sixtyth part.
Alternatively, one should consume that divine elixir together with honey;
by practicing this for only a month, one may live for ten thousand Brahma-days.
By means of its urine, excrement, and sweat, copper becomes gold.
In a windless place, having taken mercury, realgar, and water— Āk 1,23.462.
One should grind it on a grinding stone until it becomes a fine paste (naṣṭapiṣṭa);
then, one should steam it for seven nights and encase it with the three metals.
In an instant, one may attain invisibility and become a lord of the Vidyādharas, surrounded by hundreds of Siddha maidens for as long as fourteen kalpas. (Āk 1.23.464)
During all those days, one should give rice cooked with *śāli* grains along with ghee and combined with milk; one should perform this daily in this manner. (Āk 1.23.465)
(The Ritual for Warm Water):
I shall explain the procedure for warm water; listen with a concentrated mind.
Wherever one sees warm water, there indeed one should make one's dwelling. (Āk 1.23.466)
If one eats chickpeas there every day for a month, having fasted throughout the night, one shall live for eight hundred years. (Āk 1.23.467)
By means of his urine and feces, copper becomes gold;
likewise, hot water combined with ferrous sulfate (kāśīsa) and sulfur (gandhapāṣāṇa). Āk 1.23.468.
One should add mercury equal to a fourth part and copper equal to ten parts;
by rubbing them all together, they will become a "lost-and-ground" (naṣṭapiṣṭa) mass in an instant.
By merely being smeared with that, copper becomes gold.
When it has been poured with that water, the wise man should apply a counter-deposit (*prativāpa*). Āk 1.23.470.
And copper becomes gold with the luster of the rising sun; and silver, when poured by that same method, attains the state of gold. Āk_1,23.471 //
One should consume bhallātaka with warm water and a handful of sesame seeds;
by practicing this for two months, one shall live for three hundred years. (Āk 1.23.472)
Having rubbed together mercury, sulphur, realgar, copper sulfate, cinnabar, and pyrite with hot water for one watch (yāma), one should smear silver leaves [with the resulting paste]. Āk 1.23.473.
O Goddess, having caused it to circulate, one should blow upon it; thus, O Mistress of the Gods, it shall become fourteen-colored.
By this sequence, O Goddess, the copper becomes sixteen-colored. (Āk 1,23.474)

Having separately ground one part each of gold and silver, along with two parts each of *kāntaloha* and mica, with hot water, one should bring it to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*) through smelting. (Āk 1.23.475)
One should hold that [substance] in the mouth for one month; thereafter, one will possess a vajra-body.
One should consume that powder, the size of a barley grain, with honey and clarified butter. (Āk 1.23.476)
Just as copper becomes gold when purified by its impurities for a full pala, one should eat kuluttha beans boiled in hot water and subsist on milk. Āk 1.23.477.
One should bathe with warm water every year until one reaches a hundred years of age;
one should also cook milk, warm water, and a decoction of *triphalā*. (Āk 1.23.478)
One should cook milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in a vessel of *kānta* iron; by eating it, one attains a long life.
(The Ritual for Mountain Water) Hereafter, O Dear One, I shall explain the procedure for mountain water (*śailodaka*). Āk 1,23.479.
It is of four kinds: clay, water, earth, and stone slabs;
some pierce in an instant, while others pierce over the course of days. (Āk 1.23.480)
When wood that has been cast into water on the surface of the earth is seen to have become petrified after six months—whether it be one fortnight, one month, or so on. (Āk 1.23.481)
O Goddess of gods, that which pierces both externally and internally is proclaimed as such;
[the substances are] cinnabar, yellow arsenic, sulfur, and realgar. (Āk 1.23.482)
It removes their odor and acts as a penetrator (*vedhaka*); otherwise, O Goddess, it is merely a brick, unfit for use and useless. (Āk 1.23.483)
On the stone slab called Paryaṅka, at the edge of the Śrī forest on Mount Śrīśaila,
situated there on the bank of the river Bhagavatī, it shall pierce [the target] in an instant.
In that place, at Gokarṇa, there is piercing [of the soul] in one day;
at Bhadrāṅga, it occurs in three days; and at the end of the three sacred sites (Tristhalī), it lasts for three years. (Āk 1.23.485)
At Dhāreśvara, it occurs on the fortnightly day; at Karṣāpurī, for one day;
at Brahmeśvara, it occurs monthly; and at Vyāghrapurī, for a single day. (Āk 1.23.486)
At Aghoreśa there shall be a monthly [observance], and likewise again at Siṃhadvīpa;
for one day at Brahmagiri, but at Vindhya it is a piercing in an instant.
On Mount Mālyavat, however, there is Vāsara; on that same mountain is Kṣaṇavedhin; and on the lovely Kiṣkindha mountain, on the bank of the Pampā, is Kṣaṇodaka.
O Goddess, two yojanas further to the west of that is the Bhūśaila mountain; there, on the Veda mountain, one should stay for three days.
Elsewhere, wherever the nectar originating from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva may be found, there too this supreme method of vajrification is applied. Āk 1.23.490.
I shall describe its origin so that the practitioner may understand it:
[it arose] from the body of the Boar who lifted up the earth. (Āk 1.23.491)
From that sweat which fell, the supreme Śailodaka was born; when it reached the mouth, it became momentary, but at the region of the ear, it became a full day. (Āk 1.23.492)

By piercing with both arms for three days, one becomes a piercer of a month; by piercing with the sides, a piercer of six months; and by piercing on the other parts of the body, [one pierces] for a year—all these yield equal results. (Āk 1.23.493)
Having performed protection for that field with the Aghora-weapon mantra and having offered the bali-oblation to the directions,
one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times and then take up the supreme nectar.
O worshiper of the gods, during autumn, summer, spring, or winter, [one should offer] in an iron vessel, a copper vessel, or one made of kāntaloha. Āk 1.23.495.
One should add eight palas of stone-water and one pala of milk;
having boiled it until only the milk remains, a person should drink it for twenty-one days.
He shall live for a thousand years, free from wrinkles and grey hair;
or else, eight palas of milk mixed with one pala of water.
One should consume the milk residue; one obtains the fruit previously described. One should boil eight parts of water with horse gram (kulattha) until eight parts remain. (Āk 1.23.498)
One should cook clarified butter with four times that amount [of the powder] until only the ghee remains;
after three weeks, one should lick it mixed with honey and sugar, as Bṛhaspati did. (Āk 1.23.499)

Having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old and a lifespan of a thousand years—of this there is no doubt—one should take the remaining *kulattha* beans mixed with honey and ghee in a one-fourth portion. (Āk 1.23.500)
One should consume one karṣa [of it]; by doing so for a month, one will live for ten thousand years.
One should also perform anointing and rubbing [the body] with that perfected oil. Āk 1.23.501.
One shall suddenly conquer scabies, eczema, ringworm, and leprosy;
freed from wrinkles and graying hair, one attains a lifespan of a thousand years. (Āk 1.23.502)
Whoever rises at dawn and drinks a handful of water from a mountain spring shall,
after six months, live for a thousand years, free from wrinkles and grey hair.
Alternatively, O Goddess, one should grind the *sūtaka* with water;
after one month, O Mistress of the Gods, it will become a lost-powder (*naṣṭapiṣṭi*).
If one consumes it for just a month, he shall become free from old age and death;
or else, one should smelt that mercury with gold using a fire of khadira wood.
The pill named Sundarī wards off all weapons;
its practitioner, having attained mastery himself, shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars. (Āk 1.23.506)
Then, with that very water, one should cook milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with half as much milk;
by practicing this for only a month, one becomes free from wrinkles and gray hair.
Having cooked sixty-three hundred *pathyā* fruits with that water and mixed them with honey, one should place the entire quantity in a vessel and set it in the ground. (Āk 1.23.508)
Having risen each morning, one should consume that [substance] one by one day after day;
freed from wrinkles and gray hair, one shall live for a thousand years. (Āk 1.23.509)
One should eat either *kuluttha* beans that have become as hard as stone with honey and clarified butter;
by practicing this for six months, one shall live for a thousand years. (Āk 1.23.510)
Beginning with the kūṣmāṇḍa fruit, whatever fruits there may be, and even iron objects cast into water, one would eat them as if they were stones. (Āk 1.23.511)
And by subsisting on milk alone until it is digested, a man shall attain a vajra-body;
O beloved, one should rub abhraka with that water and boil it. Āk 1.23.512.
One who eats it combined with the three pungents (kaṭutraya) shall live for a thousand years; or else, one karṣa of that [substance] rubbed with its own water [may be taken]. Āk 1,23.513.
Situated within the water of that mountain, like a seed inside the fruit of the *iṅgudī* tree,
its hardness arises after a period of three times that duration.
If it is held in the mouth for six months, it makes one’s body vajra-like; possessing strength equal to ten elephants, one rejoices together with the gods. (Āk 1.23.515)
Having taken the three myrobalans (triphalā), one should throw them into that mountain water;
when that [water] has become solidified as stone, one should take it and then grind it into powder.
One should consume well-digested mercury along with that [elixir], saturated with ghee and honey, for one year; thereafter, one should subsist on milk alone. (Āk 1.23.517)
Resembling the rising sun, intelligent, and pleasing to behold,
with dark, curly hair, he shall live as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars.
One should combine mercury, yellow orpiment, realgar, pyrite,
cinnabar, and poison— all together in one place.
One should grind it on a stone mortar with the juice of *mātuluṅga*;
having formed it into a pill, one should then cast it into the middle of water. (Āk 1.23.520)
By that, mercury (tāra) and copper (śulba) certainly become gold; if one employs it for one month, one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair. (Āk 1.23.521)
He, possessed of great strength and prowess, lived for a thousand years;
yet, by merely adding a powder of turmeric that had turned to stone, [his life was ended].
The naga attains a blood-red color, with a luster like that of the rising sun, when it is cast into mountain water, or onto the earth, or into a rocky crag, or even into mud. (Āk 1.23.523)
Having determined the duration of time, one should then bind the mercury;
it is blown with red alkali and amalgamated with an equal amount of gold.
Having obtained the second refinement of all metals with a hundredth part [of mercury], the alchemist pierces [them] with a thousandth part. Āk 1.23.525.
One should hold that pill in the mouth, and one certainly attains divinity.
(Certain formulations of pills:
[It may be prepared] from *nicula*, *kakubha*, *kiṃśuka*, or even *madhuka*. (Āk 1.23.526)
Or within the fruit of the *iṅgudī*, or in the two types of turmeric, or in fresh ginger, or in the *amṛta* tuber, or in the aforementioned tubers and medicinal herbs. (Āk 1.23.527)
Having fashioned a hollow in that [place] and having cast [the substance] therein, one should cause it to oscillate by means of that very [instrument];
then, having carefully wrapped it with a paste of triphalā and vyoṣa. (Āk 1.23.528)
Having placed gold with one's foot, one should join mercury to it;
by casting that into *śailodaka*, a pill shall become like a diamond. (Āk 1.23.529)
The extraction should be performed as before; as before, it shall bestow success. When held in the mouth, however, it grants a lifespan of a thousand years. (Āk 1.23.530)
Through the yoga of the second drawing-in, she pierces ten thousand [times];
when held in the mouth, she herself bestows a lifespan of ten thousand years. (Āk 1.23.531)
Through the third application of sublimation (*sāraṇā*), it becomes capable of piercing a *lakṣa*.
If one holds that pill (*khoṭa*) in the mouth, a man attains a lifespan of a hundred thousand years. (Āk 1.23.532)
O Goddess, that fourth [recitation] is the piercing of ten million; of this there is no doubt.
His life shall last for ten million years, and he attains the power of moving through the sky. (Āk 1.23.533)

With five [times ten million], there would be one hundred million; with six, there would be one billion, until his life is as long as that of the moon and sun, possessing infinite strength and vigor. (Āk 1.23.534)
And the seventh [goddess] also bestows [the fruit]; she is the supreme pill known as Sāraṇā, renowned as Khecarī, impelled by Bhairava. (Āk 1.23.535)
But he who should eat even a single grain of that for one month shall become a perfected one with a vajra-body, beloved by celestial women. (Āk 1.23.536)
He sports with the enjoyments of the sky-goers at his own will and shall attain the state of Śiva.
O beautiful one, hear now of its various kinds of fruits and its medicinal pill (guṭikā). Āk 1,23.537.
One should digest purified and bound mercury with sulphur;
when three times the amount of sulphur has been digested, one should then prepare gold with it. (Āk 1,23.538)
One should cause the mercury to be reduced to ash, and by means of that [ash], the mercury is turned into gold.
That ash should be digested within the mercury in equal proportions with the lord of fluids (rasendra). (Āk 1.23.539)
By means of that digested *sūtaka*, one should strike the *vajraratna*;
that *vajra* becomes ashes resembling the red hue of vermilion. (Āk 1.23.540)
One should digest that ash in mercury three times its quantity, O worshiper of the gods;
one should then extract the essence of gold and fashion a pill (*ghuṭikā*) with it. (Āk 1.23.541)
Having placed that [object], encased in the three metals, in his mouth, the practitioner becomes devoid of shadow; he thus becomes invisible even to gods and dānavas. (Āk 1.23.542)
For a hundred thousand years he shall be free from wrinkles and grey hair;
[he shall behold] the wielder of the trident, joined with his spear, adorned with the qualities of jewels and the like.
One should wear upon the face and the hand the "obstructor of all weapons," namely:
the void (*vyoma*), the essence of honey (*mākṣikasattva*), silver (*tāra*), copper (*tāmra*), and the weapon of the gods (*surāyudha*).
O lady of excellent hips, that pill consists of steel, mercury, and gems adorned with various qualities, combined with the three sweets. Āk 1.23.545.
Remaining in the mouth, it directly destroys gray hair; there is no doubt about this.
O Goddess of the Gods, Śiva and Śakti, as well as gems, white cows, and elephants [are obtained]. (Āk 1.23.546)
One should prepare equal parts of gold, silver, and mercury;
then, having placed female reproductive fluid within a tiger-skin pouch, one should wrap it with a lotus fiber.
Having thus wrapped it with white [silk], one should place it in a secret location;
in battle, in the royal court, in gambling, in divine matters, and in desire, victory shall be attained. Āk 1.23.548.
Vaikrānta, abhraka, kānta, sasyaka, and surāyudha shall be equal in measure to the kāñjika produced from vibhītaka and other such ingredients. (Āk 1.23.549)
Then, having refined it, one should join it with the juices of the *sūta*; this auspicious pill, rubbed with the juice of the virgin (*kumārī*), is thus prepared. (Āk 1.23.550)
When placed in the mouth, it destroys disease, death, and old age; of this there is no doubt.
O lady of excellent hips, [it consists of] the five *tāras* and the two *sūtakas*. (Āk 1.23.551)
There should be three parts of sky (black), one part each of gold and copper, and half a part of tin; by this division, the pill becomes as beautiful as the goddess Amarā. (Āk 1.23.552)
By this, one becomes truly inexhaustible and ageless, possessing great strength;
likewise, one [should take] one pala of ashes and one pala of mṛtakānta. Āk_1,23.553.
One pala of honey, one pala of *śilājatu*, one pala of *viḍaṅga*, and likewise one pala of powdered *pathyā*. (Āk 1.23.554)
Having combined all of that together, one should grind it with honey and clarified butter;
from this, one should fashion three hundred and sixty pills. (Āk 1.23.555)
If one should eat them one by one daily for one year without interruption, he shall live for a lifespan of a hundred years, possessing great strength like Rudra. (Āk 1.23.556)
(Some are like elixirs of rejuvenation.
Hereafter I shall proclaim the elixir of mercury-ash (*rasabhasma-rasāyana*), which is to be known as a supreme, divine medicine that requires no restrictive regimen. (Āk 1,23.557)

Take *āmalakī* and other such [herbs], *kānta* iron, mercury (*pārada*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*), each in equal parts with *vākucī*; these should be ground with the juice of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīriṇī*). (Āk 1.23.558)
One should cook it in a sealed crucible (mūkamūṣā) together with the juice of *meghanāda*;
then one should consume it in sequence, starting with one *māṣa*, then two *māṣas*, and then three times that amount.
O Goddess, for three years at most, one should give half a niṣka per foot;
then for six, seven, and eight years respectively, according to the measure of a niṣka.
Free from old age and deformity, he shall eat divine food,
and [receive] some gold coin, or even half a coin, fashioned with gold.
Whoever consumes it conquers all diseases within three years;
with a lifespan of eight thousand years, one becomes a piercer of the target at twelve *lakṣa*s.
In the sixteenth year, O Goddess, he becomes possessed of a divine form;
the Mūlabandha is the highest, while the Sārabandhana is middling. (Āk 1,23.563)

Thus is the threefold binding, the lowest being the binding by cooking. One hundred palas of *abhayā*, along with *akṣa* and *dhātrī*, are boiled in eight parts of water until one-eighth remains. This is enriched with ghee, honey, and sugar, and made variegated with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*). It is prepared with ten palas each of juice and iron, both in its digested and reduced states. (Āk 1,23.564)
Take *viḍaṅga* equal in measure to mercury (*rasa*), along with *abhra* (mica) and *kāntaloha* (magnetite), mixed with honey, *bilva* marrow, and rice.
Having formed a paste with snow-water, place it in an iron vessel for one month; this paste, purified by three days [of processing], is most excellent. (Āk 1,23.565)

At the time of reclining, he who frequents the left eye, possessed of dense and firm meditative concentration, with the pride of an elephant in rut, free from all defects, all-seeing with the divine eye, and as radiant as the god of love to women—he is the preeminent hero. (Āk 1.23.566)
Possessing a body like a rain-cloud, with hair whose tips were curled at the ends; pure like a horse, a true poet and a master of artistry;
moving with the gait and gestures of a bull, with a slow and deep resonance; he lived by the moon, stars, and sun in this world like the elephant of the gods. (Āk 1.23.567)

A pill made of gold, copper, and mercury, placed within an *abhraka* stone inside an *iṅgudī* fruit, is a perfected pill produced by the waters of the mountain; it is indeed auspicious and known as "Sundarī," the name of the Immortals. Āk 1,23.568.

Antimony containing gold, copper, and silver, as well as a ball of *vajra*, gems, mercury, and *mahīrāja* [minerals], when cast into the hollow of an *āmalaka* wood and buried in the earth or a mountain, is extracted [transformed]. (Āk 1,23.569)
Then, having attained a stone-like state within the mouth by means of days that produce a body of diamond,
[the practitioner should prepare] a pill (*golaka*) composed of silver, excellent gold, copper, and mercury, constrained by a wooden apparatus.
The pill made from the juices of *śailavāri* and *sundarī* is called *khecarī*. (Āk 1.23.571)

One should eat a palāśa seed that has been cast into mountain water and transformed into stone by means of honey and ghee; after twenty-one days, having taken it on each successive day, a man shall be known as one who lives for a thousand years. Āk 1,23.572.
Sūtaka and abhraka, combined with vajra and tīkṣṇa, and joined with hāṭaka, shall become a *gulikā* known as *khecarī*. (Āk 1.23.573)
One should place the mercury situated within the fruit of the *karañja* tree back into that very same [fruit];
held there within the water of a mountain spring, it bestows a lifespan of a thousand years. (Āk 1.23.574)
In *tinduka* [oil], the lifespan is two thousand years; in *jambīra*, three thousand;
and in *mātuluṅga* and *nāraṅga*, four and five thousand years respectively. (Āk 1.23.575)
Six thousand [times] on a plantain fruit, seven on a jackfruit, and ten thousand on a vibhītaka fruit. (Āk 1.23.576)
O highly fortunate one, there are fourteen thousand [merits] for a coconut;
thirty thousand for a *pathyā* fruit; and furthermore, one hundred thousand for an *āmalaka*.
From a decoction produced from *abhrapatra* kept for a day and night in water containing mica, the extracted mercury binds [the essence], destroying death and poverty. (Āk 1.23.578)
Through the application of the sequence of attraction (*sāraṇā*), the body becomes like a diamond;
in both mercury and elixirs (*rasāyana*), it undoubtedly pierces a hundred thousand targets. (Āk 1,23.579)

Having formed a pill from the essence of a maiden's menstrual discharge mixed with clay, a person should hold it in the mouth; through blowing upon it, the vital essence (sattva) falls out, which one should then retain.
By practicing this application for six months, one indeed attains freedom from old age and death;
for mercury mixed with lead and combined with *srotoñjana* is blown [into a crucible]. (Āk 1.23.581)
One should hold that pill in the mouth, for then one certainly becomes invisible; whatever procedure has been prescribed for water in the Śiva-āgama [is to be followed].
"Alas, one might perform the elixir (*rasāyana*) on the body after a hundred years of time;
this previously described method of *baddhajāraṇa* is the lowest form of *bālajāraṇā*. (Āk 1,23.583)
The supreme and indeed rare *baddhajāraṇā* shall now be heard:
he who causes the unbound [mercury] to digest [the essence] will go to destruction as he wastes away. (Āk 1.23.584)
The food of one who is bound digests, and when it has been digested, his mouth becomes open;
one with an open mouth gives a bad face—this is the characteristic of the common and the supreme. (Āk 1.23.585)
(The Methods of Binding:
The first is the ordinary [binding], which, by virtue of its resistance to fire, serves as a solvent for great gems and the like;
it should be performed first, with the "devouring" [process] occurring on all sides. Āk 1,23.586.
O Goddess, this [mantra] would indeed be common and merely a maker of a physical body;
however, when bound without a *grāsa*, it becomes the bestower of divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*). (Āk 1.23.587)
The Mūlabandha is the best, the Sārabandhana is middling, and the Pākabandha is the lowest; thus, there are three kinds of binding.
The *mūlabandha* is that great bond which consists of the contraction of the root;
the *sārabandha*, however, is the bond that is called the bond of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
From among the sixty-four root-mantras, there may be some binding by means of a root-mantra;
the limbs of beings such as the Daityas and others consist of root-limbs that are composed of deities. (Āk 1.23.590)
And the stone is indeed honored by both the perfected ones (siddhas) and human beings;
through the pedestal, the melting, and the contraction, there shall be a threefold binding. (Āk 1.23.591)
The previously mentioned contraction-binding (*saṃkocabandhana*) is performed with divine medicinal herbs;
when the mercury (*sūta*) is bound by fluxes (*druti*), it is called momentary-binding (*kṣaṇabandha*). (Āk 1.23.592)
Abhraka and harabīja, along with gold in a sixteenth part,
should be smelted in an open crucible and purified with glass and ṭaṅkaṇa.
When the mercury is blown while rotating clockwise and fused with the seed-syllable of Hara, O lady of excellent hips, it leaves the crucible and remains fixed like a bird in a cage. Āk 1.23.594.
With a dose of even half of a half-raktikā, one may pierce even mountains;
by consuming it, O Goddess of Gods, a man becomes equal to Rudra. (Āk 1.23.595)
He sports through the seven worlds, possessing prowess equal to Śiva. (The procedure for the fusion of the fluxes:
Vajrakanda, Guḍūcī, and Uccaṭā, combined with the others. Āk_1,23.596.
Abhraka (mica) is quickly assimilated; otherwise, there is no union [with the mercury].
[This is achieved] with black agallochum, musk, garlic, and asafoetida. (Āk 1.23.597)

When combined with the menstrual blood of a woman, the flower of the *pālāśa* tree, and sesame oil, and heated until they are thoroughly rubbed together, all the *drutis* (mercury preparations) will merge into the mercury. (Āk 1.23.598)
(Vajrabandha;
accomplished through the rite of the ten joints:
O you who are worshipped by the gods, I shall further proclaim another Vajrabandha.
A woman should consume sulphur for twenty-one days. (Āk 1.23.599)
That dust is beneficial for the binding and digestion of the king of mercury (rasarāja).
One part of diamond ash and three parts of pure mercury [are used]. Āk 1,23.600.
One should rub [the substance] with the dust of *dvipadī* until it reaches the state of a paste; then, one should apply a leaf-coating using a quarter-part of gold. (Āk 1.23.601)
One should add the beautiful juice of *somavallī* along with finely powdered borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) in an eighth part of that [quantity], and one should grind it with great care. (Āk 1.23.602)
Having crushed that dried substance into a fine powder and placed it inside a crucible,
one should heat it while it is contained within a blind-pot (andhamūṣā), combined with a fluxing agent (krāmaṇa).
O Goddess, the great elixir (mahārasa) becomes a "pierced hundred" (śatavedhī) when it is solidified;
one should purify it by repeatedly adding *sauvīra*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and glass (*kāca*). Āk 1,23.604.
The unexhausted [debt] is settled with gold, and a Samāvarta ceremony is performed;
then one should cause it to pass through the fingers with the increase of one unit at a time, along with the finger-joints (saṃkalaiḥ). Āk 1,23.605.
With a thread of one strand, one *saṅkalī* is said [to be made];
with a thread of three strands, however, a second *saṅkalī* is said [to be made]. (Āk 1.23.606)
With a mercury six times [the weight of] the [other ingredients], the third *saṅkalī* is formed;
with a mercury ten times [the weight], the fourth *saṅkalī* is formed. (Āk 1.23.607)
O Goddess, by fifteen-fold multiplication, the fifth *saṅkalikā* occurs;
O Goddess, by twenty-one-fold multiplication, the sixth *saṅkalikā* occurs. (Āk 1.23.608)
O Mistress, when multiplied by twenty-eight, it is known as the seventh *saṅkalikā*;
when multiplied by thirty-six, the eighth *saṅkalikā* is formed. (Āk 1.23.609)
The ninth *saṅkalī* is considered to consist of forty-five qualities;
fifty-five [qualities] are recorded as the tenth *saṅkalī*. (Āk 1.23.610)
And thus, through gradual increase, the *saṃkalī* becomes tenfold;
in the first [stage] it pierces ten, and in the second it pierces a hundred.
In the third [stage], one becomes a piercer of a thousand; in the fourth, a piercer of ten thousand;
in the fifth, a piercer of a hundred thousand; and in the sixth, a piercer of a million. (Āk 1.23.612)
In the seventh [stage] one becomes a piercer of the *koṭi*; likewise, in the eighth, a piercer of ten *koṭis*.
In the ninth, however, one is a piercer of smoke; in the tenth, a piercer of sound.
When bound with all the *saṃkalīs*, the piercing (*vedha*) becomes tenfold;

The wise one should mix that ash with mercury in equal parts;
he should cause the silver to be consumed by the mercury and rub it with horse urine. (Āk 1.24.13)
One should seal it in an andhamūṣā crucible with a gentle fire for one day and night or three nights; thus the mercury becomes fire-resistant. (Āk 1.24.14)
By touching it, one will turn all metals into silver.
(The fifth method: the accomplishment of red vaikrānta.
The ritual application of the red [stone] shall now be described; it destroys old age and poverty. (Āk 1.24.15)
One should saturate its powder seven times with water from the *vyāghrī* bulb;
then, one *pala* of that [powder], one *pala* of gold, and one *pala* of pure mercury [should be combined]. (Āk 1.24.16)
All of it shall become pure ash; then one should add a hundred parts of gold. That entire ash becomes equal in luster to pure gold. (Āk 1.24.17)
One should then mix that ash with mercury and again with gold;
O Goddess, it will become fire-resistant, and thereafter it becomes the most excellent mercury. (Āk 1.24.18)
The mercury becomes all-piercing, and the great elixir becomes ten-million-fold piercing.
(The sixth method:
One should mix the essence of red vaikrānta with gold. Āk 1.24.19.
One should digest it equally with mercury after having caused it to flow; then, by means of a thousandth part, one shall pierce the metals—of this there is no doubt. (Āk 1.24.20)
(The seventh method: the perfected black vaikrānta.
Take one part of black vaikrānta and one hundred parts of pure mercury; grind these two together in a mortar until they become a fine powder. Āk 1.24.21.
One part of this powder and one thousand parts of gold should be rubbed together until ash is produced. (Āk 1.24.22)
One should blow [the crucible] in a blind mūṣā until it becomes a solid mass (khoṭa);
one should cause a pedestal to be made for it, which consumes an equal portion [of the ingredients]. (Āk 1.24.23)
One should transmute all metals into gold by mere touch;
one should then grind that powder along with mica and mercury together. (Āk 1.24.24)
One should cause it to sweat and digest; then it becomes capable of withstanding fire. That mercury, once processed, penetrates all metals.
(The eighth variety: yellow-colored vaikrānta-siddha.
Even with yellow-colored vaikrānta, the procedure for red and black is prescribed.
Furthermore, yellow vaikrānta powder combined with gold powder—Āk 1.24.26.
Having mixed the powder of yellow mica with a great mineral essence (mahārasa), it should be subjected to sweating and grinding; after one month, it becomes capable of withstanding fire. (Āk 1.24.27)
(The elixir of blue vaikrānta ash):
Blue-colored vaikrānta is killed when combined with mercury;
it is then joined with black mica and mixed with honey and ghee. (Āk 1.24.28)
O Goddess, by consuming the maṇḍala, one shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars;
indeed, according to the application of whichever specific yoga corresponds to whichever [individual]. (Āk 1.24.29)
Having mixed the juice of *guñjā*—measured at one *guñjā*—with the three kinds of honey, one should consume it with milk, ghee, and *śāli* rice, while avoiding all other food. (Āk 1.24.30)
(Ninth method:
One should grind the mercury combined with the essence of vaikrānta in the acid of *luṅga*;
one should heat it with hot water and then fill it with water. (Āk 1.24.31)
One should blow [a bellows] upon sattva and sūta mixed together; this results in the binding of the mercury (rasabandhana).
Having cast the bound mercury into the mouth, one beholds the cavities of the earth. Āk 1.24.32.
(Tenth method: One should grind one *niṣka* of mercury that has been saturated with horse urine for one day; O Goddess, having thus ground it, it becomes dead. Āk 1.24.33.
Having performed this for four days with equal proportions,
one who is pure in mind should proceed with equal measures of rubbing and fomentation as previously described.
One should take one part each of the seven pairs [of herbs] and eight *pala* of the root of *Śalyāviśalyā*; these should be ground with water for one day. (Āk 1.24.35)
One should apply a *puṭa* (roasting) for seven days inside a *bhūdharīyantra*.
That purified ash should be consumed; one *guñjā* of it constitutes a *maṇḍala*.
The first, the fifth, and again the middle one are praised as single;
O Goddess, when bound as before, the mercury becomes a "piercer of the peak" (koṭivedhī). Āk 1.24.37.
(The *kāntabandha*:
Magnetic iron of red color, with a luster equal to lac-dye, resembling the blood of a woman who has been pierced; its powder, when combined with mercury— Āk 1.24.38.
One should rub it with goat's blood; when heated, it becomes a *khoṭa*, O Dear One.
That mercury is a hundredfold penetrator (*śatavedhī*), and it shall be a remover of diseases. (Āk 1.24.39)
One should wear a pill in the mouth and live for a thousand years;
[the pill made from] yellow-colored magnetite has a luster equal to refined gold. (Āk 1.24.40)
O beautiful one, he should transmute the metals by mere touch;
(this is the capala-bandha, the first type).
Lāṅgalī, karavīra, citraka, and girikarṇikā.
One should apply a coating to the crucible using woman’s milk, *ṭaṅka*, and *sauvīra*;
[the mixture should contain] mercury twice the amount of *capalā*, and gold twice the amount of mercury. (Āk 1.24.42)
One should reduce it to a fine powder and heat it within an *andhamūṣā* crucible;
the mercury (*rasendra*) situated therein becomes an excellent *khoṭa*. (Āk 1.24.43)
One should pierce lead with a hundredth part [of the essence], and it becomes the color of a guñjā berry;
by that hundredth part of lead, copper becomes red-hued. (Āk 1.24.44)
With that hundredth part of the copper, one pierces the silver to produce gold.
(The second method:
Six parts of capala and seven parts of silver [are used]. (Āk 1.24.45)
There are eight parts of gold and nine parts of mercury;
when combined, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, they constitute thirty parts. (Āk 1.24.46)
One should apply a paste of *citraka*, *kaṇavīra*, *lāṅgalī*, and *gṛdhraviṭ*, crushed with the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga*, as a coating for the crucible. (Āk 1.24.47)
Having blinded it, O Goddess, one should heat it; it becomes a beautiful *khoṭa*.
Pierced with a tenth part of that *khoṭa*, the *nāga* becomes ruddy. (Āk 1.24.48)
When copper is pierced by that *nāga* [mineral], it becomes as red as a *guñjā* berry;
when silver is pierced by that copper, it becomes gold. (Āk 1.24.49)

(The third method: O Goddess, take volatile mercury with a golden luster mixed with half its weight of quicksilver; having added gold to the quicksilver, one should grind it for a moment with realgar. (Āk 1.24.50)
Lāṅgalī, citraka, breast milk, kaṇavīraka, and vulture droppings—one should use all of these as a coating for the crucible. (Āk 1.24.51)
When that [substance] situated in the middle is blown [with fire], it becomes a beautiful *khoṭa*;
one should pierce this as previously described, and it becomes seedless gold. Āk 1,24.52.
One should cast the powder of capala into a well-heated iron vessel;
having prepared mercury together with its seed, one should cause it to be sown upon the capala. (Āk 1.24.53)
The mercury, red as lac, is bound like a great elephant with a goad; (this is the binding by sulfur; the first method).
One *pala* of pure mercury and one *pala* of sulfur.
Then, having combined and thoroughly ground it with the juice of *dhuttūraka*, one should kill it by means of the *cakra*-yoga; the mercury (*sūtaka*) is reduced to ashes. Āk 1.24.55.
When heated in an andhamūṣā crucible, the *khoṭa* becomes excellent;
it pierces white gold, lead, and even the "moon and sun" (silver and copper). Āk 1.24.56.
(Second method: One *pala* of pure mercury and one *karṣa* of sulfur should be ground together with the juice of *devadālī* in a smooth mortar. Āk 1.24.57.
One should rub it with the fingers of the hand until it becomes a fragrant paste; one should then rub it for one day with the juice of the jambīra fruit alone. Āk 1.24.58.
One should prepare an auspicious pill combined with the five fluxing agents; one should then coat that pill with a paste of the root of the *palāśa* tree. (Āk 1.24.59)
By means of a combination of white glass (śvetakāca) and borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), the impurity (khoṭa) should be heated;
one should purify it with effort until it reaches a state of stainlessness. Āk 1,24.60.

O Goddess, that [mercury] becomes solid; then one should take three parts of lead (pannaga), and afterwards color it a hundred times with a mixture of copper (śulba), mica (abhraka), and human skull (kapāla). Āk 1.24.61.
This *khoṭa* is a penetrator (*vedhaka*) by a thousandth part in both gold and silver.
(The third method:
When mercury has been killed with sulphur, one should cause the dead metals to flow [into it]. (Āk 1,24.62)
Furthermore, having refined the gold again, consume it in equal parts;
once processed with copper and silver, the mercury penetrates the brass. (Āk 1.24.63)
(The fourth method: Having made the mercury equal to gold, one should grind it with half as much sulphur, combined with the powder of *dvipadī* and endowed with *ṭaṅkaṇa*. (Āk 1.24.64)
Then the *khoṭa* becomes burnt to powder, dried, and heated;
when pierced by a sixteenth part of mercury and the moon, it becomes gold. (Āk 1.24.65)
When that [mercury] is joined with half a part of gold, it attains equality with the *mātṛkā* (the mother-substance).
Through the application of *saṅkalikā*, the piercing (*vedha*) becomes ten times superior. (Āk 1.24.66)
Just as it is with gold, so it is with silver when joined with the seed-syllable *vyāṭi* and bound by the third *saṅkalā*; this pierces six hundred *nāgas*. (Āk 1.24.67)
If, by this same process, gold [is produced] from that [iron] increased fourfold at each step by a thousandth part, then there would be seven layers. (Āk 1.24.68)
O Pārvatī, it turns the eight metals into divine gold;
having powdered that again, one should subject it to a *puṭa* (roasting), and it becomes ash. (Āk 1.24.69)
O Goddess, by consuming one *pala* of this as a wholesome food, all diseases are conquered;
with two *palas*, there is the longevity of Brahmā; with three *palas*, it becomes the longevity of Viṣṇu. (Āk 1.24.70)
O Goddess, if four *pala* are consumed, one becomes the Lord (*īśa*); if five *pala*, one becomes [Īśvara];
if six *pala* are eaten, O Goddess, one becomes the body of Sadāśiva. (Āk 1.24.71)
(Fifth method:

One should grind together equal parts of mercury, sulfur, silver, and the fat of *meṣavallī* for three days; [the resulting paste] should be applied to tin in the proportion of one part [of the paste] to four parts [of tin]. Āk 1.24.72.
Tin placed in an andhamūṣā crucible and blown with a bellows is solidified in an instant.
(The sixth method: the procedure for the fragrant paste.)
O Goddess, powdered sulfur should be impregnated with the juice of *markaṭī*.
One should meditate upon it one hundred times, and the ash of the living being departs;
one should cause it to be placed in an earthen vessel together with the mercury. (Āk 1.24.74)
One should heat sulphur combined with the juice of *markaṭī* by means of the sun's heat;
mercury swallows it, and in an instant, a paste (*piṣṭikā*) is formed. (Āk 1,24.75)
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, one should saturate the sulphur with the juice of *tilaparṇī* seven times, drying it repeatedly in the shade.
O beloved, having purified and cast one *pala* measure of mercury (*sūta*) into the middle of a crucible (*mūṣā*), it should be combined with the juice of *narendrī*.
Furthermore, one should cause the processed sulphur to be digested in a *vālukāyantra*; the sulphur should be added again and again, little by little, bit by bit. (Āk 1.24.78)
By this sequential method, the fragrant paste is produced;
indeed, the powder of sulphur (gandhapāṣāṇa) [is prepared] with the juice of gold.
One should perform the ritual of seven recitations seven times with menstrual blood; then, one *pala* of pure lead should be placed in a crucible. (Āk 1.24.80)
One should give processed sulphur combined with human bile;
by swinging it over the heat of the sun, it becomes a paste in an instant. (Āk 1.24.81)
O Pārvatī, one should take sulphur as a fine powder and saturate it seven times with sour chickpea juice (*caṇakāmla*), and likewise seven times with the menstrual blood of a woman. Āk 1.24.82.

Into the midst of the liquefied mercury (sūtaka), one should cause camphor, sulfur, and mercury to be given; having cast them into a cow-pen, after seven days there will be a fragrant paste (gandhapiṣṭikā).
(The immobilization and piercing by means of a paste of sulphur):
Having ground the seeds of *kaṭukośātakī* and the bulb of *cāṇḍālī* with breast milk, one should apply that paste [to the mercury]. (Āk 1.24.84)
One should seal it in the *bhūdhara* yantra; it will be immobilized, of this there is no doubt. One should cause it to undergo complete revolution within the middle of a golden casket. (Āk 1.24.85)
With that very same eighth part, one should cause the piercing of the naga to be performed;
with that very same sixteenth part, one should cause the piercing of the silver (tāra) to be performed. (Āk 1.24.86)
(Seventh method: One pala of fragrant powder and eight palas of nāga-paste should be used to smear the nāga-leaves; thereafter, one should dry them in the shade. Āk 1.24.87.
One should smear the leaves of the *nāga* tree with a paste of *āṭarūṣaka* seeds; O Goddess, one should then apply three layers of wild lotus petals over them. (Āk 1.24.88)
That divine nāga-dust, possessing a luster red as vermilion, is not consumed;
one pala of that nāga-dust [is combined] with eight palas of copper powder. (Āk 1.24.89)
One should grind it for one prahara with the juice of vāsaka itself;
then, by means of a pātanāyantra, one should kill the copper (śulba), and that [copper] dies instantly. Āk 1.24.90.
By means of that very sixteenth part, one should cause the piercing with mercury (tāravedha) to be performed;
thus divine gold is produced, fit for adorning the ornaments of the gods. (Āk 1.24.91)
Whatever fragrant paste there may be, one should first kill the *nāga*;
with that *nāga* one should pierce the copper (*śulba*), and into the copper one should pierce the silver (*tāra*). (Āk 1.24.92)
Divine gold is produced; this is declared to be the Siddhayoga (the eighth method).
Sulfur, combined with honey and rubbed with the seed-syllable of Hara (HŪṂ), [is used]. (Āk 1.24.93)
Gold situated on the ground becomes silver after one month;
by anointing with that very [substance], all forms of leprosy are destroyed. (Āk 1.24.94)
Combined with *ghana*, it destroys diseases of the wounds;
by practicing this for one year, a man shall attain a lifespan of a thousand years. (Āk 1.24.95)
(The Talaka-seal:
One *pala* of pure mercury and one *pala* of *talaka*, having combined these and then thoroughly rubbed them with the juice of *unmattaka*. (Āk 1.24.96)
One should kill [the mercury] by means of the wheel-machine (*cakrayantra*); the quicksilver (*sūtaka*) becomes reduced to ashes.
When it is blown [with fire] while contained within a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it becomes an excellent *khoṭa*.
The mercury should successively transmute tin, silver, and copper;
one *pala* of pure tin and one *pala* of mercury [are to be used]. (Āk 1.24.98)
These two *pala*s of *tālaka* should be rubbed with the juice of *unmatta* and killed in a *pātanāyantra*; by blowing [with a bellows], one should bring it to the state of a *khoṭa*.
The essence of white mica, silver, iron, and pyrite,
when placed in a blind crucible and heated, instantly becomes a solid residue (khoṭa).
One *pala* of that *khoṭa*, one *pala* of mercury (*sūtaka*),
and one *pala* of *tālaka*— having combined all these together, one should then grind them.
One should kill [the mercury] in a *pātanāyantra* by heating it, thereby bringing it to the state of a solid mass (*khoṭa*). (Other minor bindings:
One *pala* of pure mercury and one *pala* of lead (*pannaga*). ĀK 1.24.102.
One should grind two palas of realgar together with all [the other ingredients] in one place;
by heating it in a *pātanāyantra*, one should bring it to the state of a solid mass (*khoṭa*).
One *pala* of gold-dust and one *pala* of sulfur,
having combined these and then thoroughly rubbed them together with the juice of *dhuttūraka*, [one should proceed].
One should kill [the mercury] in a pātanāyantra and, by heating, bring it to the state of a khoṭa; likewise, the essence of black abhraka, kānta, tīkṣṇa, and gold [should be processed]. Āk 1.24.105.
One should take equal parts of pure silver and copper sulphate (mākṣika);
when heated in a sealed crucible (andhamūṣā), it instantly becomes a solid mass (khoṭa). Āk 1.24.106.
One *khaṭapala* of that [substance], one *pala* of mercury (*sūtaka*), and two *palas* of realgar (*kunaṭī*)—one should grind all of this together. (Āk 1.24.107)
One should kill [the mercury] in a *pātanāyantra* by means of heating, thereby bringing it to the state of a solid mass (*khoṭa*).
One *pala* of black mica (*abhraka*) and likewise one *pala* of mercury; ĀK 1,24.108.
O beloved, one *pala* of *sūtakā* should be combined with everything else and ground for two *praharas* with the juice of *unmattaka*.
One should grind it for one day together with ṭaṅkaṇa (borax), and afterwards, one should fashion it into a pill and allow it to dry in the shade. (Āk 1.24.110)
The *khoṭa* that has been blown [into a flame] within a great crucible becomes *sūtaka*.
One should purify that *khoṭa* by means of a mixture of glass (*kāca*) and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) dissolved in liquid. Āk 1.24.111.

Having processed it together with gold and refined it through three cycles of *sāraṇā*, one should apply the *vedha* (transmutation) of copper using that very [refined substance] in a proportion of one-thousandth part. Āk 1.24.112.
By this sequential method, the mercury becomes "piercing ten million" (koṭivedhī).
Take two palas of *palāśa* seed and one pala of mercury. (Āk 1.24.113)
Having ground it with the sour juice of *jambīra*, one should cause it to dry in the shade.
Then [one should add] *tumbīkā*, *meghanādī*, *kākajaṅghā*, and *bhūlikā*. (Āk 1.24.114)
One should place [the substance] smeared with breast milk into a crucible and blow it with charcoal from the khadira tree; it becomes an indestructible *khoṭa*. Āk 1.24.115.
Having been rubbed in *palāśa* oil until it becomes a liquid paste, it is placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated; at that very moment, it becomes a solid bolus (*khoṭa*). Āk 1,24.116.
O Pārvatī, having thoroughly ground it with previously purified mercury and an equal amount of gold, one should fashion a *golaka* (globule) and make it firm. Āk 1.24.117.
The seeds of the *brahmavṛkṣa*, cotton seeds, *vibhītaka*, *yavaciñcā*, *vandhyā*, and black mustard—these combined together. (Āk 1.24.118)
O Goddess, by smearing a ball made from all these ingredients finely ground together, the stabilization of the paste occurs through seven roastings (*puṭana*). (Āk 1.24.119)
Then, having added a large amount of flux, one should blow [the fire] into the crucible;
then, having processed that mercury and combined it with an equal amount of gold—Āk 1.24.120.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should pierce the moon and sun with a hundredth part;
then, by that very same yoga, one should effect the stabilization of the *piṣṭī*.

Then, having refined it with gold, there is a thousandfold transmutation; in this manner, through the sequential application of yoga, one should effect transmutations by the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions.
Having fashioned a ball-shaped mouthpiece from seven layers of cloth, by means of that alone for one year, he shall become free from wrinkles and grey hair. (Ākāśagupta 1,24.123)

Then, one should combine that mica (abhraka) with the flowers of the *cāṇḍālī* and *rākṣasī*, along with honey, clarified butter, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, in the midst of the eight great minerals (*mahārasa*). (Āk 1.24.124)
One should grind mercury equal in weight to lead or tin, or else gold,
silver, mica, or the essence of mica, for two *praharas*.
Then, O beloved, having dried that ball in the shade and placed it inside a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*), one should apply a light *puṭa* and blow upon it; it becomes an excellent *khoṭa*.
Raṃbhā, vīrā, the milky sap of snuhī, kañcukī, yavaciñcikā, dīnārī, gorambhā, mīnākṣī, and kākamācikā. (Āk 1.24.127)
For mercury processed with these, rebirth does not exist;
through the sequential application as before, it becomes a beautiful pill (*khoṭa*). (Āk 1.24.128)
Viṣṇukrāntā, Vakrāṅkābalā, and likewise Tulasī;
Mahāsomā, Ahivallī, and Sūryāvarta, O beautiful one. (Āk 1.24.129)
The mercury, rubbed with these, should be brought to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*) as before;
[using] the milky sap of *snuhī*, fermented gruel (*kāñjīra*), and the seeds of gold.
One should grind mercury with *kañcukī*, *lāṅgalī*, *indravāruṇī*, *viṣamuṣṭikā*, and water from the roots of the *pālāśa* tree. Āk 1.24.131.
The wise one should cause an equal amount of mercury to be mixed with equal gold and made into a paste;
he should then macerate half of that paste with the juices of the great medicinal herbs.
Having rubbed it for three watches (yāmas), the wise one should form it into a ball;
having bound the paste, he should cook it in scented oil. Āk 1.24.133.
One should cause the globule placed in a blind crucible to dry in the shade; then, having applied a light seal, one should heat it in a fire of *khadira* wood. (Āk 1.24.134)
O Goddess, it arises like dross; one should heat it together with gold.
It remains undiminished when mixed with gold, and a complete amalgamation (*samāvarta*) occurs. (Āk 1.24.135)
At that very moment, the man becomes a being with a divine body;
the mercury, when colored and transmuted, penetrates all metals. (Āk 1.24.136)

When the mercury has consumed equal portions [of the ingredients], one should grind it with the juices of medicinal herbs; having made it into a "lost-pounded" (naṣṭapiṣṭa) consistency, one should heat it according to the previous method. Āk 1.24.137.
But the divine *khoṭa* is born; it is a penetrator by means of a sixteenth part.
When bound through the application of *saṅkalikā*, it pierces ten times more than that. (Āk 1.24.138)
Alternatively, one bound with powder should pierce [the target] ten times more effectively;
likewise with *mṛgadūrvā*, *candravallī*, and *pakvabimbā*.
O beautiful goddess, one should grind together kāṅkṣīlā, karavīra, the seed of unmattaka, and a pala of kākāṇḍī. Āk_1,24.140.
The wise one should cause an equal amount of mercury to be mixed with equal gold and made into a paste;
or else, having purified it, he should mix equal mercury with equal [gold]. Āk 1.24.141.
One should grind the mahārasa powder with the juices of medicinal herbs; having ground it for three yāmas, the wise one should form it into a ball (golaka). Āk_1,24.142.
One should cause the ball placed in a blind crucible to dry in the shade; then, having applied a light *puṭa* and blown [with a bellows], it becomes a *khoṭa*, O Dear One. (Āk 1.24.143)

The extraction of mercury is neutralized by the juices of *mṛga*, *dūrvā*, and *uttamāsoma*, as well as by the roots of the three [plants] beginning with *lāṅgalī* and by asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*). Āk 1.24.144.
The wise one should cause a paste to be made joined with equal gold; or else, he should cause a paste of silver to be made with equal mercury. Āk 1.24.145.
By means of the sequential application as before, the *khoṭa* becomes excellent;
having placed it in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) on the ground, one should heat it with a fire of the intensity of a *karṣaka*. (Āk 1.24.146)
Then, by means of a powder-binding (*cūrṇabandha*) for one day and night or for three nights, that powder-binding effects a penetration (*vedha*) ten times greater [than before]. (Āk 1.24.147)
And mercury processed with *śūlinī* and combined with *srotoñjana*,
through the application of a paste as previously described, becomes an excellent *khoṭa*.
Srotoñjana, satagara, and mercury combined with the three creations (sṛṣṭitraya) will quickly become capable of enduring fire; such mercury performs all rites. Āk 1.24.149.
One should bind together golden mica, silver mica, copper mica, iron mica, tin mica, and lead mica, along with mercury. (Āk 1.24.150)
Just as medicine ground with whatever is available, endowed with great potency, [is used] with gold, silver, mercury, and likewise with iron, tin, and lead; Āk 1.24.151.

Having made a paste with these [substances], either individually or combined together in equal proportions, one should kill [the mercury] according to the previous procedure within a *garbhayantra* using a fire of chaff. (Āk 1.24.152)
Having given equal portions of the *sūtaka* again and again, repeatedly, there arises the various *khoṭa*, the great mercury bound with *kānta*. (Āk 1.24.153)
Through the application of *saṅkalikā*, piercing (*vedha*) becomes ten times more effective. [This is] the *nigalabandha* [method].
There are five [types]: *khoṭa*, *poṭa*, *bhasma*, *dhūlī*, and the fifth is *kalpa*. (Āk 1,24.154)
