Through these methods of binding and yoga, the fruit of all fetters arises:
the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, the seeds of binding, and *guggulu*. (Āk 1.24.155)

O beautiful one, having added double the amount of rock salt (*saindhava*), the wise practitioner should grind it; then, having formed a pill (*piṣṭikā*) with this paste, he should bind it. (Āk 1.24.156)
Having fashioned a very firm and auspicious crucible the size of a *bilva* fruit, one should place salt at the top and bottom and pour the mercury into the middle of the crucible. (Āk 1.24.157)
The wise one should place the powder of burnt conch-shell and other substances into the middle of the crucible,
and then firmly seal its opening with salt-clay.
One should cause it to be mixed with salt from a sandhole and have it dried in the shade;
this is called the "iron-shackle bond," which is not even told to one's own son. (Āk 1.24.159)
One should apply gentle heat to the earth using a fire of husks and grain-chaff for one day and night or three nights, having carefully applied the *puṭa* seal. (Āk 1.24.160)
One should bring mercury (*rasendra*) to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*) by heating it well with charcoal of *khadira* wood;
having repeatedly added *sauvīra*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and glass (*kāca*), one should purify it. (Āk 1.24.161)
When the mercury is not yet exhausted, it mingles with gold and a "reversion" (samāvarta) occurs;
one should effect that equal-part consumption using purified mercury. Āk 1.24.162.
One should heat the lord of juices (rasendra) according to the previous method and bring it to the state of a solid bolus (khoṭa).
Through the application of the saṅkalikā process, the penetration (vedha) shall be ten times greater.
One should grind the exudate from *palāśa* seeds, *kokilā*, *unmattavāruṇī*, combined with the juice of *śūlinī*, along with rock salt. (Āk 1.24.164)
Having made a wrapping with the paste, one should bind it with a chain, using a leaf of mica along with *vajra*, *arka* milk, and sea salt. (Āk 1.24.165)
Bound with these—tāpya, iron dross, sand, and clay—the great mercury of Pārada becomes fixed in its fetters. (Āk 1.24.166)
He does not transgress the boundary, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore;
he is the supreme restrainer with the fingers of oil, the sun, milk, and kataka. (Āk 1.24.167)
The seeds of *kākaviṭ* and *brahma*, *lāṅgalī*, and another called *nigala*;
*vākucī*, the seeds of *brahma*, and the bones of a crab, O beautiful one. (Āk 1.24.168)
One should prepare sea salt, Śāmbara salt, common salt, the best of fetters, the milky sap derived from *snuhī* and *arka*, and the seeds of *brahma*. (Āk 1.24.169)
One should grind seeds of *kanaka* with eight parts of salt;
another *nigala* consists of the roots of *gojihvā*, and another is [made from] female menstrual blood. (Āk 1.24.170)
Vākucī, seeds of Brahma, the milks of Snuhi and Arka, rock salt, Jvālinī, and crow dung constitute an excellent and superior formula for loosening bonds. (Āk 1.24.171)
Salt, borax, alkali, realgar, orpiment, and sulphur, as well as amlavetasa, mākṣika, and cinnabar, taken in equal parts; (Āk 1.24.172).
One should grind together the milk of *snuhī* and *arka*; this is the supreme binding.
One should wrap the paste with one of these bindings. (Āk 1.24.173)
Having prepared a *khoṭa* as before and placed it within a salt crucible (*loṇamūṣā*), one should perform the transmutation (*vedha*).
Now I shall describe the second method, the "Ball" (*golaka*), which is the supreme means for stabilizing the paste (*piṣṭikā*). (Āk 1.24.174)
Having ground rock salt, mica, and guggulu with the urine of a two-hoofed animal, one should wrap the resulting paste in clay eight times over. (Āk 1.24.175)
One should apply gentle heat to it on the ground using a fire of husks and grain-chaff for one day and night or three nights, and bring it to the state of *khoṭa* as before. Āk 1.24.176.
Vākucī, seeds of Brahmā, the sky, a pure gem, sauvarcala salt, saindhava salt, ṭaṅkaṇa, and likewise guggulu. Āk 1.24.177.
One should grind that urine very finely with the dust of *dvipadī* (two-footed insects);
having enveloped the paste with this powder, one should bring it to the state of a solid mass (*khoṭa*) as before. (Āk 1.24.178)
(The Procedure for the Intoxication of the Rasa;
First Method) Now,
O Supreme Goddess, I shall explain the intoxication of the rasa.
Bāhlīka, saindhava salt, kanyā, dhūśara, garlic, and vacā. (Āk 1.24.179)
One should grind the juice of all parts of the *meghanāda* (blue water lily) and *kākamācī* (black nightshade) until it is smooth;
having formed this into a ball, one should wrap it on the outside with *hiṅgu* (asafetida). (Āk 1.24.180)

Having placed it in a salt-preserved vessel, one should cook it for a day over a fierce fire; when it has cooled to the touch of one's own body, the liquid situated at the bottom of the vessel [is extracted]. Āk 1.24.181.
Having taken the powder and bound it with a thick, double-layered cloth,
one should place an equal amount of sulfur above it in the *somānala* apparatus.
Having added the fragrance again, one should cook it; thus the fragrance becomes sixfold.
O Goddess, that mercury, once processed (*mūrchita*), digests [the essence] and destroys all diseases. (Āk 1.24.183)
(Second method:
One should grind sulphur and iron chloride in equal parts with purified mercury for one *yāma*, making it smooth, and place it inside a glass flask. Āk_1,24.184.
Having coated the flask with seven layers of clay and rags, one should dry it in the heat;
then one should cook the flask in a sand-bath apparatus for twelve praharas.
O Goddess, that mercury is born; it becomes liquefied and colored.
(The third method:
Half a part of mercury and one part of sulfur should be ground together for two watches in the hot sun. (Āk 1.24.186)
Then, one should grind it for three days with the juices of white jayantī;
thereafter, having formed it into a ball, one should seal it within a crucible. (Āk 1.24.187)
Having dried it, one should blow upon it slightly and then cast that heated substance into water;
having taken up that mercury (rasendra), one should saturate it with the juices of *gokṣura*. Āk 1.24.188.
The mercury becomes stunned (*mūrchita*), auspicious, and the remover of all diseases;
(the characteristics of bound mercury:
it is imperishable, easily fusible, radiant, pure, and heavy. (Āk 1.24.189)
Furthermore, when it bursts and returns [to its original state], that bound mercury is called "bound by leeches" (*jalūkābandha*);
[this refers to] the leech-like binding through rubbing (*mardanajalūkā*).
One-eighth part of the mercury should consist of gold or indeed of lead.
One should grind ripe *śleṣmātaka* fruit, seeds of *kokilākṣaka*, and the powder of sesame oil-cake in a heated mortar. (Āk 1.24.191)
One should also pour the juice of the five parts of the *śālmali* tree into that; it should be massaged until a leech-like growth (*jalūkā*) arises, and then one should cast it away. (Āk 1.24.192)
One should grind together camphor, vākucī oil, rock salt, borax, long pepper, and the hairs of the *kapikacchu* plant with water. (Āk 1.24.193)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, by placing this aforementioned leech in a heated mortar for three weeks, a divine leech called Mardana is produced. Āk 1.24.194.
During the fertile period of women, however, it should be applied into the cavity of the womb; it removes their intoxication and pride, yet causes them to become overwhelmed by passion. (Āk 1.24.195)
In childhood, the leech should be applied at eight finger-breadths; in youth, it should be ten finger-breadths;
and for those who are mature, it should be twelve finger-breadths. (Āk 1.24.196)
Whoever wears that [substance] upon the head, his virility shall become firm.
[This is] Manmathajalūkā;
one-eighth part of mercury, along with gold or lead. (Āk 1.24.197)
The bark of the *śālmalī*, *hastikanda*, the root of *nīla*, and the leaves of *muni*—
all these should be ground without weariness in a heated mortar with their juices.
Having added ripe śleṣmātaka fruit, kokilākṣaka seeds, and the well-ripened pulp of a bilva fruit, one should grind them together. (Āk 1.24.199)
As long as the leeches are produced, one should place camphor and other substances therein as before and grind them in a heated mortar for twenty-one days. (Āk 1.24.200)
The leech named Manmatha, as before, yields its fruit;
[it is] Kandarpajalūkā.
One-eighth part of mercury should be combined with gold or even with lead. (Āk 1,24.201)
One should grind ginger, *bhṛṅgī*, *varā*, honey, goat’s milk, cow’s ghee, and cow’s urine together in a heated mortar for twenty-one days. *Āk* 1.24.202.
As long as the leech is produced from camphor and other ingredients as before, it should be rubbed for twenty-one days; thus a beautiful leech is produced. (Āk 1.24.203)
O Queen of the Gods, the one called Kandarpa bestows fruits as previously described.
(Madanajalūkā) One should rub four niṣkas of mercury in a mortar for three days. Āk 1.24.204.
One should gradually add three palas of mango resin and milk from a large *śamī* tree, sufficient for the purpose of kneading. (Āk 1.24.205)
This plant called Madanā, known as Jalūkā, arises as a bringer of auspiciousness for men,
acting like a liquefier of fire and ghee for women who are intoxicated with passion and pride.
By means of the sequential application as before, it becomes a means for arresting the emission of semen;
being of various colors and likewise transparent, it is held in the womb like a leech. (Āk 1.24.207)
That which is bound by birth is characterized by the attachment of a leech.
Āk, 1, 25 (Paribhāṣā): I shall proclaim the technical rules; listen to them with careful attention.
(The Section on Medicine:
O Goddess, half [of the mixture] is perfected mercury, and one-third is gold ash. Āk 1.25.1.
One-quarter part of silver ash, one-sixth part of copper ash, one-eighth part of magnetite and mica, and one-sixteenth part of the nine gems; Āk_1,25.2.

Aiming for the Lord of Mercury (Raseśvara), one should give [the gift] to a wise physician of mercury, a perfected master of mercury (rasācārya), for the sake of attaining one's desired goal. Āk 1.25.3.

(Kajjalī and Paṅkarasa: When mercury is rubbed with mineral substances such as sulphur and others that are free from moisture, until it becomes very smooth and resembles collyrium, it is called *kajjalī*. (Āk 1.25.4)
When that [substance] is also rubbed in a good liquid, it is known as *pākarasa* (the essence of digestion).
[This is called] *piṣṭī*.
Then, in a mortar, one should take mercury equal to one part of *arka*, and sulphur equal to half a *niṣka*, even in minute quantities.
When ground under the intense heat of the sun, it becomes a paste in the form of fresh butter. Āk 1.25.5.
Having ground the mercury together with sulfur and milk in a mortar, [one should proceed].
Through grinding, it becomes a paste; that is considered *piṣṭī* by others.
A *pātanapiṣṭī* is a paste made with mercury and one-fourth part gold. (Āk 1.25.7)
That would be a *pātanapiṣṭī* made from silver and so forth— namely,
a gold-powder (*hemapiṣṭī*) or a silver-powder (*tārapiṣṭī*)— wherein the silver or the gold has been treated with mercury, sulfur, and other such substances. (Āk 1.25.8)
And though that mass of gold and silver was repeatedly drawn out, even after throwing away the dross at the edge of the gold, its color did not diminish. (Āk 1.25.9)
The seed prepared by means of gold-extraction is the coloring agent for mercury;
having repeatedly cast molten copper combined with *tīkṣṇa* [iron] into it, (the metal becomes) *lohaka*. (Āk 1.25.10)
Excellent metal emerges from the juice of the *likuca* fruit when it is mixed with its own fragrance.
Gold that has been colored by this—whether it be "red gold" (*hemaraktī*) or "silver-red" (*tāraraktī*)—is designated as *hemaraktī*. (Āk 1.25.11)
Cast into molten gold, it produces an excellence of color;
it also serves to dye silver and brings about the coloring of seeds. (Āk 1.25.12)
In this very way, one should prepare the beautiful *tāraraktī*, which indeed dyes silver and even dyes seeds. (Āk 1.25.13)

(candrānaladalam) A different metal processed with mercury—whether dead, bound, or otherwise—is transformed from white into yellow; this is indeed the well-known "petal" (*dala*) of the Moon and Fire. (Āk 1.25.14)
Combined with mercury bound by the immortal radiance (ābhāsa), or processed with another metal, that petal indeed becomes white or yellow. Āk 1.25.15.
Iron that has been heated and quenched seven times in its own liquid is beautiful; two *palas* of this pair, or alternatively, two *palas* of copper ash [should be used]. (Āk 1.25.16)
Having placed everything in a crucible, one should heat it firmly seven times; that is called ayonāga, which is effective for both the body and metals. (Āk 1.25.17)
By means of the essence, its pill is prepared in a sāraṇā apparatus; when held in the mouth, it destroys all urinary diseases without exception. (Āk 1.25.18)
It provides firmness to the teeth and makes the eyes like those of a vulture;
likewise, it cures other diseases born of the bodily constituents (kṣetraja) as well as ailments occurring above the clavicle. (Āyurveda 1.25.19)
Copper killed with honey and raised [to its original state] ten times, and likewise purified lead— these two, each weighing four *pala*, [are to be used]. (Āk 1.25.20)
When blue antimony has been struck [with mercury] and rises up again seven times, this is indeed proclaimed as the perfected *śulbanāga*. (Āk 1.25.21)
The lord of elixirs (sūtendra) prepared by him, when held in the mouth of men, destroys the entire multitude of urinary disorders completely within just one month. (Āk 1.25.22)
By eating wholesome food for a year, one becomes free of graying hair along with wrinkles;
possessing the keen vision of a vulture and a radiant gaze, one is endowed with complete health. (Āk 1.25.23)
(Piñjarī):
When iron is cast into another metal, heated, and quenched in a liquid, it becomes pale-yellow in luster; this is designated as *piñjarī*. (Āk 1.25.24)
The sixteen parts of the moon and likewise the twelve parts of the sun, when combined together, are called "Candrārka" (Moon-Sun). Āk 1.25.25.

(Quenching): If another metal is cast from a blowpipe into a metal being held [in the crucible], that is called quenching (*nirvāpaṇa*) by physicians; indeed, it is also known as *nirvāhaṇa*. (Āk 1.25.26)

One should cast the additive (nirvāhaṇa) into the substance to be processed in equal proportion; likewise, the additive to be sown (āvāpya) or the seed to be sown (vāpanīya) is treated like the visible [substance] when its portion is seen. Āk 1.25.27.
(Vāritara [Definition]):
That which, when dead, floats upon water—that indeed is vāritara.
(Rekhāpūrṇa [Definition])
That which is rubbed between the thumb and the forefinger enters into the space between the lines. Āk 1.25.28.
That dead iron is designated by the name *rekhāpūrṇa*. (The characteristics of *niruttha* ash:
When combined with molasses, *guñjā*, things pleasant to the touch, honey, and clarified butter... [Āk 1.25.29]
It does not return to its original state; thus it is called "non-rebirth" (*apunarbhava*).
When [the gold] is combined with iron and smelted together with silver, it would be licked [by the tongue]. (Āk 1.25.30)
Then that iron is said to be "irreversible" (*niruttha*), meaning it does not undergo rebirth;
likewise, if silver or copper is smelted, it will certainly not adhere to the copper. (Āk 1.25.31)

Then, when it has acquired its specific color through the particular process of extraction (*nirvāhaṇa*), the best of physicians should consider that seed to be "pure" (*niruttha*) silver. (Āk 1.25.32)
That which is soft and variegated in appearance is called the seed (*bīja*);
indeed, this very thing is designated by physicians as the "extraction" (*uttāraṇa*). (Āk 1,25.33)
The destruction of one of two mixed metals by means of a blowpipe,
after it has been blown [into a flame], is declared to be *tāḍana*. (Āk 1.25.34)
(Dhānyābhra):
Powdered mica combined with rice and tied in a cloth is placed in sour gruel (kāñjika);
when it has emerged from the cloth after being rubbed out, it is called dhānyābhra. (Āk 1.25.35)

When the essence (sattva), combined with alkaline, acidic, and liquefying agents, is heated in a mineral furnace, that refined substance which emerges from it is designated as "essence" (sattva). Āk 1.25.36.

(On the single *kolīśaka*): When [the mercury] has reached the ears of the crucible by means of the blowing of the *kokilā* from the summit of the furnace, it is considered a single *kolīśaka*. (Āk 1.25.37)
(Kokilas suitable for fomentation, etc.):
*śikhitrāḥ*, *pāvakocchiṣṭāḥ*, *mṛtāṅgārāḥ*, and *kokilāḥ*—these are synonyms for *kokila* charcoal, and they are interchangeable with one another. (Āk 1.25.38)
For the liquefaction and the extraction of the essence (*sattvapāta*) of charcoal from wood, *mādhūka* and *khadira* woods are auspicious;
for difficult liquefaction, bamboo is used, and for steaming (*svedana*), *bādara* wood is auspicious. (Āk 1.25.39)

(Regarding mercury extracted by means of cinnabar: That mercury which is drawn out from [mercury] situated within the apparatus called *vidyādhara*, having been rubbed with the juice of fresh ginger, is said to be "extracted by means of cinnabar" (*hiṅgulākṛṣṭa*). Āk 1,25.40.
(Tin attracted by sound:
Brass joined with a small amount of tin, when struck by a tin tube, releases that tin; indeed, that copper is called "attracted by sound" (*ghoṣākṛṣṭa*). (Āk 1.25.41)
(Regarding the secret serpent-lore: Twenty palas of pure snake [flesh], having been made into a paste, should be rubbed upon a stone with silver-milk (*rūpikā-dugdha*). (Āk 1.25.42)
Having enclosed it within a pair of earthen saucers, one should cook it using the "boar's pit" (kroḍapuṭa) method;
one should carefully cook it that many times until ash is produced. Āk 1.25.43.

Having thoroughly rubbed that [substance] with jaggery, guggulu, guñjā, clarified butter, and borax, one should seal it inside a crucible; then, having raised it again by heating, [one proceeds]. Āk 1.25.44.
Having again prepared a wheel with that [substance], and having smeared it with mercury weighing one pala, one should smear it with the juice of white *arka* and with realgar (*śilā*). (Āk 1.25.45)

In this manner, one should indeed administer twenty measures (vāra) using the "elephant-step" (gajapuṭa) method; moreover, at every single measure, one should certainly perform the rite of raising the Nāga.
One should thoroughly soak it ten times with the liquid of blue light;
thus is that lead perfected, remaining in the measure of one *karṣa*. (Āk 1.25.47)
This excellent [method] for the alchemy of mercury has been proclaimed by the one known as Guhyanāga;
when this metal called *nāga* is melted in the measure of one *niṣka*, [the result is achieved]. (Āk 1.25.48)
He certainly swallows a golden probe a hundred thousand times his own size;
heated with oil, that gold surely adheres to him and he certainly vomits it up. (Āk 1.25.49)

This is declared to be the Guhyana-ga, the Bhairava of the Independent Power (Svacchandabhairava). Having repeatedly and firmly smelted a sharp, excellent naga endowed with blue collyrium, [one attains the goal]. (Āk 1.25.50)
That which is soft, black, and melts quickly is called a "superior nāga.
(Regarding *utthāpana*:
The re-emergence of one who has died is designated by the term *utthāpana*. (Āk 1.25.51)
(Ḍhālana):
The pouring of a liquid substance into another liquid is considered ḍhālana. (Capala)
A nāga weighing thirty palas, rubbed with the milk of a bhānu plant.
One should crush it and then seal it in a crucible until only one karṣa remains; even after a thousand such sealings, it never undergoes depletion. Āk 1.25.53.
"This Nāgasambhava has been instructed by the commentators to be 'capala' (fickle/unstable);
indeed, in this manner, even vaṅga should be made 'capala,' without a doubt. (Āk 1.25.54)
Mercury that has been touched by a hand that has itself been touched by that [substance] alone becomes bound;
such mercury is recommended for alchemical transmutations of metals (*dhātuvāda*), but not for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*). (Āk 1.25.55)
For this was proclaimed by the Lord of the World named Karpaṇa:
[the powder] of *bhrāmaka* and *aśmarī*, finely ground and combined with a fifth part. (Āk 1.25.56)
One should grind it for one day with the root-water of the *kumārī* plant, or else continuously for one day with the fresh juice of *śārṅgerī*. (Āk 1.25.57)
In this manner, one should grind the purified mercury for two days with an equal amount of lead,
and likewise with an equal amount of tin.
One should apply it ground finely with ten *niṣkas* of *rasendra*;
having combined it with the primary paste, one should triturate it as before. (Āk 1.25.59)
Then, having made a paste of mercury and *rasaka* with *śāṇa* and *rasendra*, one should combine it with the previous substances and the previous medicinal powders. (Āk 1.25.60)
Then, having washed it with warm sour gruel (kāñjika), one should dry it;
[one should take] half a pala of purified mercury along with eight guñjās of the juice of *sasyaka*. Āk 1.25.61.
Having ground it with fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika), one should prepare pills the size of black pepper;
then, having placed them in a *vajramūṣā* crucible and secured the seal at the joint. (Āk 1.25.62)
One should indeed blow [the furnace] properly with nine bellows equipped with fire-tips;
then, having gathered the essence located within the crucible from all sides, [one should proceed]. (Āk 1.25.63)
One should heat it in an open crucible and purify it with a blowpipe;
for that essence [is purified] by ten *śāṇas* of ash and salt. (Āk 1.25.64)

Having ground it with sour gruel (kāñjika), one should purify it by means of a sealed crucible (puṭayoga); when it has reached the measure of three niṣkas, [one should treat it] with the previously mentioned ash. Āk 1.25.65.
Having blown upon the naga [mercury] eighty times, one should indeed cause it to be extinguished; by this much, that previously prepared elixir is by no means diminished. (Āk 1.25.66)
This [mineral] has been designated as *capala* by Śambhu, the Lord of the World;
by means of this as well, mercury is quickly and easily bound, just as before. (Āk 1.25.67)
When that [mercury] has been processed ten times with the powdered roots of *kāravallī*, it becomes liberated from the serpent and consumes its entire meal. (Āk 1.25.68)

The mercury, having digested its meal, becomes exceedingly superior in quality when it is easily processed in an open crucible; indeed, this mercury brings about the perfection of both the body and base metals. (Āk 1.25.69)

(Washed by earth-cobra: Having been washed with the urine and dung of a cobra and thus having its impurities removed, that which is black in color is indeed called "washed" (*dhauta*) by the alchemists. (ĀK 1.25.70)
(Dvandvānam):
The fusion of two substances through heating is proclaimed as *dvandvāna*.
(Bhañjanī)
When the additive is greater than the numerator by one unit, it should be made homogeneous with the denominator.
A colored paste made from fibers, or a "bhañjanī" fashioned by a speaker;
a *phullikā* produced from the paste of *pataṅgī*; and the state of silver or gold in metal. (Āk 1.25.72)
Having remained for a few days, this [dye] fades away; it is considered *phullikā*.
It is like the color of a moth (*pataṅgīrāga*), produced from copper partially saturated with juice, or from another [substance] after a long time. (Āk 1.25.73)
That which is poured out is designated as *pataṅgīrāga*;
indeed, it is that which is produced by the casting of other substances, such as metals, into the molten [mass]. (This is *āvāpa*). Āk 1.25.74.
That is considered the addition (*āvāpa*), the counter-addition (*pratīvāpa*), and the covering (*acchādana*).
(Regarding the consecration:
when the metal has been liquefied and remains in the fire, one should pause for eight *nimeṣas*. (Āk 1,25.75)
The sprinkling of water around [the vessel] is known as *abhiṣeka*.
Having caused either lead or tin to melt, one should pour it over [the object] a hundred times. (Āk 1.25.76)

The beating of that substance with a liquid upon the aforementioned material is indeed its consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Casting the heated [substance] into water is *nirvāpa*; it is also called *tapana*. (Āk 1.25.77)
The process of pouring [the metal] back and forth should be performed with a very pure molten metal;
when the fire has bright flames and is accompanied by the rising of white smoke, it is called *śuddhāvarta*. (Āk 1.25.78)
That time, when the vital essence (sattva) emerges, should be known as the "Pure Revolution" (śuddhāvarta).
When, during the blowing [of the bellows], a flame resembling molten metal is seen, it is the "Line Revolution" (rekhāvarta). (Āk 1.25.79)
This inclination toward fluidity is called a "swirl" (*rekhāvarta*).
That which is cold within one's own limbs yet hot externally, being cold while situated in fire, is said to be "cold to one's own limbs" (*svāṅgaśītala*). (Āk 1.25.80)
That which draws out the coldness of fire is called *vahniśīta* (fire-cold);
it is indeed [the method of] *svedana* (fomentation) for one situated in a *ḍolāyantra* (swinging apparatus), using alkaline substances, acids, or medicinal herbs. (Āk 1,25.81)
Cooking, known as "sweating," causes the loosening of impurities;
it is performed with the aforementioned medicinal herbs, along with all types of sour liquids and fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*). (Rubbing. Āk 1.25.82.
Pounding, known as "rubbing" (*mardana*), destroys external impurities. (Mūrchana:
Rubbing with the prescribed medicinal substances causes the loss of the "ground-to-paste" state (*naṣṭapiṣṭitva*). (Āk 1,25.83)
For that *tanmūrcchana* is the destruction of the sheaths consisting of water, earth, and fire;
it is indeed the reduction to a state of being ground [into powder] (*piṣṭitva*) through the destruction of one's own form—this is what is called "the pulverized" (*naṣṭapiṣṭi*). (Āk 1.25.84)
Increase [of the mercury] by means of the "conquered" (*jita*) flux is called *naṣṭapiṣṭi*.
(Regarding *utthāpana*:
It is the restoration of its original form again through the application of heat from sweating and other such methods. (Āk 1.25.85)
This is called "its arousal," which destroys the impairment of fainting (*mūrchā-vyāpatti*).
Regarding "falling" (*pātanam*):
it is the [movement] upwards, downwards, and sideways of the mercury that has been rubbed with the prescribed medicinal herbs while situated within the apparatus (*yantra*).
The act of causing [the poison] to exit is said to be performed with the perception of "causing it to fall"; it destroys the casing produced by contact with the Vaṅga serpent. Āk 1.25.86.
(Blocking:
For three days, [one should apply] a juice mixed with water and rock salt. Āk 1.25.87.
Stability is that which nourishes within the *kumbha*; this is called "restraint" (*rodhana*).
[It is] for the sake of ceasing the fickleness of that [vital energy] which has gained its potency through restraint. (Āk 1.25.88)
The sweating that is performed upon the vessel is indeed called *niyamana*. (Dīpana:
It is combined with minerals, stones, roots, and so forth, within the interior of the vessel. (Āk 1.25.89)

Sweating for three days for the sake of the meal-portion is considered by the wise to be "dīpana" (the kindling). (Regarding the measure of the meal-portion: this is the quantity of the mercury to be consumed, consisting of the substance to be eaten. (Āk 1.25.90)

It is said to be "this much," which is described as the measure of the morsel (*grāsa*). Furthermore, *jāraṇā* consists of the circulation of the morsel, the melting of the womb (*garbhadrāvaṇa*), and likewise digestion (*jāraṇa*). (Āk 1.25.91)
Thus, the threefold *jāraṇā* has been described by the excellent commentators;
furthermore, there are three other designations: *grāsa*, *piṇḍa*, and *parīṇāma*. (Āk 1.25.92)
Digestion (*jāraṇā*) is considered to be of two kinds: with mouth (*samukhā*) and without mouth (*nirmukhā*).
Digestion without mouth is said to occur through the taking up of seed (*bīja*) in due proportion. (Āk 1.25.93)
(Purification and Incineration by Confrontation) Pure gold and silver are designated as the "seed" (*bīja*).
The introduction of the seed in a proportion of sixty-four parts is called the "mouth" (*mukha*). (Āk 1,25.94)
When this has been done, the mercury becomes possessed of a mouth, eager to swallow, and becomes capable of devouring even hard metals. (Āk 1.25.95)
This indeed is called "face-to-face" (*samukhī*), the digestion of the nectar of digestion (*jāraṇāmṛtajāraṇā*).
Through the union with divine medicinal herbs, it remains manifest within the crucibles. (The "faceless" [digestion], *nirmukhacāraṇā*. Āk 1,25.96.
He who possesses the mouth of a *rākṣasa* consumes all metals and other substances;
*cāraṇā* is considered to be the casting of the mercury-bolus into the stomach. (Āk 1,25.97)
(Garbhadruti): The melting of that which has been swallowed within the womb is declared to be *garbhadruti*.
(Bāhyadruti).
Having indeed liquefied the dense sentient beings and so forth externally, [one should proceed]. Āk 1.25.98.
For the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of the lord of mercury (*rasendra*), that is called external liquefaction (*bāhyadruti*).
It possesses non-adhesiveness, fluidity, brilliance, and likewise lightness. (Āk 1.25.99)
Non-union with the fluxing agent (*sūta*) is the fivefold characteristic of liquefaction (*druti*);
through the application of medicinal herbs, clarified butter, and so forth, the metals, ores, and other substances are [liquefied] at all times. (Āk 1.25.100)
That which arises in the form of liquefaction is proclaimed as *druti* (melting);
(*jāraṇā*) is the transformation of the swallowed [substance] through the application of *biḍa*, mechanical devices, and so forth. Āk 1.25.101.
This is called *jāraṇā* (digestion); its varieties are in the tens of millions.
[It is performed] with *viḍa*, alkalies, acids, sulphur and other substances, as well as with urines and salts. (Āk 1.25.102)
That is proclaimed as *viḍa* for the sake of digesting the swallowed mercury (*rasagrāsa*);
for it is through the digestion of perfected seeds, *sattva*, and so forth, that the mercury is indeed colored (*rañjana*). (Āk 1.25.103)
That which generates a yellow or other color is declared to be *rañjana* (coloring);
indeed, *sāraṇā* (coating) is the casting of gold and so forth into a crucible containing oil. (Āk 1.25.104)
Sāraṇā is proclaimed as that which increases the intensity of penetration (*vedha*) in metal;
indeed, it is mercury itself when cast into a substance combined with a penetrating medicinal agent. (Vedha) Āk 1.25.105.

That which is known by the experts as *vedha* (piercing) is said to be of many kinds: *lepa* (smearing), *kṣepa* (throwing), *kunta* (spear), that called *śabda* (sound), and that designated *dhūma* (smoke). (The varieties of piercing) Āk 1.25.106.
(Leepavedha):
By means of an application (*lepa*), one makes base metal into gold or likewise silver;
that is to be known as *lepa-vedha*, and in this case, the *puṭa* is the "pig-shaped" (*saukaraka*) one. (Āk 1,25.107)
(Projection Piercing): The casting of molten metal is known as piercing by projection (*kṣepavedha*). (Spear Piercing): *Kuntavedha*.
And that which is the impact of a liquid substance held by tongs. // Āk 1.25.108 //
The *kuntavedha* is said to be that which produces qualities such as goldness;
the *dhūpavedha* occurs when smoke is produced from the essence cast inside a fire that is smoldering. (Āk 1.25.109)
The production of gold and other [precious metals] from base metal through the process of fuming is called *dhūmavedha*;
indeed, *śabdavedha* occurs when the mercury is held in the mouth and the metal is blown upon with a blowpipe. (Āk 1.25.110)

The production of the nature of gold or silver is proclaimed as "piercing by sound" (*śabdavedha*). (Utpāṭana) is the removal of impurities and the like from a massed substance by means of mercury (*sūta*). Āk 1.25.111.
The manifestation of color is said to be its extraction (*utpāṭana*);
[this is] *svedana*, [performed] by sealing [the substance] with alkaline salts, acids, and medicinal herbs inside a vessel with great care. (Āk 1.25.112)
That which is buried in the ground is declared to be *svedana* (perspiration);
it is the careful confinement within a vessel of mercury combined with medicinal herbs, [known as] *saṃnyāsa*. (Āk 1,25.113)
The constant casting [of the mercury] into the interior of a crucible joined with fire is called *saṃnyāsa*.
These two—*sveda* and *saṃnyāsa*—are certainly the two methods for the King of Mercury (*rasarāja*). (The virtues of *svedana* and *saṃnyāsa*) Āk 1,25.114.
They produce the power of qualities and likewise bring about swift pervasion.
Āk, 1, 26 (on instruments):
That by which the *rasa* is restrained is called an instrument (*yantra*).
(1. The mortar-machine:
The mortar-machine is said to be of two kinds for tasks such as grinding and so forth. Āk 1.26.1.
O Goddess, the mortar may be made of iron or even of stone;
the stone suitable for the mortar should be blue or dark, smooth, firm, and heavy. (Āk 1.26.2)
The *khalvayantra* (mortar machine) is said to be of two kinds for the purpose of grinding mercury and other substances.
It is sixteen finger-breadths in height and nine finger-breadths in width. (Āk 1.26.3)
The rubbing board should be twenty-four finger-breadths long and twelve finger-breadths wide;
alternatively, it may be twenty finger-breadths long and ten finger-breadths in height. Āk 1.26.4.
That mortar should be known as a standard measure; it is excellent for the grinding of medicinal juices.
The mortar is circular and sixteen finger-breadths in width. (Āk 1.26.5)
It should be four finger-breadths deep and extremely smooth in the middle; the base should be flattened for massaging, and it should have a handle at the top for easy grasping. (Āk 1.26.6)
For this circular mortar is exceedingly pleasant for grinding;
likewise, one may have an iron mortar made of magnetite (kāntaloha) of this same kind.
Below, a trough (*droṇikā*) should be constructed, suitable for igniting the fire.
It should indeed be nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height, equal to one *kalā* (one-sixteenth) in its length, and nine finger-breadths in width; likewise, it should be six finger-breadths deep.

At the neck, it should be two finger-breadths wide, very smooth, shaped like a half-moon, and provided with a grinding surface (*gharṣa*) ten finger-breadths long; this is considered the instrument known as the *khalva*. (Āk 1,26.8)
In this case, a charioteer weighing five palas should be crushed for the sake of purification. Āk 1.26.9.
One should indeed purify these and other substances according to their respective suitability.
(The heated mortar):
A mortar for iron is nine fingers deep and six fingers wide. Āk 1.26.10.
The pestle is eight finger-breadths long; this indeed is called the heated mortar.
Having fashioned the hearth in the shape of a mortar and having filled it with charcoal, [one proceeds]. (Āk 1.26.11)
Having placed that [substance] in it, one should indeed blow upon its side with a bellows;
therein the paste, well-combined with alkaline salts and acids, should be thoroughly rubbed. (Āk 1.26.12)
When heated, it flows out with extreme velocity; of this there is no doubt.
When processed with kāntaloha iron, this mercury becomes ten-million-fold more potent. (Āk 1.26.13)
(2. The Khavalabhīya or Valabhīya instrument): In an iron vessel of the instrument, there are two rings on the sides;
a similarly shaped but much smaller vessel with a compartment for the illumination of the rings. Āk 1.26.14.
Having placed it upon the previous vessel, one should pour the condensed liquid onto a small vessel; then, having filled the large vessel with *kāñjika* vinegar, [one should proceed]. (Āk 1.26.15)
One should thus heat it for two watches (six hours) for the purpose of raising the mercury;
that is the *khavalabhī* apparatus, which brings about the excellence of the mercury. (Āk 1.26.16)
In a vessel made of fine, beautiful material, the essence will become more excellent.
(3. *Ūrdhvapātanayantra*) It should be exactly eight finger-breadths in measure, perfectly circular, and flattened at the base. Āk_1,26.17 //
From four finger-breadths below the neck, it is provided with a hollow channel,
four finger-breadths in width, deepened, and firmly bound.
And such a vessel at its base is sixteen finger-breadths in width, and it is provided with a handle nine finger-breadths in width. (Āk 1.26.19)
Having poured liquid into the first jar, one should place another jar upside down over it;
this [upper jar] should be concave on top and surrounded by a firm rim. (Āk 1.26.20)
One should pour water into a trough-shaped vessel and ignite a fire beneath it;
this is indeed the *ūrdhvapātana* (upward-throwing) apparatus described by Nandin. (Āk 1.26.21)
(4. The downward-descending apparatus):
One should place another shallow dish, turned upside down, upon that vessel; this dish should have its inner surface smeared with mercury. ĀK 1.26.22.
Having cast it into a muddy pit, one should set fire to its head;
this is indeed proclaimed as the "downward-falling" machine (adhaḥpātanayantra). Āk 1.26.23.
(5. The Tiryakpātana yantra:
One should pour the mercury into a long jar provided with a bent lower nozzle;
one should indeed insert that nozzle into the interior of the belly of another jar. (Āk 1.26.24)
There, having properly sealed the lower parts of the two jars with clay, one should kindle a fierce fire beneath the jar containing the mercury. Āk 1.26.25.
One should pour sweet, cool water into the other jar;
this is indeed called *tiryakpātana* by the commentators (*vārttikas*). (Āk 1.26.26)
Indeed, a triad of yantras has been taught for the three types of *pātana*; without these *pātanas*, the mercury (*sūta*) incurs excessive defects. (Āk 1.26.27)
Why is he not liberated from those three faults by means of the three upward leaps, through the two-fold division of ripening and the mutual conjunction of substances? (Āk 1.26.28)
Indeed, by shifting the contents from one vessel to another, various qualities may arise;
for instance, rice grains might become broken by the water in a mortar, or they might be deprived of their moisture. (Āk 1.26.29)
The very act of causing it to fall is proclaimed as the "great purification" (*mahāśuddhi*), known as *taṇḍulī*.
(6. *Kacchapayantra*) One should place [the substance] into a wide-mouthed vessel filled with water. Āk_1,26.30.
Furthermore, having properly prepared a wide and level basin in its center with clay, one should place mercury in the middle of it. (Āk 1.26.31)

Having applied *biḍa* salt both above and below, and having carefully sealed it with a *malla* [lid], the *puṭa* is applied according to the appropriate method; that is what is described. (Āk 1.26.32)
Indeed, that apparatus known as the *kacchapa* (tortoise) has been described for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury;
having fashioned an iron crucible provided with a circular base, [one should employ] this intermediate apparatus. (7. Intermediate Apparatus) Āk_1,26.33.
It should be measured by a span (*vitasti*), fashioned from gold or made of iron, or even produced from bell-metal; it should be worn two finger-breadths below the neck.
One should provide a ring two finger-breadths wide at the middle of the neck,
serving as a holder for the lid, with a bracelet as broad as a tamarind leaf.
Having placed a vessel with its opening covered, its neck intact, its joints joined, and its base free from holes, one should indeed turn it face downwards. (Āk 1.26.36)
One should suspend it by means of a mechanical device at the top, having restrained and dried it;
then one should place the rim of the vessel to maintain the heat of the *puṭa*. (Āk 1.26.37)
Such a yantra would be known as "intermediate";
by means of this, one should digest (jārayet) mercury, even that which has been liquefied and placed within a crucible. Āk 1.26.38.
(8. The Tāpikāyantra) Having made a crucible of clay, firm and measuring one cubit [aratni], very solid in its middle part and provided with a two-finger-wide opening; Āk_1,26.39.
One should place a khārī vessel made of kāntaloha over the substance, and fill the crucible on all sides with purified sand. Āk 1.26.40.
Having placed it upon the hearth, and repeatedly adding liquid dungs, one should then kindle the fire until the flame reaches the size of a big toe. (Āk 1.26.41)
One should digest all substances such as iron and mica over the mercury;
this is called the *tāpikāyantra*, which is easy to use for the digestion of mercury. (Āk 1.26.42)

(9. Garbhayantra) Having placed substances such as mercury into a vessel, and having again placed gold and other materials into a crucible, one should then add acids and salts on top and cook it over a furnace; that is the *pratigarbhayantra*. Āk_1,26.43.
(Regarding the *garbhayantra*):
One should then very carefully seal the *khorī* with the *malla*, or having placed the substance in the *sthālī* or the *mallā* or the *khorī*, one should seal it with the *malla*. (Āk 1.26.44)
Having cast [the substance] such as silk cloth and sealed it, the cooking process takes place in the *garbhayantra* (inner vessel apparatus).
A circular iron cup with a curved tip and an upward-pointing handle is the *pālikāyantra* (ladle-shaped apparatus). (10. *pālikāyantra*) Āk 1,26.45.
This is indeed the *pālikā* apparatus for the purpose of digesting the *bali* [mercury];
it is a water-receptacle of four *prasthas*, with a mouth-opening of four finger-breadths. (11. The *ghaṭī* apparatus) Āk_1,26.46.
This is declared to be the water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*); it is also remembered as the "filling" (*āpyāyana*) [wheel].
Having fashioned a circular pit and having placed a jar (*malla*) therein—(12. *iṣṭikāyantra*). Āk 1,26.47.
Having placed there a beautiful brick in the center of the pit, one should construct a rim around the pit, one finger-breadth in height. (Āk 1.26.48)
Having placed the mercury there, one should throw a cloth over the mouth of the pit;
then one should add sulfur and close its opening with a crucible lid. (Āk 1.26.49)

Having properly sealed the space between the two brick-enclosures with clay, one should apply a *puṭa* (furnace) made of forest lotuses known as the "pigeon" (*kapota*), but not exceeding that measure. (Āk 1.26.50)
This is the *iṣṭikāyantra*; by means of it, one should digest the sulphur (*gandhaka*).
Having placed [the crucible] upon a pot and having properly sealed the pot, [one proceeds]. (13. Vidyādharayantra) Āk_1,26.51.
Having poured water into an upper vessel, one should ignite a fire beneath it;
this is the Vidyādhara yantra for the purpose of extracting cinnabar. (Āk 1.26.52)
(14. The Ḍamaruka apparatus) By placing an inverted vessel over another vessel, [the contents] are sealed;
that apparatus is called the ḍamaruka, and it is beneficial for the purpose of binding mercury. Āk_1,26.53.
(15. The Navel Apparatus) One should make a pit in the center of a wrestling arena; therein one should place mercury together with sulphur.
Around the pit, one should construct a wall three finger-breadths high. (Ākāśabhairava-tantra 1,26.54)
Then, one should properly cover it with a crucible shaped like a cow’s udder, having sealed it thoroughly with clay mixed with water, as will be described here. (Āk 1.26.55)
The fine dust of digested dross (*kiṭṭa*), mixed like a linctus with a decoction of *barbūraka* and combined with powdered jaggery, [is to be used]. (Āk 1.26.56)
This is indeed called *jalamṛt* (water-clay), which is truly difficult to break with water.
(*Vahnimṛtsnā*:
Fire-clay) is made from the residue of chalk and *paṭu*, rubbed together with buffalo milk. (Āk 1.26.57)
The clay from a fire-site is indeed capable of withstanding the intense heat of a fierce fire;
mercury, when obstructed by these two types of clay, is unable to move. (Āk 1.26.58)
Then, having poured water [into the vessel], one should ignite the fire below;
this is declared by Nandin, the knower of reality, to be the *nābhiyantra*. (Āk 1.26.59)
By this, pure sulphur is digested in the crucible without emitting smoke.
*Grastayantra*) The crucible is situated within the belly of another crucible, being perfectly round at both its beginning and end. (Āk_1,26.60)
And that which is flattened at the base is called *grastayantra* by the wise;
indeed, it has been proclaimed by the experts in mercury for the purpose of binding the lord of elixirs (*sūtendra*). (Āk 1.26.61)
(17. The Balance Apparatus) There are two crucibles shaped like eggplants; at the bottom of their necks, indeed, a straight tube one span long is attached, containing sulfur. Āk 1.26.62.
There, one should pour the mercury into one [crucible] and the fragrant powder into the other;
having sealed the openings of the two crucibles, one should place them in a sand-vessel (*vālukāyantra*).
One should ignite a fire below; this is declared to be the *tulāyantra*, which is prescribed for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of minerals such as *śilā*, *tālaka*, and *gandhāśman*. (Āk 1.26.64)

(18. The Pot Apparatus) Having placed copper or other metals in a pot and having closed its opening with a lid, that which is cooked while situated within the pot is known as the *sthālīyantra* (pot apparatus). Āk 1,26.65.
(19. The Furnace Apparatus: One should place fine sand inside the interior of a large vessel, with a height measuring one span (*vitasti*); then, one should set [the crucible] therein. (Āk 1.26.66)
A well-baked earthen crucible, twelve finger-breadths in height and six finger-breadths in width, with its interior made exceedingly smooth. (Āk 1.26.67)
It should have a five-fingered cover, be sharp-pointed and closed like a bud; it should be neither too short nor too long for the receptacle, smooth at the neck and outside. (Āk 1.26.68)
And one should place six palas of finely powdered fragrance inside the crucible;
then, having set down a stable iron tripod to support it, [one should proceed]. (Āk 1.26.69)
And upon that, one should place a crucible made of iron or of magnetite;
into it, one should pour purified mercury measuring twenty palas.
One should saturate mercury with sulphur and *ṭaṅka* using the juice of garlic, having covered it with the previously mentioned lid while [the fire] has its flame directed downwards. (Āk 1.26.71)
One should join the joints together with lime, clay, molasses, and so forth;
once the joint-binding has dried, one should pour sand over it. (Āk 1.26.72)
Then, having sealed the mouth of the vessel, one should ignite a fire beneath it;
thus, for as long as three watches (yāmas), there arises the production of sulphur.
The smoke adhering to the lid, having fallen off, would dissolve into the liquid;
and thus, having absorbed the sixfold fragrance, the mercury becomes ruddy. (Āk 1.26.74)
It produces all the distinguished qualities specified in the Kalpas;
for this is indeed the Koṣṭhikāyantra as proclaimed by Nandin. (Āk 1.26.75)
(20. Vālukāyantra) Having carefully placed five āḍhaka measures of sand powder into a vessel, mercury, pills, and so forth are cooked; that indeed is the vālukāyantra. Āk_1,26.76.
(21. Salt-mechanism) Thus, by the depositing of salt, the salt-mechanism is described.
(22. Incense-mechanism)
Having fashioned an iron vessel eight finger-breadths wide and eight finger-breadths high.
In the region two finger-breadths below the throat, where the *jātādhāra* has arisen, one should insert a metal rod horizontally into it. // Āk 1.26.78 //
One should place thin gold leaves upon it;
one should also place beneath the vessel the incense that is to be described right here.
One should indeed cover that vessel with another vessel turned upside down;
having smeared the seam with clay, one should ignite a fire beneath it. (Āk 1.26.80)
By that [process], the black impurities are destroyed according to the prescribed method;
the mercury moves with speed, and the internal essences melt within the crucible. (Āk 1.26.81)
Indeed, the fumigation of gold leaves with sulphur, realgar, collyrium, or the fumes of a dead snake is proclaimed as the supreme method. (Āk 1.26.82)
For the purpose of transmutation (*tāra*), one should fumigate the copper leaves with dead mercury (*mṛtavaṅga*);
and one should also fumigate them appropriately with primary and secondary minerals (*rasa* and *uparasa*). Āk 1.26.83.
This is declared to be the incense-burner (*dhūpayantra*) for the purification of substances used in *jāraṇā*. (23. The Mortar Apparatus [*kandukayantra*]:
Having poured the liquid into a large pot and having firmly tied a cloth over its mouth... (Āk_1,26.84)
Having placed the substance to be sweated therein and having sealed its opening with clay, one should ignite a fire beneath it; that apparatus is called the *kanduka* (ball) instrument. (Āk 1.26.85)
(24. The Ḍhekīya Machine) One should insert a bamboo tube into an opening below the neck of a vessel;
having made two attractive bronze bowls into a hollowed-out pair filled with water. (Āk 1,26.86)
One should firmly join the tube to that [crucible] and ensure it is made secure;
the mercury, previously placed therein with the appropriate substances, is deposited within that crucible. (Āk 1.26.87)
Heated by the fire, he falls down into that water from the tube;
indeed, it lasts only as long as the entire vessel remains hot. (Āk 1.26.88)
The union of the mercury occurs; this is the *ḍhekī* apparatus (*somānalayantra*).
Fire is above, water is below, and the collection of the mercury is in the middle. (Āk 1.26.89)
This is declared to be the *somānala* [apparatus], which digests substances such as *gagana* (mica) and the like.
(26. *Nālikāyantra*) The mercury contained within a metal tube is placed in a vessel filled with salt. (ĀK 1.26.90)

One should cook this [substance] once it has been stopped by means of the *nālikā* machine (the *pātāla* machine), having joined it well with joints, directly in a divine vessel. (27. *Pātālayantre*) Āk 1.26.91.
Its mouth should be eight finger-breadths wide and its length sixteen finger-breadths;
having joined it with well-fitted joints, one should apply a coating of cloth and clay. (Āk 1.26.92)
In that *pātālayantra*, one should cause the mercury and other substances to fall.
(28. *Dīpikāyantra*) It is situated upon a lamp placed on an earthen pedestal located within a *kacchapayantra*. // Āk_1,26.93 //
That upon which the mercury falls is called the *dīpikā* machine (the *gaṅgāsāgara* or *bhaṭṭī* machine); it is twelve finger-breadths in height and sixteen finger-breadths in length. (Āk 1.26.94)
The vessel should be made of copper or clay, very smooth, flat, and auspicious;
below the rim, there should be a trough two finger-breadths in height.
One should place another vessel of equal size, well-fitted, inside the trough;
its neck should be joined to the joint of those two [vessels] and made like the mouth of a cow. (Āk 1.26.96)
Having placed the substance to be cooked in the lower vessel mixed with a liquid, and having applied a clay seal at the joint, one pours water onto the upper part of the apparatus. (Āk 1.26.97)
Having placed that apparatus upon the hearth, one should ignite a fierce fire beneath it;
consequently, no other substance emerges than the mercury residing within that very material.
This Gaṅgāsāgara machine is indeed known as the Bhaṭṭi machine;
it extracts the excellent liquefaction of jaggery, flowers, fruits, and so forth. (Āk 1.26.99)

(30. The Swing Apparatus) When a vessel whose belly is half-filled with a liquid substance has its handle placed horizontally at the mouth, and the mercury is suspended by a thread [from that handle], ĀK 1.26.100.
One should heat that which has reached the state of *tatta* [liquid heat]; this is known as the *ḍolāyantra* (swing apparatus).
(31. *Koṣṭhīyantra*) Having constructed a four-faced furnace (*cullī*), one should place the vessel therein. Āk_1,26.101.
Having placed the medicinal substances therein and sealed that vessel, this is celebrated by those local experts as the *koṣṭhīyantra* (the crucible apparatus). Āk 1.26.102.
(32. The Embryo Apparatus) One should fashion a crucible from clay, very firm, three finger-breadths in circumference and four finger-breadths in length, with a circular opening. Āk 1.26.103.
Having finely ground twenty parts of salt and one part of guggulu, one should grind them together again and again, repeatedly. (Āk 1.26.104)
Having applied a firm coating to the crucible with a mixture of salt and clay, the wise one should gently heat it in a fire of dried cow-dung, or in a fire of husks, or on the ground. (Āk 1.26.105)
In one day and night, or in three nights, the mercury (rasendra) shall attain the state of ash.
This is declared to be the *garbhayantra*, which effects the reduction of the paste (*piṣṭikā*) to ash. (Āk 1,26.106)
(33. Haṃsapākayantra):
Having filled a shallow pan with sand, one should place another shallow pan upon it; there, one should cook [the substance] slowly over a mild fire. Āk_1,26.107.
Then, with the five alkalis, urines, and salts, including viḍa, it is called *haṃsapāka*; that is the vessel described by the best of alchemists. (Āk 1.26.108)

(34. Crucible apparatus: Having made two iron crucibles measuring twelve finger-breadths [in length], one should provide a tube at the openings of the two crucibles and seal them properly. Āk 1.26.109.
In one [vessel] pure *sūtaka* is placed, and in the other pure sulfur;
water should be poured beneath the *sūtaka* and fire should be cast upon the sulfur. (Āk 1.26.110)
One should indeed digest the mercury with six times its weight of sulphur according to this very sequence;
this is to be known as the *mūṣāyantra*, as proclaimed by the perfected Nāgārjuna. (Āk 1.26.111)

(35. The Breast-Machine) A vessel made of kāntaloha iron, twelve finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in height, O Goddess; three finger-breadths below the vessel is auspicious. Āk_1,26.112.
A low vessel and a lid made of copper, flattened and auspicious—this "breast-machine" is excellent for the digestion of metallic pastes. (Āk 1.26.113)
(36. The Nāgamāyūra Machine) One should have a pair of bell-shaped crucibles made from lotus-circular iron;
one should place mercury in one and poison in the other. Āk 1.26.114.
One should place a snake-shaped tube at the mouth of a poison crucible;
indeed, one should place a peacock-shaped tube at the mouth of a mercury crucible. Āk 1,26.115.
The wise one should join a serpent’s mouth to the face of a peacock;
he should apply three joints with diamond-clay (vajramṛd) so that it becomes firm. (Āk 1.26.116)
O beloved, water beneath the crucible, poison beneath that, and glowing embers below—this serpent-illusion machine is indeed excellent for the incense of poison. Āk 1.26.117.
(37. The Wheel Machine:
A pit one cubit in length and two spans deep [should be made];
in the middle of the pit, however, there should be a crucible twelve finger-breadths in length. Āk_1,26.118 //
One should fill the auspicious crucible, two *vitastis* in height, with sand;
outside of that, [place] a fire of dried cow-dung chaff, and within the crucible, the mercury, O Dear One. (Āk 1.26.119)

This wheel-mechanism is recommended for the process of reducing mercury to ash. (38. Khecarayantra) One should place a crucible resembling a plantain flower, with a perforated base, into a well-positioned vessel. Āk_1,26.120.
One should fashion [the mold] facing downwards and coat it firmly with diamond-clay;
then, one should place another vessel over it, facing downwards, ensuring they are well-sealed together. (Āk 1.26.121)
One should place vatsanābha [poison] in a crucible within an upper vessel; one should skillfully smear the mercury [into it], and above the apparatus is the deceptive mercury. (Āk 1.26.122)
This *khecarayantra* is for cooking [the substance] with a mild fire from below; it is generally excellent, O Dear One, for the perfected mercury when subjected to the fumes of poison. (Āk 1.26.123)

(39. Kāpāliya-yantra) Having placed mercury and other substances in a vessel, one should place a crucible made of gold, silver, or other materials upside down over it; having sealed the joint with clay, one should fill the space inside the crucible with sand. (Āk 1,26.124)
Having prepared this *kāpāliyantra* (sand-vessel apparatus), one should cook it over a mild fire;
it should have a concealed opening and be joined with a soft cloth and a finger’s breadth [of clay]. (40. *Vālukāyantra*) Āk 1.26.125.
One should fill a dried glass flask with three parts [of liquid] and place it in sand within a vessel that is one span deep. Āk 1.26.126.
One should cover [the vessel] with other [substances] that fill its portion;
having sealed the mouth of the jar with a lid, one should smear the joint with clay and bake it. (Āk 1.26.127)
Because it does not burn even the grass placed in its cauldron, this is indeed the *vālukāyantra* (sand-vessel apparatus) situated upon the back of a water-jar;
one should cook the mercury-balls and other substances in it. (ĀK 1.26.128)

(41. The Salt Apparatus) Thus is described the salt apparatus (*lavaṇayantra*) by means of the deposition of salt; it consists of a copper vessel whose mouth has been internally coated with a paste of *rasāla*.
Having smeared the joint and the bottom of that vessel with clay and salt, and having filled that vessel with pungent substances or alkaline ashes, one should cook it as before. (Āk 1.26.130)
(42. Bhūdhara Yantra):
One should cover the crucible containing mercury, with all its parts buried in sand, inside the apparatus with glowing blue lotuses; that apparatus is called the Bhūdhara. Āk_1,26.131.
(43. The Nālikā Machine) One should make a hole by the side of the jar the size of a thumb; the bamboo tube or even a reed tube should be as thick as that. Āk 1.26.132.
One should join the tube to the opening and place a small vessel at the tip of the tube;
having cast resin from the *sarja* tree or similar substances into the jar, one should seal its mouth. (Āk 1.26.133)
One should ignite a fire below; this is called the *nālikāyantra* (tube-contrivance). (44.
*puṭayantra*) One who knows the measure of fire should place [the substance] inside a pair of earthen saucers (*śarāva*) amidst dried cow-dung (*karīṣa*). (Āk 1.26.134)

One should cook the medicinal juice for one watch (three hours) in a crucible apparatus on the hearth; [this is] the Pātālayantra. [Alternatively,] one should place a wide-mouthed pot in a pit containing water and cow dung. (Āk 1.26.135)
Having placed it within the mouth, one should fill another jar;
one should then set down a vessel provided with five openings upon the face. (Āk 1.26.136)
One should fill that jar with substances suitable for immersion in oil and seal the mouth of the vessel with a shallow bowl; then one should apply a *puṭa* (heat-sealing) treatment all around it.
One should employ oil that has fallen through apertures in those respective applications; for this "underworld machine" (pātālayantra) causes all the oil to fall down. Āk 1.26.138.
One should collect wood, bark, seeds, meat, bone, bamboo, and talas;
having placed a ladle made of donkey-bone or similar material into a pot, one should put a bronze vessel upon its mouth. (46. Incense Apparatus) Āk_1,26.139.
O Goddess, one should place water below and ignite the fire;
the oil situated in a vessel of magnetite (kānta) heals all wounds. (Āk 1.26.140)

O Goddess, this incense apparatus (dhūpayantra)— also known as the downward-pressing apparatus (adhaḥpātanayantra)— was described by Nandin as being shaped like a round gourd, of equal thickness, with a long neck and provided with holes. (Āk 1.26.141)
O Dear One, one should cast substances such as seeds and the like, along with oil, into that [fire];
one should place hair into its mouth and set it down facing downwards. (Āk 1.26.142)
One should insert a tube into the hole of a jar that has a perforation;
one should place a crucible inside the jar and set a small vessel beneath the tube. (Āk 1.26.143)
Indeed, the downward-descending apparatus (*adhaḥpātanayantra*) is excellent for the extraction of oil.
(48. Another downward-descending apparatus:
One should place a support level within a large bronze vessel. (Āk 1,26.144)
Above that, one should place another very firm earthen vessel four finger-breadths deep;
this heated vessel should be set within the previous vessel.
Having placed [the first vessel] upon it, soaked with sandalwood, black aloe-wood, and honey;
likewise, the second vessel, and the third as well, should be prepared in that same manner.

Having placed [the vessels] one above the other, one should place an earthen pot upside down over them; then, having placed the pot upon a bronze vessel, one should cleanse it with water. (Āk 1.26.147)
Indeed, the downward-dropping apparatus (*adhaḥpātanayantra*) causes the fragrant oil (*gandhataila*) to fall. (The crucible:
The crucible is called *krauñcikā*, *kumudī*, and *karahāṭikā*. (Āk 1,26.148)
That which is desired by alchemists as a digestive agent and a friend to fire is called a *mūṣā*;
because it steals away the defects (*doṣa*), it is designated as a *mūṣā*. (Āk 1.26.149)
Even if the material for it were clay or iron, a single kākī coin that has emerged from the mouth of the crucible is better. (Āk 1.26.150)
Fie upon even a hundred thousand [gold pieces] for the proud who bow down before the wicked!
Just as one should well-seal the cracks in the joints of a crucible and its lid when they are joined together. (Saṃdhilepa) Āk 1.26.151.
Clay that is capable of both melting and cooking, with closely joined joints and bonds—
white, coarse, red, or pale-yellow— is the best for the purpose of crucibles (*mūṣā*). (Āk 1.26.152)
For that which can withstand long-term inflation is highly praised for the purpose of making a crucible;
in its absence, one made of ant-hills or clay is recommended.
The clay that has been pounded with burnt husks, hemp, lime, horse-dung, iron, and a rod is indeed suitable for the purpose of making crucibles. Āk 1,26.154.
White stones, husks, burnt [substances], firebrands, hemp-rags, and the dross of *laddi* should be combined as appropriate with the clay of the crucible (*mūṣikāmṛd*). (Āk 1.26.155)
Taking three parts of clay, two parts of hemp and *laddi*, one part of lead, and half a part of slag from burnt husks, stones, and the like,
one should cut these into pieces and fashion them into a *vajramūṣā* crucible for the extraction of metallic essences (*sattvapāta*). (Āk 1.26.156)
(Yogamūṣā):
Clay originating from an anthill, mixed with burnt charcoal and husks, combined with various *viḍa* salts, and smeared with those same *viḍa* salts. (Āk 1.26.157)
The crucible fashioned by her is called the *yogamūṣā*;
the mercury processed in this [crucible] becomes even more excellent in its qualities. (Āk 1.26.158)
(Vajradrāvaṇamūṣā):
Equal parts of *gārā*, *bhūnāga*, and *dhauta*, along with hemp, burnt husks, and clay for the crucible, mixed together and combined with buffalo milk. (Āk 1.26.159)
For the *krauñcikā* crucible, which will be described and is proclaimed to be of many kinds, when fashioned by her, is beneficial for the liquefaction of diamonds. (Āk 1.26.160)

By blowing upon it with a pair of bellows, it does not melt with fire; [this is] the *gāramūṣā* (iron-clay crucible), enriched with six times its weight of burnt clay, and provided with dross, charcoal, and hemp. Āk_1,26.161.
A crucible made from black clay is called a *gāramūṣā*.
A *vajramūṣā* consists of equal parts cloth, charcoal, and husks, with four times that amount of clay.
A crucible made from all these materials mixed with an equal amount of clay is designated as a "vajra-mūṣā" (adamant crucible); it can withstand the heat of a *yāma* [of fire]. Āk 1.26.163.
A crucible mixed with the powder of the red group of minerals and processed with the liquid of the red group is designated as the *varamūṣā*; it is also called the *svarṇamūṣā*. (Āk 1.26.164)
A crucible made of clay and prepared by being smeared with *kṣiti* and *khecara* is called a *varṇamūṣā*; it is employed for the enhancement of color (*varṇa*). (Āk 1,26.165)
Thus, the silver crucible has been described by means of the white group [of substances]. Now, the *biḍa* crucible:
Produced from various kinds of clay and smeared with various kinds of clay.
For the purpose of alchemical transmutation (deha-loha-artha-yoga), it is called *biḍamūṣā*;
though distressed by the liquid, it withstands fire for four watches (*caturyāma*). (Āk 1.26.167)
When the crucible has reached a state of liquefaction due to the application of heating, its removal for a brief moment is called *mūṣāpyāyana* (the replenishing of the crucible). Āk 1,26.168.
In a crucible shaped like an eggplant (*vṛntāka*), the neck should be twelve finger-breadths long;
it should be as firm as a *dhuttūra* flower above, with its joints well-fitted together. (Āk 1.26.169)
Eight finger-breadths long and provided with a hole, that shall be the *vṛntākamūṣikā*;
by means of this, one should extract the essence (*sattva*) from soft substances such as potsherds and the like. (Āk 1.26.170)
The Cow’s Teat Crucible: A crucible that is shaped like a cow’s teat and has a lid provided with a spout;
for the liquefaction and purification of substances, that crucible is known as the Cow’s Teat. (Āk 1.26.171)
(The Mallamūṣā):
The *mallamūṣā* is specified as that which is formed from the union of two crucibles;
it is proclaimed for the purpose of steaming substances such as the juices of *parpaṭī* and others. (Āk 1.26.172)
A *pakvamūṣā* is a vessel made of clay that is strong and well-fired;
it is called a *pakvamūṣā* when used for firing medicinal powders (*poṭṭalī*) and the like. (Āk 1.26.173)
The *golamūṣā* is mouthless, spherical in shape, and contains the substances to be fused;
it is called the *golamūṣā* because it restrains volatile substances. (Āk 1.26.174)
That which is shaped like an elbow at its base and gradually widens toward the top,
thick like a large eggplant, is known as the *mañjumūṣā* crucible. (Āk 1.26.175)
And that [crucible], used for the cupping and melting of iron, mica, sattvas, and so forth,
is a box-shaped crucible (*mañjūṣāmūṣā*), which is deeper than it is wide. (Āk 1,26.176)
A crucible known as a *mañjūṣā*, measuring six finger-breadths in size, should be buried in the ground; one should then apply the *puṭa* heating process over that crucible. (Āk 1.26.177)
( *Musalamūṣā*):
That crucible which is flattened at the base, circular, and eight finger-breadths in height is called the *musalā* crucible;
it is likewise used for mercury bound by a wheel. (Āk 1.26.178)
(Another is the *vajramūṣā*): six parts of burnt charcoal, red ochre, black clay, *gāra*, and the dross of charcoal—this is proclaimed as the *vajramūṣā*. (Āk 1.26.179)
A crucible made from burnt bricks, burnt husks, anthill earth, and hemp bark combined together is considered to be like a diamond. Āk 1.26.180.
(The blind crucible and the open crucible:
The crucible is traditionally held to be of two kinds—the open crucible and the blind crucible.
The open crucible should be understood as being shaped like a shallow bowl (*śarāva*). Āk 1,26.181.
And that [process] is praised by the Vārtikas for the extraction of the substance;
furthermore, the Andhra crucible should be made resembling the shape of a cow's teat. Āk 1.26.182.
Combined with a covering, with the head slightly raised, this is beneficial for applying leaf-ornaments, as well as for coloring and the blending of two substances. (Āk 1.26.183)
That very [vessel] is provided with openings, pleasant and deep, and suitable for Sāraṇa;
it is a crucible of ash consisting of two parts of sesame ash combined with one part of brick. (Āk 1.26.184)
It should be known as the *bhasmamūṣā* (ash crucible), which is beneficial for the purification of mercury (*tāra*).
(Another is the *vajramūṣā*:
husks and cloth burned in equal parts, with clay added in four parts. (Āk 1.26.185)
The *vajramūṣā* is proclaimed as being joined with a stone vessel. (Regarding the characteristics of the clay used for the crucible, the blowpipe, and the furnace:
The clay may be black, red, yellow, or white in color. (Āk 1.26.186)
The first is the best, the last is the worst, and those in between are considered middling;
having burned the impurities of elephants and horses until they have reached a state of blackness. (Āk 1.26.187)
One should grind vāśā, vajralatā, and the leaf of an anthill together with its clay in vajra-water until it reaches a state of whiteness. Āk 1.26.188.
One should crush these and bind them with a bamboo tube and a crucible;
[using] ant-hill earth, iron dross, and white stone, each separately. (Āk 1.26.189)
Take one part each of burnt husks, hair from a woman's head, and [the other ingredients];
having made them equal portions, one should grind that entire mixture with goat’s milk. (Āk 1.26.190)
With that [substance], one should firmly prepare a crucible and a sealed capsule for two *yāmas*;
having dried the mercury and cast it therein, one should seal it with *kaṃsa*. (Āk 1.26.191)
The "vajra-furnace" and other such methods are prescribed for the complete killing of mercury;
two parts of potash (mokṣakṣāra) combined with brick and bell-metal [are used]. Āk 1.26.192.
That crucible in which it is prepared is the best for purifying silver;
it should be mixed with the red group of substances and saturated with the red group of substances.
When applied with a paste made from the red group [of substances], it is used for gold-work; when mixed with the white group or saturated with the white group, it is likewise employed. (Āk 1.26.194)
An ointment prepared with the white group [of substances] is recommended for cleansing white [parts of the body];
however, when mixed with the fecal group or saturated with the fecal group, it is used for other purposes.
A crucible prepared with an application of the group of feces (viḍ) is used for the digestion of the liquefied metal;
it should be mixed with the group of alkalis and thoroughly saturated with the group of alkalis.
A crucible coated with an ointment made from the group of alkaline substances is beneficial for the extraction [of mercury] (the procedure for revolving within the crucible;
the color-puṭa).
One should apply a coating to the crucible using a mixture of mercury, borax, and guñjā seeds.
If one applies a coating of charcoal to the *prakāśā* crucible, the wise man should place the substance into that crucible and cause it to revolve. Āk 1.26.198.
In a crucible colored with a paste, one should employ red earth, sal-ammoniac, sulfur, and mercury.
(The nature of the substances being processed:
When gold is being processed, it is yellow; when silver, it has a white luster. Āk 1.26.199.
In the case of a sharp [substance], one resembling water is recommended when it is white in color;
indeed, for the restraining of mercury, a mechanical device (yantra) is superior to medicinal herbs. (Āk 1,26.200)
Even when accompanied by medicinal herbs, their essence is bound by means of a vessel (*yantra*)—
the *koṣṭhī*—
for the purpose of precipitating the *sattvas*, and for the purification of those already precipitated. (Āk 1.26.201)
Furnaces are of various forms; their characteristics are now described:
(either a mine-furnace or a charcoal-furnace), they should be one *rāja-hasta* in height, and half that measure in length and width. (Āk 1.26.202)
And that [mandala], square and enclosed by a wall made of clay, should have its door on one side, provided with a width of one span. (Āk 1.26.203)

The door, measuring one and a half spans (vitasti) and being very firm and auspicious, should be constructed beneath the *dohala* for the purpose of blowing [the bellows] as is appropriate. (Āk 1.26.204)
The northern wall above the upper member should be one *prādeśa* in measure, and indeed a door of one *prādeśa* in measure should be made above it. Āk 1.26.205.
Then, having blocked the joint of the door with bricks and smeared it, and having filled it with charcoal, one should blow upon it with two bellows. (Āk 1.26.206)
One should introduce the substance for the subduing of the fire-breather through the upper opening;
and one should repeatedly apply five *sattvapātana* globules at a time.
This is the furnace for ores used in the extraction of metallic essences (*sattva*).
For the "underworld furnace" (*pātālakoṣṭhī*), one should dig an auspicious pit in firm ground, measuring one span in depth. *Āk_1,26.208*
Then, in the center of that, one should fashion another circular pit,
endowed with a width and depth of four finger-breadths.
From the pit to the edge of the earth, it should be provided with horizontal petals;
it should be slightly elevated and sloped inward toward the outer pit.
One should place a clay wheel provided with five holes upon the cavity of the crucible;
having filled the furnace with coals (*kokila*), one should heat it with a single bellows. (Āk 1.26.211)
Indeed, this is the Pātālakoṣṭhikā furnace for the precipitation of mild substances and for those materials that require intense heating; thus it was proclaimed by Nandin. (Āk 1.26.212)
The crucible (*gārakoṣṭhī*) should be twelve finger-breadths deep and one span (*prādeśa*) in width;
it should be four finger-breadths high and provided with a rim (*valaya*).
One should place a crucible containing many holes upon a ring;
having cast the minerals therein, one should heat them in a closed crucible (vaṅkanāla).

The curved tube (*vaṅkanāla*) should be made from crucible clay, firm and measuring one *aratni* in length; its opening should indeed face downward, and the tube should be five finger-breadths long. (Āk 1.26.215)
It is called the "curved tube" (*vaṅkanāla*) and is renowned for providing firm inflation.
This is designated as the *gāragoṣṭhī* furnace, which destroys the produced metal. (Āk 1,26.216)
The crucible (koṣṭhī) is prescribed for the preparation of mercury and other substances;
it should be twelve finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths at its base.
That which involves blowing across [the fire] is for the purification of soft substances;
*puṭa* is the indication of the proper measure for the cooking of substances such as juices and the like. (Āk 1.26.218)
A cooking process that is neither deficient nor excessive is desired; medicine is beneficial when well-cooked.
Likewise, the non-recurrence of iron and other metals, their increase in quality, and their intensity [result from such processing]. (Āk 1.26.219)
From the *puṭa* there arises non-sinking in water, the filling of lines, passion, lightness, swift pervasion, and illumination. (Āk 1.26.220)
Even from the processed lord of mercury (sūtendra), the quality of the metals increases;
just as fire, though situated outside, enters into a stone through the application of heating in a crucible (puṭayoga). Āk 1.26.221.

For it is certain that the attainment of qualities in metals occurs through pulverization; having cast the medicinal substance to be cooked into a double-layered saucer-casket, [one should proceed]. Āk_1,26.222.
Having enclosed it within a *garuḍapacana* crucible, that is called a *puṭa*;
[specifically] the *mahāpuṭa* is performed in a square pit measuring two cubits in both depth and width.

When the crucible is filled with a thousand forest lotuses and the medicinal herbs for the *puṭa* process are securely confined within its cavity, one should carefully place it upon the grinding stone. Āk 1.26.224.
One should place five hundred forest lotuses upon the crucible;
one should ignite the fire therein—this is known as the *mahāpuṭa*. (Āk 1.26.225)
(The Gajapuṭa):
Square and hollowed out to the measure of a king’s forearm, it should be filled with pebbles and gravel up to the neck; then one should place [the substance] therein. (Āk 1.26.226)
One should place there the *kumudī* vessel filled with the substances for sealing;
one should then deposit half as many *garuṇḍa* vessels as there were *chagaṇa* vessels previously.
This is declared to be the *gajapuṭa*, which bestows great qualities.
(The *vārāhapuṭa*):
likewise, when the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is two *aratnis* in measure, the *puṭa* is called *vārāha*. (Āk 1.26.228)
(The Chicken-Basket): That basket which is on the surface of the ground, two spans in height and likewise two spans in width at its base—that is the chicken-basket (*kukkuṭaka-puṭa*). Āk 1,26.229.
(The Dove-Method Pouch):
That pouch which is placed upon the ground with eight forest lotuses for the sake of the ash of a recently deceased infant is called the *kapotapuṭa*. (Āk 1.26.230)
(Gorvarapuṭa):
Dried and powdered cow dung trampled by the hooves of cattle within a pen is designated as *gorvara*; it is the most excellent for the preparation of mercury (*rasa*). (Āk 1.26.231)
(Govarapuṭa): Where a *puṭa* is administered using cow dung or even husks, that is called a *govarapuṭa*, for the purpose of preparing the ash of mercury (*rasabhasma*). (Āk 1,26.232)
(Bhāṇḍapuṭa):
When a thick vessel is filled with husks, provided with a crucible in the middle, and heating by fire is performed, that is called bhāṇḍapuṭa. (Āk 1,26.233)
(A sand-pouch:
A vessel covered with a lid both below and above, wherein the apparatus is filled with heated sands—that is indeed a sand-pouch (*vālukāpuṭa*). Āk 1,26.234.
(Regarding the earthen crucible: One should properly bury it two finger-breadths deep in fire-bearing soil; that apparatus which has a crucible on top is called the *bhūdhara* crucible. (Āk 1.26.235)
(The *lāvakapuṭa*):
A crucible (*puṭa*) made with husks or cow-dung, sixteen *mātrās* high, is called the *lāvaka* instrument; it is used for the successful processing of soft substances. (Āk 1.26.236)

When the measure for the number of *puṭas* has not been stated, those skilled in reasoning and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*) should determine the appropriate *puṭa* by considering the relative strength or weakness of the substance to be processed (*sādhya-dravya*). Āk 1.26.237.
(The nature of small jars and so forth:
Small jars, cups, and bowls made of glass, iron, or clay; likewise, *rūpikās*, established *kūpikās*, globes, and baskets. (Āk 1.26.238)
Caṣaka, kaṭhorī, vāṭikā, khorikā, kañcolī, and grāhikā are indeed synonyms. (Āk 1.26.239)

The fires for the threefold processing of mercury, the secondary minerals (uparasa), and the metals are [achieved] through the methods of *garuṇḍa*, *kāṣṭha*, and *kolīśa*; these are each further divided into three types. Āk 1.26.240.
Among those, there is the *garuḍapuṭa*, the one known as the *kukkuṭapuṭa*, the one known as the *varāhapuṭa*, and there is also the *gajapuṭa*. (Āk 1.26.241)
The best [rods] are made from wood grown in the forest; those produced in a cow-pen are middling;
inferior are artificial wood or that derived from the *khadira* and *asana* trees. (Āk 1.26.242)
Alternatively, that which is produced from a heartwood tree, two vitastis in length and as thick as a stout forearm,
is excellent for the cooking of mercury.
The preparation of wood for the fire is known to be mild, moderate, or fierce;
the embers should be produced from *khadira* wood or from trees belonging to the *triphalā* group. (Āk 1.26.244)
Carṣā ores produced from the most excellent trees are the best for the process of smelting.
