Āk, 2, 1 (The Procedure for Purifying and Killing the Secondary Metals):
Śrī Bhairavī said:
O God of gods, O Consciousness-Bliss, O Bestower of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss! By you alone was I previously awakened to the method of aesthetic essence (*rasa*). (Āk 2.1.1)
Now, O Lord, by your grace, I wish to hear about the secondary minerals such as fragrances, and the metals beginning with gold. (Āk 2.1.2)
O Lord, please tell me the characteristics, the origins, the processing, and the qualities of rubies and other gems, so that I may understand them. (Āk 2.1.3)
(The secondary minerals:
Śrībhairava, sulphur, realgar, mica, antimony, orpiment, cinnabar, and red ochre.
Capala, aśmajabhūnāga, haridrāśman, and agnijāraka; // Āk 2.1.4 //
Kharparī, tutthaka, kaṅkuṣṭha, girisindūra, ṭaṅkaṇa, kampilla, viṣa, kāsīsa, gaurīpāṣāṇa, and bhūkhaga; Āk 2.1.5.
Poddāraśṛṅgī, sindūra, tuvarī, rasāñjana, nīlāñjana, sauvīra, srotoñjana, and aphenaka. (Āk 2.1.6)
Flower-ointment (puṣpāñjana), conch-shell, pearl-oyster, and cowrie-shells; sābuṇī, the nine alkalis, cīnakṣāra, and ākhumāraka. (Āk 2.1.7)
Sal resin, bdellium, lac, alkalis, and salts; gorocana, sour wood-apple, glass, slag, and sand. (Āk 2.1.8)
These are known as the secondary minerals (*uparasas*) for the work of the King of Mercury (*rasarāja*).
(The twelve metals: gold, silver, copper, iron, the essence of mica, *tīkṣṇa*, and *muṇḍaka*. (Āk 2.1.9)
Bhujaṅga, trapusa, rīti, kāṃsya, and vartaka—these twelve are the metals; maṇḍūra is the dross of iron. (Āk 2.1.10)
(The Nine Jewels): Ruby, pearl, coral, emerald, topaz, diamond, sapphire, go-meda stone, and cat’s-eye—these are, in order, the jewels of the nine planets. (Āk 2.1.11)
(The nine secondary gems: The sun-loved, the moon-loved, the star-loved, and the lovely; the vaikrānta, the nṛpāvarta, the sasyaka, and likewise the vimalā. (Āk 2.1.12)
And one should point out these nine as the secondary gems (*uparatna*): [mercury, mica, sulfur, iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, and gold].
(Sulfur:
Purification of Sulfur)
The first method:
one should purify the birth-characteristic, the genus, and the odor from this. (Āk 2.1.13)
Having placed milk mixed with clarified butter in a vessel, one should cover its mouth with a cloth;
having sprinkled powdered fragrance upon it, one should seal it with a lid. (Āk 2.1.14)
Having placed the vessel on the ground, one should apply a light covering over it;
then, once the fragrance has quickly melted into the milk, one should employ that pure substance in various formulations. (Āk 2.1.15)
(Second method: Oil from *kaṅguṇī*, mustard, or *eraṇḍa*;
or oil from safflower; or ewe’s milk, clarified butter, cow’s milk, or *cāranāla*. (Āk 2.1.16)
One should fill one of these vessels almost to the brim, seal its mouth with cloth, and then place fragrant powder upon it. (Āk 2.1.17)
Then, having enclosed it with an iron vessel and placed a shallow pan over its back, one should melt it completely with blue lotuses along with fire and then remove it. (Āk 2.1.18)

Having ground that with the juices of *dhuttūra* and melted it while dry as before, one should perform the process again in this manner; thus the sulfur (*gandhaka*) will become perfectly purified. (Āk 2.1.19)
(Third Method) One *yāma* of sulfur should be ground with the juices of *bṛhatī*, *ajagandhā*,
or else with those of *bhṛṅgī*, *dhuttūra*, and *tilaparṇī*. (Āk 2.1.20)

Having taken that [mercury] and equal amounts of ghee, one should cook it for a moment in an iron vessel; once it has been liquefied by the fire, one should indeed cast it into goat’s milk. (Āk 2.1.21)
In this manner, one should perform the purification seven times; thus the sulphur attains purity.
(The fourth method: Castor oil, *karañja* oil, and goat’s milk [should be placed] in a vessel. (Āk 2.1.22)
Having cast [the powder] into its mouth and bound it with a clean cloth, the wise one should impregnate the sulphur with decoctions of *dhūrta* for a day and then dry it. (Āk 2.1.23)
One should place that powder upon a cloth over the previously prepared vessel;
having covered it, a small packet should be given on the back by the disciple alone. (Āk 2.1.24)
Having quickly taken the fragrance, it should be processed with the juices produced from the *dhuttūra* plant;
likewise, it should be melted and processed again, and then melted once more thereafter. (Āk 2.1.25)
Having taken [the powder], it should be processed seven times with fish gall in the sun;
thereafter, one should grind it together with the powdered seeds of *kośātakī*. (Āk 2.1.26)
One should soak it with juices derived from bees for seven days in the intense heat of the sun;
then, having washed it with water and dried it, one should roast it for a moment over a gentle fire. (Āk 2.1.27)
Then, having melted it in an iron vessel smeared with ghee, one should quench it;
situated within the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, it becomes perfectly purified. (Āk 2.1.28)
(Fifth method:
Or one may process sulphur for the duration of one watch (yāma) with the juices of *madyabrāhmī* and *jagandhā*, or with *bhṛṅga* and *dhuttūra*, or with the juice of *tilaparṇī*. (Āk 2.1.29)
Having taken that [substance] mixed with ghee, one should cook it for a moment in an iron vessel over a mild fire; once it has quickly melted, one should cast it into the milk of a ewe. (Āk 2.1.30)
When this has been done seven times, the sulphur becomes pure. (Sulphur Oil; First Method)
Or *devadālī*, *amlaparṇī*, or else *nāraṅga* or pomegranate. (Āk 2.1.31)
One should take as much liquid citron juice as is available for one part, and add a quarter-part of sulphur along with borax mixed with that liquid. (Āk 2.1.32)
Dried in the sun for three days, the liquid should be added again and again;
[the ingredients are] dhattūra, tulasī, black garlic, and devadālī. (Āk 2.1.33)
The root of the *śigru* tree, *kākamācī*, camphor, the two types of *śaṅkhinī*, black agallochum, musk, *vandhyā*, and *karkoṭakī*—these in equal parts. (Āk 2.1.34)
Having ground [the substances] with the juice of citron (mātuluṅga), one should cast them into castor oil;
with this, one should saturate the previously mentioned sulfur placed in an iron vessel. (Āk 2.1.35)
When heated three times with an equal amount of honey, it becomes free from its odor; this shall be known as sulphur oil (gandhakataila), which one should employ in all formulations. (Āk 2.1.36)
(Second Method) Alternatively, one should coat a cloth seven times with the milky sap of the *arka* and *snuhī* plants.
Then, having ground sulfur with fresh butter, one should smear that [cloth] with it. (Āk 2.1.37)
One should hold that burning wick at the bite with its tip facing downwards;
the oil will fall into a vessel below, which should be collected and employed in medicinal formulations. (Āk 2.1.38)
(The precipitation of the sattva of sulphur;
the first method: Sulphur, having been rubbed for a long time with the oil of *kuberākṣī*, [is processed].
When strongly heated in an open crucible, it releases its essence. (Āk 2.1.39)
(Second method) Alternatively, having placed previously purified sulfur inside a vessel and covered it with a copper lid, one should pour cold water into that [vessel]. (Āk 2.1.40)
Having kindled a gentle fire beneath it, one should remove the hot water;
in this manner, one should repeatedly pour cold water over the top. (Āk 2.1.41)
The essence of sulfur, when heated by fire, is gold-colored and performs all functions;
yet one should not extract its essence from it, for sulfur itself is of the nature of that essence. (Āk 2.1.42)
Thus some others who know the true nature of sulfur declare [the process of] the liquefaction of sulfur (*gandhakadruti*): "Alternatively, powdered sulfur combined with mustard oil... (Āk 2.1.43).
Having placed that cloth upon a garment, one should have a firm wick made from it;
then, having wrapped it with thread, one should soak it thoroughly with cow's ghee. (Āk 2.1.44)
Having extracted it with tongs and prepared a wick, one should light it from below;
the resulting liquid will have the color and taste of the juice of a ripe mango fruit. (Āk 2.1.45)
(The Qualities of Sulphur): Sulphur is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), hot in potency (*vīrya*), pure, and laxative;
it cures erysipelas, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), itching, worms, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and consumption (*kṣaya*). (Āyurveda-kalpa 2.1.46)

It pacifies eye diseases, is aphrodisiac, overcomes the afflictions of poison and disease, bestows all accomplishments, is strengthening, destroys the three humors, and is a rejuvenative elixir. (Āk 2.1.47)
Haritāla is also called godantī, tālaka, naṭamaṇḍana,
girijālalita, pīta, atigandha, and biḍālaka. (Āk 2.1.48)
(Various types of haritāla:
Haritāla is said to be of two kinds: that called *pattra* (leaf-like) and that designated as *piṇḍa* (mass-like).
(The leaf-like haritāla:)
(Physical properties:
It is gold-colored, heavy, glossy, capable of being made into thin leaves, and radiant. (Āk 2.1.49)
That which has leaf-like scales is called *tālapattra*, while that with many scales is an elixir (*rasāyana*); [this is known as] *piṇḍatālaka* (the physical properties).
It is leafless, like a mere lump, possessing very little essence, and likewise heavy. (Āk 2.1.50)
The extraction of the "female flower" (strīpuṣpa) from that [haritāla] yields a small amount of the active principle, known as piṇḍatālaka.
(Regarding the defects of consuming impure haritāla:
It causes disorders of wind, phlegm, urinary disorders (prameha), and the like, and it destroys longevity. (Āk 2.1.51)
The cracking of the heat and the contraction of the limbs [occur when using] unrefined yellow orpiment.
(Purification of Yellow Orpiment;
First Method)
Having reduced the talaka to fine particles, one should add a tenth part of ṭaṅkaṇa.
It should be washed with juices from *jambīra* fruits and then washed again with *kāñjika*;
having bound it in a fourfold cloth, one should cook it for a day in a *ḍolāyantra*. (Āk 2.1.53)
Tālaka (orpiment) attains purification by being sweated for a day with powdered *ārana* (sour gruel), with juices from *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin gourd), or with the decoction of *śālmalī*. Āk 2.1.54.
(Second Method) Having ground it, one should saturate talaka three times with a thickened decoction of Brahmamūla that is like honey, and then with buffalo urine. (Āk 2.1.55)
One should give ten *utpala* flowers and repeatedly form a sealed packet (*puṭa*).
Thus it should be cooked twelve times; once purified, one should employ it in the yogic applications. (Āk 2.1.56)

(Third method: Having tied the mineral calamine (*tālaka*) in a cloth packet (*poṭṭala*), one should cook it for one *yāma* in fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) mixed with powder, using a swinging vessel apparatus (*dolāyantra*), and then [cook it] in the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd. (Āk 2.1.57)
One should cook it for one watch (yāma) in sesame oil and for one watch in water of the three myrobalans;
thus, having been cooked in a yantra for four watches, the mineral cinnabar (tālaka) becomes purified. (Āk 2.1.58)
(The precipitation of the essence of *tālaka*;
first method: Lac, *rājī*, sesame seeds, *śigru*, borax, salt, and jaggery.
Having crushed it with the value of lac, one should seal the hollow crucible. (Āk 2.1.59)
One should seal it with the pātālayantra; the essence will certainly fall out.
(The second method: One should grind tālaka with milks or with the decoctions of sarpākṣī. Āk 2.1.60.

One should generate the sattva as before, confined within a crucible with perforations (the third method). Lac, turmeric, jaggery, drumstick tree, borax, salt, and sesame seeds [are used]. (Āk 2.1.61)
One should grind *sattva* equal to these with the milky sap of the sun-plant (*arka*), or for one day with the milk of *vajriṇī*, or with the juices of the *kūśmāṇḍa* gourd. (Āk 2.1.62)
Having smeared the interior of the *chidramūṣā* crucible with that paste, one should seal it;
then the essence (*sattva*) is to be extracted from the *pātālayantra* by means of heating in a *puṭa* or by blowing. Āk 2.1.63.
(Fourth Method) One-eighth part of the *tālaka* should be combined with mercury and *ṭaṅkaṇa*;
this should be rubbed for three days with the juices of *kūṣmāṇḍa* and the milks of *snuhī*. (Āk 2.1.64)
That bola should be taken in a crucible with a hole, and the essence [sattva] extracted as before.
(The fifth method:
Sixteen parts of *tāla*, along with poison (*viṣa*), mercury (*pārada*), and *ṭaṅkaṇa*... (Āk 2.1.65).
One should mix equal parts of the powder of white cloud-mineral (śvetābhra) and tin (vaṅga), and grind them together with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka* for two days. (Āk 2.1.66)
Having placed that ball inside a glass flask, one should firmly coat that glass flask all over with clay mixed with cloth to the thickness of one finger's breadth. (Āk 2.1.67)
Once it has dried, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire in a sand-oven (*vālukāyantra*).
When the liquid has evaporated, one should then properly seal the opening with clay and salt. (Āk 2.1.68)
One should cook it over a fierce fire for as long as twelve watches;
once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should remove it, break the vessel, and collect [the substance]. (Āk 2.1.69)
The sixth type is the *tālasattva* which is fixed upright, resembling a crystal stone;
it has been meditated upon and sprinkled with the milky sap of the *snuk* plant, or with the juices of *snuhī*, twenty-eight times over. (Āk 2.1.70)
One should grind together sesame, mustard, *śigru*, salt, and the five "friends" (*mitrapañcaka*) in equal parts with purified mercury for one day. (Āk 2.1.71)
When heated inside a crucible with a hole in an earthen vessel, it releases its essence.
(The qualities of orpiment:
Purified orpiment is excellent; it removes skin diseases, death, and old age. Āk 2.1.72.
*Manaḥśilā* (realgar) produces good fortune and fragrance and increases supreme longevity. *Manaḥśilā*, *kunaṭī*, *nāgāsyā*, and *raktagandhaka* are its synonyms. (Āk 2.1.73)
Nepālikā, Nāgajihvā, Kalyāṇī, and Saptanāmakā—these are the varieties of *manaḥśilā*.
*Manaḥśilā* is said to be of three types: Śyāmāṅgī and Kaṇavīrakā. (Āk 2.1.74)
And that which is called a "fragment" (khaṇḍa) is likewise conceptualized by distinguishing its specific form;
it is considered to be dark, red, coarse-limbed, heavily burdened, and blackish. (Āk 2.1.75)

Tejasvinī is radiant and weightless; Tāmrābhā has the luster of the kaṇavīra flower; Kaṇavīrakā is powdered and has extremely red limbs; Sabhārā is characterized by being broken into pieces. Āk_2.1.76.
The superior [variety] mentioned above is proclaimed to possess abundant *sattva*.
(Regarding the defects of using impure *manaḥśilā*: It causes urinary stones, dysuria, weak digestion, and constipation. (Āk 2.1.77)
Mind-ore (manaḥśilā) that has not been purified causes leprosy and fever.
(The Purification of Mind-Ore: One should cook mind-ore for three days in a dolāyantra with the urine of a goat. (Āk 2.1.78)

For the sake of purification, one should heat realgar seven times in cow's urine, goat's bile, and ghee while it is being heated in the sun; likewise, one should process it with the juices of *jīvantī*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *raktā*, and *agastya*. (Āk 2.1.79)
One should cook it for one *yāma* in a swing-oven (*dolāyantra*) with goat’s urine, and wash it with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*); it may be employed in all formulations. (Āk 2.1.80)
The mineral (śilā) should be processed in the juice of Agastya for seven days and purified;
(this is the first method for the extraction of the essence [sattva] of realgar).
Like a palm tree, the extraction of the essence from the stone and its purification are likewise performed. (Āk 2.1.81)
Realgar (manaḥśilā) should be infused for one day with beef and the sour juice of citron;
it should then be infused with the juices of red and yellow flowers and with yellow [pigments]. (Āk 2.1.82)

At the end of the day, one should grind [the substance] for one watch (yāma) combined with the five "friends" (mitra-pañcaka). Having placed that pill inside a glass flask, [one should place] that glass flask... [Āk 2.1.83]
One should firmly coat the cloth with clay to the thickness of one finger on all sides;
once it is dry, one should bake it slowly over a mild fire in a sand-vessel (vālukāyantra). Āk 2.1.84.
Once the liquid has dried up, one should properly seal the opening with clay and salt, and cook it over a fierce fire for as long as twelve yāmas. (Āk 2.1.85)

Having removed it while still warm from one's own body and having broken open the vessel, one should extract the mineral essence of the stone, which clings to the upper part and resembles the rising sun. (Āk 2.1.86)
(Second method: Manahśilā should be infused for three days with water from Agastya and Śigru trees;
through the application of Tālaka and medicinal herbs, its essence becomes like gold. (Āk 2.1.87)
(The properties of realgar:
Realgar is pungent and hot, slightly bitter, and it conquers phlegm and wind;
it destroys itching, consumption, and cough, and removes the effects of poison, spirits, and sluggish digestion. (Āk 2.1.88)
(mākṣika) *Mākṣika* is honey-ore (*madhudhātu*); it may also be called *mākṣīka*, *hemamākṣika*, *tāpya*, *tāpija*, *tārkṣya*, and that which originates from the Tāpī region. (Āk 2.1.89)
(Various types of *mākṣika*):
*Mākṣika* is of two kinds: *hemamākṣika* (golden *mākṣika*) and *tāramākṣika* (silver *mākṣika*).
Among these, the first type of *mākṣika* originates from Kānyakubja and resembles gold. (Āk 2.1.90)
That which is produced on the banks of the Tāptī, possessing five colors like gold and abounding in stones, is called *tāpya*; it is said to be endowed with excellent qualities. (Āk 2.1.91)
Furthermore, due to differences in their golden forms, each of these is again threefold:
that known as *kādamba*, that called *kāravella*, and that designated as *taṇḍulīyaka*. (Āk 2.1.92)

(The defects in consuming impure honey: O Goddess worshipped by the gods, honey that is not purified indeed causes suppression of breath, debility, impairment of the digestive fire, and eye disease; it even kills the consumer. (Āk 2.1.93)
(Purification of honey;
first method:
Honey [should be purified] with human urine and decoctions produced from *kulattha* beans.
With vetasa, the group of sour substances, ṭaṅkaṇa, and the three pungents (kaṭutrika).
It should be cooked for one day in a *ḍolāyantra* (swing-furnace) placed inside a *sūraṇa* (mountain ginger) root;
then it should be cooked for one day with the juices of plantains. Once extracted, it should be ground with clarified butter. (Āk 2.1.95)
One should purify it by cooking it in a *puṭa* with castor oil. (The second method:
Three parts of honey and one part of borax. Āk 2.1.96.
Alternatively, one should cook it in an iron vessel with the juices of *mātuluṅga* or the juices derived from *jambīra*, until the vessel becomes a beautiful red color. (Āk 2.1.97)
Even copper-colored silver ore is purified by this means.
(The third method: One should rub the root of the *śigru* tree with the exudations of the *agasti* flower. Āk 2.1.98.

One should grind *pāṣāṇabhedinī* with liquids and honey with these [same substances]; then, having formed a pill from that, one should roast it in a crucible (*mūṣā*) using ten *utpala*-measurements of fuel. (Āk 2.1.99)
Furthermore, by grinding it again and again and then applying it in six *puṭas*, it becomes purified. (The fourth method:
Honey, milk, and sour gruel (*āranāla*), each in eight parts [of mercury]. (Āk 2.1.100)
One should fill a vessel with four parts of cow’s buttermilk and one part of the juice of *kulattha* beans; then one should cook it with one part of honey. (Āk 2.1.101)
One should cook it again for one *yāma* in a *ḍolāyantra* over a gentle fire;
then, having removed it, one should grind it with the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga* and ten blue lotuses (*utpala*). (Āk 2.1.102)
One should perform this process of sealing again and again for twelve days; thus the *mākṣika* becomes pure and may be employed in all formulations. (Āk 2.1.103)
(Fifth method: Having reduced honey into small particles, one should place it into a lump of *jālinī* and *meghanāda* and cook it in a dolāyantra using a decoction of *kulattha*. (Āk 2.1.104)
In a decoction, that iron attains purity; it is highly recommended for the killing of iron [in the sixth method]:
in oil, buttermilk, cow's urine, *kaulūttha* ferment, or sour *kāñjika*. (Sixth Method) Āk 2.1.105.

The wise one should purify honey-lead (*mākṣika*) in order to eliminate the defects of the mountain [ore], using a decoction of *kuluttha* and *kodrava*, human urine, and *amlavetasa*. (The seventh method. Āk 2.1.106.
Having placed it within the interior of a *sūraṇa* tuber, one should cook it for a day in a *ḍolāyantra* with borax, the group of acidic substances, or the three pungent spices. (Āk 2.1.107)
Mākṣika should be cooked for a day with the juice of plantains, blown with fire, then removed, ground, and purified by means of *puṭa* applications using castor oil and clarified butter. (Āk 2.1.108)

(Eighth variety: Pure gold-colored [mercury], either melted or reduced to small particles, should be placed in a paste of *punarnavā* and subjected to sweating (*svedayet*) in a decoction of *kaulūttha*. (Āk 2.1.109)

Alternatively, combined with rock salt and smeared with *bījapūra*, it should be placed in a cloth packet and steamed for one day in a *ḍolāyantra*; it will certainly attain purification. (Āk 2.1.110)
(The method for precipitating the essence of *mākṣika*;
first type:
It should be saturated with cow’s milk, *snuhī* latex, and castor oil.
Honey, having been ground for one day, is made into pills. (Āk 2.1.111)
This procedure for *sasyaka* is also [applicable] during sublimation like that of *abhra*.
(The second method: One should steam *mākṣika* in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) with *sāranāla* for one day. (Āk 2.1.112)
Having powdered it, one should cook it with honey and ghee in an iron vessel for a day;
then, taking it up, one should saturate it in the heat with the milk of the *vajrī* plant for the duration of a day. (Āk 2.1.113)

One should rub [the substance] for a day with house-soot mixed with clarified butter and honey; when heated in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), it becomes a sattva resembling a guñjā berry in color. Āk 2.1.114.
(Third method: Honey, having been saturated a hundred times with the juice of plantain roots in the sun, should be cooked for one watch (yāma) with ghee and Vātāri oils. (Āk 2.1.115)
By blowing [on it] as before, the essence becomes like a cochineal insect (*indragopa*).
(The fourth method: One should grind honey for a day with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, and with breast milk. (Āk 2.1.116)
Kaṅkuṣṭha and ṭaṅkaṇa, mixed with one-quarter part [of the base metal], when heated in a closed crucible (mūkamūṣā), will become a sattva resembling a gem. Āk 2.1.117.
(Fifth Method) One should successively saturate fine honey seven times with the juices of plantain root, *tulasī*, and citron, using each juice separately. (Āk 2.1.118)
When [the breath] is obstructed and blown, the auspicious *sattva*, resembling the beak of a parrot, will fall.
(The sixth method.
One should meditate upon it for fourteen days with the group of urine and the group of acids. Āk 2.1.119.

One should grind *mākṣika* with acidic substances under intense heat for one day; then, having combined it with the five allies (*mitrapañcaka*) and formed it into pills, one should heat them strongly. (Āk 2.1.120)
Like the sky, the essence [of mercury] becomes copper-colored through a curved tube;
(this is the seventh method.
It should be processed with the milks of Snuhī and cows, and with castor oil. Āk 2.1.121.
Honey treated with the five friends (pañcamitra) for seven days and then made into pills should be melted as before; by that, the essence (sattva) becomes like lac. (Āk 2.1.122)
(Eighth variety:
For seven days, one should take honey combined with kaṅkuṣṭha, milk, and the juice of plantain, along with the five "friends" (mitrapañcaka). (Āk 2.1.123)
One should massage the processed substance for a watch (yāma) or a day with oils that ward off wind;
one should cook it over a mild fire until the globule (golaka) becomes liquid. (Āk 2.1.124)
The *sattva* [of the gem] has the luster of a *kiṃśuka* flower; it arises from the vein like the sky.
This is the procedure for all pure [gems], including even *sasyaka*. (Āk 2.1.125)

(Ninth method: Having pulverized pure *mākṣika* [honey-ore] and ground it with some kind of acid, one should wash it with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), whereupon it will settle at the bottom like gold powder. (Āk 2.1.126)
Having collected that, one should cause it to be digested and blow upon it; it releases the essence (sattva).
One should employ this wherever seeds are to be sown. (Āk 2.1.127)
(Tenth method: One should quickly saturate honey with water from plantain leaves;
then, having cooked it for one day with *gandharva* oil, honey, and clarified butter, [it is ready]. (Āk 2.1.128)
Then, one should place that heated substance into a baked vajra-mūṣā crucible;
one should then add an equal amount of iron-joining agent into it. (Āk 2.1.129)
One should firmly place [the substance] in a crucible within a furnace and heat it with two bellows using charcoal produced from Khadira wood. (Āk 2.1.130)
When combined with *vaṅkanāla*, the essence of *tāpya* certainly falls down.
(The eleventh method: One should take equal parts of *māṇibandhya* and *vaiṣṇava*. (Āk 2.1.131)
Having ground [the ingredients] with the juice of citron (phalapūra), one should place them firmly inside a sealed crucible;
then, having coated it well with charcoal derived from trees, one should fire it in a *puṭa* oven. (Āk 2.1.132)
Having drawn out that which has arisen from the *kukūpaka* [furnace] and cooled it to the temperature of one's own body, one should grind it;
then, having ground it with the juices of ripe *phalapūra* fruits as before, [one should proceed]. (Āk 2.1.133)

The wise practitioner should perform the *puṭapāka* (sealed cooking) with dried cow-dung cakes until that medicinal paste, which has been crushed with sour fruit juice, is thoroughly cooked. (Āk 2.1.134)

Just as iron sharpened on a whetstone and smeared with copper attains the color of that copper, so too does pure *garuḍa*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *nīraja*, and mercury [attain their respective qualities]. (Āk 2.1.135)
Combined with ghee and honey, along with jaggery and an equal amount of *guñjā*, one should place it in a crucible as before and blow it with a fire of *khadira* wood. (Āk 2.1.136)
A person of weak disposition is like an elephant or like a cochineal insect;
he surely falls, there is no doubt—such is the word of the Omniscient One. (Āk 2.1.137)
When Vaiśvānara becomes white, radiant, and soundless, then one should know that the *sattva* has fallen; it is never otherwise. (Āk 2.1.138)
(The qualities of honey:
The two types of honey—bee-honey and flower-honey—are astringent, bitter, sweet, and pungent;
they are heating, act as rejuvenatives (*rasāyana*), and dispel skin diseases, consumption, hiccups, and vomiting. (Āyurveda-kalpa 2.1.139)
Mākṣika mineral destroys all diseases, is the very life-force of mercury (rasendra), and is supremely aphrodisiac;
it is the unifier of two metals that are difficult to fuse, possesses superior qualities, and is the foremost among the ancient elixirs (rasāyana). (Āk 2.1.140)
(Regarding mica: The origin and other details of the "cloud" (mica) were explained at the beginning in the section on elixirs (*rasāyana*);
now I shall fully describe its processing as well as its qualities. (Āk 2.1.141)
(The method for preparing mica ash;
the first type:
One should grind *dhānyābhraka* with the juices of *meghanāda* for one day.
Having added one-hundredth part of ṭaṅkaṇa, one should then cook it in a gajapuṭa.

One should prepare three types of *puṭapāka* with the juices of *mustā*, *sūraṇa*, and *varṣābhū* taken individually; five with the juice of *kāsamarda*; and another five with *varā* and cow’s urine. (Āk 2.1.143)
It should be rubbed with decoctions of the roots of the *nyagrodha* tree for ten *puṭas*, and then six times with the juice of *jambīra* and three times with cow's milk. (Āk 2.1.144)
One should perform four operations in sequence: grinding, heating in a crucible, cooking in a pot, and roasting in a *puṭa*; and with each *puṭa*, one should add borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*). (Āk 2.1.145)
For the moonless cloud indeed arises; one should employ it in all yogas.
This is the general purification, but the specific [purification] is now being declared. (Āk 2.1.146)

(Regarding the specific refinement for the process of incineration: One should grind the "moonless" dead sky, which has undergone the general refinement, with decoctions of substances that remove various diseases, and cook it in a *puṭa* vessel. (Āk 2.1.147)
One should perform the ritual three times and seven times; it shall become the remover of each respective disease.
This specific consecration shall be the remover of each respective disease. (Āk 2.1.148)

In the forenoon, the grinding should be performed; at midday, the heating of the vessel; in the afternoon, the cooking in the pot; and at night, the application of the *puṭa* (herbaceous) method in due order. (Āk 2.1.149)
O Supreme Goddess, the processing of mica is said to be fivefold:
the preparation of the grain-mica, the precipitation of the essence, and the purification. (Āk 2.1.150)
Likewise, there is the rite of making one well-remembered and the rite of making one immortal;
[these are performed] for the killing of a being of dense essence, and for the killing of one with dense leaves.
Cinnabar and borax are declared to be the most excellent [for this purpose] in succession; these two are recommended.
(The second method: One should cook *dhānyābhraka* with a decoction of *mustā* in twenty-five *puṭas*. (Āk 2.1.152)

O Goddess of the Suras, [one should perform] one *puṭa* with cow's urine, likewise with decoctions of *triphalā*, with the juice of *kāsamarda*, and once with cow's milk; [this is repeated] three times. (Āk 2.1.153)
Indeed, the moon becomes "moonless" (niścandra) in the clouds; one should employ it in all yogas.
When endowed with specific refinements, it shall become the remover of various diseases. (Āk 2.1.154)
(Third Method) One part of grain-sulphur and two parts of borax, having ground them together, should be sealed in a blind crucible and blown with a fierce fire. (Āk 2.1.155)
One should employ this powder, which is naturally cooling, in all formulations;
when combined with specific preparations, it becomes a remover of various diseases. (Āk 2.1.156)
(Fourth Method) One should grind *dhānyābhra* with acidic liquids and then place it in the sun;
thereafter, one should apply a *puṭa* (roasting), followed by sprinkling with acid and grinding again. (Āk 2.1.157)

Then, after being subjected to twenty cycles of milking, one should place the *abhraka* (mica) that has been stabilized by the *puṭa* process into milk; having stirred it with milk and placed it back in the milk, one should set it out in the sun. (Āk 2.1.158)
One should prepare the packet in this manner repeatedly for twenty-one times;
[using] rice, *vajravallī*, *tālamūlī*, and *punarnavā*. (Āk 2.1.159)
One should grind śārṅgerī, marica, and balā together with milk, along with pūrvābhra, using each of these individually for three days at a time. (Āk 2.1.160)
Having placed it in the sun, one should cook it in a sealed vessel again and again;
thus, when the sky [of the mercury] becomes free of its lunar spots and attains the luster of soot, it becomes "dead. (Āk 2.1.161)
(Fifth method: One should add black pepper equal to one-tenth the weight of dried *dhānyābhraka* (grain mica);
it should be ground with the group of sour substances (*amlavarga*) and soaked in sour liquids for three days. (Āk 2.1.162)
Once that has dried, it should be strongly heated in a crucible using charcoal from the *khadira* tree;
then, having covered it with an upper vessel, one should sprinkle it with some kind of acid. (Āk 2.1.163)
One should sprinkle that very grain six times, again and again, with sour liquids made from the roots and leaves of *agastya*, *śigru*, and *varṣābhū*. (Āk 2.1.164)
Having ground the mica, one should sprinkle it with that [liquid] six times and subject it to heating;
then, having washed it with sugar, honey, clarified butter, and cow’s milk, that mica should be ground again. (Āk 2.1.165)
Having sealed it with six layers of clay, one should cook it, grinding it again and again with the juices of *matsyākṣī* and *ekavīrā*, and thus cook it three times. (Āk 2.1.166)
In this manner, mica (*abhraka*) becomes moonless (*niścandra*) when cooked in *gajapuṭa* [furnaces];
one should employ the cinnabar (*sindūra*) of leaf-mica (*pattrābhraka*) in all formulations. (Āk 2.1.167)
(The sixth method: One should grind *dhānyābhra* for one *yāma* with the fresh juice of *matsyākṣī*, and then cook it in *gajapuṭa* vessels seven times with the juice of *tulasī*. (Āk 2.1.168)
Likewise, with the juices of *kokilākṣa*, the juices of the seven *kumārī* plants, similarly with the juices of white *dūrvā*, and likewise with the juices of *vyāghrī* and *kandara*. (Āk 2.1.169)
Likewise, it should be processed seven times with the juices of *punarnavā*, and thereafter with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*);
thus the "cloud" (*abhra*) becomes moonless, and one should employ it in all formulations. (Āk 2.1.170)
(Seventh Method) One should grind equal parts of *dhānyābhra* and *ṭaṅkaṇa* with cow’s urine, *tulasī* juice,
*vākucī*, and *sūraṇa* for one day, and then cook it in a *puṭa*. (Āk 2.1.171)
Having ground it again and again with liquids, one should cook it in a *puṭa* at the ends of the days.
Having repeatedly sealed it with *puṭas* in this manner, the mica (*abhraka*) becomes moonless (*niścandra*).
(The eighth method. Having ground the bark of the root of *peṭālī* with sour *āranāla* [vinegar], Āk 2.1.173.
One should grind the mica with those juices for one day and then bake it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
in this manner, seven such applications should be made, followed by seven applications with curd. (Āk 2.1.174)
Similarly, by means of the juices of *yavaciñcā*, mica becomes moonless (*niścandra*);
this is the ninth method.
Alternatively, *dhānyābhra* [mica] may be treated with the milks of the sun-plant (*ravikṣīra*) or with the juices of the root of the sun-plant (*ravimūla*). (Āk 2.1.175)
Having ground it repeatedly, one should cook it in a *puṭa* [furnace] seven times; thus it will certainly die [become calcined]. (The tenth method:
One should place *dhānyābhraka* (grain-sized mica) within *tuṣāmla* (sour gruel made from husks) in the sun for one day. (Āk 2.1.176)
Having ground that ball for one watch (yāma) and enclosed it, one should cook it in a gajapuṭa;
likewise, having placed it within cotton-water, one should cook it by placing it in a puṭa. (Āk 2.1.177)
In this manner, having placed it within cow's milk, one should grind it and cook it in a *puṭa*;
thereafter, one should repeatedly treat it with sour liquids, cow's milk, and cotton wool. (Āk 2.1.178)

Through the sequence of heating, grinding, cooking in a vessel, and encapsulation (puṭa), when the twenty-first encapsulation is reached, the mica becomes free of its metallic luster (niścandra). Āk 2.1.179.
The procedure for the immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) of all killed clouds (*abhras*):
(The qualities of *abhraka*)—*Abhraka*, *gagana*, *bhṛṅga*, *bahuputra*, and *umābhava*. (Āk 2.1.180)
The vermilion of leaf-processed abhraka is supreme nectar, highly beneficial;
it destroys the three doṣas, bestows strength, is aphrodisiac, promotes health, and is pure. (Āk 2.1.181)
It is the remover of all diseases, gentle, an antidote to poison, and a rejuvenative elixir.
(Synonyms for cinnabar:)
Hiṅgula is darada; and raso-dbha-va is powdered mercury (cūrṇa-pārada).
Rasagarbha, suraṅga, lohaghna, and siddhipārada [are the subtypes of cinnabar].
Cinnabar is to be known as being of three kinds: carmāra, śukatuṇḍaka, and [the third]. (Āk 2.1.183)
Among those, one should employ the first, the *haṃsapāda*, for the act of piercing;
one should know that to be inferior, while the *śukatuṇḍa* is middling. (Āk 2.1.184)
O Supreme Goddess, one should employ the Haṃsapāda [mantra], which is most excellent and performs all rites, on the path of the ritual of blood extraction. (Āk 2.1.185)
Its essence is indeed that of mercury, derived from the three types of Darada;
[the first is] *śukatuṇḍa* (physically characterized by its properties).
Resembling gold-dross, it has that same appearance and is a destroyer of the *tīkṣṇa* [poison]. (Āk 2.1.186)
The leather-worker is of a sharp nature, while the Śukatuṇḍaka is well-pleased;
the Haṃsapāda possesses similar qualities.
Resembling a hibiscus flower, with feet like those of a swan, he is most excellent. (Āk 2.1.187)
It is excellent for alchemy, for the extraction of all mercury, for the coloring of all [metals], for the calcination of metals, and for the work of improving their color. (Āk 2.1.188)
Likewise, in the binding of color (rāgabandha) for mercury (rasaka), it is known as the foremost;
free from impurities, defects, and the like, it is honored in all undertakings. (Āk 2.1.189)
(Regarding the purification of cinnabar):
Cinnabar, having been processed seven times with sheep’s milk and the group of acidic substances, certainly attains purity through diligent effort. Āk 2.1.190.
(The Extraction of the Essence of Cinnabar):
Cinnabar, when subjected to sublimation in a *pātanāyantra* over a body of water, undoubtedly releases an essence resembling mercury (*sūtaka*). (Āk 2.1.191)
(The Qualities of Cinnabar): Whatever qualities are proclaimed for mercury (pārada), those same qualities indeed exist in cinnabar (hiṅgula).
It is said to remove acute fever (navajvara) and to destroy contagious fever (sampātajvara). (Āk 2.1.192)
(Gairika: Gairika is a mineral of the mountain; it is a red mineral and is also called gavedhuka. (Sub-types of gairika:)
Gairika is said to be of two kinds; among them, the first is svarṇagairika.
Furthermore, there is another variety, stone-gairika; the former is the most excellent in its qualities.
(The qualities of gairika:
It is blood-red, smooth, unctuous, sweet, aphrodisiac, cold, and light. (Āk 2.1.194)
Red ochre (raktagairika) is beneficial for the eyes, destroys blood-bile disorders, and removes poison, hiccups, vomiting, and fever caused by heat; it is excellent and counteracts gold. (Āk 2.1.195)
Pāṣāṇagairika is said to be hard and copper-colored.
Capala pierces the body, lohavedhī pierces iron, and capalā binds mercury. (Āk 2.1.196)
Capalā is manifold and possesses the nature of all metals; it takes the form of gold, silver, copper, lead, and tin. (Āk 2.1.197)
Sharp in form, bell-metal in appearance, red, and likewise uneven;
possessing the nature of volatile mercury and the essence of sattva-metals, that poison possesses the quality of green metal. (The nature of the fickle one. Āk 2.1.198.
Having obtained the volatile substance known as *viṣa*, one should cause it to be administered to the lifeless [subject];
one should completely eliminate it by means of a sealed crucible (*puṭa*) using forest-born dung, along with its smoke. (Āk 2.1.199)
One should indeed avoid its smoke and touch from afar;
for by eating it or touching it, one dies instantly. (Āk 2.1.200)
From observing smoke, a headache and fever arise; when the applied seal has thus been pacified, one should then take up the "restless" [state]. (Āk 2.1.201)
(The qualities of the fickle:
By its mere touch, even a diamond perishes in an instant;
such indeed is declared to be the inherent nature of all fickle things. (Āk 2.1.202)
In the sequence of the King of Nagas, Vaṅgastambha, it is highly praised;
they turn all metals into gold and silver. (Āk 2.1.203)

Furthermore, when purified by means of reasoning (yukti), it likewise penetrates [the target] even without the seed-mantra (bīja)—whether a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million times. (Āk 2.1.204)

Supported by the *vajra*, the king of essences (*rasarāja*), and the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should pierce the metals with smoke; once the essence has been digested, it will dissolve of its own accord. (Āk 2.1.205)
Having emerged from that flickering body, the Great-Souled One [became] *śilājatu*—that which is born of stone, mountain-born, rocky, and mineral-like; *śilājatu* is indeed *śilājatu*. (Āk 2.1.206)
Bitumen (śilājatu) is said to be of two types; that which resembles cow's urine and the like is a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
And there is another preceded by camphor; among those, the first is remembered as being of two kinds. (Āk 2.1.207)
Between these two, the one with a sentient being is superior in quality to the one without a sentient being;
[it is like] the snow-capped mountain compared to the feet scorched by the fierce sun in summer. (Āk 2.1.208)
Mineral pitch (śilādhātu) may exude from mountains containing gold, silver, or copper.
(The qualities of mineral pitch:
That which is produced from a mountain containing gold is like the Japā flower in color and is heavy. (Āyurveda Saṃhitā 2.1.209)
Accompanied by its essence, it is supremely delicious; it is that supreme elixir, born from the mountain containing silver in its womb, sweet, pale-white, and heavy. (Āk 2.1.210)
Śilāja (bitumen) cures anemia and especially conquers diseases of the bile;
that which is produced from a mountain containing copper ore is blue in color, dense, and heavy. (Āk 2.1.211)
Śilāja (bitumen) destroys phlegm and wind; it is sharp, hot, and an excellent digestive stimulant.
That which, when thrown into fire, takes on the shape of a lingam and emits no smoke, is indeed [the best]. (Āk 2.1.212)
That which is dissolved even in water is indeed established as *śilājatu*.
Black, smelling of cow’s urine, resembling *guggulu*, containing sugar-like particles, soft, earthy, unacidic, astringent, oily, and heavy—such *śilājatu* is excellent. (Āk 2.1.213)
And everything that is bitter or pungent should be sweet, neither too hot nor too cold. (Āk 2.1.214)

It is aphrodisiac, a conqueror of the three doṣas, a purgative, beneficial for the eyes, and a rejuvenative; it destroys consumption, swelling, abdominal enlargements, and hemorrhoids, and removes urinary disorders and retention of urine. (Āk 2.1.215)

Surely it pacifies fever, anemia, and swelling; it removes urinary disorders and weak digestion; it cuts away excess fat and pacifies consumption (*yakṣman*); it uproots diseases of the roots. It destroys the spleen and cures abdominal and cardiac colic; it removes undigested matter (*āma*) and destroys all skin diseases. What more can be said? It is beneficial for both the body and for metal. (Āk 2.1.216)

Whatever qualities reside in mercury, the secondary minerals, the lord of metals, gems, and base metals, those dwell in the mineral *śilādhātu* for the sake of conquering old age and death. (Āk 2.1.217)
*Bhūnāga*, *kṣitināga*, *bhūlatā*, *raktajantuka*,
*kṣitija*, *kṣitijantu*, *viṣaghna*, and *raktatuṇḍaka*. (Āk 2.1.218)

Those eyebrow-creepers from which blood does not flow constantly, even though they generally grow in a soil of blood—those should be gathered; one should cause the being that bestows the wealth of poison-removal to descend into them.
If mercury, the lord of alchemy, moves through them by that method, evenly, by means of the application of the *sāraṇā* machine;
This bound [mantra] pierces the ten million-fold [obstacles]; one should employ it in battle, or in the solar [rite]. (Āk 2.1.219)
(The qualities of the *bhūnāga* substance:
The essence produced from the *bhūnāga* overcomes poison, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and death;
it brings everything under control, destroys all diseases, and is an elixir (*rasāyana*). (Āk 2.1.220)
When processed by the art of *jāraṇā* in the king of essences (*rasendra*), it becomes capable of piercing ten million times;
in an instant, it consumes red metals such as gold and the like. (Āk 2.1.221)
(The first method: causing the *bhūnāga* essence to descend.
One should wash with water the clay of the *bhūnāga* born from red earth.
As long as there remains even a single sentient being, that very world is indeed one in which all beings have been purified.
One should strongly heat that [substance] together with the five friends in a crucible;
having broken the crucible, one should take that essence and the dross again. Āk 2.1.223.
Thus, by heating it three times, one should collect what remains as pure essence.
(The second method:
One should place earth from a *bhūnāga* [ant-hill] along with actual *bhūnāgas* into a vessel. Āk 2.1.224.
One should sprinkle it repeatedly with water for six months or until the end of the year;
by this procedure, one should extract its essence just like the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*). (Āk 2.1.225)
(Third Method:
One should have blood-born *bhūnāgas* devoured by a peacock kept in a cage during the autumn season; one should always collect their excrement. (Āk 2.1.226)
Lac, resin of the Sarja tree, Sarjikṣāra, Guggulu, and Mitrapañcaka; wool, alkaline salts, Patu, Nīla, the serpent, and Indragopaka. (Āk 2.1.227)
Fish, a blue lizard, the shell of a tortoise, rabbit bone, honey, peacock, conch, and copper sulfate (tuttha), along with all parts of a peacock's excrement; Āk 2.1.228.
Having placed everything inside the crucible, one should blow it strongly with a fierce fire;
then, having broken open the crucible, one should take that essence and the dross again. (Āk 2.1.229)
Thus, by performing the dhamana three times, one should extract the remaining essence. (Haridrāśman:
Haridrāśman, Niśāgrāvan, Pītāṅga, and Pītakarṣaṇa. Āk 2.1.230.
That which contains the essence of that [mineral]—white or golden—is excellent for the alchemy of mercury (*rasarasāyana*).
(Agnijāra:
Agnijāra is known as *agniniryāsa*, *agnigarbha*, and *agnija*. (Āk 2.1.231)
Vaḍabāgni, mala, jarāyu, arṇavodbhava, agnijvāla, agnijāra, and sindhuplava are declared to be the ten [names]. (Āk 2.1.232)
The placenta of a sea-monster (agninakra) cast out upon the ocean and dried by the heat of the sun is known as *agnijāra*. (Āk 2.1.233)
The membrane (jarāyu) burns like fire upon contact; it is slippery and floats upon the ocean [of fluids].
It is of four colors, and among them, that which is reddish is the best. (Āk 2.1.234)
(The qualities of Agnijāra:

Agnijāra is pungent and hot in potency; it destroys abdominal diseases, removes phlegm and wind, increases pitta, and cures blood disorders, derangements of the humors (*sannipāta*), colic, and other wind-related ailments. (Āk 2.1.235)
Agni-jāra destroys the three doṣas, cures dhanu-vāta and other wind disorders, enhances the potency of rasa, and likewise acts as a digestive stimulant and a catalyst for digestion. (Āk 2.1.236)
(Kharparī [Rasaka]) Kharparī, rasaka, tuttha, kharparī, and amṛtasambhavā are synonyms.
Rasaka is said to be of two kinds: dardura and kāravellaka. (Āk 2.1.237)
The *dardura* is said to be "with-bites" (*sadaṃśa*), while the *kāravellaka* is "without-bites" (*nirdaṃśa*).
Of these two, the former is auspicious for the falling away of the *sattva*, and the latter is for medicinal substances and the like. (Āk 2.1.238)

Externally, it resembles a dense mass of living beings; it is beautiful like turmeric, transparent like a shard, and like *tuttha* (copper sulfate), it is excellent and possesses a slightly raised center. (Āk 2.1.239)
(The qualities of kharparya: Rasaka destroys all the *doṣas*, eliminates *kapha* and *pitta*, cures eye diseases and consumption, and serves as a coloring agent for iron and mercury. (Āk 2.1.240)
Nāgārjuna has described two types of mercury: both are known as the most excellent perfected mercuries (siddharasa), which are supreme for the purpose of transforming the body and metal. Āk 2.1.241.
Both mercury and its derivative (rasaka), by which they have been made fire-resistant, will undoubtedly grant the accomplishment of both the body and the metal. (Ākāśabhairava-tantra 2.1.242)

(The extraction of the essence from kharparī: Having ground together the powder of jayantī and triphalā, turmeric, jaggery, and ṭaṅkaṇa—each being one-quarter part of the mercury—one should smear this paste onto crucibles. (Āk 2.1.243)
Having bound the two tubes together in a pair, one should dry them in the hot sun;
then, when the crucible is heated, the essence (sattva) is to be extracted by means of the pātālayantra or by means of a sealed crucible (puṭa). (Āk 2.1.244)
(Purification of Kharparī):
One should saturate *rasaka* with the menstrual blood and urine of a woman in her courses for one day;
by rubbing it with those very substances for another day, it attains purification. (Āk 2.1.245)
(Regarding *mayūratuttha*): *Mayūratuttha*, *tuttha*, *nīlāśman*, and copper ash;
*mayūragrīvaka*, *sasyaka*, and *kṣveḍanāśana*, O Beloved. (Āk 2.1.246)
Resembling a peacock's neck when ground, it becomes like cow's milk;
when thrown into water, it floats—this is *māyūratutthaka*. (Āk 2.1.247)
Alternatively, one should rub tuttha—which resembles a parrot’s plumage and is marked within by golden spots—on iron that has been combined with an acid. Āk 2.1.248.
This mayūratutthaka becomes like iron or copper.
(The purification of mayūratuttha:
One should grind tuttha with the excrement of a cat and a pigeon. Āk 2.1.249.
Having added one-tenth part of ṭaṅkaṇa, it should then be cooked in a mild fire-pit (*mṛdupuṭa*);
thereafter, a fire-pit with curd and a fire-pit with honey should be applied for the purification of *tuttha*. (Āk 2.1.250)
(The precipitation of the essence of peacock-tuttha:
One should grind together equal parts of *tuttha* and *ṭaṅkaṇa* until they are finely reduced;
having placed that in a crucible and sealed it, one should blow it with a fierce fire. (Āk 2.1.251)
A being resembling an *indragopa* insect falls [from the sky] without a doubt.
(The qualities of *mayūratuttha*:
Tuttha is pungent, astringent, and hot; it removes leucoderma and eye diseases. Āk_2.1.252.
Kaṅkuṣṭha is praised for neutralizing all poisons and defects, and it bestows a radiant complexion.
(Synonyms of Kaṅkuṣṭha)
Kaṅkuṣṭha and kākakuṣṭha are purgatives that impart color. (Āk 2.1.253)
Kaṅkuṣṭha is said to be of two kinds: that consisting of gold and that consisting of silver.
Kaṅkuṣṭha destroys wounds, parasites, and fever; it removes colic, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and abdominal tumors (gulma). (Āk 2.1.254)
(Girisindūra):
The red juice found within the stones of great mountains, when dried, is designated by the name *girisindūra*. (Āk 2.1.255)
Girisindūra is said to pacify the three humors (tridoṣa), act as a purgative, bind the essence of mercury, strengthen the body and the metals, and is beneficial for the eyes. (Āk 2.1.256)
(Ṭaṅkaṇa):
Ṭaṅkaṇa, ṭaṅkaṇakṣāra, rasakṣāra, rasādhika, lohadrāvī, rasaghna, subhaga, and raṅgada are its names. (Āk 2.1.257)
The *navāhvaya* (also known as *kṣāraśreṣṭha*), which grows on the banks of the Mālatī river, destroys urinary calculi, dysentery, and immobile poisons. (Āk 2.1.258)
It is proclaimed by the masters headed by Nāgārjuna as that which brings about the perfection of alchemy (*rasasiddhi*).
(Kampillaka) is like fine powder, rich in luster, and exceedingly abundant. (Āk 2.1.259)
That *kampillaka* is considered to be a mineral product from the country of Saurāṣṭra.

It destroys bile, ulcers, flatulence, and constipation; it removes phlegm, abdominal diseases, worms, and tumors (*gulma*); it cures colic, piles, fever, and swelling; and as a purgative, *kampillaka* eliminates impurities. (Āk 2.1.260)
The vatsanābha poison, beginning with its methods of extraction and so forth, is indeed declared at the outset to be an elixir (rasāyana). (Āk 2.1.261)
Amṛta, vatsanābha, viṣa, ugra, mahauṣadha, garala, maraṇa, nāga, stokaka, and prāṇahāraka are synonyms for poison. (Āk 2.1.262)

It is declared, O beloved, to be the remover of all skin diseases, the destroyer of all ailments, and the bringer of cessation to diseases such as those caused by the derangement of the humors (sannipāta). Āk 2.1.263.
Kāsīsa is known by the synonyms dhātukāsīsa, kesara, haṃsalomaśa,
śodhana, pāṃśukāsīsa, śubhra, and sattvāhvaya. (Āk 2.1.264)
Kāsīsa is known to be of three types: white, black, and yellow;
furthermore, it is called kāsīsa, puṣpakāsīsa, and hīrakāsīsa. (Āk 2.1.265)
Others have declared that it is fourfold—yellow, black, white, and red.
Kāsīsa is hot, possessing alkaline, astringent, and sour tastes, along with a bitter quality. (Āk 2.1.266)
It pacifies wind and phlegm, is beneficial for the eyes, and is supremely coloring;
it removes dysuria, urinary calculi, skin diseases, itching, wounds, and poisons. (Āk 2.1.267)
(Gaurīpāṣāṇaka):
Gaurīpāṣāṇaka is yellow, with a distinct body, and exists as a powder; it binds mercury, is unctuous, destroys the bodily humors, and enhances the potency and vigor of mercury. (Āk 2.1.268)
(Tuvarī and Phaṭakī:
Bhūmistuvarikā, Phullatuvarī, Rañjikā, Kṣiti, Citrabhū, Cīnakāra, and Mañjiṣṭhārāgadāyinī. (Āk 2.1.269)
Khagastu, phaṭakī, and dugdhapāṣāṇa cure eye diseases;
the mineral known as karpūra-stone dyes with the color of mañjiṣṭhā. (Āk 2.1.270)
The *podāraśṛṅgī* is greenish-yellow in color and is found in the region of Gurjara; it grows on the slopes of Mount Arjuna. (Āk 2.1.271)
Lead-sattva pacifies wind and phlegm, removes impurities from the male organ, is excellent for binding mercury, and is the best for dyeing the hair black. (Āk 2.1.272)
Sindūra, sindūranāgagarbha, saimantika, vīrapāṃsu, nāgabhava, rakta, nāgareṇu, gaṇapatibhūṣā, and suraṅga are its synonyms. (Āk 2.1.273)
It brings good fortune, beauty, auspiciousness, and a ruddy complexion. Sindhūra is pungent, bitter, and hot; it heals wounds. (Āk 2.1.274)
O beloved, whatever qualities exist in vermilion (hiṅgula)—namely, the supreme pacification of leprosy, poison, itching, and erysipelas—those same qualities reside in timuruka. (Āk 2.1.275)
(Rasāñjana):
Rasāñjana is produced from mercury (*rasodbhūta*), it contains mercury within (*rasagarbha*), and it is born before mercury (*rasāgraja*).
When bell-metal (*rīti*) is being smelted, its dross (*kiṭṭa*) is indeed rasāñjana. (Āk 2.1.276)
In its absence, however, one should prepare a medicinal preparation for children made from the decoction of *dārvī*; likewise, an artificial medicine may be prepared from the decoction of *dārvī*.

That which is produced from a decoction of *dārvī*, which expands when placed upon the throat and applied to the eye, is designated as *rasāñjana*; it is an astringent, pungent, and bitter. (Āk 2.1.278)
Slightly warm, it removes phlegm, is scarifying and scraping, light, pacifies hemorrhaging and bile, and destroys diseases of the eyes. (Āk 2.1.279)
Rasāñjana, tārkṣyaśaila, and varyañjana, as well as rasanābha and agnisāra, are celebrated as having twelve names. (Āk 2.1.280)
(Regarding *nīlāñjana*):
*Nīlam* and *nīlāñjanam*, as well as *cakṣuṣyam* and *vārisambhavam*, and *kapotakam* and *kāpotam*, are declared to be produced from the earth of Śakra. (Āk 2.1.281)
Blue antimony is said to be cooling, pungent, bitter, and astringent;
it is beneficial for the eyes, destroys phlegm and wind, is an antidote to poison, and is a rejuvenative elixir. (Āk 2.1.282)
(Sauvīrāñjana):
Sauvīra collyrium is unctuous when rubbed on a stone surface;
having the luster of collyrium and the appearance of stone, this natural variety is the best. (Āk 2.1.283)
Sauvīra collyrium is beneficial for removing *rakta-pitta* (bleeding disorders), destroys poison, hiccup, and eye diseases, and cleanses and heals wounds. (Āk 2.1.284)
(Srotoñjana: synonyms) Srotoñjana is known as srotodbhava, srotanadībhava, vāribhava, and likewise another.
The essence of *sauvīra*, the essence of pigeon-dung, the summit of an anthill, and that which is called "equal to the sages" (*munisaṃmitāhva*).
This is *srotoñjana*: it has the shape of an anthill's peak, possesses the luster of a blue lotus when broken, and has the hue of red ochre when rubbed. (Āk 2.1.286)
Srotoñjana is cold, pungent, and astringent; it destroys worms.
This elixir (rasāyana) should be administered with meat broth; it is supreme for increasing breast milk. (Āk 2.1.287)

Srotoñjana is cooling, unctuous, thirst-quenching, sweet, and scraping; it is beneficial for the eyes and removes hiccup, vomiting, nausea, and the provocation of kapha, pitta, and blood. (Āk 2.1.288)
From the agitation caused by the churning of the exhausted Vāsuki, poisonous drops of sweat rose from his mouth and fell upon other continents. (Ahiphena) Āk 2.1.289.
Wherever they fell, they grew in the form of shrubs;
the people say that the resin produced from them is called *aphena*. (Āk 2.1.290)

There are four types of "foamless" [mercury]: digestion (*jāraṇa*), killing (*māraṇa*), retention (*dhāraṇa*), and extraction (*sāraṇa*). I shall describe their characteristics in due order. (Āk 2.1.291)
White is said to be *jāraṇa* (digestion), while black color is *māraṇa* (killing).
Yellow color is *dhāraṇa* (retention), and likewise, variegated is *sāraṇa* (integration). Āk 2.1.292.
Jāraṇa digests food; māraṇa bestows death; dhāraṇa stabilizes youth; and sāraṇa extracts the essence from impurities. (Āk 2.1.293)

Free from froth, it destroys the derangement of the humors (sannipāta), is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and induces clarity; it cures malabsorption (grahaṇī), diarrhea, and even impotence. (Āk 2.1.294)
Synonyms for *puṣpāñjana* are:
*puṣpāñjana*, *puṣpaketu*, *kaustubha*, and *kusumāñjana*.
Rītika, rītikusuma, rītipuṣpa, and puṣpaka. (Āk 2.1.295)
Pushpāñjana is declared to be beneficial; it cures bile disorders, hiccups, and burning sensations.
It destroys poison, cough, and fever, and removes all diseases of the eyes. (Āk 2.1.296)
(Conch):
Śaṅkha, arṇavabhava, kambu, jalaja, pāvanadhvani, kuṭila, antarmahānāda, śvetapīta, and sunādaka are synonyms for the conch shell. (Āk 2.1.297)
*Sasvana*, *dīrghanāda*, and *bahunāda* are names for the conch dear to Hara (*harapriya*).
*Kṣullaka* and *kṣudraśaṅkha* refer to a small conch; *śambūka* and *nakhaśaṅkhaka* refer to the same. (Āk 2.1.298)
Conch shell is pungent in taste, cooling, and bestows nourishment, virility, and strength;
it destroys abdominal tumors, colic, phlegm, and asthma, and removes the defects of poison. (Āk 2.1.299)
The small oyster shell (*kṣullaka-śukti*) is pungent, unctuous, a reliever of colic, and digestive;
it is also the mother of pearls, as are the large oyster shell (*mahāśukti*) and the common oyster (*śuktikā*). (Āk 2.1.300)

She who causes pearls to burst forth is praised as Muktāsphoṭastotikā; she who brings forth pearls is known as Mauktikaprasavā, as well as Mauktikasūḥ and is likewise remembered as Muktāmātā. (Āk 2.1.301)
Pearl oyster shell is pungent and unctuous; it removes asthma and heart disease, pacifies colic, improves the appetite, is sweet, and is an excellent digestive stimulant. (Āk 2.1.302)
Jalaśukti, kṣudraśukti, and krimisusphuṭikā are varieties of water-shell.
Jalaśukti is pungent, unctuous, digestive, and a remedy for abdominal tumors and colic. (Āyurveda-kalpa 2.1.303)
Likewise, *kaparda*, *kapardaka*, *varāṭa*, *kaparda*, and *varāṭikā* [are names for cowrie shells]; they are antidotes to poison, appetizing, digestive, and strength-giving. (Āk 2.1.304)
Moving and unmoving, moving and excellent, he is the child’s plaything;
the *varāṭikā* is yellowish, knotted at the back, long, and round. (Āk 2.1.305)
That [elixir] designated by the physicians of mercury as "moving and unmoving" (carācara) is best when weighing one and a half niṣkas, and middling when weighing one niṣka. (Āk 2.1.306)
The smallest [dose] is proclaimed to be three-quarters of a niṣka;
it destroys disorders such as indigestion and colic, and cures chronic diarrhea and consumption. (Āk 2.1.307)

Pungent and hot, it stimulates digestion, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and removes wind and phlegm; it is prescribed for the digestion of mercury and is highly recommended among the substances used for *biḍa* salt. (Āk 2.1.308)
Other types of human hair are heavy and increase phlegm and bile;
the shell of a cowrie (kaparda) is pungent, bitter, and hot, and it cures earache and wounds. (Āk 2.1.309)
It destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and colic, and eliminates disorders of the eyes.
*Sābuṇi* is all-alkali (*sarvakṣāra*), multi-alkali (*bahukṣāra*), and the alkali of the *samūha* group (*samūhakṣārasābuṇi*). (Āk 2.1.310)
Stomakṣāra, mahākṣāra, malāri, kṣāramelaka, sarvakṣāra, and atikṣāra are beneficial for the eyes and cleanse the bladder. (Āk 2.1.311)
Navasāra (sal ammoniac) cures upward-moving wind and worms, and like vit salt, it cleanses the mouth;
it is produced from bricks when the wood of the *karīra* and *pīlu* trees is being burnt. (Āk 2.1.312)
This alkali is *navasāra*, known by the name *cūlikālavaṇa*;
it facilitates the digestion of mercury, liquefies metals, and stimulates the digestive fire. (Āk 2.1.313)
It destroys abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and dryness of the mouth, and it digests meat and other foods that have been eaten.
(Saurāṣṭrī) Then, one should saturate the saurāṣṭrī a hundred times with cow bile. Āk 2.1.314.
Having heated it, one should cause the being to fall; this is the extremely secret *krāmaṇa* [charm].
First is the name of the mouse, then the name of the stone (*ākhupāṣāṇa*). (Āk 2.1.315)
This substance known as *ākhu-pāṣāṇa* (mouse-stone) is an iron-ore conglomerate;
it is a mouse-stone that is astringent and removes vomiting, cold, and fever. (Āk 2.1.316)
In rites for deliverance (*tārakarma*), it is to be fully honored; it cuts through fat and bad flesh.
*Sarjarasa*, *rāla*, and *sarjarasa* are indeed yakṣa-incense, beloved by the fire. (Āk 2.1.317)
The resin of the *śāla* tree is beloved by the gods, fragrant, and dear to incense-lovers.
*Rāla*, however, is said to be of five kinds: red, yellow, white, and black. (Āk 2.1.318)
They should be known to be of various colors; among them, the black variety is superior in quality. The red variety, however, is cool, unctuous, and astringent-bitter in taste. (Āk 2.1.319)

Guggulu removes wind and bile, and destroys eruptions, itching, and ulcers. In ancient times, it restored the beauty, fortitude, courage, and splendor of the gods who had been defeated by the lord of the Dānavas and were deprived of their luster.
Beholding it, Viṣṇu indeed created the nectar-like guggulu, which bestows strength, a beautiful body, and victory.
Generally, city-trees grow in desert lands. (Āk 2.1.321)
Scorched by the rays of the sun in summer, they emit guggulu resin.
Guggulu is said to be of five kinds: Mahiṣākṣa and Nīlaka; Āk_2,1.322.
Padma, Kumuda, Suvarṇa as the fifth, O beloved, Mahiṣākṣa, and Nīla—these are the ones that bestow qualities upon elephants. (Āk 2.1.323)
Kumuda is for horses, and Svarṇavarṇaka is for men;
[these should be applied] in castor oil, sesame oil, or ghee. (Āk 2.1.324)
One should perform purification with decoctions of the five bitter herbs and good guggulu; one should cook it in a *dolāyantra* until it becomes pure. (Āk 2.1.325)

Thus, having grasped this pure [practice], one should apply it to the various yogas; thereby, diseases such as scrofula, glandular swellings, and so forth, as well as wind-disorders, are destroyed. (Āk 2.1.326)
Yavakṣāra (barley alkali) is known as amṛta, pākya, yavaja, yavaśūkaja,
yavaśūka, yavāhva, yavapākya, and yavāruja. (Āk 2.1.327)

Barley-alkali (yavakṣāra) is pungent and hot; it relieves the pain of abdominal enlargement caused by phlegm and wind, and is supreme in removing undigested matter, colic, urinary stones, dysuria, and the disorders of poison. (Āk 2.1.328)
*Sarjikṣāra* is *sadyaḥkṣāra*, *sarjika-kṣāra*, *sajjī*, and *suvarjika*.
*Sarjīka* is pungent and dry; it is sharp and removes the afflictions caused by *vāta* and *kapha*. (Āk 2.1.329)
It destroys abdominal tumors, constipation, and hemorrhoids, and removes urinary disorders and diseases of the stomach.
(Lavaṇakṣāra) is also known as loṇāra, lavaṇottha, lavaṇāsura, and lavaṇameda. Āk 2,1.330.
Resin-derived salt, alkaline salt, and saline alkali—these salts and alkaline salts are extremely hot and sharp, and they cause an increase in bile (pitta). (Āk 2.1.331)
Alkali and salt slightly alleviate the pain of wind-born abdominal tumors (*vātagulma*) and similar conditions.
Vajraka, vajrakakṣāra, the best of alkalis, and vidāraka are synonyms. (Āk 2.1.332)
Sāra, the essence of sandalwood, smoke-origination, that which is born from smoke, elephants, extremely hot vajra-alkali, sharp alkali, and rodhana. (Āk 2.1.333)
It is the supreme alleviator of gulma, abdominal diseases, distress, constipation, and colic.
Sāmudraka is called sāmudra and sāmudralavaṇa; it is auspicious. (Sāmudralavaṇa) Āk 2.1.334.
Sea salt is light, beneficial for the heart, and does not aggravate wind, blood, or bile.
It causes a burning sensation, destroys phlegm and wind, stimulates digestion, improves the appetite, and is pleasant. (Āyurvedadīpikā 2.1.335)
Saindhava is known as śītaśiva, nādeya, sindhuja, śiva, śuddha, śivātmaka, pathya, māṇimantha, and navābhidha— thus it has nine names. (Āk 2.1.336)
Rock salt (saindhava) is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, digestive, and appetizing;
when used as a nasal drop (nasya), it is pure, destroys the three doṣas, and overcomes wounds, defects, and constipation. (Āk 2.1.337)
Saindhava salt is to be known as being of two kinds, white and red, respectively;
of these, the white variety is rich in qualities regarding its taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation (vipāka). Āk 2.1.338.
*Kācalavaṇa* is that which arises from blue glass (*nīlakāca*), as well as *kācatilaka*, which is produced from glass;
it is known as *kākasauvarcala* and is considered to be produced by boiling (*pākyaja*). (Āk 2.1.339)
Glass-origined [substances], heart-fragrance, that-time-salt, kuruvinda, glass-dirt, and katiman—these are the fourteen. (Āk 2.1.340)
The salt known as *kāca* is appetizing, slightly alkaline, and associated with *pitta*;
it causes a burning sensation, destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, stimulates digestion, and relieves abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and colic. (Āyurvedadīpikā 2.1.341)
Biḍalavaṇa:
Biḍa, biḍaka, khaṇḍa, kṛtakṣāra, āsura, supākya, lavaṇakhaṇḍa, dhūrta, and kṛtrimaka—these are the ten [types]. (Āk 2.1.342)
Biḍa salt is hot, salty, digestive, and subdues wind;
it improves the appetite, destroys indigestion and colic, and eliminates abdominal tumors and urinary disorders. (Āk 2.1.343)
Sauvarcala, rucaka, tilaka, hṛdyagandhaka, akṣa, kṛṣṇalavaṇa, rucya, and likewise kodravika [are types of salt]. (Āk 2.1.344)
Sauvarcala salt is light, alkaline, pungent, and hot; it alleviates abdominal tumors and colic pain.
It conquers upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), abdominal pain, distress, constipation, and loss of appetite. (Āk 2.1.345)
*Amlavetasa* is sour, a piercer (*vedhin*), acid in taste, and free from reeds (*vītavetasa*).
It is also known as *vetasāra*, *amlasāra*, *śaravedhī*, and *vedhaka*. (Āk 2.1.346)
Nīla, Bhedana, Bhedin, Rājāmla, Amlabhedana, Amlāṅkuśa, Raktasāra, Phalāmla, and Amlanāyaka. (Āk 2.1.347)
The two types of *amlavetasa*—namely *sahasravedhī*, *vīrāmla*, *gulmaketu*, *dharākṣidhā*, and *śaṅkhamāṃsādidrāvī*—are indeed acidulous. (Āk 2.1.348)
Amlavetasa is extremely sour, astringent, hot, and a conqueror of vāta;
it is supreme for curing kapha-type hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, undigested matter (āmadoṣa), and loss of appetite. (Āk 2.1.349)
*Kāca* (glass/quartz), *tuṣārasāra* (essence of frost), *rasakhoṭa*, and *malāpaha* remove [impurities]; *śṛṅgārī* and *abhradhārī* remove all diseases of the eyes. (Āk 2.1.350)
*Chagaṇa*, *piṣṭaka*, *chagaṇa*, *chāṇa*, *utpala*, and *vanotpala*; *kariṇḍa*, *upalaśāṭhī*, and *varaṭī* are synonyms for dried cow-dung (*chagaṇa*). (Āk 2.1.351)
That ash, renowned for removing defects from mercury and iron, is celebrated for the destruction of misfortune.
Embers (*aṅgāra*) are considered to be the remains of fire, the sparks of the fire-crested one, and are known as *koliśas*. (Āk 2.1.352)
And the *kokilā* are embers extinguished without water;
*sikatā* refers to fine sand produced by a current, moistened with water, consisting of minute particles. (Āk 2.1.353)
That sand removes fatigue through sprinkling and cures the *sannipāta* disorders.
(Purification of the minor metals:
One should saturate green vitriol (*kāsīsa*) for a day with the juice of *jambīra* fruits in the heat of the sun. Āk 2.1.354.
Tungsten (ṭaṅkaṇa), red ochre (gairī), kaṅkuṣṭha, cowrie shell (varāṭikā), conch shell (śaṅkha), and blue antimony (nīlāñjana) should each be purified day by day. Āk 2.1.355.
One should rub śilājatu with cow’s milk, decoctions of triphalā, and the juice of bhṛṅga in an iron vessel for one day; thus it becomes purified. (Āk 2.1.356)
Cinnabar, processed with sheep's milk and the sour group of substances (amlavarga) seven times with care, certainly attains purity. (Āk 2.1.357)
Sūryāvarta, vajrakanda, kadalī, devadālikā, śigru, kośātakī, vandhyā, kākamācī, and vālukā. (Āk 2.1.358)
One should diligently infuse these with a single essence together with the three alkalis, salts, and the group of sour substances for one day. (Āk 2.1.359)
Sauvīra, kāntapāṣāṇa, pure śuddha bhūnāga, and all the secondary minerals (uparasas) should then be processed separately day after day. (Āk 2.1.360)
Then, the wise one should cook those [substances] with their respective fluxes in a dolāyantra for one day;
all the secondary minerals (uparasas), individually, are purified—of this there is no doubt. (ĀK 2.1.361)
With *punarnavā*, *meghanāda*, *kapittha*, *jambīra*, and *tinduka*; with *agasti* flowers, *kumuda*, barley, *ciñcā*, and *amlavetasa*. (Āk 2.1.362)
With *vanasūraṇa*, *bhūdhātrī*, *maṇḍūkī*, and *karavīraka*; with *kāravallī*, *kṣīrakanda*, red lotus (*raktotpala*), *śamī*, and *ghana*. (Āk 2.1.363)
With the horns of a ram, the fat of a rabbit, *śakravāruṇī*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*;
with oil, fish-fat, *vyoṣa*, and these juices, along with *kāñjika*—ĀK 2.1.364.
With all or any of these [substances], one should cook the mica-leaf and other minor minerals in a swinging apparatus (*ḍolāyantra*) for three days for the sake of purification. (ĀK 2.1.365)
Āk, 2,
2 Śrī Bhairava says: I shall describe the sequence of the origin and other details regarding all metals, such as gold and the rest.

Gold: its synonyms are *svarṇa*, *suvarṇa*, *kanaka*, *ujjvala*, *kāñcana*, *kalyāṇa*, *hāṭaka*, *hiraṇya*, *manohara*, *gāṅgeya*, *gairika*, *mahārajata*, *agnivīrya*, *rukma*, *hematapanīya*, and *bhāsvara*. (Āk 2.2.1)

Variegated with the colors of Jāmbūnada gold, Aṣṭāpada, Jātarūpa, Piñjana, and Cāmīkara; possessing immense splendor with a hue as tawny as refined gold, they were radiant and pure like glowing lamps. (Āk 2.2.2)
Maṅgalya, Saumerava, Śātakumbha, Śṛṅgāra, Candra, Araja, Jāmbavān, Āgneya, Niṣka, and Agniśikha—these are the names of gold extracted from the ocean of the eyes. (Āk 2.2.3)
(The varieties of gold:
Native, innate, produced by fire, and produced from a mine. Āk 2.2.4.
Gold produced by the transmutation of the lord of mercury (rasendra) is said to be of five kinds;
it is indeed that by which the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), born of the quality of passion (rajas), is enveloped. (Āk 2.2.5)
That is declared to be the primordial (prakṛta), difficult to obtain even for the gods;
by it Brahmā was enveloped at birth, for that is indeed innate gold. (Āk 2.2.6)
The unbearable Śaiva splendor emitted by Agni was swallowed; that which was thus designated became gold, known as *suvarṇa* because it originated from fire. (Āk 2.2.7)
This divine triad of gold, endowed with sixteen qualities, makes the body free from old age and disease merely by being worn. (Āk 2.2.8)
That gold which is produced from the mines of mountains is known as *khanija* (mineral-born);
it is enriched with fourteen colors, and when consumed, it removes all diseases. (Āk 2.2.9)
That which is produced by the transmutation (vedha) of the lord of mercury is declared to be "born of transmutation" (vedhaja);
for that born of transmutation is indeed the most excellent elixir (rasāyana), supremely pure. (Āk 2.2.10)
Gold may be of two kinds: having a reddish luster or being yellow in color.
(Regarding the forms of gold that are acceptable or unacceptable:
it is red when heated, white when cut, and has the luster of saffron on the touchstone. Āk 2.2.11.
Gold that is heavy, glossy, soft, clear, free of flaws, and reddish-yellow—rich in the sixteen colors—is recommended for both the body and metalwork. (Āk 2.2.12)
The leaf is white-bodied, hard, rough, discolored, and dirty;
when burned it becomes white and black, and when rubbed on a touchstone it turns white and light. (Āk 2.2.13)
Gold that is neither purified nor dead produces a host of diseases; it destroys happiness, virility, and strength. Therefore, purification is proclaimed. (Āk 2.2.14)
(Refining Gold):
Ant-hill earth, soot, red ochre, brick, and salt—these are the five clays [to be used] with *jambīra* fruits or *vāranālaka*. (Āk 2.2.15)
Having ground [the substance], one should smear it upon a gold leaf and place it covered with ashes inside a crucible;
one should apply the *puṭa* treatment as long as it remains liquid, by which means it becomes purified. (Āk 2.2.16)
One should purify gold by means of *puṭapāka* (sealed heating) using clay impregnated for five days with the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga*, along with ashes and salt. (Āk 2.2.17)
One should soak the five earths for three days with the sour juice of *mātuluṅga*;
then, with rock salt and powdered earth, gold is purified as before. (Āk 2.2.18)
One should heat [the substance] and pour it successively seven times with each of these liquids: oil, buttermilk, cow’s urine, sour gruel, and horse-gram water. (Āk 2.2.19)
This purification is praised for gold and other metal leaves; likewise, one should pour [mercury] upon molten lead and tin for the sake of their complete purification. (Āk 2.2.20)
One should first dissolve gold in the juice derived from *kāñcanāra* seven times; thereafter, the gold will certainly become fit for ritual application. (Āk 2.2.21)

One should smear gold leaves with (1) gold ash, lead powder combined with mica, and mixed with the milk of a *vajrī* plant; then, through the application of a *puṭa* [firing] process, one should coat them. Āk 2.2.22.
Having ground a dead snake with the milky sap of *snuhī* or with some acidic liquid, one should smear a gold leaf, seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa*. (Āk 2.2.23)

Having taken the dead lead (mṛtanāga) in an eighth part [of the mercury], one should grind it with sour liquids; having sealed it, one should cook it in a gajapuṭa fire as before, combined with lead. (Āk 2.24)
Thus, through repeated heating, it certainly dies eight times.
[Then] pure mercury equal in amount to gold ash, along with sulphur and pyrite, together with acidic liquids— (Āk 2.25)

Gold is killed by eight layers [of reagents] according to the procedure as before; (this is gold ash [3]). One should place an amount of pure gold equal to the purified mercury in a mortar and form it into a ball. ĀK 2.2.26.

Having placed sulphur above and below [the substance] in equal amounts to the whole and having sealed it, one should apply thirty *vanotpala* [measurements] of heat; in this manner, fourteen *puṭas* should be given. (Āk 2.27)
The ash becomes free of impurities; fragrance should be applied again and again.
(Gold ash [4]) Having melted one *tola* of gold and one *māṣa* of pure lead... Āk_2,2.28.

Having cast that powder and taken it, one should grind it with an equal amount of fragrant honey (gandhamākṣika) using an acid for one watch (yāma); then, having sealed it, one should cook it in a mild *puṭa*. (Āk 2.29)
Furthermore, the fragrance should be applied repeatedly; it dies after ten applications.
(Regarding the killing of gold by means of juices and so forth:
one should prepare leaves of gold and smear them with the ash of the juice. Āk 2.2.30.
By means of a paste of sour substances, one should perform a *puṭapāka* on gold; it will attain a state devoid of life.
Alternatively, gold that has been subjected to a *puṭapāka* with *tāpya* (calamine) goes to the state of ashes. (Āk 2.2.31)
Alternatively, one may reduce a dead elephant to ashes through the application of stone;
or else, a Yoginī smeared with the fragments of a dead thunderbolt [should be used]. (Āk 2.2.32)

It is reduced to ashes by secondary minerals (uparasa), primary minerals (rasa), and great minerals (mahārasa); and when smeared with substances ground with acidic liquids (amlapiṣṭa) and subjected to heating in a closed crucible (puṭita), it likewise attains the state of ash. Āk 2.2.33.
(5) For the killing of gold: one should grind mercury double the amount of gold with sour gruel for one *yāma*.
Having added *āroṭa* and *mākṣika*, equal in quantity to the gold, into a crucible—Āk 2.2.34.
Upon its surface, beaten gold should be applied; upon that, purified *mākṣika* [pyrite] equal in weight to the gold; and upon that, sulfur equal in weight to it. (Āk 2.2.35)

One should place all the powdered ingredients inside a sealed crucible and heat it strongly; once it has cooled naturally, the ash should be collected, and five parts of this should be taken. (Āk 2.2.36)
One should grind together one part each of ṭaṅkaṇa and white glass;
these three, mixed with honey and clarified butter, should be formed into a ball. (Āk 2.2.37)
One should cause one part of grain-cloud (dhānyābhra) to be placed both below and above [the mercury]; having sealed it, one should heat it intensely in a crucible for two ghaṭikās. (Āk 2.2.38)
Ash that has been rendered inert is produced; one should employ it in various formulations.
(Gold-killing, 6) One-fourth part of killed mercury, ground with some acid, [should be added] to gold. (Āk 2.2.39)
Having smeared [the substance] on a leaf, one should cook it in a *puṭa*; thus it is certainly killed by eight [applications].
Such is the method for killing all pure metals. (Āk 2.2.40)
(7) [The Alchemy of Gold]:
Having added one part of pure *mākṣika* (pyrite), one part of *cāroṭamākṣika*, and two parts of mercury (*sūtaka*), one should grind these three with acid. (Āk 2.2.41)
Having smeared one part of a gold leaf with [the mercury] and rubbed it with acid, one should heat that globule forcefully in a *pātanāyantra* for three *yāmas*. (Āk 2.2.42)
In this way, gold is killed and becomes non-reverting; of this there is no doubt.
(The Killing of Gold) By means of *yavaciñcā* powder, *vṛkṣabhallātaka*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* [sodium carbonate]... (Āk 2.2.43)

Having smeared gold leaves with these juices and enclosed them, one should cook them in a *gajapuṭa* fire; by grinding them with those same juices and applying seven such *puṭas*, the gold is killed. (Āk 2.2.44)
Having applied a paste of pīlu, kaṅkuṣṭha, bukkāṇa, and sauvarcala that has not been ground to the leaves of gold, it is killed by seven puṭa-firings. (Āk 2.2.45)
(The Qualities of Gold):
Gold is nourishing, unctuous, sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect, removes the defects of poison, is cooling, and possesses astringent and bitter properties. (Āyurvedadīpikā 2.2.46)
It is pleasing to the heart, bestows luster, provides strength, is flavorful, heavy, and scraping;
it promotes intelligence, intellect, and memory, heals wounds, and grants purity of speech. (Āyurvedadīpikā 2.2.47)
