It pacifies wasting diseases and insanity, is beneficial for the eyes, and is a rejuvenative tonic; it pacifies the three *doṣas*, is gentle, promotes longevity, is pleasing, and pure. (Āk 2.2.48)
Through the power of retention (dhāraṇā), sovereignty that bestows wisdom, vigor, and a beautiful voice arises. Ākāśagarbha 2.2.49.
Āk, 2, 3 Śrī Bhairava:
(synonyms for silver)
Silver is *raupya*, *śubhra*, *vasuśreṣṭha*, *rucira*, *candraloha*, *rajata*, *taptarūpya*, *candrabhūti*, and *raupyaka*. (Āk 2.3.1)
Kaladhauta, saudha, and candrahāsa are varieties of silver (tāraka).
It is considered to be of three kinds: innate, produced from a mine, and artificial. (Āk 2.3.2)
For each preceding type of silver is surpassed by each succeeding one in its own qualities;
silver produced from mountains such as Kailāsa is naturally superior. (Āk 2.3.3)

For that which is touched by it becomes the destroyer of great diseases for embodied beings; indeed, that silver which is produced on the peaks of the Himalayas and other mountains [is such]. (Āk 2.3.4)

That which was tin, upon being placed upon the sandals of Śrī Rāma, attained the state of silver; this is declared by the knowers of such things to be a supreme elixir (rasāyana) of mineral origin. Āk 2.3.5.
That which is called "silver-footed" is artificial, yet it cures all diseases;
its nature is like silver that is neither graspable nor ungraspable.
It is dense, glossy, heavy, and smooth; it is white when burned or cut, and soft. (Āk 2.3.6)
Silver that is rich in color, clear like the moon, possessing an even luster when heated or cut, white as a conch shell, smooth, and free from flaws is auspicious. (Āk 2.3.7)
Silver that is red, yellow, black, dry, cracked, light, thick-bodied, or rough—these eight types of silver are to be rejected. (Āk 2.3.8)
A leaf that is hard, artificial, rough, discolored, and dirty, which fails when subjected to heating, cutting, or hammering, is considered silver of middling quality. Āk 2.3.9.
It causes burning, diarrhea, and the wasting away of semen, strength, and life;
therefore, one should purify and then kill silver that is neither pure nor dead. (Āk 2.3.10)
Silver attains purity when melted with *nāga* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*;
it becomes pure if cast three times into oil derived from *jyotiṣmatī*. (Āk 2.3.11)
A heated and then reheated silver leaf should be sprinkled [with water]; it shall attain purity.
Or, in the case of its being produced by a Piśāca, it shall attain purity once it has been cast [into the fire]. (Āk 2.3.12)
One should collect silver that is free from defects and has been taken out of the water;
one should immerse it seven times in water produced from a white jar. (Āk 2.3.13)
One should thoroughly rub silver ash with water extracted from the *kuraṇḍa* and *munipuṣpa* flowers;
then, having smeared the silver leaves, one should perform the *puṭapāka* (encapsulation) using *vanotpala* flowers. (Āk 2.3.14)
It dies, of this there is no doubt—whether it has been smeared with mercury-ash or with the group of acidic substances (amlavarga)—by means of the application of *puṭa* as before. (Āk 2.3.15)
One should grind talaka, mercury, and tin with acid;
having smeared the leaves of silver with this and subjected them to heating in a closed crucible (puṭa), one should reduce them to ashes. (Āk 2.3.16)
It dies by means of combinations of fragrances and the like, or it perishes through the Vaiṣṇava [process].
One should cook silver ash with the milky sap of *snuhī* and smear the leaves of silver (*tāra*) with *tāpya*. (Āk 2.3.17)
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* and cooked it, one should cook it again with the previously mentioned [substances];
by forty such *puṭas*, the silver will be thus cooked and become dead (*mṛta*). (Āk 2.3.18)
Having smeared silver leaves with equal parts of silver ash (5), mica, long pepper, rock salt, and sour substances,
one should seal them and cook them with seven puṭas. (Āk 2.3.19)
By grinding it again and again with juices, it dies; there is no doubt about this.
(Silver ash [6]) One should prepare a paste of silver using the juice of *likuca* and mercury. ĀK 2.3.20.
Having placed sulphur below and sealed it within the interior of the crucible, one should subject it to sudation in a *vālukāyantra* for one day with a steady fire. (Āk 2.3.21)
Having ground mercury until it is cool to the touch and mixed it with sour calamine, one should subject it to twelve *puṭa* cycles; the silver will then be reduced to ash. (Āk 2.3.22)
Silver ash (7):
Mākṣika [pyrite] powder, rubbed with the juice of *luṅga* and subjected to gentle heating (*puṭita*) thirty times, becomes that silver ash which is "without residue" (*niruttha*). (Āk 2.3.23)
There will undoubtedly be the liquefaction (*rāga*) of all metals when there is an excess of *puṭa* applications.
(Silver ash [8]) Four parts of silver leaf and one part of pure *tālaka* [are to be used]. (Āk 2.3.24)
One should grind silver leaves with the juices of *jambīra* fruits, smear them [with the paste], dry them, seal them, and then roast them in a *puṭa* fire using thirty *vanotpala* plants. (Āk 2.3.25)
In this manner, through fourteen folds, it certainly dies without residue.
(Silver ash [9]) One part of silver leaf and one-fourth part of dead tin. Āk 2.3.26.
Alternatively, one part of the fragrant ingredient should be smeared with a paste of *jambīra* fruit;
having enclosed it within three layers of clay, it should be cooked in twenty-five *vanotpala* fire-pots. (Āk 2.3.27)
It dies; there is no doubt in this. Sulfur should be applied again and again.
Having made mercury and sulfur equal in measure, [one should add] the root of *kākatuṇḍa*. (Silver ash, 10) Āk_2,3.28.
One should knead that paste with buffalo milk and wash it with water;
then, having placed it within a ball of turmeric, one should place that ball in horse dung. (Āk 2.3.29)
Having cast it [into the crucible] for twenty-one days, one should extract it again from that interior;
having ground that [substance], the leaves of *tāra* (silver) should be smeared with some kind of acid. (Āk 2.3.30)
Through twenty *puṭas*, ash is produced; there is no doubt about this.
With that ash ground with acid, one should smear a copper razor. (Āk 2.3.31)
One should know that when [the base metal] becomes ash, it is as if dead; [this applies to] gold and silver.
(The qualities of silver: Silver is unctuous, astringent and sour, and its taste is sweet in its post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*). Āk 2.3.32.
It stabilizes youth, is cooling, scraping, and conquers wind and bile; it is aphrodisiac, improves the appetite, is strengthening, and kindles the digestive fire. (Āk 2.3.33)
Āk, 2, 4 Śrī Bhairava:
(Copper)
Tāmra, mlecchamukha, śulba, tapaneṣṭa, udumbara, tryambaka, aravinda, raviloha, and ravipriya. (Āk 2.4.1)
There is the red [sindūra] from Nepal and the red mineral (raktadhātu) produced by the moon-like hand;
there is also that from the Mlecchas and that from Nepal, and between these two, the Nepalese is supreme. (Āk 2.4.2)
That which originates from a mine other than Nepal is called *mleccha*;
it is very glossy, soft, red, capable of withstanding heavy striking, and heavy. (Āk 2.4.3)
The best copper, which is unchanging and excellent, is said to be from Nepal; it has a white, black, or reddish luster, is left-handed (vāmabhedi), and is hard. (Āk 2.4.4)
Furthermore, that which is black even after being washed is the copper of the Mlecchas;
it is pale, blackish-red, light, and characterized by cracking. (Āk 2.4.5)
Copper with rough surfaces and impurities is not desired for alchemical work (*rasakarma*).
Indeed, the defects of copper—excessive salivation, delusion, dizziness, burning, and piercing pain—are difficult to suppress.
Through purification, it becomes free from its own defects and, like nectar, becomes equal in taste, potency, and post-digestive effect (*pāka*). (Āk 2.4.6)
It causes vomiting, fainting, vertigo, insanity, various diseases, leprosy, and colic. (Āk 2.4.7)
Copper that is impure does not destroy life, beauty, or strength, nor does it vitiate the bodily constituents (dhātus); therefore, one should purify and then kill [the copper]. (Āk 2.4.8)
(Refining Copper): Copper combined with alkalis and acids, melted and heated with red ochre (*gairika*), should be cast into buffalo urine and cow dung seven times. (Āk 2.4.9)
Freed from five defects, it is produced in seven days;
having smeared copper leaves with the juice of *nimba* and rock salt. (Āk 2.4.10)
By blowing upon them and casting them into *sauvīraka* eight times, they are purified;
likewise, by being smeared with nimba-water and heated eight times. (Āk 2.4.11)
Copper leaves are purified by rubbing them with the juice of *nirguṇḍī*;
furthermore, a copper leaf placed within the midst of *kumārī* leaves [is likewise purified]. (Āk 2.4.12)
When folded and freed from impurities, it becomes white;
thus purified, the copper is divested of all defects. (Āk 2.4.13)
It becomes a supreme elixir that transforms both the body and the metals;
Śiva or Nandikeśvara alone would recognize this purification. (Āk 2.4.14)
Copper that has been struck by mercury seven times, having arisen [from its impurities], becomes liberated from all defects and becomes like nectar. (Āk 2.4.15)
Having smeared a copper leaf with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, salt, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should heat it and repeatedly sprinkle it with the juice of *nirguṇḍī*. (Āk 2.4.16)
After twelve washings, it becomes pure through plastering, heating, and sprinkling;
one should grind chalk and salt with buttermilk and sour gruel. (Āk 2.4.17)
A copper leaf smeared with that [substance] should be heated repeatedly and quenched six times in sour gruel and in *nirguṇḍī* juice for the sake of purification. (Āk 2.4.18)
One should sprinkle heated copper plates with the juices of bitter plants, repeatedly coating them with sour gruel, salt, and fermented rice-water. (Āk 2.4.19)
One should heat it repeatedly and pour water over it three times; it will certainly attain purity.
One should cook a copper vessel for one watch (yāma) over a strong fire with cow’s urine. (Āk 2.4.20)
It is purified; there is no doubt in this matter. Now, the procedure for killing [the metal] is also described:
one should smear copper ash with an equal amount of sulfur ground with acid. (Āk 2.4.21)
Having pierced the leaf at the stalk and enclosed it in a sealed crucible (puṭa), one should cook it;
then, having extracted it and powdered it, one should add sulfur equal to one-quarter of its weight. (Āk 2.4.22)

Having repeatedly ground [the ingredients] with jambīra fruits, sour gruel (āranāla), or the juices of mṛgadūrvā, one should cook it while adding aromatic substances, enclosed within four layers [of cloth]. Āk 2.4.23.
Having ground it with the juices of *mātuluṅga*, one should administer one *puṭa*;
likewise, one *puṭa* should be given with white sugar, and it will become dead (reduced to ash). (Āk 2.4.24)
(2) One should apply a paste of copper ash and double the amount of sulfur with the juices of *pāṣāṇabhedi* and *matsyākṣī*; having sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire. Āk 2.4.25.
Then, having added an equal portion of fragrance and stirred it with liquid extracts, the copper ash will certainly be perfected after being processed through seven such coatings. (Āk 2.4.26)
(3) Copper ash:

One should grind mercury three times the weight of copper with the acid of *jambīra* fruit; first, having placed it inside a crucible along with a leaf of *dhuttūra*, [one should proceed]. (Āk 2.4.27)
Upon its surface, one should throw powdered sulphur equal in weight to the copper;
upon that, one should place rubbed copper and an equal amount of sulphur as before. (Āk 2.4.28)
Having covered it with *dhūrtapatra* leaves and sealed it in a "gaja-puṭa" (elephant-seal) vessel, one should cook it;
when it has cooled to the touch of one's own body, the powder will certainly be dead [calcined]. (Āk 2.4.29)
One should wash a copper leaf with a little fragrance or acid;
then one should smear the leaf while it is still moist with mercury mixed with a quarter-part of copper. (Āk 2.4.30)
Having smeared that [copper] again with double the amount of sulfur ground with acid, one should apply well-ground *amlaparṇikā* above and below it. (Āk 2.4.31)
Having sealed that mass inside the interior of a vessel, one should cook it on a stove for one watch (yāma) according to the copper-cooking method; it will certainly be reduced to ashes. (Āk 2.4.32)

One part of mercury and two parts of sulphur should be ground for one *yāma* with *kanyā* juice; having placed an equal amount of this upon a copper leaf, one should seal it inside the interior of a crucible. (Āk 2.4.33)
One should place a layer of good clay and salt over the joint on the side, and then, together with cow dung, cook it on the hearth for four watches (yāmas) upon the back of a vessel. Āk 2.4.34.
Water should be applied again and again until it becomes cool upon one's own body; then one should crush [the powder].
There is no doubt that [the subject] dies; this should be employed in all formulations. (Āk 2.4.35)
(6) Having taken well-digested copper, one should then add these six equal parts: tin, bell-metal, lead, the essence of steel, and magnetite. Āk 2.4.36.
One should melt all of them together in one place according to the measure of copper;
using a blowpipe, one should do so until only the *arka* remains. (Āk 2.4.37)
First, one should immerse that *arka* plant in the water of *nirguṇḍī*;
then, one should sprinkle the powder of its root onto the *arka* seven times. (Āk 2.4.38)
With that copper, one should fashion a beautiful, scar-free pill;
having smeared it with double the amount of sulfur and a third part of mercury relative to the sulfur. (Āk 2.4.39)

One should grind either pure mercury or that produced from cinnabar with the juice of *bījapūraka*, or with the juice of *jambīra*, or one should thoroughly grind it with the juices of *likuca*. (Āk 2.4.40)
Having dried that for three days, one should then place it inside a vessel;
having positioned a copper pot above it with its opening facing downwards, [one should proceed]. (Āk 2.4.41)
Afterwards, one should apply a firm coating and place an earthen vessel [upon it];
one should smear that [vessel] with great care so that it does not crack when wetted. (Āk 2.4.42)
Then, having placed the *adhikullī* [ladle] and filled it with water below,
one should kindle the fire (*vītihotra*) according to the sequence of soft, medium, and intense.

Having taken six days [of processing], when the vessel has cooled to the touch of one's own body, one should diligently break it open and extract the mercury that has been killed by the metal. (Āk 2.4.44)
Then, having indeed pulverized this, one should employ it as desired.
(The purification of copper ash:
Five parts of various kinds of dead copper [are used] for the sake of purification. (Āk 2.4.45)
Having placed one part of white glass, one part of white borax, and one part of mica-leaf mixed together inside a crucible, [one should proceed]. (Āk 2.4.46)
Having poured [the liquid] upwards and then restrained it, one should take up the copper once it has been blown [with a bellows] and has become perfectly cool;
thus the copper becomes free from defects and shall be a remover of all diseases. (Āk 2.4.47)
Alternatively, one should grind killed copper with a single acid;
having enclosed that ball inside a *sūraṇa* root, one should coat it on all sides. (Āk 2.4.48)
One should cook it dry in a *gajapuṭa* fire; it will become a remover of all the *doṣas*, and it never causes vomiting, dizziness, or purging. (Āk 2.4.49)

Having smeared [the vessel] with copper ash (tāmrabhasma), and having covered the copper leaves with a paste made from sulphur (gandhāśman) ground with the juice of *vilva* fruit, one should seal them inside a crucible. (Āk 2.4.50)
One should cook it properly for exactly one watch (yāma); once cooled, one should extract it and grind it into powder.
Indeed, a dose of one *valla* of that ash, wrapped in a betel leaf— Āk 2.4.51.
Then, having induced vomiting and purging after two watches (six hours), it destroys the fever of men accompanied by colic and flatulence. (Āk 2.4.52)
Poison and *gara* certainly cause vomiting with great force;
in this case, wholesome food and cow's buttermilk mixed with rice should be administered. (Āk 2.4.53)
In cases of excessive [dosha] accumulation, excessive vomiting, or extreme confusion, one should apply cooling remedies according to the specific requirements of each situation. (Āk 2.4.54)

In the case of excessive vomiting, one should consume cooled sugarcane juice that has been strained, or alternatively, one should cook a decoction made from bilva fruits together with sugar. (Āyurveda 2.4.55)
The bark of *barbūra* should be drunk with buttermilk during purgation.
(Copper ash [8]) [is prepared] with mercury equal in weight to copper, and with an equal amount of *balī*. Āk 2.4.56.
Having prepared a smooth kajjali, resembling split soot, with a thickness of half a tāla and a width of half that again, using stone [grinding]. (Āk 2.4.57)
Within the interior of a crucible as specified in the chapter on mechanical devices, one should alternately insert lampblack and copper leaves. (Āk 2.4.58)
One should cook it until the end of the watch (three hours), and once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should powder it.

Taken by licking with two *vallīs* of copper, accompanied by appropriate vehicles (*anupāna*) for each specific disease, this certainly destroys chronic abdominal pain (*pariṇāma-śūla*), abdominal enlargement (*udara*), and jaundice-fever (*pāṇḍu-jvara*);

it removes tumors (*gulma*), spleen disorders, liver ailments, consumption, loss of digestive fire, urinary disorders (*meha*), diseases of the bladder (*mūlāmaya*), and malignant dysentery (*duṣṭa-grahaṇī*). This is the destroyer of all diseases. (Āk 2.4.59)

Copper is bitter and astringent, sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and hot in potency (vīrya). It is slightly warm, pacifies pitta and kapha, and brings an end to abdominal pain, skin diseases, indigestion, and chronic wasting. It acts as a purgative for both the upper and lower tracts, destroys poison, removes obesity, stimulates hunger, and alleviates hemorrhoids, consumption, and anemia. It is beneficial for the eyes and is a supreme scraping agent (lekhana). (Āyurvedadīpikā 2.4.60)
Āk, 2, 5 Śrī Bhairava: (The Origin of Mercury)
Now the origin of the metals known as kāntāya, tīkṣṇa, and muṇḍa is described:
while the great ocean was being churned by the hosts of gods and asuras, [Āk 2.5.1].
In ancient times, the nectar that sustains the gods arose therein; as it was being drunk by the deities, tiny drops fell from it. (Āk 2.5.2)
Having realized that they had descended to the earth, Dhūrjaṭi, the charioteer,
concealed them within the surface of the ground by transforming them into the form of iron stones.
"Those men who are overcome by evil diseases shall not worship these"—thus were these drops of nectar protected by Śiva in the past. (Āk 2.5.4)
For their sake, I shall briefly describe the clear method of accomplishment for the purpose of destroying leprosy and other diseases, according to my own understanding. (Āk 2.5.5)
Iron is likewise of three types, known as *kānta*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *muṇḍa*;
one should know it to be a hundred times more effective than all other elixirs (*rasāyana*). (Āk 2.5.6)
(Ayaskānta: synonyms) Ayaskānta, kāntaloha, kānta, and kṛṣṇalohaka are synonyms for magnetite.
Magnetite, great iron, and black iron constitute the seven kinds [of iron].
The defects arising from the consumption of impure iron:
"Impure iron—neither purified nor killed—causes heart pain, weakness of the digestive fire, great diseases, and likewise death through its consumption. (Āk 2.5.8)
(The Procedure for Taking Kānta): Therefore, the purification and the killing of kānta are prescribed.
Mercury is like a rutting elephant, and kānta is said to be its goad. (Āk 2.5.9)
Having examined the field, it should be accepted with great effort;
however, O beautiful goddess, one should avoid that which has been exposed to wind and sun. (Āk 2.5.10)
Whatever beautiful object is situated on the ground, one should consecrate it with goat's blood;
one should wrap it with a hide smeared with goat's blood. (Āk 2.5.11)
Having wrapped it in a goat-skin, one should place it on the ground as before;
after seven months have elapsed, one should take it out and cast it into a water-jar. (Āk 2.5.12)
It should always be worshipped with red flowers and red perfumes and ointments; it is filled with wine and meat, and should be employed for the sake of alchemy and elixirs. (Āk 2.5.13)
When refined with goat's blood, it becomes a *bhrāmaka* and a *cumbaka*;
through this sequential application, O Dear One, it becomes a *drāvaka*. (Āk 2.5.14)
Without *kāntaloha* (magnetite), mercury does not penetrate the body anywhere;
mercury is ineffective without *kānta*, and *kānta* is useless when devoid of mercury. (Āk 2.5.15)
The application combined with magnetic iron (kānta-sūta) sustains the body; previously, I have explained all the properties of magnetic iron according to the prescribed method. (Āk 2.5.16)
Now I shall fully explain the purification and the qualities of *kānta* [iron].
(*Kāntaloha*:
Purification)
The beautiful leaf, naturally smeared with rabbit's blood, was considered nectar. (Āk 2.5.17)
O Goddess, by heating it three times with fire, one should abandon the natural impurity of kāntaloha.
(Kāntaloha:
Purification: Mountain)
Take sixteen palas of triphalā and boil it in water that is eight times the quantity of the triphalā. (Āk 2.5.18)
Having reduced that decoction to one-fourth and adding five *palas* of *kānta* iron, one should heat the leaves and pour [the liquid] over them seven times. (Āk 2.5.19)
In this very way, the impurity arising from iron is dissolved;
one should cook powdered *kāntaloha* in eight times its quantity of cow’s urine. (Āk 2.5.20)
Washed again with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and dried, it attains purity.
Ratnamālā, haṃsapādī, gojihvā, triphalā, and amṛtā—Āk 2.5.21.
One should grind these—gopālī, tumburu, and dantī—with cow urine; then, having heated it repeatedly, one should immerse iron leaf in that paste twenty-one times. (Āk 2.5.22)
One should moisten the *kāntaloha* for the removal of all defects.
(The sequence for the accomplishment of *kānta*:
For the sake of accomplishing *kānta*, the procedure must be performed preceded by mantra. (Āk 2.5.23)

The word "udbhavodbhava" (O you who arise from arising) should follow [the name], ending in the dative case and followed by "amṛtāt paraṃ svāhā"; with the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning, this mantra is established for the act of crushing. (Āk 2.5.24)
For the protection of mercury and iron, O Dear One, this very [mantra] is the sole source; at its end, one should join "phaṭ" without "svāhā. (Āk 2.5.25)
The Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by "namas caṇḍa vajrapāṣāṇa," and thereafter "mahāvajrasenādhipataye namaḥ. (Āk 2.5.26)
The word *saru* should be repeated twice for the sake of the power of the Great Vidyā;
then follows the mantra *tatas tvāha*, which is honored in the rite of offerings (*balikarman*). (Āk 2.5.27)
Having performed the *bali* offering with this very [mantra], one should carry out the ritual as prescribed.
(The procedure for iron ash) Then, one should grind five *palas* of vermilion with breast milk. Āk 2.5.28.

One should smear the leaf of the beloved with exactly five *palas* of that [substance], seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire; then it should be processed again with the decoctions of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (Āk 2.5.29)

Having ground cinnabar with *jambīra* fruits or fermented gruel (*āranāla*) in a proportion of one-twentieth, one should smear it [onto the metal], seal it in a crucible, and heat that metal again. (Āk 2.5.30)
One should seal it in a crucible and roast it at night, and in the morning one should saturate it with liquid extracts;
by doing this for eight days, the three types of iron are indeed killed. (Āk 2.5.31)
(Procedure for Iron Ash [2]) One should prepare kānta, tīkṣṇa, and muṇḍaka iron so that it resembles the leaf of the *ciñcā* tree;
having placed it in an earthen vessel, one should expose it to the heat and fill it with the juice of *dantī*. (Āk 2.5.32)
Furthermore, one should repeatedly heat the leaf until it floats by itself;
when it dies due to the intense heat, one should grind it into powder and apply it. (Āk 2.5.33)
(The Procedure for Iron Ash [3]):
A powder of *kāntaloha*, *tīkṣṇaloha*, and *muṇḍaloha* should be processed in the sun for three days with the juices of *matsyākṣī*, and for three days with the juices of *citraka*. (Āk 2.5.34)

One should macerate it for three days with the juices of *trikaṇṭaka*, for one day with the liquid of *sahadevī*, for three days with cow urine, and for three days with decoctions of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (Āk 2.5.35)

Then, having ground it with the aforementioned liquids, one should apply a series of *puṭas* (roastings) in succession; having sealed it, one should roast it using *gajapuṭas*. Thus, once it is dead, one may employ it in medicinal formulations. (Āk 2.5.36)
(4) The Procedure for Iron Ash: Stirring with an iron ladle in either a pot or an iron vessel, one should cook the iron powder with a decoction of triphalā for one day. (Āk 2.5.37)
Having ground that bolus with the decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and sealed it within a crucible, one should cook it by means of a *puṭapāka*;
one should cook it for a full day and night inside a pit sixteen finger-breadths deep, in a place free from wind. (Āk 2.5.38)
In this manner, one should prepare the *sthālīpāka* three times, ending with the *puṭa*;
[using] *bhṛṅga*, fresh ginger, *tālamūla*, and the root of *hastikarṇī*. (Āk 2.5.39)

Having ground the roots of śatāvarī and vidārī together with triphalā water, one should cook them in a pot as before; the paste should then be processed three times with *puṭa* applications. (Āk 2.5.40)
Then it should be cooked again with decoctions of punarnavā and daśamūla, as well as with a decoction of bṛhatī and the juices of bījapūra. (Āk 2.5.41)

Having first ground [the ingredients] individually with the juices of *brahmabīja*, with decoctions of *śigru*, and also with cow’s milk, one should cook them in a sealed crucible (*puṭa*) in the previously mentioned pit. (Āk 2.5.42)
One should impregnate it with that very liquid for the duration of one *yāma* at the end of each *puṭa*;
having thus ground each [ingredient] individually, one should perform the *puṭa* and the impregnation in successive order. (Āk 2.5.43)
One dies; there is no doubt regarding this—[the preparation of] the lovely, sharp *muṇḍaka* [iron].
(The procedure for iron ash, 5) Having made pure mercury and sulphur in two parts into a kajjalī within a mortar, ĀK 2.5.44.
One should grind equal parts of the two powders with the juice of kanyākā for two *yāmas*; then, having extracted it, one should place that ball in a copper vessel.

Covered with castor leaves, when it has become excessively hot after half a watch [of the day], one should place it upon a heap of grain; thereafter, at the end of three days, one should remove it. (Āk 2.5.46)
Having ground it, one should strain it through a cloth; thus it becomes a true water-soluble extract (vāritara).
It becomes lovely, sharp, pure, free from residue, and "dead" [in its potency]. (Āk 2.5.47)
In this manner, one should indeed dissolve gold and other metals and reduce them to powder like iron;
now, the perfected formula (siddhayoga) that came directly from the presence of the Siddhas is declared.
O Goddess, I have experienced this which removes all diseases:
one should not cook iron [preparations] with less than five palas nor more than thirty palas. (Āk 2.5.49)
(6) The Procedure for Iron Ash:
The bark of the *arjuna* tree should be ground and thoroughly stirred with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).
Into that mixture, one should add fine iron powder (*kāntacūrṇa*) and place it in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*). (Āk 2.5.50)
One should heat it for one day in the sun, filling it repeatedly with liquids made from *arjuna* or *sāranāla*; thus one may kill the three types of iron. (Āk 2.5.51)
One should rub the powder of *kāntaloha* with the juices arising from the leaves of the *kukkuṭa* plant for one day;
then it should be rubbed in the intense heat of the sun with the juices produced from the *trikaṇṭaka* plant.

Vandhyā, bhṛṅga, and punarnavā should be processed with cow's urine for one day; furthermore, triphalā should be boiled in cow's urine, and [the previous mixture] should be impregnated with that decoction. (Āk 2.5.53)
Then, having rubbed it with effort for three weeks, one should seal it in a *gajapuṭa* and cook it for one day; thereafter, one should rub it with a decoction for one day. (Āk 2.5.54)
One should grind it by day and seal it (in a *puṭa*) by night for a period of twenty-one days;
indeed, by these twenty-one *puṭas*, the three types of iron are killed.
(8) The Procedure for Iron Ash:

Having ground together pyrite, realgar, turmeric, and a quarter-part of black pepper with acidic liquids, one should smear this onto a leaf of *kānta* iron; as it is heated again and again, one should quench it [in the liquid]. (Āk 2.5.56)
One should wash it again with water seven times in a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*);
then, one should pound it with an iron rod and grind it in the water of the three myrobalans. (Āk 2.5.57)
One-sixteenth part of the metal should be given of *mākṣika* and *śilā*; having ground it with acid and sealed it, one should cook it in a single *gaja*-named crucible. (Āk 2.5.58)
The ash produced is free of impurities and is beautiful, sharp, and "shaven" (muṇḍaka).
(The Procedure for Iron Ash, 9) Having smeared a sword with the marrow of the *tinduka* fruit, [place it] in the hot sun. (Āk 2.5.59)
One should keep it inside a bronze vessel for one day, until it thoroughly cracks open.
One should apply the paste again and again, and at the end of the day, one should grind it down. (Āk 2.5.60)
Combined with a decoction of triphalā, one dies in a single day;
[this is prepared] with five palas of triphalā when reduced to one-eighth part of its original water. (Āk 2.5.61)
The clarified butter should be equal to the decoction, and the iron filings should be equal to the clarified butter;
one should cook this in a copper vessel, stirring it with an iron ladle. (Āk 2.5.62)
One should cook it over a mild fire until that liquid is digested;
one should add sugar equal in weight to the iron and remove it once it is well-cooked. (Āk 2.5.63)
This is known as the great elixir (mahāmṛta), the dead metal that carries the yoga; this procedure applies likewise to magnetite (kānta), steel (tīkṣṇa), and even iron (muṇḍa). Āk 2.5.64.

One should cook dead iron, equal in quantity to ghee, inside an iron vessel; once the ghee has been digested [by the iron], one should take it up and employ it in all medicinal formulations. (Āk 2.5.65)

Oṃ Oṃ! I consume the Lord of Nectar; obeisance! That vessel into which water does not spread like a drop of oil upon water, in which asafoetida does not release its own scent, and in which the paste of neem does not manifest its bitterness; wherein milk turns to curd during cooking and iron assumes a pointed shape on the ground—that alone is declared to possess the characteristics described, and nothing else. (Āk 2.5.66)
(The nature of the iron-smelting process:
Iron smelting is said to be threefold, consisting of soft, medium, and hard.
The first is like a mound of mud; the middle is the "lump-cooking" (*piṇḍapāka*). (Āk 2.5.67)
The third stage of cooking, O beloved, is the "rough-cooking" (*kharapāka*), which resembles sand;
having understood the color and smell of the metal from the fire, one performs the examination of the ash that has no residue (*nirutthabhasmaparīkṣā*). (Āk 2.5.68)
Then, having removed it, one should place the pure substance into another iron vessel;
[the ingredients are] iron, elephant, lion, sulphur, realgar, and vermilion. (Āk 2.5.69)

All this dead iron should be smelted with the five friends (*mitrapañcaka*); if it thus becomes non-recurrent, it is beneficial as "water-crossing" (*vāritara*) iron that should be employed. (Āk 2.5.70)
One should take iron combined with honey and clarified butter, joined with silver, heated in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), and collect it once it has cooled naturally. Āk 2.5.71.
If the silver contained within the metal is of the same quantity as before, then that metal will be rendered "niruttha" (rendered inert); otherwise, one should perform the process again. (Āk 2.5.72)
One should grind equal parts of sublimed sulphur and iron together in a mortar for one day with the juice of kanyākā, then seal it and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire. (Āk 2.5.73)
Thus, the extraction of all metals should be performed in this manner. (The qualities of the ashes of magnetite and other ores:
Magnetite vermilion bestows longevity, health, strength, and vigor. Āk 2.5.74.
It is excellent for strengthening the body, it brings about sharpness of the senses, it pacifies the three *doṣas*, and it destroys the disease of *rājayakṣman*. (Āk 2.5.75)

It destroys fever, hemorrhagic disorders, jaundice, and other such ailments—the eight great diseases—and whatever medicinal formulations remove specific diseases, this [preparation] shall likewise remove those very diseases. (Āk 2.5.76)
(Tīkṣṇaloha: synonyms) Tīkṣṇa, śastrāyasa, śastra, piṇḍa, piṇḍāyasa, and śaṭha.
An iron sword, sharpened and fierce, and a blade made of steel from Muṇḍaja.
Iron is said to be of three kinds: *citrāyasa* (variegated iron), *cīnaja* (Chinese iron),
and *muṇḍaloha* (mundane iron).
Muṇḍa, muṇḍāyasa, loha, kṛṣṇalauha, and that which is produced from stone.
The killing of *tīkṣṇa* and *muṇḍa* [iron] by means of the *kāntaloha* type [of magnetite];
(*tīkṣṇaloha*: [the killing of] sharp iron).
Regarding its medicinal properties:
sharp iron (tīkṣṇaloha) is astringent, sour, bitter, pungent, and light. (Āk 2.5.79)
It is cooling, scraping, and dry; it conquers phlegm, bile, blood disorders, and anemia.
It destroys urinary disorders and all types of colic; it is sharp and possesses qualities superior to those of *muṇḍā*. (Āk 2.5.80)
Mundaloha (iron filings) is beneficial for the eyes, astringent, sweet, and bitter; it is scraping, alleviates wind, is cooling, and destroys worms, bile, and phlegm. (Āyurvedadīpikā 2.5.81)
It conquers swelling, abdominal enlargement, colic, hemorrhoids, leprosy, anemia, and urinary disorders. (Āk 2.5.82)
Āk, 2, 6 Śrī Bhairava:
[The sub-types of tin (verbal suffixes)].
Tin is said to be of two kinds: pure (khuraka) and mixed (miśraka).
Among these, the pure is superior in its qualities, while the mixed is deficient in qualities. (Āk 2.6.1)
White, soft, glossy, melting quickly, and heavy— these are the physical properties [of gold].
(From the *Miśraka* section on physical properties.)
The *khuravaṅga* should be soundless; the *miśraka* is dark and white. (Āk 2.6.2)
Tin (rasa) has the following synonyms:
trapu, trapusamārūpa, vaṅga, kuṭila, hima, kurūpya, viccaṭa, raṅga, pūtigandha, and rasāhvaya. (Āk 2.6.3)
It is clear, unable to withstand heat, cool, characterized by fine leaves, and light.
When base metal is destroyed and silver is produced, that alloy is called "excellent" (śreṣṭha). Āk 2.6.4.
(1) Having melted tin and cast it into the juice of *nirguṇḍī* mixed with turmeric, the "hoof-tin" (*khuravaṅga*) is purified in three cycles; of this there is no doubt. (Āk 2.6.5)
Tin purified by two methods is thoroughly cleansed when ground with sour buttermilk, varṣābhū, vṛṣa, and sindhu, and placed inside a bitter alābu gourd. Āk 2.6.6.
Then, having smeared the leaves of vaṅga with the milk of *arka* and *satāla*, one should apply light *puṭa*-firing using the alkalis of the bark of *bodhi* and *ciñcā*. (Āk 2.6.7)
Having ground it, one should apply the ash to mercury and other substances; this is what is proclaimed [as the purification of tin].
One should purify tin as one does lead; likewise, [one should purify] the milky sap of the *aśvattha* and *ciñcā* trees. (Vaṅga-śuddhi 2) Āk 2.6.8.
One should grind that ash and an equal amount of yellow orpiment with an acid,
or alternatively, having stirred them with the juice of *palāśa* leaves, one should seal them in a crucible (*puṭa*).
Having removed [the dross] with a tenth part [of its weight], one should grind it together with *tāla*;
(this is the purification of tin) then, having stirred it with the previous liquids and sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire. (Āk 2.6.10)
With twenty-one layers [of clay], tin becomes dead [calcined] and destroys diseases;
[this is done by placing] a ball mixed with the powders of *śirīṣa*, *rajanī*, and *kumārī* [inside]. (Āk 2.6.11)

A leaf of tin coated with *sūta* (mercury) and formed into a ball (*golaka*) by thorough rubbing, having been sealed and cooked in small *puṭas*, becomes dead according to the previously stated number [of cycles]. (Āk 2.6.12)
Having ground the leaves with the juice of *akṣa* and *bhallātaka*, one should apply a coating;
then, having placed them in the midst of sesame chaff and sealed them, one should cook them with *puṭa* applications. (Āk 2.6.13)
Forty elephant-loads of [processed] tin produce ash.
(The qualities of tin: Tin is sharp, hot, and pungent; it slightly aggravates the wind (*vāta*). (Āk 2.6.14)
It destroys diseases of fat and phlegm, kills worms, and cures urinary disorders;
it is cold, astringent-salty, removes jaundice and burning sensations, and is laxative. (Āyurvedadīpikā 2.6.15)
Tin and lead are slightly scraping and increase bile; they possess those same qualities [as tin].
Lead, however, is dull, cold, and is called *yavaneṣṭa* (beloved by the Yavanas) and *bhujaṅgama* (serpent-like).
(Sīsaka) Lead, however, is dull, cold, and is called *yavaneṣṭa* (beloved by the Yavanas) and *bhujaṅgama* (serpent-like). (Āk 2.6.16)
The serpent desired by yogins, the uraga, the kuvaṅga, and the paripiṣṭaka—these are known to be soft black iron that purifies the eyelashes and the pupils. Āk 2.6.17.
Sirāvṛtta is vaṅga (tin), and cīnapiṣṭa is sixteen [parts];
lead (sīsa), however, is equal to vaṅga in terms of its rasa, vīrya, and vipāka. (Āk 2.6.18)
(The defects resulting from the consumption of impure lead and mercury:
Lead and mercury that have not undergone proper processing are known to cause leprosy, abdominal tumors, and pain;
they are also said to produce urinary disorders, anemia, fever, and disorders of phlegm, wind, and bile. (Āk 2.6.19)
Lead that melts quickly, has a great weight, is black when cut, and is brilliantly bright, yet has a foul odor and is black on the outside, is pure; otherwise, it is not. (Āk 2.6.20)
One should apply a paste of powdered *nirguṇḍī* root mixed with the milk of a *arka* plant;
then, having dried the leaf of the *nāga* tree, one should melt it and pour [the liquid] over it. (Āk 2.6.21)
Having smeared it and melted it, one should sprinkle it seven times for the sake of purification.
[One should take] seeds of *niśātumburu*, *kokilākṣī*, and *kuberaka*. (Āk 2.6.22)
Gaurīphala, Mallikā, Mokṣa, Brahmā, and Mayūraka—one should saturate the ashes of these, as they are available, with the milk of the Vajrī plant. (Āk 2.6.23)
In the midst of that, pure molten lead should be poured seven times;
it should be well-melted with the powder of buffalo bone and sprinkled with urine. (Āk 2.6.24)

Just as pure tin [is purified], so too is lead [purified] by means of the urine of a snake's bones. (Lead ash) Ashes from the bark of the *aśvattha* and *ciñcā* trees are added in a fourth part of the amount of the lead. (Āk 2.6.25)

Having cast it into the furnace, one should cook it in the fire, stirring it with an iron ladle until it becomes ash; having removed that [ash], one should take realgar equal in weight to the ash. (Āk 2.6.26)
Having ground [the mercury] with *jambīra* fruits or *āranāla* vinegar and sealed it, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
When it has cooled on its own, one should grind it again and place it in twenty parts of *śilāmlaka*. (Āk 2.6.27)
Having cooked it thus in sixty layers, the "Nāga" [mercury] becomes non-volatile (nirutthita).
Alternatively, the leaves of the Nāga plant, smeared with powder, [should be placed] in a shallow pan. (Āk 2.6.28) [Nāgabhasma (2)]
One should cook it for one *yāma* over a mild fire; that ash should then be fried in an iron vessel with the juices of *citraka*, stirring it with a wooden pestle. (Āk 2.6.29)
The liquid should be added repeatedly until the sixteenth watch;
one should press it firmly with a staff, having extracted it with *citraka* and *dāru*. (Āk 2.6.30)
Having stirred it and then restrained it with the sixfold [process], one dies quickly;
[this is] nāgabhasma produced from *ciñcā*, *akṣa*, sugarcane, *bhallātaka*, *vāsā*, and *vajralatā*. (Āk 2.6.31)
And with ashes produced from *apāmārga*, *arjuna*, and *aśvattha* trees, one should roast [the substance] firmly in an iron vessel using a staff made of *pālāśa* wood. (Āk 2.6.32)
He will die in exactly seven days; there is no doubt about this.
Having ground the ashes of a *nāga*, *agastya* [root], and *bhūnāga*, one should smear them on the vessel and purify it. (Āk 2.6.33)
One should melt the lead (nāga) in that vessel; once the lead is molten, one should throw in the alkali of vāśā and ciñcaṭa, and stir it with a stick of vāśā wood. (Āk 2.6.34)
One should cook it on the hearth for one watch (three hours), then remove it and mix it;
having ground it on a stone slab, it should be combined with the alkali of *vāśaka* and *tāpya*. (Āk 2.6.35)
One should cook four equal parts of the aforementioned naga for twenty-one layers;
for two layers, one should add the ashes of *ciñcī* along with the juice of *vāśā*. (Āk 2.6.36)
The *nāga* mineral has the luster of vermilion; it is lethal yet accomplishes all tasks.
Lead is extremely hot, unctuous, and bitter; it subdues wind and phlegm. (Āk 2.6.37)
It destroys the defects of urine and seminal fluid, stimulates digestion, and alleviates *āmavāta*. (Āk 2.6.38)
Āk, 2, 7 Śrī Bhairava:
(synonyms for brass).

Rīti (bronze), kṣudrasuvarṇa (inferior gold), sitakanaka (white gold), piṅgala (tawny), pittalaka (brass), lohitaka (red), ārakūṭa (copper), piṅgalaloha (tawny metal), and pītaka (yellow)—these are the nine types [of alloys]. (Āk 2.7.1)
Brass is of two kinds: *rītikā* and *kākatuṇḍī*. (Examination of Brass)
When heated and cast into sour gruel (kāñjika), it is considered *rītikā* because of its copper-like luster. Āk 2.7.2.
Thus, that which is born black is considered to be *kākatuṇḍī*.
(Examination of Brass: Quality)
Heavy and soft, yellowish like a pigeon, full of pith, and capable of withstanding beating.
The style is thus auspicious: very smooth, with soft limbs;
pure, glossy, gentle, cool, beautifully colored, and well-proportioned like a leaf from a reed-pen. (Āk 2.7.4)
The *rīti* known as *aśvattha* is proclaimed to be auspicious, resembling gold in appearance; however, it is of inferior quality when examined.
The *pāṇḍu* [variety] is yellow, coarse, and rough; the *barbara* is incapable of withstanding friction. (Āk 2.7.5)
A foul-smelling and light consistency is not desired in tastes and so forth. (Qualities of consistency:
A bitter-tasting consistency is parching, kills small creatures, and cures blood-bile disorders. Āk 2.7.6.
Kṛṣṇā removes skin diseases through its application; it is hot in potency yet cooling in its effect.
(Rājarīti: Properties)
The *kākatuṇḍī* style is characterized by the application of *sneha* (smoothness) and follows the qualities of royal conduct.
The royal alloy (*rājarīti*) is described as being similar to *rītikā* in its qualities.
The two types of *rītikā* are dry, slightly bitter, salty, and laxative. (Āk 2.7.8)
Brass (rītikā) is excellent; it destroys pāṇḍu and vāta, and increases strength, virility, and longevity.
It is pungent, bitter, and hot, and it eradicates splenic disorders and abdominal tumors. (Āk 2.7.9)
When used dry, it destroys phlegm, blood, and bile; when used sweet, it [nourishes].
(Rājarīti: synonyms)
The royal style is Kākatuṇḍī; the princess is Maheśvarī. (Āk 2.7.10)
Brāhmaṇī, brahmarīti, kapilā, and piṅgalā; kāṃsya, saurāṣṭrika, ghoṣa, kaṃsīya, and vahnalohaka. (Āk 2.7.11)
Dīptaloha, ghoṣayuṣya, dīptaka, and navāhvaya—these are the nine names [of bronze].
It is produced with one-eighth part copper and two parts of kuṭila. (Bronze:: Production) Āk 2.7.12.
When melted, bronze becomes [malleable]; that which originates from Saurāṣṭra is auspicious.
A voice that is sharp yet soft and gentle, slightly dark and bright. (Āk 2.7.13)
Brahminical bronze (kāṃsya) is praised as being of six kinds: stainless, glowing red, white and radiant, soft and luminous, resonant with sound, and glossy and pure. (Āk 2.7.14)
The finest bell-metal is said to have a thousand streaks of dense fire-like lines.
Copper that has been smelted in fire becomes dense, rough, and unable to withstand being beaten into a solid mass. (Āk 2.7.15)
One should discard bronze that has lost its luster after it has been polished seven times;
for humans, everything contained in bronze—except for ghee alone—is [unwholesome]. (Bronze: medicinal properties) Āk 2.7.16.

Bell-metal (kāṃsya), when used for eating, bestows health and happiness; it is wholesome, habit-forming, light, bitter, and hot, and it is scraping, clarifying to the eyes, and beneficial to vision. (Āk 2.7.17)
It cures worms in the digestive tract, destroys wind and bile, and is beneficial when consumed as food.
Vartaloha is circular, sharp, and round; it is an alloy of iron. (Āk 2.7.18)
Nīlikā, nīlaloha, lohaka, and vaṭṭalohaka; kāṃsya, ārka, rīti, loha, and ahijāta—these are the varieties of vartaloha. (Āk 2.7.19)
That very [substance] is called "the five metals" by those who know of metals; everything prepared in a vessel made of it should be preceded by other condiments. (Āk 2.7.20)
Free from acidity, it is highly digestive, a purifier, and auspicious.
(Regarding the purification and killing of *vartaloha*):
when molten *vartaloha* is cast into horse urine, it becomes purified. Āk 2.7.21.
Round iron, encased in both sulphur and mercury, is killed;
it should be applied according to the prescribed method in those various respective portions. (Āk 2.7.22)
Vartaloha (cast iron) is pungent and hot, yet bitter and cooling; it conquers phlegm, pacifies bile, is sweet, and cures burning sensations and urinary disorders. Āk 2.7.23.
It is parching, appetizing, anthelmintic, beneficial for the eyes, and a purifier of impurities.
(The procedure for the purifying ash of pitta-dominant substances and others:
One should saturate the three alkalis and five salts seven times with sour gruel. Āk 2.7.24.
One should smear the leaves of bell-metal with that paste, seal them, and roast them in a *gajapuṭa*; thus they attain purity, and not otherwise. (Āk 2.7.25)
Having subjected them to a process of killing (calcination) similar to that of copper, one should employ them in all [preparations].
These metals, once killed, become like nectar; when properly administered, they destroy even great diseases.
Through the yoga of constant practice, they bring about the perfection of a firm body and the destruction of illness, birth, and old age. (Āk 2.7.26)
Gold and silver are destroyed by *nāga* and *tāpya*; copper by *gandha* and lead by *śilā*;
tin by *tāla*, and the three types of iron by *nārīpaya* and *hiṅgula*. (Āk 2.7.27)
In the same way, mercury immediately destroys iron, even that which is as hard as adamant, when it is combined with mica and sulfur.
I shall explain the true essence (*sattva*) of *vajrābhra* (adamantine mica); listen, O Bhairavī!
The essence of mica is of four kinds: hard, soft, and liquid. (Āk 2.7.29)
And the seed should be known as possessing qualities; from that, each subsequent stage follows in sequence.
(For the purpose of precipitating the sattva, there is the accomplishment of *abhraka* [mica]:
*dhānyābhraka* should be placed in the milk of *ravikṣīra* under the heat of the sun for a period of days. (Āk 2.7.30)
One should grind that finely on a stone slab and confine it in a shallow earthen dish;
one should cook it properly in a *gajapuṭa* and then cook it again in the milk of a *ravi* plant. (Āk 2.7.31)
One should perform the mardana and puṭapāka in this manner seven times;
likewise in the juice of jambīra and in the juice of nicula. (Āk 2.7.32)

This is the most excellent, perfected "dense" [elixir] (ghanasiddhi), free from the moon (niścandra), for the descent of the vital essence (sattvapātana); it may be prepared with the essences of mercury, sulfur, and mica, either individually or all combined. Āk 2.7.33.
Having finely ground powdered mica (dhānyābhraka) and sealed it within a crucible, one should cook it in a gajapuṭa fire;
[adding] lac, guggulu, burnt wool, sarja, sal resin, and salt. (Āk 2.7.34)
Rabbit bone, small fish, turmeric, the five friends (*mitrapañcaka*), the five products of the buffalo (*pañcamāhiṣaka*), and marking-nut (*bhallātaka*)—all in equal parts. (Āk 2.7.35)

One should grind all of that together with an equal amount of *siddhaghana* for a day until it is free of lumps; from that, pills (*vaṭakas*) the size of one *karṣa* each should be prepared. (Āk 2.7.36)
One should strongly heat [the ore] in a crucible furnace with charcoal produced from *khadira* wood;
by heating it for three watches alone, the pure essence falls out. (Āk 2.7.37)

One should perform this process three times using hard, fine-grained [ore] that is free from glass and potassium carbonate (ṭaṅkaṇa), in order to extract the essence (sattva) from its dross. Āk 2.7.38.
Furthermore, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall describe another mild-natured [substance], the mild-natured *abhraka* (mica):
guggulu, ṭaṅkaṇa, guñjā, sarja, sarjarasa, and jaggery. (Āk 2.7.39)
Small fish, barley-alkali, glass, oil-cake, suraṇa, bhūlatā, the three myrobalans (triphalā), vahnī, milk-yielders, kanda, and punarnavā. (Āk 2.7.40)
Dhuttūra, lāṅgalī, pārā, balā, sulphur-sevaka, cow’s milk, and the five salts—all these [should be used] with twice as much honey. (Āk 2.7.41)
The six dots, the shell of a small snail, the bones of a hare, pigeon dung, the three pungent spices (tryūṣaṇa), the Indragopa insect, and the Śigru plant. (Āk 2.7.42)
One should grind wheat, mustard, and mica with goat's milk;
thus, whether used individually or all together, they should be ground for the duration of one watch (yāma). Āk 2.7.43.
One part of this bolus, two parts of processed mica, and one part of buffalo fat—mix all these together in one place. (Āk 2.7.44)
Pills weighing one karṣa each should be prepared and dried slightly in the shade;
one should repeatedly cast them into a crucible furnace heated by acacia wood charcoal. (Āk 2.7.45)
One should strongly heat five *ghuṭīs* and five [units] in the curved tube;
it becomes a soft, pure essence that destroys disease, old age, and death. (Āk 2.7.46)
One should perform this process three times; that residue causes the precipitation of the essence (*sattva*).
By this sequential method, one prepares *kāntaloha*, *sasyaka*, and *mākṣika*.
Other ores, such as tin and lead, along with pure earth and clay, release their own molten mass and each separately receive this [molten iron]. (Āk 2.7.48)
Taking mica-essence (abhrakasattva) of soft nature (abhrakamṛdusattva),
together with equal parts of glass (kāca) and borax (ṭaṅkaṇa),
one should repeatedly blow it three times while it is contained within a vajra-muṣā crucible. (Āk 2.7.49)
One should grind together the group of sour substances (amlavarga), the leaf of *snuhī*, and the seeds of *bimbī* along with their bark;
then, one should pour the heated [mercury] onto this mixture seven times. (Āk 2.7.50)
Its soft and bright essence destroys disease, old age, and death.
(Soft Essence of Abhraka) There should be ten parts of perfected abhraka and three parts of pure [mercury]. Āk 2.7.51.
One part each of well-purified borax, pyrite, and mercury, along with one part each of wool-ash, silk-ash, and barley-alkali, should be mixed together. (Āk 2.7.52)

It should be ground with the groups of urine and acids as previously described for the duration of a day; combined with the five limbs of a goat, the extraction of the essence (sattvapātana) is performed as before. Āk 2.7.53.
Having taken the actual dead [iron] and processed it, it becomes stainless and soft.
I shall now describe the "cooking of the seed" (*bījapāka*), which is supremely beneficial for this *abhraka* ore. (Āk 2.7.54)

One hundred palas of perfected abhraka (mica), gold, silver, arka (copper), and kānta (magnetite); mercury, the three aromatics, mākṣika (pyrite), vimalā (antimony), abhralatā, and mountain-born [minerals]. Āk 2.7.55.
Blue antimony, kaṅkuṣṭha, ferrous sulfate, and cinnabar—each of these should be ten niṣkas; then there shall be red ochre and borax. (Āk 2.7.56)
Indragopa, jaggery, guñjā, honey, clarified butter, guggulu, sarja-alkali, barley-alkali, and bedbugs constitute the "nine-fifths" (navapañcaka) [formula]. (Āk 2.7.57)
One should grind together small fish bones, rabbit bones, buffalo horn, *ālaka*, the two types of *pañcamūla* taken separately, and the five products of the buffalo (*pañcamāhiṣa*). (Āk 2.7.58)
And from these, pills should be prepared and dried slightly in the shade;
as before, one should administer the essence, which removes disease, old age, misery, and death. (Āk 2.7.59)
This seed-essence is the most excellent for medical practice, debate, and alchemy.
O Pārvatī, I shall now describe the purification of the essence of mica (abhraka-sattva). Āk 2.7.60.
Having reduced that essence into fine particles and combined it with the five friends, one should place it in a crucible with glass positioned both below and above it. (Āk 2.7.61)
Having sealed it, one should blow it in the forceful fire by means of the charcoal of khadira wood;
in this manner, one should blow it seven times in succession, and it will become stainless. (Āk 2.7.62)
Having purified it along with the sattva, one should grind it in an iron mortar;
one should rub it with decoctions of triphalā for one watch (yāma) and dry it in the heat. (Āk 2.7.63)
One should perform the cooking and the sealing according to the prescribed method in this manner repeatedly;
one should thus prepare forty sealings with juices produced from *mārkava*. (Āk 2.7.64)

Having performed five layers with the five nectars separately and three layers with sugarcane juice, [the pill] becomes like the rising sun, possessing dense essence and granting excellent accomplishment. (Āk 2.7.65)
(Procedure for Abhrakasattva-sindūra 1) One should grind purified mica into a powder in an iron mortar;
into that, one should add one *niṣka* of sulfur for every hundred *niṣkas* [of the mica]. (Āk 2.7.66)
One should grind it for one day with the juice of a *kumārī* plant;
then, having heated it in the sun for one watch (*yāma*), one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* (elephant-seal) vessel. (Āk 2.7.67)
In this manner, one should prepare a hundred layers and repeatedly apply the fragrance; O Śivā, the essence of mica will then take on the hue of vermilion and the pāṭala flower. (Āk 2.7.68)
(Procedure for Abhraka-sattva-sindūra, Part 2) One should grind very pure abhraka-sattva in an iron mortar.
Then, one should add one hundred *niṣkas* of that [sattva] along with half a *niṣka* of *mākṣika*. Āk 2.7.69.
Having ground it for a day with the milks of *arka* plants and sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
in this manner, one should perform a hundred *puṭas*, adding *mākṣika* (pyrite) in each successive *puṭa*.
This is the cinnabar of sattva, which destroys disease, old age, and death.
(The procedure for abhraka-sattva-cinnabar, 3) Having separated that sattva from the metallic flakes, the wise one [should place it] in an iron mortar. Āk_2,7.71.
One should crush it with an iron rod combined with a decoction of *varā*, and place it in an iron vessel for the duration of one *yāma* in a hot, arid climate. (Āk 2.7.72)
Having made the *sthālīpāka* coarse, one should cook it at night in a "gaja-puṭa" (elephant-seal) vessel;
in this manner, one should perform seven such puṭas with the fresh juice of *mārkaṇḍa*.
Likewise with the juices of the *kumārī* plant, similarly with the juices of the *citramūla* root,
likewise with the juices of *nīlī* leaves, and similarly with the juices of *punarnavā*.

With seven decoctions made from the juices of the Meghanāda plant and the roots of the Vaṭa tree, one should likewise add sulphur in an extremely fine powder in a hundredth part [of the total weight]. (Āk 2.7.75)
One should rub it with lemon juice and cook it in a vessel or in a *puṭa* over heat;
one should proceed in this manner for ten days, then again heat it by a hundredth part. (Āk 2.7.76)
Having cast [the ingredients] with the husks of grain and having crushed them, one should cook them in a vessel or a *puṭa* over heat;
in this manner one should proceed for ten days, and then cook it again with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). (Āk 2.7.77)
One should perform the fivefold folding with the juices of five different types of sugarcane; then, one should place pure cinnabar into the mica-ash that has the luster of vermilion. (Āk 2.7.78)

Then, having ground a twentieth part of the solid [substance] with breast milk, one should seal it in a crucible and, having placed it in a *bhūdhara* (earth-pressing) apparatus, perform a light *puṭa* (roasting). (Āk 2.7.79)
In this manner, one should prepare twenty layers by repeatedly applying cinnabar;
through this sequential process, the essence becomes like vermilion in appearance.
This is the general consecration; however, the specific [consecration] is now declared:
whatever substance removes a particular disease, that very substance shall become the remover of that disease. (Āk 2.7.81)

(Procedure for Abhraka-sattva-sindūra, 4) One should grind very pure abhraka-sattva in an iron mortar with the juice of *muṇḍī* leaves; having rubbed it for one day, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa*. (Āk 2.7.82)
In this manner, ten layers should be applied using the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī*,
as well as with decoctions of *vaṭa* roots and the juices derived from the roots of *peṭārī*.
Likewise, with the juices of the *kakubha* tree and similarly with the fresh juice of *jambu* bark, one should prepare sixty layers; then, one should place [the ingredients] into that. (Āk 2.7.84)
One should grind cinnabar with breast milk for a day using a twentieth part [of the milk];
then, having sealed it within a crucible, one should apply a mild fire-packing (puṭa) in an earthen furnace. (Āk 2.7.85)
In this way, one should prepare it in twenty ways; it will certainly become the color of vermilion.
(Regarding *sthālīpāka*:
*Sthālīpāka* is said to be of three kinds: soft, medium, and hard. Āk 2.7.86.
O Dear One, the first [type of] cooked rice-mass is like a mound of mud; the middle one is like a ball of dough;
the third is a hard-cooked mass, resembling sand. (Āk 2.7.87)
Then, the cooked rice (sthālīpāka) prepared with a savory sauce, or combined with realgar,
should be placed in an earthen vessel (bhūdhara) that has been heated to either a mild or moderate degree.
Having placed [the substance] in a small crucible, it should be given [as an ingredient], excluding mercury and cinnabar;
a hard-baking process (kharapāka) must be performed, and one should cook according to the procedure using a gajapuṭa. (Āk 2.7.89)
(The Procedure for the Immortalization of Iron Ashes and All Mortarized Metals, including Abhraka):
I shall declare the supreme secret, the immortalization [of substances]; listen. (Āk 2.7.90)
Taking sixteen parts of the decoction produced from the three myrobalans (triphalā), eight palas of cow’s ghee, and ten palas of purified abhraka; Āk 2.7.91.
Having combined them in an iron vessel, one should cook them over a gentle fire; once the liquid has been digested, one should take it up and employ it in all formulations. (Āk 2.7.92)

For indeed, even *abhra* (mica), which removes old age, death, and disease, [is ineffective] without a post-digestive drink (*anupāna*). One should therefore employ appropriate post-digestive drinks so that it may become a remover of various specific diseases. (Āk 2.7.93)
Sindūra, gray hair, wrinkles, the sharpness of the sense faculties, and even the qualities of mica and leaf-metal belong to the *kaṭhina* type of *abhrasattva*. (Āk 2.7.94)
Sindūra from Mṛdu-sattva destroys all diseases; it is a divine elixir that eliminates wrinkles, graying hair, poverty, and death. (Āk 2.7.95)
It pacifies the three *doṣas*, is gentle, stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, and is auspicious; it destroys the entire network of fevers, as well as *grahaṇī* and diarrhea. (Āk 2.7.96)
It cures urinary calculi, dysuria, consumption, anemia, halīmaka, hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, skin diseases, and ailments arising from vāta and pitta. (Āk 2.7.97)
It cures diseases arising from phlegm that are difficult to overcome, as well as ulcers such as abscesses and various types of colic; it also destroys sterility in both men and women. (Āk 2.7.98)
Whatever diseases are removed by various medicinal formulations, those same diseases are likewise subdued by mercury;
whatever qualities exist in mercury, those very qualities also exist in the essence of the seed (bījasattva).
One should blow away the dross produced from iron using charcoal from *akṣa* wood; then one should repeatedly sprinkle it with cow's urine inside an *akṣa* vessel six times over. (Āk 2.7.100)
This is declared to be maṇḍūra; one should employ it when pure and finely ground.
One should boil triphalā in cow’s urine and slowly sprinkle [the powder] with that decoction. (Āk 2.7.101)
(Maṇḍūra-bhasma):
Iron dross that has been thoroughly heated until it crumbles by itself—once it has crumbled, one should collect it and grind it; this is the maṇḍūra to be employed. (Āk 2.7.102)
Whatever qualities are found in killed hair, those same qualities are found in hair-ash (muṇḍakiṭṭaka).
Therefore, one should employ iron rust everywhere for the pacification of disease. (Āk 2.7.103)
O Shaven-headed One, *muṇḍa* is ten times more effective than *kiṭṭa*; *tīkṣṇa* is a hundredfold more effective than *muṇḍa*;
and *kānta* is a hundred-thousandfold more effective than *tīkṣṇa*—it produces its full benefit through consumption. (Āk 2.7.104)

Iron rust (maṇḍūra) cures anemia, consumption, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, and jaundice; it destroys all types of colic and urinary disorders, stimulates digestion, and is supremely beneficial. (Āk 2.7.105)
Cold, bitter, astringent, and sour, it destroys heart disease and splenic disorders.
(Regarding the quantity of substances for the killing of mercury and so forth:
O Goddess, one should purify the king of mercury (rasendra) using two thousand palas [of the aforementioned substances]. Āk 2.7.106.
One may perform alchemical operations with a thousand, a hundred, fifty, or even half of that; however, one should certainly not do so with less than twenty-five. (Āk 2.7.107)
One should not perform the smelting of iron beyond thirty palas, O Goddess; likewise, one should smelt the essence of mica for less than five palas. (Āk 2.7.108)
Gold weighing more than five *palas* and less than one *pala* should not be purified;
likewise for silver and copper, O Dear One, one should purify and then kill [them]. (Āk 2.7.109)
It should possess a density like that of iron and likewise have thick leaves;
it should not be less than five palas, nor should one make it more than twenty palas.
O Goddess, there is liquefaction, purification, and the killing of lead and tin;
however, one should not perform purification or the killing of diamond (vajra), whether it be below or above the gold coin (niṣka). Āk 2.7.111.
O Sovereign of the Gods, one should likewise fashion gems such as rubies and the like. (Āk 2.7.112)
Āk, 2, 8 Śrī Bhairava said:
Whether in the great ocean, in a river, on a mountain, or even in a forest,
O Goddess, it is a mine of jewels because of the weightiness of that which is contained within it. (Āk 2.8.1)
Within them appear jewels that remove the defects of demons, poison, serpents, and diseases, as well as those that are of inferior quality. Āk 2.8.2.
Produced by a corrupted being and afflicted by [the three] humors, they increase through defects and diminish through the perfection of virtues. (Āk 2.8.3)
Māṇikya, śoṇaratna, ratnarāṭ, raviratnaka,
śṛṅgārin, raṅgamāṇikya, tarala, and ratnanāyaka are synonyms for ruby.
Rāgadṛk, padmarāga, ratna, śoṇopala,
saugandhika, lohitaka, kuruvinda, and śarenduka.
The first is called *māṇikya* or *padmarāga*, and the second is *nīlagandhi*.
(Ruby: Examination)
It has the luster of a lotus petal, being clear, glossy, heavy, and radiant. (Āk 2.8.6)
A ruby with rounded, elongated, and symmetrical limbs is said to be the most excellent among gems purified by examination for those who uphold the earth. (Āk 2.8.7)
One who desires welfare, prosperity, and fame should always maintain [the treatise];
thereafter, the examination of those [treatises] and so forth is described according to the scriptures. (Āk 2.8.8)
(The varieties of rubies:
Siṃhala, Kālapura, Andhra, and that situated in Tumburu—these are the four types of source-land for the production of that ruby. Āk 2.8.9.
In Siṃhala, there is the unsurpassed red *padmarāga*;
that which originates from Kālapura is yellow and is known as *kuruvinda*. (Āk 2.8.10)
O beloved, the *saugandhika* variety of *andhra* is said to have the hue of an *aśoka* sprout;
that which is found in *tumburu* is described as having a dark-blue luster and a blue fragrance. (Āk 2.8.11)
In the middle [region], the ruby (māṇikya) should be known as of middling quality according to the distinction of its field;
four qualities of the ruby have been proclaimed by the eminent sages. (Āk 2.8.12)
Glossiness, weight, purity, and deep redness are the qualities of a ruby (*māṇikya*).
A ruby stimulates digestion, acts as an aphrodisiac, and removes the afflictions caused by phlegm, wind, and consumption. (Āk 2.8.13)
It destroys spirits, vampires, and sins; it eradicates diseases born of karma;
it is a source of great merit, a jewel, and the supreme bringer of great fortune. (Āk 2.8.14)
It destroys all spirits, seizing-demons, insanity, and poisons, and is the supreme subduer of the humors (*doṣa*).
[Muktā] is synonymous with *muktā*, *saumyā*, *mauktika*, *śauktikeya*, *tāra*, *tārā*, *śauktika*, and *tārakā*.
The essence of water is cool and free from dust; the constellation is the moon-jewel, which is white. (Āk 2.8.15)

*Muktāphala*, *binduphala*, *muktā*, *śaukteyaka*, *śuktimaṇi*, *śaśipriya*, *svaccha*, *hima*, *haimavata*, *śubhra*, *sudhāṃśuratna*, and that which is called *bhasaṃkhya*—these are the names for pearl. (Āk 2.8.16)
The pearl-gem clearly arises from eight sources: the elephant, the serpent, the fish, the boar, the head [of a bird], the bamboo, the conch, and the water-bearing oyster shell.

Among these, the colors are generally pale-red, blue, yellow, and white; however, while these seven are frequently found, the other—namely that which comes from the oyster—is most abundant. (Āk 2.8.17)
Resembling a star, perfectly pure, exceedingly free [of flaws], lustrous, large, stainless, and without blemish;
That pearl which possesses such weight that it cannot be measured on a scale, being priceless, bestows happiness. (Āk 2.8.18)

Pearl is sweet and very cooling; it alleviates eye diseases, destroys poison, cures the aggravation of *rājayakṣman*, and increases the nourishment of diminished semen, strength, and vitality. (Āk 2.8.19)
Pearl is cooling, unctuous, clear, and increases radiance. (Āyurveda 2.8.20)
It cures burning sensations, thirst, vertigo, fainting, hemorrhagic disorders, fever, and poisons;

it is beneficial for the eyes, subdues wind, blood, bile, and toxins, and delights all the sense organs. It pacifies thirst, burning sensations, fever, grief, and delusion; it is cooling, removes fatigue, and is wholesome. Blessed, auspicious, and a sustainer of life, it bestows good fortune and luster. All these qualities belong to pearls as an ornament for the neck; indeed, the Moon is pleased with that very root. (Āk 2.8.21)
Coral is synonymous with *pravāla*, *aṅgārakamaṇi*, *vidruma*, and *ambhodhipallava*. (Āk 2.8.22)
The earth-born gem is the red-bodied coral, a jewel with red sprouts and tendrils;
it is that auspicious creeper which grows upon the bridge in the midst of the ocean.
That which is called vidruma is intensely red, difficult to obtain, and radiant in appearance.
(Coral: Examination:
Good Quality)
Being hard, this [earth] becomes stone through the process of baking. (Āk 2.8.24)
That which is called coral is red, bestowing excellence of color, beauty, and luster;
it is perfected when it is clear, glossy in appearance, round, lovely, even, and heavy. (Āk 2.8.25)
A firm, solid mass with a colored body is said to be the best coral; it has the luster of a ripe bimba fruit and resembles the japā flower. (Āk 2.8.26)
Coral that has a luster like a parrot’s beak is exceedingly beautiful; [however, this refers to its appearance when of inferior quality].
A petal that has the luster of autumn [leaves], is thin, curved, rough, and hollow; Āk 2.8.27.
A coral that is pierced, black, or extremely light will cause defects; one should discard an inauspicious coral that is pale-colored or covered with water. Āk 2.8.28.
Coral that is soft, glossy, and well-colored is beneficial as a vidruma gem.
It brings wealth and grain, is purifying, and destroys the fear of poison and serpents.
Coral is sweet and sour; it subdues the humors such as phlegm and bile. It bestows vigor and luster upon women, and when worn, it grants auspiciousness. (Āk 2.8.30)
*Marakata*, *rauhiṇeya*, *gārutmanta*, and *harinmaṇi* refer to emerald; *sauparṇa* refers to that which was vomited forth by Garuḍa; and *budharatna* and *aśmagarbha* refer to cat's-eye. (Āk 2.8.31)
The enemy of poison (the peacock), possessing the power of the wind, is the Gāruḍa [mantra], equal to Rudra;
it was obtained in the ocean of the Turuṣka region on Mount Samīrārohaṇa. (Āk 2.8.32)
That region became dark with their shadows and turned into a mine of emeralds; from that specific cause, emerald was born, possessing both defects and virtues.
Its defects are said to be of seven kinds, its qualities of five kinds, and the luster of the emerald gem is of eight kinds. (Āk 2.8.34)
It is said to be ununctuous and parched, as well as having eruptions and pustules; moreover, the abdomen is devoid of luster, lacking radiance, and likewise soiled. (Āk 2.8.35)
[An image] that contains gravel and stones, is rough, joined with threads, variegated in color, mottled, and brings all manner of fear. (Āk 2.8.36)
It is said to be stainless, clear, heavy, and endowed with weight;
it is smooth, free from dryness, devoid of dust, and free from impurity. (Āk 2.8.37)
"Deep red and abounding in luster—these are remembered as the five qualities;
an emerald endowed with these is supreme in removing all sins. (Āk 2.8.38)
Emerald destroys poison, is cooling and sweet in taste; it removes undigested matter and bile, is appetizing, provides nourishment, and destroys malevolent spirits. (Āk 2.8.39)
Lustrous emerald is clear, auspicious, and removes all defects;
it bestows beauty and good fortune, is purifying, and destroys spirits, planetary influences, and poisons. (Āk 2.8.40)
(Puṣparāga: synonyms) Puṣparāga is yellow; it is also called pītasphuṭika and pītaratna.
Yellow stone, guru-ratna, yellow gem, and puṣyarāga. (Āk 2.8.41)
Slightly yellow, with a pale luster, transparent, and captivating by its brilliance.
It is known as the *puṣyarāga* gem by those who examine jewels.
(Puṣparāga:
Examination:
Good Quality)
A topaz that has a golden luster, a rounded head, and is as pure as a glowing ember;
which is yellow-bodied, heavy, and glossy—is highly praised. (Āk 2.8.43)
(Puṣparāga:
Examination:
Poor Quality)
A topaz (puṣyarāga) that is rough, scratched, light, white, black, pale-yellow, sandy, dirty, or marked with spots is not recommended. Āk 2.8.44.
Topaz is sour and cold; it subdues wind and is an excellent stimulant of the digestive fire.
Through its retention, it bestows longevity, prosperity, and wisdom upon men. (Āk 2.8.45)
The Puṣyarāga gem is auspicious and pure; it bestows wealth, good fortune, and fame;
it grants eloquence of speech, is pleasing to the heart, destroys poison, and is supreme in overcoming the bodily humors. (Āk 2.8.46)
*Vajra*, *indrāyudha*, *vīra*, *bhidura*, *kuliśa*, *pavi*, *abhedyam*, *asiram*, *ratnam*, *dṛḍham*, and *bhārgavakam* are recorded as synonyms for the thunderbolt (*vajra*). (Āk 2.8.47)
Clear, possessing the luster of lightning, smooth, beautiful, light, and capable of scratching [other substances].
One with six spokes and sharp edges, or one with very gentle spokes, shall bestow prosperity. (Āk 2.8.48)
(Vajrākarā and vajrabhedāśca):
Pauṇḍra, Mataṅga, Himācala, Saurāṣṭra, Supāra, Kosala, Kaliṅga, and the bank of the Peṇṇā river—these eight are designated as the diamond mines. (Āk 2.8.49)
That which originates from Prapauṇḍarīka is dark; that born on Mount Mataṅga is slightly yellow;
that produced in Himavat and Surāṣṭra is copper-red; and that from Supāra possesses a black luster. (Āk 2.8.50)

They say that the diamond produced in Kośala has the luster of a full-blown śirīṣa flower; that from Kaliṅga has a golden brilliance; and that which arises on the banks of the Peṇṇā river resembles the nectar-rayed moon. Āk 2.8.51.
The regions of Kaliṅga and Kosala, Mount Mataṅga and the Himālaya, as well as Saurāṣṭra, Pauṇḍra, Kauberaka, Karasū, and Pāraka. (Āk 2.8.52)
In the Kṛta and other ages, these two are known as the sources of diamonds; among the sources of diamonds, there are indeed three types: the mine, the stream, and the scattered. (Āk 2.8.53)
O leader of the gods, the place of origin is taught to be threefold:
the points, the sides, and the edges, numbering six, eight, and twelve respectively. (Āk 2.8.54)
Thus they speak of the qualities of the diamond, whose tip has a clear and sharp edge:
(the defects of the diamond) are impurity, a spot, a line, fear, and likewise a crow's foot. Āk 2.8.55.
These five defects have been fully described as residing in diamonds; an unpurified diamond may cause leprosy, burning sensations, and heaviness of the limbs. (Āk 2.8.56)
It causes pain in the heart and sides, as well as jaundice; therefore, its purification is now described.
(Vajraśuddhi) Having taken a bright diamond, one should place it inside the bulb of a *vyāghrī* plant. (Āk 2.8.57)
Having smeared it with buffalo dung, one should cook it over a fire of dried cow-dung;
after twenty-four hours, one should remove it and sprinkle it with horse urine. (Āk 2.8.58)
In this manner, being cooked again and again, it becomes purified after seven nights by means of *meghanāda*, *śamī*, *śyāmā*, *śṛṅgī*, and *madanaka*.
Kulattha, vetasa, agastya, sindhuvāra, and ākhukarṇikā—having again prepared a decoction of these with horse urine... [Āk 2.8.60]
Having cast the *vajra* into *jambīra* juice, one should cook it for three days with horse urine using the method of the *ḍolāyantra*; thereby, it attains purification. (Āk 2.8.61)
One should cook the *vajra* contained within the bulb of *vyāghrī* in a *dolāyantra* using decoctions of *kuluttha* and *kodrava*; after seven days, it attains purification. (Āk 2.8.62)
Having placed a decoction of *kulattha* and *kodrava*, horse urine, and the milk of *snuhī* into a vessel, one should cook therein a *pavimantra* located within the bulb of *vyāghrī*. (Āk 2.8.63)
In a swing-oven (ḍolāyantra), having extracted [the substance] day and night, one should place it back again;
having smeared the bulb with clay in a "thunderbolt-bulb" (vajrakanda) vessel, one should cook it in a "gaja-puṭa" fire. (Āk 2.8.64)
Once it is cooked, sprinkled with digestive liquids, and smeared with clay, the diamond (vajra) placed inside the tuber of *vyāghrī* should be baked in a *puṭa*. (Āk 2.8.65)
Having extracted [the substance] after a day and night, one should sprinkle it with horse urine or sprinkle it with *vajrī* milk; thus purified, one should kill [it]. (Āk 2.8.66)
(The slaying of the pure vajra by means of a different caste): The slaying of the pure vajra belonging to the brahmin caste and others will now be explained.
[One should use] *aśvattha*, jujube, *bhaṇḍī*, honey, and crab bone. (Āk 2.8.67)
Having ground [the ingredients] together with the milk of the *snuk* plant, one should smear [the mixture] inside the crucible;
thereafter, one should place the diamond (*vajra*) into its midst along with those medicinal herbs. (Āk 2.8.68)
Having carefully covered the vajra, one should then seal the crucible;
furthermore, one should roast it with a great *puṭa* known as the "elephant. (Āk 2.8.69)
A diamond of a different species is perfected with a single firing;
likewise are *karavīra*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *darada*, and *udumbara*. (Āk 2.8.70)
Having ground it together with the milks of the *arka* plant, one should place a diamond of the Kṣatriya class into the resulting ball; as before, it will certainly be killed. (Āk 2.8.71)
(The killing of a Vajra belonging to the Vaiśya caste:
One should grind sūraṇa, garlic, and conch shell together on a stone;
one should also grind balā, atibalā, gandha, and tortoise bone. (Āk 2.8.72)
One should place a diamond of the Vaiśya class into a ball made from the milk of the *uttarāvāruṇī* plant; as before, it will become dead. (Āk 2.8.73)
(Regarding the killing of one of the Śūdra caste by means of Vajra):

One should grind together sūraṇa, garlic, conch-shell, and realgar in equal parts; having formed a ball with this using the milky sap of the banyan tree, one should cook it as previously described. (Āk 2.8.74)
That *vajra* which belongs to the *śūdra* caste is properly brought to death by that [method];
however, the male and female *vajra* are killed by those respective medicines previously mentioned. (Āk 2.8.75)
By means of the four types of medicinal herbs alone, death occurs for the neuter *vajra*.
(The slaying of the *vajra*)—the general procedure for the slaying of all *vajras* shall now be described. (Āk 2.8.76)
Having smeared a pure vajra with the blood of bedbugs, one should heat it again and again until it is the color of fire, and then repeatedly cast it into the urine of a donkey. (Āk 2.8.77)
One should smear and heat it in that same manner twenty-one times.
Having ground realgar with bedbugs, one should throw it into that globule. (Āk 2.8.78)
Having sealed the crucible, one should heat it intensely and then immerse it in horse urine;
having withdrawn it, one should repeat this process seven times, and it will become dead (calcined). (Āk 2.8.79)
(2) Vajramāraṇa:
ramie’s horn, snake bone, tortoise shell, bitumen, sulfur, magnetite, *munipuṣpa*, and *satālaka*. (Āk 2.8.80)
The three alkalis, the five salts, meṣaśṛṅgī, indravāruṇī, vajravallī, mūṣakarṇī, and the buds of badarī. (Āk 2.8.81)
The excrement of a rat, breast milk, the latex of *snuhī* and *arka*, the five parts of *śarapuṃkhā*, and the bones of a donkey and a ram. (Āk 2.8.82)
