The seed of *peṭārī*, the flower of a woman, the excrement of a pigeon, realgar, and the flowers of *vākucī* and the five parts (*pañcāṅga*) of *timira*. (Āk 2.8.83)
The five parts of the *dhātrī* tree, *gorambhā*, horse urine, *haṃsapādī*, *vajrakanda*, *bṛhatī* fruit, and *sūraṇa*. (Āk 2.8.84)
One should mix *gojihvā*, crab meat, and the group of urines; all of these together, or individually as available, well-kneaded into a ball. (Āk 2.8.85)
One should place that mass inside a crucible and seal it within a blind-muffler (*andhamūṣā*);
then, having ground horse-gram (*kuluttha*) and *kodrava*, one should stir them into horse urine. (Āk 2.8.86)
One should pour that heated [substance], which has emerged from the crucible-cavity, into the middle of it;
in this manner, one should repeat the process twenty-one times. (Āk 2.8.87)
Taking that vajra again, one should place it in a ball made of crushed bedbugs mixed with *tāla*, seal the crucible, and blow it in a fierce fire. (Āk 2.8.88)
Thus, having been heated in this manner seven times, one should pour it into horse urine;
by this sequential application, it will certainly become dead. (Āk 2.8.89)
One should grind that dead [substance] in a mortar; this is declared as the Siddhayoga.
(Vajramāraṇa 3) Bhrāmaka, dead tāpya, peṭālī, seeds, and ṭaṅkaṇa—Āk_2,8.90.
Milk, uttaravāruṇī, sulphur, realgar, mica, the seed of the tamarind, meṣaśṛṅgī, female menses, and amlavetasa. (Āk 2.8.91)
The five ingredients of *śarapuṃkhā*, rabbit bone, and bitumen—these, either combined or individually, should be finely powdered according to their availability. (Āk 2.8.92)
One should rub [the diamond] with the milks of *snuhi*, *arka*, and *uttaravāruṇī*, as well as with breast milk;
having placed the diamond into that mass and sealed it, one should heat it firmly. (Āk 2.8.93)

Having ground together *guḍūcī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *mustā*, and *uttaravāruṇī* with the decoctions of *kulattha*, one should throw [the paste] into that same decoction. (Āk 2.8.94)
Having placed that vajra in the crucible as before and having sealed it, one should blow upon it in that manner;
then one should perform the pouring [of the liquid] twenty-one times. (Āk 2.8.95)
One should heat talaka seven times in combination with bedbugs;
one should then sprinkle it with horse urine—that *vajra* will certainly die. (Āk 2.8.96)
(4) *Vajramāraṇa*:
One should take the root of the three-year-old *uttha* cotton plant and grind it;
or one should grind it with the natural juices of the three-year-old *nāgavallī*. Āk 2.8.97.
One should cast the vajra into that crucible, seal it, and cook it in a "gajapuṭa" fire;
thus, by seven such puṭas, each one [of the ingredients] becomes cooked. (Āk 2.8.98)
Having ground together talaka, kāsīsa, saurāṣṭrī, and the ashes of apāmārga with the decoctions of kulattha, one should thoroughly heat the vajra in that [mixture]. (Vajramāraṇa 5) Āk 2.8.99.
One should cast [it] for twenty-one times; it dies, of this there is no doubt.
One should grind amlavetasa together with the ash of vaikrānta. (Āk 2.8.100)

One should place that vajra into the crucible, blow it while it is inside a blind-sealed crucible (andhamūṣā), sprinkle it with horse urine, and then place it back into the original crucible. Āk 2.8.101.
Having obstructed it, one should blow upon it and then sprinkle it again; one should do this twenty-one times.
It dies; there is no doubt about this. One should employ this in all yogic applications. (Āk 2.8.102)
(7) *Vajramāraṇa*:
Having ground for a moment the "mouth" [of the crucible] made from *kāntapāṣāṇa* with the milk of *uttarāvāruṇī*, one should place that ball inside it and cook it for a day. (Āk 2.8.103)
One dies by [using] human oil or scented oil; there is no doubt about this.
(Vajramāraṇa 8) Then, one should grind realgar and sulfur with breast milk. Āk 2.8.104.
One should cook that ball containing the *vajra*; the *vajra* will become dead [melted] in the previously mentioned oil.
(Vajra-māraṇa 9) Having ground *vimalā* with the milk of *snuhī*, one should place it into that ball. Āk 2.8.105.
Having sealed the crucible with a vajra, one should blow it with a fierce fire once it has dried;
then, having cast the vajra into the urine of a horse, one should retrieve the vajra. (Āk 2.8.106)

Having thus prepared it in seven ways, one should then grind it with *tālaka* and *matkuṇa* to form a ball; this should be cast into that [mixture], and the *vajramūṣā* crucible should be sealed. (Āk 2.8.107)
It should be blown [into flame] as before and sprinkled seven times; it will become dead.
(Vajramāraṇa 10) Having smeared the vajra repeatedly with the blood of a bedbug, one should place it in the sun. Āk 2.8.108.
Once the plaster has dried, it should be dried again, repeating this for up to seven days;
one should sprinkle it repeatedly with the juices of *viṣṇukrāntā* and *peṭakārī*. (Āk 2.8.109)
That vajra, having been heated again and again, becomes dead after being processed one hundred times.
(Vajramāraṇa) One should take powdered sulphur and saturate it seven times with female menses. Āk_2,8.110
Again, having stirred it with female menstrual blood, one should heat that vajra well; by sprinkling it and heating it twenty-one times, it becomes deadened (mṛta). Āk 2.8.111.

(12) Vajramāraṇa: Having cast the *vajra* into a large pearl-oyster shell from a river, one should meditate upon it repeatedly in the sun’s heat with the juice of any one of the following: *snuhī*, *arka*, or *uttamakanyā*. (Āk 2.8.112)
One should grind it with the flesh of a black lizard and wrap it again;
properly held in the clay of *bhūnāga*, it attains the state of ash. (Āk 2.8.113)
(13) Vajramāraṇa:
A diamond, when wrapped with the roots of *raktamūla* and the buds of *meghanāda* ground together and then heated, is completely reduced to ashes. (Āk 2.8.114)
(14) For the Vajramāraṇa [process]:
having placed the vajra inside a citron fruit and sealed it, one should coat the exterior with clay;
after removing it from a *puṭa* (earthenware crucible), one should cook it likewise in a *śatapuṭa*. Āk 2.8.115.
(1) Vajramṛdūkaraṇa:
Anointed with the juices of *nāgaparṇī* and wrapped in its own leaf, if it is placed between the knees for one watch (*yāma*), that diamond (*vajra*) will attain softness. (Āk 2.8.116)
(2) For the softening of the diamond:
one should place the diamond in the center of the seed of the *mātṛvāhaka* plant;
or else, one should cook it for a day in a *jambīra*-fruit vessel using a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*). Āk 2.8.117.

Having extracted [the mercury] after one day and night from a decoction of *kulattha* and *kodrava*, or from a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), one should place it again inside a *jambīra* fruit. (Āk 2.8.118)
Or, having cast [the substance] into the seed-mantra of Mātṛvāhaka, one should cook it as before;
it should be cast in again and cooked again, and at the end of three days, one should extract it. (Āk 2.8.119)
One should collect the sprouts of the *badarī*, *vaṭa*, and *nimba* trees;
having ground them, one should place the previously prepared *vajra* into that mass. (Āk 2.8.120)
Having wrapped that ball in an *aśvattha* leaf and placed it between the knees, or having worn it on the side of the body for a day, one certainly becomes soft. (Āk 2.8.121)
(3) For the softening of diamond (*vajramṛdūkaraṇa*):
one should grind mercury and fine powder of iron (*tīkṣṇa*) with sour gruel for a day;
one should place the diamond inside that globule and wrap it on the outside with thread. (Āk 2.8.122)
Wrapped with betel leaves and placed upon a heap of grain, one should, at the end of the month, remove it and smear it with the juice of the *nāgalatā* creeper. (Āk 2.8.123)
Wrapped with its petals and placed between the knees, it becomes soft;
or else, the powder produced from *kānta* iron, or the surface of *kānta* stone, [should be used]. (Vajra-softening, 4) Āk 2.8.124.
One should grind it for one day with a sour preparation containing honey;
then one should place the *vajra* within that sphere along with *nimba*, cotton, and *kodrava*. (Āk 2.8.125)
Then, having thoroughly ground the leaves with *nāgavallī* (betel) leaves, it should be wrapped and placed between the knees; at the end of the day, it will attain softness. (Āk 2.8.126)
(5) Vajramṛdūkaraṇa:
One should cast an iron nail into the center of an eraṇḍa tree or into its fruit.
After extracting it after exactly one month, [one should place it] between the knees as before. (Āk 2.8.127)
Diamond becomes soft at the end of the day; there is no doubt about this.
(Vajra-softening, 6) One should place diamond wrapped in partridge meat inside the mouth. Āk 2.8.128.
One should wrap the mouth of an extremely large frog with thread, bury it in the earth to a depth of one cubit, and after one month, dig it up. (Āk 2.8.129)
Having confined a frog within a sealed crucible, one should cook it properly in a "gajapuṭa" (elephant-oven).
That vajra, situated within the aforementioned sphere and placed between the knees, [should remain there] for a day. (Āk 2.8.130)
One should first prepare vajraudana directly, and afterwards one should add the ingredients to be brought in;
however, the killing of all those who eat the vajraudana shall occur as before. (Āk 2.8.131)
(Vajradruti) The three alkalis, asafoetida, sour chickpeas, amlavetasa,
jvālāmukhī, ikṣuraka, and the fruits of sthalakumbhī. (Āk 2.8.132)

Having finely ground purified diamond with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, one should place it within a ball of that paste; then, having bound it securely in a cloth, one should cook it with force. (Āk 2.8.133)
By means of a swinging apparatus (*ḍolāyantra*) in fermented grain liquid (*dhānyāmla*), [the diamond] becomes liquefied after eight months;
or, having placed the diamond inside *vajravallī*, it is rendered immobile (*nirodhita*). (Āk 2.8.134)
It should be sprinkled while placed in a vessel of sour gruel; after seven days, it attains a liquid state.
There are three methods for the killing of *vajra*: ash, rice-gruel, and liquefaction. (Āk 2.8.135)
It is declared by the masters headed by Nāgārjuna to be a binder of the vital essence (*rasabandha*).
And the diamond (*vajra*), endowed with the six tastes, removes all diseases. (Vajra-qualities) Āk_2.8.136.
It pacifies all evils, bestows happiness, strengthens the body, and is a rejuvenative elixir;
it is a diamond, the supreme jewel, meritorious, and increases fortune and prosperity. (Āk 2.8.137)
It bestows longevity, prosperity, vigor, and fame; it conquers all evils and produces life-force, strength, physical well-being, beauty, and luster. (Āk 2.8.138)
When consumed, it destroys diseases; when dead, it is a diamond—of this there is no doubt.
The blue [stone] is the solar jewel (*sauriratna*), the blue stone (*nīlāśman*), and the blue gem (*nīlaratnaka*). (Āk 2.8.139)
The sapphire (*nīlopala*), the grass-grasper (*tṛṇagrāhī*), the great-blue (*mahānīla*), and the well-blue (*sunīlaka*);
therein the indranīla gem is fourfold according to the distinction of its species. (Āk 2.8.140)
One with a white luster is of the Brahmin caste; one that is red is of the Kṣatriya lineage.
The Vaiśya caste is indeed yellow, while the Śūdra has black radiance.
(The qualities and defects of the blue [color]):
It has an appearance like the juice of indigo, resembling the *vaiṣṇavī* flower;
it resembles the *lavalī* flower and has a luster like that of the blue water-lily (*nīlendīvāra*). (Āk 2.8.142)
Resembling the flax flower and possessing a luster like the wings of a blue jay, she bears a radiance equal to that of the black *trikaṇikā* flower. (Āk 2.8.143)
It has a luster like the neck of a peacock, resembling the throat of Śambhu, shining with a brilliance equal to the body of Viṣṇu, and possessing a radiance like the wing of a bumblebee. (Āk 2.8.144)
These shadows of the great sapphire gem bring auspiciousness: heaviness, glossy luster, excellent color, and a darkening of the sides. (Āk 2.8.145)
These five qualities are proclaimed as being like grasping a blade of grass:
he is not pale, his body is stainless, smooth, heavy, and radiant. (Āk 2.8.146)
The *indranīla* that is grass-like in its hold, soft, blue, endowed with auspicious marks, and difficult to find, is praised as auspicious and the destroyer of all sins. (Āk 2.8.147)
Nīla bestows longevity, fame, strength, fortune, and health; it is slightly bitter and hot, and it subdues phlegm, bile, and wind. (Āk 2.8.148)
Whoever wears it on his body, that [gem] becomes a bringer of auspiciousness; it is the sun-gem (sauri).
Gomedaka, gomedha, rāhuratna, and tamomaṇi are synonyms for the gomedaka gem. (Āk 2.8.149)
This gem is called *svarbhānu*, *ṣaḍāhva*, and *piṅgasphaṭika*.
That which resembles cow's urine, is soft, glossy, warm, possesses a pure luster, and has weight;
which is reddish like gold and suitable for the illustrious—this, the virtuous declare, is the gem known as *gomedaka*. (Āk 2.8.150)
Having a luster like a drop of honey and a radiance similar to cow's urine or clarified butter.
Gomedaka that is gold-red, heavy, clear, and glossy is auspicious;
whereas that which is white, black, devoid of color, or marred by flaws such as cracks and lines is not. (Āk 2.8.152)
One should reject a *gomedaka* gem that is rough, reddish-pink in appearance, or defective.
(The qualities of *gomedaka*: The *gomedaka* jewel is purifying, conducive to fame, and increases prosperity. (Āk 2.8.153)
Gomedaka is auspicious, produces luster, is unctuous, and removes all poisons;
it is sour and hot, and it conquers disorders caused by the provocation of Vāta. (Āk 2.8.154)
This *dhṛta* (worn amulet) is an illuminator and a digestive aid, as well as a destroyer of sins.
(Vaiḍūrya:
Vaiḍūrya, the banner-jewel (*keturatna*), and likewise that which is born from the sprout of the sound "kha. (Āk 2.8.155)

The Vaiḍūrya gem, born in the Viḍūra region, is known by five names; it was produced from the roar of the lord of the Daityas, which was like the conflagration at the end of an eon that agitated the ocean, and it is a preeminent jewel of many colors, delightful with its splendor and luster. (Āk 2.8.156)
Not far from Mount Viḍūra, whose ridges are lofty.
At the border of Koṅka and Cola, that mine of jewels is said to be located;
there, against the roar of the lord of the Daityas, [the sound] is like the deep thundering of clouds. (Āk 2.8.158)
Indeed, lapis lazuli gems appear with the arrival of the rainy season; those that are slightly black or white resemble white clouds or smoke. (Āk 2.8.159)
That which is examined by experts in the colors of gems is called *vaiḍūrya*;
it possesses a luster equal to that of bamboo leaves, a cat's eye, or a peacock's throat. (Āk 2.8.160)
Lapis lazuli is considered excellent when it has a smooth surface, is heavy, clear, and possesses its characteristic qualities;
it is inferior when marked by lines, light, translucent, or stained with the appearance of charcoal or mud. (Āk 2.8.161)
One should discard a lapis lazuli that is discolored, rough, black, or defective.
Lapis lazuli that is clear and lustrous increases affection, longevity, and strength. (Characteristics of Lapis Lazuli) Āk_2,8.162 //
For by wearing it, this auspicious [gem] indeed removes all planetary influences and poisons;
lapis lazuli is sour and hot, and it destroys phlegm and wind. (Āk 2.8.163)
It pacifies abdominal tumors and colic, is adorned, and brings auspiciousness.
(The five jewels:
ruby, pearl, diamond, sapphire, and likewise emerald. Āk_2,8.164.
The "five jewels" are said to remove sin, misfortune, and poison; [the nine jewels are:
gomedaka, topaz, lapis lazuli, and coral. (Navaratnāni) Āk 2.8.165.
One should point out these nine gems together with the five jewels.
Now, as for the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*): it is the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*), the heating-jewel (*tapanamaṇi*), the burner (*tāpana*), and the sun-loved (*ravikānta*).
The *dīptopala*, the *agnigarbha*, the *jvalanāśman*, and the *arkopala* are names for the sun-stone (*vasu*). Āk 2.8.166.
In color, it is like white mica or a white cloud, resembling the moon upon the snowy mountain. (Āk 2.8.167)
Stainless and endowed with luster, such crystal is said to be the best;
it is found in the Himalayas, Siṃhala, the Vindhya mountains, and likewise on the banks of the Revā. (Āk 2.8.168)
In a place where rubies originate, there may be various kinds of crystal;
among them, one is sun-crystal (sūryakānta) and another is moon-crystal (candrakānta). Āk 2.8.169.
Merely by the touch of the sun’s rays, it vomits fire at that very moment;
that is called *sūryakānta*, a crystal pierced by a gem. (Āk 2.8.170)
The sun-gem (sūryakānta) is hot and pure, a rejuvenative elixir; it subdues wind and phlegm, promotes intelligence, and through worship, bestows satisfaction from the Sun. (Āk 2.8.171)
(candrakānta), indukānta, candrakānta, candrāśman, saṃsravopala, śītāśman, candrikādrāva, and śaśikānta— thus it is of seven kinds. (Āk 2.8.172)

That which is glossy, white, or yellow, and which brings about a state of mental composure for sages on all sides, and which melts upon contact with the rays of the moon—this is the noble gem known as the *candrakānta* (moonstone). Āk 2.8.173.
The moonstone (candrakānta), however, is cooling, unctuous, and removes bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations;
it is pleasing to Śiva, clear, and destroys the influence of planets, misfortune, and poison. (Āk 2.8.174)
Sphaṭika (rock crystal) is white stone, a stainless gem, and a star-stone; it is clear. Its potency is both cooling and heating; it destroys bile and wind of the eyes and cures swelling. (Āk 2.8.175)
Indeed, I have previously described to you the characteristics and other qualities of *kānta*, as well as *vaikrānta*, *vikrānta*, *nīlavajra*, and *kuvajra*. (Āk 2.8.176)
Gonāsa, Kṣudrakuliśa, Cūrṇavajra, and Gonasa; white, red, yellow, blue, and the color of a pigeon. Āk 2.8.177.
It is indeed eightfold: dark, black, and variegated;
in the absence of diamond (vajra), however, vaikrānta is equal to it in taste, potency, and other qualities. Āk 2.8.178.
Eight-sided, with eight facets, hexagonal, smooth, and heavy, and endowed with pure or mixed colors—this is called vaikrānta. (Āk 2.8.179)
Vaikrānta is purified by being steamed in a decoction of horse gram (kuluttha), along with the three alkalis, the five salts, fat, urine, sour gruel, and kodrava grain. (Āk 2.8.180)

One should cook [the substance] contained within the bulb of *vyāghrī* for seven days in a *dolikāyantra*, together with equal parts of fish oil and ghee, along with *kulattha* beans and sour gruel (*kāñjika*). (Āk 2.8.181)
(Vaikrānta ash:
Vaikrānta of a molten color certainly attains purity;
it should be sprinkled with horse urine, heated and [sprinkled] repeatedly for fourteen times. (Āk 2.8.182)
Then, one should cast [the substance] into a ball using the five parts of *uttaravāruṇī*;
having sealed the crucible and cooked it in a *puṭa*, one should extract it again and place it back into the ball. (ĀK 2.8.183)
Having cast [the substance] and sealed it, one should thus roast it seven times until it turns to ash. (The essence of vaikrānta:
One pala of vaikrānta and one pala of ṭaṅkaṇa. (Āk 2.8.184)
It should be infused for one day in the milk of the sun-plant (*ravikṣīra*) and ground for one day with the juices of the *śigru* plant;
then, one should separate one *karṣa* each of *guñjā*, oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), and fire (*vahni*). (Āk 2.8.185)
Having made a pill with this, one should strongly heat it in a crucible furnace;
the essence derived from *vaikrānta* will become as white as a conch shell, a *kunda* flower, or the moon. (Āk 2.8.186)
(2) Vaikrāntasattva:
One should grind equal parts of vaikrānta and vajrakanda together with the milk of snuhī, buffalo butter, and honey for one day. Āk 2.8.187.
From sublimation as before, the essence (*sattva*) becomes like a *indragopa* insect.
(The essence of *vaikrānta*: 3) One should grind the powder of a barren woman's [menses] together with *vaikrānta* equally in the shade. Āk_2,8.188.
By means of goat urine for one day, the essence becomes like silver;
(this is the essence of vaikrānta) which is killed by eight layers of heating when combined with the juice of *gandhanimbuka*. Āk 2.8.189.
Vaikrānta, having been processed by the yoga of precipitating the essence (sattva), formed into pills, and heated in a crucible for one ghaṭikā, will release its essence. Āk 2.8.190.
(Vaikrānta liquefaction: White-colored vaikrānta, when saturated with amlavetasa for seven days, will undoubtedly melt thoroughly in a hot sun; of this there is no doubt. (Āk 2.8.191)
One should place in a vessel ketakī juice, tuttha, rock salt, and svarṇapuṣpikā, all combined and resembling indragopa insects. (Āk 2.8.192)
One should subject vaikrānta to sweating within that [apparatus] for seven days; it will attain a state of liquefaction.

Indeed, vaikrānta bestows longevity, produces strength and complexion, is highly aphrodisiac, grants wisdom, removes all defects and intoxication, kindles the digestive fire, possesses qualities equal to those of iron (pavi), is energetic, and truly effects the growth of the body, strength, and blood. (Āk 2.8.193)
Rājāvarta, āvartamaṇi, āvarta, rājāvarta, and anala are synonyms. (Āk 2.8.194)
Now I shall describe the characteristics of rājāvarta mercury:
by its color it resembles a bumblebee, and it is of two types according to its processing.
One should know that one [type] has the form of powder, while the second consists of a globule;
when combined with a drop of gold, it possesses stable coloration and bestows stability. (Āk 2.8.196)
It is highly skilled at enhancing the color of mercury-born cinnabar;
it is excellent for coloring lead and is preeminent in the process of coloring silver. (Āk 2.8.197)
It is considered the bond of passion for all those with fickle desires; the *rājāvarta* gem has a slight red hue mixed with a great luster of blue. (Āk 2.8.198)
A teacher who is gentle is excellent; any other is considered mediocre.
Indeed, [the instruments] should be steamed with lime-water mixed with the juice of nimba and cow urine. (Āk 2.8.199)
Minerals such as rājāvarta and others are purified after two or three applications.
Rājāvarta, powdered and combined with the juice of *luṅga* and sulphur, [is thus processed]. (Rājāvarta ash) Āk 2.8.200.
By being processed seven times [in this manner], rājāvarta becomes dead [i.e., reduced to powder].
(Regarding *rājāvartasattva*:
One should cook rājāvarta in an iron vessel with buffalo ghee. Āk 2.8.201.
For one day, it should be mixed with milk and five parts of *mitra*;
for five nights, it should be mixed with *rajanī*, until it has been made into a solid mass. (Āk 2.8.202)
Through the application of khadira charcoal, it releases its essence within the crucible; it cures urinary disorders, consumption, hemorrhoids, anemia, phlegm, and wind. (Āk 2.8.203)
Rājāvarta is illuminating, digestive, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
Sasyaka is known as *garuḍodgāra*, *kālajit*, and *viṣasāraka*. (Āk 2.8.204)
Having drunk the Kālakūṭa poison, that Garuḍa was unable to endure it;
then, emerging from the belly of the thief, he became a gem in many pieces. (Āk 2.8.205)
Mahārasa is sasyaka; it is endowed with five lusters:
white, black, yellow, green, and deep red. (Āk 2.8.206)
The *atisthita* fire, which receives oblations from all sides and assumes every form—whether white or green—is commended for the rite of neutralizing stars. (Āk 2.8.207)
Red, black, and yellow sasyaka is recommended for goldsmithing;
it destroys all diseases and removes the fear of poison and untimely death. (Āk 2.8.208)
Vimala is stainless, pure, and clear; it is a clear mineral.
That which is called "numbered by arrows" (five) is praised when made of two parts of silver and gold. (Āk 2.8.209)
Vimala is said to be of three kinds, beginning with that made of gold and followed by that of silver;
the third is the vimala of bell-metal (kāṃsya), which is distinguished therein by its luster. (Āk 2.8.210)
Circular, with well-defined corners, smooth, and provided with a polished surface, it removes wind and bile, is aphrodisiac, pure, and a highly effective rejuvenative. (Āk 2.8.211)
The first [type] is prescribed for gold-making; the second for aphrodisiac practices;
and the third for medicinal preparations. Among these, each preceding one possesses superior qualities.
(Vimalaśuddhi):
Vimala, having been steamed in the juice of *āṭarūṣa*, becomes pure;
one should first cook vimala with the water of plantain root. (Āk 2.8.213)
Then one should cook them for four watches (yāmas) in a dolāyantra with amlavetasa, dhānyāmla, and sheep’s urine; this is their most excellent purification. (Āk 2.8.214)

One should macerate it for a day with the juices derived from *kārkoṭī* and *meṣaśṛṅgī* and those produced from *jaṃbīra*, in the intense heat of the sun; thus, the *vimalā* is certainly purified. (Āk 2.8.215)
O Vimalasattva, one should soak [the substance] in the juice of the *śigru* tree with *kāṅkṣī*, *kāsīsa*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
combined with *vajrakanda*, using the sap of the *kadalī* plant. (Āk 2.8.216)
One should blow [the furnace] containing the essence of *mokṣaka* placed inside a blind crucible;
its sattva, resembling the moon and the sun, will undoubtedly fall out. (Āk 2.8.217)
Peroja, haritāśma, viṣārāti, and harinmaṇi are synonyms for peroja;
in terms of taste, potency, and post-digestive effect, it follows the qualities of sasyaka. (Āk 2.8.218)
Āk, 2,
9 Śrī Bhairavī said:
O Lord, what kind of auspicious medicinal herb is there that performs the work of mercury?
By what means is there ash and mercury, and by what means is the binding of the pill? Āk 2.9.1.
"O Sūta, having become lifeless, how can he bestow life? And O Śaṅkara, how does that which is itself lifeless cause life to exist? (Āk 2.9.2)
"O Śiva, explain this doubt of mine so that I may understand it.
Śrī Bhairava said: "Listen, O Bhairavī; I shall tell you all of that which is unprecedented. (Āk 2.9.3)
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, it is not known even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other lords of the gods;
it destroys wrinkles, gray hair, and disease, and shatters death and poverty. (Āk 2.9.4)
The divine medicinal plants of the *kula* lineage, which grant perfect accomplishment, are the producers of the elixir;
yet deluded fools wander about, deprived of these *kula* medicinal plants. (Āk 2.9.5)
Furthermore, no success whatsoever arises from the juices of ordinary grasses and herbs;
therefore, with every effort, one must come to know the family herb (kulauṣadhi). Āk 2.9.6.
The sixty-four divine medicinal herbs are established within the Kula;
yet the deluded do not know them, being infatuated by the delusion of Śiva. (Āk 2.9.7)
Divine medicinal herbs grow in mountain caves;
mercury never undergoes fixation by means of the juice of such ordinary herbs. (Āk 2.9.8)
That which is inexhaustible does not remain at all if it is devoid of the family-herbs;
for those [poisons] that are lacking the family-herbs do not destroy even the sky. Āk 2.9.9.
But that mercury, O lady of excellent hips, does not remain in the midst of fire;
it neither becomes a solid bolus (khoṭa), nor ash, nor indeed does it act as a medicinal substance. (Āk 2.9.10)
Certain substances undergo transformation when being smelted and do not remain as they were;
gold does not remain unchanged during heating, melting, scratching, or cutting. (Āk 2.9.11)
O Dear One, that mercury does not pierce [the metal] beyond a hundred times, nor until that gold has been sold for one full year. (Āk 2.9.12)
One should never give [the mercury] for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa, nor for the sake of pleasing her;
O Goddess, when the mercury has been processed with a divine herb (divyauṣadhi), [it becomes effective]. (Āk 2.9.13)
O Pārvatī, mercury that is free from kālikā is always [efficacious];
mercury free from kālikā takes away the time of another. (Āk 2.9.14)
It pacifies the impurities of even the eight metals in an instant;
who indeed would say that mercury, having fallen into a great swoon, is dead? (Āk 2.9.15)
By the very essence of divine herbs, he whose consciousness was lost is restored;
the mercury, composed of the five elements, remains as Sadāśiva. (Āk 2.9.16)
Rasauṣadhis, mahauṣadhis, siddhauṣadhis, and likewise others known as divyauṣadhis—these four types have been described by me. (Āk 2.9.17)
Divine medicinal herbs are enumerated; among them, those are the most excellent:
namely, trees, creepers, climbing plants, shrubs, grasses, and vandānikā. (Āk 2.9.18)
The medicinal herbs that effect the binding of mercury are proclaimed to be of six kinds:
Somavallī, Mahāgulmā, Yakṣaśreṣṭhā, and Dhanurlatā. (Āk 2.9.19)
It is known as Somāhvā, Gulmavallī, Yajñavallī, Dvijapriyā, Somakṣīrā, and Somā; it is remembered as Yajñā and Divyalatā. (Āk 2.9.20)
Somavallī is pungent, cold, and sweet; it alleviates bile and burning sensations, pacifies specific types of thirst, is digestive, and acts as a rejuvenative. (Āk 2.9.21)

Having five parts and enriched with fifteen petals, shaped like a serpent and having joints red as blood—that *somavallī* plant, when brought on the full-moon day, performs the work of binding the mercury. (Āk 2.9.22)
In the dark fortnight, one petal falls away each day, and in the bright fortnight, it grows again until the creeper becomes fully extended.
Its bulb, when taken on the full moon day and bound to mercury, renders that mercury into a body-transforming elixir (dehaloha) combined with gold. Āk 2.9.23.
This creeper named *somalatā* is exceedingly difficult to obtain; by means of it, mercury (sūtendra) is bound, and one becomes a "piercer of a hundred thousand" (*lakṣavedhī*). Āk 2.9.24.
The characteristic mark of the twenty-four types of *soma* is clearly evident in alchemy (*rasāyana*).
Even the *soma* tree itself performs the binding, killing, and other operations of mercury. (Soma-vṛkṣa) Āk 2.9.25.
The creeper brought from the day of the full moon is superior in its qualities;
it is called Mahiṣavallī and Pratisomāntravallikā. (Āk 2.9.26)
Apattravallikā is said to be kāṇḍaśākhā and payasvinī;
it is remembered as being equal to somavallī in its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect. (Āk 2.9.27)
(Sthalapadminī) Now, therefore, hear the ritual for the divine herb *sthalapadminī*.
It resembles a lotus in its leaves and is likewise similar in its flowers. (Āk 2.9.28)
Upon its breaking, milk flows out, red in color and most beautiful;
having stepped upon it with his left foot, he should gaze at the circle of the sky. (Āk 2.9.29)
And one should see the circle of planets and constellations joined with the stars;
O Goddess, at a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas, that is to be known as the terrestrial lotus-pond. (Āk 2.9.30)
*Gonasā* is a creeper having the form of a *gonasa* [serpent], adorned with variegated circles;
it pacifies old age, disease, and death, and is capable of binding and killing mercury (*rasa*). (Āk 2.9.31)
(On *Uccaṭā*) Now, O beloved, I shall explain *uccaṭā*, which effects the binding of mercury;
its stalk should be only one, and it should be entwined with hair. (Āk 2.9.32)
And in front of that, O Goddess of Gods, there should be a flower resembling a parrot's beak, and its petals should resemble the feathers of a parrot. (Āk 2.9.33)
O Pārvatī, take that bulbous root, which is shaped like a tortoise, with milk resembling vermilion, from which wax-like resin flows; having gathered that, O Pārvatī. (Āk 2.9.34)
One should pierce all metals, and they become gold.
She is called Īśvarī; she is a certain woman whose form is equal to that of Īśvara. (Āk 2.9.35)
Exuding abundant milk, binding the essence of seeds,
and possessing leaves resembling those of the *nimba* tree, it is called *bhūtakeśī*. (Āk 2.9.36)
That by which the charioteer is not slain is indeed the charioteer, for he is the binder;
this creeper, resembling crushed collyrium, is called the *kṛṣṇalatā*. (Āk 2.9.37)
The garlic vine (*laśunavallī*), which resembles garlic leaves, removes all poisons and binds even seedless mercury. It is known by the name *laśunavallī*. (Āk 2.9.38)
The *kṣaratkṣīrā* and the *sukandā* bind the essence with speed;
the *rudantī* has leaves resembling those of the *caṇa* plant, and its flowers are likewise. (Āk 2.9.39)
Indeed, she is renowned by the name Rudantī, for she rains down water from below;
she seems to weep upon seeing people overwhelmed by death, misery, and old age. (Āk 2.9.40)
It should be known as fourfold—yellow, red, white, and black. Having digested the mercury like a cloud, it destroys [its defects], binds it, and acts as an elixir (*rasāyana*). (Āk 2.9.41)
The tuber of *musalī* is like its root; its leaves have the shape of its foliage.
Known as *sukṣīrā* and *romaśā*, it is called *vārāhī*, which binds fluids. (Āk 2.9.42)
The *saptapattrī* is considered to be that which is complete with seven sprouts and seven leaves;
it is an elixir that destroys old age, and by means of it, mercury is bound. (Āk 2.9.43)
The *nāginī* is said to be a creeper whose body is like the coils of a serpent;
it destroys the poison of snakes and the like, and it binds the flow of one's own vital essence. (Āk 2.9.44)
The *sarpiṇī* and the other, the *latikā*, have stems curved like a serpent; they possess milky sap and glossy leaves, and they bind even young mercury. (Āk 2.9.45)
The *chattriṇī* has stalks and leaves like an umbrella; it is neither too low nor too high.
Known as *chattriṇī*, it yields good milk and is considered to be a binder of the vital essence (*rasabandhakarī*). (Āk 2.9.46)
(Gośṛṅgī):
Produced from stone on a mountain, possessing a bulbous root shaped like a cow’s hoof, it exudes milk when wounded; this Gośṛṅgī is a binder of mercury. (Āk 2.9.47)
The *jyotirlatā* is said to be threefold by name: consisting of a tree, a bulbous root, or a creeper.
At night, that creeper, which binds mercury, blazes upon the mountain. (Āk 2.9.48)
(Raktavallī):
That divine creeper which has red sap and leaves, whose body is not overly extensive, is designated as Raktavallī; it binds mercury. (Āk 2.9.49)
(Padmavallī):
That leaf-creeper which has leaves shaped like lotus petals is called *patravallī* by those who know its essence;
it possesses milky tubers, grows in water, and does not remain on dry land, for it is bound to its sap. (Āk 2.9.50)
Kākinī is rich with the color of thick thorns; she is called the Kākinī creeper. She binds the mercury and destroys old age and death. (Āk 2.9.51)
The *cāṇḍālī* is designated as such because she bears three or four petals; she is red with a bulbous root of milk, and by her the elixir is bound. (Āk 2.9.52)
And the Caṇḍālakanda is said to exist in its varieties as the one-leaved, the two-leaved, the three-leaved, the four-leaved, and the five-leaved. (Āk 2.9.53)

The copper-creeper (*tāmravallī*), which possesses leaves and flowers of copper color and is endowed with latex, is called *tāmravallikā*; it is the means for accomplishing mercury, base metals, and so forth. (Āk 2.9.54)

The yellow creeper (*pītavallī*), which is exceedingly rare and possesses the sap of its yellow leaves, stalks, and flowers, is called *pītavallikā*; it is beneficial for the process of binding mercury. (Āk 2.9.55)
(Vijayā):
Having white *kṣīrāḍhakī* leaves as its foliage and not being very large, this plant is renowned as Vijayā; it is beneficial for the process of binding mercury. (Āk 2.9.56)
Possessing a triangular bulb and covered with variegated leaves, it is called *mahauṣadhī*; it is exceedingly beneficial for the binding of mercury. (Āk 2.9.57)
Devadālī,
rich with leaves the color of a peacock’s neck and thick with the fragrance of sandalwood—
this divine plant called Devadālī binds the vital essence (rasa) in an instant. (Āk 2.9.58)
(That which has the scent of butter: "Having the scent of butter" means it has a bitter fragrance like that of an ointment;
when it contains milk and bears red flowers, mercury is bound by it. (Āk 2.9.59)
The *gāruḍavallī* has milky sap and red flowers, with leaves like those of the *badarī*;
it is called *gāruḍavallī* because it quickly binds mercury. (Āk 2.9.60)
The *tumbinī* is declared to be a creeper provided with its leaves and flowers;
its fruits are combined with bitter and red milky sap and are binders of mercury. (Āk 2.9.61)

The *bhūtumbinī* is that which has leaves similar to those of the *tumbinī*, does not spread excessively, and is endowed with fruits resembling those of the lime tree (*nimbū*); it destroys all diseases and binds the essence. (Āk 2.9.62)
The *gandharvā* has leaves like those of the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍa*), is milky, and is not very broad;
it is indeed called *gandharvā*, for by means of it the juice may go to a state of bondage. (Āk 2.9.63)
*Vyāghrapādī*:
that which has leaves resembling a tiger’s paw, bears red flowers, and is milky;
it is designated as *vyāghrapādī*, and it certainly binds the mercury. (Āk 2.9.64)
The *mahauṣadhī* has leaves resembling those of the *saptacchada*; it is slender-bodied and not very broad.
It is called *mahauṣadhī*, and it binds and destroys [the flow of] the *rasa*. (Āk 2.9.65)
The creeper named gomārī has leaves resembling those of the bamboo;
having obtained its root, an excellent elixir is prepared. (Āk 2.9.66)
That [plant] which has leaves in the shape of a trident and fruits like those of the *śamyāka* tree is designated as *triśūlī*; it is renowned for its power to bind mercury. (Āk 2.9.67)
*Rutasī* has leaves like those of *rutasī*, its fruits are leaf-like, and it possesses milky tubers;
it is called the *rutasī* creeper, born of the mountain, which binds [the flow of] mercury. (Āk 2.9.68)
(Tridaṇḍī):
Adorned with beautiful flowers and a forehead mark (tilaka), and endowed with the three red fruits, she is called Tridaṇḍī in the ritual for the binding of mercury (rasabandha). (Āk 2.9.69)
*Bhṛṅgavallī*:
Rich in leaves with a color like that of a bee, milky, and bearing yellow flowers—it is called *bhṛṅgavallī*; it is employed for the binding of mercury. (Āk 2.9.70)
The *camarikā* creeper, rich with leaves shaped like yak-tail fans (*camara*) and bearing a milky moon-like substance, binds mercury. (Āk 2.9.71)
The *karavīralatā* is a creeper possessing leaves and flowers resembling the form of a horse's head;
it is called *karavīralatā* because it is an excellent binder of mercury. (Āk 2.9.72)
The *vajravallī* resembles the leaf-covering of the *koraṇḍa* tree; its flowers have petals like those [leaves], and its bulb contains excellent milk.
That *vajravallī* has a pungent and bitter essence, its leaves are marked with the sign of a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and it binds mercury. (Āk 2.9.73)
The *vāravallī* possesses red latex and is endowed with petals resembling those of the *bilva*;
it binds mercury and destroys diseases. (Āk 2.9.74)
(Rohiṇī):
That which has the shape of a hemp flower petal, possesses ten flowers, and is mixed with milk is designated as Rohiṇī; it is the binder of the king of essences. Āk 2.9.75.

*Bilvinī* has leaves with the shape, color, and appearance of *jyotiṣmatī* leaves; it is glorious and is declared to be used in the procedure for binding mercury (*rasabandha*). It is called *bilvinī*. (Āk 2.9.76)
(Gorocanalatā) The Gorocanalatā is endowed with leaf-vines possessing the luster of gorocana; it liberates beings and binds the mercury. Āk 2.9.77.
(Karīrī):
The *karīrī* herb, which grows on the peak of Śrīśaila and resembles the *mārkaṇḍī*, releases red milk when wounded; it binds the essence (*rasabandhinī*). (Āk 2.9.78)
That which has leaf-joints (*pattrasīsa*) like a leaf and yields fruit after three years is known as *akṣarā*; it is a firm binder of mercury. (Āk 2.9.79)
(Leafless):

Like a *somavallī* plant deprived of its leaves, yet endowed with the essence of collyrium (*kajjala*), this "leafless" variety found on the Vindhya mountains is not very tall and binds mercury. (Āk 2.9.80)
In the first year it becomes sour; in the second year it becomes bitter;
and in the third year it is produced with sweet fruits. (Āk 2.9.81)
The *kuṭajavallī* creeper, when combined with its excellent leaves and fruits, immediately removes fever caused by *pitta*.
This creeper known as *kuṭajavallī* consists of those fruits and is provided with those leaves. (Āk 2.9.82)
Sweet, with blood-like knots and binding the king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*), it is known as *mūlakanda*; it possesses roots, fruits, and leaves like those of the radish plant. (Āk 2.9.83)
The *brāhmaṇī* creeper, possessing milky sap, certainly effects the binding of mercury;
it is the mountain-born vine of the *pārijāta*, with leaves like the petals of the *śatapuṣpa*. (Āk 2.9.84)
*Kṛṣṇakṣīraphalā* is said to be *brāhmaṇī*, which binds mercury; it is also called *munivallī*, *agastipatratatpatrā*, and possesses similar reddish flowers. (Āk 2.9.85)
That creeper, known as *munivallī*, has the scent of ghee and destroys [excessive] tastes; it resembles the *nimba* tree in its leaves, flowers, and fruits. (The *nimbakā* creeper. Āk 2.9.86.
The creeper by whose roots the mercury is bound is called the *nimbakā* vine;
it is renowned as *tilakandā*, possessing roots, fruits, and leaves. (Āk 2.9.87)
The milky creeper (kṣīravatī), when bound in the intense heat of the sun, produces mercury;
its flowers, fruits, and leaves are like those of the flax plant (atasī). (Āk 2.9.88)
For that *atasī* creeper is a binder of mercury; it is called the "Bodhi-creeper" when combined with the milk from the leaves of the Bodhi tree. (Āk 2.9.89)
It binds the king of essences (*rasarāja*), just as Acyuta bound the lord of the Dānavas;
it is known as *madyagandhā*, possessing no stem but endowed with fruit and leaves. (Āk 2.9.90)
Its bulb quickly and certainly brings about binding.
(Kūrmalatā):
Kūrmalatā is said to have a bulb in the shape of a tortoise; when combined with milk, [it acts as described]. Āk 2.9.91.

The *mādhavī* creeper has flowers resembling jasmine blossoms and binds with its sap; it possesses roots like those of the *mādhavī* root itself and is provided with the leaves of the betel vine (*nāgavallī*). (Āk 2.9.92)
The creeper called *mādhavī* has its sap bound by its roots;
likewise, the *viśālā* creeper has white leaves and bears white flowers and fruit. (Āk 2.9.93)
That [vagina] is also designated as "vast" (viśālā), for it binds mercury;
it has a bulbous root like the coil of a great serpent and petals resembling its hoods. (Āk 2.9.94)
This great *nāgī* creeper binds mercury;
it has a bulb shaped like a frog (*maṇḍūkalatikā*), and its leaves resemble the leaves of the *maṇḍūkī*. (Āk 2.9.95)
This is called the maṇḍūkalatikā; the elixir is bound by its roots. (The udumbara creeper:
It possesses leaves like those of the udumbara fruit, and its fruit has the shape of the udumbara fruit. Āk 2.9.96.
That which is called *sodhumbaralata* is the binder of the king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*);
it is the *citravallī*, which has a milky bulb, leaves like those of the banyan tree, variegated foliage, large fruits, and is very long.
That is called the Citravallī; the mercury (rasendra) is bound within the interior of its fruit. Āk 2.9.97.
Thus, sixty-four divine medicinal herbs of great power have been proclaimed.
Bound by these, the *rasa* of men accomplishes the purpose of alchemizing the body;
[the plants] are *somavallī*, *somavṛkṣa*, and then *sthalapadminikā*. (Āk 2.9.99)
Gonasā, kāravallī, uccaṭā, īśvarī, bhūtakeśī, kṛṣṇalatā, and laśunavallarī are to be known [as synonyms]. (Āk 2.9.100)
Rudantī, Vārāhī, Saptapattrī, Nāginī, Sarpiṇī, Chattriṇī, and Gośṛṅgī bestow all accomplishments. (Āk 2.9.101)
The one named Jyotis, the threefold red creeper, the leaf-creeper, Kākinī, Cāṇḍālī, and the copper creeper. (Āk 2.9.102)
Pītavallī is to be known as Vijayā and Mahauṣadhī; Devadālī is to be understood as Navānītagandhinī. (Āk 2.9.103)
Garuḍavallī, tumbinī, bhūmitumbinī, gandharvā, and vyāghrapādī are to be known as great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadhī). Āk 2.9.104.
Then there are gomārī, triśūlī, rutasī, tridaṇḍikā, bhṛṅgavallī, camarikā, and karavīralatā. (Āk 2.9.105)
Vajravallī, vāravallī, rohiṇī, and likewise bilvinī; also gorocanalatā, karīrī, and akṣarā. (Āk 2.9.106)
Apattrī, kuṭajā-vallī, mūlakandā, brāhmaṇī, ghṛtagandhā, nimbavallī, tilakandā, and likewise atasī. (Āk 2.9.107)
The Bodhivallī, Madyagandhā, Kūrmavallī, Mādhavī, Viśālā, Mahānāgā, and Maṇḍūkavallī are to be known [as such]. (Āk 2.9.108)
The Udumbara creeper and the Citravallī, O Goddess worshipped by the gods—these sixty-four are declared to be divine medicinal herbs of great power. (Āk 2.9.109)
Āk, 2, 10 Śrī Bhairava: (Born of the Snowy Mountains)
Himajā, kāñcanakṣīrī, yavaciñcā, mahādrijā, himāvatī, pītadugdhā, recanī, and paṭuparṇikā. (Āk 2.10.1)
Its milk is *hemakaṅkuṣṭha*, *pulaka*, and *recana*; it is also *tejovatī*, *bahurasā*, *kanakaprabhā*, *tīkṣṇāgnigarbhā*, and *suravallarī*. (Āk 2.10.2)
Himajā is pungent and bitter, a purgative that subdues all types of wind (vāta);
it destroys worms, consumption, and abdominal diseases, and it removes fever caused by bile (pitta). Āk 2.10.3.
*Kāravī*, *kāravī*, and *kāravallī* are astringent and hot; they remove phlegm, cure cough and asthma, are strengthening, and should be known as regulators of the bodily fluids (*rasa*). (Āk 2.10.4)
*Kaṭutumbī*, *kaṭuphalā*, *rājaputrī*, and *mahatphalā* are synonyms for *kaṭutumbī*.
*Kaṭutumbī* is pungent and bitter; it cures vomiting, asthma, and nausea. (Āk 2.10.5)
Kāsaghnī cleanses and removes swelling, wounds, pain, and poison;
tiktatumbī is bitter, while kaṭutumbikā is pungent. (Āk 2.10.6)
The *tumbī* is known by synonyms such as *kaṭu*, *tikta*, and others;
the creeper named *jyotiṣmatī* has the brilliance of fire, and that *jyotirlatā* is also called *kaṭabhī* and *supiṅgalā*.
The Sarasvatī [medicinal plant] is radiant, purifying, bestows intelligence, and is difficult to digest; it is immortal and equal in number to the sun. Āk 2.10.7.
The *liṅginī* shall have many sons; she is a sovereign, a creeper of Śiva. (Āk 2.10.8)
The Svayambhū, the Laiṅgī born from the liṅga, the Citraphalānvitā, the Ayaḥstambhakārī, the Liṅgabījā, and the Śivavallarī. (Āk 2.10.9)
She possesses the *liṅga*, is pungent and dry, foul-smelling, and a rejuvenator (*rasāyanī*);
she is divine, the bestower of all accomplishments, and the controller of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*). (Āk 2.10.10)
Pātālagaruḍī, Tārkṣī, Sauvarṇī, Garuḍī, as well as Vatsādanī, Dīrghakāṇḍā, Dṛḍhakāṇḍā, and Mahābalā. (Āk 2.10.11)
O Pārvatī, these names—Dīrghavallī, Dṛḍhalatā, and Darśanā—are all synonymous;
this plant brings everything under control and destroys the poison of snakes and other creatures. (Āk 2.10.12)
Girikarṇī, kaṭabhī, gardabhī, dadhipuṣpikā,
sitapuṣpī, viṣaghnī, and śvetāśvakhurapuṣpikā. (Āk 2.10.13)
Girikarṇī is cooling, bitter, and destroys complications of pitta;
it is beneficial for the eyes, removes the defects of poison, and pacifies the three doṣas. (Āk 2.10.14)

Nīlapuṣpā, mahānīlā, nīlagirikarṇikā, and nīlādrikarṇī are cooling and slightly bitter; they destroy bloody diarrhea, fever, and burning sensations. They alleviate pratardika, insanity, intoxication, fatigue, pain, and the affliction of labored breathing, and they are removers of poison. (Āk 2.10.15)
The *ākhukarṇī* is a ground-crawling plant that runs along and possesses many feet. (Āk 2.10.16)
Sutaśreṇī, Dravantī, Nyagrodhā, Mākṣikāhvayā, Citrā, Mūṣakapucchī, Pratyakśreṇī, and Śabarī. (Āk 2.10.17)
The *sutaśreṇī* is pleasing to the eye, pungent, and removes the poison of rats;
it cures defects of the wounds and destroys diseases of the eyes. (Āk 2.10.18)
Kṛṣṇikā, Bahuparṇī, Pratyakśoṇī, Śabarī,
Pūtiparṇī, Śivā, and that which possesses joints like the ears of a mouse (Āk 2.10.19).
Ākhukarṇī is pungent and hot; it alleviates phlegm and bile, is laxative, destroys abdominal distension, colic, fever, and pain, and is an excellent digestive. (Āk 2.10.20)
Vārāhī is the sow, the female boar, the daughter of Krodha, the one who has calved once, and the beloved of Viṣvaksena;
Kaumārī is the daughter of Kumāra, the leaf of Brahmā, the three-eyed one, the daughter of Krodha, the one who has calved once, and the beloved of Mādhava. (Āk 2.10.21)
Vārāhī is bitter and pungent; it removes poison, bile, and phlegm. It cures skin diseases, urinary disorders, and worms; it is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and an elixir. (Āk 2.10.22)
Devadālī is said to be of three kinds: white, black, and yellow.
The white variety alleviates diseases; the black and yellow varieties are for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*). (Āk 2.10.23)
Devadālī is also known as kośaphalā, dālī, lomaśapattrikā, kṛṣṇabījā, kaṭuphalā, vṛttakośā, and amlavallarī. (Āk 2.10.24)
Jīmūta and Kaṇṭakaphalā remove poison from the head; Veṇī removes poison from the eyes; Turaṅgikā and Jālaphalā are enemies of *gara* poison; [and] Sāramūṣikā. (Āk 2.10.25)
Devadālī is sharp and hot, pungent, and it removes anemia and phlegm; it destroys hemorrhoids, dyspnea, and cough, and it cures jaundice and lūtikā. (Āk 2.10.26)
She who causes all metals to liquefy, who removes catarrh and the poison of serpents—
(Aindrī)— is Aindrī, Indravāruṇī, Aruṇā, Mṛgādinī, Gavādanī, Kṣudrasahā, Indracidbhaṭā.
Sūryā, Viṣaghnī, Ruṇakarṇikā, Amarā, Suparṇikā, and Phalatārakā; // Āk_2,10.27 //
Vṛṣabhākṣī, gavākṣī, pītapuṣpā, and indravallarī. (Āk 2.10.28)
Hemapuṣpī, kṣudraphalā, vāruṇī, bālakapriyā, raktā, urvāru, viṣalatā, cakravallī, and viṣāpahā [are synonyms]. (Āk 2.10.29)
Amṛtā and Viśālā are to be known by twenty-nine names;
Indravāruṇikā is bitter, pungent, cooling, and purgative. (Āk 2.10.30)
Mahendravāruṇī, Ramyā, Cakravallī, and Mahāphalā remove abdominal tumors, bile disorders, enlargement of the abdomen, phlegm, worms, skin diseases, and fever. (Āk 2.10.31)
That is Mahendrī, Vṛttaphalā, Trapusī, and likewise Trapusā; also Ātmarakṣā, Viśālā, Dīrghavallī, and Mahāphalā. (Āk 2.10.32)
It may be called Bṛhadvāruṇī or Saumyā; it has fourteen names.
It is to be known as Māhendravāruṇī, which was previously described as possessing excellent qualities. (Āk 2.10.33)
In terms of taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation, this [gojihvā] is slightly superior in its qualities.
Gojihvā is also known as kṣurapattrī, adhaḥpuṣpā, and adhomukhī. (Āk 2.10.34)
Gojihvā is pungent, sharp, cooling, and destroys bile;
it pacifies wounds and removes the poison of the seven-toothed snake. Āk 2.10.35.
*Kākatuṇḍī*, *kākanāsā*, *kākasiṃhī*, and *raktalā*;
likewise *kākadantī*, *kākapīlu*, and *vṛttaraktaphalā*. (Āk 2.10.36)
Kākaprāṇā, valkaśalyā, kṛṣṇabījā, rañjakī, and kākatuṇḍī are sweet, cooling, and remove pitta. (Āk 2.10.37)
*Rasāyanī* (the elixir plant) provides firmness and specifically removes grey hair.
*Raktapādī* has leaves like those of the *śamī* tree and leaves like those of the *khadira* tree. (Āk 2.10.38)
*Saṃkocanī*, *samaṅgā*, *namaskārī*, *prasāraṇī*, *lajjālu*, *saptaparṇī*, *khadirī*, and *maṇḍamālikā*. (Āk 2.10.39)
Raktamūlā, tāmramūlā, svaguptā, añjalikārikā, and lajjālu are pungent and cold; they destroy pitta and diarrhea. (Āk 2.10.40)

Lajjālu, also known as Vaiparītyāhva, removes swelling, burning sensations, fever, dyspnea, ulcers, skin diseases, and afflictions caused by phlegm; it is pungent, hot, and alleviates phlegm and nausea. (Āk 2.10.41)
When used as a fixative for mercury, *punarnavā* produces various types of cognition.
*Punarnavā* is said to be of three kinds: white, red, and black. (Āk 2.10.42)
Punarnavā is a destroyer of poisons; kaṭhillā cures eye diseases; pṛthvīkā, sitavarṣābhū, dīrghapattra, and sitāṅgakā are synonyms [for punarnavā]. (Āk 2.10.43)
White *punarnavā* is warm, bitter, and removes phlegm and poison;
it cures cough, heart disease, colic, hemorrhage, anemia, swelling, and the afflictions of wind. (Āk 2.10.44)
Another *punarnavā* is called *raktā*, characterized by its circular leaves;
it is known as *vaiśākhī* and has red limbs throughout. It is a supreme remedy for swelling and a destroyer of poison. (Āk 2.10.45)
Punarnavā is new, fresh, and the autumnal creeper;
it is red, pungent, a restorative, and a destroyer of swellings. (Āk 2.10.46)
Known as Śyāmā, Nīlavarṣābhū, and Dīrghapatrā, Punarnavā destroys the disorder of menorrhagia, and subdues jaundice and bile. (Āk 2.10.47)
Blue *punarnavā* is bitter and pungent-hot; it is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) that removes heart disease, anemia, edema, asthma, wind, and phlegm. (Āk 2.10.48)
*Atyamlaparṇī* is sharp and sour, causing itching, and known as *vallīsārasā*; it grows in forests, dwells in the wilderness, is rich in tubers, and has coarse leaves. (Āk 2.10.49)

Atyamlaparṇī is pungent and sour; it destroys splenic pain, subdues wind, stimulates the digestive fire, improves appetite, and removes diseases of the abdominal tumors (gulma) and phlegm (śleṣman). (Āk 2.10.50)
*Karkoṭakī* and *kārkoṭakī* are two kinds; the barren one is inferior, while the other is excellent as it destroys [diseases] through its fruit.
It has soft thorns and round fruits, and it grows in the forest. (Āk 2.10.51)
The goddess Vandhyā, Vandhyakārkoṭakī, Nāgārāti, Nāgahantrī, Manojñā, Pathyā, Divyā, Putradātrī, Trikandā, Śrīkandā, Kandavallī, and Viṣaghnī are synonyms for this plant. (Āk 2.10.52)
Yogīśvarī, Vyāghrapādī, and Kanyā are names for the plant called Ṣoḍaśā; it is also known as Vandhyā and Karkoṭakī. It is bitter and pungent, hot in potency, and removes phlegm (kapha). (Āk 2.10.53)
*Śarapuṅkhā* destroys poisons such as those from immobile beings; it is used for binding mercury and in elixirs (*rasāyana*).
That which has a shaft (*puṅkhā*) resembling an arrow (*śara*) is called *śarapuṅkhī*. (Āk 2.10.54)
The *śarapuṅkhī* has three varieties—white, red, and black—and is thorny;
even the white variety is rich in qualities and is used in medicinal applications and for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*). (Āk 2.10.55)
But *kaṇṭapuṅkhā* would be another [name], as would *kaṇṭasāyakapuṅkhikā*;
likewise *kaṇṭaspṛśā*, *kuṇḍī*, and *kaṇṭakaśarapuṅkhamūlaniryūha*. (Āk 2.10.56)
They quickly cure indigestion, cholera, and extreme emaciation;
all varieties of *śarapuṅkhā* are pungent, hot, and destroy phlegm and wind. (Āk 2.10.57)
It destroys indigestion, colic, and worms, and is supreme for pacifying *grahaṇī*.
*Mārkava*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *bhṛṅgāhva*, and *keśarañjaka* are synonyms for *bhṛṅgarāja*. (Āk 2.10.58)
Pitṛpriya, Brahmapattrī, Keśya, and Kuntalavardhana; another is Pīta, Svarṇabhṛṅgāra, Harivāsa, and Harapriya. (Āk 2.10.59)
